The only thing I hated was the voice acting, and hence, most of the cutscenes. I'm not an Anime fan and I'm not into anthropomorphistic animals. But as big of a problem as that may seem, I still found the game an enjoyable experience.

Edit: As of December 25, 2014 (Merry Christmas)
I really love this game. Danny Baranowsky does a beautiful job at making the music catchy and fit the theme of the levels. The game is incredibly hard, split into 4 zones (4th zone is locked as of the early access). Once you beat one zone (each zone is made up of 3 normal levels and a final boss, all of which are amazing and the music to the bosses are amazing as well) the next zone opens up. I've unlocked Zone 3 and it's nearly impossible for me. I mean, come on, there's a chess boss where the pieces move exactly like in chess, it's absolutely badass.
There's a daily challenge much like Spelunky and SpiderMod for Isaac, and I've seen scores of people who have beaten the game, so it IS possible, it's just really hard. Don't let the challenge discourage you from getting it. Enemies have a distinct pattern (except bats, ♥♥♥♥ those guys), and you have to attack the enemy between their attack pattern to hit them unharmed, however if you stay in a square or attempt to move into a square that an enemy moves onto at the same time, you get hit. There is some knowledge you gain only by playing the game, such as attack prioritization. For example, the game prioritizes your attack over all enemies', so if you attack a 1 health enemy that's going to attack you at the same time, your attack is registered first and the enemy dies without you getting hit, but if the enemy has more than 1 health, you get hit because you didn't kill the enemy on that beat.
When you get hurt or die it's ALWAYS because you messed up the enemy pattern, I've never felt the game cheated me on damage or death. And don't think the game is trial and error on knowing the enemy patterns, they nearly always have a tell when they're about to attack so you can attack them in between.
There are very, very minor bugs in the game, sure a good amount of them are userend, meaning you might mess up thinking how something works and try to use it incorrectly only to have it mess you up (such as learning how the Cat of Nine Tails works, I hate this weapon), but the actual bugs in the game are barely noticeable and the creator does an absolutely fantastic job of updating the game and squashing bugs, he's very very active on the /r/necrodancer subreddit as well as the Brace Yourself Games forums where there's a bug database that you can add to or search through to see if a bug you found has already been seen.
The visual style is nice, the pixelated art works fine, the level art is looks good. Most enemies groove out to the music so it's pretty cool.
There's also a feature where you can use your own music and the game will process it and determine the beat of the music, so far it's pretty accurate though it does seem to have very minor issues with certain songs. But I really like the original music so I'm probably not going to change it.
The more I play this game, the more I'm loving it. I fell in love with the Binding of Isaac and have about 230 hours in it, I can EASILY see myself outplaying that game in this one. Seriously, the music is some of the best I've heard in a game, the gameplay is fresh and the creator is constantly updating and improving the experience. Is it worth $15? ABSOLUTELY. I would not skip a beat even if this game was $30 dollars or even full retail at $60. The replay value is immense and if I get 200 hours in this game, even if the game was prices at $60, I payed $3.33 per hour, and I say that's an amazing deal. If the game is on sale (which it is for the Winter Sale), I say with 100% certainty that it is worth your time to buy it.

--------------------------------
FINAL IMPRESSION OF THE GAME
--------------------------------
Before we get started, I should mention that this used to be a first impression review of the game after I bought it and played through the original version on the Nintendo 3DS. Some comments in the comment section may not add up to things written here, now that I actually finished playing through the steam port.
With that said,  Let us begin and keep this short because english isn't my native language and the grammar mistakes become more apparent if I keep going on any longer. This is my final impression after playing through this on the regular difficulty.
Like I said before, this game originally came out on Nintendo's handheld the 3DS and was followed by a sequel a couple of months after. This game is an action-rpg that puts high emphasis on a tower-defense-, arcade-like feeling and stage progression. It was a nice little game that worked they way it was intended to be, but didn't really stood out and was good for short sessions... on a handheld!
--------------------------------
POSITIVES:
+ Colorful 8-bit graphic for characters
+ Minor changes in graphics and animation
+ Instead of two screens you get one with everything
+ The use of both sticks for each character instead of the shoulder buttons
+ Controlling two characters works fine and isn't confusing for hands and eyes
+ Arcade-like RPG with stage progression
+ Time attack and survival mode after playing through the game once
+ A game for short sessions in between
+ Easy to get into
+ The cheat codes from the 3DS still work on this version
NEGATIVES:
- The use of 8-bit character sprites doesn't fit in some parts with the 16-bit backgrounds of the stages
- Stage backgrounds really look like they came straight out of RPG-Maker
- Minor changes in graphics and animation, which doesn't amount to anything
- You can control two characters, but you don't have to. Just set the witch on wind magic and you don't have to aim at all and got one hand free for other stuff
- The final and only true boss battle has become insultingly easy after a certain change in the port
- Despite the arcade-like nature of the game, you will get bored after a short while
- No reward in playing through the game and that "unlockable function" was not worth it
- Time attack and survival mode should feel like rewards, but they don't...
- The "cheat codes" unless they added new ones, are actually the friggin' difficult settings of the game
- It gets really repetitive after a while, but that was a also a problem of the handheld version
- The (to me) useless update for the screen size to be changed through Alt+Enter, despite the fact that the size could already be changed through pressing F1 on the keyboard. Unfortunaly the instructions for this are almost completely obscured by the english title on the title screen and only become visible after changing the language to either japanese or chinese! Seriously, WHY!?
- Barebones option menu that only allows you to change either language or which stick should be used for either of the two characters
- The game sound cannot be changed from within the game itself
--------------------------------
OVERALL:
Well, that final impression turned out to be mor negative than my initial first impression of the steam port. And yet it still gets the thumbs up from me. Why? Because I still enjoyed the game for what it was even though some flaws became more apparent on the bigger screen. The game really works as a nice little distraction for a few minutes and just like on the 3DS, everything works the way it was intended to be. It's just a shame that the game feels like it has less to offer on the big screen than on two tiny ones.
If you already own the original and the sequel on 3DS, then there is no reason to buy the steam port. Those who don't own any of the two games, should really consider if there isn't any better alternative to this.

I'm finally writing a review in response to devs saying I cannot warn potential buyers on the forum anymore. (or I'll get banned for "whinging"  - When valid complaints are called "whinging" you know the devs don't care at all about making things better for the players)
Be aware when purchasing that the "rookie only" servers you will have access to have been specifically set up by the developers to create a "fake" community that provides a pleasant experience for new players, however you will be locked out in no time flat (way way way before you've had any chance to learn the basics) and by then

Their sole motivation for making "rookie only" servers was to provide a pleasant experience for new players during the refund window (hence why the change happened at the same time valve introduced their refund policy)  In truth all it has done is led to a lot of upset people quitting after being locked out of "the only good servers"  (There's a reason we've had a steady influx of new players for over a year, and yet the playerbase hasn't grown even the tiniest bit)
This game is great in a lot of ways. It blends FPS and RTS genres better than most others that try, and playing Aliens is an absolute blast. The game still recieves semi-regular updates (whether that's a good or bad thing depends on who you ask) and the playerbase is small but incredibly solid. (aka it's not "dying")
Unfortunately the community for NS2 is extremely high skill, elitist, and toxic as hell. In addition to high skill players making it feel like you're playing against aimbotting wallhackers, people will rage at you from everything from being unable to kill another player, to not being in the perfect position at the right time...
You can literally be screamed at no matter what you do... For instance if you're commanding Marines and your base gets attacked by 3-4 Aliens.
Stay in chair = You idiot jump out and save the base
Jump out and die = You idiot never ever ever jump out of the chair
TL:DR - Game is great fun, but devs are horrible at balancing, have no interest in improving the game (only improving sales) and "rookie only" only exists to keep new players happy during the refund window. Avoid rookie only for your first game or two for a view of what the real NS2 is like. (god-like players ruining balance, elitists yelling at the lesser skilled, players getting votekicked for not doing what others think they should be doing, etc)  If you like it enough, then return to rookie only for as long as you can (which will be pathetically short)

Simple and efficient well-crafted turn-based game.
You play with a small squad (from 3 to 12 members). There is more or less 40 missions. You usually need 10 to 20 turns to finish missions. (I would say 20 min to 1h30 per mission?)
There is 8 distinct kinds of soldiers (captain, scout, engineer, paladin, berserk, etc...) You chose how they progress after each mission : skills points and attributes points, how you equip them and which talents you learn or improve, depending on soldier's class. (For example: strike harder with blade or gun, strong short range shooting or long range, personal or mass boost -defensive or offensive-, more movement points, cover, radar, healing, attacks with penalties for ennemies, turrets, more abilities uses, capture, repair, etc...)
Before each mission, you can freely re-attribute skills points, attributes points and talents points, to modify you soldiers as you need.
There is a big development's tree used to chose which classes you will improve, which gears and abilities you will unlock, and which items you will be able to use. There is a lot of separate branches, and you cannot reset this tree, so your "battleforce" really depends on it.
You can entirely  create and chose which soldiers you use during missions, even if sometimes some soldiers or some classes are forced on. All soldiers progress during the game, even if soldiers you use a lot progress faster.
There is a "capture tactical points" mechanism in many levels. With tactical points, you can deploy new sodiers in mission, get new items to help you, and you usually want to protect it. It's not the core of the game (you don't do so many captures or deployments), but it's definitely a big part of the gameplay.
There is a totally black "fog of war", so you have to explore and discover maps, ennemies and objectives.
There is sometimes secondary objectives (places to go) on maps to get more xp, but usually you don't know if there are secondary objectives in a mission, and you don't know where it is.
The game push the player to move quickly and to kill a lot. The less you need turns to beat a mission (and the more you kill per turn), the more you receive XP.
There is small randomness in ennemies'creation.
There is no randomness for maps. So, if you retry a level, you will know what to do and where to go.
Sometimes (not too many), you have to do some choices, so the order of mission will change... and you can't do all missions in one playthrough.
When you finish the game, you can start again with your team and stronger ennemies to continue your progress.
The game saves automatically every turn. (So if you quit during a turn, you will have to start again. It can be useful if you did a bad move.) You can never save by yourself. During a mission, or at the end of a mission, you can restart the mission. (Except for ironman mode.)
The combat system is relatively complex, but there is an in-game "library" to briefly explain all concepts... if you want understand. There is some tutorials missions, to explain really basic stuff.
There is randomness during fights. Even if you can definitely influence it, and you can probably deal with it, the difference between a strong critical hit and a dodged one is obviously big.
You have to deal with a "heat" mechanism which inflicts damage if you do too many actions every turns.
There is a story and a universe around the game. You learn it mainly by talking with 2 or 3 NPC between missions. (You can skip it.)
I like turn-based games, and I enjoyed this one. It was fun to play, to find the best solution, to improve my soldiers, to discover the game. I liked different kind of soldiers and different abilities. Even if it's "simple", I think that the team successfully diversify missions. There is a lot of interesting soldiers, talents, gears and items, and the game is still well-balanced.
I liked to be able to play an entire mission in small game's session... and to know the length of a mission before I start it, based on the turns goal.
Personnally, I'm not fan of all mechanisms. (If I want more xp, I have to play fast rather than safe... I don't like the fog of war most of the time, because for some level you need to know the map to make best tactical decisions... The development's tree is big, with a lot of branches, so you cannot enjoy all classes during a playthrough, it's a little bit sad... You have to play always with same soldiers if you want the best progress for them, so you can't easily try all of them... It seems that the best way to play is to focus on some abilities and to avoid overheating, so you don't have enough talents points and heat to really use all interesting talents during fight.) But it's just details! The game is well crafted, the small team behind the game seems to be nice, so I can easily recommand this game, if you like this kind of game and if you liked what you saw in videos and screenshots.
Definitely, it's for people who like turn-based tactical games.

I originally picked this game up just because it was a turn based strategy game, and I love games that reming me of the many hours I put into Fire Emblem.
Sound: My first instinct here is to say that it has an 8-bit or 16-bit feel. Because the theme, it has space, steampunk, and a bit medieval history. It blends all the themes and their sounds, and makes for a very nice feel to add to the game.
Graphics: This game could have been on the old Nintendo or Sega systems back in the 90's. For the younger generation, this game is probably awful looking, but I just love it. The nostalgia of playing a game that could have been a game  from my youth is just great. The colors of the Templars and the other factions are simple but feel right. The templars are a rustic metal, while the Xeno seem like they're straight out of a circuit board.
Gameplay: Plays like most tactical strategies, you can only move so much each round and attack. This game takes a different kind of system, where if you attack before moving, your AP gets removed from your movement as well. Each of the different classes have armor and weapons you can equip between chapters. But the catch is you have to use the Requisition tree to unlock them. It also is where you unlock the more advanced units. This makes each playthrough interesting as you cannot really unlock all of the features in each playthrough.
Replay Value: I am still working on my first campaign, but I already see the skill trees and talents that I messed up. A scout doesn't need much melee points, so focus on his ranged skills. I could play this a hundred times, and might just possibly do so.
Story: The story so far seems a bit confusing, but it does seem in depth enough. It has lore and backstory, much like you'd get out of Elder Scrolls or Warcraft. I feel that as the game develops you will get more details to make the reason you're in this fight more obvious.
Opinion: Overall, I'd give this game an 8/10. It has given me something to sit down and enjoy after a long day. I can play a level or two and then move onto something else. I can pick it back up the next day, and not feel like I've lost anything. I managed to pick it up on sale, but the standard price for the game is not bad for an indie game. I definitely say if you like tactical strategies, Fire Emblem, or just a general history buff, Templar Battleforce has something for you.
*Edit: I would like to add that I love that the team is putting time into making the game look and run better than the initial launch. I am enjoying the new character designs they did, and the UI changes. Keep up the good work.

Aragami is pretty much a stealth only game, since once you have been seen, it is hard (but not completely impossible) to complete the area you are in. Enemies that have seen you will alert others making it harder to surprise them. But that kinda makes it appealing, since it is that stealth the game is all about. There is no HUD, all the meters are on the character, which sometimes makes for not such great visibility of them, but most of the time it just helps the whole experience.
There are a few bugs in multiplayer (like loosing connection and having to start the chapter over again), but nonetheless multiplayer is where the fun really begins. And nothing compares to the feeling of your first simulkill, supressing the urge to high-five your partner in crime. The levels are spacious enough to loose your comrade out of sight, with a little icon helping to regroup if needed. There is plenty of things to do for two players in the maps, and plenty of enemies to be avoided or executed.
The two play-styles, peaceful and murderous, both exist, with peaceful often being the easier route (and also the faster). In my opinion though, killing all enemies is way more fun, and thankfully - to this date - the game does not punish you for doing so. The story is nothing really spectacular or new, but dramatic and fetching nonetheless.
To put it in a nutshell, Aragami is what is to be expected at the price, and more. There are some bugs, especially in multiplayer and the HUD sometimes not being clearly visible due to the fact that it is on the clothing of the main character, and some features like collapsing platforms, that only work in singleplayer, but it is Indie, and judging by the changelogs, always improved on. I definitely recommend buying it, cause it is a heck of a lot of fun, and I recommend playing it with a friend.

To preface this review, I have beat the game. This review is not out of frustration for not being able to accomplish that, but it is out of frustration from the game in general.
For a match 3 game the concept is novel, adding a requirement of matching specific tiles to progress.
Unfortunately once the novelty wears off, it becomes a chore. And the novelty will wear off, because the game is stacked against you in multiple ways, and requires you to lose repeatedly to complete tasks and buy upgrades (which soon become an artificial barrier to gameplay) before winning it even becomes possible.
The main barrier to fun in the game is the manner of losing - not the inevitability, as with Tetris, but the speed at which it can happen. Every obstacle requires a specific type of match - attacks or keys - and the game can at whim decide to deprive you of these, leaving you helpless to do anything but wait until defeat.
Other problems with the control system compound this. For instance, sliding the tiles is not well designed. If you click a tile, it can only slide by the first direction the mouse moves. So if you want to drag a tile upwards but your mouse moves a LITTLE to the left first, your tiles will try moving left and right instead. You can try again while the mouse button is held down, but you've lost that time.
The matching detection is not great either. When you line or nearly line up a match, their tiles illuminate, however when you let go the tile you're moving can fit to an adjacent space, meaning the match does not occur and you have to start again. Once more, this costs time.
The game needs resource management - trying to keep a healthy number of attack tiles and keys on the board at all times to be ready for any obstacles that arrive, but a couple of things ruin this as a concept and make the game even less fun.
The monsters - particularly boss class monsters - require a LOT of matches and items to defeat, during which time you're losing time AND they hit you which also costs a nasty chunk of time. It goes without saying that despite the whole upgrade system, matching attack tiles is just not effective enough to keep the game balanced.
The game can and does throw numerous amounts of the same obstacles at you consecutively, such as two chests, a door and then another chest. Even if you kept a healthy number of keys available at the start of this, you probably won't have enough to get through it all which leads to a lot of lost time and defeat. The same applies to multiple tough monsters.
Matching tiles or using an item JUST before you arrive at an obstacle will cause it to be wasted. There's no tolerance whatsoever. This can lead to situations where you're not blocked by an obstacle, and too afraid to do anything because you don't want to lose the matches you can see available to you. This is contrary to the game's advertised element.
Finally, when you match tiles, more appear which can result in combos. Normally in this kind of game these are desirable, but in this game they can and will punish you by decimating a resource you can see yourself needing soon - for instance, if you're fighting a monster with a chest behind it, a few keys may fall in during the fight, matching with the ones already on the board and severely depleting the keys. Then when you win the fight you won't be able to deal with the chest.
Furthermore, when newly-fallen tiles create combos, this takes time during which you are unable to slide any tiles to make more matches. This results in awkward situations where you can see multiple matches you want to make but are unable to do so because a useless combo is ongoing and killing you in the process.
You do get a very limited number of items, but most of the time an item does not even clear one of its respective obstacles. After a few hours of play to finally be able to challenge for the game's namesake 10,000,000 points (yes, you need to play for a few hours before winning a game even becomes a possibility), key items will not be enough to open a three-lock chest or door, and you will need at least three damage items to defeat a single monster.
This game had promise, but its execution is disastrous. Its visuals and music are very fun for a few hours, but they do not last the extended periods of time demanded of you when the game becomes an unfair and repetitive grind.

I bought this game two days after a friend of mine showed me a few screens of the alien-species (Kharaa) two or three years ago.
I couldn't stop playing it for two weeks, it was something entirely new.
Playing the marines was nothing like playing Counter Strike or similar games. You move much slower and can't crouch, just walk and run. You have to use a flashlight when the power nod in your area got destroyed and the weapons you can use are limited to a pistol, an axe, a...wielder(? healing-thing), a mashine gun, a shotgun, a flamethrower, a grenade launcher, mines and a few different types of grenades. On the other hand you can research jetpacks and Exos (those gigantic roboter suits).
The beauty of this team are the many cool things you can build. Other than the armory (storage for weapons etc.) you can build sentry guns to defend your base against aliens or small tank-like mashines to attack the enemy.
The aliens are my absoloute favorite. You can play as Skulk, Gorge, Lerk, Fade or Onos, everyone of those has their own pros and cons, but I prever the Skulk. I love hoding in dark corners, waiting for a stupid marine who walks around on his own and killing him before he even gets what's happening. At the beginning, it was quite hard to master the fast, wild movements of every alien (except for the onos...can't call that "fast"), I had to get the hang of it to actually harm any marines, but it didn't take much time.
With the Gorge being able to build countless different structures to support his team, there are many tactical possibilities to finally destroy your enemy's commander station.
Which brings me to the actual clue of the game: The need of a commander. Without a commander, the team can't research new structures and weapons (marines) or new abilitys and upgrades (aliens). Also, the commander is essential for a great teamplay. He coordinates attacks, can drop healing- or ammo-packs for marines and cysts for aliens, spreading the area controlled by them. Also, he's the one dropping ressource-gaining towes all over the map for both teams, so if you lost your commander and those get destroyed, you can't buy better weapons (marines) or evolve to higher creatures (aliens) anymore. A good commander brings you half-way to victory, but of course the other players actually listening is almost as important.
The incredible high amount of tactics and teamplay won me over in minutes and I still love playing this game with friends or with random people on the servers.
Only flaw is the training-mode. The bots (especially aliens) tend to get stuck in the ground or walls, leaving you alone to defend your base. It's a good way getting used to the commander-job, however, or getting the basics.
I can only recommend this game with high praise, but you should be sure to have a computer that can take it. Before I got the hadware-upgrade, the game wasn't exactly fluent, even though I lowered the graphics. Now, it runs perfectly.

This is the best game of the Master collection set. If you need to save money, this is the one to buy. It has better economic balances than either of the two preceding games (Dawn of War and Winter Assault). There are diverse races to choose from. The campaign map is set up like a game of risk, so you direct the war rather than following a linear campaign. Heroes advance in power through their wargear. You earn wargear by accomplishing special objectives over the course of a campaign. Eventually you unlock them all, so I wouldn't call it customization. The enemies push back. All of this is true for Soulstorm as well, but it falls short. Dark Crusade has a better world map in every way (it is easier to see where armies are, which territories you can move to, and what bonuses you have acquired), you can fortify your positions effectively, and the wargear, while barely different, is better.

Let me preface this by saying I love Orcs Must Die and I played this since before it came to Steam. I bought the first one shortly after its release and I have been in love with it ever since. I still fire it up occasionally just to kill a couple Orcs. When the 2nd one released I felt like their focus on Multiplayer detracted from the experience of the single player. It was still possible to play on your own, but at least the first part was a chore.
And now we come to this. Single Player? Forget it. Much like games like Smite, which the Siege Mode reminds me of, there is no single player. This is a Multiplayer only title. Single player is in there only in the Practice Levels, so congratulations, I hope you got friends to play with, because coordinating with a bunch of strangers in a PUG match, about how to build kill boxes is neigh impossible.
The Maps are even more Lane based, reminding me of Mobas like Smite where minions are pushed down lanes, and this example becomes even more glaring in the Siege Mode where two teams fight each other. You have to build traps and send minions down the lane.
Speaking of building traps, remember how fun that was in OMD 1 and 2? Yeah, not so much here. Traps do not seem to have any impact on the Orcs. Sure, it does Damage, but there are no animations corresponding to it. It doesn't feel like the traps hit the Orcs. Sure they throw them up in the air, but it lacks the visceral feel the first two games had.
The Oomph that made the first two games so enjoyable is gone. Gone are also other mechanics such as Headshots. They even make fun of it during the Tutorial saying “Aiming for the head does nothing but feels good”. No it doesn't. It makes no difference. It feels like I do a pittance of damage to the enemies, and I do not even get rewarded for aiming properly. Every Hero coming with their locked in weapon abilities and one special thingy. I am writing thingy because its not even guaranteed to be a trap.
Some Heroes and their abilities are clearly designed for PvP. Its more than clear that the MOBA like Siege Mode is where they want you to play with most of the heroes.
The Animations of the Heroes are also a bit stilted and overall I can't but help feel like the B-Team has been working on this. Like they gathered the interns, gave them some pointers and access to the graphic assets and let them run wild. Now you might be saying “But its beta”, yeah well Beta doesn't excuse the poor Animation quality in my book. It also doesn't excuse how floaty the traps feel, or how grindy everything became.
Speaking of grindy.. I hope you like random rewards and booster packs. Traps are now cards, which you have to find in chests. But fear not you occasionally get a chest and hope you get something useful out of it. If not.. don't worry the cashshop is quite in your face, so don't worry about leaving some money. And of course heroes have to be bought. You can earn them (or rather craft them) Warframe style. Grind, grind, grind with random rewards, hoping you get what you want and then grind some more.
It makes me sad that this is what OMD has turned into. Nothing I enjoyed in OMD 1 and 2 is being found in this game. Instead I get a soulless cash grab. And if you haven't caught on by now.. Avoid like the plague, it will just ruin your fond memories of OMD.

Let's get the important stuff out of the way first, because persuading you is very much in
interest:
Should you buy Duck Game? YES.
Duck game is, by the numbers, a run-of-the-mill 2d pixel platformer.
But real life isn't by the numbers.
Made by a single solitary developer for the Ouya (How about that!), Duck Game is as simple as they come. Choose a duck. Shoot the other ducks. Last player standing wins. Rinse and repeat.
But by applying this formula to an excellently crafted pixel-sprite based world with incredibly snappy controls, a plethora of weapons from flower to flamethrower, a physics engine that is not only predictable and reliable but at the same time able to provide endless laughs and surprises, simple duck-based arcade humour and a crisp netcode and UI, you get an outstanding, fast-paced four player quacking frenzy that's made me laugh more than any other game has even come close to doing.
It's just
.
So if you have any friends at all, and don't hate having huge amounts of fun, then I cannot reccomend Duck Game enough. There's good reason why this is one of only four games I've ever given the honour of being chosen to sit in my "Favourites" category.

The Binding of Isaac is about surviving levels of foundations with the most horrendous looking things you have ever seen. At first you may find yourself surprised at what you see, but later its all natural to you, given enough time on the game. It's a game full of NES styled references and vulgar tones, and I wouldn't have it anyother way. If you are a strong follower of Catholism, I suggest not to buy it unless you feel you will get a hoot out of it like I have.
This game is a commitment, in a good way of course. It gives you constant goals and obstacles which makes it never a dull moment. There are 7 characters to choose from, all very diverse, you must learn how to play with all of them to progress the game. Most of them are easy to navigate but some like Eve and XXX take patience and good evasion to beat the game (and its all preference on who you like).
I find once you unlock Cain, he's a great character for initial damage and speed. As long as you dont get the Technology 2 (dlc item) you will be fine.
That's another thing, the dlc. People always decide to purchase it on Steam sales along with the standard game. This is a big mistake for some people as the dlc makes the game a step more difficult with enemies and few of the bosses (Carrion Queen, Bloat, im looking at you). Without the dlc, you are able to find the game more progressive, without having the responsiblity of the right trinket and fighting super sins (yes, thats a thing). I recommend to hold off until the next sale of the dlc (or buy it if you can't wait) just so you are able to grasp the mechanics of the game without dying constantly.
Overall, Edmund McMillen (the creator) has made a game that has created a popular cult following for a game, as the community shares secrets and tips to the game. Its a game where I had found determination in, until I 100% it, plus dlc. The only problem I found in the game was characters like Judas or Samson will always get the same rewards from treasure rooms,  once you play with them, which gives a lack in hopes for random items.
If you love the Legend of Zelda styled dungeons and a game that will give you 250+ hours I would suggest this masterpiece.

One trick you might want to try while leaning the game is going to Character Select and using The Bard. Normally, the main character has to hit the beat or take damage, and if the level song finishes before you reach the Exit, a trapdoor automatically opens up underneath you, limiting your time to uncover secrets. The Bard doesn't use the beat system, and lets you play the game move by move like a more traditional Rogue-like, with no time limit, letting you learn the enemy patterns and secret tricks before going back to the much more hardcore main heroine.
Very complete for an Alpha! Necrodancer takes the nail-biting indecision involving most Rogue-likes and blows it away by setting everything do a beat. You dance, the monsters dance, the floor lights up when you're doing things right, the fun takes over and you find yourself enjoying the challenge of having to think fast!
There are many items to discover, inventory management and spell/bomb use is controlled by hitting two directions at once, but the game shows surprising intuitive depth for only have four buttons you can push, and can truly be played on a DDR pad! Enemies run on a pattern, although with several monsters in the room at once it gives Dance or Die an entirely new literal meaning. There are lots of secrets to discover, and the soundtrack of solid from start to finish.

This game is basically Bejeweled with RPG elements. I love Bejeweled with over 60 hours clocked in on Bejeweled 3. If you're familiar with those types of block matching games, it's pretty easy to pick this up and play.
The game can be frustrating. You need to make appropriate matches to meet the needs of your character who is running a dungeon at the top of the screen. If there's a locked door or chest, you need to match keys. If it's a monster, you need to match swords or staves. When you're not doing that, you want to match wood and stone to upgrade various shops. Sometimes you just don't get the types of blocks you need and the game delivers a brutal beating if you stop to consider your options. You have to keep matching non-stop to advance. If you hesitate, it's over. Some of the dungeon objectives are survival-based like "stay alive for 90 seconds." It's not as easy as that sounds. As you upgrade your armor, weapons, and abilities, however, the game's difficulty decreases. One ability, for example, reduces the number of keys to open locks to just one key.

At surface level, the gameplay is simple match three before time runs out.  The added twist of needing to match specific blocks to pass obstacles in engaging and implements well.  As was mentioned in another review, you will occasionally have several of the same obstacles in a row, which will see you run out of the blocks you need.  This doesn't seem incredibly common, and may just be a fluke of the radomness of the obstacle generation.
It will take a lot of runs to get the resources you need to escape.  This isn't much of a problem, as it's incredibly nice to have an actual objective in a game like this.
One  gripe with the game is that it seems to be perfectly geared for playing on tablets or other touch screens, and that using a mouse handicaps you.  It's a minor problem, and one that might just be because I'm terrible at games.
There are currently some bugs with achievement completion, but that only matters if you care very much about achievements.
In all, it's a charming little puzzle that is definitely worth the price.

Where do I begin with Templar Battleforce? This lovely little game first caught my eye when I was trolling around the internet looking for video games that gave me the ability to play customizable soldiers clad in epic battle armor. This little gem caught my eyes and I've been hooked ever since.
In Templar Battleforce, you play an elite force of genetically modified humans who are capable of cognizant recall of their ancestor's memories. They, along with a convoy of more "all natural" human beings have fled the core of the galaxy to seek their fortunes, and survival, after an epic war ravaged their homeworlds in a past war. They come under attack during their exodus and are forced to make landfall on a set of desert worlds. From here, the story of the Templars truly begins.
In this game, you will control a customizable taskforce of Templar warriors. Your force is broken down into multiple different unit types: Your "Blade Class" Captain (Basically, the proper Player Character), Soldiers, Scouts, Engineers, Hydras (Flamethrower equipped heavy infantry), Neptunes (Autocannon/HMG equipped heavy infantry), Paladins and Berzerkers. Each class evolves as you spend a limited pool of requsition points to unlock new abilities, equipment, and options for your units.
The Requisition Tree deserves special mention because of how in depth it is. Every class has no less than three branches they can develope along, and given the relative rarity of the requisition as a resource, you will have to carefully mold your taskforce, selecting which classes and which abilities you desire to define your Templars with. Will you try for a generalist approach, taking each class and combining the smaller number of individual powers to create a greater sum than the whole? Will you focus on one or two classes, creating an army that is solid because of the uniform excellence of a Templar unit type? Will you stride into the battle with guns blazing, Neptunes holding the fort and laying down massive walls of firepower while the Soldiers press ahead and annhilating xeno scum with plasma blasters? Will you take up axe and sword, forming mighty shield walls while augmenting and healing your brothers and sisters in the middle of cyclone of melee combat? The choice is yours, and if you play the campaign through, New Game Plus will reward you for your diligence and victories in the face of defeat.
The campaign consists of a series of linked missions. This is where the meat of the gameplay is. Each mission will have its own objectives and peculiarities. While they tend to follow a fairly similar layout from one mission to the next (Kill enemies, survive against timers, take strategic points), each mission does in fact have its own peculiarities. You will cleanse infested landscapes with mighty flamethrowers, you will assault into alien ships to plant bombs in the core of the vessels, you will retreat through canyons and pver bridges while burning the earth during your retreat, you will investigate derelict space hulls, you will save desperate people from the middle of nightmarish scenarios, and you will secure cities against invading forces. Each of this mission types will come with their own peculiarities, their own specifics in terms of victory objectives, and each will have a larger place in the game's overarching plot. So, while the missions will have similar formulas, you will never truly play the same fight twice.
The mechanics on the field are rather simple at the end of the day. You have a topdown isometric perspective, wherein you command your units on a tactical grid. Movement points, action points, special attacks and abilities, unique battlefield requisition, and more will all be at your disposal. Each character is commanded individually, giving you the ability to maneuver your forces and utilize your strengths in strategic coordination. Soldiers can lay down fields of cover fire while your melee units advance, meanwhile your scouts move up ahead to find enemies and peg them with high powered sniper rifles or venomous needlers. Cap it off with your engineers setting up turrets to organize a defensive peremiter for your Neptune to hold with his suppressive fire so your strike force can advance deeper into enemy territory, and you'll find victory in your sights. Or do it another way. If you're familiar with tactical turn based squad games, then you will be right at home with Battleforce Templar, no matter your preference for command.
All of this is topped off with a world full of lore and personality that is revealed through the journal of your Captain and his/her interactions with the various NPCs you will meet in both missions and peaceful zones between campaigns.
Likewise, the music  tracks to this game, while somewhat limited in number, definitely set the tone for the missions. Each soundtrack is crafted with an emotional theme in mind, ranging from an uplifting ballad of defiant action against the enemy to stress inducing choruses that are played when the mission's stakes are high and the price of failure is higher.
Finally, the developer(s) for this game are actively improving upon their creation all of the time. Since I first obtained Templar Battleforce, there have been at least three full mini campaigns introduced, several revisions and additions to the Requisition Tree, expanded lore entries and dialogue options, expansions to enemy unit types, and a multitude of bug fixes, weapon rebalances, and class expansions. This is clearly a labor of incredible love from a dedicated company that wants to deliver the best experience possible to their customer base without shelving the cost of expanded content on their fans. They're doing this old school, and they're doing this right.
If you are a fan of Tactical Turn Based Strategfy games and love to support developers who put their player base first, this game comes HIGHLY recommended.

I really like this game a lot. I think that there are a few things that are off, but it's really enjoyable to play. I also respect that there have been so many patches and additions. There are a couple things that are kinda
otherwise a very good game.
It's tactical and turn based. It's heavily reminiscent of Warhammer 40K so if you're a fan of that you might like this, or hate it depending on how much you like warhammer. The plot is simple. you're a templar dood who takes command of a squad. You're trying to locate the source of xeno scum and wipe them out, essentially.
The turn based combat seems a little weird at first, but once you understand how it works it can work pretty well. You spend AP by doing actions or you spend move points by moving. if you move first, you don't spend action points, but if you shoot first you spend move points. Like if you have 6 move and action points. You move 3 spaces and then shoot for 3 action points. You would have 3 action points and no move points left. This means it's often better to stand firm and fire a whole bunch and encourages stationary combat. Which is good as well because the enemy is mostly melee. There are defintiely ranged enemies too though and there aren't just xenos, but they are the main enemy.
There's also a 'heat' system where if you take too many actions your templar can overheat and take damage. This restricts you from shooting and moving too much.
I feel as though the 'requisition' system is neat too, but kinda makes me spread too thin. It's better to focus on a few classes, like 4 of them than to try and get them all. I also don't like that there is soldier and then heavy weapons because they function essentially the same. Paladin and berserker are similar too, but they have the distinction of being a healer and a pure melee which is nice, but there could be more variety in them.
The other classes are pretty varied though and quite fun to mess with. I like that engineers can lay turrets or specialize in capturing. Scouts can kite or be big hitters and armor penetrators or dedicated stealth scouts. Stealth works pretty uniquely too since it's not just 'turn invisible now you're invisible' but that you increase your stealth and stealth levels make you harder to detect. The only downside I can see is it's hard to tell if your guy is actually 'stealthed' since stealth levels reduce the range the enemy can detect you at. You kinda gotta manually do it?
Anyway I would definitely recommend the game. I like the game, the devs seem responsive in fixing bugs and adding in some content and making the game as a whole better. Some real love was put into the game and it makes the game even better as a result. I would like to see another templar game come out!

Earth Defense Force is a third person shooter pitting you against hordes of alien invaders, said invaders are using giant robots and huge bio-enginereed insects to invade our world:  it's up to you to stop them in the 15 campaign missions.
-alien units are well designed and animated
-intense, frantic combat against hordes of insects and robots
-most of the environment can be destroyed, cars blow up and buildings crumble to dust when hit with rockets: this adds a slight strategic layer to things cause doing so increases your line of sight (at the cost of cover) and gives the alien insects less surfaces to crawl on
-dialogue is generally funny, the game really doesn't take itself seriously with soldiers joking and abesnt-minded intel officers taking their time to explain how to beat a boss
-a good amount of armors and weapons to unlock and level up
-very fun when played in coop
-when not playing coop AI companions are quite competent and generally quite effective
-graphics are a tad bland and levels generally look all the same
-unremarkable voice acting
-gameplay is overall simple and boils down to going from point A to B shooting everything that moves
-some enemy waves last a bit too long
-no tutorial whatsoever, thankfully it's easy to pick up and any doubts can be cleared by looking up a FAQ
-a bit on the short side
-leveling up armors takes quite a long time, you'll have to grind missions once you're done with the campaign or simply replay it selecting a higher difficulty
EDF comes out as a straightforward game that offers plenty of mindless fun, shooting tons of enemies and leveling the city using the various over the top weapons at your disposal is truly enjoyable.
There's not much of a story, the characters are cliched and the ending feels hurried but the fact is the game isn't really interested in that stuff: what it wants is to offer you an huge b-movie inspired alien armada-and a few bosses-to blow up alone or with friends: and it does so really well.
I'm not sure the game has alot of staying power once it's done, there's a campaign remix mode that adds different foes and ups the ante a bit but it doesn't really change things much, so you'll have to play survival with friends or just grind campaign missions again to level up everything.
At its sale price of 3 bucks EDF is a really fun albeit simple and short game: if you're into third person shooters and like its campy b-movie style it will not let you down.

One trick you might want to try while leaning the game is going to Character Select and using The Bard. Normally, the main character has to hit the beat or take damage, and if the level song finishes before you reach the Exit, a trapdoor automatically opens up underneath you, limiting your time to uncover secrets. Very complete for an Alpha! Necrodancer takes the nail-biting indecision involving most Rogue-likes and blows it away by setting everything do a beat. You dance, the monsters dance, the floor lights up when you're doing things right, the fun takes over and you find yourself enjoying the challenge of having to think fast!
There are many items to discover, inventory management and spell/bomb use is controlled by hitting two directions at once, but the game shows surprising intuitive depth for only have four buttons you can push, and can truly be played on a DDR pad! Enemies run on a pattern, although with several monsters in the room at once it gives Dance or Die an entirely new literal meaning. There are lots of secrets to discover, and the soundtrack of solid from start to finish.

Dust: An Elysian Tale is a hack-and-slash Metroidvania game with RPG elements: levelling up, equipment, stupid side-quests about collecting items, characters who won't shut up, and a dreadful yet entirely serious plot about the amnesiac warrior Dust battling hordes of evil monsters and the genocidal General Gaius.  Comic relief is provided by Dust's companion, a winged fox thing called a "nimbat".
Oh, and everyone in the world is a furry.
Artwork is attractive, particularly the hand-painted backgrounds and other terrain. Dust himself is well-animated, but less attention went to the enemies: many of the enemy sprites look fine when standing still but terrible in motion.
The real problem is that there are few puzzles and little platforming, just screen after screen of of mooks with occasional interruptions for dialogue. The game lives or dies on the quality of its combat, and that combat isn't enough.
A tutorial early in the game explains Dust's starting combos, and a combo-counter in the top right helpfully lists the number of strikes. You might be encouraged into thinking that this is going somewhere, but it isn't: there are no new moves coming to string together into fun combos; and long combos have no effect other than granting bonus experience. Combat actually gets worse when you learn the next and final moves, involving tapping the "Dust Wind" button to whirl the sword around like a fan or fly through the air. This is particularly effective because Fidget is capable of launching projectiles, which are multiplied by the Dust Wind. Most of the game will involve spamming these attacks as much as possible.
One reason the late game gets easier is that you find items which multiply Fidget's power. These multipliers stack, so her hundreds of hits that do very low damage are eventually multiplied 8x or more and the game is renamed "Fidget: Unstoppable Killing Machine".
While impressive for a game largely developed by one person, Dust doesn't feel like a labour of love in the same way as recent classics like Fez or Guacamelee (which, incidentally, also has far more interesting combat). It's OK, but, for me, that's not enough. If you like endlessly spamming the same attacks, though, it sure is the game for you.

Just wanted to put a note out there to say thanks and let you know that the app is working great for my group and my DMing needs!
I use it through Steam on my MacbookPro, take my own TV to my friend's house and lay it out flat, then hook it up to AppleTV. We've been playing D&D in person for a couple years now, and I used to spend a small fortune on printed maps. No longer. We've been using InfinitasDM for a very long while now, and I can't tell you how much money it has saved me in the long run, nor how much we love the Fog of War feature (a little soft around the edges for my tastes, but meh, it works!) We don't use your tokens and instead use our own on the TV surface, but I have used the drawing tools and they're very handy!!
I especially love that I can upload whatever jpg I want to splay across the screen--I've been able to upload monster imagery and player handouts so everyone can see all at once what they're up against and read things without having to pass things around. This was the interface I was looking for when I wanted to start using digital maps. I didn't want to use two computer screens and turn our gaming sessions into technological nightmares of set up--I originally used this on my iPhone, it was that simple. I'm beyond happy with what you've put together, and I hope it sticks around for a very long time. It has become a necessary and indelible part of our gaming experience, and I'd be hard pressed to replace it.
I can't thank you enough for adding yet another level of categorization for file management--having 4 layers instead of 3 made a huge difference in how I prep my stuff each week. I know that happened a long time ago, but I'm just now getting around to posting...
The only thing I would love is the capacity to import imagery into a layer over the top of the imagery already there, or be able to split the screen. I know that completely mangles the interface, but being able to see a pic of a monster in the corner of the screen could be really handy sometimes.
I'm not sure, ultimately, whether I'm using your app the way you intended, but I have to say it is exactly what I needed regardless of its full capabilities. I can scroll through multiple desktops on my Macbook, using one for Infinitas DM and others for other programs or browsers (using it in conjunction with D&D Beyond, Kobold Fight Club, and a dice roller has literally Rocked. My. World.). I'm able to load pretty large images (in jpg only not jpeg--that makes a difference for some reason), and that means the quality of the picture for my players is just that much better when I zoom in (it's so cinematic when I do that--they love it!!). I don't have to use the tokens and the players feel more involved (thank-you for fixing the map-resizing issue when opening a different image--that one change saved us so much time re-positioning everything!!).
We haven't played your downloadable adventures, but I appreciate that you've taken the time to create them. They're visually stunning!!! Someday!!! :)
Thanks again for making this. My pocketbook, myself, and my group are very very happy. Weirdly, the quality of life has improved since I don't have to struggle so hard to prep--making analog out of digital was very time consuming... Thanks so much!!

Everyone can sympathise with the fact that there is always that cousin or sibling who just happens to overshadow you in every little thing you do - just like X-COM overshadows this little beauty.
(FYI anyone who saw the word 'templar' in the name expecting to see Altair in space.....no....just no...)
First things first - Its not X-COM. Similar pretence. Similar style. But not X-COM. It is a great game with a well thought out story and gripping mechanics. The retro style graphics gives a wave of nostaliga and the difficulty levels ensure all players can have whatever level challenge they wish. The turn based system is excellent and merged with a time limit it ensures you cannot slowly (and safely) crawl through a level. The 'heat' mechanic is a breath of fresh air and you are forced to play sensibly to ensure your templars do not overheat and turn into metal burritos.
There is limited replayability factor, and there is additionally nothing new with this 'alien invasion' story and the turn based mechanics. But that doesnt detract from the fact that Templar Battleforce hits the spot and succeeds to add its mark to the turn based genre.
I would seriously reccomend this to anyone who enjoys turn based strategy games. It is certainly worth the small price to play this little gem.

I use this program for the two games I run weekly. My groups now have zero interest in running without using them, as we use a Duchess gaming table, with an LED tv for our battle map. Infinitas is dead simple to use for my purposes (I am not using a lot of advanced features), as I am taking pre-generated maps, importing them (by encounter/area) within the respective 'worlds' (campaigns.. hell's rebels and giantslayer), then using the split display between the gm view on my laptop, and the PC map view on the LED battlemap.
I have tried to use other programs to get the digital maps on the TV, but all of the ones I tried were too complicated for my tastes; I do a lot of prep on my own, and this program does exactly what I want - fog of war, PC/digital-battlemap, etc. I've never had a performance problem as I have read others have had here - the program is snappy.
My only complaint, if there even is one (as it is so minor) - is there's no "square" option for the fog of war eraser. Getting into corners while erasing (whether via mouse or finger) can be dicey on the fly, if I don't want to reveal a room next to the one I am currently erasing.

Earth Defense Force: Insect Armageddon is a pretty fun game if I do say so myself.
There are some negatives to point out. EDF is a little repetative in its objectives. Essentially you're moving from point to point, killing swarms, and that's the crux of it. Another negative to point out is that the dialogue is pretty corny and cheesy. Your squad-mates chime in with very cringey things to say and it's not even funny; you'll involuntarily sigh when you hear them . Also your character's name is "Lightning"....yeah.
With that being said, if you're able to ignore the negatives, this is a very fun title. EDF: Insect Armageddon is a pretty neat gem on Steam. It's worth a look.

Gameplay - (based on "normal" difficulty) 8/10 - Nothing too challenging on normal, but on any higher difficulty perma-death is active for your templars ; however, as far as I'm aware you are able to retry a mission if you feel you could perform better. The interesting part comes from the "heat" system which I won't go into explaining but it certainly makes it stand out somewhat from other turn-based strategies
Aesthetics - 8.5/10 - Very stylised and definitely not for everyone, but I personally enjoyed the clarity that was brought about by the simplicity
Story/ Dialogue - 7.5/10 - The concept of the leviathan mech suits and the templar lineages is pretty interesting, but overall the story really comes down to humans vs aliens and I spotted more than a few typos throughout the story and additional flavour text you can get between chapters
Top-down Steampunk/XCOM in space - As your templars level up they gain access to not only more stat points but also more gear points, allowing them to wield superior equipment requisitioned from the templar armoury. Many of the abilities you unlock are able to affect multiple targets at once encouraging you to keep your troops close in order to maximise your effectiveness.
Depending on the difficulty you're playing on you can permanently lose templars - but as tragic as this may be it is not game over. Any new templars you bring in gain a chunk of experience proportional to your captains own experience. Veterans that haven't been used in battle for a while will also maintain this level of experience so that you do not have to constantly hire new templars in order to change up your strategy.
Overall - given the price - I would say this game is definitely worth picking up for the ammount of gameplay you can get from a single playthrough; even more so if you intend to play through multiple difficulties.

One trick you might want to try while leaning the game is going to Character Select and using The Bard. Normally, the main character has to hit the beat or take damage, and if the level song finishes before you reach the Exit, a trapdoor automatically opens up underneath you, limiting your time to uncover secrets. The Bard doesn't use the beat system, and lets you play the game move by move like a more traditional Rogue-like, with no time limit, letting you learn the enemy patterns and secret tricks before going back to the much more hardcore main heroine.
Very complete for an Alpha! Necrodancer takes the nail-biting indecision involving most Rogue-likes and blows it away by setting everything do a beat. You dance, the monsters dance, the floor lights up when you're doing things right, the fun takes over and you find yourself enjoying the challenge of having to think fast!
There are many items to discover, inventory management and spell/bomb use is controlled by hitting two directions at once, but the game shows surprising intuitive depth for only have four buttons you can push, and can truly be played on a DDR pad! Enemies run on a pattern, although with several monsters in the room at once it gives Dance or Die an entirely new literal meaning. There are lots of secrets to discover, and the soundtrack of solid from start to finish.

Binding of Isaac has become one of my favourite indie games and there is no surprise why:
Starting a new game I was already amused by the classic 'room battles' with almost a different foe each time. When reaching my first treasure rooms I felt a sense of satisfaction that I was being rewarded for my progress, the item I collected not only transformed my abilities but transformed isaac himself! I instantly knew that I needed these items to survive this game let alone improve my character, making looting a very important part of the game. After my exploring and looting I finally came across to the boss room and in turn, my first challenge! Although this was the first room therefore the easiest boss, I felt a little helpless as it was my first encounter and had no idea what this boss was capable of which made the fight much more exciting for me. Unfortunately my first playthrough was cut short in the second stage (stupid pointers getting a lucky shot).
Starting up a second playthrough I noticed the changes straight away, the levels were completely different from the first! The layout of the floor, items rewarded, even the boss had completely changed! This is what makes Binding of Isaac so addicting for me, it's never the same twice.
Now I've covered the experience playing the game yet I still have so much to talk about! Being run on flash it works ridiculously well; there is rarely any lag at all and I can't say that I've witnessed any crashes or glitches, you can tell this game was very well put together and a large amount of effort and care was put into making this the perfect indie game.
Another part of the game is the beautiful music, oh the music! Words are not enough to tell you guys how much I love this soundtrack; its simple yet catchy tune when exploring the first floor, fast-paced battle theme that really gets you in the mood for victory! I love how eerie and darker the music starts to get as you progress further down the basement. There's not one negative thing that can be said about this soundtrack. Hat's off to you, Dan!
Personally, after getting to know the back story of this game (not saying anything about it because spoilers) this has really got me to tell my mother how much I love her :( displays that games can hit you on a much deeper level.
I've been playing Binding of Isaac now for at least half a year, I've achieved so much and beaten the game many times, I've even brought Wrath of The Lamb Expansion (but a review on that is for another day). But I still think that I've not fully 'completed' the game therefore I'm still enjoying it as much as I did on my first playthrough, no matter how many times I click on the 'start' button :)
So the question is this: would I recommend this game to be played by any kind of gamer and not just indie lovers? Its a big fat yes, this will be the best £3.99 you'll ever spend on steam!

Do I have quite a bit of hours? Yes.
So the question is: Why would I not recommend a game that I have spent so much time playing?
It is simple. I have been playing on modded servers all the time. And those are now being killed by the devs.
This game is not bad. Infact I love it's concept and with some mods it is just the game I spent my weekends playing as you can tell by the playtime. But the game is changing in a direction that I cannot support. It is going all out competitive where it feels like the devs are trying to kill the part of their community that consists of casual non-league gamers.
While supposedly focusing on new players and player retention (as stated by themselves) the devs have painfully neglected and put off large parts of the existing playerbase. Especially the community that enjoys large servers or total conversion mods.
When you see a server browser what is the first thing you do? Yes, sort by players.
And then? Yes, join the top most that has room.
Why is that? It is because you like playing a multiplayer game with a lot of other players and it is way more forgiving for a new player if there are more people that can compensate or help you learning the ropes.
The devs think that this is ruining your fun as a new player. So they have hid all servers not fitting their dogmatic view on what a true NS2 server is. Leaving you to competitive low population servers by default unless you find the hidden quirks in the menus to unlock the other servers. This effectively kills the influx of new players to those modded servers denying them the upkeep and having those communities die a slow death.
If you like spending hours watching tutorial videos and training on bot servers before you are fit to join an official server go ahead and buy it. You might like going all league and competitive. But if you are looking for a game to play once in a while look for something else, you will probably not enjoys this (anymore).

At first glance it appears to be a simple poker mmo with micro transaction options.  Everything is going well; you are winning; you're unlocking higher-level tables (which you can't afford yet), until you get to level 13.  At level 13 you are no longer allowed to play at the "low-stakes" table, and instead you are forced to move on to the higher tables, whose buy-ins are 10-13% of your bankroll at this time.  It appears that there are bots floating around these more expensive tables (if you scroll through the screenshots section, you will see a few players that show up everywhere).  The bots yolo their chips every hand, forcing you to potentially lose big and quickly need to pay real money for more fake chips.
Also:
-Tables are not consolidated; once people stand up their seats are never filled until the room empties out.  You can switch between tables, and virtually all of them have only one or two people sitting at them; (people = bots in this review).
-Chat feature is limited to emojis.
-You cannot play with your steam friends.
-Betting options are narrow (1/2, 3/4, Pot, All-in).  As I mentioned before with the higher stakes tables, any competitive hand is going to lay waste to your allotment of free chips.

As someone that Kickstarted this app, I was really looking forward to the potential of this program. But I have tried with every update to give it the benefit of the doubt, but this program is has so many glaring issues that I don't feel like anyone should pick this up until some major issues are addressed on both the Steam and mobile versions of the app.
Problems
Ease of use/Learning How to Use: On the mobile version, there is no link to or in app version of a manual or quick tips. It wasn't until just now that I found out there was a manual on Steam to look at and download, but that is something that should be connected in the program itself, especially in the mobile version.
Controls: Because of the above problem, understanding the controls can be confusing. One of them being that everything still works as if on a touch screen, so you have to click and hold to choose anything. This is something I also seems to lag a bit on the Steam version. Another is the fact that the zoom with a scroll wheel is very slow and that it's turned off if you have any drawing or erasing tool selected. So you must constanly selecte and unselect just to navigate around the page you are on.
Tools:
1.) Eraser - This has been brought up before and the Dev has said it's just the two smallest sizes that have issues, but I'm sorry, I tested it myself on both mobile and the Dev is only correct if you are zoomed in pretty deep in the map and go quite slowly alone the line, then in may work with the largest size eraser. Go to fast and it just erases random line segments. Same if you are looking at the map too zoomed out. So it's really not a eraser as it's a bad, manual, undo tool. When I think or erase, I think of the "click and swipe, everything is gone" tool that every other drawing program from Paint to Photoshop has.
2.) Drawing tools - there is a lot of lag on line creation if you, like the eraser, are not super zoomed in. This is both on an iPhone 6 plus and a PC with an i7, 32Mbs of RAM, and a Quadro k4000 video card with no other apps running.
3.) Map Links - Because of the unresponsive touch based controls, this menu pops up more than I like and you can click out of it. Once it's up, you MUST choose something and then click and hold it--hopefully not bringing up the menu again, which does happen--to be able to drag and delete it. There needs to be a X in a corner to close that out.
No freedom of creativity - Despite the possible versatility of the app, it doesn't allow for the GM to create freely, but to a very structed method.
1.) World -> Region -> Location: You can only have those three subgroups (which is kind of odd since how many games are going to hav more that one world), so a location in a location is going to be mixed in with other locations. Not only that, once they are made, they can't be upgraded or downgraded. So if you wanted to have your first arc in a city, you'd think, "Okay, World would be the city, Regions would be districts, and locations being hotspots and POIs." then the next arc makes the party travel, the world would be bigger and more can be created. But since you can't shift anything, it rapidly becomes disorganized.
2.) Map and grid size - No matter what you want to draw, you get a huge canvas with very small grids to draw on. If i need to make a tavern, I don't need that much space to work with. And it would be one thing if it saved how much I'm zoomed in when i close a map, but it doesn't. This is another basic funtion of a drawing program sorely laking in this app.
3.) Can't make a document without a map - One of the assets that is supposed tomake this app useful is the ability to have documentents with lore and dialouge and notes ready for the GM to use. But you cant make any of them with out a Map created first. If we go back to the City arc I brought up, I may have notes on the greater world there incase they are needed, but I don't need the map yet. But right now you need at least a blank map before you can make any documents and you can't get to thos documents without opening that map, which feels very laborious and rigid for digital tool.
I hope the dev gets to really work on this and do some major changes and optimizations, but this feels like a proof of concept/alpha build of a program, not a finished produnct and as someone that backed this I don't feel this should out for sale yet.

I love the idea of this software. On paper, it's just what I am looking for. Something specifically designed to run a tabletop game with a screen for battlemaps with fog of war. I am reveiwing if from the standpoint of using it with a PC and on that platform, it's really lacking in basic usability.
Until I went and hunted around on forums where the developers where answering questions similar to mine, I was pretty convinced that the software was just bugged and broken.
It turns out that many of the features are built around the idea of 'click and hold' which is not anything the average PC user ever uses. This design choice is clearly for touch enabled surfaces. I get that but this software is being sold for PC with zero concessions for that platform. I really hope this changes. Also, if you want to use your purchase on another platform, you have to buy it again. On top of that, I see no way for you to share your files from one device to another. There is basic infrastructure lacking (user accounts, syncing between devices, etc).
There's also issues with placing markers. It seems that, depending on how large or small you decide to make a map that you import effects the size of the markers you place. On some of my maps they are tiny, on others they cover a large portion of the map. When you are placing a map, it's impossible to tell how big or small you are making the map. Again, this may not actually be true, but from a UI standpoint it's either impossible to tell or very criptic in it's notification to the user.
I'm glad that someone decided to make this product, but I wouldn't recomend it at this time, simply for the fact that I would not reward releasing software that isn't ready for release on the platform that you are buying it for, in my case, PC.
EDIT: One of the devs pointed out that tokens on the screen when you go to scale your map are there to set the relative size of the map image. I never infered that from the tokens on the screen as they are off center and there is no text explaining why they are there. Frankly, I thought their display was a bug.
As for the long press use throughout the software, I was told this is detailed in the user manual, which it is but I still question how many people actually look at a manual, muchless assume one even exists. I know I didn't. It's not my go to solution to learn how to use relatively simple software. I hope the devs decide to make some simple UI design changes that hold the user's hand a bit more instead.

TLDR; A good game that's worth buying for fans of turn based squad combat. Lot's of content, good class and progression system, flexible difficulty settings, rich back story, runs smoothly to boot.
If I had to describe this game in one word it would be: functional. There's no beautiful art or pretty effects, but what's is there gets the job done. The core gameplay is solid and the game runs smoothly, which to me is the most important thing a game has to get right before anything else.
Gameplay consists of turn based battles where you command a squad of space-marine-esque warriors called Templars. They come in various classes which gives them access to different abilities. The combat system can be a bit dense if you try to understand everything at once, but the game does a decent job off telling you what you need to know at any given time and if you really want to dig into the system there is a "Library" section that explains the game rules in detail. One thing I esspecially appreaciate about the interface is: tooltips, tooltips everywhere. Don't know what a stat does, just hover over it and a tooltip will appear and tell you what it feeds into, how likely am I to kill that alien?, hover over it and a tooltip will pop up giving you hit percentages and average damage.
In a game with a dense rule set like this I'm thankful that the devs made sure I could always quickly access enough information to make a decision and there are plenty of decisions to be made, both in and out of mission. Character progression consists of assigning points to their base stats, their special abilities(called talents) and giving them better gear. Below this is a requisition tree where you spend a requisition points to unlock new talents and equipment for your characters. I think this tree is very well planned out as it offers multiple ways to specialise your character classes, and many pieces of equipment can be used by more than one class, thus you can expand your options for other classes even as you level up only one. The limited amount of talent points each character gets means that you will inevitably create multiple characters of the same class and specialise them differently. For example: the scount class can be used as a fast stealth unit, or speced to be a high damage sniper.
The missions themselves are varied enough to be interesting. Most of the objectives consist of finding a thing or getting your entire squad to a certain place, but the map design and narrative keep this from getting boring. The game also provides a variety of difficulty settings from easy to the hardcore-permadeth-single-autosave difficulty for the ultra masochist. I have not finished the game yet but 18 hours in it looks like there's still plenty more content.
On the surface the game lore feels like it draws a lot of influence from Warhammer 40k, but I feel that it ultimately stands on it's own. Yes you have a force of elite warriors in mech-suits, yes you have a race of completely unsympathetic biological killing machines, yes you have cultists working to undermine humanity from within, but it's not like WH40k has a monopoly on these tropes and Templar Battleforce puts enough of it's own spin on them to keep things interesting. I find the concept of the Templar Lineage particularly fascinating.
The game's story is mostly delivered through text in "cutscenes" and through conversations in "secure areas"(missions where you can just walk around and talk to NPCs). This is fine if you don't mind reading text and enduring a little low budget storytelling. I think the devs did a decent job of breaking up the text and avoiding gratuitous exposition dumps, but your mileage may vary. If you really don't care for the story you can quickly skip over the text anyway.
My opinion on this game is summed up in the TLDR.  Make no mistake this is a niche game, but it does what it sets out to do. It's fun, polished and great value for money.
