You there! You like sci-fi? You like turn-based TACTICAL (yess, all caps!) games? You like RPGs with deep customization of characters and squad? You like story-driven scenarios with lots of objectives? You like to have access to the mechanics of the rules? You like all of the above except the sci-fi genre (you prefer goblins and wizards, is that it?)?
Well you have to at LEAST read on.
I've only played 2 missions (2 times the first one, 1 time the second), and let me tell you this : this game is serious stuff!  Now you might say ''Pfff, you barely played the game, how can I give credit to your review?''. Because just browsing through the interface, options, library, menus, tech trees, character sheets, etc., you'll get the feeling you know you like to have from this kind of game. The feeling of satisfaction. The feeling of devotion and attention to details from the devs.  The feeling that you'll spend quality time playing the game. The feeling that your decisions in-game actually matter.  And... the feeling that you won't see much of your family and friends for the next few weeks!
Honestly, I know nothing from the Star Traders universe, but I'm familiar with Warhammer 40k and StarCraft with their space marines. The Templars in this game hits the same chords : who doesn't like hulking machines decked-out in heavy weaponry ready to fire at every alien shenanigans they come by? On a more serious note : the Templars are really well done and diverse.  The lore behind them is also very interesting, and I love how it reflects into actual character customization. In this game, you can respec your Templars at-will between each mission, so you'll never be locked in your choices of character upgrades.  It lets you try different skills without the drawback of having to lvl another character.
What I really like is that information is not hidden. If you haven't noticed yet, I like to look at menus, tooltips and interfaces a lot because to me, these are the things that make or brake games like that.  And the ones found in this game are simple, easy to use and easy to know what is what.  From the font, to the colors used to identify different rolls, to its sound effects, you simply cannot have difficulties navigating through your character sheet, assigning orders and planning your moves.
Now to actual gameplay and features. After only 2 missions in, I see the enormous amount of tactical and strategic plays you'll have to make to succeed in this game.  From using the terrain to your advantage, to capturing Tactical Points to get more reinforcement and supplies, while having to carry out your mission in a timely fashion, this game offers a deep experience.  It let's you take your time to plan out your strategy. Turn by turn, yes, but also before deploying into the actual mission.  You have to select your gear, your talents, your skills, etc.  Because you want to succeed, yes. But you also want to survive.
Templar Battleforce offers a wide selection of game difficulties that will satisfy casual to semi-hardcore to full hardcore players.  Permanent death not your cup of tea? Play easy or normal, where your Templars carry on to other missions if you succeed even if they were defeated in battle.  You like to play with permanent death but don't want to lose everything if you screw up? Demanding and Hard difficulties let you abort and retry your missions without penalty, but you can chose to carry on and accept the death of characters if you succeed the mission.  Then there are harder game modes where decisions are final.  You died? Sorry pal, you are dead.  No turning back.
And finally, the amazing support of the devs.  The devs are real soldiers.  They have placed an Overwatch over their game.  As soon as you ask a question.. BAM! an answer comes right away.  They never seem to overheat.  And they are really dedicated to implement player suggestions into the game.  Browse through the community hub and you'll see. They put out guides, they ask for game files to track stats, they actively participate in discussions, they give interviews and are clear about the future of the game (no DLC), and most importantly, they update the game frequently. The game is even available on mobile platforms and they plan to share saved files eventually.
So by all means, if you hesitate about buying this game, you shouldn't. If you are into tactical turn/squad-based games, you will like it. If you don't like that type of game then.. what are you exactly doing reading about it? :P

Binding of Isaac has become one of my favourite indie games and there is no surprise why:
Starting a new game I was already amused by the classic 'room battles' with almost a different foe each time. When reaching my first treasure rooms I felt a sense of satisfaction that I was being rewarded for my progress, the item I collected not only transformed my abilities but transformed isaac himself! I instantly knew that I needed these items to survive this game let alone improve my character, making looting a very important part of the game. After my exploring and looting I finally came across to the boss room and in turn, my first challenge! Although this was the first room therefore the easiest boss, I felt a little helpless as it was my first encounter and had no idea what this boss was capable of which made the fight much more exciting for me. Unfortunately my first playthrough was cut short in the second stage (stupid pointers getting a lucky shot).
Starting up a second playthrough I noticed the changes straight away, the levels were completely different from the first! The layout of the floor, items rewarded, even the boss had completely changed! This is what makes Binding of Isaac so addicting for me, it's never the same twice.
Now I've covered the experience playing the game yet I still have so much to talk about! Being run on flash it works ridiculously well; there is rarely any lag at all and I can't say that I've witnessed any crashes or glitches, you can tell this game was very well put together and a large amount of effort and care was put into making this the perfect indie game.
Another part of the game is the beautiful music, oh the music! Words are not enough to tell you guys how much I love this soundtrack; its simple yet catchy tune when exploring the first floor, fast-paced battle theme that really gets you in the mood for victory! I love how eerie and darker the music starts to get as you progress further down the basement. There's not one negative thing that can be said about this soundtrack. Hat's off to you, Dan!
Personally, after getting to know the back story of this game (not saying anything about it because spoilers) this has really got me to tell my mother how much I love her :( displays that games can hit you on a much deeper level.
I've been playing Binding of Isaac now for at least half a year, I've achieved so much and beaten the game many times, I've even brought Wrath of The Lamb Expansion (but a review on that is for another day). But I still think that I've not fully 'completed' the game therefore I'm still enjoying it as much as I did on my first playthrough, no matter how many times I click on the 'start' button :)
So the question is this: would I recommend this game to be played by any kind of gamer and not just indie lovers? Its a big fat yes, this will be the best £3.99 you'll ever spend on steam!
Haven't been able to discern what the pro strategies are, but it's certainly a beautiful game and a fun one for six newbies to learn at a LAN or something.

One of the games that made rogue-likes popular again, even though it really isn't a rogue-like, but offers some rogue-like elements like randomized dungeons and permadeath.
This game offers lots of replayability, thanks to the randomized dungeons and the huge amount of items you can find and unlock.
It also provides quite a challenge, depending on what item combinations you are using. While you might breeze through one run thanks to some incredibly powerful items, you might get decimated very quickly in another.
And items alone won't do. Hone your skills in dodging not only some really messed up enemies, but their projectiles and traps, too or you will perish sooner than you think! And death is the end. No reload. You start again from the beginning (you will keep unlocked stuff unlocked though, of course).
If you think the base game doesn't already offer enough, get The Wrath of the Lamb DLC to get even more stuff! More enemies, more items, more rooms, more EVERYTHING!
Be advised that this game runs in Flash, which can mean a bit wonky performance and no controller support (among other things).
Also, a remake called Rebirth should come out sometime next year, which will get rid of Flash and will offer yet even more new content. But don't wait for it, because this game in its current state is more than worth it anyways!

Coincidentally or not, Spintires was very recently struck by a rash of seemingly out-of-nowhere bugs that have caused it to crash or malfunction in various ways. And according to this post on Reddit, it's actually Zagrebelnyj's doing: It alleges that he's inserted “time bombs” into the game code that are responsible for the troubles. There have been four of them so far, each eventually fixed—unofficially—by a user.
Oovees, however, denied what it called “press speculation” about the game being intentionally sabotaged. “The situation on the bug is that we became aware of a major bug last week that caused the game to stop for some users. We have been working on this with Pavel since it came up. Progress on the next planned update has been suspended while we sort the bug issue,” it wrote on its forums. “We believe we have now identified the problem and are now testing at this very moment a hot fix provided by Pavel, who is also ready to help further if needed. We're fully focused now on making the game work properly again, so please allow us to get this sorted first and we'll then be able to explain what has caused this and then carry on with future updates we have planned.”
Despite the apparent imminence of a fix, however, Oovee has suspended sales of Spintires on Steam. It's still listed, but there's currently no option to purchase it, or even follow or add it to a wishlist. I'm not a coder, but that seems like a rather extreme step to take in the process of fixing a conventional bug—and I'm not a conspiracy theorist, but the sudden appearance of crippling bugs nearly two years after a game's release seems a little hinky, too.

10,000,000 is an arcade match-3 RPG with base management mechanics. Now, that may sound schizophrenic, but all the features actually mold together quite well to create a strange but fun experience. The gameplay consists mostly of dragging rows of cubes in order to match 3 of a certain type of cube, thereby helping you pass whatever obstacle you are currently faced with. Unfortunately, the game often gives you tons of whatever you need the least of at a certain time, leading to quite a lot of frustration. I remember one run in which I started out with a ton of keys.
“Yeah!” I thought. “I’ll be totally set for this run!”
I was then presented with about  10 or 15 obstacles in a row that required keys, and I ran out about halfway through and had to simply bide my time until the one match that I needed came along, using up all of my special items and powerups in the process. Now, whether that was built into the engine or I just have the worst luck in the world remains to be seen, but that kind of thing happens extremely frequently.
The gameplay sometimes gets as annoying as the music (an extremely loud 8-bit tune in an endless loop), with the aforementioned situation of having everything except the one thing that you need providing nearly endless frustration. The goal of the game is to get 10,000,000 points in a single run, because apparently that will help you somehow escape the prison you are in. While in a run, you can collect special items for use in a pinch, as well as building materials, gold, and experience. You can use the building materials to fix and upgrade your base. What benefit do base upgrades give? They help you waste all your gold and XP getting upgrades for your equipment.
Later on in the game, the price of training skills and getting upgrades becomes completely outrageous, whilst you are left sitting on a huge pile of wood and stone with nothing to spend it on. One thing I did like about the game was the difficulty curve. As you gather more points and complete objectives, you rank up and are forced to face harder and harder monsters. Thankfully, this gives the game a natural flow. Every time you rank up, the super-hard boss monsters that used to always kill you before you could get any matches in become commonplace grunts.
Overall, 10,000,000 is a fun game, and it is definitely worth 5 bucks for the hours of gameplay you will undoubtedly get from it. While many players like me will ragequit often, you’ll always be coming back for more. I hope we can see a more polished and less frustrating sequel sometime in the future.

This game, there's too much good to say about this game! Crypt of the Necrodancer is one of the best rhythm dungeon crawler I've ever played (And the only one :P).
But that aside. Crypt of the Necrodancer is a must get for any rhythm game lover! The way the game functions is absolutely perfect! Not to mention the soundtrack that comes with the game on default, the soundtrack had me hooked the instant I heard it. Combine it with moving to the music to move around. And if you don't like the music the game provides, you can put your own mp3 files in it's place which makes for even awesomer gameplay! Each enemy moves with their own patterns and memorizing each and every one is quite the trip. From mere movement pattern, mirroring patterns, heck even the boss patterns are fun to memorize.
This game while not focused on the graphics, is what makes it so enjoyable. The game focuses on the gameplay and not the graphics for once. I set my alarm to make me get up and by the game on release date before school started and every cent was worth it ^.^

I haven't played this for quite some time (A few years maybe?), there have been a number of updates I've not seen. So instead, I'll point to the overall mechanics of the game.
Assymetrical gameplay is a very brave thing to attempt in a game, even some games that attempted it (e.g Planetside) later flattened the playing field substantially. Playing as an alien in NS2 is fun, traversing vent systems, clinging to ceilings and pouncing on marines is pretty immersive. It's quite interesting to see gameplay from the perspective of 'the alien menace,' when so many other games are about marines etc. hunting down aliens.
Marines... I didn't enjoy them so much for personal reasons. If you wandered too far from your teammates you could be cut down very quickly by an even vaguely coordinated pack of skulks. Also quite immersive in that regard. This isn't really a balance issue, it's more about the ability to cooperate.
Some of the issues I've read about in other reviews, such as uncooperative teammates, is unfortunately a common gripe with multiplayer. Unless you play together with a group of friends and use TS, someone is always going to ignore the commander and do what they like.
When I played at the time the 'Rookie System' didn't seem to do very much. You could join a server that was 'rookie friendly' and still find players much more experienced than you playing there. At the same time,  no one wanted the responsibility of commanding, but were very good at back-seat commanding if you made a mistake.
At the time, there was no tutorial. I imagine that's changed, or at least I would hope. There was a 'tutorial' where you could run around a map and had little hud markers explaining what cysts were, power cells and other upgrade structures, but it didn't really explain HOW to play the game. As a result, I feel a lot of people probably didn't pick up competency very quickly and became disenchanted with it.
Lastly, there are a number of negative reviews which mention a toxic community. I haven't really had much experience of this myself, but this is going back years now. You should definitely heed those warnings, they seem fairly consistent. Many also reiterate that the game is dead.
To summarise; the gameplay is enjoyable, immersive and an interesting step in game design that hopefully will be used as a reference for how to create assymetrical gameplay enjoyable, in the future. However, the community is apparently a small group full of toxicity, so put on your thick skin.
I can only recommend this game to people who could convince maybe 20 people to play it with them occasionally. Otherwise, you will probably be disappointed.

Infinitas DM is a great tool for local play sesisons. It's great for me for a couple of reasons: Firstly, I'm insanely unorganized and this is an awesome tool to keep everything in one place. I have all of my world names, cities, NPC names, flavor text etc all in one place to reference. I cannot express enough how much that will help me moving forward.
Second, it is SO nice having detailed maps with multiple layers to edit. I've been able to make some of my own using the in app tools, and even that has been useful for making a couple of quick areas I needed in my campaign. I've never had a good way of doing fog of war live before (seriously, this is one of the best reasons to get the app). If I have a dark dungeon I only want to reveal partly at a time, I can screenshare the partially revealed dungeon on my TV and monitor the entire dungeon from the DM view only on my device. I can't wait to see how this goes with my players live, since this isn't something I've ever really been able to do before. You can import maps you've already made elsewhere, and add fog of war features from here too, so it's nice being able to use pre-existing maps frequently.
Third, and this one is minor compared to the previous points I mentioned, but I love the tokens you can place. The NPC tokens are pretty straight forward, just your basic coins, but there are added little pictures you can drop into your maps that are really neat (treasure chests, skull and crossbones, potions, etc). I think these add a neat touch to my maps that I think my players will enjoy. It adds a cool incentive to exploring and gives a good visual of the rewards you can get. Again, this is a pretty minor thing, but I just though it was a nice touch.
Side notes:
The eraser tool is tough to use on mobile, but seems to work better on the steam version. I'd recomment doing the majority of your creating in the steam client, but I know this is something the developer has addressed already so it's not a huge deal.
Another note, THIS IS NOT ROLL20. This app isn't really designed for online play. This is something you'd use for a local session to broadcast live to your players. It's great for creating a campaign, broadcasting your campaign, but you'll be doing yourself a diservice if you're just looking for a cheaper alternative to Roll20. I would highly recommend this app to people who have a lot of local, in person sessions, not so much to those who exclusivly host online sessions.
TLDR; this app is simple, effective, and great for managing and running a campaign. It doesn't take long to learn, and the instruction manual addresses anything I didn't find to be intuitive. I highly reccommend to any DM who frequently hosts local sessions with their crew.

One of the most fun and interesting multiplayer shooters. Oh, and its VERY arcade!
The game has two competing sides that play vastly differently, which is something rarely seen in multiplayer games, especially shooters. Playing as aliens is nothing like playing marines. Moreover, commanding makes the game actually a Real Time Strategy with other players as your units! However,  each side is limited to one commander, so if you enjoy NS2 as RTS, then you might have a hard time playing it this way when there are other players who want to be a commander too.
Nonetheless, there's a lot to enjoy in this game when played as FPP too. Not only because every unit (as aliens) and every different weapon (as humans) changes the style of the gameplay, but also because the game is quite intense and atmospheric (this is probably the best looking game I have ever seen too!). I highly recommend checking this game to everyone who like multiplayer action games, especially the arcade ones.
The only drawbacks I can think of are infuriating loading times. I have never seen a game that would load maps even one third of a time as a NS2 maps load. This is quite annoying.

There's potential here, but in the current state it's missing a lot of features I would expect from a map editor. It needs a LOT of work before it's worth any money. There are no shaping tools, just free draw and line draw. There are a lot of buttons that I think are supposed to be for adding symbols or tokens to the maps that appear to just not work. Really common keyboard shortcuts are missing (no undo, copy, or paste that I can find). If you have a tool selected you cannot change your zoom level or move the maps around, and I see no real reason for that. It also has no way of connecting people to your game online that I could find, so I'm not entirely sure how you're supposed to share these maps to play with. It seems inconsistent for saving changes; it looks like it's supposed to work with auto save but in the few minutes I spent with this it failed to save work I'd done for a location, and I don't know why.
For maps you're better off just getting a basic grid image and editing it in MS Paint. For managing a campaign as a whole, you're just as well to use a basic text editor.
[edit] Folks in the comments for this review have provided some explanations for what's lacking here. They don't change my assessment of the software at all, but it might change yours.

Templar Battleforce is a top-down turn based tactical battle game in the form of classics such as the original XCOM with a dash of Warhammer 40k flavour thrown in for good measure.
The game is well balanced in my experience. Enemies generally spawn and behave reasonably, encouraging the player to keep up the pace without being overwhelming- at least on the difficulty I have played so far). Enemies and Templars alike have a wide range of interesting talents to select from, none of which have struck me as redundant so far. The tech tree is expansive and detailed, with missions providing enough unlock points to facilitate experimentation while you find the layout that works best for you. The Templars also feature a system akin to genetic memory that allows for full respec between missions. While flavourful, this also allows you to experiment with a variety of builds without having to worry about making your units suboptimal in the later game or having to maintain more copies of each class than you need.
The developers clearly love their creation and have demonstrated a level of interactivity, responsiveness and support that I find very impressive.
If you like the genre, I absolutely recommend this game.

Templar Battleforce Review, 2015-11-02
Templar Battleforce is a squad-based tactics game made by the Trese Brothers, and boy howdy, it scratches a real tactical itch for me. Gameplay wise, it's crisp, smooth, and responsive, although the game seems built for a tablet screen (much like The Banner Saga). The squad building aspect is quite appealing, with several different classes, each with their own unique skills and equipment restrictions.
Missions are a mixed bag, ranging from "Take and Hold" types to "Race Against the Clock", and everything in between. Difficulty is fairly equal, with a few missions harder than others. Perma-death of your squaddies isn't an issue unless you're playing on Demanding difficulty or higher, which I heartily recommend for the adrenaline rush.
All in all, after buying several games recently and having my expectations dashed and my wallet drained, Templar Battleforce leaves me satisfied and wanting more. Consistent updates after launch make this a gem to buy and play, plus it supports indie development.
***EDIT: February 26th, 2016***
Oh man. I wish you could give this game multiple recommendations, and here's why.
After several months since I bought this game, the devs have done consistent tweaks and updates since then. And after some digging, I've discovered that the Trese Brothers have done this with not only Templar Battleforce, but also with their other titles! Middle-school-age me, a big Tenchu fanboy, would've been really happy playing this. By less nostalgic standards, the game is okay! It lacks the polish to be great, but it's definitely worth playing if you're hurting for a good stealth game. You play as a shadow-themed ghost ninja called Aragami and sneak around fantasy Japan in the aftermath of an Avatar-like war between elemental clans. The game's gimmick is that as a shadow elemental, darkness affects your mobility as well as visibility. Safe movement is mostly handled by shadow teleportation, a short-ranged teleport between darkened areas.
It's more a stealth game than an action game. Guards are dangerous, but it's mostly mitigated by the minimal backtracking and ample shadows for quick exits. All guards have unblockable one-hit kills, ranged attacks, and you are never completely invisible. That's a dealbreaker for some, according to other reviews. They're easy to kill but it's risky, too. There are enough of them it's often faster and safer to bypass whichever ones you can.
As a stealth game, level design is king. Mostly it works! An early example: the cemetery map. Lots of cover, irregular shadows, with the low visibility working both ways. The map has a lot of variety. It's fun to stalk between shrine shadows, close enough for a guard to see, and teleporting past him just as he faces you. Sometimes the game gets hard, especially when navigating around guards in narrow spaces. When the level design involves that while also being highly visible, which happens at least twice, it doesn't work as well.
The game has flaws. The boss fights in particular are bad. The first one has an Arkham City Mr. Freeze gimmick that's not telegraphed (it looks like a recent patch changed that, thankfully.) The second is an aimbotting archer. The third is less bad but they move erratically enough to feel random. There's also a trap mid-way through the game that involves a few blind jumps which can kill you. A bad-in-a-fun-way thing is that the geometry can be exploited sometimes. I managed a pair of really lame sequence breaks first time through, and got out of bounds a few times too (I wasn't able to repeat one of them recently, it might've been patched.)
There's a letter score ranking and three award "medals" at the end of a level. The scoring system is superfluous, but the medals encourage specific playstyles. The medals are "yurei" (not triggering alerts,) "kami" (not killing anyone,) and "oni" (killing everyone.) First time through I played for "yurei" and "kami." Having upgrades, in late game and on replay, changes things dramatically! It is much faster, easier, and more "oni." Playing lethally feeds into a feedback loop of enabling safe exploration, finding more upgrades, and being more lethal. It's a weird choice considering early game disincentivizes unnecessary killing. I'm guessing an early version of the game awarded upgrades based on story progress instead.
The game's story is finding macguffins to save a princess. There's obvious plot stuff toward the end. I suspect it was made obvious to add dramatic irony to a fairly thin story. Dialogue is handled by gibberish over text boxes, but different characters have different VA's, and proper nouns are audible in the gibberish (a great little detail.)

I really wanted to be able to give this one a positive review. Even with the rose-tinted glasses of having played and immensely enjoyed the original EDF. The first had its good and bad points, but it was the good points that salvaged the game's bad ones. Yes, repetative gameplay is pretty much the staple of this series, but it never got too boring because of the campy, B-horror tone, the hilarious enemy physics (dead ants bouncing gloriously into the heavens) and the scale and variety of the creatures.
Unfortunately, IA seems to have decided to do away with all that. Gone is the humor. Replaced with a more serious (but still somehow silly) gritty approach. Gone are the physics and the scale. Gone is the variety (well, you get some variety...if you like Spider Type A, B, C. Mix that up with Bee Type A, B, C, etc.). It's nice to have larger maps to explore, but they're hardly inventive or varied enough.  Overall, it was a pretty dissapointing experience.

Pro:
-Unique gameplay, offering synergy between RTS/FPS unlike very few games.
-Can be very fun if you have balanced teams, and/or cooperative team-mates.
-Establishes very different playstyles between the two factions; Kharaa (Aliens) and Marines.
-Rewards in-game potency with actual long-term results.
-Lifeform specialisation can be very rewarding if you play effectively (I played Fade/Jetpacker myself)
Con:
-Horribly designed skill system; mathematically sound however doesn't represent skill, just elo.
-Very linear gameplay after you play 100+ games. (Onos stomp or Exo/ARC rushing or just concedes)
-Community is often highly toxic and elitist, alienating rookies on larger servers.
-Playerbase is definitely dead, literally nobody plays the game at peak times.
-Mods for this game do not balance the game effectively, matching it based on elo averages, not actual skill.
-Worst hit registration I have seen in a long time, with larger servers making it unbearable due to horrible ping.
-Only specialist weaponry appears to live up to an auditory experience, with base assault rifles feeling like they shoot potatoes.
TL;DR: Good for a short time, more frustrating than fun after 50+ hours.

Summary for those who don't like to read:
Pros
-Solid mechanics
-RPG tactical
-The RP system
Cons
-No distinquishing features or mechanics from other members of the genre
+The game seems to over rely on its own version of 'genetic memory'
-Terrible story telling that can't seem to keep track of what character's should know
-Unforgivable showing vs telling in a game with "Genetic memory"
-Bland unrelatable characters
I'd rank this game really as a 2 out of 5, barely. Mechanically everything works, but I don't find anything compelling in this game to, say, the game's from the UFO series, or even XCOM EU (and I hate that game). Or almost any other RPG tactical. Combat is pretty tame. You've got different points that award increased attack and defense to whoever holds them. A supply system that rewards you for holding tactical points with more characters on the field. Additionally, classes, talents, skills, etc which can be used to differentiate the different characters. There's also an RP upgrade system where you use points to unlock equipment, skills, etc. Also, the AI seems fairly straightforward so far, no twists, but it was early in the game (I doubt I'll have anything more to say on that). Together, it is solid, but if you search through most tactical games, you'll find most have a good chunk of the above in one form or another. However the dev's are still working on the game and we could see mechanical improvements. And besides that I hear what you're saying, "But dark, that's no reason to rate the game 2 out of 5, it should be at least a 3 out of 5 for these reasons!"
Well, my astute audience, my main issue is with the story. Some other reviewers are going, "OMG, the story is brilliant! Buy the game!" Obviously I disagree. For starters, I find the very idea of "Genetic memory" to be laughable. Might as well go, "Magic" (I'm doing jazz hands, fyi). But I gave the game a chance and set aside how silly that concept is. No, despite that, my main issue is that the dev's seem to be wishy washy about this "Genetic memory" and memory of the ancestors thing. In one scene, for instance, our main character 'knows' that a big baddy will come through a gate and so tells everyone in the party that it will occur. My immediate response was, "Wait, what?" At one point or another every person in your party would've had an ancestor that probably witnessed this sort of event so why the devil is our protagonist saying that? Are they just that kind of annoying a**hat? Wouldn't it make more sense to just do ancestoral flashbacks that way we get the info and it can be cool at the same time (show vs tell, devs)? Ugh, anywho, when the big bad does pop out what it is has to be explained to the protagonist via helper helpington (or reddish shield guy if you prefer). This isn't to mention how annoying it is when we're told a whole bunch of history to things that our character was indirectly a witness to.
And I can hear the buzz of the annoying uncritical fanboys, "But we get to make chhhooooiiiccccessss!" Okay, okay, sure, but the game has essentially murdered my interest in it at this point with these crimes against story telling and no amount of 'choice' makes up for that. Especially since this isn't the first game to do "You've got choices now!" Bland emotionless characters aren't helping either (at least at this point). Of course, the ultimate sin is that we're 'told' about this lineage. I don't see why we couldn't have an overarching family/lineage tree in the UI somewhere to give us all of the backstory. Even give all of those non-descript recruits a place in that tree. Seems like a better idea than what is currently in game. I imagine there should even be a few family feuds in there. This "Genetic memory" thing could be intriquing if done right, as it is, its a snore fest with no mechanical traction to get us anywhere to the more interesting points.
Anywho, I'm certain a solid chunk of peeps are all going, "Pft, I don't care about any of that," or "You're totally missing the point, X and Y and Z happens!" To the first, okay, but there are people that do. To the second, I don't really care. At this point the game has failed from a story telling perspective and in major unforgivable ways. I came in wanting to see what would transpire and now I no longer do. The writing up to this point is crap and the mechanics weren't enough to tide me over until X or Y or Z. So, for those like me, where story can make or break a game, this game, as it is now, is not worth buying.

TEMPLAR BATTLEFORCE has a very strong tactical table top character. From the color rich style of the units and the board style maps to the Warhammer 40k heroic writing style it all gives off a very flamboyant grim science fiction feel with undertones of Fasa's Battletech universe. It has a very detailed leveling and character design system with tons of skills to unlock not to mention all sorts of futuristic upgrades to the multiple weapons systems such as scanners, heat disipating improvements, energy and physical shields, heavy weapons and melee weapon upgrades, enemy detection and stealth avoidence addons etc etc.
The enemies are pretty much Tyranids in behaviour and looks which is done perfectly creating a xeno terror out of your worst H.R. Giger nightmares. Things really get tense when they start to increase and swarm in numbers. They definitely test my strategic skill as i figure out if its best to fight, flee or repair my suit among many other choices. There are plenty of buffs like shields to decrease damage, a commander inspiring skill to motivate units in combat, terrain which increases defense and attack bonuses, overwatch mode, etc etc.
Incredibly well done game which for turn based feels very fast paced and hectic. The music is also quite atmospheric capturing a mix of gloom and heroic persistence to fight on against impossible odds to shatter the darkness and bring forth a piercing beam of light transmitting hope into the mentally crushed and spiritually hopeless.
TEMPLAR BATTLEFORCE a tour de force of epic warfare in a brutal universe of unrelenting all consuming terror. If you value your gaming happiness you will purchase this sacred work with its devastating armaments of annihilation and praise the ancestors for the battle bliss to come!

Aragami is a positive addition to the stealth genre.  It features intelligent level design that requires careful attention to level geometry, light sources, and shadows.  The selection of enemies is quite limited, but the way they are distributed throughout each area makes for a fascinating experience despite the fact there are only two enemies in the game outside of the boss battles, which are all very stealth oriented and sometimes frustrating.
I would really like to commend the development team for the excellent 3d in-game cutscenes, music, and overall look and feel of this game.  It feels like a movie at times, and has an interesting story that is revealed in bits and pieces as things progress.  It reminds me a bit of Okami or Shadow of the Colossus in its presentation.
The various stealth powers and special moves are creative and useful.  Co-op play was wonderful, my wife and I played the entire game together without any problems and had a great time doing it.  Having the option to have one player distract guards by intentionally making noise, using special powers, or being almost spotted while the other player sneaks up on enemies to perform stealth kills is great.
Overall length of the game is about 10-15 hours depending on how fast you go.  For 20 dollars this is a perfect stealth title to pick up which fans of Tenchu, Splinter Cell, or Metal Gear would most likely enjoy.

Fallout Shelter is a base-building survival game set in the, you guessed it, Fallout universe. You are the overseer of a vault, and need to perform various tasks to build up and grow your vault.
Pros:
-Simple and easy to get into and play, making it the perfect time-waster. Most objectives or completing of tasks or quests take time (anything from a few minutes to a couple of days), making it an idler of sorts as well.
-Set in the Fallout unverse, with some references towards other Fallout games being made as well
-Mechanics are simple, build a vault and ensure that there is enough power for the vault, and food and water for your dwellers. There is also quests which your dwellers can go on to find weapons, outfits or junk to craft the latter.
-There is steam achievements, but they take quite some time to get, as you need to grind to get them.
Cons:
-Microtransactions is the only thing which irritates me in this game, especially for the Nuka Quantum Cola, which is basically a speed boost item within the game. The game kind of tries to force you to use it if you want to skip objectives or get something done immediately.
Overall, this is a great time-waster worth a look if you enjoy the Fallout series and are looking for something to play.

Aragami is a stealth game set in Japan, you play as a spirit of vengeance known as Aragami and you play the game with a companion called Yamiko who is imprisoned by 6 artifacts. You stealthfuly traverse levels with abilities that only work in shadows and can only regain mana in these shaded areas. The game has 3 tokens for every level to add a challenge if the player wants to do so. You can either kill all enemies, or no enemies, and you also can not be seen. Of course this encourages more then one playthrough since you obviously can't kill everyone and also be a pacifist. There are also hidden scrolls across the maps that you can collect to upgrade abilities. A ability I recommend early on is to upgrade to the ability that allows you to see all collectibles on the map since this will be usefull later on. If you want to easily complete the game I recommend doing a pacifist run first while getting as many collectibles and abilites as you can while also staying hidden, then plowing through the second playthrough with majority of abilites and killing everyone.
As I don't want to ruin the story since it is crafted very well, I'll try to say what I feel is necessary. In the game Aragami has no memory of who or what he was, all you get is some flashbacks at the begining with nothing to go on. The more artifacts and scenarios you go through, the more flashbacks are shown to you. The ultimate goal is to gather all artifacts and bring them to where Yamiko is imprisoned to set her free. Now for a quick run down of Pros and cons to end this little review.
PROS
-The soundtrack suits the mood for all scenarios you go through
-The ending is a big suprise if you get engaged
-Full of content and replayability for the price
-New comers to stealth will have a blast and love either stealthfully taking out gaurds, or going for challenges
-The game has gorgeous visuals, reminds me of LOZ: WInd Waker HD
- Great level design
- Great story
CONS
-The cape you wear shows you your mana, it frequently clipped into Aragami and made it hard to see the full bar.
- Easy for beginners, but anybody who plays tons of stealth games can get through this game at least in a day or two if you only want story, 2 if you want to complete the game 100%
-There is a bug that when you teleport and restart the chekpoint, the level resets but you go to the area you targeted, I found this by accident during the final boss. (Hopefully will be fixed)
- Only two types of enemies (Archers and Swordsmen)
- Swordsmen are easily fooled and don't posses a threat unless you stand still, and Archers aren't a problem what so ever.
Overall Aragami is a great game for it's price, and to me, doesn't have any serious flaws that breaks immersion or ruins gameplay. Overall I give Aragami
8/10

The game has several game modes:
It starts with two low buy-in tables, a 250 chip buy in table and a 1-5k buy in table, both have 5 seats at the table, which means small tables, you get to win more often!  The 250 table isn't available after you "level" to 13, which will happen eventually just playing the game... winning, losing, getting trophies, everything gets you experience.
After those low buy in tables, you'll see your first "cashgame" saloon.  Cashgames have 8 seats, and turbo cashgames move a little faster because each player has less time to decide to bet/call/fold.
Then you'll see you first "Sit and Go" table.  Sit and Go games have 5 seats, like the starter saloons, but there is a set fee to play.  The first Sit and Go game costs 10K to join, but when you sit at the table, you have 3k in chips.  You're then locked in that game, which has increasing blinds, meaning the game can't go on forever.  Eventually players lose all their chips, and the last two players standing win a prize.  Second place is the entry fee returned, and first place is 3.5 times the entry fee (35K at the first Sit and Go arena)
Next is the first "Big Win" tournament.  Big Win games go on for 24 hours, or at least once I saw a 12 hour game, with 8 seats at the table.  The first Big Win has a 10K + 1K buy in, meaning you pay 11K, but get 10K in chips for the tournament.  Then you play as far as your chips will take you.  At the end of the time, your ranking in the tournament will determine if you win a prize or not.  10K chips won't win anything, so you have to improve from your start to have a chance of leaving the tournament with anything, because the chips in the tournament are only for score; you don't get to keep them after the game, but you'll get chips if you win a prize.
"Push or Fold" is the next game type you'll see.  Push and Fold is like a very fast cash game, with 5 seats at the table.  The first has a buy in of 10K + 1K again, pay 11K chips to get 10K in game, but you can leave the game and take your chips with you in this one, unlike the Tournament. Push or Fold features very high blinds, so it is difficult to sit back and fold on your first two cards if you don't like them, because you'll go broke fast that way.
Then further down the line, there is a "Royal Poker" saloon, which is a 5 seat table, where the deck has only 10 through ace cards... maybe a good place to try and get the rare Royal Flush achievement? I haven't played this game yet, as it has a big 150K buy in!
And finally, if you click the little map to zoom out, you'll see a place to play blackjack.  No other players, just you and the dealer.  I played a little to get a couple of the blackjack trophies, but it was pretty dull for me.
Speaking of Trophies! Virtually anything you do in the game will earn you credit towards trophies.  For instance, your first win with a straight will get you a trophy! trophies earn you extra experience, as well as gold coins.
Gold coins?  Well, those are used to buy hats! yep! lots of cool hats to be found... the special VIP hats have animations and sometimes sounds, and are pretty cool, except the disco hat scares the crap out of me every time the guy wearing it wins cause it makes a lot of noise :D  You can also buy pins, roses, or other decorations for your hats, and you can buy different colored shirts.  If you play a girl character, the shirt color is also your glove color, so I got some pretty purple gloves, and a few cheap hats...forgot to mention those Big Win tourneys want you to wear different hats... there's usually a cheap hat you can buy and not spend a lot of gold.
Experience? Yes, you gain levels in this game.  Looking at someone's level is a good way to get a general idea of how much they've played the game so far.  Everything you do earns stars.  1 star for losing a hand, more for winning.  Stars for trophies too.  I think you actually get a few chips for leveling up too.
Want to spend some real money?  You don't have to, but if you run out of chips and don't want to wait for more free ones, you can buy chips, and there are always deals for cheaper chips too.  You can also buy gold, which is great if you want to support the game AND get one of those cool VIP hats I'm so envious of... considering how much I've played already, I'll probably buy some gold at some point and buy a neat hat.  Gold never seems to go on sale though, which is disappointing
Social system:  The game doesn't have a direct chat system, so you can't talk to other players using your own words, however, there are emotes and short quotes you can say as you wish, stuff like "nice bluff" and "well played" or if you're more trolly "scared?" or maybe just post a face sticking your tongue out at them... I like this system personally, as I don't care for angry trolls, or people talking about what cards they have, or stuff like that, but if you're looking to make lifelong friends, it is pretty hard to do just posting giggle faces at each other :D
A last note on free chips: you can get them both by waiting on the 4 hour timer, and by making friends, and getting gifts from them.  Friends can only give you 100 chips at a time, once a day, and you're limited in how many total gifts you can give out a day too, but it is something in addition to the 4 hour timer if you're really broke and desperate for your poker fix.
Some complaints I have about the game:
1. Gold never on sale! Come on Devs! chips are always, always on sale...why not gold??
2. EDIT: this bot issue I discussed was fixed, so you'll no longer see the bots.  For a while the bots which were only supposed to appear to new players in the 1-5K poker shack, first two hands, instead stuck around while other players joined the table, which caused more experienced players to see the bots too.  These bots now all leave the table after feeding the new player some chips in the first two hands, before experienced real people are allowed to join that table.  I am still mildly disappointed that the new player gets tricked into playing against unlabled bots, but it is only for two hands, and the hands are supposed to help feed the new player some chips so...
3. I...uh...forgot... if I remember I'll come back here and edit again :D
What I like about the game:
1. Free Poker!
2. Fun Poker!
3. Winning! at Poker!
I hope this long review helps people decide to try out this fun and exciting game.

I love this game. Have thoroughly enjoyed playing 23+ hours so far and I think I'm about halfway through. Bottom line, if you're into squad based combat games, and don't need fancy graphics, this game is for you. It's kind of like XCOM but without the stragteic base management, instead the strategic management is more about spending your xp wisely, equipping your troops correctly, and unlocking the parts of the trees that your soldiers need to upgrade gear/abilities.
I hope these guys come out with an expansion, or another game. They have got everything right from the actual gameplay perspective, all they need is a little more polish on the graphics (better and more varied animations, a bit better UI) and sounds, but those are just a matter of getting better assets, not a fundablement problem with the game.
Good
* Writing is crisp and impactful without delivering walls of text. You also don't have to read pages of exposition up front, the game drops you in the middle of the action and the story without the need to explain everything up front. If you don't mind learning-as-you-go (I really enjoy it) then it's a great experience.
* Excellent balance of difficulty, fun, and excitement. I've felt challenged on most levels (occasionally I breeze through one), and even lost a few levels.
* The equipment and leveling up systems are great. You unlock gear through a requistion process, but you don't buy individual pieces, instead you can then assign it to any soldier. When you level up you get to assign 2 different and independent stats while leveling a talent which are the abilities you can use in game.
* The soldiers classes feel /very/ different from each other and there are about 10 of them. Even small loadout changes can really flavor how they behave and operate on the battlefield. You also have a lot of choices on how you want to mix/match meele/ranged.
* The game doesn't reward you for "farming" during the mission at all. Get in, get the job done as quickly as possible, and keep your soldiers alive. You get extra xp and requsition points for doing the right thing (not for sitting at a spawn and camping).
* The in-mission replenishment system is great. You defend control points and those give you supply points which you can use to purchase stuff like medpacks. These control points aren't in every map, and generally if there are any you have to bring an Engineer.
* The mission flavors are great. I always feel like I'm doing something new. They do a great job of mixing up "defense, escort, push, speed, explore" kind of maps. I have actually picked out different flavors of teams based on that. The size of your team also changes, and there are occasionally NPCs that come with you (which can be a fun way to play with a class you haven't unlocked through the requisition system already).
* The mechanics of the game are great, and there's a lot of stuff in the character page that helps explain stuff. I would comment that it's kind of hard to get a feel for if you're pumping a stat too hard. IT would be nice to see the dice rolls and calculations which drive the game so that you could get a better idea if you've put way too many points into accuracy.
Bad
* The sound effects are pretty terrible. The music is OKay, but the gunshots and alien damage noises are really repetitive and often times I have a hard time telling what they are suppose to be.
* There is no "walk range" indicator that shows you what tiles you can move to. This also becomes a problem when you're starting out on a new tileset because it can be hard to tell which tiles you can move onto. You basically just have to experiment.
* Graphics are barebones and animations are a little stiff as well as having exactly one animation for each action. No idle animations either. It's servicable, but not great.

Overall a solid game and good value for the money at the initial release but needs fine tuning. Thankfully did not enounter any bugs on my first play through (demanding difficulty). Balance could use some improvement. None of the maps felt particularly challenging, so much as occasionally tedious. Some levels are near impossible to complete in the target number of turns (if you approach them with no prior knowledge) and can spiral into runaway heat as you search for the right order to activate switches. Once know the correct path to take for routing power / unlocking doors, they are easy. These sequence should really be randomized and the maps balanced accordingly. Other than that, most maps can generally be rushed in half the number of target turns or less. MP is the single most important attribute. Buffed scouts with 12+ MP will wreck many maps. Beat the end boss in 7 turns on first try (target 30)... felt like the easiest map in the game. RNG can be silly with the map initialization. After 30 missions I will rate this game
Overall: 9/10
Pros:
Very fun, best turn based strategy I have played since tactics. For $10 you can't go wrong here if you are a fan of the genre
Huge skill trees and tons of loadout options. <3 customize
Free respecs for your toons whenever you want!
Not a terrible story so far.
Insane value
I can tell the replay value will be huge based on the req page and many difficulty settings.
Cons:
Hard to predict dmg. Sometimes you get hit but armor soaks 100%, sometimes you get 100 to zero'd by that same single mob in a single turn.  Simply put the damage calculations are wildly random because of too many factors. Armor, deflection, dodge, block, parry, evasion compete against damage crit accuracy and penetration. There may even be more I can't remeber.
Some things are either buggy or just not clear. Overwatch skill will sometimes hit a target each step he takes in the box. Sometimes tho it won't hit him even once regardless of LOS. Sometimes stats do not update on your character sheet until you get into battle, forcing you to add up all your bonus's to have an idea of what your crit or block is, and even that is off from time to time.
Some of the load out relics need cost adjusted. It is very hard to equip most relics without huge sacrifices at every other equipment slot and they are far from game breaking. Honestly most of them are noob traps as is.
The cons I listed are have very little impact at med-hard difficulty, and none at less than medium. For insane difficulty tho it can be frustrating.
All in all though if this is your favorite genre and you have ten dollars to spend you would be a fool to pass this up. I can't wait to see what these guys do in the future.

Fallout Shelter is a base-building survival game set in the, you guessed it, Fallout universe. You are the overseer of a vault, and need to perform various tasks to build up and grow your vault.
Pros:
-Simple and easy to get into and play, making it the perfect time-waster. Most objectives or completing of tasks or quests take time (anything from a few minutes to a couple of days), making it an idler of sorts as well.
-Set in the Fallout unverse, with some references towards other Fallout games being made as well
-Mechanics are simple, build a vault and ensure that there is enough power for the vault, and food and water for your dwellers. There is also quests which your dwellers can go on to find weapons, outfits or junk to craft the latter.
-There is steam achievements, but they take quite some time to get, as you need to grind to get them.
Cons:
-Microtransactions is the only thing which irritates me in this game, especially for the Nuka Quantum Cola, which is basically a speed boost item within the game. The game kind of tries to force you to use it if you want to skip objectives or get something done immediately.
Overall, this is a great time-waster worth a look if you enjoy the Fallout series and are looking for something to play.

sorry guys.  i really wanted to like this game.  i mean i REALLY REALLY wanted to like this game.  i have been an EDF fan since GDF days.  i thought, how hard could it really be to make an EDF game?  even i know the formula, these developers surely couldn't have messed it up.
how to make EDF game
1. fill stupidly large area with large amounts of generic destructible objects, i.e. rocks, buildings, etc.
2. put bugs or robots or aliens or something on the map - lots of them, like wayyyy too many
3. make tons of weapons of radically varying levels of actual usefulness and cram them in
4. create mission scenarios that are all as vague as humanly possible cuz they are all the exact same: kill everything
5. crank all engine physics up into the red, then do it again 2x for good measure
just like that, i've made a good EDF game.  so what went wrong here?
EDF is not an action 3rd person shooter series.  it is sooo slow, missions are mind-numbingly long, it's repetitive beyond all reason and you never really feel like you've made any progress in the games because nothing has changed.  you're doing the exact same thing you were 2 missions ago.  literally - nothing has changed.  it has a heavy hypnotic, zen-like quality to it - clearing a massive map is simple but tedious, and there is a special kind of old school arcade pleasure in glancing at your minimap occassionally to see the field of red dots slowly thin.
in insect armageddon, they have forgone that slower pace, and put in it's place a weird checkpoint system where enemies come in individual waves.  they made a decision to have the bodies "vaporize" instead of just explode into the distance - a damn shame considering the gonzo physics has always been a huge draw for these games.  the cheeky humor is intact, although they went for more starship troopers than godzilla.  the guns definitely blow stuff up.  but it just doesn't hit the spot, not for a long-time EDF fan anyways.
if you're looking to scratch that meditative, map-clearing arcade itch, i highly recommend just picking up Lost Planet: Extreme Condition instead if you don't own it already.  it's not the same as an EDF game and hopefully one day we'll get a real one here but for now it'll have to do.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Not sure why everyone raved about this game. If you're used to, say, BigFish point-and-clicks, yeah this will feel "deep." But while the overall ideas of the story are interesting, the actual dialogue and narration are awful, with the salient story points being told to the player rather than shown (which should be the entire point of a video game, SHOWING rather than telling). This makes the storyline feel wandering and convoluted.
Essentially it feels like there was one person or team in charge of the story, and they would say, "okay now we need some gameplay here" and another person/team would make a level based on acquiring whatever is needed to progress the story. The story itself is trying to be far grander and deeper than the game earns the right to pretend to be.
The biggest sin of Satinav, however, is not only that it often falls into the trap of "use item on other item and hotspots until something progresses because how the hell was the player supposed to figure that out," but worse, that the achievements are TERRIBLE. It is near impossible to get 100% on this game without a walkthrough due to the utter stupidity of some of the hidden achievements. And, crime of crimes, there are two SEPERATE achievements for completing the game on each of the two difficulties. No, you don't automatically get the badge for finishing it on easy if you finish it on hard. So even though it's possible to get all the other achievements in a single play by saving and reloading certain branch points, it's necessary to play the entire game through twice.
Yes, Satinav is pretty and the characters are slightly less one-dimensional than the usual point-and-click fare, but if you want a game that's going to move you or enthrall you, look somewhere else.

I really like this game and I just finished the campaign a moment ago (for the Blood Ravens). Dawn of War Dark Crusade is an expansion to Relic's real time strategy game Dawn of War, which is set in the Warhammer 40, 000 universe of table top wargames. I highly recommend it to any real time stategy fan who loves the grittines and toughness of battles which are primarily set in a distopian future where every alien you meet wants to kill you and eat you for jujubes :D, and that's not all; Your government, which is the Grand Imperium of Man, constantly drafts new recruits in the billions in order to sacrifice to The Emeperor, who uses His powerful psychic mind in order to stave the forces of Super Hell (or Chaos for short) which constantly gobbles up any known dangerous substances in order to get high for the dark gods. The 7 major races are The Blood Ravens; The Emperor's own space marines who came to the planet Kronus to search for the secrets of their lost history. The Ork's or should I say 'Da Orks', only come for the tendency of following their Ork Chieftains for the sake of the Waaaagh!!!! in order to satuate their cravings for constant battle. The Eldar, a mysterious alien race which are a splinters of their former empire 10, 000 years prior to the 41st millenium, have come to Kronus in order to stop their ancient enemies, known as the Necrons, from rising from their tomb worlds and purging the galaxy clean of all sentient life. The Necrons were metallic warriors who slumbered eons ago iduring the aftermath, which in Eldar legend was in the aftermath of the so called 'War in Heaven'. Then there are the imperial guard, chaos and the tau (my favourite), and for that YOU can explore for yourself. For the 4 races I've mentioned there is a ton of lore to explore and unfortunately I cannot tell you all of it. If you think Halo, Startrek  and Starwars had tons of lore, you have never read the Lore of 40k, it is just a massive game world that you need to delve into. As for this game I give a solid 9/10. Please relic in the name of the emperor, where is Dawn of War 3?

Out for a big price (20€, probably more on dollars?), this point and click adventure actually has its good points.
I played it in English although it has subtitles and such in Italian but as always, translations are not that great.
Set in the realm of Andergast, you follow the adventures of the main character Geron who's like an outcast in his society, and gets cursed and so.. starts his journey.
The gameplay is quite simple, since we have a 2D point n' click adventure with lots of dialogues with NPCs, things to collect and combine in your inventory and nice backgrounds in which your adventures will take place.
More specifically, the two main characters have both a unique ability; Geron can destroy items while Nuri, who's a fairy, can restore them.. so, as in every other good point and click adventure, your action in the inventory is fundamental - you'll have to deal with items, combine or use them in the right way and so on.
The English voices actors are quite enjoyable and the backgrounds and the whole graphics are good - there could have been put way much work, both in the artwork and in the character design but anyways it's still nice as it is.
So, if you love these kinds of adventures and maybe you're not a newcomer well this one could bring you memories from past games.. it has often a retro style, and the developers have proven another time to be great in their fields.
Moreover, the logic puzzles/riddles are almost never so difficult - there's a difficulty curve, but nothing unplayable really - so it's great since you can enjoy the story flow without interruptions.
I won't write a long review 'cos there are as of today more than 900 reviews and for sure they're better than mine, so I'd like only to share my feelings :)
I'd recommend to put the game in your wishlist, 'cos even if the game needs I think at least 15 hours of playtime (maybe more than 20 if you're like me) it doesn't deserve 20€.. it has no replayability, even though the story is very good and well developed.
Yeah, I don't agree with other players that thought that this game is above the average of the good point and click adventures. It's a "big" game, for what concerns graphics and such, but I think that there are many other adventures (many of them not set in a fantasy world by the way) that are free and better than this one.
This game has a big advantage for the graphic, music and sound compartment and the story setting and the plot are for sure great, although it isn't a brilliant title. It's great, but 20€ are definitely too much.
Stick with these developers if you liked this adventure anyways, it's sure a great game. Make sure to play it in English even if you're not a native speaker; of course, since the developers are Germans, probably the original German game is even greater but I don't speak a lot of Deutsch so well, since English is the only other well-developed language (and has voice acting and such) I'd suggest you to play in English and not in Italian for the well-known reasons of almost every review of mine.
Geron and Nuri (whose appearing in the game will change a lot!) are really two greatly developed characters and they manage to make the whole story good in the fantasy genre. Get this game if you can :)

As a long-time fan of the old point-and-click adventure genre, I've been happy with the recent resurgance of the genre, and Chains of Satinav is definitely worth playing for anyone of like mind.
Pros: This is not a pixel-hunt, thankfully, nor is it a "try every item on every other item" series of hopeless guesses. The puzzles are generally intuitive/solveable, and items you need to pick up or interact with tend to be visible without being obvious. The story is compelling and engaging, as is the cast of characters. The voice-acting was surprisingly good. Most importantly, the game feels like it matters. I laughed at the jokes, and I felt regret at the less pleasant choices you have to make in the game.
Cons: There *are* a couple of puzzles that may require you to get desperate and/or consult a walkthrough to get past (though probably not more than a couple for those typically familiar with the genre). The ending could have been more satisfying. I'm a sucker for "epilogues," particularly in games where I care about the characters, and this one feels like it could have used a better wrap-up.
All in all, a solid 8/10.
Bonus: I had no idea going in that this was placed in the same world as the cult-classic German RPG series "The Realms of Arkania." I slowly started to recognize names of distinctive things (like the gods from those games), which made it all the more interesting having enjoyed Star Trail a great deal. Fans of those RPGs will appreciate the references, but you don't need any Arkania-specific knowledge for the game, and you'd probably never feel like you're missing out on something if you aren't familiar with those games.

Crypt of the Necrodancer genre blends rhythm based mechanics with rogue like/lite much more successfully than Limp Bitzkit's attempt at blending rap and rock. Think traditional turn based rogue like/lites but each beat of the game's music is it's own turn. It's a simple, but very well executed catch that adds a lot of flavor to the game.
The pixel art is gorgeous, with detailed textures and animations, the up beat electronic music, though seemingly off themed from the game's more fantastical setting, is catchy and works well with the designed mechanics. If you're not a fan of the music (because you are probably insane), you can always play your own music which the game will build stages out of.
Crypt of the Necrodancer also comes with a variety of different modes and features for you to explore, including hardcore, training, and a pile of items and upgrades to unlock. Even as an early access (or perhaps, especially because), it feels very complete. Further improvements from this point will feel more like free DLC than the game subsidizing for missing content.
Overall, Crypt of the Nectrodancer is a very unique take on the rogue like/lite genre. It executes it's genre blending perfectly, offering easy to understand, but challenging mechanics, catering to the hardcore and beginners.
Pros:
- Excellent music
- Great pixel art
- Unique genre blending
- Lots of features and promotes replay
Cons:
- Those unfamiliar with rogue-like/lites could find this repetitive
- Custom music could use some tweaking

A brave soldier plods along his patrol, further into the cover of darkness, away from the glow of a pale moon.  A vengeful shade lurks within the shadow, eager to bring swift finality to his prey with ferocious grace.  A wisp of air is the last sound the man hears as a piercing anguish gives way to black.
Aragami is a story of unrelenting revenge and canny manipulation, told through intermittent flashbacks experienced by the protagonist.  Summoned by a young girl, held captive by the Kaiho army, Aragami has one night to retrieve six talismans to free the girl’s retainers.  Armed with a host of supernatural powers and the prowess of an assassin, this enigmatic specter commences his journey into the night.
Stealth serves as the lifeblood for all virulent pursuits in Aragami, and clever use of shadow is mandatory for progression.  Teleportation mechanics allow the player to blink from shadow to shadow, stalking the enemy before administering an ephemeral haze of lethal embrace.  Kill animations are visceral and ritualistic in their aesthetic; however, there are only a handful of available executions based on the angle of approach the player takes. Navigation through each level is expedited by teleportation but also requires a delicate balance of strategy and awareness.  Dancing between shadows can prove difficult at times, as I struggled on occasion to warp to my destination and found myself stuck within the environment once or twice.
Skills acquired, in the form of “shadow abilities,” include Kunai shadow knives, Shinen traps, which erupt in shadow and pull unsuspecting victims into the void, and targeted shadow generation for precise maneuvering.  Chaining these supernatural abilities together often results in satisfying scenarios which reward tactical improvisation. Energy, charges and light exposure are all visible via Aragami’s cloak, which serves as an innovative HUD, lending itself to the games clean aesthetic appeal.  Kaiho samurai patrol every corner of the environment, while archers scout for surreptitious threats.  Generally speaking, being spotted by an enemy will result in certain death, which forces stealth but allows the player to decide if they will extinguish their foes or circumvent them entirely. Unfortunately, enemy variation is also lacking, as it feels like you’ve been dispatching the same two enemies all game long.  Redundancy aside, challenging, fluid and decisive combat drew me in and kept me ardently embracing progression.
Fireflies hover around flickering flames which illuminate smooth stone graves and tufts of grass.  Fog conceals pernicious intent, while pagodas breach the sky with imperial allure. An incandescent moon saturates the sky with a silky radiance, as viscous crimson envelops steel below.  Aragami is an exquisite game to behold.  Cel-shaded graphics, layered with strokes of vibrant color and soft outlines, provide a refreshing visual aesthetic akin to Wind Waker.  Hauntingly melodic sounds evoke feelings of melancholy and loneliness, while providing an elegant backdrop for the visual experience.  I often found myself taking a break from the action and absorbing my surroundings for several minutes at a time.
Fans of the Tenchu and Mark of Kri franchises of yore, will find themselves at home within the context of Aragami.  While the game is less complex than the aforementioned titles in many aspects, it achieves a compelling level of immersion as a result.  For those in love with the stealth genre, this game is a worthy addition.

One of the most gorgeous hand-drawn action-platformer I've ever experienced, DUST: AN ELYSIAN TALE does a lot right when it comes to quasi-Metroidvania gaming. Apart from the terrific graphics, it has a great combo mechanic (just wish it had more of them), and the game does a good job of pacing its power-ups. Crafting is a unique way of equipping new, more powerful items. The last level of the game is especially satisfying to fight in, especially those hovercrafts that can be wrestled to the ground in one big, satisfying explosion. But the game is not without problems. For one, though the in-game graphics are amazing, the hand-drawn animated cutscenes looks awful (I'm also not exactly a fan of the artstyle). Worse are the characters, which are either annoying (Fidget) or one-dimensional. The dialogues never amount to much apart from lines that you've heard of tons of tmes. The ending is especially disappointing, with the last boss being utterly underwhelming (as opposed to, say, the last boss of Guacamelee, who was intimidating and fun to fight against), and the finale is a bunch of cliches all put together. I groaned when Ginger asks, "Dust?" in the end. That said, despite being letdown by the game during its final moments, DUST is still very much worth playing. 7/10.

If there was ever an RTS that's insanely addictive, this is it! It's very well polished, has a great tutorial and is very well balanced.
What makes the game a real winner is that it's easy to play, but hard to master. Camera manipulation, map scrolling, location bookmarking, building, recruiting, resource management, unit selection, unit grouping and unit direction feel very natural and logical and have been very well implemented. This is often something that is done so poorly in many RTS's and ruins what would have otherwise been a good game, but DOW makes it easy, which means that I can crack on with the more complicated management of my bases, armies and resource gathering.
I also love the element where you take a bit with you at the end of each mission to the next mission because that makes logical sense if you're running a war campaign, instead of starting each new mission with 1 builder unit.
One thing that can be improved is troop path finding, including formations. Then again, I still haven't found and RTS that does this overly well and I just have to micro-manage my armies more like usual.

Dark Crusade was probably my favorite RTS throughout my college years. While my friends were busy playing Starcraft, commanding the forces of Terrans, Protoss, and Zerg, I was busy fighting wars in the 41st Millennium, taking on foes ten times my greater and defeating them with honor and earning glory. This was also the version of Warhammer 40K's Dawn of War series that got me into modding, giving me a sweet, sweet taste of what the penultimate prize of Modding experience would be promised to me upon getting Soulstorm.
If you've ever gotten the previous two, Dawn of War and Winter Assault, you'd know gameplay-wise that nothing's really changed. However, with the addition of two new factions; the popular Necrons and the mysteriuos Tau Empire; and new units for all other factions (including Grey Knights for the Blood Ravens, which remains my favorite unit choice to this day), it definitely shines in front of its predecessors. That, and with an awesome campaign where you can play not just one but all seven factions, promising continuous replayability even after you've beaten the campaign once...there's nothing here that's not to like.
I'd be a fool not to recommend Dark Crusade. Any RTS player would be a fool to deny that this game stood the test of time. Stop reading the review, fork out some cash or grab that debit/credit card, and get the sodding game. The best part about it all is that the multiplayer options are compatible with all versions and are standalone, so you only need one game to have fun. I recommend giving it a go, it's worth it. Let's keep this game alive. For the Emperor

- I like asymmetrical gameplay. Makes things interesting, although it has it's drawbacks at times.
- The fact that commanders and "soldiers" need to work together is interesting and refreshing.
- Playing as alien is especially interesting, Skulk in particular
- The map design allows for strategical attacks, defense and traps.
- Graphics are good. Though I don't actually care about graphics if the gameplay is meh.
- As soldier you need a skilled commander, but as commander you need skilled soldiers. It can be very frustrating if you have to trust others to do their job but see them fail horribly. Balance is always a hit-or-miss, so meh.
- Simply put, the game is dead. There are hardly any servers with people on, and if there are any, they are either full or rookie only (which I can no longer play on). The very few with slots remaining have terrible pings, for me as European at least. Which brings me to...
- The netcode. A monkey could have made this better. Lag compensation is already a heretical concept and whoever made this up deserves to be shot, but it's just super trash in this particular game. Hits and shots feel so delayed and unresponsive at anything above 30ms (and even there it's not exactly spot on either). Usually you'll see your enemy not taking any damage or getting one-shot, same applies vice versa.
- To increase your win chances, it's all about bunny-hopping like there's no tomorrow. There should be a cooldown on jumping.
- The variety of weapons and abilities could be more diverse...especially since certain combinations are vastly superior to others, making most abilities pointless. And marines can do just fine with their rifles. The other weapons feel more like support tools, aside from the Exo-Suits, which are kinda end-game though.
