For an Indie game this is very well done. It's got a good setting for a fun TBS game. The heat component is great for adding that little bit of extra tactics into your turn choices, and the tech tree is nicely spread out with lots of options to play the way you want to play. That being said, there are A LOT off little things that throw wrenches into the gameplay. The spawning system for enemies is very random. While they mostly spawn next to tiles that look like holes for skitterings to crawl out of, sometimes they spawn on the space directly next to you for absolutely no reason. Additionally, the leveling system takes a huge factor of risk vs reward out of the game, because every unit you recruit will automatically be the same level as the units you've had since the beginning. Units you don't bring into combat still level up, and the skill tree becomes a little washed out because of this. Basically you can lose your geared up Hydra by charging him ahead, and not have to worry because you can spend SP to get another one of the same level with no hassle. It's a shame, because if the game progressed a little more smoothly within the realm of Risk vs. Reward, it would be a 10/10. All together though, a wonderful little Indie game, Well worth the money, and well worth the time played. 8/10 would recommend.

Templar Battleforce - Review : Omni Horizon
Templar Battleforce - Review: By Andrew Salfinger Rating: 8/10
“Templar Battleforce is a must have for all fans of tactical strategy games!” ~ Omni Horizon
Hello, my name is Andrew from Omni Horizon, Below you will find our first video game review.
Read the review @
Backstory:
Trese Brothers the company behind Star Traders RPG, 4X Empires, Heroes of Steel, Cryber Knights, Templar Assault and age of Priates are back again with Templar Battleforce the fourth game set in the Star Traders sci-fi world.
The game follows Templar Knights are a martial order sworn to protect the Star Traders – the last known free humans. Under the guidance of the Templars and the prophet Shalun, the Star Traders departed the ruins of the Galactic Core – leaving behind the desolation wrought by the great Galactic War. Guided by the prophet, the Star Traders sought a new home among the stars. Across the multi-generational journey of the Great Exodus, many ships have disappeared, fallen behind, or splintered from the main fleet – scattering the Star Traders to the galactic winds.
With the Great Exodus coming to an end, the Star Traders founded new colonies on the few remaining habitable worlds. The Templar Knights are called upon once again to defend the Star Traders and their new colonies from an ancient threat.
Review:
Templar Battleforce is a pickup and plays squad tactical grid combat game, with a focus on defending or advancing through swarms of enemies while completing objectives via set scenarios. It shares common ground with other squad tactics games like Xcom and the more recent Warhammer 40K games. It adds its own spin on progression by blending tabletop RPG attributes, light tech tree management, and weapon/gear loadouts to give it its own unique feel and tone to the genre.
Some players who may be new to this type of game may find it overwhelming so let’s break down the basics. Each turn every character in your unit will have six “move points (MP)” This will allow you to move six squares after using up all MP the character will not be able to move till the next player turn. If you use up all six MP this does not mean you can’t attack, for that each character also get five “AP” you will use these to use abilities and attack when it’s the players turn. Planning this stage is also recommend since different abilities will use different amounts of AP. You can do this by clicking on a character in your unit then at the button of the screen you will see your characters ability then right clicking on one will tell you how much AP it will use.
The game fills great, and from a small indie team they have done an amazing job. You can fill the love and passion they have put into this game. The combat is quick and quite challenging; you can kill an enemy within one turn, tho it can also happen the other way around so you will need to be on your toes with your strategy. In this game you don’t just want to grab, shoot get out of there, you will need a plan. It’s important to have each member of your squad cover and support one another, because if any single member is left exposed they will quickly be overwhelmed. At the end of the day crowd control is the key of the game, you are also often playing against the clock. You’re encouraged to race through and complete each scenario as fast as possible. If you stay put and try to bide your time you will usually lose by getting overwhelmed.
One of the great things within the combat turn is “free forming” where any of your characters can do any action in any order you wish, You don’t even have to use them all before moving to another character or ending your turn. This was a nice change from the normal, you have to do it in this order or else type gameplay and opens up the strategy and adds a new layer of gameplay.
Progression is handled within the game a couple of different ways. One of them is with the “Requisition” system or skill tree. On First glance there is a lot going on here but the Requisition is broken down into sections like engineer, scout, soldier, captain and so on, you can pick the skills in order of what type of unit you want to play and focused on.
Other ways are with traditional skills and attributes, as well as weapon/armor/augment loadout you take into battle.There is some light customization with a color swap, portrait swap and renaming to personalize, but it is not very in depth. Some more options and perhaps different graphics for the more robust armor and weapons would help give the characters a little more distinction and personality.
The game also haves things called ”Tactical Points" that you can capture and control on the map. They generate currency over time you can use to resupply, deploy extra squad members and give your squad bonuses. Tho be careful the enemy can and will try to destroy these “Tactical Points,” so I always felt compelled to protect them and at some points it can be critical in some levels. However, it can also be a misleading lure; where you could get caught up in stands off against the enemy when you should instead be pushing ahead.
The UI in the game is easy to use and to understand, I like the style and fit’s the game it does not feel out of place. The games UI also haves some useful tooltips for most elements in the game and does a good job of explaining. You can also change the UI by hitting “TAB,” this will allow you to see all characters within your unit.
Music in the game I quite liked for an indie game tho nothing stood out, some are catchy and help capture the mood, but some tracks seem cut short and can become weary after several plays. Sound effects are also serviceable but nothing amazing. The game is also all text based with no voice acting but that was expected due to voice acting costing a lot, and if they went the cheap route it would have ended badly.
Let’s talk about the story. I was surprised with how it expanded and was not expecting much from it due to it being a squad tactical game, it could however, be more robust. That is not saying it’s not any good and that you should skip away. The story does give you hints and what you should do among other things. The focus however is on the combat and how you handle it yourself in battle. Most of the plot and background development will happen through cut scenes, monologs, dialog trees and discussions with the fellow crew at headquarters. It would have been nice if it tied in with more of the other Star Traders games.
The graphics in the game are not bad, it haves a nice grunge alien look to them. Some people may find it bland and, or lacking, This is an indie and graphics comes second to gameplay and everything else. The main seller for this game is the combat, and they did an amazing job of that. Templar Battleforce has made a better tactical strategy games, and then most other AAA ones that have come out in the past couple of years.
Another thing I really liked about this game is when you start it up, I love the main menu in this game, it just set the mood for myself the subtle animation and effects used in it was great.
Read the review @
With that all said I found my self-liking this game much more than I originally thought I would, and I kept wanting to come back for more, so with that said I give the game 8/10. I can’t wait to see what game they come up with next.

This seems to be because some things had to be balanced, de-emphasized or made a bit faster. It makes sense for the type of game because it is now more focused on multiplayer. However this takes out much of the charm the other two games have had for me.
So in summary: If you are looking for Orcs Must Die gameplay, this game only sort of delivers. It has a different purpose, and I'm sure it's good for people who like that. But for me? I'm going to take a pass. I hope they do another game more like the other two in the future.

A low budget version of Tenchu, where the protagonist picks up the blink spell from Dishonored, with a dab of Mark of the Ninja in regards to skill progression. I like the fact that this is pure stealth gameplay, there is no going to a 'fight' mode once you've been discovered. There should be more stealth games that do this. I really like the fact that you have to hop from shadow to shadow. For some reason, it reminds me of the 'don't step on the lava floor' game everyone plays as a kid.
This game was mostly fun. There were some very annoying aspects that filled me with a lot of rage though. Getting the blink spell to appear exactly where you want it is an exercise in extreme frustration a good portion of the time. Usually, this was not a huge deal, but this made boss battles difficult in a cheap way, I didn't feel as though my skill was lacking so much as I couldn't get the goddamn cursor to register in the exact spot I wanted to warp to in time for me to not die. Also, later you have lightning that randomly drains a portion of your shadow power, which I couldn't stand. Maybe these issues are less of a problem to your younger and less crotchety gamer.
The default control scheme for the mouse and keyboard is abysmal, and it's as if it wasn't even fully tested using this mode (why is the stealth kill button spacebar instead of left mouse? Completely counter-intuitive), so it will likely require some modification. In a related matter, my pinky was constantly tired, as I was holding down control with it for 99% of the game. I really wish the developer had made sneak the default mode of walking; it's a STEALTH game, after all.
Oh, and why does the Esc button do absolutely nothing? This is inexcusable. I'm sure I'm missing some menu I never learned how to get to, but to quit the game, I would just alt+tab out of it and then kill the process. During the second boss battle (which was very annoying to me), this caused me to have to jump back 2 or 3 checkpoints when I started it back up again. That was the last straw. I was done with it at that point. I didn't finish it, but I got pretty close. Still, I don't have time for this kind of frustration. Admittedly, I probably suck more than most of you kids out there, so if you're a 12-15yo with nothing but time on your hands, this likely won't be a problem for you.
As rough as this game is when it comes to control, it's still worth recommending, I think. I got 20 bucks worth of entertainment out of it, since I played it for about 9 hours. Still, if I could actually fully control the game to the level which should be expected, this would truly be a great game.

This is a pretty good time if you can get it cheap. It's not a 'real' EDF game as it was outsourced to an entirely different studio halfway across the world but thankfully they understood enough to keep things goofy. The biggest departure from the Sandlot EDFs is this game's modern Western mission structure where it's all waypoints and overt setpieces as well as the odd (infuriating) linear vehicle segment. It kind of made me realize the canon EDFs are a lot better designed than they typically get credit for as they manage to get a lot of these moments to happen organically (like, in IA there will be an anthill and a prompt for you to stick a bomb on after which a counter starts running and you have to deflect waves of insects until it blows. In canon EDF there would just be an anthill with bugs streaming out so you end up deciding for yourself to wade in and destroy it so they'll stop coming. The end result is remarkably similar)
Anyway until one of the proper EDFs gets a PC port this isn't a bad way to scratch that itch.

It has plenty of room to grow and branch off with new content to be added and all sorts of new gear, traps, etc.
Basically, if the game didn't run well, had bad gameplay or looked terrible, leave a negative review, but it doesn't. I woke up today thinking about this game, and it took me an hour of thinking to decide what kind of review I would write for it.
My negative review today is based solely off my experience with the community that plays this game.
I got this game in order to play the puzzle-like games that I've seen so many YouTubers play. It looked fun, and my friend had played those a lot, so I got it so we could get on and test the waters since most videos I watched were a couple years old.
These days, those puzzle games have very low population and most of the maps that servers run, according to my friend, aren't nearly as good as older maps. We couldn't get a decent game after a few hours.
So we tried the 2nd most popular game mode: Star Wars RP. We were locked in a "training room" on the most popular server for a good 30 minutes with nothing to do besides stare at walls with training material on it. We asked for a trainer multiple times, only to be confronted with a wall of angry Star Wars roleplayers that just sat there and stared at us ominously. We eventually decided to walk outside the training room in order to explore the area, and got incarcerated for 15 minutes. After that time, we tried again, and quickly got incarcerated for 15 minutes. We cut our losses after an hour and quit for the night.
The next day I tried again on my own and actually got a trainer to show me how to play on a different server. Most of it is about memorizing marching formations and ship statuses of alert. I got all those down, and was allowed to explore the area and walk freely after about 45 minutes of training. Most people were nice, but after a couple hours I was quickly discouraged. Everybody spent most of their time standing around and bickering about non-RPers. I tried to progress in the ranks to no avail because of silly trick questions and stuff. So I tried the combat against NPCs. Well, at the lowest rank you get 1-shotted by mobs that run way faster than you and it takes a few shots to take them out. So, that was a no-go without progressing through the ranks. I felt I was stuck in being a private without being able to successfully play the mind games that the community set forth for people to progress through the ranks.
So, I decided to try the most popular game mode online. DarkRP. It was great. It was similar to the old custom map "LoaP" (Life of a Peasant) from Warcraft III. More Grand Theft Auto elements and building, though. I had some good times and bad, buying guns and drugs as a gangster and printing fake money. I had some great fun for maybe 15 hours or so over the course of a few days.
But then, the community. Playing as a thug or gangster, I figured I could jump people in alleys that weren't really doing anything other than hanging out in sketchy alleys for no reason. So I started to "claim territory" by murdering anybody that wouldn't talk to me or tell me what they were doing in my hood, figuring if anybody had an issue with it, the police force RPers on the server would come clean up the neighborhood and force me out. Instead, I was teleported to a room alone with a GM of the server and interrogated about what I was trying to do to the server and was told that what I was doing was not allowed because it's just not allowed to go around killing people. I apologized and pressed on.
Amidst a few fun experiences, I came across quite a few people around my age that would RP, fail because of some people in the community or GM interference, and then just stand around complaining about how children had ruined most servers and so on. Sounded pretty improbable. I couldn't see kids really enjoying that kind of stuff. I wouldn't have been allowed to play this kind of RP game with people ages 20-40 when I was a kid anyway.
So I built a small base according to the strict rules of the server. Raiding has no real benefits. You don't get money or anything from it. All you get is the accomplished feeling of having destroyed someone's creation and means of making money. However, lots of people raid bases anyways because of course there are many people on the internet that thrive off of watching others fail.
So I built this base according to the building rules of the server. Switches and triggers in plain sight, no path blocking, and no closing in of your money printers behind a wall that can't be surpassed. I was able to build a base that had a few puzzles in it that I felt would protect me pretty well against raiders. Set up my money printers, and made my money back after an hour or so.
At one point, I walked outside my house to go hang out outside the police station, puff on my vape pen, maybe get arrested for it, talk♥♥♥♥♥♥to the cops from my jail cell.... the usual RP stuff I'd do as a gangster on that server. A gun dealer (imo a character I should do business with) walked up and killed me. Fair enough, I never reported people for random killings and just acted as if maybe he was RPing as if I owed him money or something from a gun one of my homies bought or whatever. So I was running around, and got teleported to my base. Right in front of the gun dealer. Turns out he was a GM. He was furious. He couldn't figure out how to raid my base and came to the conclusion that I used illegal path blockers to totally prevent a raid. He sounded maybe 10-11 years old. I assured him there was a way to raid my base, I just made it into an IMO really good puzzle game.
He wouldn't hear any of it, got another GM involved, and demanded that I take down my base immediately after showing him all of the secrets to getting to the money printers that, as I said, yield no benefit to raiders destroying - just gives raiders a sense of accomplishment in being able to watch another player fail. He threatened to ban me if I didn't comply. I really enjoyed playing on that server, so I walked him through how to access the money printers that he used his GM powers to delete in a nerd rage. He didn't understand still, so told me to delete everything anyway. This whole time, the other GM was in total agreement with him.
At this point I got pretty frustrated, told him I wouldn't come back because not only is it unfair that I had to show him exactly how he can destroy my money-making source only because he was a GM so that in the future he can cause me to fail whenever he wants, like a kid with a magnifying glass burning ants, but I told him I also felt it unfair that even though I obeyed all the building rules, just because a child couldn't figure out the puzzles in my base, I had to delete it all. I had spent a good hour and a half building it all.
He sustained his position. Get rid of it all or be banned.
I told him it'll all get deleted when I log off for the last time, said goodbye, and never came back.
In short, this game has a lot of potential for fun if you've got 5-10 internet friends to play puzzle games with or an entire community to make a roleplaying server with. However, I wouldn't recommend this game for the majority of players who, like me, might have 1 or 2 friends that own the game. RP servers have pages of rules that you must read and comply, and even if you do... it's not likely you'll be left to your own devices because of children with magnifying glasses who just want you to be an ant for them.
So, this is why I'm giving it a thumbs down. Fun for a while, but the community sets the odds against people who don't travel in packs.

This game is really good. And this means something coming from me, who doesn't even enjoy point and click adventures and puzzle games. That's because, even if you don't like the genre, the story and characters are still good enough to keep you interested regardless. But then again, I might be biased because I got lured in by the trailer depicting a story of a guy and a girl setting out on an adventure and falling in love.  Being such a sucker for romance stories, I was sold right off the bat and luckily for me, the trailer wasn't one big lie for once in my life, like it usually turns out to be. With this game, you get exactly what you see. A point and click game in a high fantasy setting with a story of a couple who has to overcome some hardship. If you don't like any of that, you might as well just turn around and leave, but if you enjoy what you see, then good news: This game will be to your liking.
Here is what's good about this game:
- Memorable and likable characters with their own personality and growth
- A big world/universe that feels developed enough to actually make you feel like it might exist somewhere out there (I  mean, it doesn't feel like a fictional construct that was awkwardly put together by some novice author who wanted to make some quick cash with his game. You may laugh, but that's what most video game universes feel like to me these days)
- Intriguing storyline and worldbuilding with some nice plot twists to keep you interested.
- awesome OST
- Romance for all the Romance-geeks like me (even if it's just a little bit due to the not-all-that-long story)
- No handholding. Challenging puzzles (although that might just be me and my inability/unwillingness to solve them). They make sense for the most part, except for one part of the game in which logic as a whole gets disabled (Mild
spoiler)(
)
- And the very best thing for me personally: (Mild spoiler)
- And well, there is a sequel, too. For those guys who think the ending left off at a bad spot (which, admittedly, it did with its rather abrupt cut-off.)
Here's what the game doesn't do so well:
- The voice acting is terribad. At least the English one is. I usually avoid the German VOs, but given how this game is actually made by a German studio, it might be better to just listen to the German voices and use English subs. The main reason is that Geron, the protagonist, is unable to show any emotion aside from boredom in English, except for maybe a bit of annoyance here and there. He was that monotonous that at the one time he actually DID express anger , it actually felt so out of place for him that I felt genuinely shocked. Yes, that bad.
- The animation is quite rough and stuttering a lot. While some folks might be able to look  past that and even see it as the game's very own charm for following its own art style, I can definitely see a lot of people being turned off by it as well.
- Weird graphic bugs kept happening for me throughout the game. The background kept flickering with black boxes every once in a while. I ignored it, but it certainly hurt the immersion quite a bit.
- Some achievements are just diabolical. Having to repeat a certain pointless act 100 times was really unnecessary and annoying. Sure, it was done in five minutes but it felt neither rewarding nor was it fun to get it, let alone a clever easter egg of the developers. It was just downright a waste of time to get it. Plus, getting separate achievements for finishing the game on easy and hard mode for a game that has basically zero replay value is pretty stupid as well. I mean, it's a puzzle game, the fun is in figuring out the solution. You won't get the same kick out of it when you play it a second time, right? Since you already know the solution and all.
All in all, I can really recommend this game, even if you don't like puzzle games. Just open up a walkthrough of the game and merely enjoy the story which is definitely interesting. And if you liked it, there is a sequel, too, which is called Memoria. (Memoria is a good game as well, although maybe a bit of a disappointing sequel in regards of Geron and Nuri's story, given how they get treated like side characters there. But that's just my opinion)

I think it is a pretty good game, but I personally didn't enjoy it that much because the platform aspect was too difficult for me. It is a lot like Portal, with puzzles and an interesting environment, but it is also a challenging platformer, which I don't like. I'm not good a platform player. I like the Portal series because you don't die that much and you can save anywhere. The skill comes in solving puzzles, not navigating the environment. In Magnetic: Cage Closed, the puzzles aren't that hard but jumping and avoiding the knives and fire and chlorine gas is really hard (at least for me) and you can't save anywhere. The game auto-saves at the beginning of each room and in the middle of a couple of really long rooms There was one room towards the end where I probably had to try it literally 100 times before I got through. Not so fun.
As others have mentioned, the voice acting was a bit over the top. The entire game was very derivative of Portal, but I just took that as having more Portal to play. It apparently had a number of endings which I would really like to have explored, but it doesn't have saved games, so to try each ending requires playing the whole thing over each time, and I'm not going to go through those stupid twitch challenges again.
So if you like Portal and enjoy platform games, this is for you. If you like Portal and don't like platformers, look elsewhere.

This game is difficult.  Far more than I imagined.  And yet it was far easier than I expected it some respects.  Disclosure, I only made it partway into the first chapter.  The magnetic aspects of the puzzles were quite easy to figure out. The jumping aspects of the puzzles were much more difficult to pull off.  In my brief 1 hr of playtime, puzzles involving the magnet gun were not challenging at all.
The jumping puzzles, however, were rather difficult and punishing at that.  The last level I played (in Chpt 1) had a complicated jumping puzzle involving the magnet gun in which I had no idea whether I should use the magnet gun to pull myself to a far off platform, or push myself with the magnet gun to vault over the platform, or...??? something else entirely.  The puzzle didn't allow for trial and error to figure it out.  One mistake and you land in a blanket of chlorine gas and die.  Which means you have to start the puzzle from the beginning all over again.  I tried a few times and failed each time to make the jump.   So I died with no idea how to make the jump, and had to start the entire puzzle from the beginning.  Again.  My tolerance for repetition is fairly low, so I will probably never play the rest of this game.  I wish I could refund.
TLDR: the learing curve for the magnetic gun (boxes, stairs) is quite shallow and actually gets a bit boring.  The learning curve for the jumping aspects of the game is quite steep and quite punishing.  I personally detest jumping puzzles.  If I could just climb back up and try again I'd probably be playing right now instead of writing this review.  But  death on failure requiring starting the puzzle from scratch means....there are other games in my Steam backglog to play which surely have far less frustation and a more satisfying sense of progression and advancement.

10,000,000!  The name you should never call your game because it makes it difficult to find in search engines.
The game combines classic match-3 gameplay with an RPG in a way that you wouldn't think would work well, but it does.  The game is quite simple: Venture into the dungeon and match the applicable tiles on the board to fight monsters, charge up your shield, collect resources, and unlock doors and chests.  The run ends when you run out of time (HP and time are the same) and you use the resources gained to upgrade your equipment and train new bonuses.  The ultimate goal is to make a dungeon run ending in a score of 10,000,000 points.
The gameplay is quite fast paced so you will need a quick eye and hand to succeed.  There is some strategy involved with your upgrade path as well as enemy damage resistance but also the inherent factor of luck in relying on a board of random tiles.  Sometimes you will fail because you just can't get the tiles you need.  Fortunately it doesn't really matter much in the long run because you still gain resources to use for upgrades to improve your next run.
It's a nice little game, give it a try!

It's a neat little game with a fun storyline. Just like Portal and The Turing Test, you're yet another prisoner with one way communication to someone talking over the loudspeaker system. They'll remark on your progress (if you beat the level quickly, they'll say they're impressed. If you take forever, they'll either say "I'm going to fill the room with chlorine gas in 5 minutes" or they'll tell you they're disappointed by the time you get to the end of the level.
Also, and I'm not 100% sure but this is my observation, when you die, the character you control is replaced with the next prisoner down the line. I remember getting hurt in the first couple levels and there was a man screaming out in pain. After I died and restarted the level, I thought I was still the same guy until later on when they referred to me as a 'she'. I chuckled, thinking it was a quirk and the developers made a typo in the script. That is, until I found out my character was now a girl when she screamed in pain.
I haven't beaten the game yet but I've gotten through a chunk of the modules with ease. The difficulty is about as hard as The Turing Test (which isn't all too hard in the first place). It's more fun due to the storyline and the challenge combined. If there were no story, this would be a poor puzzle game. If there were no puzzles, this would be a poor story game. They compliment each other.

What do you do with this block? You put it on buttons, in order to finish the ... wait for it ... test chamber. Sounds familiar? Yep, that's Portal alright.
The big thing with this game is though, the mechanics feel so very clunky, which makes the puzzles more frustrating than what they need to be. The graphics feels... I don't know, they're very brownish, which makes it all feel "meh", not very pleasing to the eye at all, and there has been games where it can be very much brown but still pleasing to the eye - like Borderlands or Gears of War, to name two examples.

The Binding of Isaac is based on the eponymous biblical story  of Abraham and his son Isaac where God asked Abraham to sacrifice his only son, but spared Isaac in the end because Abraham had been willing to make the ultimate sacrifice for Him. Unlike biblical Isaac, the Isaac in this game isn’t about to stand for that. He escapes to the basement where he fights his way through various level of horrors. The player takes control of a naked, crying Isaac as he fights through the basement using his tears. Along the way, the player picks up various objects that usually help, though some hinder, Isaac’s quest.
Isaac may be a little too crude and possibly offensive for some. There’s a lot of potty humor in it, and some of the monsters are ghastly distortions of children and fetuses with names like Larry Jr.  Also, some may take offense to how religion is used in this game. Most of it made me chuckle and roll my eyes at the same time, but I wouldn’t recommend it for everyone. This is the type of game that will leave you thinking about what some of it means when you're NOT playing it. Overall, I thought this was a fun 2D shooter masquerading as a less challenging game.

A surprisinly satisfying turn based tactics game that exceeded expectations.
While it shares many similarities with "Space Hulk" or the old "Incubation: Time Is Running Out" game, TB stands out due to the large amount of customization it offers in terms of unit classes, abilities and gear thanks to it's branching tech tree that you gradually unlock. You can never have everything and have to make important decisions on how to build your squad which encourages experimentation, provides replayability and most importantly variety.
Level design also goes beyond just corridors and there are maps that are both large and small, open and constrained and there are relevant strategic decisions to be made with where you move and how you position your units. There's high ground, choke points, buildings, obstacles which can all make areas easier to defend or more difficult to attack depending on where you're standing.
Visuals are low budget but nice and clean, I find the game pleasant to look at. Music is decent but the tracks are few and fairly short which can make them feel repetitive and grating assuming you're paying attention in the first place (the game tends to suck up concentration).
Overall I definitely recommend Templar Battleforce over something like Space Hulk simply due to the superior variety it offers in terms of rpg elements, abilities, gear, level design and different enemy types.

This may be one of the best Free-to-play games on smartphones in my opinion, and here it is on Steam roughly 2 years after the original release. With its gameplay being building rooms and later upgrading them for more resources for your Vault (somewhat similar to something like Clask of Clans in that way), upgrading rooms (and even rushing them) do NOT require Nuka Cola Quantum (aka the games "premium currency"), instead, rooms will upgrade the instant you purchase it with the games basic currency, Caps. The mechanic to Rush rooms to get the resources instantly is a great idea, and it works well in the game! Basically, rushing a room has around a 30% chance of failing, and it increases by +10% each time you do it, the counter will go back down to 30% if you allow the room to work naturally. If the Rush fails, there will be a disaster in the room (ie a fire or a Radroach infestation), if thats the case, the Dwellers (more on them in a second) assigned to the room will have to douse the flames/fight off the radroaches. For the Dwellers aspect, you must rebuild civilization by allowing dwellers to become members in your Vault. Each Dweller has a set of S.P.E.C.I.A.L. skills: S for Strength, P for Perception, E for Endurance, C for Charisma, I for Intelligence, A for Agility, and L for Luck. Dwellers high in strength can work best in the Power Generator rooms, which are vital for powering your Vault. Dwellers high in Perception  work well in Diners, which supplies food for your Vault. Dwellers high in Endurance can work well in Storage rooms. Dwellers high in Charisma do well with, well, talking; Charisma only affects males/females conversing with someone of the opposite sex, which will end up causing the female to become pregnant and after 3 or so hours will birth a new child, which he then grows up to become another worker in the Vault. Dwellers who have high Intelligence will work best in Medbays or Science Labs, where they can produce Medkits and AntiRadiation Packs. Dwellers high in the Agility stat can work well in the Water Treatment rooms, which supply water to the Vault. Then Luck affects the Rush mechanic, allowing the chance of a disaster to go down a little bit. Strong Dwellers are also very capable of venturing out in the wasteland; giving a dweller a weapon (which helps them during Radroach Infestations or Raider Invasions) will allow the Dweller to survive in the wasteland, out there he can find Caps, guns, and outfits (which will help stats for Dwellers) and return them to the Vault. Combat in the game is simplistic, Dwellers will automatically attack threats and fight fires, its your job to heal them though, if they wont survive, you can assign them to another room so they can flee and survive. If they die, you have 24 real life hours to revive them with Caps, which can be handy. When you reach 18 Dwellers, you can build the Overseer's Office, which allows Quests to be unlocked. Quests are like sending Dwellers out into the wasteland, except you select 3 which meet the Quest requirements (i.e. level and weapon power) and you send them to a certain location which can take anywhere from 1 hour or 21 hours in real time, to speed this up you can use Nuka Cola Quantum. When they arrive at their destination, they travel as a group and will fight enemies. However, combat in Quests is VERY different from regular battles in the Vault, and it is, in my opinion, a little hit or miss. If Dwellers walk into a room where there are enemies, they are locked into fighting and cannot flee (I learned that the hard way), so if you intend on doing quests, i strongly advise packing tons of Stimpacks. Aside from that, combat is a bit deeper, it's still simplistic, but you can tell which Dwellers should target what enemy, and there's a random chance a checkmark crosshair will show up above an enemy, which once clicked, pauses the game and enters a timing minigame where you must click the crosshair when it's as close to the center as possible, doing so will give a critical hit that's 5x more powerful than the basic attacks. Quests do, however, offer a chance to score tons of loot that can be used later in crafting (which I myself have not reached yet).
Side Note: if you've played a Fallout game, you will most likely recognize a ton of familiar aspects of the game. As the game, in my opinion, stays very faithful to the Fallout franchise in terms of style and presentation.
If you enjoy Fallout games or Free-to-play games in the style of crafting rooms and ect., you will most likely enjoy this game, whether it be for Steam or smartphone. I give it 4/5 Stars. If you do plan on playing this game, I hope you enjoy it! ^u^

Solid stealth game for 20€
I bought Aragami at release and tested it instantly. As a stealth game veteran I was very impressed by the almost bugfree and beautiful game i got at release. I need to confess that i didn't play through it completely in singeplayer, but instead played through it with my friend Graudy.
But lets talk about the game.
Graphics
Even though Aragami was developed by a small indie dev team, the Artstyle is very unique and supports the very authentic mood. The contrast between light and shadows is a very big part of the gameplay and represents itself also in the leveldesign.
Soundtrack
Just listen to it. Just go and listen to it.... Its very calming and goes with the flow of the game.
Powers
Being a shadow ninja brings its advantages. You can get different powers by unlocking them with skillpoints you find spread in the levels.
Here you have to unlock at least the power to teleport from shadow to shadow, (totaly not inspired by Dishonored I swear #*cough*#) and the power to create shadows.
Of course the possibility to play through the game without powers would have been a nice options for hardcore ninjas, but that is not the purpose of this game. The powers go from kunais, to invisibility. There are 6 different powers which i dont really wanna spoil at this point, but I can say that they all work very well.
Gameplay and Controls
The controls are solid and work very well. powers on e, attack on space, leftclick for creating a shadow and right click for teleport. This may sound very simple, but I can guarantee you that it is all you really need.
The game starts with a good intro level, which teaches you the basics of the game, by introducing them one after another.
It is Idiot secure but not boring ;)
The game gets consistently harder as the player gets better at it, which keeps it at a challenging but not frustrating difficulty level, exept for the bossfights which are a little hard, even in coop.
Coop
Love it. 10/10
Played it with my stealth noob friend XD. We had a lot of fun playing and strategising together and I could observe his skill rising from level to level, up to a point where we didnt even have to do a countdown for coordinated kills anymore;)
It is a lot of fun playing together.
Summary
This is one of the best indie stealth games ive played so far. It comes at a price of 20 bucks which really isnt much for 10 hours of fun with your friends or alone of course. It is of course replayable level by level for getting all of the medals.
After all I can only recommend this cheap and awesome game to stealth gamers and gamers that want to get into stealth.
If you are one of those people:
"What are you waiting for. Go play the damn game;)"

Recently I beat the game “Dust an Elysian Tail”. I heard about it on the ActFur podcast.
Basically it's a side-scrolling adventure game with anthropomorphic characters. You play as Dust, a blue furred swordsman that has lost his memory. You are joined by a talking magic sword and a flying little helper thing named Fidget. Together you must discover your past and save... the land or something. You know it'll happen at some time in the game.
The gameplay starts out decently. I was glad that a steam game had such well implemented xbox 360 controls, but turns out that it was released on the xbox live marketplace too. So the game doesn't get extra points for that. The sword combat uses 2 buttons and a third button to use Figdet's magic. At first I thought the combos would make for challenging gameplay with tight controls, but then you learn the dust storm in which you spin your sword around like a deadly fan. After that the second sword button that was used for combos is dedicated to the dust storm and the sword combos are a pain to pull off after that because now it'll just turn you into a murder tornado most of the time. While doing this you can get your little flying squirrel friend to shoot magic into your dust storm and fill the entire screen with magic lens flares and dying enemies. Later in the game this will drop the challenge curve off a cliff while you breeze through the ending. But throughout the entire game the combat is nothing short of a cluster-♥♥♥♥. It's got a level up system and item crafting system where you get materials from dead enemies. The gameplay felt like a small upgrade from a free flash game.
The plot of the game is peculiar. If you think twokinds has the best storytelling ever, this is a couple steps down from that, so you might enjoy it. Early on in the game you learn that you were in some army under the command of a some general whom is basically a furry hitler. You were participating in the genocide of creatures called “moonbloods”. Thing is, not much has changed since the memory loss since you've been slaughtering moonbloods since the beginning of the game. Your character wonders if he's doing the right thing in a cutscene, then afterward you cut back to gameplay of you racking up combos of murdering these creatures. The plot and the gameplay are so inconsistent. After I learned the moonbloods were faced with extinction (despite the infinite supply of them on repeated areas), I tried to avoid combat then pretending the moonbloods I had run into were all just had brain damage that makes them inexplicably violent. Turns out you can't move to the next area if there are enemies nearby. So not only do they make you feel evil for killing enemies, they force you to kill them to gain experience, complete quests, and just travel around the place. Plus the story never explains why the feral moonbloods keep hitting you with sticks throughout your journey.
Anyways, the tone of the game feels setup by the art style. The landscapes are constructed from beautifully constructed hand-painted set pieces. The good guys are attractive, and the bad guys are unattractive. While this is sadly common, I thought the game would move away from that. But the only exception seems to be the fat-chinned furry Hitler at the end. Even when you find the sane moonbloods, they've been made to look nice. Your little fuzzy magic thing is always quick to point out what is ugly and what is pretty. The landscape, the monsters, and on occasion the other characters. The shopkeeper is apparently ugly, because he has to hide in the shadows of his little tent to keep you from dicing him to pieces upon sight. Without giving away spoilers, the game makes it very obvious that a sequel is planned. It's mentioned that there are four other swords of Elysium. Wow, a number of magic swords. That's certainly not a cliched plot device. In the ending cinematic, the last line of spoken dialog is one of the characters basically telling you there's going to be a sequel.
I didn't feel like the game was amazing or even very good. It's decent and certainly looks nice I suppose. The only reason I bought the game was because of the furry art style. So if you want an adequate adventure game with a furry art style, this game is an option. Just don't expect to be blown away by it.

First i know this could not match Mafia 1 and even less Mafia 2 (one of the best games i've ever played) but to turn the game into this? first the plot, the story is unconvincing, the gameplay is pretty much ok also the graphics are pretty nice and the soundtrack is amazing, but despite that the game is really shallow and repetitive and overall i'm gonna talk about 2k Shady way of doing bussiness lately.
Story: Mafia 3 sets in a fictional place called New Bordeaux (New Orleans), for Mafia 2 was Empire Bay (New York) and for Mafia 1 was Chicago. You play as Lincoln Clay, a boy raised by the black mob, orphan that at it's adult age joins the vietnam war and recieves the training to be a soldier, acording to the game a really good one, there's a minor spoiler here but everyone knows, after meeting Vito Scaletta (protagonist of Mafia 2) you get betrayed by Marconi and left to die in a fire, the game starts on a journey for revenge upon the man that took the only family Lincoln ever had, now the story itself is "good" not like mafia good but somehow decent.
Missions: This is where the games gets wrong, missions are repetitive and you will find yourself doing the same stuff over and over again, even killing the bosses is the same, honestly this part is what kills Mafia 3.
Gameplay: Game had several problems at launch and earned most of its bad reviews for having 30 fps look, which today is unnaceptable, after a few patches things got cleared out and the game is working properly now, overall really fluid, cars handling is very good, combat and cover system works and it's fun to play, you also get your friends to help you out providing ammo, weapons, upgrades, etc (for a price)
Soundtrack: Amazing as always, even it was the winner of this year 2016 Golden Joystick Awards for it's amazing soundtrack featuring some of the best songs of the 60 and 70's, gunfire and voice acting is really good, i'll saying extremely good, lipsyncing also is great.
Cutscenes: The best part of the game, this game nails this perfectly by delivering even better dialog and cutscenes that even L.A. Noire, everything is really well made and deserves to be commended by it.
Now you might be thinking "If i like this game so much, why i'm giving it a bad review", well that's because 2k decided to join other shady companies and start false adversiting the game, claiming that the steam reviews are wrong and Mafia 3 is the fastests best selling games of the last years, even claiming that their games is underdevilered, saying that mafia 3 is one of the best games of all times and everyone that thinks different is wrong, this game have a BIG flaw, it's NOT A MAFIA GAME, missions are repetivie and you find yourself doing the same stuff for the rest of the game, it's fun at first but 60 dollars is a lot of money for something like this, honestly i cannot recommend this game, not now or ever.

One word to describe NS2: unique. So what does it offer?
- hybrid FPS/RTS (the only other game I know about that does the same is Nuclear Dawn, but ND has been abandonned    by its devs and is pretty much dead)
- two completely different teams with different upgrades, tech trees, weapons, etc. encouraging different strategies
- a lot of room for in-depth teamwork
- each match is different, even on the same map = high replay value (btw maps are awesome)
- unlike most RTS, NS2 allows for surprising comebacks (too many careless mistakes by players with high value classes/equipment can cripple the winning team very hard)
- high skill ceiling (play with people of same skill or you'll be frustrated)
- constant updates
Many of the old negative reviews do not apply anymore, as the game now puts you against people of same skill. I got this game when it was on sale for 5€, but to be honest even 10€ is a joke. Steam is full of♥♥♥♥♥♥games which are more expensive and don't even get close to the amount of content and replay value that NS2 offers.
Don't get confused by the DLC, as I did. NS2 is not pay to win, everything is unlocked in the game. The DLCs are only skins, and most likely they will disappear soon anyways (one already did) due to the new NS2 item store. So expect more customization possibilites in the future.
If you think about buying this: do it. There simply is no other game like this.

I loved Orcs Must Die 1 and 2. I love the concept. The combination of PFS and TD. And I've been longing to play this game together with more than one friend (as was the fact in OMD2).
But OMD!U is another great gaming concept almost ruined by the Free 2 Play business model.
Fact: The investors and devs must earn their money some way or other.
This requires placing some portion of the game's potential behind a paywall. But this makes the game pretty much like the old days where players paid a fixed fee to unlock the whole game. The investors want max profits. So they turn to the addictive and gullible nature in most of us (and perhaps us gamers in particular). This has caused a surge in games choosing the F2P business model.
For not to be accused of making a Pay 2 Win/Pay 2 Progress-game, there must be a way to attract as many players as possible by offering a grindwall.
By promising LOUD and clear that EVERY aspect of the game is available without having to sink ANY money in the game, the investors try to attract as many players as possible.
As with spam: If only a tiny fraction of the recipients bite, then the conman will strike rich.
To maximize the desire to climb a wall, a large enough portion of the fun must be located on the other side.
If the GRINDwall is too low then players will simply play themselves over it. =Money lost.
For fear of unhappy investors the devs will have to make the grindwall very high. This makes it impossible to climb for casual gamers.
The players who are willing to sink valuable hours of their lives playing a fun-restricted game should get just enough reward - slowly enough - to keep them coming back for more.
But they should also constantly be enticed to pay money to progress faster. The progress must therefore be sufficiently slow. There are many ways to conceal slow pace: long cooldowns, ineficcient traps, puny effects, little game impact,
The promise that the game will eventually become maximum fun should always loom above the next hill.
The grindwall will gradually increase the motivation to defend all the time invested in the game by paying for quicker advancement. In OMD!U it takes the form of chests providing completely random rewards. The more expensive chest you buy the greater the chance for rare loot and greater amounts of it.
This opens up the casino-part of most F2P-games.
Since investors demand a maximization of profits, any player revealing him/herself as willing to play the casino game should be milked as much as possible before they realize they will never get to the greatest enjoyment of the game.
Or they will have to pay a LOT, to reduce the chance of the game being pegged as P2W.
These gamblers must - after all - pay for the players who doesn't pay. Patching, content development, servers and bandwidth costs money.
If the gambling system is designed right the player should believe s/he got something good. But after playing a bit they should realize that it was not that good anyways, and be tempted to protect their earlier investments by gambling some more. Rinse and repeat.
It is human nature to throw more money after lost money, in order to somehow redeem or avoid losing the earlier investments.
If you read this thinking "The game is fun as it is": As yourself how much more fun you could have had with a fully unlocked game.
If you read this thinking "I can play myself over the grindwall": Ask yourself how many hours you think you'll have to play to get to the full enjoyment that the game can offer. And if you - perhaps - have gone bored by then. Perhaps you will leave the game having never experienced all the fun it could provide? Perhaps there are other games you could have enjoyed instead? Do you think you will live forever? Time is valuable, and we gamers should ask ourselves if gaming companies respect our time or not. They should focus on making games that gives us max amounts of fun, and charge a reasonable fee for it. -Rather than having us pay both valuable time and money to never get the full game.
What if you could play every game and enjoy all its potential without having to pay with hours of reduced enjoyment?
When you go to the cinema you can expect to pay a bit in both money and commercials. But after that you get the full movie, from start to finish, in all its glory.
But what if they offered a Free 2 Watch business model like F2P:
- The movie starts great. You love the story, and decide to keep watching.
- But there are loooong scenes of the hero brushing his/her teeth, eating dinner, reloading weapons, shooting the breeze. It is OK to watch. Not fun, but OK.
- You will never get to see all the scenes of the movie (or its complete ending). Because when you do you're off the hook and have no incentive to keep wathing.
- Some of the audience will decide their lives are worth more than their money, and will start gambling. They will have to pay for all the rest who still take up seats. But will get to skip some of the teeth-brushing and weapon reloading scenes.
- And no one will get to know what the movie wold have been like if it was provided Pay to Watch as the director intended.
Back to the walls:
If a paywall is too low then the game will quickly be pegged as Pay 2 Win. And since this is both a PvP-game as well as PvE-game the devs cannot allow players to purchase themselves to power. If this happens the game will receive crippling reviews and bleed players quickly.
As you can see: The whole F2P concept - by inherent design - ruins games.
Investors could not give a damn about this fact. They are in it to earn money. They do not care about your enjoyment.
The devs are paid by the investors, and have little say. They are victims of this just as we gamers are.
Why should we accept this?
I implore you: Make a principal decision. Make a statement by supporting the paid games and refusing to play F2P. Let's all contribute to sending the destructive F2P business model to the junkyard of financial history.

10,000,000 is one of those great little casual time wasters that you can pick every once in a while to grind for 5 more minutes then put back down again until the next time. The core gameplay mechanic is the basic tile matching we've seen in so many games by now, 10,000,000's own little unique aspect to this rather tired mechanic is that instead of moving individual tiles you move entire columns. This however does not change the concept significantly and if you have played a tile matching game in the past you'll figure this one out in no time at all.
The interesting aspect of 10,000,000. And what separates it from so many other similar games, is the way it approaches the timing mechanic. on top of your screen you have a little guy running along in a dungeon, as he progresses he will encounter various obstacles such as doors and monsters each pushing him slowly out of the screen if you do not match the right tiles on the board below. This creates quite a bit more purpose than your usual tile matcher where you just match what you can, as quickly as you can. Here you might wanna save those keys in case you run into a chest, or be careful not to spend too many swords and staffs if you think you're getting close to a tough monster.
The game also feature a small metagame, as you match tiles and progress through the dungeon you earn wood, stone, gold and experience which can be used to open up shops and improve your various abilities.
All in all 10,000,000 is a fun little game, nothing spectacular, nothing really exciting but a solid time waster. Unfortunately while the time waster genre as such is perfect for mobile games it does not fit quite as well on the PC and although this one of the best examples I've seen in a long time it still doesn't quite measure up to the standards that you would expect from a game that costs money.

This game could have gone so wrong. But it gets it just about exactly right ...
It's a combination of simplicity and focus off control, and two game genres that unexpectedly enhanced each other.
The controls are that of a rythm game: up down left right (or ABXY on a gamepad, with full-featured remapping options). Two keys can be pressed together in a combo. But instead of just mimicking the symbols and combos you see on the screen, you are improvising patterns that allow you to defeat monsters. It's like jamming with a band more than it is playing a faithful cover of a song.
The basic roguelike elements are there, too: monsters, upgrades, loot. But instead of soaking hits or luring monsters to choke points, you're moving smoothly through the dungeon, boldly weaving between monsters, improvising a dance of death. The various weapons modify your patterns in interesting ways, and using bombs and potions requires being quick with the combos.
It's a rythm game that doesn't dictate your moves, and a roguelike that encourages you to be bold and take risks. And as a result, it's both one of the best roguelikes and best rhythm games I've played to date. It's also very polished for an Early Access game. I heartily recommend it :-)

Here I want to concentrate on one annoying fact:
The game saves automatically (usually only at the beginning of a chamber) in ONE savegame.
This means two things:
1. Some chambers are pretty time consuming. When you die after 10 minutes figuring out the whole thing (and dying happens quite often) you have to do everything from the start. I can live with that but I just don't see a reason why there is no save or quicksave option.
2. The bigger problem is: The game has 9 endings. If you want to find them all you have to play the entire game again for each of them since there is NO level selection (apart from time trials) and you can't save when making a decision.
This isn't just a problem for completionists like me -
Some endings are just like: "You're dead - Thanks for playing. Now start over - you're not allowed to play this chamber again and choose a different outcome"
Of course one might argue that playing the whole game again and making different decisions also gives you a different experience but that's just not the case.
I'll try to explain without spoilers:
You get to the 7 main endings by making a decision near the end before entering the final 3 hard chambers. You can choose Path 1, 2 or 3. Depending on which path you take you get to the very same 3 chambers but in a different order (wow! so different from each other!).
At the end of each path you make another decision that leads you to one of the endings. (Path 1=2 Endings, Path 2=3 Endings, Path 3=2 Endings).
The first playthrough is fun because you have to solve puzzles but playing it the second time is a chore since you just know all the solutions already.
TLDR: Great game but you have to replay it 9 times to find all the endings because you can't save yourself and there is no level selection.

NO FIGHTING IN THE WAR ROOM
DEFCON is the second title from the brilliant independent company Introversion Software. It's a haunting and daunting game, where you are charged with the offensive forces of a portion of the world as a timer ticks down the stages of the US Defense Readiness Condition system. (5 is peacetime, 1 is nuclear war.)
Gameplay consists of placing buildings such as radar sites, missile silos and air bases in your chosen territory and assembling your naval fleets with aircraft carriers, battleships and submarines. As the DEFCON clock ticks down, air and naval combat is enabled, then at DEFCON 1 nuclear strikes from silos or submarines is authorized against population centers and military installations. Your overall goal is to lose the least; to get away with less civilian megadeaths (millions of deaths) than the other combatants. Hence the game's slogan: EVERYBODY DIES.
The macabre nature of gameplay combined with the chilling NORAD-command-screen aesthetic and melancholy music makes for a tense game pretty much every time you play. Especially if you're not terribly good at it like me. That, and the main menu is nifty and there's good mod/AI support.
Anyone who is interested in the Cold War or wants a dark twist to their RTS gaming owes it to themselves to at least try this game.

Templar Battleforce is a "pickup and play" squad tactical grid combat game, with a focus on defending or advancing through swarms of enemies while completing objectives via set scenarios. It shares common ground with other squad tactics games like Xcom and the more recent Warhammer 40K Space Hulk games. It adds its own spin on progression by blending table top RPG attributes, light tech tree management and weapon/gear loadouts to give it its own unique tone and feel.
Combat is quick and challenging, often you can kill a enemy in 1 turn but if you aren't careful they can do the same. It's important to have each member of your squad cover and support one another, because if any single member is left exposed they will quickly be overwhelmed. At the end of the day CROWD CONTROL is the name of the game, you are also often playing AGAINST THE CLOCK. You are encouraged to race through and complete each scenario as fast as possible. If you stay put and try to bide your time you will usually lose by attrition and get overwhelmed. By this same token exploration can be a double edged sword where exploring the map might uncover bonus experience or a cache, but you might stretch your characters too thin and risk becoming too weak to finish your objective. Buffs and enhancements have limited use so you need to use them with some finesse, this also ties into the pressure to speed through the level in as few turns as possible.
The combat turn is free forming where your characters can do any action in any order you wish. The characters don't have to complete all of their actions before selecting the next character. There is no turn order. For example: your soldier can shoot someone, then have your captain buff the squad, then go back to your soldier to setup overwatch, then have your captain push ahead all on the same turn.
Another wrinkle to combat is there are forward points or "Tactical Points" that you can capture and control on the map. You use these as staging areas; they generate currency over time you can use to resupply, deploy extra squad members and give your squad bonuses. You will often feel compelled to protect these "Tactical Points," especially since the enemy can destroy and capture them too. Maintaining these points can be critical in some levels. However in other levels the Tactical Points can be a misleading lure; slowing your game down where you get caught up in standing off against the enemy when you should instead be pushing ahead. Caught up in a struggle over Tactical Points will cause you to lose momentum and eventually lose to attrition as many levels will have unlimited enemies.
Another thing to be wary of is that while many of the enemy spawn points are marked and easy to identify, many others are much more subtle and not so easy to identify, this can lead to some frustrating moments (especially at higher difficulties) as spawning enemies can freely move and attack on the same turn that they appear. This can compounded by squad members' short line of sight. Members that can counter act this with the "Sensorkit Scan" will be invaluable.
Death on lower difficulties will give you back your characters after you finish the level, but on higher difficulties death is permanent. The game is very different depending on the difficulty setting you chose: on low to medium difficulty the game is more akin to a Sci-fi RPG with a core party you can rely on regardless of what happens. At higher difficulties you get more of a Xcom experience where you have to live through the loss of your veteran members killed in action.
Progression is handled in a split of traditional skills and attributes, a branching tech tree, as well as weapon/armor/augment loadout you take into battle. You can respec your squad skills without detriment. With unlimited respecs you can adjust to whatever scenario the game throws at you and experiment without the worry of being stuck with skills you dislike. There is some light customization with color swap, portrait swap and renaming your characters, but it is not very in depth. Some more options and perhaps different graphics for the more robust armor and weapons would help give the characters a little more distinction and personality.
The story is serviceable but not very robust which is understandable for a squad tactical game. The focus of the game is the combat and how you handle yourself in battle. Most of the plot and background development will happen through cut scenes, monologues, dialog trees and discussions with fellow crew at headquarters. I actually hope more plot, origins and history of Shalun will be added in future updates to flesh out this games plot ties with the other Star Trader games a little more.
The UI is easy to understand and most things are clean and well explained.There are useful tool tips for most elements in the game. However I do feel some key information ought to be included in the tool tips such as remaining AP/MP and perhaps armor and deflection. Toggles for animation speed, and more general game options would be welcome additions too.
Music ambiance is decent, some tunes are catchy and capture the mood or situation, but some tracks seem cut short and can become weary after several plays. Sound effects are also serviceable but nothing amazing.
In Summary:
Overhead Squad Tactical Grid Scenario Combat Game with some twists and a unique approach to progression.
Fight as a Templar Captain in part of the Star Traders universe taking flavor from Dune, Space Hulk, and some Hindu.
PRO
Simple and challenging combat that is easy to pickup and play.
Lots of scenarios, varied difficulty settings, and an ever growing list of content (due to updates) help give the game long legs and high replayability.
Great overwatch mechanic that is tactical without destroying balance.
The devs are very involved and receptive to community feedback and the game is always improving as a result.
CON
Characters could use some more customization to make each member feel more like your own.
Very little game options to tailor your preferences.
Music and sound effects are serviceable but could still be better, particularly music loops could be longer and more varied.
Some enemy spawn locations are hard to make out leading to frustrating moments.
Many levels require a "core" set of classes and don't leave much room to experiment with the less used classes. Edit: Devs have added a swap out member mechanic which does help this a bit.
OTHER
The Tutorial levels can drag a bit and do a bit of hand holding, I'd suggest playing through it just once for the plot points or to get the basics down and then skipping ahead to the main game from there.
The setting is akin to Space Hulk but has it own subtle spin and ties into the other Star Traders games from a Templar prospective, I hope more plot and Star Trader history is added in future updates.

Templar Battleforce is one of those games that had no right to be as good as it is. It's a game of dizzying depth and what it lacks in raw graphics it makes up for in gameplay.
If anyone played the Space Hulk videogame and felt it lacking then Templar Battleforce is the answer. It plays very much like a mix of Space Hulk (both the boardgame and the videogame) and X-COM, though it's by no means a clone of either of these games. Templar Battleforce brings to the table many new features such as 'Heat' for your Templars, an opposite of HP that means every move you make or action you take will put your Templar one step closer to overheating. The mechanic forces you to give your men a rest every few turns or risk taking unwanted damage over time. On top of that certain battlefield have Tactical Points which can be captured by you or the Xenos. Once these points have been captured you can spend the SP they generate to call in more soldiers or ordance, or upgrade your team. Any recruits you call in that survive the battle will become veterans, and can be deployed in every battle from there on.
From a fantastic lore to fantastic gameplay to rather decent music Templar Battleforce is well worth the price that it's being sold for.

The Binding of Isaac is based on the eponymous biblical story  of Abraham and his son Isaac where God asked Abraham to sacrifice his only son, but spared Isaac in the end because Abraham had been willing to make the ultimate sacrifice for Him. Unlike biblical Isaac, the Isaac in this game isn’t about to stand for that. He escapes to the basement where he fights his way through various level of horrors. The player takes control of a naked, crying Isaac as he fights through the basement using his tears. Along the way, the player picks up various objects that usually help, though some hinder, Isaac’s quest.
Isaac may be a little too crude and possibly offensive for some. There’s a lot of potty humor in it, and some of the monsters are ghastly distortions of children and fetuses with names like Larry Jr.  Also, some may take offense to how religion is used in this game. Most of it made me chuckle and roll my eyes at the same time, but I wouldn’t recommend it for everyone. This is the type of game that will leave you thinking about what some of it means when you're NOT playing it. Overall, I thought this was a fun 2D shooter masquerading as a less challenging game.

Templar Battleforce is a turn-based squad tactic game. Your units gain experience and requistion/technology points in missions. The more side objective you achieve and xenos you kill the more xp and rp you get. With xp you can level your units, with requisition you can buy new skills, classes and weapons, powerfull relics in the requisition tree. The tech tree is rather large.
There are 8 classes: Captain, Hydra, Neptune,  Berserk, Soldier, Engineer, Scout and Paladin.
The classes have different equipment and skills. Your progression choices on attributes when leveling have impact on the gameplay. A unit with high fortitude and melee skill is good in melee as you can aspect. But you can also decide to try different builds. A standart bearer with excellent party buffs for your captain? Or a soldier with high grenade ability and melee skills? It is your choice.
The requisition system is interesting and motivates to get more rp to get better equipment and classes. Some are even essential for progress in the game. The paladin as healer or the engineer for capturing strongholds in the level, where you can get reinforcements.
The tactical gameplay is very good. You have a little rng here, because every actions success is based on dice throws. But if you invest xp intelligently into your units you get nearly 100% chances on attacks and up to 60% block evade for incoming attacks. It is possible to create 'useless' units, if you invest wrong, But you can respec your units anytime in the hq to prepare for missions on normal difficulty. The AI behaves human like. It does not circumvent your overwatch field, it is not omniscent and makes errors. A human player could not know where you place your traps or overwatch so it does not cheat to win. The AI has many units to make the missions more interesting. After 10 missions i had killed 500 aliens. More then in any other turn based tactic game i played before. The missions can get quite difficult when you are slow and not focused on your objective. After all you are fighting against hordes of aliens, stopping and resting will get you overwhelmed quickly. The missions are quite interesting and different. Some times you have to escort a bomb carrier into the heart of an alien cruiser or defend a bridgehead for some time. Or you have to kill a boss while being attacked by waves of aliens. Killing the boss will win the mission.
Your units have movement points and action points to spent. You should move before using action points, because any left movement points are spent when you use your action points.
The grafics and sounds are adequate. They are 2d, every unit is animated. Unfortunately there is no movement range indicator for enemies, so you have to learn the movement patterns of the different enemy units. Most have 6 movement range like your units. Do not expect Xcom remake like grafics.
If you like the old star quest or space hulk boardgames this game is made for you. It is space hulk on steroids, with tech tree and a roleplaying stat system and an interesting atmosphere and story.
I encountered many bugs but not one software bug in this game. Performance is flawless. Very nice product.
I am not a fan of pointy review score, but i would give this game a 10/10. My personal game of the year.

tl;dr - Don't be fooled by its' looks, this is a tremendous game for the price.
Don't be turned off by the simplistic graphics and interface - this is a solid strategy game for the turn based tactics crowd.  The strategy is much more refined than that of its' nearest relatives, and the missions force you to think creatively about how to best combine your units to face situational challenges - dividing your forces to reach multiple objectives, fighting against a timer, deciding whether or not an optional objective is worth the extra turns it will take to complete, etc.  The combination of units which advance, and also persist through the campaign even if they die(and also respec'd at will), allows you to experiment freely with specializing your forces using a very deep tech tree and equipment loadouts to develop your own playstyle, or prepare any particularly challenging levels with a customized force.

Magnetic: Cage Closed is your run of the mill first person puzzler with flaws. I found myself getting frustrated with many aspects of the game.
Pros:
- Someone who enjoyed Portal and wanted to play a cheaper cousin would be satisfied with this game.
- I guess the magnet gun is cool?
- The soundtrack was enjoyable. It sounded tense, which I guess fit well with the atmosphere the game was going for.
Cons:
- The controls are so annoying! Controlling the magnetic forces while in the air was very difficult at times and awkward to handle.
- This story format is tired. I'm a prisoner in a strange place with trials to solve to gain my freedom, and there is a voice over the loudspeaker that doesn't like me.
- Was there even a point of setting the magnetic level? Anything below the highest level was useless.
- This game has no mercy. Traps everywhere. If you die in any part of the chamber you have to start the whole thing over.
- Although I don't mind easy puzzle games, for some reason I felt like the puzzles in this were too simplistic. I didn't feel like required you to be clever at all. The only times I got stuck in this game were when the controls were too hard to use. I would know how to get from A to B but I couldn't accomplish it with my hands. Basically, every chamber requires you to push buttons to get past it.
- The transition tunnels from level to level got old quickly. Crawling into the same looking tunnel over and over and over.
I finished the game in a little less than 5 hours. I would have finished it in 4 had it not been for the constant dying. Unless you are a die-hard fan of first person puzzle games, I wouldn't bother with this one.

This game is a big slide puzzle that has an ever changing picture.  It may sound complicated and overwhelming at first, but it really isn't that hard by any means.  You slide squares on an x/y axis to make three-in-a-row matches vertically and horizontally.  Depending on what you have matched up has a specific effect as to what happens to your adventurer.  Combining swords or wands will make your adventurer attack enemies that stand before him.  Combining shields and treasure chests will grant the adventurer bonuses to help him last longer.  Bigger combos make for bigger points, and your goal is to break the coveted 10,000,000 mark in one game.  If you like slide puzzle games, you'll find yourself playing this casual game for awhile.

I want to recommend this game on the sheer philosophical level that games are an art form to be experienced.
This game made me feel things.  As gamers we've slain zombies, killed Nazi's and even exploded innocent towns in fallout.  And yet, through all the years of gore and hyperviolence this simple vectorized representation of the world has made me feel more guilt than any video game I've played.  This game is unsettling to it's core and has made a huge impact on me.
The soundtrack is, in my opinion, perfection and lends a staggering amount of gravitas and torment to the game.  Even when you're winning, it is disturbing to think you so easily caused 5.8 million deaths in Tokyo.  In the background you hear the final gasping cough of a women as she succumbs to radiation poisoning or the cry of a mother over the death of her newborn.
Even if unintended, this game makes a moving and bold statement, all represented by a very detached and matter-of-fact way.
At least try the demo!

DEFCON is a unique strategic game that employs a great sense of atmosphere and immersion through its simplicity. Because of its simplicity the importance of the interactions with other players becomes paramount to the enjoyment of DEFCON - and it works. It may seem risky that the game relies on the performance of the players, but the design and art of the game (the soundtrack in particular) induces players to act in a paranoid and tenacious fashion. There is deceit, lying, trickery, backstabbing - it is like a game of poker, but with fantastically chilling music and nuclear weapons. DEFCON is a very fun game and I would recommend it to anyone.
