It’s a 2D point 'n click adventure game, with beautiful hand-drawn and awe-inspiring backgrounds (have your finger ready to hit the F12).
There you will:
•	find three main characters: a bird-catcher, a fairy (not at all like Tinker Bell) and a raven
that speaks;
•	solve puzzles and get out of baffling situations;
•	talk to people or... things (a lot);
•	collect and use items (more than a lot);
•	even obtain a couple of extra skills.
Cutscenes and background narrative illustrate the progress of the story.
It’s not a hard game. I will put it as difficult for those of you who are new, though courageous, at this and a brain teaser for those who are not [new].
Arm yourself with a good deal of patience and prepare to travel through a world of wonder, unveiling a lovely story of courage, perseverance and endurance.
As for installing and playing, I did not have any troubles. But if it happens, just look it up in the game discussions. Sometimes is only a question of just leaving the default configuration settings as they are. Try different combinations and choose the one that works for you.

I'd compare this to Templar Assault, but if you've played Templar Assault, you've probably already bought this game.
If you haven't, Templar Battleforce is a grid-based, turned-based strategy game where you lead a squad (well, more like a platoon) of armored infantry across a variety of battlefields. While most "budget" tactical games either limit you to a handful of units with flexible progression or offer you a choice of otherwise bland troops with one unique trait apiece, Templar Battleforce gives you eight classes each with a broad selection of upgrades and gear that have minimal overlap with the other classes. Each of your soldiers levels up seperately and has their own stats and skills, making it easy to specialize even soldiers in the same class for different roles.
The scenarios are objective-driven, usually encouraging a fighting advance, though more defensive and other goals pop up. Maps do not seem to get reused, keeping things relatively fresh. Enemy variety is broad enough to encourage keeping your squad flexible, without becoming confusing.
Graphics are in the screenshots. Clear and atmospheric, they are about what you'd expect from a 2D game made by three people. Similarly, the sounds and music are serviceable, if less than cinematic quality. Still, the strength of the game lies in the gameplay rather than presentation.
Replayability includes multiple difficulties, New Game+ modes, and the option of exploring different paths on the Requisition tree, which unlocks class upgrades and gear. While characters themselves can have their talents, skills, and attributes respecced freely between missions (an ability explained in the fluff), the requisition tree is less flexible.
I'm told there are about 50 scenarios, so I'd guess about 15-20 hours to blow through them all if you're an experienced gamer playing on Normal.
All in all, Templar Battleforce is an excellent value for anyone who enjoys turn-based tactics games that mix relatively simple mechanics with plenty of options for customization and strategy.
Also, there's minimal randomness. While attacks can miss and criticals can happen, rarely is an individual attack going to make a difference in mission success.

is a point and click adventure game that is set in a mystical land with fairies, knights, and magic. On paper it sounds like a lovely experience and indeed, I did enjoy playing it. However, it also has its fair share of faults including but not limited to a mediocre story and, at times, illogical solutions for puzzles. I feel if you enjoy point and click games of this nature you can find an enjoyable experience here but there are better games in this genre and newcomers would be better playing those. This title is in no way a bad game, I was able to get into it and enjoy playing it but I do feel it’s a very middle-of-the-road game.

The story has players take control of the lead character named Geron. Geron is just an average boy who is training to be a bird catcher which is very convenient seeing that is town is becoming plagued with crows. This is a symptom of a much larger problem and after Geron meets Nuri, who is a fairy, they end up embroiled in a deadly plot. Because of her heritage as a fairy, an evil prophet needs Nuri to play a harp that will help him take over the world. Geron wants to protect her from this as well as save his kingdom from the evil prophet. The two travel far and wide to find a solution to their problem and a way to defeat the prophet once and for all.

While the story itself is a bit on the cliche side, I still wanted to learn about the world it took place in. I wanted to learn more about Nuri and fairies, I wanted to know why Geron had magic, I wanted to know more about the prophet as well. However, the game doesn’t deliver on a lot of the topics it sets up. Geron has one spell that can destroy minor objects but we don’t know why. He’s just a normal boy so why does he have that spell? Nuri is a fairy who doesn’t want to return to her world and while we learn why from visiting it, we never hear this from Nuri or learn of her experiences there. Which is the biggest issue here, the characters aren’t developed well.

Geron has little to no backstory and spends a large bit of the game having to babysit Nuri. Nuri is a vapid idiot with no sense of danger or her surroundings. She would probably walk off of a cliff if Geron wasn’t there to tell her not to do so. She is sweet and innocent, but aside from her small bit of magic,  totally useless. The game also throws in a moment where the two kiss which is out of place since there had been no romantic hints or interactions beforehand and I’m never given the impression they love each other. The prophet’s motives are explained but his powers aren’t nor his real connection to fairies. The game has so much potential to flesh these characters out very well so that players invest more in their struggles but it doesn’t come to pass. In the end I found myself wanting to finish the story so Geron could just go home and live a normal life, with or without Nuri.

While the story could have been improved so too could the gameplay. The gameplay consists of a series of puzzles you have solve by finding items that may be of use to you at some point, knowing where to use these items and also when to combine items. You also have two spells, Geron’s that destroys things and Nuri’s that reconstructions them. Since it’s a point and click game, you will be using your mouse for everything. You can interact with other characters, talk to them look at them, give them items and such. You can look at items as well, pick them up and use them when needed. The issue lies in solving the puzzles, sometimes they’re pretty straightforward and other times the solution makes no sense at all. The latter happens a lot when you end up in the fairy world and while I admit a land of magic doesn’t always make sense this doesn’t help when I’m trying to play a game. I ended up needing a guide often because there aren’t many in game clues to help you either. Nuri never has anything intelligent to say so she’s of no help and while you can check hotspots to see where you can interact with something there is an achievement that relies on you not using it often at all. If the main part of your gameplay is solving puzzles and a large portion of them do not make logical sense then there is an issue.

But before the story and gameplay, what you notice first is the artwork in the game. Yes, even with its other faults the gorgeous artwork helps support this game a great deal and helped me get through it. The atmosphere is lovely and everything looks hand painted. Every land Geron and Nuri travel to offer players a new visual experience and while the game leans towards a darker tone things still remain vibrant. Be it in a beautiful forest or a death-filled ogre camp, there is great attention to detail everywhere. What isn’t that amazing, however, are animations especially when characters talk. This may be because the game is from Germany so perhaps the lips move to fit German better, but I don’t think that it is the case. I just feel the mouth movements seemed very generic and don’t match the English dialogue well. And the voice acting is also hit or miss, I was fine with it for the most part but it isn’t anything to be remembered. The music fit the game and I liked it but the soundtrack is not memorable.

I hate to sound overly critical of
because it is not a bad game, I enjoyed myself as I played it. But I was hoping for more from it, especially with how gorgeous the artwork was, I was hoping the story at least matched it. What we end up with is a mediocre point and click game that looks beautiful. It has in game achievements that also translate to Steam achievements but many are annoying and at worst tedious, like breaking something one hundred times. One also requires you to play the game twice, pointless, as the game has no replay value. You can also enjoy the Steam trading cards if you fancy. If you see this game on sale then I recommend it but you may also want to grab the sequel as well because the ending is rather abrupt and leaves you with a few unanswered questions.

Oh man, this game. I've now played this game 3 times through on Normal/Dark/Insane and am still missing a few sidequests that are only available on certain plot decisions. This game is massive and very well done. Here are some random pros & cons for things that immediately come to mind:
Gorgeous. This game is gorgeous. Especially if you grab an improved textures mod. (see related con)
Story-rich. The story is grandiose and tons of fun to be a part of. There are quite a few story-altering decisions you will make throughout the game as well, providing a dynamic and involved experience.(one decision determines a good third of the game that differs completely should you have chosen differently) There were a couple choices where I had to pause the game for like 20 minutes while trying to decide what I wanted to do. Intense stuff. LISTEN TO ALL DIALOGUE, TALK TO EVERYONE. You won't regret it.
Combat is very dynamic and an absolute blast. You really need to think about the best way to approach certain encounters. Alchemy can alter things drastically for example, so don't skimp on the potions/oils(especially on higher difficulties!). Certain enemies need to be approached certain ways, some are very resistant to sword or magic, some can shield up and block all damage so you need to approach them from another direction or use a specific sign, etc... Very well done and very well thought out by the development team.
Game starts out pretty damn difficult during the prologue. You start very weak and then slowly gain strength until all at once, you are suddenly quite over-powered. This could be a pro or con depending on what sort of gaming experience you prefer. There *are* a couple mods that smooth out the combat system and even out your ascension to badassness, although I would highly recommend you not touch any sort of mods til you've completed your first playthrough.
Quite a bit of nudity and corny sex scenes. May or may not be your cup of tea.
While the game is gorgeous, it is also quite resource intensive. I had serious issues with my 560m, almost unplayable. My desktop's gtx 780 had no issues. Check out benchmarks for your specific card and make sure you can run it decently.
QTE's(Quicktime Events) are a part of this game and they are lame. There are a couple encounters where if you miss a QTE prompt, you are dead. Playing on insane, this feels cheap and lame. *Luckily*, You can turn these off via Gameplay Options, which I would highly recommend.
Prologue is pretty damn linear. Don't let this turn you off though. It's necessary for the introduction of the story. Make it to chapter 1 and things improve greatly.
A lot of people have reported that the controls feel "clunky", especially during the prologue. I was one of these people. But seriously, stick with it. It gets better. Also, graphic settings affect control sensitivity. Higher = better response. I also played the game with a controller, so that could have some impact.

Pros

Cons

-Not Giant Mechas/Godzillas
-Certain weapons are tied to certain Classes
Ok, so overall the game is NOT as good as EDF 2017. Sure, the game looks great, but the designs are highly "western". They've removed those chromed Hectors and flying ships (like in 1950s sci-fi movies) for more Americanized grimdark enemies. Very little color in the game at times, ants and spiders practically blend into the Detroit setting (which is the ONLY setting). You play a very short amount of levels in city that looks the same. No green fields with small buildings, no ravines, no beach areas, no different city changes, no underground missionss.

"Dust: An Elysian Tail" (developed by Dean Dodrill) is a 2D action-platformer RPG released on Steam in 2013 and Xbox 360 (Live Arcade) in 2012. You get to play an anthropomorphic samurai in a well-animated picturesque world made of various anthropomorphic animals (and a talking sword), gradually uncovering your mysterious past as you gain skills, craft items, collect treasures and complete quests.
On the hardest of all difficulty levels (hardcore, tough, normal, casual), I completed 100% of this game (including all Steam achievements), which often proved impossible without impeccable gameplay (especially at the beginning). To beat the final boss, I needed to be at the maximum level (i.e. level 60); and it was still a pretty intense challenge. I got about 40 hours of gameplay out of this game, but I wasted about half that time attempting to progress and achieve things, only to die and have to restart from the last save.
Going beyond the frustrations of my many failures in the game, I can't think of anything in this game that I didn't either like or love, except maybe the music, which was just "o.k." as it did at least fit the atmosphere well enough. In my opinion, the story was fairly original and its delivery would often get as intense as the game's battles.
As the main character (and with your "sidekick"), you can potentially create many powerful combos as you grow your set of skills. By the end of the game, you may find yourself flying and slashing through a pretty big area, killing several monsters at once with your sword and magic powers (making combos in the triple digits). There's even an optional side-quest and achievement that expects you to make a combo of at least 1000. You may not have to worry too much about creating combos though. I often found myself accidentally failing combos, only to create other combos that still helped me cause damage. You gradually get the hang of the battle's ebb and flow; and combos become second-nature.
From what I could tell, you can immerse yourself into the story by choosing "casual" mode and listening to character interactions between the quick-and-easy battles and dungeon quests. If you just don't care about the story though, then you can skip (through the pause menu) any cutscene that suddenly comes-up, so that you can go straight to kicking-butt again. Battles are the most fun on "hardcore" mode, but expect to hear the main character's death rattle a whole lot (from 1-hit kills) while in that mode. The game normally costs $15 USD on Steam (as of this post) and I'd say that it's worth the price overall. Although, it probably depends on whether or not all of the above sounds appealing to you at all.

I generally don't write reviews for games, but I felt like this one deserved some genuine praise.  It isn't perfect by any means, but I have enjoyed every moment of the game, frustration and all and want to give my sincere appreciation to the developers.  Haven't given co-op multiplayer a try yet, but the fact they put it in at all is pretty awesome in my book.
It has a great visual style, though optimization might be lacking a bit as it drops frames on my PC which is a custom built, higher-end gamine rig.  The music and audio are fantastic.  I didn't buy the soundtrack, but I honestly might.  Voice over is mostly short sound bites made to sound like ghostly Japanese as queues for who is talking.  The story is conveyed largely through text bubbles and short animated flashbacks.  This didn't bother me, but at times characters were 'talking' during gameplay with text on the lower portion of the screen, trying to murder fools while story elements are being conveyed was distracting (this is rarely an issue though).
As you play, you unlock abilites that make the game easier as you find scrolls that give you skill points.  This gives the game a relatively compelling feeling of progression as the tools in your arsenal expand to make dispatching foes easier and more satisfying.  Level design is varied and generally really good as there typically several ways to approach each one.  End of mission stats and rank are rewarded based on kills, if you set off alarms, enemy bodies found, collectibles, etc.  For those pacifists out there, it would seem there is an option to play pure stealth and try to avoid leaving a trail of carnage in your wake.  Not really my style but if there's an achievement for it, I'll go back.  :)
If you played any of the Tenchu games on Playstation or Xbox back in the day, this game is very much in the same vein as those titles.  If you enjoyed those titles, then I can easily recommend giving this game a shot.  If you enjoy stealth games in general, then this is kind of a no-brainer.  This is a great indie game, and I couldn't be happier to have it in my library!

Magnetic: Cage Closed is a first person physics puzzle platformer that tries to imitate Portal a little too hard.
Unfortunately it lacks the charm and fun gameplay that made Portal so enjoyable. The story is rather similar to Portal but unfortunately the writing is nowhere near as good. To exacerbate the issue the game also suffers from some pretty bad voice acting.
The core gameplay is also very similar to Portal. You process through a series of testing chambers while solving some simple puzzles. However, this time around you armed with a Magnet Gun instead of the Portal Gun. Magnet gun can either pull or push magnetic objects and you can also use it to boost your jumps.
The puzzle design isn't particularly inspired and most of the puzzles are rather easy to solve. The gameplay also suffers from the poorly implemented magnet gun physics.
Finally, the game looks rather dated for a 2015 release. The models tend to be blocky and the textures are often low resolution.
Not recommended, just replay one of the Portal games instead.
The good:

The bad:

- Wonky magnet gun physics

I would call this a supernatural Splinter Cell with Assassin's Creed dynamics, in a setting of ancient Asia. I can't compare it to Tenchu, since I don't play on, nor own any consoles. So, why those two games? Because light, shadow, and stealth are important, killing is (so far) optional if you can make it, but the swift assassin-style killing mechanics really befit the character.
I find the gameplay very efficient, refreshing, and fluent. You will not miss jumping at all, unlike some reviews have stated, you will not need it. In fact, it would likely be a hindrance, or a way for you to accidentally get discovered hitting the wrong key if jump were available. The game is well paced, balanced and overall fair. I don't even mind dying and having to start from the last save point; which is rare. You can try out different strategies, see what works and what doesn't, or stick to your strategy and just pace your approach right. There isn't one way fits all, there is the way that works best for you.
You will find new abilities along the way, and slowly progress in what you can do. A keyword is patience and stealth. Ideally kill only if you need to.
As far as performance is concerned, I find this game very well optimized. My system is slightly below or at par with the requirements, and the gameplay is absolutely smooth (Core2Quad Q9400 2.66 GHz, 8 GB RAM, GeForce GTX 660Ti 2 GB, Windows 7 x64, nVidia drivers 350.12). All graphics options on default (high), with motion blur and vsync turned off. I enabled adaptive sync within the driver as well as triple buffering, shader cache, and set max pre-rendered frames to 1.
So, in conclusion, if you like well paced stealth games with relative freedom, and good progression, then this is for you. Don't even think twice. Another plus is the very helpful developer who definitely reads comments and responds with helpful advice. That is rare and very much appreciated!

This is a puzzle game at heart. If you line up 3 or more coloured tiles they disappear from the grid, they disappear. In much the same fashion as Bejeweled, new tiles then fall down from the top of the grid to fill in the now empty space. The only way this differs from Bejeweled is that instead of swapping two tiles, you instead can drag any row left or right, or any column up or down in its entirety to make a match.
However, this is only half of the game, and is frankly the boring bit. Each set of tiles you clear does something different, with the aim of keeping your man running through the dungeon above the board as long as possible. So sword and staff attack monsters, shield defends you, keys open locks, backpack provides items, and wood and stone help you upgrade your base. So this balance of keeping the right tiles on the screen, especially when different monsters are weaker to different attacks, is what keeps this game enthralling.
That said, it does have some problems with artificial difficulty. Your health/stamina is represented by how far along the top of the screen your man is. Once this runs out, you have to restart the level for another try at the high score. However, as your man runs through the dungeon, the time it takes to slide backwards along the track  gets shorter and shorter, decreasing your max health no matter how well you are playing. As a result, you often need to start at a later checkpoint to have any chance of progressing to a higher score. I'd have much preferred just a straight run through increasing power/health monsters than a backwards slide down my character's own abilities.
So overall:
Negatives:
The match game is Bejeweled and requires little strategy.
Decreasing power through out a run gets on my nerves.
Positives:
The dungeon combat system is inspired and brings the strategy that Bejeweled lacks.
The power increase due to upgrades between runs is well thought through and well paced.
If this game had an endless mode, that is a mode where monster health/attack power went up constantly until you die, I'd recommend this in an instant.
But without this it lacks replay value as you feel like you're hitting a hard-coded wall instead of the limits of your own ability.
So a reasonable game for 3$, is enjoyable, just don't expect too much playtime from it.  7/10

In a market already saturated by great MOBAs OMDU falls flat.
There's no compelling reasons to choose OMDU over Smite, if you're looking for a 3rd person MOBA, or Heroes of the Storm, League of Legends, or DOTA2. Yes, there's traps, but they're so incidental to the gameplay that they're almost not even worth thinking about.
The traps, by necessity can't just outright slaughter waves as you'd expect from the game's sister titles. Counter to a traditional MOBA where mobs fight each other in lanes, in OMDU the traps are the only thing standing in the way of the mobs, and because once the traps are placed they're untouchable by the other team they serve merely to reduce pressure on one lane; you still have to run back to do something about the wave. This results in a large portion of the gameplay that simply doesn't feel good (not that you're given the space to design fun mazes even if it did).
Remove the traps from the equation and you're left with tepid, uninspired PvP that feels a pillowfight, floaty and not very impactful, and a leveling system that's easily unbalanced and makes it hard to recover if you're behind. There's simply no reason to choose OMDU over a more refined, better balanced MOBA at the moment.

The forced attempts at humour also are not helping very much.
Let me summarise the story for you:
The bad guy, bad guy dies but not really, the main protagonist goes from zero to hero and sets on the quest to protect oval-faced fairy, who looks like a human girl and acts as hippie junky with IQ of a shoe and no regard for danger.
Bad guy trick the girl, turns her into a musical instrument, our hero goes on and saves her by using trickery, and turns her from the musical instrument into an animal (no, not the goat unfortunately for him).

Riptide GP2 is a racing game in which you earn money and XP as you race. You use the money to buy upgrades and more jet-skis, and the XP lets you level up, which gives you money and SP that then can be used to learn new tricks and passive abilities. The usefulness of buying jet-skis and upgrades is pretty obvious, and tricks/passive abilities are necessary to build boost and earn points in the freestyle events.
I've played most of the game and I doubt I'll beat it anytime soon because unlocking the last set of events requires  getting first place in almost every prior event, barring three events in which you have to place second, which makes the game feel like a massive grind. This is especially true if you made the same mistake I did and bought a not so great bike towards the  end, as they are really expensive and such an error can set you back quite a bit while you save up for a better bike.
This  wouldn't be so bad if it weren't for the freestyle events, which require you to get a certain score doing tricks within the time limit. However, the issue with that is that the first time you see these events it will be very hard to succeed because you have few tricks and repeating tricks earns you fewer points. this is especially troublesome towards the end because you can only buy tricks with SP, so you basically have to grind until you can buy tricks.
I typically enjoy the grind, and I will keep playing the game on and off until I eventually beat it, but it's definitely something you should know about this game.
Graphically, the game is nothing spectacular by today's standards, but I liked the aesthetic and the game runs great on my laptop.
As for the gameplay itself,  the campaign is fun and the AI is challenging until you buy your way to a much better bike, the  tracks are varied, even if their themes are sparse, and there's a fair variety of vehicles even if you should only buy half of them untiil you have fully upgraded your best watercraft. The online multiplayer is dead and their third mode is a neat way to challenge your friends with your best time on the available racks, but that requires your friends also owning the game to participate, so I could not even try it.
Ultimately, I recommend the  game because I am having fun with it, but I strongly suggest buying it during a sale.

I simply loved Hydro Thunder. So, when they said this was made by the same company, I was very interested. But, after playing it for a bit, I'm a little disappointed. I think the designers missed the entire point of what made Hydro Thunder FUN. It was the over-the-top and wacky environments, the huge drop offs, the sound of the jet engines engaging, the massive jumps, the hidden passageways... just simply EVERYTHING about it. It just made your eyes pop out and made you giggle at every turn.
But, sadly, all of that is gone in Riptide GP2. There is no joy like there was in HT. The environments in Riptide are stale and sterile. I haven't found any hidden passages or anything fun about the racetracks at all. They just seem bland and utilitarian. Gameplay is straightforward, and feels underwhelming. There is a bit of sensation of the water moving your craft around a bit, but it just doesn't feel like anything special. Graphics are decent, but about as interesting as looking at your refridgerator. Sound is, well, just simply sound. Nothing visceral and heart-thumping.
To earn boost, you have to do tricks, ala SSX. But why? What was wrong with the boost system in HT? Surplanting the boost system with a long list of unnecessary tricks is a complete distraction to the racing experience and isn't particularly fun.
Now, granted, I"m not really far into the game yet. But that's another thing. I SHOULD be much further along by this time. I have to keep racing the same races over and over and over again to earn upgrades, because there's no chance of affording a new craft anytime soon. And the upgrades don't seem to improve my times. So I just have to keep doing the races over and over until I get lucky or something. It definitely feels like the type of game where "you'll win when the game DECIDES to let you win, and not a moment before then." Which means absolute tedium, frustration, boredom, and irritation, which is the opposite of FUN.
It's just not as good, not as fun, not as engaging, not as smile-producing, nor as memorable as Hydro Thunder. Not by a nautical mile.
There's ♥♥♥♥ing dinosaurs in it. Don't think, just buy it.

It’s a fun way to kill time. If you pick it up on sale for $2.09 like I did, you really can’t feel too badly ripped off.  Buy it cheap. Play it in short bursts of 30-45 minutes as a warm up to something more tactical and it should last you a solid 10-15 hours before it becomes tired.
Track selection is limited. Watercraft selection though limited has a lot of customizable upgrades in a market that is under catered.  I like racing games though I’m tired of racing in cars. I want jet skis, weaponized hovercraft, airplanes, even snowmobiles, and this sates my appetite in short bursts.
There is a reasonable variety of unlocks, upgrades and tricks that should allow for some reasonable replayability which should double for every friend you can talk into buying it. The VR ghost challenge like feature is fun, if you can get the game cheap for yourself and some friends.
Apparently there is also a sequel which is third in the series overall called ‘Riptide Renegade’ which looks far superior, I have every intention of purchasing it when it goes on sale for $4.99 or under until then if you like aquatic arcade racers, you really can’t go passed Riptide GP 2.
Give it a half hour spin twice a week and the fun factor should last you 3 months or 6 months to a year depending on
how competitive you are with your friends.  Expect online multiplayer to be dead and if you go out of your way to unlock and upgrade every hydro jet, then god knows.
On weekends I generally use Riptide GP2 as a warm up before running headlong into Hand of Fate, rolling over to Elder Scrolls Legends and finishing up with a session of Street Racing Syndicate which when compared to Riptide GP2 is effectively like  taking a hot bath and dropping a Valium.
If Ii put 26 hours into this game over 12 months, then I’ve had my fun with it. In short bursts it’s perfectly serviceable and compulsively playable if you’re as keen to unlock and upgrade all the hydro jets as I am.  The core gameplay loop is repetitive, soothing and an even satisfying no-brainer.
I’ll buy a lot of games in bulk, I’ll play them for between half an hour and an hour and a half and I’ll end up refunding about 80% of them.  I don’t care about price, it’s the principle. Life is too short for bad games. If it’s not fun I ask for money back.
I wouldn’t pay full price for Riptide GP2, especially not since Riptide Renegade is out. If you can get it on sale and pick it up cheap you really can’t lose.  I paid $2.99 for Cards of Cthulhu and that stopped being fun around the 45 minute mark. Riptide GP2 suffers no such problem.
At the time of this writing I’ve put 3-hours into Riptide GP2 and I’m not tired of it. Even if I quit next week I still feel I’ve gotten my money’s worth out of it.  It’s not worth $7 when Renegade is worth $10. It was definitely worth $2.09 on sale.
It’s not the prettiest game,  it’s not the best optimized, its showing its mobile heritage, its age is obvious and its soundtrack is generic however in spite of all of the games more than noticeable flaws it’s still a fun time-killer with an arcade feel, probably aimed at time poor old muppets like me.
If the sequel is half this good I’d even consider dropping a fiver for it in the good faith they’ve fixed the floaty controls, upped the graphics and gotten some better background music.  If you can pick it up for less than the price of a cup of coffee… do it.  You will not regret it.

Edit: April 26- I figured I'd try yet again to play Spintires, and guess what? It actually is working for me again.
Do I still love this game? Sure.
Am I going to change the recommendation? No.
Why? Because the game is going to Xbox and PlayStation.
What's the issue with that? Let me explain.
You see, Spintires is a great game with lots of promise. But I cannot understand why anyone would think that a still-beta game should be released on consoles while its PC counterpart only gets minor and sparse updates and has a severe lack of actual objective. Multiplayer seems fun (although it still never works for me), but other than that, I can't see any reason someone would want this game in its condition with no mods. That's the only thing that keeps me coming back.
The other reason I despise the console releases is that this game IS NOT FINISHED IN THE SLIGHTEST, and can't seem to fix jack shi`ite in this game, yet they insist they split their power into trying to branch out into two other systems and tackle three sets of issues at once. Have you ever tried to build two project vehicles at the same time, while trying to keep your daily driver in barely running condition? Yeah, I know from experience that it doesn't work well when you've got nearly no power or money behind it.
Tl;dr- The devs are trying too hard to expand themselves with this game far too fast while trying to grab as much money as they can and letting the modding community continue to limp the game home on two cylinders. I do love the game, but I can't let anyone I know blow thrty bucks on this beta.

I do however recommend playing with a controller even though keyboard and mouse works great, controller is still better.
You will probably want to play it once because once you know the story there will be no point in playing again so if you played on casual you are simply wasted your time because it was too easy and you can finish it in few hours. I'm thoroughly enjoying this game so far. The gameplay is relatively simple, but it makes you feel like an absolute badass. Would definitely recommend to anyone who liked Dishonered, or stealth games in general. Well worth the £15, definitely worth the £13.50 I paid in the sale.
EDIT
I feel like I didn't have a full opinion of the game before, so here we go. Aragami is a beautiful, simplistic game, but its simplicity does not detract from the experience. Crouching on rooftops and descending great heights with an aerial kill feels fantastic, and sneaking up behind someone, and essentially making them a human bomb, is such an incredibly fun thing to do and has entertained me for longer than it should have. These are just 2 out of so many more different ways to deal with enemies. Aragami is a genuine stealth game; you die in one hit, with no way to defend yourself other than quickly shadow leaping, or sometimes perhaps a lucky spam of the spacebar.
The visuals of Aragami are wonderful. I found myself thinking of Amaterasu a lot playing through the game, sort of ironic considering she's the goddess of the sun and in this you play as a shadow assassin. Anyway, it's a pleasure to look at.
Of course, Aragami is not a perfect game, but nothing is. Maybe it's just me being a bit of a weeb, but I didn't really find much wrong with this title, and any faults I did notice were few and far between.
So, in conclusion, I think this game is easily worth the money you'll pay for it. Aragami is a joy to play through, and the level editor adds a level of replayability you just couldn't get otherwise. If you're considering buying this game, now is the time! The £7 ish is a steal for such an amazing game. 10/10, would 100% recommend.

Natural Selection 2 is one of those very old, very hardcore games with a small, but dedicated community. What awaits you is a deep experience that goes beyond the average shooter, requiring good aim, good teamwork, and good strategy.
If the "small dedicated" community part scares you, don't be afraid. People grossly exaggerate how bad the community is, when I've had only one time where someone raged at me for being a noob. What you'll more often find are passionate players who are willing to assist and help people new to the game.
Your first games will be difficult; they will be hard and confusing. But if you are up to the task, a deep game with a helpful community awaits you.
As for the game itself, it can best be described as a starcraft game. Zerg vs. terran, but the players are zerglings and the marines with a commander on each team. New players tend to always be more comfortable with the marines as they're more identifiable with other shooter games, but trust me, the aliens are just as interesting and fun to play. Both sides are very balanced,  But the marines are a bit simpler at first.
For marines, check your corners, nooks, and crannies. The best way to kill the aliens is to not let them sneak up on you. In fights, it's better to aim at the skulk that ISN'T attacking you, but your teammate. You can then both keep each other safe, as it's easier to aim the farther away the skulk is. ALAWAYS BUY A WELDER! Welder = armor = live longer = more shooty shoot. Welders are also dirt cheap.
As for aliens, group up and attack simultaneously. Only attack if you're sure you'll get something good out of it, don't blindly rush the marines. Use odd angles to pounce on them, and sack yourself for the good of the team. It might not be glamorous, but the first skulk who gets shot first is just as valuable as the skulk who came from behind and got the two kills. Even as a new player, you can use yourself as a distraction, and trust me, you'll be appreciated.
~
To wrap up, this is a hard, deep game with a dedicated but small community. That community is willing to help you. The game is also willing to help you. The game also has 'rookie' or new player only servers so you aren't getting butt♥♥♥♥ed by veterans with 2000+ hours in the game. Definately worth $60, but always way cheaper than that :)

Before the review, quick note about myself.
- 16 hours played at time of writing.
- All achievements, All S ranks
- Trained Scriptwriter
But you're here for the game review, so let's get onto that.
This is a stealth game, and it's all it tries to me. If you're specifically looking for a 'ninja' game, be aware this game does not include the following;
-Jumping
-Dodging
-Rolling
-Combat
But that's ok! As a spirit of vengeance, here's what you do have;
-Conjuring Shadows
-Frequent short controlled teleports
-Assassinations
-Various other powers such as decoys and traps
This is not one of those stealth games where it's afraid it's too simple and that you as a player are going to get bored so it continues to tack on more and more mechanics and enemy types to a point of feeling unfair or too frustrating.
What it does is confidently give you TWO enemy types and interesting geometry. Later on there may be parts that make you want to pull your hair out or just stare at what you need to do with bewilderment, but at no point will that game ever make you exclaim '♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t'. It sets it's rules and sticks by them being very difficult yet fair. The one exception will be mentioned later in the review.
While some may think only two enemy types aren't enough, this game takes a page from Portal's book and really, expertly, uses what it has to create interesting levels.
The levels are also fairly open, too often in a stealth game the choice to not kill anyone and ghost a level is far harder than the lethal route. But with the open levels, if you want the medal for killing all enemies, you need to make the choice and actually hunt everywhere, not just within the linear path you traveled. As such, going for a ghost run is about the same challenge as going for the kill all run for very different and equally satisfying reasons.
My only real complaint is the lack of feedback during the final boss. It's very difficult to tell if you are doing it correctly, or even making any progress. It's the one time the game breaks it's own rules and could use some further tweaking in patches down the road.
Visuals, Music and Story: Subjective, but I liked them.
A similar title would be Styx: Master of Shadows, if you liked that, or stealth focused games in general, you'll like this.
*Minor edits now that all achievements achieved.

In a market already saturated by great MOBAs OMDU falls flat.
There's no compelling reasons to choose OMDU over Smite, if you're looking for a 3rd person MOBA, or Heroes of the Storm, League of Legends, or DOTA2. Yes, there's traps, but they're so incidental to the gameplay that they're almost not even worth thinking about.
The traps, by necessity can't just outright slaughter waves as you'd expect from the game's sister titles. Counter to a traditional MOBA where mobs fight each other in lanes, in OMDU the traps are the only thing standing in the way of the mobs, and because once the traps are placed they're untouchable by the other team they serve merely to reduce pressure on one lane; you still have to run back to do something about the wave. This results in a large portion of the gameplay that simply doesn't feel good (not that you're given the space to design fun mazes even if it did).
Remove the traps from the equation and you're left with tepid, uninspired PvP that feels a pillowfight, floaty and not very impactful, and a leveling system that's easily unbalanced and makes it hard to recover if you're behind. There's simply no reason to choose OMDU over a more refined, better balanced MOBA at the moment.

I find it rather odd that this game has a mixed rating.  Allow me to change that with this review.
To begin with, I saw Markiplier playing this game, and seeing it was a free game, I thought to give it a try.  What I experienced is a MOBA that innovates the formula in a different way by combining tower defense strategy with it.  I enjoyed building my own trap schemes to kill enemy minions and being able to choose my own minions to send to battle rather than the staple soldiers that just charge forward and attack the first thing they see.
There are currently two modes: Survival and Siege.  Survival is a 5 player Co-op to defend your rift rom enemy waves and after an x number of waves, another portal will open allowing minions to charge from that portal and thus needing to split the team to make up for a lack of defense at that segment.  Siege is a 10 player PvP that acts similarly to Survival, but the key difference is that there is an opposing team of players trying to take out your rift while you do the same to theirs.
Minions are a wide variety of high defense, long range, and quick Get-From-Point-A-To-Point-B mindset.  Choosing which minions get sent out can change the attack strategy quite a bit whether you want a bulwark team of bears, ogres or giants that can take on any hero, trap or guardian or a speedy team of satyrs and kobolds that can take down enemy gates faster so they can reach the opposing team's rift portal.
Traps themselves are also quite effective and the fact that some heroes have their own unique trap or glyph adds more personality to the game.  One gripe I do have for traps is that some can be godawful expensive and being that you want to be able to add to the trap scheme as quickly as possible, it can be a setback to wait for enough coins for a better trap, but it's just the case of compromise whether to put something down now or save up for it later.
Finally the heroes, while not at SMITE or LOL levels of variety (yet), offer a unique hero for any occasion.  I find myself liking Stinkeye and Blackpaw the most, the former with his intricate ability to use totems to give him a edge in any situation and the latter for his ability to move quickly on the map and quickly wittle down any enemy's health.
Overall, it's a very fun game and a very fun MOBA, if that's your thing.  If you want a change from the typical 3 lanes, 3 towers in each lane, rehashed schematic, give OMCU a try.

Once you reach an ending, that's it. Your save is done. You cannot resume from any point to  go for the other endings, you need to play the entire game through again. And when most of the endings are literally just "You died", this feels like a massive slap in the face and removes all drive to see any of the others.
The game is 3 hours long, which is short enough to leave you disappointed at how short the whole experience was, but also long enough to remove all urge to slog through the game again to see another ending,
All in all, for some fairly meh puzzles, many weak endings, and a short playtime, this game is definitely not worth its normal price.

Between this and Renowned Explorers, it's been a surprisingly good month for indie strategy/rpg games.
This one has you take control of a squad of super powered troops, think 40k space marines and you'd feel very much at home. You take your squad through turn based missions not unlike Xcom tactical phase or Jagged Alliance (if you remember Laser Squad then that's an even better comparison) and the game uses both an AP and MP system as well as an overheating system (keep running around, firing wildly and using abilities wantonly will quickly overheat a Templar's suit and cook the pilot inside!).
MP+AP might confuse some people at first as AP uses up MP too, but it also allows you to take more complex moves then allowed in say..xcom unless you have a ton of perks. Ex: you can have a Templar throw a grenade for 1AP, fall back with remaining MP then end your turn by using up all your APs into firing action.
Combined with overheating, this means optimal use of your Templars can be trickier then it seems especially in hectic situations. If I'm making it out to be tedious though, rest assured, it isn't. It enhances gameplay and contributes to the feeling you are commanding a squad of walking tanks.
Inbetween missions you unlock equipment, abilities and new Templar classes in a tech tree of sorts as well as levelling up and gearing up your Templars. At first the options are limited as you'd expect, but you quickly start unlocking stuff and your Templars are able to carry more equipment as they level, increasing build flexibility as the game goes on.
The game can be played with ironman settings and permadeath if desired.
The best points of this game are definitely the squad development which is far more extensive then any other title of this genre I've played and lots of action, you'll quickly rack up hundreds of dead xenos.
As a 40k fan I was quite partial to the design and feel of the Templars themselves too, a couple of missions has human enemies and/or allies and the difference between normal squishy humans and your power armored behemoths is quite satisfying.
Graphics is probably going to be the biggest barrier for people who care about that. Visuals are perfectly serviceable and clear and I like the blood splatter and gooey messes aliens leave, or for that matter the bloodied wrecks of dead Templars, but I recognize that people born a lot later then me might have more picky tastes so check out screenshots and see if that doesn't bother you.
Pros:
-Exelent rpg mechanics and squad development mechanics, so many games have the rpg tag yet have rather shallow level up mechanics and this isn't one of them. Tooling up your templars is just a joy in this.
-Linked to the above, you can respect stats and talents any time, so no fear of making "bad" builds and you can experiment more.
-Missions are nicely varied in the objectives and challenges you need to overcome.
-Great gameplay overall.
Cons:
-Graphics are clear and functional but unlikely to impress. Animations as well can be described as such.
-Apart from maybe 1-2 music tracks, don't recall the music to have been particularly memorable.
-There is a story and even some choices to make but this isn't really a game you play for the story. That said, I found the Templar lineage part of the background quite cool and liked how it justified respeccing Templars within the lore.
Overall as far as squad based tactical games go this is a really good title, 100% reccomend it.

is a point & click adventure game that's not easy to review. There are both good and bad things to say about every single aspect of this game.
For example, the graphics. The backgrounds are very nice. But character animation is just awkward. And every time any of the characters is talking, you'd swear the developers did everything they could to make sure the character's mouth
fits the words being spoken. It's uncanny!
Or take the voice acting: some of it is very decent and some of it is almost cringeworthy.
I felt another duality with the setting, the story and the characters. They certainly showed a basic charm that made me want to continue playing for the better part of the game. But after a while I found that
never went beyond that basic charm: the story never unfolded much after the basic premise was explained at the beginning of the game, the characters never showed any real depth although there seemed to be plenty of room for that, and at the end the story just seemed to drag on as if the game had outstayed its welcome.
Same for the puzzles. In the first half of the game, the puzzles are logical and therefore fun to solve. After that, more and more puzzles are far-fetched and therefore frustrating to solve. The only way to solve some of the later puzzles would be to just try everything on everything, or to look up a guide. Both options mean taking away a considerable part of the fun of playing an adventure game.
Sure, you can use a 'hint' button, marking all the objects you can interact with. But there's a Steam Achievement for not using that button a lot, so you end up not using it at all if you want the achievement. Also, the problem is almost never that you missed an object you can interact with, but that you just can't guess what the developers were thinking. The solution usually is going back and talking to everyone and clicking with every item on every object you can interact with... again... and again after that.
You see, there are a
of 'preconditions' to this game's puzzles. Often you realize what you need to do but you can't perform an action until you did something else or talked to someone again. Often it was clear to me what I was supposed to do but Geron couldn't do it... yet, so off I went looking to fulfil the precondition, which often had its own preconditions. In the end, this results in a lot of 'trying everything on everything' over and over again, until you get the 'chain of events' right, exactly according to the progressive scheme the developers had in mind.
It doesn't help that the game itself gives you contradictory clues. Two examples:

makes it a game you can both love and hate simultaneously. So do I recommend it or not? Okay I'm not even close to finished with this game.  However, I can imagine that some people might be nibbling on whether to purchase this or not, so here is my first impression.
Summary:
Pros: I like the theme, I like the combat, I like the customization of the different character's abilities.  So far I'm definitely on track to get my money's worth and then some.
Cons: Personalities between the different templar are not very distinct (more about that below)
If you like being a paladin/templar type character and like commanding squads in turn based combat I think you'll really enjoy this game.  Consider that this is an early impression, that may be subject to change later on.
Detailed Version:
I bought this game for the promise of commanding a team of badass templar/paladin type characters.  Any time I have the option in an RPG to play a paladin type class, that's what I go with.  It was the theme of this game that really hooked me.  You get to play the good guys, and fight some mean old space aliens.  Nothing wrong with that.  I do hope that as the game goes on I get the opportunity to explore the belief system of the templars a little.  I like to geek out about that kind of stuff.
The meat of the game is the turned based combat in which you use your templars to fight against Xenos.  The combat works well.  It's easy to jump right in to the action and pick it up as you go.  I don't think its revolutionary or anything but that doesn't bother me.
Coupled with the combat is the all important customization.  Each level you get points that help you specialize in different types of abilities.  This is another main draw for me.  Rather than just a few different units with set roles there is the potential for enormous specialization.  At just over two hours I haven't even scratched the surface of the what I can do.
The problem so far with the game is that none of the templar characters are distinctive.  The "captain" of your squad has generic dialogue that makes he or she indistinguishable from your other squadmates.  The captain doesn't have an established name or backstory, none of them do.  They're all here to protect the remaining humans from the Xenos, and any other threats.  That's it.  I'll have to see how the rest of the game unfolds, but my main criticism for now is that I'm not really invested as I should be in the plight of these generic templars.  Some humor, maybe a character who's faith is challenged by seeing his people go through this, or anything to change it up a little would be appreciated.
I'll update this post once I feel I can do the game justice with a full review.  With my criticisms in mind I still say with confidence that I like this game, and I think others will too.  I definitely look forward to playing through this interesting game, and leading my noble templar to victory.

In a few words, Templar Battleforce is a 2D XCOM set in a backdrop that is heavily inspired by Warhammer 40k. It is somewhat rough around the edges but is surprisingly easy to get into if you have a general idea of what to expect.
The core tactical combat gameplay is very well done and even exceeds games like XCOM in some areas such as flexibility and variety. While the internal mechanics of combat suffer from the opaqueness of the dice rolls system and of the damage mitigation formula, the game offsets this with ample toolips and a set of starting missions which guide new players through all they need to know to enjoy the game. Extra praise is deserved for both the tooltips and tutorials as these two elements are rarely well done in indie games and are often quite mediocre in AAA releases.
Combat itself is familiarly intuitive and draws much of its allure from the fairly deep customization options and progression available. First off you have a sort of tech tree which controls the pool of equipment, active abilities, and recruitable templar classes available. Every templar in your band belongs to a class which defines which active abilities are available and which equipment can be equipped. In addition to equipment and talents (active abilities), every templar has two sets of defining statistics which can be increased by one point each level. You will end up customizing talents, equipment, and attributes for each templar every time he levels up which will be every 1-2 missions. This is so since you can freely respec any templar between missions and you will want to do this when new abilities or equipment become available, which happens almost after every mission depending on how you choose to progress the tech tree. This opens ups the ability to experiment freely with your squad build and keeps you from worrying too much about planning your progression ahead of time.
I was also very happy with the mission design so far (about 10 missions in). The length of each mission is right on target with about 30 mins on average and the overall pacing is excellent so far. The time I’m spending in mission and out of mission leveling my army is at a good ratio to prevent being fatigued with either aspect. The missions themselves don’t drag out with most missions aiming for around 15 turns on average to complete which keeps each turn and what you do in it very significant. The heat mechanic plays an important role here. Heat builds up from using abilities and moving and decreases a small amount each turn and will decrease a lot in a turn if no or almost no actions are taken during that turn. Maxing out on heat will start causing hitpoint damage to the templar so this helps keep the action tense makes you consider every action you take or don’t take during a turn.
I have a few small gripes with the game which affect my enjoyment of it in very limited ways. No ability to change keybindings is regrettable but not critical since the default scheme is workable if somewhat inconvenient. The way vision works could use improvement as your templars can only seem to see 5 squares away which can lead to very awkward ambushes. Enemies can attack the same turn they spawn which is annoying but since they don’t spawn in packs, for the most part, this is nowhere near as big an issue as it was in XCOM. There is plenty of room for the UI to be improved and enhanced with such features as moving the camera via mouse screen edge scrolling, highlighting interactable elements on mouseover, indicating which squares either your unit or an enemy unit can move to this turn or the enemy's next turn. The Devs have indicated that some of these fetures, edge scrolling in particular, will be added in future updates.
This is a game I would highly recommend to anyone who enjoys turn-based tactical RPGs in the style of the recent XCOM or going further back to Temple of Elemental Evil and Pool of Radiance. The story is very adequate for a game where the story is arguably not the main focus and works very well to build up the right atmosphere of tension and heroics and this is a type of game that benefits greatly from having that kind of backdrop. The ample depth of progression available for your “army” and each templar along with way the game encourages experimentation will keep most players hooked.

Sometimes the old ways are the best ways, especially when you refine the old ways and give them the polish they had back when old was new. Much is the case with Dust: An Elysian Tail
Dust is a 2D Sidescroller with an emphasis on metroidvania gameplay with an emphasis on fluid combat with added RPG traits like equipment and experience. You play as an unknown swordsman with no memory of who he is, on a quest to save the land from evil in a fully-voiced epic story. The story is provided through cutscenes and quests that guide you through the different areas, which are usually blocked off from each other by some barrier that requires an item located somewhere else. If you ever played Symphony of the Night or Super Metroid you know what to expect, though it's not quite as varied.
The combat is the main focus of the game. You have only one weapon, but it has many combos and moves you can perform with it. You have the choice between normal, fast attacks and the ability to spin your sword around like a buzzsaw, which done in the air spins you like a corkscrew and propels you forward. The spin also generates wind which sucks up pickups and blows things around.
You are accompanied by a flying creature named Fidget, who you can use to fire little projectiles which when sucked up by your tornado explode and do a variety of different attacks based on what type of projectile Figet has equipped. This drains a mana bar which recharges quick enough to be very devestating.
As you gain experience you can level a variety of stats: health, magic, etc. Experience comes as orbs that drop from fallen foes, as well as a bonus from your combos: a counter keeps track of your subsequent attacks which give bonus XP if you keep attacking. Leveling is important to keep up with the hordes of enemies everywhere which get stronger as the game goes.
The graphics are beautiful. It's a 2D game but the sprites are very VERY detailed, no 16-bit here. It's on par with games like Odin Sphere and Rayman Origins/Legends. You can just look at the screenshots and see how good it looks. It animates even better. The hardware requirements are slightly high for it, but it's worth it.
My one problem is the game tends to be slightly repetitive at some points, your sword attacks don't change much, so you'll be doing mostly the same moves through the whole game, but it's only a minor problem, since the combat can still get pretty intense.
I'd recommend this game to those who want a nice brawler with a good story to compliment it. Metroidvania lovers may find it lacking as far as that goes, but it's not too bad, just no Super Metroid. The combat is fun and varied dispite the lack of progression and theres plenty of challenge to be had. The story is great and the voice acting is well-done. It's decently priced and tends to go on sale a lot as well, so give it a try.

I'm not big on writing reviews to be honest.
I've only written one to date but this game deserves some attention.
I was very reluctant to purchase this game at first because there has just been so much low budget stuff on steam of late but because I had a little change in my wallet and the fact the game is priced correctly I decided to give it a go.
I have to say I am more than delighted with my purchase.
Trese Brothers have done a fantastic job, both with the game and with their community interaction.
They are a credit to game development and how dlc and support of a game should be managed.
The big guns out there, could learn a thing or two from these guys.
I won't go into the story or key features here as you can read all that from the game store page but I will say that the features they list are correct and the game does what it says.
The squad customization is truly inspiring, if a little daunting at first.
What I mean by that is, you don't have AAA graphics here so the tons of equipment and various skills and talents throw lots of numbers at you instead, which can be the daunting part.
However, given a little time and some missions into the game you start to come to terms with it all and then you can't help but want to play more missions to earn more RP to get that new piece of equipment or unlock that new Templar type.
What I like most about building your Templars though, is the fact that you really feel the difference in the changes you make.
A lot of games fail in that regard, you get excited about a new piece of kit or a skill and it proves totally underwhelming in actual combat. Not so here.
You get a new sword and all of a sudden you're single hit killing those low level Xeno's that used to need two hits.
Crowd control is a thing, and now your Templars are ready for it!
I feel the game also does a good job of satisfying the needs of players who like varying skill levels. I often see the arguments about casual and hardcore gamers now, well to me all games should be capable of supporting both by the use of difficulty levels.
Trese Brothers have added many difficulty options to suit all players and each level has a good description of what it actually does so the player isn't left guessing and trying to figure it out themselves (Yet another thing the Brothers should be commended on).
The game does so much right and the Trese Brothers really have poured love and affection into their game and will continue to do so (for Free, I might add).
*Edit: All of the below minor complaints from me have been patched and fixed and the devs continue to update the game. Brilliant devs and they deserve huge credit for everything they do.*
The very few minor things I disliked or found confusing about the game are already being responded to and were the majority have voiced an opinion are being changed.
Things like the speed of text during cutscenes, I'm slowing down in my old age and I find I am having to rush to read which breaks immersion of the story for me. It confused me because during missions you have to click to forward text and I felt this should be the same for cutscene text.
During the starting missions of the game, before you really know what is going on, you are asked to activate a gate but the switch you use to do this just looks like any other map flavour tile and the fact you can click on it is not immediately obvious.
I lost a few turns here, while thinking to myself, Alright I'm in the area you told me to go to, why isn't something happening? Because you didn't click the switch dumbass. Well it wasn't really that obvious game :D
The open and closed deployment before going into a mission confused me because whenever it said open I was clicking furiously around the screen for some way to take the Templars I wanted into the mission.
Before I finally went to the forums and read that 'open' means you can get a control point in the mission which will allow you to call in more Templars as opposed to actually allowing you to take what you want from the beginning.
And closed meant there would be no control point and what you get is what you have for the full mission. (This is something the devs are addressing and will be updated to allow you to take what Templars you want outside of what is actually needed for the scenario, like an engineer or scout etc).
Lastly the fact you left click on an enemy to see their stats but also left click on an enemy to attack them.
In the later missions of the game it is important to watch your Templars heat and balance moving, damage and other various skills.
So I often want to check the health left on an enemy to be sure I can kill it in another way before taking a shot with the same Templar again.
The current system can lead to mistakenly taking shots or using a skill you did not want to.
You can unselect your Templar or their skill before clicking on an enemy to avoid this but I feel it is a little clunky and could do with being changed.
As I said, these things are already been looked into by the Trese Brothers and overall I think they did an amazing job with this game.
I definitely recommend this game to anyone who loves Turn based strategy and squad building games and if you are new to the series and just dipping your toe in I couldn't fault you starting here.
Well worth a purchase.
I hope when the Trese Brothers grow into producing AAA titles they remain true to their current values and continue to price their games correctly and support them as they do now.
Thank you Trese Brothers.
I look forward to what I hope will be a very long and bright future for you in video games.

Warhammer 40k Dark Crusade is the 3rd entry into the Dawn of War series and its a strong contender in the RTS market despite not being as mainstream as the Starcraft or Stronghold series. If you enjoy games like Company of Heroes and Starcraft then this is a can't miss title.
The game is set on the planet Kronus where the Imperial Guard rule in the name of the Emperor but all is not well on Kronus. The Ork invasion has begun anew on this planet and with all the fighting above the ancient killing machines known as the Necron have awaken which in turn has caused the Tau to appear on the planet in an effort to stop them from annihilating all life on the planet. Of course all this extra violence has attracted the attention of the Blood God of Chaos attention and brought the Chaos Marines onto Kronus. And with the Chaos Marines the Eldar quickly came in tow to stop them from ressurecting more demons and overtaking more planets. The Space Marines (namely the Blood Ravens) are ordered to cleanse the planet now for it is considered overrun with the Alien, the Unclean, and the Heretic. Upon their arrival on the planet they are told their are precious artifacts on Kronus that must be reclaimed at all costs and thus order the Imperial Guard to evacuate from Kronus in order for them to purge Kronus and reclaim the artifacts. The Guard promptly refuses and sparks an intense war with the Blood Ravens. This all quickly turns into a nasty open war.
How this war plays out however is solely up to you however. The game gives you a decent background for each race and the events leading to the war but it has not true canon story beyond that. Your campaign mode consists of picking 1 of several races (Space Marines, Imperial Guard, Eldar, Orks, Chaos Marines, Tau, or Necrons) and then using them to conquer the entire map. The campaign starts off on the world screen where you can reinforce your territories launch attacks or upgrade your Honor Guard, which are essentially free beefed up versions of your basic units, as well as upgrade your commander unit with Wargear, items that add health attack or other bonus abilities to your commander unit. Each race has its own Stronghold which if taken will kick them from the game for that campaign. Capture all strongholds to win.
All in all the game looks great despite some age, it sounds great and has a decent soundtrack and its positively steeped in lore for every race. Theres dozens of novels written on this series. I highly recommend this game to any and all fans of RTS games. Gotta cut this one short since Steam wont let me write any more about this game! For the Emperor!

This is a tricky one. After my first 15 hours, I got bored and wrote a rather bad review. However, after dusting the game out of forgotten diskspaces for a second time, I actually found it rather enjoyable and when I got my two gaming buddies to get it, it turned into a blast. (Literally)
So, let's take a look at the game itself, shall we:
EDF is a franchise that was actually around a bit longer, but usually console-exclusive. EDF:IA is (afaik) the sole PC-avaible title of the franchise.
The original franchise relies on 'So bad it's good again'-style of voice acting, cinematics, plot and really doesn't try to take itself too seriously. Combine that with a full-arcade 'omg shoot the aliens' exploding spamfest, and you got a rough draw of what EDF does.
This specific instance of the instance is, as mentioned, the only PC title and, sadly, wasn't developed by the original developers, but by a foreign group. And many fans complain that EDF:IA is nowhere near as good as any of the old titles and a bad joke compared to EDF:2025 (one of the more recent titles).
EDF:IA itself is straight forward: Aliens invade Earth, you are an elite soldier group with absurd weapons utilizing endless ammo, and now fight your way through a 15-mission campaign. Doing so, you unlock more and more powerful weapons, till killing the enemies actually becomes a sidequest next to leveling the entire battlefield. Because that is what you can literally do: Level the (exclusive) city-maps to a heap of rubble. And damn, that's satisfying. Especially because your teammate is a jettrooper direly trying to get into a high spot.
As with it's ancestors, the main progression point of EDF:IA lies in unlocking new weapons for the four playable classes. Not that every class comes with 5-6 weapon categories, with dozens of (often unique) weapons each, from which you can bring exactly 2 to each mission.
Standard assault rifles? Sure. SMG's for the Tac Officer? Jep. Rocket Launchers? Duh! BIG rocket launchers? Too.
Tactical Nuclear missile launchers which fires rockets slower then a hulking heavy? Included. Giant multi-missile 8-tuble super-sized nuclear flare ANTI-AIR rockets? Je, this game goes silly at times.
Of course, the game DOES have a fair number of downpoints: First off, it's limited campaign. You get one campaign of 15 missions, which maybe cover ~3-5 hours. Then you get a 'Campaign Remix' which plays on the same maps, but with different objectives and enemy groupings. And lastly a rather crude Survival mode. The game offers 3 difficulty degrees which SEVERELY ramp up said difficulty: On Normal, you have to put effort into actually dieing. On Hard, you will despare in the first mission because those tiny ant enemies suddenly survive your best rocket launchers and actually kill you in a few hits. On Inferno... let's say I didn't yet make it into Inferno.
Creativity in enemy design is another weak suit of the game: You get Ants. Spiders. Ticks. Wasps. Robots. Then you get Robot Ants, Robot Spiders, Robot Wasps. And another Robot Spider. The game tries to compensate for that by making jokes via the radio. "Hey intel, what can you give us on this new enemy?" "Well, it seems to be... a robot ant! Probably faster, better stronger and more dangerous." "... Thanks, intel..."
And, one of my biggest complaints, is the stupid AI for your squadmates. When playing solo, your team will be filled up (toggleable though) with AI troopers which are... simplistic. They follow you around, shoot aliens with a rather solid accuracy and do their job quite well on Normal, dieing occasionally. On Hard, however, the AI dies rather regularyly, because it doesn't grasp the concept of dodging attacks, or eventually avoiding those incoming instakill carpet bombers. From what I'Ve heard, it becomes completely useless in Inferno.
Which clearly states one thing: This is a MULTIPLAYER COOP GAME, to the core. And boy, once I got my buddies into buying this, we had loads of fun blowing up aliens, buildings, each other and some more aliens. And AI teammates, occasionally. But mostly aliens.
Of course the game has no terribly comlex depth, past organizing a solidly spread out weapon layout, assigning directions/roles to the team (F.e. the heavy battle suit takes care of the frontline, the tac provides carpet bombing support with his launcher and the jet keeps an eye out from above and snipes distant enemies) and learning the bosses' movement patterns to avoid the hard-hitting special attacks.
But the sheer amount of enemies and the intense difficulty ramp-up make the game very challenging, nontheless. (Or maybe the fact one of my teammates keeps insisting on using the 9999 damage missile launcher which oneshots most enemies and players alike, and keeps killing either himself or somebody else.)
Final judgement? 7/10
Solid game, not as good as I would have hoped for, and judging by the countless critique definitely not a high point of it's franchise. But if you get two buddies to play it with, you will very well be busy fragging robot ants for dozens of hours to come. And for a price of mere 10€, this makes it a really nice budget purchase.

Witcher 2 is the successor to Witcher 1, all in all the game boasts high graphical fidelity, challenging and tactical combat, a vast array of side missions, dialogue options, and choices to make that affect the outcome of the endgame. After completing the game twice with two different endings each time, i feel the game has alot of content and requires a few playthroughs to get the most out of it. Witcher 2 is a great example of how a well made RPG can destroy the competition and make for an excellent gaming experience. Just looking around the towns you enter you will find all sorts of things to do such things as pub brawls, dice games and a number of well made sidequests that dont feel too grindy or boring as they have interesting characters and events that make you want to seek out more adventure.The main quests as well as sidequests also have different ways to approach your objectives. Do you want to go stealth and try to stun guards as you make your way to your objective? or go a different path to avoid the enemies altogether, or perhaps you want to go in sword slashing with blood and limbs flying? your decision.  Witcher 2 also features many references to movies/books such as Lord of the rings (  wont spoil which references ) Although there are some optimization issues the game runs quite smoothly even on older hardware. Although there are minor gripes such as the lack of in-game grapgical and controls menu, this is all done in the config menu at the launcher, as well as the sometimes annoying repeating dialogue from random NPC'S. Despite the very minor problems and annoyances, The witcher 2: Assassins of kings is a standout RPG with few faults, and i look foreward to the sequel Witcher 3: Wild hunt, comming february 2015.
The good:
- High graphical fidelity even though a slightly aged game.
- Many dialogue options (sometimes its hard to pick due to emotional attatchement to certain characters)
- Nice Tactical combat - the use of different swords for different enimies works well.
- Interesting characters and plot points.
- Side missions arent boring.
The bad:
- Some optimization issues.
- Main story quests are a little short ( but they are fullfilling )
- Some of the random Npc's repeat the same lines of dialogue.
- Configuration menu ( unable to change grapgics or controls in-game )

As others have stated many times, this game is either trying way too hard to be Portal, or trying way to hard to differentiate itself from Portal and failing. Either way, it's a game where a silent female protagonist is forced to run through a regiment of dangerous experiments for reasons that aren't entirely clear, her only weapon a color-coded "gun" that she uses to evade traps and put boxes on buttons, while a sadistic antagonist mocks her at nearly every turn. She escapes the lab and gets the chance to turn the tables on her tormentor. It is different from Portal in that the featured tool is a magnet gun that pushes/pulls objects and the player, and it has multiple endings (9 different endings based on the choices you make throughout the game) It's pretty short: my first (and only) playthrough took less than three hours including breaks.
The game is nice in that the story was compelling enough to keep me playing and the voice acting and script is, if not good, at least passable. However, when it comes to the challenges, Magnetic: Cage Closed just doesn't measure up to its spiritual predecessor. Puzzles are extremely easy and solutions obvious the second you walk into the level. Instead of the "Eureka!" moment that makes puzzle games so much fun, you get the "Oh." moment of realizing you were missing something obvious because you forgot to look up, walked past something important, etc. The Magnet Gun doesn't have the same versitility as the Portal Gun: It's clumsy and lackluster, and there's only so many ways you can incorporate it into a puzzle. Your options pretty much begin and end at hovering, moving slightly faster, and picking up boxes from far away.
Overall, Magnetic: Cage Closed is a more boring Portal. I thought the choice aspects were neat, but didn't care enough to go back and explore every option. The level transitions are slow, repetative, and irritating, the featured tool just isn't as cool or fun to use as the Portal Gun, and the writing is merely "good enough."
It definitely feels unfair to compare this title to the gem that was Portal, but even on its own it doesn't hold up as a puzzle game because the challenges are so simple and the main mechanic loses its novelty after a few minutes of roleplaying the part of a slow, fleshy mag-lev train.
Buy it on sale if you're looking for your First Person Puzzle Platformer fix, but don't get your hopes up if you're looking for the next Portal.
