I have been looking for a sequel to Tenchu, or at least a game like it... well the search is over.  This game did it, and they did it creatively.  Tenchu was fun to play but throwing the grappling hook and flying on an angle to climb a roof was more mystical than realistic (which is fine because the ninja are mysterious).  However the game Aragami has a more believable way of doing this using the Aragami's nature that draws its power from the shadows.  It reminds me of Rikimaru saying "I am a shadow".
The same downside is present in this game that the original Tenchu games had as well, limited number of levels.  In any case it still had more scenes than the original tenchu which had only 10 levels, and I played it over and over again. Still I expect to play this numerous times like I did with Tenchu, and it aparently also has a co-op mode for playing with friends online (which clearly wasn't availabe for Tenchu back on the PS1).  Also (like Tenchu) most of the levels aren't really difficult if you have played stealth games like this before. Sentenced to death and left in labyrinth of traps and torment prisoner XE-47632 has only one hope. Make it out alive and reclaim her freedom. Can you help?
Let’s start off with the obvious, yes it is portal like but this game offers far more than just that and aren’t all puzzle platformers going to be compared to the farther of the genre. With an intriguing story, challenging puzzles and a branching story with 9 different endings this game stands up on its own and shouldn’t be ignored.
You begin with very few answers, trapped in a massive underground complex and your only hope of freedom is to make it through each puzzle alive and using your wits, will and a prototype magnet gun. With the constant heckling of the warden and the unsettling words of the prison psychologist your only contact with the outside world you must help XE-47632 survive. The game offers you many choices throughout your journey and each has an impact on the ending that you will achieve. Some may be subtle but some may lead you to totally different out comes.
The sound design is outstanding, with the score adding depth to the game whilst the voice actors really nail the feeling they are trying to convey. I felt the dichotomy of the two main characters come off really well, two sides of the same demented coin toying with rats in a maze, you just happen to be one of the rats.
Whilst not having the polish of a AAA title it still looks great. The models are well done and very detailed, the sets are suburb and lend to the overall feel of the game perfectly. Even the weapon is designed brilliantly. I adored the use of manikins instead of people; always in the back of my mind was I truly alone with no one else here. Is this all a test or am I actually going to be free.
The difficulty of each puzzle was just right in my opinion, some take it easy on you even though they require some thought at least but a few of them really tax your mind and figuring each one out was highly satisfactory. Even the few times you could shortcut the stages felt great, like you were cheating but as a lot of the have associated achievements they knew what they were doing.
This game is a must have for puzzle platformer addicts. It’s fun, intriguing and challenging. Even a novice at puzzles like me can enjoy it immensely. The story, the lore and the characters, each plays their part perfectly and I for one would love to see more of facility 7.

I woke up today thinking about this game, and it took me an hour of thinking to decide what kind of review I would write for it.
My negative review today is based solely off my experience with the community that plays this game.
I got this game in order to play the puzzle-like games that I've seen so many YouTubers play. It looked fun, and my friend had played those a lot, so I got it so we could get on and test the waters since most videos I watched were a couple years old.
These days, those puzzle games have very low population and most of the maps that servers run, according to my friend, aren't nearly as good as older maps. We couldn't get a decent game after a few hours.
So we tried the 2nd most popular game mode: Star Wars RP. We were locked in a "training room" on the most popular server for a good 30 minutes with nothing to do besides stare at walls with training material on it. We asked for a trainer multiple times, only to be confronted with a wall of angry Star Wars roleplayers that just sat there and stared at us ominously. We eventually decided to walk outside the training room in order to explore the area, and got incarcerated for 15 minutes. After that time, we tried again, and quickly got incarcerated for 15 minutes. We cut our losses after an hour and quit for the night.
The next day I tried again on my own and actually got a trainer to show me how to play on a different server. Most of it is about memorizing marching formations and ship statuses of alert. I got all those down, and was allowed to explore the area and walk freely after about 45 minutes of training. Most people were nice, but after a couple hours I was quickly discouraged. Everybody spent most of their time standing around and bickering about non-RPers. I tried to progress in the ranks to no avail because of silly trick questions and stuff. So I tried the combat against NPCs. Well, at the lowest rank you get 1-shotted by mobs that run way faster than you and it takes a few shots to take them out. So, that was a no-go without progressing through the ranks. I felt I was stuck in being a private without being able to successfully play the mind games that the community set forth for people to progress through the ranks.
So, I decided to try the most popular game mode online. DarkRP. It was great. It was similar to the old custom map "LoaP" (Life of a Peasant) from Warcraft III. More Grand Theft Auto elements and building, though. I had some good times and bad, buying guns and drugs as a gangster and printing fake money. I had some great fun for maybe 15 hours or so over the course of a few days.
But then, the community. Playing as a thug or gangster, I figured I could jump people in alleys that weren't really doing anything other than hanging out in sketchy alleys for no reason. So I started to "claim territory" by murdering anybody that wouldn't talk to me or tell me what they were doing in my hood, figuring if anybody had an issue with it, the police force RPers on the server would come clean up the neighborhood and force me out. Instead, I was teleported to a room alone with a GM of the server and interrogated about what I was trying to do to the server and was told that what I was doing was not allowed because it's just not allowed to go around killing people. I apologized and pressed on.
Amidst a few fun experiences, I came across quite a few people around my age that would RP, fail because of some people in the community or GM interference, and then just stand around complaining about how children had ruined most servers and so on. Sounded pretty improbable. I couldn't see kids really enjoying that kind of stuff. I wouldn't have been allowed to play this kind of RP game with people ages 20-40 when I was a kid anyway.
So I built a small base according to the strict rules of the server. Raiding has no real benefits. You don't get money or anything from it. All you get is the accomplished feeling of having destroyed someone's creation and means of making money. However, lots of people raid bases anyways because of course there are many people on the internet that thrive off of watching others fail.
So I built this base according to the building rules of the server. Switches and triggers in plain sight, no path blocking, and no closing in of your money printers behind a wall that can't be surpassed. I was able to build a base that had a few puzzles in it that I felt would protect me pretty well against raiders. Set up my money printers, and made my money back after an hour or so.
At one point, I walked outside my house to go hang out outside the police station, puff on my vape pen, maybe get arrested for it, talk♥♥♥♥♥♥to the cops from my jail cell.... the usual RP stuff I'd do as a gangster on that server. A gun dealer (imo a character I should do business with) walked up and killed me. Fair enough, I never reported people for random killings and just acted as if maybe he was RPing as if I owed him money or something from a gun one of my homies bought or whatever. So I was running around, and got teleported to my base. Right in front of the gun dealer. Turns out he was a GM. He was furious. He couldn't figure out how to raid my base and came to the conclusion that I used illegal path blockers to totally prevent a raid. He sounded maybe 10-11 years old. I assured him there was a way to raid my base, I just made it into an IMO really good puzzle game.
He wouldn't hear any of it, got another GM involved, and demanded that I take down my base immediately after showing him all of the secrets to getting to the money printers that, as I said, yield no benefit to raiders destroying - just gives raiders a sense of accomplishment in being able to watch another player fail. He threatened to ban me if I didn't comply. I really enjoyed playing on that server, so I walked him through how to access the money printers that he used his GM powers to delete in a nerd rage. He didn't understand still, so told me to delete everything anyway. This whole time, the other GM was in total agreement with him.
At this point I got pretty frustrated, told him I wouldn't come back because not only is it unfair that I had to show him exactly how he can destroy my money-making source only because he was a GM so that in the future he can cause me to fail whenever he wants, like a kid with a magnifying glass burning ants, but I told him I also felt it unfair that even though I obeyed all the building rules, just because a child couldn't figure out the puzzles in my base, I had to delete it all. I had spent a good hour and a half building it all.
He sustained his position. Get rid of it all or be banned.
I told him it'll all get deleted when I log off for the last time, said goodbye, and never came back.
In short, this game has a lot of potential for fun if you've got 5-10 internet friends to play puzzle games with or an entire community to make a roleplaying server with. However, I wouldn't recommend this game for the majority of players who, like me, might have 1 or 2 friends that own the game. RP servers have pages of rules that you must read and comply, and even if you do... it's not likely you'll be left to your own devices because of children with magnifying glasses who just want you to be an ant for them.
So, this is why I'm giving it a thumbs down. Fun for a while, but the community sets the odds against people who don't travel in packs.

Aragami is a stylized, supernatural stealth game developed by Lince Works, which places
players in the role of a vengeful shadow, known as, you guessed it, an Aragami. Its available for
PC, Mac, and PS4 (no love for xbox this time around) and runs on the unity engine. On the
surface, Aragami might not seem all that different from other stealth games you might be familiar
with, such as Splinter Cell and Metal Gear, but its fast paced gameplay and beautiful art direction
might be enough to set it apart. This isn't just a stealth game, it's a supernatural stealth game, and I
say that because unlike the aforementioned Splinter Cell and Metal Gear game series, in which you
take on the role of a special agent, bound by the laws of physics, in Aragami you are a shadow
spirit, who's only method of moving vertically through the game's various environments is by
teleporting between shadows. There is no jump button in this game, and while it might seem
strange to think of a ninja who doesn't know how to jump, or swim for that matter, this mechanic is
really Lince Works' way of shaking up the stealth genre. Sure, the shadow leap ability in this
game is simply copy and pasted from “blank's” Dishonored, but because Aragami uses this ability
so much, and so quickly, it really changes up the overall feel and pace of the core gameplay. If the
player wanted to, they could plod along slowly, using shadow leap only when necessary, and
waiting patiently for that brief window when the enemy patrol patterns to shift and you can slip by
un-noticed, like you would in most stealth games. But what I really love is that Lince Works seems
to have said “to hell with all waiting, lets get this moving, shall we?,” and gave us the ability to
teleport about at will like meth-crazed adrenaline junkies, or perhaps simply a really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off
shadow demon. This game really does make you feel like you a playing a spirit, with powers far
beyond that of your average secret government agent, allowing the player to hop quickly along
through levels, and string together some extremely satisfying kill combos. While it could be
argued that this ability to teleport about constantly, coupled with the ability to create your own
shadows for you to teleport to, might make the gameplay a bit too easy, or cast it out of the stealth
genre all together; but I would say that Aragami still feels like a stealth game, and that the fast
pacing, and ability to simply skip past a lot of the more meticulous and annoying sections, such as
waiting for enemy patrols, is a breath of much needed fresh air.
Aragami has the standard line up of features we have come to expect in stealth games,
such as making a sound to distract guards and break their patrol pattern, a good variety of kill
animations, a skill tree, hiding bodies, placing traps, and ranged golden gun kills. But with
Aragami's fast paced gameplay aside, it really was this game's art direction that really made it
shine. Everything from the stellar soundtrack to it's stylistic lack of UI (which admittedly stole a
few pages from Dead Space), seems lovingly crafted. The UI in this game doesn't really exist, and
all the player's information is instead displayed on the protagonist's cape, which really adds to the
slick, stylized look of this game. Sadly, the cape often gets entangled with the protagonist's body,
making things hard to see, but luckily most of it isn't all that important anyway. Just teleport,
teleport, teleport again, and of course, remember to stab, stab, stab!
The game's story plays out through a combination of lackluster in-game cinematic's with
prompting dialogue boxes, and some well drawn slide show scenes, which can overall be pretty hit
or miss. Without spoiling anything or going into too much detail, you are a vengeful spirit
summoned to help a woman in need, which later unravels into a deeper plot involving a quest to
save the empress from, get this, the Forces of Light. I didn't find the story to be very memorable, to
be honest, and found myself clicking through a lot of it. But, the game also gives you an
achievement called “I Don't Care” the first time you skip a story cut scene, so I think even the
developers would agree that we aren't really here for story.
Aragami's lengthy campaign takes the player through a number of varied locations and
can also be played in co-op online multi-player. Unfortunately I didn't really get a chance to play
any of the co-op mode before putting together this review, but I did watch some footage and it
looks like a welcome addition that I am eager to try. All in all, I would say this game is most
certainly worth the price of admission, but fails to be unique enough for me to say it is a must
have, especially if you have played other stealth games in the past. But, if you are a fan of the
stealth genre and know what you are getting into, Aragami can be a lot of fun. It is incredibly
satisfying to chain multiple kills together while you zip about with supernatural speed. The art
director for this game deserves a standing ovation, as this game's style has left a strong impression
with me. I'd give this game an 8/10.

I don't think there has been a solid successor to Wave Race 64. Is Riptide GP 2 even a competition for the classic? Depends how invested you are in racing games and how much you yearn for something like Wave Race. I will recommend this game, but with great caution. I enjoyed the game the more I played, but there was a point where I started noticing a few missing elements.
Riptide GP2 is a sea-doo racing game that provides multiple modes. One of the main modes is career mode. In this mode, players have to progress and compete through multiple levels in order to attain a 3 star ranking. Once players have acquired enough stars (max of 3), they may move on to the next stage. There is also a leveling system regarding the rider and the player collects points after each race. With these points, the player may buy new sea-doos, customize their sea-doo or rider and upgrade their current ride. Players can also unlock new tricks using their points. The more complex the trick, the more boost the player will receive. I am glad there is a trick system in place, but I feel it's a little bit too rigid. I felt there was a little more control and creativity with Wave Race while Riptide relies on a combination system. Meaning, you have to hit "left + right" simultaneously with both thumb sticks in order to do a trick. The tricks are cool; issue is that it will be difficult to do more than one trick per jump. The more tricks you land, the more boost you get. You are allowed to activate your boost whenever you'd like during the race. There are quite a bit of events to do, but the game is quite difficult even on normal mode. Any small mistake can cost you a few seconds which can make a world of a difference when completing the final lap. The
is pretty decent for the most part. It feels like a little bit more could have been done to engage and immerse the player of having the feeling of racing on a sea-doo.
The
are actually pretty good in the game. The collisions between the water and the sea-doo aren't perfect, but is still smooth. Riders and sea-doos themselves look pretty cool and the arenas are neatly designed. The only issue with the visuals/animations here is when players collide - there isn't much of a reaction. I've landed on top of AI's and they have landed on top of me and my player was fine. Did not fall or tip into the water. I think this was a huge missed opportunity as this could have been that motorcycle road rage game on the water. On the plus side to the animations, they made the execution of the combos really neat. A simple move can be upgraded and can become complicated and unexpected. It was definitely awesome how they put together the simple with the complex.The menus are also easy to navigate. The
are alright. I haven't noticed much difference between sea-doos or collision sounds. I think a little more could have been done here to make the player feel like they are creating the splashing and crashing sounds.
Overall, the game is pretty decent especially for the price I paid (under $4). The difficulty can be a bit of a turn off, but once you get the hang of things its certainly rewarding. If you are hungry for a split screen or a Wave Race like game, this is it. I would recommend waiting for a sale. For future Riptide games, I would definitely recommend a small option of sea-doos to start with, put in animations/neat collision systems for when players collide or land on top of one another, and keep the different types of races/games going with battles or sport like games. It can be a bit grind-ey, but does have its moments of beauty.
RATING : 6.9/10

Crypt of the NecroDancer is a rhytm based dungeon crawler with some roguelike elements and great tunes.
CotN is a turn based game where every beat serves as a turn. This means that if you miss a beat you miss a turn. You basically need just 4 buttons to play the game: left, right, up and down. These are used also in combination to use items and spells by pressing up+left to eat an apple i.e. though you can assign a single button for these functions also.
You find consumables from the levels to heal yourself, spells like fireball or freeze and different weapons and armors. There are also diamonds that serves as a currency in the games hub where you can purchase persistent additions to your adventuring. Besides additional health the rest of the upgrades are added to the map generation for you to find.
Enemies are varied as in how often they move (in beats) and in which patterns (up and down, following you etc.) and bosses are tougher and more damage dealing creatures of course.
What makes CotN different is the rhytm-system. Roguelike-type-of-games are usually hard already but NecroDancer makes you do important decisions on the fly and likes to punish the player for hesitating. If you thought Spelunky was hard you've seen nothing (this is a warning). You have to study the movements patterns of the enemies and find the right timing and way to deal with each enemy. This changes with your gear since some weapons allow you to attack diagonally and you have to consider the right timing to launch that spell you've been saving.

makes the game look messy particularly in the second zone.

Very glad I got this game.  I'm a fan of racing games, used to play one called "Jetboat Superchamps" where I made it to the end after many weeks.  Like that game, Riptide GP2 has AI competitors that add to the challenge, getting in your way, bumping you as you head for a ramp, pushing you against a wall, giving you a target to catch up to and pass...  Courses here are good so far.  Never confusing, there are always visual clues that help you know which way to go.
The hydro jets handle well, when you hit the water at an angle you can feel the slowdown and start moving that direction.  Some near crashes will drive you under the surface.  Waves and wakes of other hydro jets affect your motion, you have to account for it in your steering.  Fun to fly off the ramps, not fun to hit a wall head-on.  Overall the driving feels nicely realistic.  I've done about 50 races so far and find it's easy to beat 2 or 3 of the 7 AI racers.  I found it hard to get 2nd or 1st place until I repeated a race a bunch of times.  To me that's a good balance, and I felt winning was due less to luck and more to my increasing skill, or my strategy of when to use speed boosts or which stunts.
I like the graphics, they don't look like a photo but to me they add to the game.  They show an interesting world with a lot of detail, yet they're very fluid and add to the immersion.  Water and things below it look great, and there's stuff going on in the background that you barely have time to see.  Sounds are good, except when you crash.  I can bounce my hydro jet off of concrete beams and all I get are some glass-breaking sounds.  I like how the sounds change in different areas.  Music did not impress me but at least I can turn it down or off separately from the sound effects.
I'm using a Logitech F310 controller in Win 10 with Nvidia GTX 750 Ti graphics, core I7 processor, 16 GB RAM.  Runs smoothly, no crashes, loads quickly between scenes.  I've never seen any lag or graphics glitches, aside from my driver's hand dissappearing inside a wall -- very minor!  Game worked with my controller right away, no setup required.
The only downside for me is the need to do stunts.  I just want to race, I don't think a sane person would ever try stunts during a race.  But you need to perform stunts to get more boost power, and you need boost power to win.  It does add to the strategy of which stunts to use when, and also which stunts to "buy" when you get experiance points.
I'm only just starting on the second series of races.  I've had a good time so far, can see pouring many more hours into this one.  Got it in a bundle a while back and just installed it.  Well worth the $6.99 price in the store today.  My granddaughter (almost 7) likes it a lot also.  She hit 3rd place in some of the races.

As of the time of this review this game is rated very positive on Steam. I have a funny feeling that if the rating system had been more than a yes/no system it would stand differently. It is by no means a bad game mind you, but it is not a very good one either. I think a lot of people have given it a thumbs up just because it isn't bad, and I am going to do the same.
Seeing that this is the first time I enter the lore of The Dark Eye, I can not say much about how true it is to the lore or how significant it is in that sense. The game doesn't seem to open much of the lore to the player and it rather feels like just a backdrop to the story we play through. The story in this game seems slightly interesting, but I feel it could have been a lot more fleshed out. It is all very isolated and intimate. For someone who's more into this universe it might do alot, I wouldn't know, but for everyone else I think it is very thin.
That being said, as a stand alone adventure game I'd say this game is mediocre. It feels a little dull and flat. Much because of the setting and also because of some of the voice-acting of the main characters being unengaging. It's sad really, as you do meet a few characters that are voiced really well, and the narrator's voice is great.  The main character does not seem to be liked by many of the inhabitants, but one never really gets to know why. As a bird-catcher in a town overrun by birds one would think they'd appreciate you a bit more. There are a lot of good things too though. The handpainted backgrounds are fantastic and there is a lot of great ideas here. The puzzles are logical and on the most part quite good and creative even though it can feel a bit outlandish at times.
There are achievements in this game, but sadly most of them are the "click this thing a 100 times and turn this 20 times". I find achievements like that a chore and very little creative. Also, to get them all you have to play through the game twice on different difficulties which is just not worth it. Other achievements include doing certain things differently, so a tip to all would be to save often and reload when one of the achievements is..uhm....achieved.
This game is a predecessor to the game Memoria and it is probably worth playing through to lay the foundations if you want to play that game. Other than that I only think it can serve as a timekiller or filler inbetween other games. I would not recommend the game to anyone who for the first time would enter into the world of point 'n' click adventure games, there are many many games that I would consider a whole lot better for that purpose. But, for established adventure fans it could be worth a playthrough, especially seeing you'd probably be able to get this game really cheap in a sale.
I give it a rating of 5/10. Just mediocre.
This opinion is of course highly subjective and your opinion might differ from mine. If you plan on buying it do not use this review as a sole source for that purpose, rather make sure to read several reviews before making up your mind.

The Dark Eye: Chains of Satinav is a point and click adventure game with fantasy and dramatic themes. It was developed by Daedalic Entertainment and released Jun 22, 2012.
The Dark Eye: Chains of Satinav takes place in the kingdom of Andergast, you play as the protagonist young Geron, a bird catcher by trade, but more well known as "the child who will bring doom".
You see, before the story even starts, poor Geron was cursed by the Seer, and so everyone in town thinks that he brings bad luck wherever he goes. Little does he realize what kind of adventure he's about to go on... But none ever to realize their journeys in these types of stories.
I don't want to give too much away of the story, because that's the driving factor of a point and click adventure game
If you've never played a point and click adventure game, it's the science of clicking on one thing, and then clicking on another thing, and then clicking on one thing with every item in your inventory.
Thankfully, since we're in the age of the internet, if you're stuck, you can look up a guide online to help you get past a part of the game where you are stuck. And I'll be the first to confess this is what I did, I was able to puzzle my way through the first two-thirds of the game... But once the Fairy chapter started... Well... Lets say I had an epiphany: the developers of this game are insane.
Insane or no, I had forgotten the satisfaction of solving a puzzle by yourself without any help... except I can't even brag about that, because I played on the "easy" mode, which gives you a hint button to show all the things you can click on. This definitely is the only reason I completed so much of the game by myself, but I honestly I ended up spamming the heck out of the button and forgetting to use my own eyes.
Point-and-click adventure games are a genre I haven't experienced since.... Some point and click adventure kid game for the Muppet Treasure Island.
There's so much good to be said about this game. I was sucked in immediately, and it doesn't feel like I actually spent 10 hours on my first play through.
The graphics are quite aesthetically pleasing. (I could comment on the animation being a bit stiff and awkward at first... but I soon grew accustom to the style and stopped noticing.) The soundtrack is spot on! The story was excellent.

Only a few hours in but I have to say I'm very impressed thus far!

I write few reviews and tend to be quite critical of the games I play.  However, I feel obligated to review this game to prevent its deceptive simplicity from harming its sales.
Though the setting may ostensibly be regarded (and not without reason) as extremely iterative upon Warhammer 40K, Templar introduces an almost neo-platonic thread early on and pursues it to a fair deal of realization.  Though your "captain's" dialogue, where present, is indistinct, the absurd degree of personalization defines your units in combat well enough.

The combat system is a bit of a black box, and at first I feared that it would be a unentertaining slog, but not only is the difficulty curve well balanced, I found myself in scenarios that really did feel like "heroism" on the part of my team.
The greatest sustaining factor in the game's favor is the advancement system.  I want to complete every mission to further characterize my units and I want to start another mission afterwards.
It would be a shame if this game were overlooked due to a poor first impression, as even an hour in I felt enitrely satisfied with my purchase.  It's ten usd and with refunds, why not?

10.000.000 is a game about numbers. You wake up in a locked up area and have to fight your way through the dungeon full of monsters. Along the way you can pick up items to aid you in the journey and upgrade your skills through Experience points and Gold gained from playing.
The gameplay consists of mixing tiles all over the place. That may sound boring, but is actually a quite interesting take on a game like this, and requires you to think about your moves and executing them as fast as possible. The game will reward you for playing well and mixing and matching the right tiles to kill the right enemies and gain resources to upgrade your buildings, which in turn allows you to upgrade your character even more.
The game is somewhat lengthy with some hours of gameplay and features no stops in the flow, unless you get matched up against a boss monster, in which the game heavily punishes you for not being prepared nor fast enough to match the right tiles. The game can feel cheap sometimes shoving a boss monster down your hallway with only a few points to go to the next rank.
The soundtrack is alright, but with only 3 songs, which may seem repetitive to some. Sound effects match the visuals nicely and fits the retro theme nicely along with the soundtrack.
All in all, the game is quite fun, not very pricey, has an above average soundtrack and will get you at least a few hours of entertainment.

Alright. "Garry's Mod"...
Garry's Mod is a sandbox game where you can play god without any kind of limitation. If you can think of it, you can make it possible. With thousands of addons made by the game community, the game offers you unlimited possibilities of doing whatever you want, creating any kind of thing that may cross into your mind and much, much more. Also the community is very active (even after almost ten years the game was released) and this means that addons and gamemodes will be always updated and of course, there are always going to be new addon releases. That's basicaly single player.
The multi player is a whole different thing. You'll find hundreds of different servers with a lot of different custom downloadable gamemodes, wich includes the well known "Trouble In Terrorist Town", "Prop Hunt", "Zombie Survival", the beautiful "Sandbox" and a lot more of'em. Of course, each gamemode with his huge variety of maps.
Now, the "problemos".
The only thing that really bothers me is the incredible potential that every addon has to practically break the whole game.
Think of the addons as an interconnected group of gears. If one of the gear falls off, the rest of the group will become completely useless.
Final verdict?
In general, i think that Garry's Mod is the definitive sandbox since your creativity it's the only limit you're going to have in every terms and because of that, wich is the thing that makes it so fun, it deserves a 9 out of 10 rate.

It's hard to achieve good puzzle mechanics in first person, and credit needs to be given to the creators of Magnetic: Case Closed for creating a solid, tactile gameplay with few (but not zero) shortcomings. However, good level design is even harder to come by (both in 2D and 3D), and the game fares much worse in this respect. Finally, there's absolutely no excuse for using the shortcomings of the game mechanics as a tool to increase difficulty. I could live with the often pedestrian level design and the large amount of unskippable intermissions, but the level where you have to move the cube from top to bottom in a maze blew my fuse as the cube kept getting stuck and I kept falling down from the narrow ledges due to the mutual attraction.
It could be such a superb game, but alas...

From what I have played of this game, I have only seen a good art-style implemented as one of the very few positives of this game. Even then some of the enemies could be modeled a little better. For the most part the presentation is the best part of this game. The shadow based stealth system, which is just as thin as say, Splinter Cell: Conviction or Blacklist, is passable for the most part. The system is either bugged or intentionally made to where enemies can spot you in shadow if you are within about 10 feet of their line of sight. Aragami has the gall to embue the protagonist to do a MGSV styled mechanic where if you are close to an enemy that spots you, you can quickly react by killing them to keep the alarm off, which the game never explains. There are three expendable weapons that the protagonist has at his disposal. They are pretty standard and feel more like leftovers from Mark of the Ninja. There is no agility to the protagonist, making you rely on the shadow blink to even get up to any height. The animation for some of the kills could be better (not that I'm saying that's a huge negative for any sort of game). This game is a stealth game that relies on checkpoints. Let that sink in for a moment because it's essentially like when you're putting together a puzzle, but when you place the wrong piece in the spot you thought it went to, the entire (or a large chunk of the) puzzle is then taken apart for you to do all over again. The ability you gain to place shadow on the groud feels like they didn't think about it for too long because they basically make you use to to just get to higher spots only due to how quickly the shadows go away. The power itself drains so quickly that I found it better to rely on the also passable level design. The shadow meter you have is also rather garbage at the beginning, especially with the shadow placing power. I'm fully aware you get more meter later on, but it's pretty bad to start with. The only time you get much verticality is when you are indoors for what little time that might be. Most of the powers seem rather ok and none are as fun as Dishonored's, or even Garrett's ultimate setup from Thief 2. At the very least, this game understands that darkness is important to a stealth game unlike Dishonored, but in the case of Aragami that's like having a sniper realize that a rifle would be better for him/her to use over per se a shotgun, but still have no clue how to use a rifle. I understand that I've only played it for almost an hour and a half, but I was sorely disappointed in this simplistically designed game. Thief 2: The Metal Age, Thief: Deadly Shadows, Mark of the Ninja, and Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory are stealth games that I would recomend against this one.
EDIT: As it turns out this game is related to a prototype for a game that I had played quite a while earlier called Path of Shadows While the site for Path of Shadows says that Aragami is a completely different game made by a studio funded by the Path of Shadows team, it looks entirely like Aragami had taken much of Path of Shadows' style. The sweet irony is that Path of Shadows plays better than Aragami and in my opinion the protagonist of Path of Shadows has a better design than that of the Aragami protagonist.

My first instinct when looking at this game was that the further I got into Magnetic, the less of a puzzle game it became. That I feel comes from an overhanging problem stemming from the fact that this game takes more than just inspiration from Portal. Taking inspitation from a another game is not a bad idea, it only becomes bad when you take the same design philosophy onto yourself without understanding what separates your own work from the original.
In theme, Magnetic takes the whole overlord enforcer setting up elaborate death traps and calling them tests from portal to a darker and more brutal extent, being set inside of a prison and and having the tests be your only way out. It makes sense and give you proper motivation to get through the ordeal... at first.
The main problem with the game comes from a conflict between the magnet gun and the puzzles, when I said this game takes its design philosophy from Portal, this is what I mean. In Portal the gun was a method of traversal; as such, all the puzzles were designed with the mindset of getting the player and objects from one point to another.
In Magnetic the gun is tool for manipulation, but the level design still bases itself on getting the player and objects from one point to another. If the game capitalize more on the guns capabilites, for instance, using magnetism to unfold a large gate or using the wall magnets as tools for puzzles rather than obstacles; it could have felt like a different game that wasn't just taking from Portal.
As a result the final levels feel more like a tedious obstacle course than actual puzzles. Any motivation to get to the end dies, and only hurts worse when you pick one of the wrong endings.

This game is phenominal.
There are not many games I recommend let alone write a review for but this is one of them. I remember playing the demo/proof of concept for this game a
long time ago and I can tell you that this game has come a long way since then.
This is a very good stealth game. Reminiscent of games like Dishonored, Dark Souls, and more but provides an experience well enough to stand on it's own two feet. It is brutal and fun. The animations are beautifully detailed, the art style is fantastic and the gameplay is hard and rewarding. If you are found by the many guards of the game you will likely die and die quickly. Death is a big part of the game given you will probably do so a lot and learn each time you die.
You enter the game as the "Aragami" or a vengful spirit made of shadows, brought to life by a ghostly woman named Yamiko. You are given a sword and brought through a quick tutorial and then unleashed the the somewhat-open world levels that the game has to offer, things such as teleportation, traps, throwing kunai and more are learned at your own pace. Each area generally has two or more entrances and two or less exits but the world doesn't feel confining. Given you are made of shadow you can only teleport from shadow to shadow, practically invisible while crouching in one. You only regenerate your powers when you are in shadow and drain when in light but are unaffected by moonlighting.
The game has a simple yet well written story and while I find the end to be predictable I was still impressed and after my time playing I found myself sitting back and reflecting on the entire thing and just telling myself that it was such a good game.
I finished the game in just under 15 hours and that's playing through each mission in the 13 mission campaign twice for an all-kill and all-stealth run, collecting all the collectables to be found to be the strongest I could be by the final boss. Unfortunately in a game as stealth-oriented as this boss fights don't really incorporate all the powers you can utilize but nevertheless it is still entertaining and enjoyable, not to mention threatening to have bosses have a general idea of where you are due to their immense power in light energy to combat your shadow energy.
Although I did get the game as a gift I would definitely recommend paying full price for this truly great experience; I greatly look forward to potential DLC further down the line.
If I had to give this a numbered score I would give it a 9 out of 10.

I find it a bit curious that there are so many reviews in English. I'd have thought that Chains of Satinav is most interesting for fans  of the Pen & Paper RPG "The Dark Eye", which to my knowledge did not really catch on outside of Germany.
The game itself- we-ell. The story is quite good, the background art really beautiful.
Unfortunately, the character art and especially animations fall a bit flat. Movement tends to be clunky and somewhat unnatural. I am usually very forgiving regarding graphics, but this could have been better with not too much additional effort.
Then there is the puzzles. Most of them are solved rather easily simply because there are not that many things you can try. Although the difficulty increases, only the chapter in the realm of the fairies offers what I had hoped for. Remains to say that some dialogues can be lead in several ways with slightly different outcomes. However, this is only interesting for achievement hunters.
Speaking of which: I don't really like them in P&C adventure games. Clicking 1.000 times on an arbitrary object is not an achievement. To be fair, the achievemts are mostly not that stupid, but still- this is an P&C, where you can't perform stunt tricks, multikills or find collectibles (the latter would be possible in Jack Keane, btw).
Can I still recommend Chains of Satinav? Certainly. Though it's not among the best P&C ever made, it is still (mostly) solidly made and very far from a bad game. And it is obligatory to any fan of "The Dark Eye".

I'm a few missions in and kinda in love. You could call this old-fashioned, because of the graphics and streamlined turn-based gameplay, but refined would be a better moniker. Everything feels intuitive, like finding a new pair of shoes that miraculously fit like a glove. The opening 'tutorial' missions play out as a prologue as much as an introduction. And they don't hold back while introducing the mechanics (at least at the demanding difficulty) like so many other games whose beginings turn into a snoozefest. On the topic of difficulty, you're given a number of options that clearly define their effect on gameplay - no mysterious 'Nightmare' mode that doesn't share with you why it might be so frightening. If you'd enjoy tactical turn-based combat on a square grid with in depth leveling and research trees - this is probably something you'd enjoy. The art style is crisp and engaging (for me personally at least) and there's a branching story-line to boot. Definitely worth the price and then some.

Before I get into the game's problems, I would like to say what's good about it. Shooting games where you fight giant insects is a rarity, so points for a concept that hasn't been explored much. The game aslo has a grand sense of scale, with huge buildings getting destroyed as collateral in the fights and huge boss-type foes that are taller than lots of the buildings themselves. It also usually introduces a new enemy or a new vehicle every mission (at least for a while). Although far from a perfectly implemented, the game also gives the player several classes with their own abilities, and the ability to change your gun loadout between missions.
However, this game has a number of problems. First, it is extremely repetitive. There is very little variance in mission objectives. It's always go here, kill all the constantly spawning enemies, repeat. There's little in terms of varied environments; Where you are on the map has almost no effect on how any given situation is approached. Combat is also repetitive, with waves and waves of the same four enemy types with an occasional bullet sponge boss. Waves of enemies tend to go on for entirely too long, and I found myself wishing for a change of scenery halfway through most of the firefights. As mentioned, most of the bosses are bullet sponges, not particularly difficult to defeat, but it takes a very very long time. Only occasionally are boss battles fun.
The system of armor classes and unlockable weapons is a nice thought, but it is poorly implemented. Weapons can be found on the battlefield, usually after killing some boss monster. However, weapons are also divided into tiers, and even after collected can only be unlocked via leveling up the armor class that uses said weapon. The problem with this is that it can take too long to level up. If you change your armors for the sake of varying the gameplay, level ups are few and far in between, so the weapons you pick up become unused, and the enemies become increasingly durable (the game uses skin swapped versions of some enemies with more health later in the game). Either the game becomes repetitive because it gradually  takes more time to kill enemies or it becomes repetitive by sticking to the same class.
Overall, the game has some good ideas, but most are not very well implemented. Some people might find enjoyment from this game, but the giant bug novelty isn't enough to salvage the gameplay

Dark Crusade was probably my favorite RTS throughout my college years.  While my friends were busy playing Starcraft, commanding the forces of Terrans, Protoss, and Zerg, I was busy fighting wars in the 41st Millennium, taking on foes ten times my greater and defeating them with honor and earning glory.  This was also the version of Warhammer 40K's Dawn of War series that got me into modding, giving me a sweet, sweet taste of what the penultimate prize of Modding experience would be promised to me upon getting Soulstorm.
If you've ever gotten the previous two, Dawn of War and Winter Assault, you'd know gameplay-wise that nothing's really changed.  However, with the addition of two new factions; the popular Necrons and the mysteriuos Tau Empire; and new units for all other factions (including Grey Knights for the Blood Ravens, which remains my favorite unit choice to this day), it definitely shines in front of its predecessors.  That, and with an awesome campaign where you can play not just one but all seven factions, promising continuous replayability even after you've beaten the campaign once...there's nothing here that's  not to like.
I'd be a fool not to recommend Dark Crusade.  Any RTS player would be a fool to deny that this game stood the test of time.  Stop reading the review, fork out some cash or grab that debit/credit card, and get the sodding game.  The best part about it all is that the multiplayer options are compatible with all versions and are standalone, so you only need one game to have fun.  I recommend giving it a go, it's worth it.  Let's keep this game alive.  For the Emperor!

To start with I must say that Witcher 2 is the best RPG I have ever played and one of the best games out there. It is an absolute masterpiece of a game with an awesome storyline, graphics that stay beautiful and full of detail throughout  the game, interesting characters and a fun and exhilarating combat.
The story is an exceptional beauty throughout , with moral choices that effect small changes like killing a character or letting them go, and huge changes that effects the entire story and leads you on different paths and goals. the game is full of cleverly thought out and designed quests, from the wonderfully interesting main plot to side quest that'll have you finding and killing ghosts , solving crimes and if you don't want to go out and discover the mysteries beyond the walls you can stay in at the tavern and earn yourself money by gambling on fights or competing in them .
The combat can be quite challenging and can require preparation like the placement of traps, the drinking of potions that will increase weapon damage , health and many more and covering your weapons in oil and poison so the sword deals more damage and has effects. This all has to be done before combat so the player must cleverly think and path his next battle. once mastered the combat is a very fun and accelerating departure from other games combats that involves hacking and slashing by simply mashing a single button till the target is dead.
The Graphics are a outstanding astonishment ( on maxed out anyway) , with an unbeatable lighting effect and texture that doesn't get poorer and poorer  the closer you get to it and focused on, the games textures stay amazing throughout .
overall Witcher 2  is an incredible game and if you have a powerful enough rig it can be an amazingly beautiful one as well, with a different but fun and creative combat and a cleverly written and presented story  Witcher 2 is a master piece of a game and without a doubt is worth buying .

It's Portal 2 without portals. Instead, your weapon of choice is a magnetic gun that works pretty much like the gravity gun in Half-Life 2. The story follows pretty much the same pattern as Portal 2, with the twist that the developers apparently got inspired by The Stanley Parable and gave the game nine different endings for you to discover. That being said, it took me about three hours to find one ending, and I didn't feel very compelled to find the others. After all game elements had been introduced, and I made it through a batch of hard levels, I felt that I've seen everything the game had to offer, and the story isn't intriguing enough.
Can I recommend this game? I guess so, I wasn't bored for three hours. I got this from a Humble Bumble though. So I had no expectations at all and my Entertainment-for-Money feeling was more than satisfied. I'd probably feel different, had I paid the full price in the Steam store (15€ at the time of writing). Would I venture out to get all endings, I guess my play time would be about 5-10 hours. Of course, you have to make up your own mind what that's worth to you. There's always a Steam sale coming.

It's reasonable to feel skeptical about buying into an unfinished game, but if the rhythm genre floats your boat then you're more than likely going to be pleased with this one. Crypt of the NecroDancer has really simple gameplay mechanics that can get you hooked fast. The difficulty, however, is anything but simple, and therein lies the charm of this game.
The tutorial does a really good job of getting you into gameplay rather quickly while laying out the rules of how to play. Everything, including you, moves to the rhythm of the music, and you study the movement patterns of your enemies to find the proper methods of eliminating them. The objective of the game becomes clear in an instant and before you know it, you're already playing. In my experience that was within the first minute. There aren't many games these days that can pull all of that off successfully, and considering this is still an alpha build I find that to be impressive.
If there's anything I don't like about this game, it's that controller support isn't all there just yet. You can use a controller just fine for gameplay, but navigating the UI is another story -- I haven't been able to do anything beyond scrolling through options, so it's a little weird to switch to a keyboard in order to make selections. Nonetheless, this is a pretty trivial complaint and is only going to be improved at some point in the development cycle. At least it allows for DirectInput controllers, so if you've been deliberately avoiding using an Xbox controller and have no desire to use 3rd party programs to emulate XInput then you still have other options.
Crypt of the NecroDancer has made me love the rhythm genre of games all over again, and I can see myself logging a ton of hours on it. I strongly recommend buying this game.

My favorite RPG of all time, The Witcher 2 continues the story of Geralt of Rivia. Very adult, shocking at times, gory and with a genuinely interesting storyline as it is based off of the Polish novels by Andrzej Sapkowski. This is not Skyrim, where your decisions are very clear cut to be "good" or "bad". Or Mass Effect, where you are graded on a light or dark scale depending on the moral direction of your decisions.
The decisions you are presented with are a series of grays, that you have to evaluate in the moment for not only the manipulation of the kingdom, but also personal gain and survival. Oh, did I mention that some of those decisions you have to make within seconds of being presented them?! No waiting around, researching which story arc you close or open depending on the decision... You have 3 seconds, and you have to deal with the consequences. The world actually reflects a bit of the Game of Thrones attitude... The good guys don't always win.
The world itself is full of political intrigue, racism towards elves and dwarves, and tensions between the kings ruling throughout the region. The world, though it can be gorgeous... Reflects this downtrodden atmosphere, and gives a very midieval "grunge" to everything. The graphics themselves are incredible, assuming you have the system for it, and have more "weight" to the textures and character models than I've experienced in some time. The last time I felt this kind of wow factor it was playing the original Gears of War back in 2006, my first real experience with Unreal Engine 3.
The combat doesn't babysit you, and if you choose not to use magic or potions you won't last long. There are various oils and gems you can augment weapons with for extra damage, potions you can consume for more resistance to a type of magic or poison, and others yet that help aid your sight in the dark depending on the mission or quest at hand. It includes an alchemy section, wherein you can craft your own potions from herbs and ingrediants you pick up through the game, as well as a very satisfying skill/ability tree that you expand upon throughout the game.
All in all, HIGHLY recommended if you can get past the difficulty.

Magnetic: Cage Closed casts the player as a convicted criminal, but instead of being sent to prison, you've been placed in a research facility, and forced to participate in a series of brutal test chambers. Each test chamber contains hazards such as flamethrowers, spike traps, crushers and poison gas. You're equipped with a magnet gun, which can push and pull blocks to weigh down pressure plates, throw blocks through the air to activate buttons and you can also use the magnetic force to gain more height and speed on jumps.

This is a first person puzzle game, so the obvious comparisons are Portal and The Talos Principle, however the gameplay isn't quite the same style. Magnetic is more of a physical challenge than a mental challenge. The puzzles, while intelligently designed, aren't particularly difficult to solve. I was never stuck for very long, experimenting with different ideas and slowly figuring out what to do. The gameplay is more about reflexes, platforming skills, and moving quickly enough to avoid the traps.
The graphics aren't amazing, but they are functional, as you would expect from a low budget indie studio. Of course this means its easy to achieve a stable 60 FPS . There are some nice visual touches though, lots of rusted metal, the occasional message from other test subjects written on the walls, or blood stains where they've fallen victim to the traps. Each test chamber is much more visually intimidating compared to Portal's bright and clean style.
A couple of NPCs talk to you over loudspeakers as you progress through the test chambers. I particularly liked the warden, who has some really sadistic dialogue. He makes no attempt to hide the fact that he wants you to die. A darker, less amusing version of Portal's Glados. Controls are fully rebindable, and work great with mouse and keyboard. I didn't encounter any bugs or crashes.
My only disappointment is that the game is quite short. I finished in just over 3 hours, and although there is a bit of replayability provided by a couple of moral choices that lead to multiple story endings, it seems that the test chambers are always the same whichever path you take.
Overall I'm giving Magnetic a positive recommendation. Maybe wait for a sale if the length is a concern, but its certainly a fun game that's worth checking out.

It's not as difficult as Portal 1 could be, and it obviously doesn't have the production value of Portal 2, but it sits nicely in between with difficult engaging puzzles, and a well told story. The voice acting falls a little flat sometimes, but is in general very good, and we learn a lot about the characters from the writing. The physics are on-point, and though I tried to break them at points I didn't accomplish anything, and honestly I really like the visual style.
Highly Recommend.

Positive:

Negative:
-Most people will be bored before they unlock even 1/10th of the game. Rather 1/20 of the game. I'm still not there.
-Lots of traps, you'll never get to enjoy because of the insane cost.
-No point in trying and testing the traps you love the most => insane cost, so you'll never have even 1/4th of the traps
-Upgrading traps is even more of a joke, even higher cost
-Hero cost is also insane
-Drop rate is horrible compared to crafting cost
-No variation at all when you play with other players => nobody can get any new traps because of the insane cost
-You can't place archers/fighters anymore. Why remove this awesome feature?
Conclusion:
This is still a beta, so things may change. They reduced the hero cost from overpriced, to less overpriced. I want to enjoy this game with other players, seeing all kinds of trap variations and fun combinations. Sadly, 80% of the player base will probably quit before reaching any new traps, due to this insane cost.
You are PUNISHED for trying different kinds of traps. There is absolutely NO WAY you'll get around testing and upgrading various traps, due to high cost, weeks and weeks of grinding to just upgrade even 1 trap. I don't mind who the developer is, but I can't believe they would enjoy their own game for a long time because of the lack of variation, only due to high costs. Orcs will prevail like this.

Got this in a bundle for the price of a Mickey D's Double Cheese so I'm not mad that the game is...let's just say, bad...but I had at least hoped it would be more like Wave Race 64.
Nope nope nope.
It kinda *looks* a bit like WR64, but the similarities pretty much end there. Oh, and lots of primary and/or bright colors, so there's that I guess...
I have NO FRIGGIN' IDEA how this game has an almost 90% positive score on Steam. As a WR64 wannabe, it's not good at all. As a standalone racer, it's equally bad.
You can't lean the rider forwards or backwards at all. HUGE absolutely HUGE deadzones on the analog sticks when using a controller (xinput, using DS3 controller via SCP, so it's not on my end). On top of that, the controls are not able to be customized whatsoever, and of course neither are the deadzones, sensitivities, etc. Yet there are a good number of PC-centric graphics option you can disable. But who even needs to disable anything? It's a mobile port with subpar graphics to begin with that can probably run 60+ fps on a moldy potato. I also don't think there are any real physics in the game. The "stunts" are a complete joke with canned animations, nothing tied to actual input except for the stick combo itself (L stick up/R stick down, etc.), and you can pull them off with a 100% success rate no problem. It also lets you stunt when not in the air, which is not only a strange mechanic to exist in the first place, but results in throwing you from your craft every single time. What exactly is the point of that? Racing the courses is WAY too easy, even with huge deadzones - almost like there's hidden assists in place keeping you on a decent line. I'd be willing to bet that there is.
The devs are working on part deux for XB1, PS4, PC, and mobile...I would assume if they want their new game to reach a wider audience, especially consoles, they will have decent controls and an actual physics engine this time. Oh, no hidden assists please, either. I wouldn't count on any of this happening though. Because mobile, amiright?

This is the same template I use to review games so that’s why the story section shows up here. There is no story in Riptide since it’s just an arcade racer but you won’t be expecting one either.
Riptide GP2’s control scheme is suited to controllers and feels smooth enough, you will sometimes find yourself a little annoyed at the course layout in the later parts of the game when you have fully souped up late-game hydro jets – I know one course in particular there’s a boat you cannot avoid hitting without ignoring your boost for a few stunt ramps which just feels like a design oversight but overall the levels are fun and I don’t try and avoid too many of them. The icy stages sometimes feel overly snakey however. I feel like I just didn’t look into this long enough but there needs to be a way to shut your boost off and I don’t think there is, if I’m wrong please feel free to let me know, that alone will bring the score up. It must be said that I love Vector Unit’s wave and water mechanics a lot though.
The music is fitting but that’s about all I can say about it. Vector Unit likes to supply their games with a fairly energetic soundtrack and cycle through it at random, that’s a little disappointing for a few people. It doesn’t seem like they put a lot of thought into how they use their soundtracks. It doesn’t stick out too much but I know some people play games solely for their scores and it seems like it’d be worth exploring in the future. Hydro Thunder Hurricane was the same way but the music in that game was actually exciting and if there was a particular track you really enjoyed you could select it at the beginning of each race. Again, it’s not something I looked too far into but the music in GP2 isn’t anything special anyway so… eh.
The game is pretty, and I love the animations your riders have for their stunts. I’m a massive sucker for crisp looking aquatic effects so I can’t complain about anything here, stunning game guys. With Riptide Renegade on the horizon I’ve been checking prerelease videos of that out and it looks even better so I would say this is something Vector Unit excels at.
I give this a 3/5, there are some things that can be improved upon and if there are some mechanics I’ve just missed then I can bump it up to maybe a 4 but it would feel generous. I have to say that I do enjoy playing it so I will recommend it, but be prepared for an annoying grind session before you can do anything fun. That would have to be my biggest gripe. You don’t start out with a hydro jet you can use for very many races so you find yourself grinding races for cash until you can get a few upgrades or a new jet and move on. The online community is pretty scarce which is another shame since VU’s Hydro Thunder Hurricane’s online play was a delightful experience in comparison. I remember playing HTH online with a few members of the dev team and remembered how stoked they seemed to be when it came to making games like this so I am very hopeful for everything they release later on down the line. Now if only we can get a follow-up of HTH I will hail Vector Unit as my indie hero.

Fallout Shelter is a freemium mobile game, that has since been ported to Steam, in advance of Fallout 4's release in order to build up hype. Sadly, that's really all it's really good for. Shelter is a 2D city builder sim where you get to live out your dreams of being a Vault Overseer, and use resources to get weapons and outfits, train your people, and send them out to collect more resources. Since quests have been added, there is a lot more to do, but there really isn't a point to the game. You collect stuff, use your stuff to make bigger stuff with bigger numbers, and use that bigger stuff to get the biggest stuff. As with all city builders, you hit a critical mass at which there just isn't anything to do with your city as it will be mostly self sufficient, and the period of time that it takes to reach this critical mass is artificially extended through the classic freemium strategy of making you wait a period of time for a certain task to be accomplished, with the option of using Nuka Cola to speed up the process. There are a lot of references to Fallout 3 and a handful to 4 and New Vegas, but there is little to actually accomplish, even through quests.
This game is good if you want a bit of a nostalgia trip for the modern Fallout games, and does an excellent job of roping in old players to come back and fire up one of the main series games again, but has no depth past that. It's best played on mobile, where you can constantly check back in on the game for the time based actions, but if you have never touched Fallout it's probably for the best to stay away.

Although it has a lot of things going against it (Match 3 puzzle game, iOS port, etc) this game is loads of fun. Don't be fooled by the store page, this isn't actually an RPG, but simply a match-3 puzzler with RPG elements.
While most M3 games have you moving one symbol around in one of 4 directions, this one has you rotating columns/rows to match 3. It takes a bit of getting used to, but well worth it.
Most gameplay is spent on the dungeon crawling. You look up on the screen, and match the symbol needed above. eg: If theres a chest, match 3 key symbols.
You cannot pass until you match the correct symbol, and theres an advancing wall that kills you (Keep ahead of it!). There are also monsters that you must kill using either Magic or Physical matches (Different monsters have different weaknesses). There are different items you can use too. Overall, a great timewaster/puzzler, but not really a puzzler.

I highly recommend this game and this is why:
Storyline:
The storyline is packed with distrust, politics and personal agendas which I found very interesting. Every character had their own ambitions, attitudes and reason for their actions. I found that I either liked or was undecided about a character, with a few characters that I hated. The storyline flowed well and almost every side quest made sense given the situation that the character was in. You even had some sidequests were you had to track creatures nest and blow them up which was fun and a different version to the usual kill x collect x formula . You were able to make multiple choses in the game and almost every chose matter towards either the main storyline or a sidequest and possibly both. Many of the choses that you choose from had its positive and negatives. You rarely got an option that seemed like the best option but more like 3 or 4 options that could be good but also could be bad. I like this and made me think of what option I should choose. Some warning there is a lot of dialogue about the political issues of Geralt's world and they do shoot out a lot of names which may push some people away. But if your intrigued about  political struggles, regicide, betrayal, mystery and even some romance then you will love this storyline.
Gameplay:
Utterly love the gameplay. It is an action rpg with a skill tree, some what, similar to diablo or other action rpgs. But the overall gameplay is different then your typical action rpg where you kill a huge mobs of monster one right after the other. In this game you do more exploring around and talking to people than killing creatures. But when you do kill creatures they are incredibly dynamic battles were you have options on how you want to kill your foe. Do you want to ensare the creature in a trap and stab it with you sword or do you want to shock it with a bomb and run in for the fatal blow. Also you do not stand their and fight the monster exchanging blows, no you try to dodge or parry the blows so you don't get killed because you can be overwhelmed in the game pretty easily if your not careful. Oh but dont forget your potions. There is an alchemy system where you can make potions using herbs that you find in abundance in the wild as well as oils and poisons that can be added to your weapon for a short period of time. These potions will increase your stats, or allow you to see in the dark, some even give you advantages at a cost of another stat being reduced. These potions are extremely helpful and usually only last around 5 to 10 minutes unless you have some points in the alchemy skill tree. Potions can only be used before a battle starts and you have a limit on how many potions you can drink. So I enjoyed thinking about what potions I should use and when I should use them. You are also capable of creating bombs, traps, armor and weapons which I have seen before, but still adds something to the game, especially the bombs and traps.
Graphics:
The graphics is just amazing for its time and I was suprised at the differences between the looks of some characters that were from the first Witcher game. I also liked how original the creatures looked  in comparison to many other games I have played. This difference added to the dark tone of the game quite well. The graphics made exploring around a lot more enjoyable overall.
Replayability:
There is some good replay value to this game. There are several different difficulty levels that you can play on, and the storyline branches out in two different ways. Therefore, you will have to play the game again to see the other part of the storyline that you missed the first time. There are also differences in sidequests depending on which storyline branch you choose as well as different results to the side quests depending on your choices.
Cons:
Yes, like all games there are some cons to this game. The big one is... the map. It might just be me but I found the map to be utterly confusing to understand.  Some things on the map that looked like walls ended up not being walls and other parts of the map that didn't look like walls ended up being walls. I was playing on the controller and there seemed to be no shortcut button to see the bigger version of the map, you had to open up the selection menu and press map every single time which got on my nerves a bit. Another con to this game is the game's inability to work properly. Sometimes the game would either slow down making gameplay difficult or just crash. Also this issue could very much be an issue with my computer and not the game. Another issue I had with the game was although the towns were well thought out and dynamic the same people walking around kept saying the exact same two or three lines every single time you would pass by them, unless you were having a conversation with them. Next time I hope that the people have atleast a few more lines that they could say.
So overall, this is a great game that you should play to get prepared for Witcher 3, which looks amazing.

Miami, 1989: meet 'Jacket', a guy living alone in his apartment whom gets various strange calls, each of which basically demand him to go to certain places and then assassinate everyone present. In order to anonymously execute these tasks, he wears animal shaped masks, the first of which he received in a package supposedly containing cookies. Following the phone caller's orders for a while, Jacket's reality eventually begins to fade, as he sees talking corpses and the like. Will he be able to keep acting out the incoming phone calls, or give into insanity as he keeps slaughtering countless people?
The game's idea is very simple: you drive to various places, choose one of the many (unlockable) masks and get ready for a killing spree. How you tackle each mission is entirely up to you: do you want to use a big shotgun and blast 3 people to pieces simultaneously? Or would you rather use a little, yet very sharp knife - killing everyone before they see you as you sneak around? Or do you not care about any of that and just want to use raw power as you punch everyone in the face? It's all possible in this gory, action packed murder simulator!
By completing missions and acquiring certain scores, you'll unlock more masks which modify your game in various small ways (e.g. start with a knife, more ammo etc). As levels get harder, it is not a bad idea to strategically pick a mask that'll greatly increase your chances of conquering each mission without too much trouble. Or, one could also act out the opposite - picking a mask that'll greatly increase the challenge of an already fairly difficult game.
Yes, you did read that correctly: the game is difficult. But luckily not unfair. More so, this game is the perfect example that any challenge can be overcome by trial and error. You may fail the first 50 times, but once you figure out that one mission which seemed near impossible, you'll most likely be able to finish it way more quickly and creatively next time.
As difficult as the game can be, it is just as rewarding (if not more) and fun, due to the many creative ways with which you can slaughter your enemies. It is also guaranteed to pump your body full of adrenaline, as this game is not really a relaxing one (well, that depends. For some, killing countless people may feel relaxing.
.
If we look at the amount of replayability there is available, don't worry: there's a lot! To start, try getting an A+ score on all chapters. This alone will greatly increase your hours spent, as it gets more and more difficult to get this highest score in the later chapters. This game is also an amazing game for people who like speedrunning, as you get a higher score for completing a chapter more quickly. Lastly, and I said this already, there are so many creative ways in which you can complete a chapter, that you can just keep on playing and still have a very different experience compared to your  first playthrough.
As far as the controls go; they are rather minimalistic and really easy to get used to. Running around is done with your familiar wasd, whereas shooting/picking up/dropping/throwing weapons is done with the mouse. Luckily, there is also a quick-restart button (the r key), which is going to become your best friend throughout this adventure.
As this is an indie game, ofcourse the art style has to be unique, right? Lots of flashy colouring and effects to suit the crazy atmosphere of the game. Combined with the highly addictive soundtrack, you'll feel like you're on drugs 24/7 (you won't believe how cheap this drug is aswell, let alone on a -75% sale!)
Mentioning the soundtrack ... Believe me when I say it is amazing. Especially Hydrogen gets me in that zone where I turn into a ruthless serial killer and laugh my♥♥♥♥♥off while chopping everyone's faces to pieces. This soundtrack, the art style and fast-paced gameplay go really well together and make for an incredibly fun overall experience.
Look no further: everyone's favourite murder simulator is here! Therefore, recommended to everyone who is not afraid to partake in a journey full of trial and error, many creative ways to kill enemies and engaging in a crazy, over the top storyline! And most importantly ... the soundtrack is just too good to pass up!

This is a first person puzzle game which uses a Magnetic gun to solve puzzles in a level. Main character is a prisoner who is on death row. Given a chance to be the lab rat for the megnetic gun prototypes. There are some very clever puzzles and some very frustrating ones as well. The point of each puzzle is to turn on switches which power on the exit door. In some puzzles there's more than one switch required. The magnetic gun will get stronger as you progress through the game and the levels get harder and harder too. Puzzles include traps such as floor spikes, flame throwers mounted in the walls, huge solid blocks which can crush you, poisonous gas. There's even a part where you go out of the puzzle chambers and into the outside of the buildings like you do in Portal 2. But in my opinion it doesn't work very well with the magnetic gun, mostly it's just walk from one part to the other. The gun is barely used on the outside.
This game will remind you of Portal every step of the way (not that it's a bad thing) minus the humor. The first chapter is a portal reference with the "Cake" part. The was you progress from one puzzle to the other, the chambers and many other similarities. Almost every puzzle the warden "Keene" will talk to you like Glados. There's more than one ending and your choices will affect the ending you get.
Graphics are run of the mill standard, nothing too impressive and not too dated as well. Good enough for a first person puzzler game.  FOV can be adjusted.
There's some good music in the game as well. The voice acting was pretty good as well. I know this is an Indie studio but imo the voice acting was superb.
I played about 4.5 hours to beat the game. The game has good replayability as there's atleast 9 different endings. The game can be addicted if you like puzzle games like me. There's time trial as well. One bad thing about the gameplay which i disliked was the transition time required to move from one puzzle chamber to the other. Once you finish a puzzle chamber you have to wait for the door animation to finished, once the door opens you have to go into the little hole and crawl to the end. This could've done a bit better and quicker. Again it's mostly like Portal 2 but instead of an elevator you crawl through the holes. In my opinion the opening of the door should've been enough. I hope they take this into consideration if they plan on making a sequel.
