I recently purchased Game Guru and I'm very pleased with my purchase. I have a lot of experience with many game engines, editors, etc. Starting with ancient programs like doomedit and Build editor for Duke Nukem 3D, to the original Unreal level editor. I've also used the Elder Scrolls Construction set for Morrowind and Oblivion. I've used both versions of FPS Creator as well. More recently, I've "played with" Unreal and Unity, but they both are complicated enough to need a lot of knowledge to use these products successfully. Game Guru and it's predecessors (FPS Creator and FPSC X10) are incredibly easy to use for anyone! (I taught my daughter how to use FPS Creator when she was in elementary school. Took about an hour.) I don't know of any other game development software that is this easy to use. Also, don't believe comments that say Game Guru is very limited in what it can do. With lua scripting you can modify and control pretty much anything. (There are some exceptions.)  However, you don't need to do any coding if you don't want to. The lua scripts included in the application are adequate for most things you will want to do. In conclusion, if you are already able to use Unity or Unreal, Game Guru might not be something you are interested in. For everyone else, this is the BEST software for less experienced developers (or,non-experienced for that matter) that I know of.

Now, I haven't played this game much, definitely not enough to some people for giving this game a +1. But what I can say, and this more or less will be agreed with, is that the game DOES NOT deserve to die, nor should it. It has an engaging, unique playstyle, and, from my experience, a nice community. But, this game definitely has some immediately apparent flaws, and honestly, some of them aren't the games fault, and the ones that are, seems to be getting fixed, or was fixed a while ago. Let's get into a couple things that deter new players, speaking AS a new player.
- The learning curve.
The second largest problem, from what I've gathered. It's too straining on new players to learn in harsh enviroments, these harsh enviroments being servers FULL of veterans, who know most of the game already. Now, just as this new player coming in, they had to learn in a harsh enviroment as well, but that doesn't mean the next batch of recruits should too, and the devs, apparently, agree. The developers have, quite recently at the time of this Review, released an update aptly named "Bootcamp", where servers can be locked to new players only, have bots(significantly updated bots) that will fill in any empty slots, and roles, such as the commander, and do decently at the job. This remedies one problem, IF the next can be fixed, which, cannot be patched in by the devs, this falls on the people intrigued by the game, and the current members.
- NS2 is considered dead/dieing.
At the time of this review, there are 322 players in-game, since servers have 32 to 42 player slots, this means there isn't all that many servers being played on. This, plus other reviews stating the game is dead, will only succeed in deterring the intrigued oncomer. The solution? Well, to put it simply, the current playerbase would need to actively sponsor the game, similar to its release. Attempt to get famous Youtubers to play the game, attracting players, and hopefully keeping them with the newest "Bootcamp" update.
- Long loadtimes
I'm only putting this here, as it seems to be a problem for my friends. They complain that the load times are too long, whereas, I, in personal experience, think they ARE on the long side, but nothing to deter people. The most I could say is that, from the updates of the past, it's been mostly resolved, so, I'm assuming it's a result of having a potato as a computer. :l
So, that's about it, IF the community gets larger within the year, I may re-make my review, as this is to just, hopefully, get the attention of newer players to buy, play and spread this game, but, you never know what the future holds, this game could end up dieing out, OR, it could sprout back up and become popular again. You never know.

Magnetic: Cage Closed
First-person puzzle
Guru Games
Gambitious Digital Entertainment
is a first-person puzzle game developed by Guru Games and published by Gambitious Digital Entertainment.
You play as a prisoner on death row that has been chosen to take part in a program that consists of him completing some chambers that, if surpassed, will grant him his freedom.
The two characters that you will hear throughout are both funny and creepy, and there is great writing involved in here.
It's the closest a puzzle game has gotten to Portal in terms of story: there are some similarities, but the presence of choices that alter the story and multiple characters make the experience feel fresh.
Powered by Unity 4, the game looks really good. The brown test chambers remind you of the setting, and some writings on the wall a-la Rat Man give an additional layer of creepiness to the game. The gun you use reminds me a lot of the one in Tripwire's The Ball, and there is just as much detail and work put into it as the rest of the environment.
More similarly to The Ball than Portal, you will complete multiple test chambers with the use of your Magnetic Gun, which can pull or push objects. Each chamber feels different and they get increasingly difficult. However, it might feel a bit repetitive if you play it in one sitting.
The levels get harder and more challenging the more you play, while never being frustrating.
While the voice acting is great, the sound effects are fine. The soundtrack serves its purpose while playing, but it is pretty forgettable.
While the game isn't really all that long, there are 9 endings and multiple choices that encourage multiple playthroughs, plus 29 achievements, secret areas and time trials that will keep you entertained for a long time.
Portal and puzzle game fans will have a blast playing this game, also thanks to its replayability, while others might want to wait for a price reduction to experience it.

Yep, it's a roguelike played via DDR. Dance pads compatible but not required. It may technically be in Early Access but I'd never know, the game seems pretty complete as is and I keep getting my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me before I can even clear Zone 2 (there being 4 zones at present).
The gameplay is pretty self-explanatory once you've gone through the quick tutorial, but is ever a matter of reflexes and quick thinking to keep yourself in one piece. Enemies are deviously varied to give you all manner of headaches to fight in conjunction with one another. Diamonds acquired through play are spent in the hub to unlock new equipment to appear in chests (as well as some passive upgrades like health). Rooms are available to help you practice fighting against specific enemies and bosses, and one character is available to let you just play the game as a regular turn-based roguelike. There's a local co-op mode of some sort too, hell if I know how that works. Hardcore mode is available for a no-upgrades run, and there's a daily one-shot hardcore challenge available, ala Spelunky.
There are a few minor sticking points.
1) You can import your own music for any of the levels you like, which is fantastic, except when the automatic beat detection--which, granted, is impressively accurate on the whole--doesn't work quite right and there's no way to attempt a manual fix.
2) The game doesn't require you to keep on the beat perfectly, there's a fair leeway in the timing and you can miss beats if you don't mind losing your current cash multiplier (that is, unless you've invoked a risk shrine); this is open to some strategizing with skipping a beat to ready yourself for an enemy, but there's no actual control function for 'skip beat' and so you're left waiting for the input grace period between beats for enemies to make their move, after which it's hard to get right back into the rhythm.
3) There's no "count in" between levels at all, so to keep your multiplier up you have to start moving again before you've even processed what's immediately around you or what the new rhythm actually is.
4) Practice rooms for monsters are great, but having to defeat a monster or boss once during normal play to unlock them seems a bit counterintuitive.
Minor gripes. Very solid soundtrack, very solid gameplay. Would probably be a HELL of a party game, with big picture running on a nice TV and a DDR mat set up.

Fallout Shelter is a freemium mobile game, that has since been ported to Steam, in advance of Fallout 4's release in order to build up hype. Sadly, that's really all it's really good for. Shelter is a 2D city builder sim where you get to live out your dreams of being a Vault Overseer, and use resources to get weapons and outfits, train your people, and send them out to collect more resources. Since quests have been added, there is a lot more to do, but there really isn't a point to the game. You collect stuff, use your stuff to make bigger stuff with bigger numbers, and use that bigger stuff to get the biggest stuff. As with all city builders, you hit a critical mass at which there just isn't anything to do with your city as it will be mostly self sufficient, and the period of time that it takes to reach this critical mass is artificially extended through the classic freemium strategy of making you wait a period of time for a certain task to be accomplished, with the option of using Nuka Cola to speed up the process. There are a lot of references to Fallout 3 and a handful to 4 and New Vegas, but there is little to actually accomplish, even through quests.
This game is good if you want a bit of a nostalgia trip for the modern Fallout games, and does an excellent job of roping in old players to come back and fire up one of the main series games again, but has no depth past that. It's best played on mobile, where you can constantly check back in on the game for the time based actions, but if you have never touched Fallout it's probably for the best to stay away.

I see a lot of praise for this game, and to be honest I can see why. Hell, I enjoy the "rhythm" aspects a lot, the soundtrack is absolutely amazing and the tileset is decent and cute, however, it fails at being a Roguelike.
Sure the dungeons, loot and encounters are randomly generated but that's the end of it. Don't be fooled by the roguelike-esque appearance, this is at heart a "rythm" game, with little to no emphasis on micro-management and rich possibilities during your run. Sure there are a lot of objects unlockable, but most, if not all of them don't change between the runs making their effects and efficiency predictable. Runes, magic items and spells are easily remembered. The combat mechanics are solely based on pattern memorization, which makes a lot of sense given the rhythm aspect of the game, but that gets old fast. All that is especially sad because there is a real sense of urgency created by the music and the need to do every action quickly but in a timely fashion, an element often missing in traditional Roguelikes.
One of the redeemable aspect for Roguelike fanatics is the Hardcore mode which pits you against a dungeon without the interference of the unlockables, thus making the whole thing a lot harder, a bit closer to a real Roguelike experience.
Bottom line I don't recommend it for Roguelike fans and that is my perspective on the game. For everyone else it's an enjoyable experience for a little while. If you manage to get past the fact that the game takes big liberties with the genre, basically doing away with most if not all its interesting aspects, it's a nice little game that won't get your attention for long but with a great soundtrack that clearly makes the experience worthwhile.

As you probably already know Riptide GP2 is a port of a mobile game.  I have tried the mobile version of this in my occasional hunting for a phone game worth playing that always ends in a solid "mobile games just aren't for me" verdict.  That was the same when trying this.  The whole time on my phone I thought man if only I had a controller this would be pretty sweet.  Well what do ya know, it is.
Some of the Hydro Thunder team actually worked on this game as well.  Now that has been a fairly sporadic series at best.  There were three games if I recall corectly.  A N64 one, an arcade one that I blew WAY too much money on as a kid, and the Xbox Live Arcade Summer of Arcade title "Hydro Thunder Hurricane".  I can honestly say that Riptide is best described as a tamed down version of Hydro Thunder on jetskis.  There you go.  Review over.  Just kidding.
The soundtrack was a dubstep mix on my iTunes in the background, because the stock soundtrack is decent, but it's pretty samey pretty quick.  The skis themselves have an almost formula 1 sound to them that's pretty cool and especially shines when one of the AI rubber bands right past you to take the win at the last second.
So yeah about that, the worst and I meen Godforsaken sin evil worst thing is this games INSANE rubber banding.  I almost gave up in the beginning it's so bad.  I could not win a race.  Why?  Because I was doing stunts to earn boost and going flat out the whole time like that games tool tip screens tell you to do.  Why does that make you lose?  Because like many games with rubber banding it just doesn't matter how fast you go.  In this game, short of a lucky crash on the AI's end, you will never win by more than a second or so.
I very quickly found myself doing enough stunts on the first lap to fill my boost meter, then steering out around every subsequent jump, then purging my boost all as the finish line is coming up.  Once I started doing this I won every single race the first try.  Well almost...
There are three types of events.  Race, which is your standard race.  And once you learn to game the AI at its own thing these become almost trivial.
There's also freestyle events, which sucks and is sucky and the games trick system isn't bad but the freestyle events somehow many to still just be boring.  Mainly due to the fact that you never find jumps big enough for actual combos.  You just bust out your moves and work through them so you aren't punished for repeating tricks.  This is not challenging at all.  What is, is leveling your character up enough to actually purchase the tricks that earn enough points to even have a hope of anything beyond 3rd place in the freestyle events.  Sound like leftover mobile game with in app purchases grinding to you?
Next we have the elimination events.  Now these are by FAR the most interresting events.  Though they left me frustrated quite a few times by the earlier mentioned overly-rubber-bandy-AI.  They are interresting though because the Race mode strategy of hang back and dump boost at the final stretch just doesn't work.  Ever.  You will actually have to consistently fill your boost bar and use it every time you find yourself in the rear of the pack with the 5 second warning of an elimination flashing on your screen.  This keeps these events feeling far far more edge of your seat than the other two.  The only issue I had was that more often then not I still just felt cheated into a 2nd or 3rd place finish due to the AI absolutely FLYING by me at the last second while I was boosting... All the while they are on a Ski that according to the stats page in your garage should never be passing you in a dead straightaway.
So all in all, why did I still sink 4 hours into this game?  It's addicting.  Cough, mobile hooks?  I wanted one of the bad A final skis as soon as I saw them.  The problem was, once I got one, the game was literally boring immidiately.  I had the final Ski less than halfway through the game's championship events.  Granted I had done a bit of backtracking, reracing old events because you 100% half to in order to upgrade your ride enough to win the events to unlock further ones.  I can only assume that the mobile version will allow you to skip this buy purchasing the upgrades with real money.
So yeah, I just don't know.  Is it worth it?  Well if you pay the full price of $7... Eh, I really don't think so.  I got this in a sale for $1 and felt satisfied.  At that point you have to ask if its worth your time.  I personally REALLY love the Hydro Thunder games and have a weird gamer fetish for driving anything on some nice pretty water.  The completionist in me hates that I will never finish this.  But the realist in me says.. "Yeah, that was 4 hours well spent.  I enjoyed that for the most part."  So  this is pretty inconclusive, but I hope that my insight here helps you work out for yourself if this port is still worth a look.

What makes Aragami great is its ability to give you options despite looking very straightforward. As you get more powers, you get more curiosity regarding the levels you completed without those powers.
There are 2 basic ways of completing the game, as a shadow and as a cleaner. Trying to be a cleaner is difficult because killing and getting away with it is a bit more complex than just dashing through the level in the shadows.
A third way of completing it would be to never move. You give yourself a rule to never use the left analog stick and just shadow dash from start to finish. This makes the game incredibly difficult but my point is that it is possible to pass it like this.
It is easy if you want to just go from checkpoint to checkpoint but if you want to experiment your stealthy abilities and enhance your skill in the game, you will find a way to set rules and challenge yourself. As you get more powers, it gets easier but you can still set rules that will make it difficult and yet you will again be able to complete the missions.
The game gives stealth freedom that is easy, difficult, fun, frustrating, annoying and amazing. It is your choice how you approach it.
Easily my number 2 stealth game right after Dishonored.

Before beginning this review and to perhaps provide some context for the initial tone of the review, Mafia 3 is the first game I have purchased on Steam and attempted to gain a refund, unsuccessfully to my regret.
Having only been a PC player and initiated into the PC master race since around this time in 2014, I never quite understood why PC players complained so much about poorly optimized games. Well fellow PC gamers I now understand, fully, why it is such an issue and how important it is.
Mafia 3 is simply one of the most poorly optimized games I have ever encountered, across the length and breadth of the game from launch to present there are recurring performance, graphical, audio and gameplay issues that make this game simply unbearable and unplayable at times.
Texture quality for example is completely awful and unacceptable for a 2016 release, often textures pop-in and out of quality going from blurry to super-bright in moments. The textures of the vehicles are simply hideous, chrome features on vehicles like the bumpers and wheels look matte in appearance with no metallic or reflective quality at all.
Character models often appear matte in skin tone and their clothes look flat, lacking any depth or shading even in its most simplistic form. In fact, you will be hard pressed at times to find any textures that look appealing or even visually correct, distance has no factor in this from examining textures in detail to casually passing them as you move around the game world.
At launch the game was controversially locked at 30 frames per second, however after instantaneous public outrage the developers amended this by implementing an FPS setting in the games visual settings menu. With this new option the players can choose either 30, 60 or unlimited FPS, however after this hasty update it’s become strikingly clear why the game was restricted to 30 FPS, it’s because the game is poorly optimized (or not at all as some, perhaps rightfully, claim).
I would consider myself an
player when playing games that offer a stealth element, or that are just straight-up stealth games, I enjoy the patient and calculating approach as I pick my targets off one-by-one without detection. The thrill of completing objectives and the mission in a stealthy, almost
way keeps me keen on a game, not all the time of course as I often appreciate the application of brute force and simply slaughtering my way through objectives.

Mafia 3 was advertised as a game that offers this sort of freedom I seek and what is expected these days of open world games, the ability to tackle objectives and opponents how you see fit helps keep a game interesting and prolong its life. However, Mafia 3 in my opinion does not offer those choices in a particularly well-polished way, the choice to stealthily remove targets one by one or go in guns blazing is there, it’s just they aren’t executed in a satisfying or even correct way.
For example, the enemy AI are, for lack of a better phrase, completely
stupid and present zero challenge to the player. At a mission area inside a factory I can simply whistle to draw the attention of enemies and kill them with a knife, two button presses and I can clear an area in the same spot just repeating the
process. The AI will not recognize their deceased friends as Lincoln discards them like chewing gum wrapper, even in broad daylight I have executed AI within line of sight to one another with no reaction. You whistle and like lemmings they follow the same route, even repeat the same tired dialogue and character models as you morosely slit one throat after another.
Even brazenly attacking a mission area feels unrefined and empty, the AI presenting no real challenge or demonstrating any useful or difficult tactics or behaviors, they may as well be crash test dummies for all their use. Though the gunplay is somewhat satisfying, with meaty weapon sounds and a slightly above average cover system it is all spoiled by poor AI and rehashed environments, which in an open world game in 2016 is inexcusable in my opinion.
The greatest reason why I, in hindsight foolishly, pre-ordered this game was for its promised narrative element, exploring sensitive issues regarding race in North America in the 1960-70’s particularly in the south and a strong, African-American lead rolled in to a crime-centered theme drew my attention and money.
However, Mafia 3 suffers oh-so greatly with repetitive, re-hashed side quests that must be completed to progress the story.
rinse and repeat for multiple zones, broken-up only by the promise of unique missions at the end of each sequence may keep you going, like the popular
analogy. It is lazy games design and story development I believe, to bait players in grinding through
content to get to the actual sustenance and reason for purchasing the game in the first place. Sandwiching the quality content between thick slices of grey, void filler is a complete turn off for me and I suspect a lot of other people as well.

As mentioned at the beginning of this review Mafia 3 is the first game I have ever purchased and attempted to return, so disappointed was I with the poor quality and failed promises of the title, the lackluster and unengaging gameplay. I needed and wanted this game to be good, after what has been a very difficult year for me personally and financially I have missed out on all the game releases this year, yet with Mafia 3 I made the exception and spent money I could ill-afford to waste on a luxury, on something which I thought could perhaps give me some joy and entertainment. I fell for the marketing, the videos and opinions of YouTubers whom I trusted,
they said with confidence.
Now I am out of pocket to the sum of £34.99 which Steam refused to refund, with a game sat uninstalled in my library and wracked with buyer’s remorse. Perhaps rather fitting of how universally awful the year 2016 has been Mafia 3 seems indicative of that, false promises, shallow content and wholeheartedly disappointing.

I have always been a huge fan of the Warhammer board games.  My first foray into this was a long time ago with some of my old friends.  I got out of the game but still have the minatures stashed in boxes around the house that i now have no time for and no space to properly work on them.  Anyway, the Dawn of war series has been a fantastic reimagining of the game for me.  Granted much of the game lacks the vast array of units that all the armies are able to field in the board game and it is not a turn based game.  Dark Crusade is the sequel to the previous two entries in the series and is a step in a new direction for the game.  The orginal and Winter Assault were story driven games based solely around the Blood Ravens in the first game and the Imperial Guard in the next game.  Dark Crusade is a way to have a single player story revolve around each race available in game by having a mini crusade span roughly an entire continent, which seems to span the entire planet or so.  Each faction has a starting location and they fight and conquer territory as they go.  Certain territories grant abilities that can affect gameplay and others add honor guard units that act as free infantry and units to fight with.  So far this has been the best game  in the series.

I thoroughly enjoyed this fine little time waster.
So, yes. It's kind of like Bejeweled. The matches you make down below push your character through combat and exploration above. Each "run" through the dungeon takes a minute or two. But as you run, you achieve a series of objectives which the game gradually presents to you, which leads to improved skills.
The game's genius is the way it rewards you not for a lifetime score, but instead for pushing your single-run high score higher and higher, until you can reach 10,000,000 in a single run. As your character improves a bit with each run, cresting your previous high score becomes theoretically easier each time you run the dungeon. Die, and you can either quit the game, or try one more run almost instantly.
It's not a deep game, but I can't think of many games that made "just one more turn" so compelling. Like, "Civilization"-style compelling. It's so easy to try again, over and over. A minute here, a minute there, next thing you know, 2 hours have gone by.

Finished the game, it is definitely a mix of magrunner and portal. I for one usually love these games and want as many to come out as possible, if they aren't short or feel like a genuine copy of better versions of the genre. I found the game fairly short, about 9 hours of gameplay.  The voice acting is okay, kind of annoying at times, but nontheless better than nothing.  I made sure to turn any music off for a better gaming experience.
The game was originally announced for March 2015 Steam launch and after waiting another 2 months for it's release, I was hoping for something longer and more challenging, per say.
PRICE POINT:  At $15 it's hard what to expect, it's not that expensive for 9 hours of gameplay, but other first person puzzle games at this price point will give you significantly more playtime.  I would wait for this game to on sale for about $5.  Games like Q-beh, Magrunner, Parallax, Portal, Antichamber, The Ball, etc were all much harder and longer and made me feel accomplished.  This game, not so much.  Once you get the basics down it's not a real challenge.
CAN I RECOMMEND IT:  At $5, I would have, at $15 I cannot for the fact that it is subpar as far as it sits.  Right now, you can play longer Portal 2 maps made for free that will leave you with a better satisfaction.  In all, IT IS A REALLY SHORT GAME with little to show.
CHEAT HINT: (?)
I don't know if this is a cheat or not, but you can use a small box to perform magnet jumps to anywhere in the game.  Stand on a small box, set your magnetic gun to the second or third most powerful settings, look straight down at the box, and just hold the right click and jump at the same time, the box will lift you up and you can mega jump almost anywhere in the game, this lets you completely avoid certain sections of the earlier puzzles.  This should probably be fixed.
Bugs:  The game can crash or have you fall through the void between levels.  The best option when you enter the end cage to crawl through is to stop as soon as you enter the transition, let the game save, then continue on through the crawl exit to the next side, if you don't let it save, you could fall through on a bug and have to restart the previous level.

Is it pay to win?
As I'm writing this review, I am just over 20 hours into the game. I've won over 20 matches, more than I've lost, I've added 3-4 traps to my itinerary, some rare, I've crafted two ability item thingies, I've crafted two trait cards and need one more to have a full deck of my own customization and I've crafted a war mage. So pay to win, I don't really think so, I haven't spent a penny. Answer: NO!
CO-OP?
This game is really about teamwork, from the beginning if you don't agree with your team mates as of which hero each of you is going to use, who defends, who attacks and who pillages, then inevitable failure is near. This is not DOTA 2 or league of legends, although it has elements of these lane pushing games. This is also Orcs Must Die, a tower defense action game. Keep in mind I mainly play siege PVP. YES!
Can smart people and dumb people play it?
It is easy to learn, my friend coached a new member of our team as of what to do and we won, despite having this newbie on our team, who at first was playing very badly and my friend told him so. By the end of the game and at our victory, he knew what to do, and in fact had collected the steak and cooked it to spawn our boss minion. But this game takes time to master, there are melee and ranged characters, with strengths, weaknesses and unique abilities, in my opinion the game is masterfully balanced, these developers know what they are doing. Some characters require more strategy, some are just ravagers, all are fun to play with and in my experience, each one caters to a different playstyle. YES!
Is it cool and funny?
Damn yes, this is a funky and funny game, just as much as the other Orcs Must Die games. It's wickedly cool, characters are hillarious, and seeing orcs dismembered, well, that's a matter of taste.
UPDATE! 70 hours in, I'm almost at level 80 (75), I have unlocked two warmages, StinkEye and BlackPaw, upgraded a trap, have loads of resources and am having lots of fun. I've won 61 matches. I love this game.
I think the negative reviews come from people who know the game is in beta and just want the developers to give away more goodies. The way I see it they've been very generous already, it's a shame people have that attitude, give an inch, take a mile. Because, I hope it doesn't put people of playing the game. My opinion, try it for yourself.

Yep, it's a roguelike played via DDR. Dance pads compatible but not required. It may technically be in Early Access but I'd never know, the game seems pretty complete as is and I keep getting my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me before I can even clear Zone 2 (there being 4 zones at present).
The gameplay is pretty self-explanatory once you've gone through the quick tutorial, but is ever a matter of reflexes and quick thinking to keep yourself in one piece. Enemies are deviously varied to give you all manner of headaches to fight in conjunction with one another. Diamonds acquired through play are spent in the hub to unlock new equipment to appear in chests (as well as some passive upgrades like health). Rooms are available to help you practice fighting against specific enemies and bosses, and one character is available to let you just play the game as a regular turn-based roguelike. There's a local co-op mode of some sort too, hell if I know how that works. Hardcore mode is available for a no-upgrades run, and there's a daily one-shot hardcore challenge available, ala Spelunky.
There are a few minor sticking points.
1) You can import your own music for any of the levels you like, which is fantastic, except when the automatic beat detection--which, granted, is impressively accurate on the whole--doesn't work quite right and there's no way to attempt a manual fix.
2) The game doesn't require you to keep on the beat perfectly, there's a fair leeway in the timing and you can miss beats if you don't mind losing your current cash multiplier (that is, unless you've invoked a risk shrine); this is open to some strategizing with skipping a beat to ready yourself for an enemy, but there's no actual control function for 'skip beat' and so you're left waiting for the input grace period between beats for enemies to make their move, after which it's hard to get right back into the rhythm.
3) There's no "count in" between levels at all, so to keep your multiplier up you have to start moving again before you've even processed what's immediately around you or what the new rhythm actually is.
4) Practice rooms for monsters are great, but having to defeat a monster or boss once during normal play to unlock them seems a bit counterintuitive.
Minor gripes. Very solid soundtrack, very solid gameplay. Would probably be a HELL of a party game, with big picture running on a nice TV and a DDR mat set up.

I see a lot of praise for this game, and to be honest I can see why. Hell, I enjoy the "rhythm" aspects a lot, the soundtrack is absolutely amazing and the tileset is decent and cute, however, it fails at being a Roguelike.
Sure the dungeons, loot and encounters are randomly generated but that's the end of it. Don't be fooled by the roguelike-esque appearance, this is at heart a "rythm" game, with little to no emphasis on micro-management and rich possibilities during your run. Sure there are a lot of objects unlockable, but most, if not all of them don't change between the runs making their effects and efficiency predictable. Runes, magic items and spells are easily remembered. The combat mechanics are solely based on pattern memorization, which makes a lot of sense given the rhythm aspect of the game, but that gets old fast. All that is especially sad because there is a real sense of urgency created by the music and the need to do every action quickly but in a timely fashion, an element often missing in traditional Roguelikes.
One of the redeemable aspect for Roguelike fanatics is the Hardcore mode which pits you against a dungeon without the interference of the unlockables, thus making the whole thing a lot harder, a bit closer to a real Roguelike experience.
Bottom line I don't recommend it for Roguelike fans and that is my perspective on the game. For everyone else it's an enjoyable experience for a little while. If you manage to get past the fact that the game takes big liberties with the genre, basically doing away with most if not all its interesting aspects, it's a nice little game that won't get your attention for long but with a great soundtrack that clearly makes the experience worthwhile.
There are some stories you will never forget, this is one of them. There is the second game, which is "Memoria", just as good. Totally recommend.

Please note: This is a "first impression" so far, not a full review.
So far, the game seems pretty amazing. It is rather quiet and has it's focus on hardcore Stealth. All mechanics are very well designed to support as well as subconciously suggest this for the player. The prime example being the "shadow power" mechanic. You are (without spoiling too much) some form of supernatural shadow being. That means all your abilities (aside from the standard sword kill) are shadow based. And light is your enemy. You spend "shadow energy" when using abilities (of which some are integral), and you will regain that energy by resting in the shadows. By doing this the developer deliberately encourages you to take things slowly and think before you act.
A.I. is a little bit simplistic here and there, and the line of sight is not the best. Shadows hide you VERY effecitvely. But the game makes up for that and cramps up the challenge by introducing different enemy types as well as having a really high guard density in every level.
The game feels like a mix of Dishonored and Mark of the Ninja. The quality and artstyle are very indie, and the design concept is very deliberate. The mechanics are focused on pure Stealth, but I feel the game has a fun way of doing it and gives you quite a few options (so far).
The plot is nothing groundbreaking, but there is some mystery involved and it is ... different than other games. So I am intriqued. I just hope the game will last long enough in terms of time / number of chapters.
Also hoping for some DLC with more levels as well as alternate appearances.
Recommended for all Stealth fans. If you liked Dishonored and Mark of the Ninja, go for it.
EDIT #1: 8 hours in. I'm in Chapter X (10) now. Seems like it actually has a nice runtime.

The Dark Crusade is considered the starting point in my campaign with the Warhammer series probably back in 2007. I always come back to this game year after year because I enjoy the single player and multiplayer game modes that include all the races unlocked out of the gate. The single player mode allows you to pick any race and drops you on the map with the rest of the races scattered across the globe. Each section of the map you win provides requisition and other bonuses to your army. The turn based "Risk style" mode begins after your first action and then allows each AI a turn in capturing territories. Similar to other RTS games, Dark Crusade is no different and allows you to construct buildings, vehicles and troops.
The maps in each territory are littered with capture points that you will need to grab before your opponent in order to gain resources to expand your base. While there isn't much story in the campaign beyond the first introduction scene, more details will unfold as you begin to win battles against the other opponents when you capture their strongholds. The main character for each race is also outfitted with war gear as you fulfill certain requirements throughout Dark Crusade. Once you start conquering section of the map, rest assured that each race will take opportunites to invade and try to force you out of the territory.
If I could recommend an RTS game then this would be the one out of all the Warhammer games. Whether it is a group of vehicles bombarding soldiers sending them flying or the up close action of Blood Ravens putting the boots to Orks for the Emperor, I feel there is never a dull moment in battle. I think Dark Crusade is the definitive pick over the newer Dawn of War games because of the maps, large scale battles and the non-linear campaign. Your best bet is to pick up the Warhammer collection, which usually pops up on sale. I had hours of time on Dark Crusade when I owned the original disc but had to purchase it again because I lost them.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is hard to review, because it is a very hit-and-miss game. Frankly, the writing is terrible, riddled with cliches and horribly abused tropes like amnesia, being reborn, or racist villians. I will admit that some of the jokes forced a smile from me, but most of writing made me more embarrassed than interested. The voice acting is extremely over dramatic and forced, the characters obnoxious and one-dimensional. I was not invested in the actual stories or characters whatsoever, and there are a ton of loose ends that are just left dangling, a lot of underdeveloped character relationships and plotlines.
The catch is that the game is fun to play. It's incredibly stupid fun, but it's fun. The combat is repetitive and has basically no variety near the end, it's really nothing more than a spam-fest. Yet it still managed to keep me playing the whole game. The game manages to pace itself very well, whisking you away to new pretty hand-drawn levels with surprising clever level design, alowing you to just spam the same flashy combos and twirl madly across the screen again and again and again. It takes no intelligence, no thought, no worrying. It's entirely a stress-free game. Something you can just burn through and enjoy. You'll forget about it in just a week or two, but it's a fun romp while it lasts. There are plenty of sidequests to help you waste more time skipping through dialog and gleefully mascaring some clusters of enemies, along with some generally interesting gimmicks, like the key system and a very good leveling system. The actual gameplay obviously had a lot of love put into it, even if that love was mindless and childish. It's very much an example that you don't have to think to have fun.

Few days ago, I made a negative review for the game. Not because the game is absolute trash but because for a F2P game, it was too heavy grind. I would have not called this P2W game as half the game is just coop and the PvP part of the game is not affected by trap upgrades and stuff like that. It's pretty much impossible for a player to pay and make the PvP unfair for those who didnt pay. But the game was feeling like a P2P because it was so long to unlock something that most people would have been disgusted before even starting to grind. Add to this the heroes and traps feel weak and the rewards for playing/leveling were not awesome. It was the perfect conditions to make this game a complete fail because only the hardcore fans, who can stand heavy grinding, would have played.
I have to admit I was very surprised how fast the devs reacted to massive complains about insane grinding. They quickly adjusted rewards for leveling, changed missions so they are not too painful and boring to do (those missions were forcing you to play a given hero and people that were not able to get their hero at beginning of the game were just rage quitting to queue again, mehhh!!). So yeah, not only surprised but impressed too. They proven they were ready to listen and bring some change to keep a good playerbase which is good. The game is not easy, you still have to grind but the grind is fair. You can unlock a new hero pretty quickly compared to before. Honestly, I think it's fair.
Now let's give the good and the bad of this game:
PROS:
- PvE and PvP (everyone will be happy!!!)
- PvE up to 5 players in coop
- Progress thru crafting
- lot of heroes VS only 2 in the OMD 1/2
- Trap upgrades are not available in PvP
- Free rotations of heroes (seems to change every week??)
- Daily quests + missions + daily rewards
- Devs seems to care about feedback as they made tons of changes since the open beta
CONS:
- Grinding required but never as heavy as it was at the beta release
- Survival (same mode as OMD 1 and 2) is not feeling as awesome as the previous games
Honestly, I like very much the idea behind the PvP and the fact that there is no trap upgrades allowed in PvP. This way, if you just unlocked traps you are as strong as a player that would have played so much hours that he would have all his traps to tier 3. And crafting a trap is much much more easier than upgrading them. So I believe it makes the P2W pretty much impossible and it keeps the game fair. A newcomer as equal chances to wreck than a long time player. Also, it's pretty easy to buy new minions so again, games wont be completely unbalanced and unfair for new players. The only issue that could happen is the balance of heroes. But this is true in almost every games like League of Legends, Dota, etc. Hero balance will be the hardest part. I hope they are going to work hard on this and listen carefuly to players review. But What I heard is like 5-6 heroes were removed from the open beta due to ♥♥♥♥♥♥ balance. They wanted to rework them before releasing them again when they would be less OP. I hope it's true because that would be just perfect to me.
The survival is the same mode as OMD 1 and 2. The traps and heroes feel weak at beginning. It's due to the fact you level up quifckly and you need to upgrade traps which take alot of time. It's going to be the hardest part. If you are playing with friends and splitting the duty of upgrading traps, it can helps alot. Also, some heroes feel weak at first but synergized very well with some traps or other heroes. This will be your job to discover the best combos and how to reveal the power of every hero. But so far, I seen some heroes I was considering poop being useful in unexpected ways.
I honestly think that when you're done upgrading your traps, the surivval mod looks like OMD 1 and 2 but more challenging as it is a 5 man coop (harder to coordinate a bigger team). And I enjoy very much what they did about the PvP. The idea is very great. I know alot of people are complaining this game is not like OMD 1 and 2. Well guess what? It is the reason it's not called OMD 1 and 2 lol. And I think it's ok the devs try new things. Bringing back the same game over and over again, this is the real boring and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ things. I prefer devs that try new things. If I wanted to play OMD 1 and 2, I would just go play OMD 1 and 2 lol. I would not play this game. So yeah, I think for a F2P, OMDU is just more than fine and enjoyable. I decided to put some money in it because the devs proved me they were listenning and the game overall is far from being broken and bad. Just try it. You can decide you dont enjoy it. But I dont believe it's a fair reason to give a negative review to say that "this game is bad because it's not OMD 1 or 2"... come on lol.

The Witcher 2 is by far THE best game I've played since TESV:Skyrim.  I've had this game sitting in my library for a long time, mainly because every time I attempted the game I played the Tutorial (tutorials never seem like a bad idea) and I'd be turned off by it instantly.  But again and again, I'd hear people talk about what a great game this was online, and so I finally forced myself to put a couple hours in before setting it down.  And I'm damn glad I did.  I can't believe it has taken me this long but I'm ten hours into a save and loving every second of it.
The game is your classic RPG, melee and magic, but with one large difference: the choices you make
.  I'm not talking Skyrim, where if you do this quest you get this item, or that quest you get that item, but rather on a vast scale, where events will unfold completely differently based on what you say or do.  Combine that with amazing graphics; maps that are intriguing, stimulating to explore, and visually stunning; characters that you can actually connect with and understand; and a complex story that has kept me craving more like each new Game of Thrones episode.
My biggest problem with the game is that it has some clunky, unintuitive menus, but after an hour or so you'll understand it to the point that it's barable.  I still have some trouble navigating it, but whatever.
The game is absolutely one of the most unique and awesome games I have played.  To those wondering, you can play this game without playing the first one.  It's not necessary as TW2 does a very good job of keeping a self-contained story.  Do yourself a favor: stop reading this review and buy this damn game.  It's the one you've wanted to play your entire life without knowing it.

Review time: Little over 3 hours
Play time: PvE / PvP
Level: 15
(Note, a review time of 3 hours to get an impression of a game is well in the resonable area)
Pros:
-The game looks wonderful, runs great
-Clean UI, simple to use button layout
-Queue system is smooth
-Built in communication works well
-Items shown clearly on how they are obtained
Cons:
-Game has been stripped down and sold off to the cash shop
-Crafting is based on pure RNG and luck
-Item Crafting is limited to PVP and PVE sets, these do not cross over thus it takes double the time
-Items are built up so the chance of obtaining them is very low
-Advancing your hero takes simply too long, you will go long periods without seeing any at all unless RNG is on your side
-Hero Selection is done after being matched up, so trying to advance one hero is limited to those you play with
Final stance:
If the game continues to grow I will return to take another look. I have been a large fan of the series for awhile and was looking forward to this game because I'd enjoy it more with more friends being able to play. But due to the limited settings and RNG ontop of RNG I will not be recommending this game at this time. I enjoy my time in games, and as an educated gamer understand that time itself does not make a game great, it's what you do in that time. In order to play well and have fun I am required to grind endlessly just to get the basic loadout, let alone advance.
I have no issues helping and funding games that show they are there to be entertaining, but I wont open my wallet for those tha simply do it out of greed.
If the RNG goes down and the game has better options to fund it. (Such as a buy option for say 30-40 that opens the entire game up) then I'll be happy to help fund there work, but nickle and dime tatics simply don't work on seasoned players.

The Dark Eye: Chains of Satinav is a very nice, above average point and click game. It rides a great line between difficulty and logic. I can only remember a few times where the logic of a puzzle or item combination seemed iffy. Otherwise, it was a pleasure to play though.
The story takes a little bit to get rolling, but once it does, I was engaged and wanted to keep continuing. The game does a good job of fleshing out some of the main characters and I did care about them. The main character is a bit on the boring side, however.
Gameplay and mechanics are solid. You can double-click fast travel when moving to a new screen and the characters running speed is good. You can zip around the game if needed. Using the mouse scroll wheel to cycle through your inventory items (with an on-screen item icon next to your cursor) really makes you efficient and certainly helps when you resort to the always classic “try everything with everything” method!
Music is very good and fits the environment. You heard it when things were happening on screen and it blended in when just walking around. The voice acting seemed hit or miss on characters. It was high quality recordings but some of the voice acting was lacking.
Graphics and animation were good. A little rough with some character movements but everything runs at 60fps. Except for the pre-rendered cut scenes which is dialed back to 24fps. Running on a 2560x1440 monitor, all the textures and art was sharp.
+Full Screen
+HD Video
+Subtitles (Way easier to read since there are a lot of fantasy names and items in here)
+Color Depth = 32
+Additional Effects = High
+Graphics, art, sound all done well
+Balanced difficulty and logic. Can get through without guide
+Save anywhere. Also, quicksave/quickload
+Good story progression
+Pretty lengthy
+Too many hints via dialog on what to do
+Voice acting tone doesn’t match scene sometimes
+Framerate hitches occasionally
+Achievement for playing the game on Easy doesn’t unlock when you beat it on Hard (usually they stack and give you both)
Fans of the point and click genre should enjoy this game and I would recommend it. The current asking price of $20 is steep, however. A solid adventure game only brought down slightly by a few small things.

The Dark Eye: Chains of Satinav is a nice point and click adventure game, and I'll recommend it to those that likes trying out games of this genre. The game's atmosphere is a mix between old fairy tales and more modern fantasy.
The characters seem like they would generally be at home in one of the old tales, they are not too deep or complex. Especially the main character is very boring, and the villain seem to just be the antagonist because he are evil.
The game is set in third person, which I like.
The love interest in the story is very naive and childish. Which fit with her character, but I disliked it a lot. She believes everything she is told, has such an open and innocent mind... Really a weird romance choice. Would fit better with the main character in a sort of purely friendly or maybe sibling sort of relationships.
The game is set in a fantasy world, with orcs and dwarves being present. And you also get the feeling of another kingdom and politics, which doesn't influence the overall plot once it starts going, but serves to build the world.
The story is your classic good versus evil battle, but it does mannage to put in a few twists here and there. At times the story is a bit too dramatic for a point and click adventure in my opinion. As someone is about to die, while you are puzzle solving... And you might, like me, miss an object, so it takes you a long time to figure out what to do. But generally the problems are not so immediate threats.
As for the puzzles themselves. They were mostly fun. Many parts were also difficult for me. Trying to figure out what to do, but I felt there were a few too many times where I was required to go back and talk to an npc, that I had already chatted with. It would have been nice if the main character or anyone else could have given hints like "Maybe I should go back and talk to X again." or "I need to find out how to get X working." As there were quite a few times where I didn't know what problem I was trying to solve or where to go. But then again, it might just be that I was bad at the game. I get stuck in most puzzle games and have to look up a guide at least once. The game also has a destroy and a fix spell to help give some variety, and try to make you think about the puzzles in a different way.

I've been waiting for this game ever since the Path of Shadows prototype. As time went on, I was worried that I may never see the full game, or that it might be a disappointment when it finally did arrive. I can tell you that I could not have been more wrong. By the time I had finished it, Aragami had blown me away in every category.
First off, I need to preface that this is (obviously) a stealth game. What some may not know going in is that this game is ONLY intended to be a stealth game. It is nigh impossible to fight the enemy head on, but that’s one of the game’s most beautiful qualities. There are a lot of games claiming to be stealth-oriented, but in reality are easiest when violently rushed through. While this game does give rewards for killing all enemies in a level, it does not reward you in any way for going massacring everyone without caring at all about the alarm. This game is brutal in punishment. If you get detected by anyone, you have to take that guy out, and you have to do it now. If he raises the alarm, you can pretty much kiss your chances of living goodbye, and that’s what I love about it.
Now let’s talk about the abilities of Aragami. Unlike PoS, this game features a skill tree. These skills are all important. My first run through, I made it a priority to get every scroll (those are the skill points, by the way) before I completed the game and not one of the abilities went to waste. I will say, however, that the most useful skill was by far the Shadow Kill. Not only does it erase the enemy’s body instantly no matter what, but it also restores one of your precious ability points, which are required to use any ability and are extremely limited without this skill. The only other way to restore ability points is through the shrines, which are single use and are mostly found in sets of two per level. As a side note, the Shadow Kill is my favorite ability just because it’s so satisfying to use.
Oh, and don’t think that the game only has about five levels or less. I was overjoyed to find a whole twelve levels, plus the tutorial level, most of which took me 30 minutes to an hour to complete the first time I tried them.
All of that said, I would like to take the time to talk about the downsides of the game. As far as the actual game goes, there’s not much bad I can say about it. I can, however, criticize the glitches it suffers from as well as a few design choices. Let’s start with the main one that you notice right off the bat. Aragami’s cape is freeform. Now, normally this wouldn’t be such a bad thing… if it didn’t get twisted around, tucked behind his sword, or bug out and expand across space-time entirely. You see, Aragami’s cape displays information that is extremely necessary to know, such as your shadow power, your equipped ability, and the amount of ability points you have for that skill. It’s not a bad idea to have a cape that moves freely, but they overdid it. Hopefully, this gets fixed in the future. Another glitch that has gotten me killed and set back by fifteen minutes many a time is the teleport. The ability to teleport is sometimes inconsistent and can either save your life or drop you into a bottomless pit or the ocean or something else like that. The main problem it suffers from is the mechanic of being able to teleport up ledges. The game is extremely picky about what you can and cannot teleport up onto. I have also experience problems with teleporting on platforms, occasionally falling through into who-knows-what bellow. While it isn’t game breaking, it is quite annoying and can frustrate the player easily. But the worst glitch I have experienced thus far is the glitch during the first boss fight. During the course of the fight, the boss is surrounded with a shield that can only be brought down by smashing the orbs around the level. After the barrier is down, you have to stab him in the back. However, in the second phase, you can get a glitch where the boss freezes doesn’t do anything ever again until you die. I’ve said it before and I’ll said it again, this wouldn’t be such a problem if it weren’t for one thing. When he freezes, you cannot stab him in the back no matter what. The only way I was able to get past the glitch was by being lucky enough to have him freeze near the edge of a stone beam sticking out of the wall and managing to execute an aerial kill. By the way, this happened even after they released the patch that had presumably fixed this. Oh, and my framerate was fine for the whole game, but I could barely hear over my computer working so hard that I was afraid it might explode.
Other than those very few things, Aragami is one of the best stealth games I’ve played this year. I strongly encourage anyone who took the time to actually get through this essay of a review (nice job if you did that) to get the game. Please support the developers who worked so long and hard on this gem of an indie game. I’m going to go get some dinner after writing this thing for half-a-freaking-hour, so you have a good day. Or… in this case, it would be night, huh?

I recently bought this game, having really wanted it. After playing through the extremely basic tutorial, I headed off to multiplayer, being weary because I've heard this game isn't very noob friendly. At first, people guided me and helped out. I was thinking: "Wow, this is actually nice. They aren't cussing me out because I'm bad, and their actually giving me tips!" However, that was about the end of my enjoyment. After a few rounds, a few people left, a few people joined, and began cussing me out for not being good enough. I figured, fair enough, not everyone is nice. I'll just go practice with bots until I get the mechanics down a bit.... Terrible idea. The bots in this game are so terrible they might as well not even be there.
Alien bots: They refuse to evolve, and I don't think they get any traits either. They also, for some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ reason, refuse to target ANY marine structure. They have an extractor right next to your base? Guess what, they won't go after it. It will live on, never to be destroyed unless you destroy it. They also seem to be able to magically bite 5 times in 1 second, killing you pretty much instantly if they get to you.
Marine bots: Each one of them has a mind of it's own... For the worse. They scatter, have no focus, and unless you're there with them, they won't build any extractors or power generators. Which leads me to something that I noticed while playing as an alien: They will destroy your harvestors, START to build an extractor, and then never finish it, leading to a very, very frustraiting bug: a hologram will just sit there, blocking you from building a harvestor, but indestructible (I got out of the hive, attacked it, but to no avail; every time it got close to being destroyed, a huge cloud of dust appeared and it would be back to the same health I found it at, about 1/4th full). Also, while playing a gorge, I blocked off an entrance to a room with clots. The marines seemed to not understand that they could destroy them, and just kept walking into them like they weren't there. This kept the hive alive for a long, long time, until I got bored and moved the clots somewhere else, and the entire marines team ran into the room immidiately.
Mechanics: They seem fine, but I have one annoying nitpick: Scrolling down while your a marine goes to the melee weapon immidiately then your secondary weapon... Scrolling up goes to your secondary weapon, then your melee weapon... That makes no sense to me, and I'll probably never get used to that.
For right now, I cannot reccomend this game. It seems like fun if you've played a lot of it and have gotten pretty good, but if you're starting out, it ends up being really frustraiting and unplayable. You can't really learn much while on multiplayer (especially when you want to try out being a commander, you'll get immidiately booted), and bots will make your worse at the game. (Or feel better about your skills, seeing how bad they are.)

Riptide GP 2 is an excellent jet ski racing game set in a future utopia so rich that mankind can afford to setup above ground water canals that go up hill. Its a fun, enjoyable, easy to play, tough to master sort of game with unlockables, upgrades and different watercraft to buy. There's a lot of content here and a healthy several hour campaign for a game where its longest races are a mere three minutes long.
Kudos to the developers for making a game where water crafting is a serious sport with helmets rather than the bikini clad fun fest it could have been. Even going for the watercraft genre shows a lot of talent. There are admirable animations of tricks and riders, the water physics feel good, because you'll never have the exact same experience no matter how many times you play on the game's thirteen circuits.
From the start of the game, you get four modes: the career, VR time trials, online multiplayer which is dead and split screen multiplayer for when you have real friends over. You are offered an optional tutorial, but the game is simple enough to understand. Use a keyboard or a 360 controller, sway your body, use your accelerator, turbo boost and perform tricks in the air to replenish your turbo meter.
The turbo boost feels quick and speedy, but its a ramping acceleration rather than a giant boost. So your best bet is to wait until that meter is full before using it. Once you use it, the turbo keeps going until you're out.
Under normal circumstances its best to use turbo in a straight away, but with Riptide GP's trick system, its best to use turbo going into low jump. Why low jumps? Because they're too low to perform tricks, but if you use your turbo, then you have just enough of a window to get a trick in. If you fail a trick, you wipe out, your body rag dolls on the water and sometimes your watercraft smacks into you. There's an easy respawn button, but it costs you time. Even if you fail the landing, you still get your turbo charged.
Tricks are easy to pull off on any jump from a ramp or a big wave. When you're in the air pressing both analog sticks right, both analog sticks up, one analog stick left and the other right. While it does replenish your turbo meter, you need to diversify your tricks. Each time you use the same trick twice, you'll get less turbo from it. Grander tricks need more air time for you to finish, but give you far more boost for your effort.
Riptide GP 2 is a game about leveling up as you earn money and experience for each event you compete in whether you win or lose. Leveling up grants you a skill point or two that you can use to unlock a new trick or ability. The abilities seem meager, things like gaining a bit more turbo from each trick and being able to perform tricks faster by a fraction of a second.
With the cash you earn, you purchase upgrades for acceleration, top speed, handling and boost. You can also purchase better watercraft and that becomes a must, because other racers will have better vehicles and you'll be left in the dust or in this case, the spray. Another nice touch about the game is choosing your exact colors and being able to randomize those colors. While you are yourself in the game, having different colors makes it feel fresh every time you get bored of looking at the same color.
There are a diverse array of event types that can change your strategy going in. There are typical races, eliminations, and hot lap challenges, but also free styles where you score points for tricks. Finishing in the top three will grant you one or more stars. Race events are unlocked by your total number of stars so you'll be replaying plenty of quick events.
The career spans nine championships and dozens of events while the VR time trials are solo races. The time trials make good use of ghosts and keeping track of your friend's times. So there's always a reason to come back and shave a few seconds off your time while competing against a ghost.
During the career, there seems to be two new courses introduced per championship, but the time trials has everything unlocked from the start. The tracks have a few different themes to tell them apart, but several courses look similar with different times of day and a variety of layouts. The two real themes seem to be rich racetrack and arctic racetrack. Some circuits are small and rely on a hairpin circle or a figure eight. If you ever find yourself going in reverse, the game reminds you of the respawn button.
While the water physics are good at making ramps, the other game physics feel a kin to the arcade. Its impossible to leap over one section of track into another. There's no way to crash your watercraft, it just realigns you, but never seems to slow you down. The only way you can fall off is failing a trick. These little details keep you playing the game.
After going through so many other racing games this feels like it stands out for a lot of reasons. Its fun, its on water and the trick system makes it far more engaging that other methods of gaining turbo. Riptide GP 2 manages to fit a lot of content into a small mobile file size. Its perhaps the largest, best looking game for around 250 MB of file size.

I picked up Dust: An Elysian Tail today for only about $4.00 with the 75% discount from the winter daily deals. And let me tell you, this game is worth all of it and more. Humble Hearts, is a one man game company founded by Dean Dodrill, and Dean  spent four years of his life putting all his soul into developing this enticing work of art. And i love him for it. When i got into this game it reminded me personally of Castlevania, in the way the the hud displays your hp and just the overall darting in and out of combat to ensure you take the least amount of damage possible. Speaking of that, the combat is engaging and fast paced making for a great challenge, with parries, dodging, and even some combo abilities that make use of your adorable companion, Fidget. It is absolutely fantastic to see a single man put such depth, and beauty into a single game. Something that big tier gaming companies i think seem to be forgetting this days. The fact that i can go on side quests, buy items at a shop, and craft more epic items at a blacksmith. Even the leveling system is reminiscent of the rpg i used to play, very simplistic but still adds a great deal to the game. The soundtrack is vibrant in the mind and compliments the atmosphere and area around you very well. I would definitely consider checking this game out. Even after when the price goes back up to $15.00. It will still be a wonderful game that you should to add to your library.

For good and bad, the water physics is a lot more like real water in this game than it was in Hydro Thunder Hurricane.  HTH's water felt like jelly.  Also, keep in mind, a boat handles waves better than a jetski.  You could kinda cushion your boat against waves when turning in HTH, whereas in this game, you are punished more for driving across them.  If you're used to HTH, you will not be "in the groove" for the first couple races.  However, it doesn't take very long to get used to.  The challenge makes the game feel more rewarding.  This feels like a water racing game trying to be more like Forza than WaveRace - if that makes any sense.  I feel like this is what Gran Turismo would be like if it was the future and the Nurburgring was covered in water.  Those are the kind of games that the steering difficulty remind me of.  At first, I didn't like that, but it's starting to grow on me.  Also, this game is in 60fps, whereas Hydro Thunder on the xbox360 maxed at 30fps.  That's a great thing for a racing game.
They're both great games, but different experiences.   This game is totally worth it, though.  Hopefully this review shed some light.

10,000,000 looks simple and, well, it is, but it's also fun to play. It reminded me of Henry Hatsworth for the NDS, without the manual platforming elements. Your character will run automatically until you bump into an enemy, door or chest. Then it's time to match key, staff, rock, wood, shield, backpack or sword tiles. Sword and staff tiles will damage your enemies, wood and rock tiles will help you build your castle, backpack tiles can give you items and shield tiles will give you a shield (did you expect anything else ?). A little counter in the top right will count to 10,000,000 while you journey along. That's right, 10,000,000. That's a lot. But in fact it will take several minutes to reach it. That is, if you upgrade your entire castle and know what you're doing. It also depends on a little factor called luck. Expect to finish it in 5-10 hours.
A fun little game, worthy of your time.

This is by far the best game I've gotten for free from Steam. It is very well balanced and well designed, and the addition of the "Quests" feature adds a more enjoyable dimension to the game than it would have otherwise. Fans of the Fallout franchise will find many familiar references, although in structure it is very different from the rest of the Fallout titles. For example, unlike other Fallout fames, there is very little strategy or tactics beyond deciding how to outfit individual characters.
Usually when you get a free game from Steam, the reasons for it being free immediately reveal themselves. This is not the case with Fallout Shelter, which is an extremely playable game that is much better than the price tag would suggest. It is true that the game is set up to offer many possibilities of spending money, but spending money does very little to make the game more playable. Paying for additional resources helps to speed up the game and increase your options a little faster, but this works very well as a standalone game without any additional money spent.
There's a great counterintuitive lesson here for game designers: the more playable the game is without extra features, the more likely players are to spend additional money on it. This is the only "pay-for-more-stuff" game in which I have actually paid for more stuff (about $5, not necessary but no regrets about it either), but it is the game that plays the best in its original form anyway. The games that play the best *without* add-ons may be the ones *most* likely to get revenue from add-ons.
This is not a rapid-fire game with much action, nor a lot of decisions to make every few seconds. It is a resources management game juggling several variables trending at different rates, and there are stretches of time where you are waiting for some clocks to wind down. On the plus side, it is a game that continues to 'play' by itself in relatively safe ways after you log off. It is an ideal game for 30m-1hour in the morning and 30m-1hr in the evening, or a game that you can switch back to once in a while while you do other things.
P.S. For those academic-minded people who like to analyze the fun out of video games, Fallout Shelter is a treasure trove for your Poli Sci or Gender Studies courses. The male and female NPC's are equivalent in all attributes except the fact that the female ones can get pregnant. This is the only game I can think of that features pregnant women, who in this game are simultaneously completely useless in a crisis and also completely indestructible. Combine that with the fact that you as a player have to practice eugenics to be successful, and you have a nice little outraged undergrad paper waiting to be written on this one.

The Witcher 2 is by far THE best game I've played since TESV:Skyrim.  I've had this game sitting in my library for a long time, mainly because every time I attempted the game I played the Tutorial (tutorials never seem like a bad idea) and I'd be turned off by it instantly.  But again and again, I'd hear people talk about what a great game this was online, and so I finally forced myself to put a couple hours in before setting it down.  And I'm damn glad I did.  I can't believe it has taken me this long but I'm ten hours into a save and loving every second of it.
The game is your classic RPG, melee and magic, but with one large difference: the choices you make
.  I'm not talking Skyrim, where if you do this quest you get this item, or that quest you get that item, but rather on a vast scale, where events will unfold completely differently based on what you say or do.  Combine that with amazing graphics; maps that are intriguing, stimulating to explore, and visually stunning; characters that you can actually connect with and understand; and a complex story that has kept me craving more like each new Game of Thrones episode.
My biggest problem with the game is that it has some clunky, unintuitive menus, but after an hour or so you'll understand it to the point that it's barable.  I still have some trouble navigating it, but whatever.
The game is absolutely one of the most unique and awesome games I have played.  To those wondering, you can play this game without playing the first one.  It's not necessary as TW2 does a very good job of keeping a self-contained story.  Do yourself a favor: stop reading this review and buy this damn game.  It's the one you've wanted to play your entire life without knowing it.
