There simply aren't enough games with dinosaurs & even fewer of these that are actually worth playing! For me, Orion: Prelude (O:P) is that rare exception. Although not much in way of a story in the game
, there is quite a tale on how Orion came to be the game it is today...
The short version is, that O:P is an evolution of previous Orion titles, Dino Horde & Dino Beatdown originally dating back to a successful 2011 Kickstarter campaign. Although recieving early criticism
, the game continued to evolve with constant updates (big & small) over the years from the developers. Spiral stuck with it! This dedication & gradual refinement of the game has resulted in an excellent first-person co-op experience, with a well rounded collection of modes, weapons, enviromental effects, vehicles & more to enjoy.
PvP isn't forgotten; it's also selectable. PvP feels more alike to a retro deathmatches, than a modern PvP
, but I mainly enjoy the co-op modes. In co-op, you essentially have to defend your power core against waves of bloodthursty dinosaurs. Dinosaur kills will reward you credits, which you can use to buy perks & weapon upgrades, in-turn helping you survive the later, harder waves. Some waves also have you securing objectives. Co-op doesn't feel ultra competitive, most of the time you don't watch your credits/kills, rather finding yourself just having fun surviving & helping your teammates! I've found the community to generally be helpful & friendly in-game too.
One of the real stand-out features in O:P has to be the enviromental effects randomly cycling on the alien world. From the day/night cycles to the extreme variety of climates & types of weather. Adds so much to the atmosphere. Couple this with excellent lighting effects through what seems to be a thicker atmosphere and the results can sometimes be spectacular! Even overwhelming! You definitely get that
when your final wave gets a night cycle with heavy rain .. you know you are gonna see an epic close quarter battle!
Along with the awesome effects, there are 3 distinct classes to mix-up the gameplay. Each has unique strengths & each you can progress/level-up in online play to unlock starting weapons, power-ups & perks. Initial learning curve isn't steep, so once you get the hang of the basic flow it becomes very easy to sink multiple hours killing dinos! O:P rarely feels like a grind; even at lower levels
you competently kill dinos & gain good XP. Plenty of dinos to go around too :)
If you can't find a friend to play with, there is also bot-support added in O:P to fill the ranks. This can be helpful to get playing quickly if server populations are low (which regrettably does happen).
The trilogy of classes are well balanced (no need for any other classes), as is the gameplay in general. Difficulty is super scalable. Weapons are mainly shared between classes so quickly become familiar, and vehicles are easy to use & offer a good range of practical & destructive uses. Repetitive? Sure, to a degree, it is the same thing over & over and despite there being a lot of 'accessories' to the spice up the character classes & tactics, modes etc, there are not a huge number of maps for each mode. I expect this will change soon with Steam Workshop support being added.
The A.I. generally employed by the dinosaurs is a fairly basic 'rush' tactic, which can feel pretty predictable
, but I find the larger dino numbers to counteract this limitation to a degree anyway. There are also the occasional technical glitches like querky physics (flying Stegosaurus anyone?) or clipping inside a dinosaur. Nothing game-breaking that I have experienced, but sure does make for some funny moments! Just like my many failed attempts at some of the more creative 'Ride a Dino for 10secs' & 'Slap T-Rex 100 times' achievements :)
O:P reminds me a bit of those classic, simple shooters like a Serious Sam or Left 4 Dead, but with a bit of high-tech sci-fi flavor. This future-tech feel across the game contradicts the jurassic era dinosaurs & remote wilderness landscapes nicely! O:P is not as complex mechanically or technically when compared to a top end AAA FPS, but its simplicity is also its underlying strength. It is great value ($1!), has strong replayability and the focused, balanced gameplay
offers a truely fun & intense, dino killin' co-operative survival experience!

Being entirely new to the series, I don't quite know how Insect Armageddon stacks up to the other Earth Defense Force titles. On its own, however, I believe it to be a solid game, doing exactly what it sets out to in a more than playable fashion.
Even Serious Sam has a difficult time comparing to the sheer scale of Earth Defense Force's battles, where the smallest of enemies is at least the size of the player and the largest stand as tall as an apartment building. With hordes in excess of hundreds at almost every turn and the player's arsenal constantly increasing in shock value and near-absurdity, things can get a bit more than hectic.
In terms of variety, EDF is a mixed bag. Much of the combat begins to drag on as the game enters the later stages of the oddly short campaign - doable in roughly seven hours by one's lonesome - as the relatively limited selection of enemies begins to show through.
In terms of weapon and playstyle variety, however, I would draw a considerable amount of comparisons to Borderlands. There are an enormous amount of interesting weapons, ranging from run-of-the-mill assault rifles to airburst missiles that rain smaller warheads down on their targets after detonation. Four different classes, such as the unmatchably maneuverable Jet and the nigh-unkillable Battle, give good options for players of all persuasions.
Graphically, the game is another toss-up. The streets of the cities feel somewhat empty and undetailed and, while undoubtedly pretty to watch and true game-changers for the battlefield environment, the collapse of buildings leaves much to be desired in their wake. Skyscrapers end up leaving little but a neatly-confined pile of rubble, cars explode piecelessly, and the thousands of enemies slaughtered in the campaign leave little but a brief, fading corpse - which, humorously, is often sent hurtling into space by some of the higher tier weapons.
However, much of the model work is definitely up to par, and while the lack of graphical options and locked framerate makes the game feel much like a console port, the game runs flawlessly.
Third party support, unfortunately, seems to be nonexistent. There's not much else to be said here; unless I've simply failed to find it, there's no possibility of a modding community for any but the most die-hard fans.
In the end, at its cheap price point of $10 USD, it'd be hard to turn this game down. If you're looking for something with longevity, that price point may be less exciting. Even still, for someone looking for a quick, frantic, larger-than-life game that charmingly follows every cliché in alien invasion movies, this is most definitely the game to be sought.

So, I just finished this game. Ignore the time it says I've played, that 2 hours is the time I spent trying to get the steam version to work. Thankfully, CDPR provides a GoG code for the DRM free version when you buy the steam one, so I ended up using that. (ETA: After playing through once on "hard", I decided to play through on "dark". Then, early on in chapter 1, it stopped detecting input from my xbox 360 controller; all my other games are still working. I thought maybe the configuration was messed up, so I tried to run the launcher, but that is no longer working. I've given up on this. I couldn't get the steam version working at all, and now the GoG version isn't letting me use controller. I still got my money's worth out of it, but be prepared for some possible issues.)
First I will say that I really like this game, but I really can't understand how so many reviewers have given it 10/10. For me, a rating like that would mean it is flawless, and while TW2 does so much so well, there are also enough flaws to make it an 8/10 at best.
Graphics: A lot of people praise this game for the graphics. As with the game in general, there is a lot I like about the graphics, and some things I don't like. There is some variety, and that is nice. You don't feel like they've applied too much of the clone brush on the locations. The people look good from far away; part of this is due to the nice reflections off armour. The faces are okay, but not so great for a game that came out several years after Crysis. There seem to be only half a dozen different faces in the game apart from the main characters. My biggest gripe with the graphics is that the colours (particularly the yellows) are blown out. I like high saturation, but when light shines on objects, the colours blow out so much that you no longer see detail in the texture. I thought it was bloom, but when I turned bloom off, it only stopped the colours from leaving the edges of the object, not from washing out the object itself. A lot of tweaking of the gamma and brightness can improve it a lot, but it's never perfect, and the default setting is ridiculous.
Gameplay: The combat takes a lot of getting used to. At first it felt laggy to me. This is because you cannot change your mind halfway through an action. If you press the attack button before the first attack has finished, it will automatically carry out the second attack. This means you have to be very deliberate about your attacks so that you don't get stuck in a bad move while you are being attacked. You cannot mash buttons with this game, and I grew to love this style of combat after a few hours of playing. There is also a great balance to it that encourages you to use a variety of techniques in a fight and change those techniques for different opponents. One thing I would have preferred is perhaps two magic bars, one for protection signs and one for destruction, or something like that. I found myself only using quen (protection) because if I used my magic for a different sign, I would be stuck without quen when I realy needed it. TW2 starts off quite linear, and I was worried it would stay like that, but thankfully it opens up a bit after the prologue. However, having played skyrim, I can say this game feels very claustrophobic in comparison.
Controls: I found a controller to be superior to K&M for this game. Keyboard and mouse may be better for more quickly choosing signs or options, but I found the controller better for combat in general. For some reason, I couldn't change the default bindings (even though it's in the options) and I found two of them in particular annoying: the Lclick and Rclick. Lclick causes you to hold your medallion, and this makes you vulnerable. Frequently in battle, I would push too hard on the left stick trying to dodge an attack and accidentally use my medallion. I would have much preferred this to be on the right stick, or perhaps down on the D-pad, which I don't think was used for anything else other than menus. Rclick is to centre view; seriously, who uses
. Left stick could have then been for autosave (wasn't binded, so I either had to use the keyboard or go through the menus.)
Story: I must admit that I don't normally pay attention to the story in games, so I don't have much to compare it to, but I managed to sit through every cut scene and follow what was going on, which is rare for me.
Style: I really like that they don't shy away from the realities of life; drunk soldiers♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in the streets, swearing, brothels, sex and nudity. It's a refreshing change from all these games that happily have you gunning down masses of innocent people, but pretend people don't have breasts. Apart from that, it's fairly typical of the genre. Perhaps leaning towards the medieval realism a bit more than other games, but still plenty of fantasy elements.
Annoyances: While most of these are fairly minor, there are enough annoyances in the game to drag its score down a bit for me...
QTEs during cutscenes! No excuse for this. I'm not a big fan of QTEs, but I'm okay with the ones in minigames (e.g. a fistfight). But when I've just beaten a really difficult enemy and it goes to a cutscene, don't flash a QTE up on the screen while the controller's on my desk and I'm having a bite of my dinner.
Door animations. I don't know who thought it would be a good idea to have an animation of you walking through open doorways, but there were a few points in the game where I got stuck in the animation and died while trying to evade enemies. Also, doors seem to have the camera attached to
rather than the character when you open the door to go through them. This can be disorienting and can cause you to go in the wrong direction.
Actions associated with camera rather than character. Basically, if you are running past an item and miss the symbol to pick it up, you can't turn the character around to get the option to pick it up again, but instead have to turn the camera around. This feels unnatural to me. In addition to this, it is really finicky in that you have to be in
the right position to get the prompt. This can make it a chore to try to pick up items. There was also a particular door that I had to go through lots of times, and would end up always looking at a poster that was right next to it rather than opening the door.
Accidentally taking off clothes. You can look through items in the inventory without actually selecting them. It starts off with the stuff you are wearing selected, and it's not that easy to tell what is selected. I would frequently search through the inventory, find what I wanted to use, click "a", and it would take my boots off or something.
Glitches. There were a few times in the game where the next thing that was meant to happen wouldn't happen. I would spend ages trying to work out where the rest of the soldiers I'm meant to defeat are, before looking up a walkthrough and finding out that I'd beaten them all and something was meant to happen. I also learnt that if you are following someone and they have an epileptic fit at the next door, something has gone wrong. There were at least half a dozen times throughout the game that I had to go back to an earlier checkpoint to proceed.
All in all, a really great game. The combat, in particular, is something I grew to love. But there are enough annoyances in the game to severely impact it, and I would not be willing to give it more than 8/10.

This is a very fun arcade racing game, though only if you're interested in the single player or have friends who also play it, as the multiplayer community seems practically dead.
I had a great time completing the single player campaign.  There is a real sense of speed here, and while the graphics are nothing to write home about, they are pleasant enough and run great on my Radeon HD4850.  It took me many tries to score 3 Stars in quite a few of the events, and some I had to come back to later after a few level ups and with a further upgraded hydrojet. The AI is decent, and I didn't notice any rubberbanding.  Crashing into other players or even the scenery only slows you down a little (or a lot if you actuall hit the scenery head-on), and the only way to wipe-out is to land back in the water in the middle of performing a "Trick".  In that case, you lose precious seconds while your hydro jet resets back on the track, and then has to accelerate back up to speed.
The game worked perfectly with my 360 controller, but didn't recognize a Logitech Attack joystick, so perhaps only the 360 pad is supported.  There is keyboard support , but I didn't use it so can't comment much about how well it works.  It's worth noting that "auto-acceleration" can only be disabled when using the controller and is forced for the keyboard.  Mouse is only supported in the menus.
The single player Campaign mode is made up of 9 "Series" of events .  The events in a series are played stand-alone - there is no "comlete these X events one after another and then total up your score to get your placement" type of tours in this game. The first "Beginner's Luck" Series contains only 4 events, but this increases all the way up to 12 events in final "All Stars Cup".  In each event you get 1, 2 or 3 Stars for placing in the third, second or first place respectively, and the total number of stars are used to unlock/qualify for latter events.
There are four types of events.  "Race" is self-explanatory.  In "Elimination," every 15 seconds the racer in the last place is eliminated until only the winner is left.  "Hot Lap" has you race a single lap against time, and "Free Style" give you 60 seconds to score as many points as you can by performing Tricks.  The first 8 series all contain a mix of these four event types, while the final "All Stars Cup" only has Races.
A core part of the game game is the character progression system.  As you place in the events, you earn experience points to level up your character, and money to purchase and upgrade hydrojets.  Every time you level up, you get 1-2 skill points to spend on either new Tricks or perks.
There are 9 hydro jets to purchase in addition to the one you start with, all with upgradable Acceleration, Top Speed, Handling and Boost attributes.  Each hydro jet has a different starting and maximum upgradable value for each attribute, and not even the most expensive hydro jet is the best at everything.  I personally prefer the  Lancer which is a Jack-of-all-trades - pretty good in every area but not the best in any.
Tricks are crucial to doing performing well in all event types as they are used fill up your boost gauge, as well as scoring points during Free Style events.  Complex tricks giving greater boost and point rewards require more skill points to unlock, and the most difficult ones even have "prerequisite" tricks that your character must have first.  As mentioned before, Tricks can only be executed while the hydrojet is in the air, and landing back on the water before the trick is completed results in a temporary wipeout.  The more difficult the trick, the more airtime is required to execute it. Using the same trick multiple times in a single event results in diminishing returns, so it is recommended to have multiple tricks of each difficulty in your repertouire.
Dissapointingly, Perks only come in two flavors - extending the boost time granted per trick, and allowing you to land a tiny bit earlier without wiping out while performing a trick (though you get less boost/point rewards if the trick isn't completely finished.)
And unfortunately the progression system is a detriment to the Online mode.  Even if you do happen to find someone playing, the chances of them being a similar level as you are very slim, which leads to very one-sided races.  There is an "Invite Friends" option though which would work much better if you have Steam friends who you know are a good matchup for you.  I played a few online matches against a couple mis-matched opponents, and didn't notice any lag - the game ran the same as offline.
There's a Split Screen option for 2-4 local players, but I couldn't try it because it seems to require each player to use a 360 controller and I only have the one.  I'll update the review if it turns out there's a way around this.
The final mode is the "VR Challenge" which has you race against the "ghosts" of your Steam friends to try to beat their times.  Again, you need to have Steam friends who play this game and have a similarly built up character to yours.
TL;DR get this game for the great single player arcade racing, unless you know you have some buddies to play with.

These words were spoken by the great Tamanegi Sensei (better known as Chop Chop Master Onion) over 15 years ago when music-based games were first making a name, and they ring even truer today as the rhythm genre takes an evolutionary step into the dungeon crawling arena.
is the holy matrimony between addictive rhythm game grooviness and challenging roguelike complexity, and I'll be damned if it doesn't hit the spot. It's amazing that a concept this unique took as long as it did to come to fruition, but it's been more than worth the wait.
Not only is the concept unique but it's done
, something we hardly ever see when a new mechanic or gimmick is introduced to the gaming world for the first time. We see so many "new" ideas that are merely just a melting pot of previously established genres. Lo and behold, these developers have obviously set out to refine and perfect their concoction of varied gameplay elements on their first attempt and that is highly admirable.
stands not only as a magnificently well-realized combination of genres but as a completely new experience of it's
and the start of what is hopefully a new trend of taking fun and risky chances in game development.
The in-game music is dark, fantastic and quite danceable itself lending to the blissful feeling of hitting each beat of the song with perfect timing. The precision of the music-based movement has lead lots of early adopters of the game to swear by playing with DDR dancepads which apparently add a lot to the fun and engaging nature of exploring the Crypt. This shows a serious level of dedication from the rhythm game community and has already garnered enough attention to spawn it's own design of custom
.
And if you somehow are crazy enough to get tired of renowned composer Danny Baranowsky's heavy electronic horror jams, the game features an intuitive beat detection function for usage of songs from your own library. The detection of beats in your songs is generally spot on, and makes trying and discovering those perfect tunes for the game infinitely explorable and replayable for audiophiles in the same way games like
and
provide endless entertainment. Even for those songs that might be a bit too fast or slow for manageable NecroDancing, there's a feature to alter the speed of in-game beats to give more accessibility for a wider range of genres.
.
There are four main floors to the game with three levels and a boss-type enemy each, but beating any single one of them won't be an easy task. You will retry many times being forced to scour every diamond, buy up all the upgrades, and loot your way through multiple plays before you succeed, but what makes this so much more of a pleasure to replay than any other games which borrow rogue elements is the musical nature of the game.
replaces the repetitive and stale turn-based combat of traditional roguelikes with the fun and engaging audio interaction of the best rhythm games made to date.
With a touch of the strategic approach of traditional tactics games, the enemies each have a very distinct pattern to their movements and attacks that the player must learn through multiple failures and awareness. Starting out you encounter the easier monsters such as slimes that move passively back and forth as well as skeletons that follow behind in a predictable way that is easy to counter. Protecting the exit of each floor are the harder and more complex mini-bosses, ranging from hulking Minotaurs that charge towards you in a straight path or determined Dragons that you must outsmart and keep just out of harm's way in order to retain your doomed life just a little longer.
Throughout your journeys into the crypt you'll have two different forms of currency, first being gold coins that you can spend within the levels at merchants on equipment and items to help you on your current run. Second, and most importantly are the much harder to find Diamonds which are the only thing that carry over into the lobby after death, allowing you to purchase upgrades to the gear and loot you come across during your runs. This adds an insanely addictive level of persistence in the same way that the character growth in
or shortcut system of
do.
The shops you purchase these upgrades from won't be made available to you that easily, however, as each of the different merchants and trainers you need will be imprisoned and strewn about the various dungeons forcing you to dance deeper and deeper to rescue the people you will rely on in the future. The game is hard and you'll die many times, but the deeper you go the more you discover, and the more you discover the easier your respective trips will become. This adds a ridiculous amount of replayability and persistence to an already engaging and genre defying new formula.
Here I am hopping and slashing away to the beat of
's 'Vampire Killer', and I come across a Blood Whip. Things could not be more perfect. Necrodancer isn't just a gimmick, it's the start of something beautiful, it's a new kind of entertainment that can be enjoyed from the hardecore-est of dungeon delving roguelite aficionados to the most casual of rhythm game fans, but there is one thing that all of these demographics must have in common; a dedication to the sound of music.

I am currently playing this game through a second time in TOUGH Mode after completing it on Normal Mode.
To summarise I would describe it as a fun game to play casually with an ok storyline with a few nice dialogue sequences and a somewhat awkward combat system that takes some getting used too if you have no controller.
The Tutorial for the game fits seamlessly into the gameplay and even adds in some humorous dialogue to go with it showing that the game doesn't take itself too seriously. The way in which you acquire some of the "special abilities" however is rather tedious and seams rather counter-intuitive, all though some of the dialogue that appears explaining why is rather amusing but only momentarily covers over a flaw in the general gameplay mechanics.
Throughout the game the dialogue between the main character and the companion is well written and makes you feel for the character although there are certain dialogue choices which the game gives you control over which actually doesn't really affect the game at all. I personally found myself becoming more attached to the companion more through the game than that of the main character, which is a shame. It employs that old "amnesia" affect that so many games employ these days, but with a slight twist to it. Without spoiling it for you your character has some what of a personality complex. The story of the game in general is ok but there are some parts which seem written to fit more around Gameplay than the gameplay matching the story which is slightly disappointing.
The actual gameplay and combat mechanics are fairly straight forward but the Keyboard setup is a little awkward. I imagine it would be a lot better to play this game using a controller. The move left - move right/dodge left - dodge right setup makes it rather fiddly to play on a keyboard. In Normal Mode this isn't a major issue but in Tough/Hardcore Mode you really need to use the dodge more in combat I find, and the mechanics for this are rather unforgiving if you are using a Keyboard/Mouse setup.
The Leveling Up system works for both your character and the weapon/gear you have and it isn't obvious throughout the game if you are of an appropriate level to continue. You can complete the game really quickly and ignore a lot of the side quests in Normal Mode and indeed completely ignore entire areas of the game which don't really add anything to the story, and makes it feel like they were added in just so you had somewhere else to go in order to level up your character so you didn't progress through the game too quickly and make the game harder for yourself by not leveling up fast enough. The actual crafting aspect of the game leaves a lot to be desired. You can find yourself picking up lots of items that by the end of the game you never really needed at all and indeed by the end of the game I had more money than sense essentially meaning by the end I could just buy everything I needed if indeed I even needed it.
I bought this game during a Steam Sale for £3 and for that price I would definitely recommend this game but I wouldn't recommend it at full price though.

Please, please do tell me why I want to pour wine on a magical prison instead of talking to the wise sage about magical prisons to see what he knows.  OBVIOUSLY, I want to pour wine on it.  And just as obviously, I'm going to use a necklace to fish with, when the game dangles a fishing pole in front of me as though it were an unsolved puzzle.  Protip: it's not; you never get the fishing pole; your companion fishes with the necklace but only if she's winched to the right height which is not actually above the hole she's supposed to fish through.  Did you know your fourth leaf is in the pig trough? Because there's no riddles for you, buddy!
At more than a dozen places, this game offers no feedback except the chance to pixel-hunt across (admittedly lovely) backdrops that scroll but only if you try to walk off the edge, which hides interaction points silently, and assuming you don't miss any of those points, you're still trying every item you've found on each one of them, hoping to randomly stumble across the one that shabby game designers welded awkwardly onto the flow of a barely-likeable story.

Ok, I just beat the game a few minutes ago, and I've been a fan of Mafia since the first one.
First and foremost, they should have called this the Godfather 3, because this really didn't feel like a Mafia game. In the mafia games things like speeding and running red lights could get the cops onto you, but not in this game. Also, the flow of the game was pretty much taken from The Godfather 1.
The music had me groaning a bit. It's got a great soundtrack, but it's all songs I've heard a thousand times in movie trailers. If this is set in New Orleans, why was there no zydeco music? I got really tired of hearing 'Paint it Black' because thats a song you have to invest yourself in and 30 seconds of that just is a bad fit. THat song is a journey.
I experienced only a few crashes, and there were textures that would disappear but for the most part everything worked just fine. My hat is off to the effects they put on Lincoln Clay when he is getting in and out of water - if you soak only the bottom half of him, only that part stays wet. The sound effects were good, the story was REALLY good, and the combat felt great.
My main quibble still is that this didn't feel like a Mafia game, and there was wayyyyyy too much grinding. 'Go here, take out these rackets, interrogate people, kill these people, secure this district'. Sooo much grinding and it really was just filler.
All the same, I had a great time and experience but there were definitely flaws. I would recommend this game if you're not expecting a Mafia game - this is a fun game, but its not Mafia.

This game is an action packed kill-fest. Despite the technical issues which I will go into further in detail, the game is surprisingly fun, albeit a little frustrating at times. First and foremost, the controls are a little jenky. Plain and simple. They do not always respond the way you want to, however, they are not terrible. The teammate A.I. is horrible. In a game where you are getting swamped left and right literally hundreds, if not more, enemies at once, your teammates ability to hold their own is very important... and the A.I. completely drops the ball. They are inaccurate, will just stand there soaking up damage and dying a quick death and also, for some reason, seem to have an inability to revive you if you fall in battle. This is especially problematic in major boss battles where you are getting swamped with 2 or more boss enemies and the usual barrage of hundreds of normal enemies and when there are few wide spread checkpoints in the level.
All this being said however, the game is unusually fun and entertaining despite these issues. There is something gratifying each time you make an enemy go splat and a great sense of accomplishment when you do actually complete a level. The charterer leveling system is fulfilling as well. Each tier unlocks new weapons, deployables and upgrades, which in turn makes playing single player more enjoyable and less frustrating. The game really shines in co-op mode however and makes most of the technical issues much more bearable. The story is really not anything that special. It is pretty much just an excuse to blow away tons of abnormally large insects, arachnids and aliens... which is just fine as long as you know what you are getting into.
Final verdict: Despite the technical flaws the game is a fun kill fest that is worth the minimal money it costs.  4/5 stars

If you start Rocket League, your goal is simple: Get the ball in the other team's goal by bumping it with your car! Everything else is a small accessory to that goal.
By comparison, just knowing the basics of Natural Selection 2 is a catacomb of logic. It makes you realize why games like TF2 and even Battlefield now focus on the idea of just having single-objective maps; diverting your focus between the five things going on at any time is often near-impossible. This is combined with very precise control requirements for each of the characters involved. For a marine, a skulk can jump across 30 degrees of your vision in less than half a second, and as any alien, having a constant arena awareness to make use of mobility is an immense challenge.
This does two things. The high skill floor causes a massive divide between skill levels. For instance, a bad skulk will get 1 kill in an entire game, and a good skulk will be undefeatable even to basic enemy marines. Second, it causes any team failure to become heavily compounded. If you've played a TF2 game with just one team member AFK, you tend to notice it. In NS2, just having someone not doing 20 things a minute as a commander can screw everyone over.
The pressure to perform well moment to moment has, sadly, turned the community pretty sour, much like a game like League of Legends. Even simple failings of the team like failing to act quickly in the face of overwhelming amounts of information (for instance, constant references to named map locations) can cause commanders to exasperate "Geez, we might as well forfeit, we have NO teamwork going on". Worse, if the team doesn't vote to concede, a completely lost match will drag on for half an hour with no map change. (Unlike a game like League of Legends, there's just no opportunities for comebacks - the entire resource system of the game encourages the "rolling wrecking ball" mentality)
Perhaps this game would be fun with months of practice, played solely with players who have similar amounts of experience; but even if you can get that first goal you'd likely just become one of the aforementioned commanders.

The game is pretty interesting when you get a chance to play it.
So pros:
+ interesting mechanics. Playing as the alien side is obviously very different from most FPS games. However, playing as the marines is ALSO very different, because you're fighting aliens. So instead of shooting one from behind cover/while running/etc. you watch the vents, ceiling and walls for skulk ambushes, try to hit those pesky super-speed flying lerks, or die if you get caught alone by a roaming fade. Or in a group, if you stumble into an onos.
+ Lots of replayability. Mastering one type of alien is difficult enough. And you can focus on a different role each time you play. The same goes for marines, even though for them it's more like mastering different types of equipment, because they play very differently(heavy and slow exosuit, which requires support to repair it, or jetpack and flamethrower/grenade launcher, which allows you to jump around the place and dodge as fast as the aliens?).
+Teamwork. Each team has a commander which coordinates the team. And that adds a very interesting aspect of teamwork many other games don't have. Constant communication and good strategies can lead to some really fun moments.
+ Execution. Feels responsive, decent variety of aliens/weapons, levels are strange, yet interesting. Don't know where Im going half the time(keep running into dead-ends, even with the minimap), but I feel that's just because Im not used to them yet.
But therein lies the problem. Getting to play it. Why?
- (Main Problem) Very few servers that have players in them. Fewer that acctually match your skill level (especially if you're a rookie). Also, using "join server" is generally a bad idea. Got dropped into a Russian server. Can't speak Russian. Great, wasted the amount of time to load everything (which, by the way, takes a long bloody time). Checked server list. 3 other servers with decent ping live, all full. I guess i can't play the game them. Sad. Guess I'll play something else.
- Long loading times. Seriously. Long enough to get really annoying. I've heard they were working to fix it but hey, hasn't happened yet at the time Im writing this yet. Loading here makes me remmember the times you could go make a cup of tea while your computer was loading. Could I make one while this game loads? Well, now there's an idea...
- NOT noob-friendly. I was lucky enough to find a game early on where there were some really nice people playing, and both losing and winning was fun (which is rare, usually losing is annoying whatever people say). And they help me learn some things. Never found the server again. Everyone just ignores you on other servers, so not to feel useless (dying as a skulk for the n-th time) i just started playing gorge (at least i don't feel like a waste of space then, at least im building things!). A bit easier as a marine, still, takes time to get used to alien moving patterns and you'll be useless at the start, if your skill level is below the others you're playing with.
Short summary:
Interesting game, whether you like to play FPS with a twist as the marine, or fight marines as the alien. Sadly, few players and huge difficulty finding a game you would enjoy at a rookie level. Thus I wouldn't recommend it unless you want it badly enough to persevere the lack of decent servers and the large learning curve (which just requires a lot of practise I suppose).

Let's start with the cons first.
-The performance is TERRIBLE. This is mostly to blame on the unity engine which is notorious for this problem, and I sincerely hope that LinceWorks will not publish another game that's running on unity.
-Some sections are very trial-and-error based. The last "boss" (yes this game has bosses) is basically "try every possible route until you find the right one", which can be frustrating.
-The third enhancement for your spotting Raven, Kurosu, turns finding scrolls into an additional errand that you're running. I would recommend unlocking this as the very last skill as otherwise you never feel rewarded for finding a scroll. I robbed myself from a ton of fun by playing the entire game chasing scrolls above everything else.
-You can't jump. Aragami is a ghost ninja that can teleport, but can't climb over a ledge. It know it's deliberate, but still... eh.
So, what did I like about the game?
-The Leveldesign is awesome in that it lets you choose your own order of objective completion. The "Teleport to the shadows" gameplay works beautiful in that the game movement never feels restrictive. It has also apparently been playtested extensively, as I never once managed to reach an out-of-bounds area despite trying. Both of these things combined result in that you never EVER feel like you're walking a path that has been pre-determined by the developers, which makes the game "feel" ridiculously good. And even on that reason alone I could recommend this game to any stealth enthusiast from the bottom of my heart.
-The soundtrack is sexual intercourse for your ears. TwoFeathers have done an excellent job at creating a perfect thematic soundtrack for Aragami, and the DLC was worth every penny.
-The game rewards you for every playstyle and it incentivizes multiple playthroughs with collectible scrolls which contain skill points and text bits about the game lore, and unlockable costumes.
And then there's subjective stuff. I felt like the cel shading graphics thematically fit the game very well and I enjoyed the story, even though it's a little bit cheesy how it throws a major plottwist at you right before the final boss.
As the credits rolled across the screen, I shed tears because I didn't want it to end.
I absolutely adore Aragami. It is by far the best stealth game that I have played in an eternity.

Yeah, rub it in my face.)  Microsoft made a BS move.  But I digress.

Aragami has been one of the most enjoyable, refreshing games for me so far this year. Playing Coop with a friend the whole way through taking only ONE break says something.
Length of the game is also not that bad from the price standpoint. Around 10 hours for a normal playthrough, and yes, we died a lot, a whole heck of a lot.
Aragami is cut up in thirteen chapters with some interesting locations to explore. Some of them are mainly boss encounters. And wow are those encounters cool.
It changes the phase of gameplay to a more intense fight, rather than a stealthy approach.
Skillsystem is also in place, giving you a range of skills to choose from, Offense and Defense. Skillpoints is aquired through exploring and finding scrolls.  And by the way, Kunai's are in. Shruiken? Not so much.
Replay value; Go for the best scores. Every chapter gives you a grade. There are also collectibles scattered around for you to find, and many of them are well hidden(Haven't found them all.... yet).
Positives-
*Great fluid gameplay
*Skill system
*Boss fights are awesome
*Exploration is rewarding
*Lovely artstyle and graphics
*Music and sound is great
*You'll die alot
Negatives-
*Some annoying animation bugs in combat resulting in dying, but happens rarely
*Story isn't that interesting, but it has a few twists
Overall Score 9/10

Good 3D engine with great potential.
Some big arugment of Game Guru is you can make a game wihtout any programming.
This let's lot of space for beginners, modders or 3D designers without coding skills.
GameGuru is developped constantly and needs some improvments in some areas, but you can already make some good action game depending on your 3D art capabilties and level design and lighting.
Pros
+ FPS template with lot of ready to use weapons and objects
+ FPS weapons are easy to swap (HUD.X and GunSpec for animations frame range)
+ Different AI scripts ready to go (melee, cover, ranged ...)
+ AI can be customized or made from scratch with Lua
+ A character creator with customisation (no other software proposes that)
+ You can bring your own AI and NPC characters and animations
+ Ragdoll made automatic
+ Code your own AI with Lua
+ Easy to understand FPE configuration files
+ Very Simple and very friendly editor  for beginners similar to Betesheda editor in some ways
+ A lightmapper
+ Making a game is fun and fast (default models can be placeholders until replaced by your own 3D art)
+ With clever textures, lighting colors, or graphic style you can have a pretty game
+ Lot of cheap DLC models addons for users that don't know how to model
+ EBE building editor (not sure about performance and if support LOD system)
Cons
- No particle system
- No Physics Api available for Lua coders to make new genre games
- Graphics needs improvment like ACE tone mapping
- Some fast and cheap global illumination lighting or baked would bring a lot
- Performance needs some work
- Lot of hard coded effects and gameplay
- Support for FBX is a big need ( FPS weapons are easy to swap but needs .X animted files)
- Needs a TPS camera and and a TPS ranged player controller
- Needs to expand Lua library (camera, physics, collision functions) to allow more game types.
- Model importer really needs a full 3D view easy to use
- Needs to be able to import collision shapes for model import (Capsule, custom concave)
- Terrain materials textures needs an editor to let people swap preconfigured textures with their own in some clicks
- No Support Tiff,TGA, Jpeg (while GG could convert them in DDS behind the scene at import)
If your goal is AAA with advanced tools and graphics use Unreal 4 instead.
Game Guru is lot more about simplicity and easy to use, and some fun.
It is somewhat similar about simplicity to Fallout 4 editor.
About Lua coding you cna do a lot (but it needs to get better for camera functions, physics, motion functions like Lerp, math Vectors like LookAt , character controller ... )
If you are a beginner or a 3D artist that doesn't know how to make a game or how to code, you'll have fun, you can make a complete game without coding quickly.
Most produced games doesn't look modern because they use the default textures, 3D assets and characters (too much photo texture baked lighting and low poly) .
Even with actual rendering to some degree , if you can bring your own 3D characters , terrain textures and 3D models assets, it willl make a huge difference on the game look and it will no more look old gen (only about lighting side).
It is cheap, it has no royalties, it comes with lot of characters and 3D models to get you started.
It's perfect for hobbysts and people that want ot have fun first, meanwhile 3D artists and advanced users can produce good results with their own content.

After about +200 hours of using and working with GameGuru it is time for a review.
I've purchased GameGuru after reading about this game engine and because of the content that is already available for the user.
I'm not very familiar with modeling nor did i ever created a game, so to find a game engine that is very friendly for the inexperienced user and easy to use was a blessing in my opinion.
But don't be fooled, even this easy to use software does not necessarily mean 'easy'.
There is a lot more to it than simply placing some items and characters on the map.
You will first want to write a story line, create a flowmap and make a list of items to use in your game creation.
There is an awful lot to learn, lucky for us, the developer of GameGuru has a big twitch list on his youtube channel in which he gives thorough explanations on the editor, lighting, shaders and so on.
Apart from that, the community behind GameGuru is very helpful, friendly and open to new and inexperienced users.
One can find an awful lot of scripts and assets which are freely shared on the community forum.
That GameGuru is capable of producing some very good games is obvious when one plays through the demo games.
However, due to the fact that this game engine is still in development and should be considered as early access, there are limitations and thus much room for improvement.
In my view, GameGuru certainly deserves a good recommendation despite the early access.
This because it is already quite good and even the inexperienced user can create his first game, easy and fast.
Personally i've been creating some testgames and made stand alone files in order to test them.
If i release a game, it must be to my satisfaction which means it has the right ambience, the right balance between assets on the map, graphical display and performance.
I'll refrain from making a list of pro's and con's due to the fact that GameGuru is still in development.

Ok, I just beat the game a few minutes ago, and I've been a fan of Mafia since the first one.
First and foremost, they should have called this the Godfather 3, because this really didn't feel like a Mafia game. In the mafia games things like speeding and running red lights could get the cops onto you, but not in this game. Also, the flow of the game was pretty much taken from The Godfather 1.
The music had me groaning a bit. It's got a great soundtrack, but it's all songs I've heard a thousand times in movie trailers. If this is set in New Orleans, why was there no zydeco music? I got really tired of hearing 'Paint it Black' because thats a song you have to invest yourself in and 30 seconds of that just is a bad fit. THat song is a journey.
I experienced only a few crashes, and there were textures that would disappear but for the most part everything worked just fine. My hat is off to the effects they put on Lincoln Clay when he is getting in and out of water - if you soak only the bottom half of him, only that part stays wet. The sound effects were good, the story was REALLY good, and the combat felt great.
My main quibble still is that this didn't feel like a Mafia game, and there was wayyyyyy too much grinding. 'Go here, take out these rackets, interrogate people, kill these people, secure this district'. Sooo much grinding and it really was just filler.
All the same, I had a great time and experience but there were definitely flaws. I would recommend this game if you're not expecting a Mafia game - this is a fun game, but its not Mafia.

As a fan of point and click games in the 90s I've felt let down in the past by more recent P&C games found in the bargain bin. But then one weekend I stuble across a Daedalic sale and picked up this little gem for the grand total of 75p, and what a bargain it was; I'd have paid more.
At first the story seemed to suffer with the old "in a time of wibblesnaps a young faropos apprentice discovered a magical snaliff that threatened the good citizens of morhop" that you sometimes get with over the top fantasy, but eventually the story became quite immersive and enjoyable.
The voice acting also gave me a few concerns at first, the blacksmith especially, but I absolutely fell in love with the voice of Nuri and then some of the later characters with good baritone joined the cast. The relationship between Geron and Nuri as wonderful to watch unfold and I found myself investing emotionally in the characters and their quest. Truly the best part of this adventure is the wonderful tale it tells and the way it tells it.
Another good point to mention is the graphics. Although the character animations are a little bit wooden, you can easily see past them when you admire the beautiful backgrounds that make up the world they live in, lots of detail went into the world and I could easily spend my time seeing new things in the background and in some cases the foreground.
As for the puzzles they make up a nice learning curve that leave you satisfied when you solve them. I may have had to seek help on one occasion, but I put that down to tiredness due to me wanting to see what happens next. Apart from that they do seem to be logical puzzles until you visit the fairy realm, and even those aren't too difficult.
TL;DR it's a good game buy it

Pros: The artwork is very charming. The two spells provide an interesting, but ultimately underutilized device.
Cons: For a game of this genre, there needs to be either some challenge/innovation in the puzzle solving, or some degree of user determination (or otherwise deep investment) in the narrative's course.  Simply put, either the mechanisms by which the narrative is unlocked piece by piece need to be entertaining and satisfying, or the decisions that move the narrative forward need to be engaging. Ideally, both.
In this instance, the plot plods on deterministically with zero input from the player as to how relationships develop, characters grow, and moral decisions are made. Which may be due to a total lack of meaningful relationships, character growth, or moral decisions in the narrative. This is a shame, as there was ample opportunity for meaningful choices to be made that were passed up instead for rather trite and forced outcomes. As to the "puzzles", there was always one solution, and it almost always veered between extremes of either being blatantly easy or almost completely unintuitive. Frequently I found myself clicking things into place with no real concept of what the intended outcome was supposed to be until it happened.

Gameplaywise, it's straightforward : you have one sword and learn several moves throughout the game. I thought this would limit the gameplay, making it boring at some point, but it didn't. The game is relatively short if you decide to do the campaign only, and becomes longer if you decide to do the subquest. You can find equipment to upgrade your sword & be more competitive in fights. The game itself is really easy, if you wish for a challenge, directly jump to the hardcore difficulty, where you really die easily if you gets hit (my advice : don't try to speedrun it, use combos & dodge as much as possible).
Graphically : it's a cel-shaded style plat-former, who really take inspiration into Don Bluth's An American Tail animated movie in terms of artstyle (they even made the same pun). At first I thought it would be a problem since I'm really not a fan of the furry genre (due to what the Internet did to it, mostly) but it really only took inspiration in the Don Bluth movie style and never try to sexualize the characters like you can see many games do whenever they try to add androgynous animal characters. So yeah, I really felt I was watching an old animated movie, with the same kind of message Don Bluth himself would be able to convey (about war, destruction of nature, etc...)
The story is cute, it's nothing great but it's very cute, very well acted, and I appreciate the voice actors' effort in the play.
One big plus for this game is the music : the music is absolutely fantastic, and one of my favourite soundtrack in videogame's history. Not even kidding.
It's charming, it's fun, it's pretty. The music is beautiful.
It is a wonderful tail... I mean tale.

This is a love letter to the DOS Era of PC gaming.
Mostly Apogee platformers Era (Duke Nukem 1, Cosmo's Cosmic Adventure, Secret Agent, Crystal Caves)

* PC-Speaker-like sounds and music.
* One button for jump, and one for shooting.

Negative points are that despite reading all the text carefully ... I still don't get what actually happened, the story of the Seer seems somehow jumbled. I'm not going to spill the beans here for those who haven't played it but it was confusing enough that I googled trying to get a story summary about the Seer - without success. That leaves me rather unsatisfied and the end was anti-climatic too in my eyes. I had a "Huh? That was it now??" moment for sure.
What I would criticize too is a more common thing with Daedalus games: female characters are always ... sweet/helpless, ♥♥♥♥♥y/hysterical or plain keyword giver without any character. This game is actually pretty fun, especially if you're already a fan of the Fallout series. It has potential for those who enjoy base-building and management-style games, as well as side quests thrown in for a *tiny* bit of story here and there. There is no overarching story, however, so don't expect there to be anything beyond a surface attachment to the characters. The downsides of Fallout Shelter are that it takes a great deal of time to accomplish anything big, and the quests timers seem to be pretty extreme. These things make it pretty clear that the developers were intentionally coming up with ways to make a little quick cash on the side, offering goods for real money to speed the processes up. Still, for a free to play game and a way to kill time when you're bored and want something "different" to play, this is a good game to try. I definitely recommend giving it a shot, especially since you get to poke the Mysterious Stranger with your mouse from time to time.

For someone who has never been a huge fan of point and click game I absolutely loved this game (and its sequel Memoria). For me, it had the complexity of a King's Quest game, but without the messing-things-up-will-lead-to-your-death-and-failure, which made it easy to sit back and enjoy taking the puzzles at my own pace and not having to worry about having not picked up a mushroom in the last area or falling to my death accidently.
Thumbs Up's:
+Great Story telling, you are looking for a good story you will enjoy this game greatly.
+You can't die or mess up. You may struggle to find the solution, but you will never run out of time and have to worry about reloading the game or missing an item earlier on.
+There's a good amount of play through, both in the player's own puzzling, but even in general content. I never felt like I cheated out of game play from cut corners.
+Controls worked very nice and smoothly. I thought the inventory layout was easy to use and access. TIP: Also, by double clicking on an exit to another screen the player can skip walking animation which is helpful in some of the more twisted and roomier puzzles.
+If you like snarky replies. Deaths are not allowed, so Geron will not do anything that will actually kill him, but that doesn't mean he doesn't have some funny, snarky quip to give you.
Thumb Middle's:
-Not a lot of replayability right away, but it's like a good book. You need to have some space to forget a bit of the storyline and how all the puzzles work, but I can see myself coming back to play this game once again after a few months or a year - and I definitely plan too!
Thumb Down's:
-I just don't have one for this game. I thoroughly enjoyed it.

Muri is a charming homage to early DOS era platforming - if you have fond memories of the gameplay found in early Commander Keen or Duke Nukem games, you'll feel right at home here. Every part of this game's aesthetic feels extremely consistent with the style they're trying to emulate, but the story is a bit complex and convoluted. Perhaps credit is deserved for trying to explore dramatic themes far beyond the scope of the gameplay, but it just felt a bit out of place - simpler character motivations would have felt more authentic to early DOS experiences.
I'm not really the sort of person who can ignore story elements, even in a game as purposefully simple as this, but Muri makes me wish I was. It has a wonderful sense of feedback for every control input, and feels like an incredibly honest love letter to a fascinating era of gaming history. Still strongly recommended.

You'll be quick to notice the downsides of this game. The graphics, controls, and features are very limited. There is no multiplayer or achievements. The game functions all around as if you were playing it on a DOS OS. While it may be nostalgic for many, the rest will find it unnecessarily limiting. The game
be better by implementing modern capabilities of computers.
However, these limitations aside, it is a very solid and fun game. If you can look past these design flaws, there is a great game behind them. It left me wondering what this game would look like as a triple A title, or if it were designed for a SNES instead of DOS. There was great potential for this game, and what little it does encompass is amazing. If it is your type of game, and you can look past the deliberate retro nerfing, you will love it.

While the Android version of Fallout Shelter was fun, the biggest problem was the lack of "end game" content (I use the term loosely, since there is technically no end). You eventually ran out of things to buy or upgrade and couldn't figure out what to do with your 200 dwellers.
The Steam version plays mostly the same, but with some simple yet crucial additions that make the game more satisfying. You can now do more with your dwellers than just move them from room to room. There are quests, random encounters in the wasteland, crafting, customization and more enemy types. On the mobile version I always ended up with too much Radaway since there was barely any need for them. In this version your base can be attacked by Radscorpions and radioactive Ghouls which you can encounter on quests, too. Now it's always necessary to keep up the production of both Stimpaks and Radaways. It's also possible to customize your dwellers' appearance in the Barbershop and collect themed interior designs.
While microtransactions exist (you can buy Nuka-Cola bottles to speed things up), it's very easy to earn what you need by completing quests, without too much grinding.
A couple of annoyances include pixel-hunting when you want to move a particular dweller hiding behind several others and end up clicking a dozen wrong things, and the frequency of attacks on your base. I've barely had time to nurse everyone back to health from the last Deathclaw rampage when another one is already starting.
Apart from these quibbles, the game remains an addictive little time-waster.

As a big fan of the first, I finally got around to playing this recently and I wish I hadn't bothered.
It's incredibly pretty, story is good, half decent voice acting but the main meat of the game - i.e combat, is dreadful.
Damage taken and done to enemies is totally out of whack (you get pretty much one shot by monsters even with fully upgraded armour and you do between 2 and 5% damage back in return), signs are pointless to the extreme (use them and you eat up vigor, so you get 2 shots early game - which is made even worse by using these it debuffs your sword damage by 50%).
The 'shield' called quen you got has now been 'fixed' by the developers so it breaks on one hit. No damage reflection at all and when you use it you reduce you sword damage by 25%. So that means you see lots of 'Geralt hits X for minimal damage' over and over.
So this forces most fights to involve repeated dodging backwards and spamming grenades as if you get in close to any group you are murdered within seconds. Quite often you'll get killed by phantom attacks where no animation plays but you got hit.
It's like a bad 80's action flick.
Then we move on to the other travesty which is the inventory - keeping your alchemy plans in your inventory adding to loads of crap you have to scroll through? - check
Running out of space constantly due to tonnes of crap in every box you find? - check
Tonnes of crap you have to keep on you but you dont need eating away that precious weight? - check
Finally selling stuff you find is diabolical, it's a 24:1 ratio on sell to buy which is crazy. (perhaps someone missed a decimal point in there?)  You are being sold a plan for 300 orens, which is more than you get for 3 quests (which are few in the
game) and loot/enemies drop 4 oren's worth of crap.
All in all its crap and I can't see myself finishing this at all when there are FAR better RPG's on the market.

Guys, if you had a PSX, you must know how amazing the Tenchu games were, and how no other game has been able to fill the hole it left (At least for me), and, in my honest opinion, this game aims to be a game that won't be forgotten, a game like Tenchu. This is great.
I don't really like stealth games, I'm pretty horrid at them, however I was addicted to Tenchu when I was a kid, and I'm loving this game, so even if you don't like stealth games, you might feel like me about this game.
For starters; the design of this game is mindblowingly good, I'm not only taking about the graphic design, which is superb, but the entire design of the game, the stages, the created language, the abilities of the game, and the one I like the most; the HUD. There's no HUD in the game, not a single thing on screen, and how you're able to measure how much shadow essence you have left, is *in* your character. If you run out of shadow essence, you're not allowed to cast skills (Light consumes your essence, while shadow increases it, great and fun system, if I can say so myself), so when you're out of shadow essence, certain parts of your character glow red, and depending on how much essence you have left, parts of your character fill with white, including the cape. It's extremely beautiful, and I don't think any other game has made such a beautiful design for a recheargable indicator.
[Picture of the character without essence]
As I said before, stealth games are not my forte, (though you have the election of not killing any enemies at all, I want to kill every single one of them, the opening of the game reveals why, though we will see how the story reveals what's right and what's wrong), and I've died in the first levels... an embarrasingly high amount of times, but I'm getting better, and killing enemies feels so good!
Anyways, since I didn't play the game enough, and I'm not very good at reviewing games, I'll have to leave this review like this until I finish this game.
Note: I didn't try the co-op yet, but I'll do it soon.

First review. Bought it on a whim as I was looking for a decent stealth game and was really surprised how fun this was. The shadow teleportation mechanic is very similar to the blink mechanic from Dishonoured so if that type of stealth mobility appealed to you then this will win you over. Levels are a little sparse looking but otherwise function well and and are well designed. Lots of moments in later levels where I would stumble upon a different route to my objective and spot multiple points of entry. No quicksave, checkpoints only but I never really ran into a situation where I was constantly restarting over and over because of difficulty. Dying just made me re-evaluate the situation and usually come up with creative ways to overcome challenges. Checkpoints are pretty forgiving and I usually never lost a lot of progress dying. As with most stealth games patience will be a virtue. One thing to note is that there is no combat, only stealth kills. I love this type of stealth but some may be put off depending on preferences. Getting caught is almost a death sentence until you get more accustomed to the controls and unlock abilities to help you get out of a jam.
Only real negatives are that the performace and framerate is uneven. A few places cause low framerate dips which is rather annoying. Also the upgrade system is a little odd. Some upgrades are wildly useful while some feel like they should've been given from the start. Overall I'd say it's worth $20. I've read on the forums that the game can be a bit buggy a well but never ran into any issues myself. YMMV on that one.

TLDR:  Simple, fun, and just the right amount of challenge...
- Controls are good and dead easy to use. Yes, they are!
- Water is pretty realistic and bouncy.
- Achievement system is realistic and achievable in 10 hours (to complete the game)
- Earning money, XP and new hydro jets do not require much grinding, they progress naturally.
- Simple hydro-jet upgrades.
- Multiplayer yet to be updated.
- It is perhaps a little bit too simple, especially if you demand more complexity from a racing game.
- Maps are simple, short and repetitive. I didn't find this much of a problem though since most racing games are pretty repetitive to me anyway. There is enough variety here to make you play differently (e.g. the icy tunnels are much trickier to boost through).
- Music is alright, though apparently is an iffy rip off of some stock-soundtrack (source: TB's review)
- Is looked down upon for being a mobile port (yet I personally feel this is irrelevant)
This game is great for anyone who wants some fun hydro-jet racing to pass the time or complete achievements, without having to grind for money or upgrades. Even better to play with friends, though up to 10 hours worth of entertainment if you do it solo.
I wouldn't recommend this game if you already like other racing games because the chances are you will find complaint with the lack of maps, detail, challenges and engine customization.

Yeah, the writing and art isn't the best in the world, but they don't make a game what it sets out to be: a game, with amazing gameplay and a masterful soundtrack to hack and slash to. That's what this game is.
The combat is fast-paced and flashy, with a bunch of fun combos and one of the most overpowered sidekicks ever. With a little practice you'll be decimating monsters by the dozens in no time.
And the music... HyperDuck SoundWorks just kills it here, every single track conveys an emotion and drives you to move onwards in your quest to find out who you truly are.
Some may jump on me for this next point, but I even like the main protagonist to a degree. Yeah, his voice actor isn't amazing but he has an interesting character. Who exactly is he? What's his purpose? Why does he have both a drive to kill yet also desires to think rationally? Well, obviously I can't answer that since it's part of the entire climax of the story so yeah.
Don't let the art style or the voice acting turn you off, this game is a must play in my opinion.

The core gameplay of this game is admittedly decent. I, presonally, found no real purchase in the versus aspect of the game. It makes otherwise good gameplay feel like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ moba that was forced into the game rather than designed into it.
The base coop mode is more of what you have come to expect from orcs must die in the past, and its done well enough. However, it does feel like it is done worse than in previous games. They reworked some mechanics (ex. guardians are stronger but VERY limited, think just a couple per map, and can only be placed in designated spots) and shifted the focus away from the traps a bit and more onto the player's character. Personally, I really dislike this choice. They did add in quite a few characters and an ingame talent choice system similar to Heroes of the Storm, but it ultimately still feels fairly hollow.
The worst part of the game has to be the progression system. There are multiple types of currency that you have to collect from various sources and the drop rate makes it feel like you are making hardly any progress at all. It basically feels like they took what was in the previous games, and took everything away from the character in order to force you to buy it all back in this game.
The absolute worst decision I can think of is also related to this progression system. Account levels are gained as you gain experience for different characters by playing them and levelling them up. The problem with this is that players that are too far apart in levels cannot play with each other in full groups. My friend showed me this game and so I decided to try it. However, because we are too far apart in levels, we can only play together with the two of us and can not get into a matchmaking group. The problem with this is that everything in this game definitely feels like it was designed for a full 5 players. The game does scale back the enemies to compensate, but the map design and everything else just screams at you the entire time that you should have 5 players and that is the way the game is meant to be played. But you can't. the game gives no indication or explanation to what is happening and you have to dig through old patch notes to figure out that they wanted to make it so that the matchmaker wouldn't just average out the players levels and leave moderately leveled people playing with one much higher level and one noob. They give absolutely no indication of when you will be able to play together the way the game feels like it was meant to be played. You just have to keep ranking up hoping this will be the one that does it. Worst system ever. I have no idea why anyone would impliment a system that actively discourages players from playing with their friends.
Its not like the problem I described above is just a newby problem either. there are 100 account levels, and as far as I can tell, a difference of 10 will mean you can't matchmake together. Again, despite my best efforts and a long time looking, there is no information other than one sentence in some patch notes a short while back explaining it.

A beautiful adventure.
The strongest elements to me are the gorgeous art, nice music and great voice acting. Nuri and Geron in particular are two wonderful characters. Their voice actors sound so nice, soothing, believable and powerful. They can be cute, funny, heartwearming, sad. It's just a joy listening to them or to be there to witness and kinda share their pain. I don't know if I had ever heard emotions projected so well only through voice between two characters. I'd love to hear them in a third The Dark Eye game, and I think it must be these two doing it close together because I am hearing them in another game, the "Game of Thrones" RPG, in more isolated roles but they just won't strike me there as much. Perhaps it's their skills and the script working magic here in combination - it looks like they were given a nice amount of freedom, or at the very least it sounds as if they were wholeheartedly enjoying their roles.
The puzzling is less diverse than in Memoria (= the sequel) but still fine in it's own, traditional right as far as I can tell. I'd say it's of the easier (not easiest, but average) kind as you won't always have dozens of items to handle and the solutions aren't as absurd as they can be for example in Deponia. You can have points of interest in the world highlighted by the press of a button, and there is a combination helper that has item labels showing up in either blue or white color depending on whether you can still do something with them or not. This mechanic was dropped in Memoria it seems, maybe because randomly using the little to average numbers of items you have works just quicker than memorizing this color coding.
The only flaws of this game I came to notice are some technical hiccups; between actions there can be very brief "freezes" which didn't annoy me but which I heard one or another player complain about on the hub. This is nothing to lament over too much I believe though because there are no real-time action scenes that would require you to have everything work totally fluently.
Which is a bit unfortunate is that, like in Memoria, audio and text will not always align, at least not when playing in English. Some lines in certain scenes may appear in text or audio which simply don't belong there but to previous ones, or one or another sentence wasn't translated properly from German (the native language of the devs) to English. This doesn't happen brutally often, but it does on some occasions and you'll notice.
What works better here than in Memoria is the the journey/adventure log, which is a relatively simply book with a short text what had happened and what you are about to do, roughly, with a world map indicating where you are (roughly as well - not that it would matter much because the game has you go through specific locations, you won't be travelling around the world by your own merit).
Also, the ending felt a little rushed; beautiful and fitting in some ways, but I was surprised it came as quickly as it did, and there isn't much of an epilogue either, which would have left me "unsaturated" if not for the fact that there is already a sequel which properly continues and somewhat ends what was started in Chains of Satinav.

The sequel Mafia 2 was criticized for this empty open world, and either as a result of this or for other reasons entirely, the third game has abandoned this format for a more conventional modern one. The result is a very mixed bag with some soaring strong points and unfortunate, tedious lows that make it difficult to answer the simple question of whether this is a good game or a bad one.
as an aside, i'll say I didn't post this on Steam right away because I was torn on whether or not to recommend it. While it's not perfect (it's in beta, people), I'm really enjoying this game.  It's different from previous OMD games in that your character and his/her abilities being used correctly are essential to winning the game - it's not mostly about the traps, although those are very important as well.  Like MOBA games, you'll be able to play a set of different heroes every week or so, and permanently unlock any hero through playing the game or paying real money.  It does take a long time to craft items and heroes, but that's to be expected.  If you could get the best stuff at the beginning, there would be nothing to work towards.
The game is in beta, so there are some issues (again, this should be expected - beta doesn't mean finished).  I haven't had any crashes, personally, but I have had people drop the game and doom a game a few times.  I have finished and won most of my matches, though, so this problem isn't completely pervasive.  The two modes are fun.  One is PvE and one is PvP.  I don't think the heroes are all greatly balanced, but they each shine in different spots.  People often don't like Gabriella, but she can wipe a wave of minions if she times her right click correctly in the middle of a trap zone.  As with any MOBA style game, you need to find the hero and role that fits you best.

The game has been through a very challenging early-access period, pivoting several times before finally landing where we are now.
Of course, if you're a new player, that won't matter to you - you just want to know if it's fun. And it pains me a bit to say it, but for me the answer is "not really" - it's incredibly competent, but not fun.
What does this mean? It's very polished, and the graphics look cartoon-y and great. In the moment, it can be a blast - but the heart and soul of the game feels missing, particularly compared to previous entries in the series.
What you're left with is fun in the immediate term, but is a barely concealed grind - grinding for currencies, grinding to upgrade your traps, grinding for experience.
This is compounded by the fact that there isn't a particularly high "skill ceiling" to the gameplay. Success is primarily related to:
1) Whether you understand the relatively simple interactions and mechanics driving the gameplay
2) How high you've levelled your traps
3) Whether you can find a team that also understands the first two points, and is aligned about a strategy.
You may really like this style, in which case your mileage may vary. But it's dropped out of my regular rotation of games because it's just not a pleasure to play.
