I am not an RPG fan at all, but Witcher 2 is a fantastic game. Beautiful visuals, fun combat, very engaging storyline with memorable characters, and a cliffhanger that has got me very excited for "The Witcher 3", a game that I before was not even considering being interested in.
Let's start with the visuals, the graphics look fantastic (for its age of course). While the graphics may not be the most realistic, the color pallete is bright, colorful, and interesting to look at whether your out in the forest, or fighting your way through ruins. The framerate was smooth the entire way through with every single graphical setting pushed to the limits. The cutscene animations were a tad repetitive, but far more intersting to look at than the terrible character animations in the new Fallout games.
The gameplay is miles ahead of the original Witcher game. The combat is fun and addicting. Pairing sword play with magical powers is genius and done very well in this game. You can blast enemies with a fire spell and follow it up with several quick sword attacks to easily finish them off, or simply switch your magic to a sort of "Force push" which enables you to quickly free some room. Now the combat sometimes gets a little fidgety when you try to reaquire a seperate target, but I found this happens very little. Other than combat, the game itself is not as interesting. A witcher is supposedly a "Monster Mercenary" yet the entire game I feel as though i only ever fought 3 types of simple monsters... zombies, harpies, and lobsters. There was the occasional boss fight here and there, but not nearly as much as you'd expect from a 30hour RPG game. I certainly hope the next game spares us from doing grocery chores (pick up this magical item.. no that one isn't good enough, run all the way here instead and get a STRONGER one) and hopefully they'll have at least side mission hunt missions that allow us to hunt crazy monsters and return their hide for coin. Thankfully, most of these boring chore missions are short and easy to complete considering the levels are pretty small.
The game world is split into 3 sections, based on chapters. The first chapter has you running through a swamp town and now and again venturing out into the colorful woods. The 2nd chapter seems to borrow very heavily from the 2nd Lord of the Rings book and has you fighting alongside elves and dwarves in a huge battle in a mountain fortress. Yeah.. I see what you did there developers... The 3rd world is probably the least interesting of the 3, featuring dreary ruins that don't really offer much interesting to explore. Thankfully, the story kept me going through the whole way through.
This games story is what you'd expect from a fantasy tale: tons and tons of unbelievably ridiculous names that nobody will ever remember making it impossible to follow anything that's going on. The general plot was pretty straightforward and easy to understand; find the big fat guy who framed you for killing a king, hence the name "Assassins of Kings." It's very difficult to stay focused on this essential goal when each chapter introduces you to a plethura of confusing names, locations, and more names. By the end, I was able to piece together what was happening, but this makes the assassins creed games seem simple in plot. Now just because some of the characters names are confusing doesn't meant hey all are. The main characters, Geralt, Triss, ... um... dwarf guy.. Ioverth? (Elf guy)... ok so they're all confusing but you'll recognize them and you do root for certain characters to live and die which is useful considering this game features a dynamic story that you can alter based on the phrases you choose in dialogue. No matter what choice I made, I felt as though I didn't make a mistake which is rare in these RPG games with dynamic stories. I never felt as though I made a bad choice and felt satisfied with the ending the game drew out for me.
In short, the graphics are good, the gameplay is good, the story is confusing but still good, and overall I highly recommend giving this game a go, especially with the new game coming out soon which already looks to be the best graphical achievement in gaming history.

Crypt of the NecroDancer is easily the most addictive game I’ve played in quite some time. It compels you to want to play more, and more, and more!
Part of this is the fantastic soundtrack that blends so seamlessly with the rhythm based rogue like.
The story is rather cliche, you’re name is Cadence and you’ve gone to look for a family member. Only to get yourself killed, and then resurrected by the NecroDancer. Now you must move to the beat and fight your way deeper into the darkness.
The game is difficult, but don’t let that dissuade you, it’s amazingly good. One of the few early access games that feels more like a completed product that some thrown together tech demo.
What’s not to love about it?
The 16-bit graphics and art style are beautiful and charming, and animations very well executed and the beat. That cursed beat that compels you to try again, and again.
In all the hours that I’ve played I’ve only made it to Zone 3, and here there is a mix of techno and metal. Ice and fire, the dungeon is separated by these two elements. With creatures embodying either of the elements, and music shifting and changing as you move from the blue to red squares.
Timing and rhythm is truly everything for the NecroDancer. All creatures in his dungeon must obey the beat, each bouncing and writhing in their own unique and horrific dance. Your yourself must do the same, although your consciousness allows you to move more freely.
The simplest way to describe the combat and various weapons is Chess. Each creature, and each weapon, works in a similar way to chess. Do you attack diagonally, or straight forward only. Do you hit ahead of you, or to the side.
You must learn each item’s use, and abilities, while doing the same for the enemies that stalk you so.
Not surprising that one of the first bosses you encounter is actually an animated chess board. With the King at the far back playing his dark melody to move and order his minions and queen. The pawns are rather useless, but ignoring them spells doom, for they quickly turn into powerful Queens once they reach your walls.
Don’t fret though, as you can also empower yourself with magical weapons, items, spells and even more life. Dotted throughout the zones are diamonds. That precious stone is used to upgrade your character and unlock more items, and spells.
Along with gems, are towns people, free them as you find them with golden keys and they will join you in the game lobby. Offering you these upgrades, and even to train you against monsters, and even bosses. For a fee of course; more diamonds.
If you can’t get enough punishment in the normal play style, there’s hardcore mode. None of your upgrades work, and you have to attempt to clear the entire game with a single run. Die, and you start again. The pinnacle of the masochist gamer.
The game is fun, more than fun. It’s a masterpiece of Indie gaming, roguelikes and rhythm games. Hell, you can even play it with dance pad. You can even import your own MP3 collection if you want. Enjoy a fantastic game, and dance!
Crypt of the NecroDancer is a must buy!

tl;dr version: Only buy it if you're 12, have zero experience making games or game content and don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about your 2016 game looking like it came from 2005. Decade old Early Access title dressed as a full program. If you're serious about making a modern game especially with MP, look elsewhere.
Full Review:
Honestly not worth the purchase.
This is a remake/rename of a program called FPS Creator. Now while the concept of an easy game maker will appeal to many, this program should be an Alpha in Early Access, but even then it should not even be considered that. I mean this program released originally in 2005. 11 years ago, and it is still lacking in many ways and far from complete.
Development is just too slow and the software lacks even the most basic things you'd expect from a game editor in 2016, things most games had already added back in the late 90's.
Sure it is easy to use, but do not expect to be making commercial games with it.
You can make Multplayer games, like 90's style deathmatches with cliche rambo esque weapons, but good luck selling it or even playing it with your friends. They will not only need your game, the content, but also a copy of GameGuru to play it. I had a custom machine gun in a game I created, friend was helping me test the level and I had to send him the gun's files for them to appear and work in his game (after I bought him a copy of GG just so we could play together.)
When I got this software the store page was extremely misdleading, only changed to more accurately reflect the true nature of this title after I pursued the devs. (Gave the impression you could make, release and sell MP games when you cannot how do you test let alone sell a game that requires the editor it was made with to work?. Imagine having to download and install Unreal to play ARK:SE or Unity to play RUST, but not only that you have to buy it and then source the content used to make the game.)
It's buggy and alot of the content included looks crap, although they have tried to make it look better. (When I bought it most textures were no larger than 1024x1024. To get many standard game features you will need to BUY scripts created by other users.) Unles you're competent in LUA scripting.
Some of the content has been made better, but so much is still early 2005 looking. Some model textures are actually low res photo's.
With ALOT of work you can make something that looks a bit decent, but the amount of effort required to make your own content like models and textures (Easy enough if you're a graphic designer to just make some 2-4k replacement textures and just 'drop them in') that you may as well just jump into Unity or Unreal and make a game for that.
Software like this could have some great potential if developed right, and developed faster. I mean the devs are friendly and communcate well with customers, but that alas does not excuse how slowly this software is beign developed and behind the times. (Heck I could grab a level editor and copy of 1997's Quake 2 and create a game faster with more stability and such faster than I could with GG)
The concept is great for a single person wanting to break into game design but the execution is terrible.
Hell, your game will not have any options to adjust graphics, instead it will auto scale to the users desktop res.
No option to rebind keys. Saving was only just added recently, (I think it was, not tested if it is or not in there I admit.)
I want to love GG, I really do, but as a gamer of several decades with some experience in level design, modelling and who is a graphic designer by trade, I think the software is laking in it's "Easy Game Creator" tagline. If someone like myself feels it is a chore to use, I imagine how bad it will be for those buying this who cannot create their own content.
If you're 12 and want to throw together some levels, happy to rely on average looking 3rd party assets and feel like you're a big game dev in front of your friend then GG might be okay.
But if you're serious about game design look elsewhere. (As I mentioned try Unity or Unreal, the GG publisher makes editors and addons for Unity BTW.) I honestly cannot see this being anywhere near complete or being suitable for creating a mainstream modern looking game for at least another 10 years.
The dev Lee needs to step up his game, or look at increasing the number of people working on the software (get the impression it's a mostly one man show.) to get it to where it should be ASAP. After a decade it's ridiculous this software is still so Alpha/EA and costs so much when in such a state.

Chains of Satinav is nothing like the other, action-oriented games set in the Dark Eye world. It’s a very slow point ‘n’ click adventure with depressing atmosphere, engaging characters and interesting motivations that move them throughout the story.
The German role-playing world of Dark Eye is not new for PC players; the setting was home for the Realm of Arkania and Drakensang games. ‘Chains of Satinav’, unlike those classic ARPGs, is a traditional point ‘n’ click adventure game with little action in it.
So little action, that it is almost boring. You move slowly, the story moves slowly, and all the voice actors speak like reading an audio book. So, even though the game is about an everyman teaming up with a fairy girl in order to save his kingdom from the icy doom of an evil wizard, it feels like watching an art film.
What is lacking in plot is gained in the exceptional characters and their motivations; it doesn’t matter if someone is the protagonist or just a one-scene character, they get the same care and detail. This not only helps in fleshing out this stereotypical story, but makes you emotionally invested in every little aspect of it.
With a fantasy setting it is easier to find new roles to seemingly everyday items, which in an adventure game translates to increased difficulty due to inverted logic. As the story progresses, this can reach the point where even veterans may get stuck for some time, especially when the game starts to add complex combination puzzles.
All by itself, ‘Chains of Satinav’ is nothing exceptional. Until you learn that this story is required to play the sequel,
. And believe me… even if this would be the worst game ever, it would be worth it to fully enjoy the greatness of Memoria.

The editor is fun, easy and quick to learn. With no coding being a plus but restrictions to customization being a con. Making a river is pretty easy but your character cannot swim, you will die the second your head goes under water. When it comes to actual gameplay which if you ask me the way this is set up the whole thing is gameplay since the editor is much like a game with how limited it actually is (there needs to be sliders and more terrian options to feel like an actual editor). The shooter A.I. are ok, they shoot back and can take cover where you tell them to but the zombies are HORRIBLE! and not at all in a good way. So I admit I was a little hesitant of Dust at first due to its furry art and its slightly overwrought, anime-style dialog. It's a"Metroidvania" game with a focus on fast and fluid combat and most importantly, great pacing.  It alternates between fighting and platforming at just the right times to keep the game interesting and more than once had me saying I would "just play until the next save point"...a dozen save points ago.
I have only complaint, which is that the game was a bit easy on normal difficulty.  This is fun in its own way as I was completely decimating enemies at the end of the game, but it also made the game a bit less fulfilling near the end as I breezed through.  To that end, I'd recommend playing on the next notch up if you're looking for a decent challenge.

First off, don't let the fact that this was originally a moble game turn you off.  In my opinion, if a game is good it can exist on any platform and still be a good game so it doesn't matter what platform it originally came out on.  With that in mind, lets review.
If you were ever a fan of Jet Moto, Sled Storm, or any other arcade stunt/racing games you'll find yourself remembering the great times you had with those games within Riptide GP2.  What the game lacks in graphics it more than makes up for in fun.  While I say that keep in mind that although the graphics might not be up to par with the current generation of games they are still fairly decent.  Furthermore, the action is smooth and I've never experienced any slow ups or lag while playing.
Physics wise the gameplay is loose.  Don't expect a realistic simulation of jet skis or water racing here.  Instead you'll find a more arcade style of gameplay physics which is, once again in my opinion here, a nice refreshing change from all the hyper-realistic gameplay that many other games try to convey.  Not that I don't enjoy some realism in my games, but sometimes its nice to just kick back and not worry about all of that.
In terms of general gameplay expect to have a blast trying to get the best time while performing some crazy stunts.  The stunt system is fairly detailed and stunts are set by your level, which gives you a chance to make your character your own.  Other customizable features are the ability to choose the colors of your ride and your rider.  It's not super detailed, but enough to make it your own.  The courses in the game seem well laid out and there's a wide variety of racers to choose from which you buy and upgrade using money you earn while racing.
There is selection of multiplayer options within the game which was somewhat unexpected.  First up is your standard online multiplayer.  I've raced others a handfull of times and the action is always smooth and fun.  Second is the race for time multiplayer in which your times on each course are sent out to your friends where upon they can race a ghost of your gameplay.  This is a nice option for those who may want to compete against others who may be on a different time scale than others.  Finally there is a multiplayer split screen option for up to four players.  Personally I have not tried this option yet and found it fairly unusual but nice within a PC game.
Overall the game is a lot of fun if your not looking for realistic racing action.  There's at least as much content within the game as there was in any of the Jet Moto games and in my opinon is well worth the price of admission.  If your looking for some simple fun races with plenty of options to play with friends you've got to try Riptide GP2.

Riptide GP2 does not project a positive introduction.  The initial bike is slow and has terrible turning capability.  To make matters worse I found the rumble to be too subtle and though the water is aesthetically pleasing the surrounding graphics are not PC acceptable though the cheap price mitigates this complaint.   There is nothing fun about the game during this phase.
Eventually through the acquisition of additional bikes, tricks and abilities the game hooks you and I found myself hooked, eagerly awaiting to participate in the next event.  A high compliment indeed.  Let it be noted that my first purchased bike was a mid range bike named as the "Lancer", essentially not exercising the option to purchase any of the slower bikes and this may be the reason why I did not experience the need to grind for cash as reported by other players on the game's forum.  The selection of the Lancer also is probably why the game hooked me as well given it's well balanced attributes and significant performance boost over the initially allocated bike.  A fun phase of the game to be sure.
Ultimately you will elevate to the more powerful bikes and upgrades for these bikes will just about maximize the bike's attributes (acceleration, power, handling and boost) and this is where the game falls apart as Riptide GP2 is a mobile port housing tracks which are CRIMINALLY too small for the higher end bikes.  It is at this point in the game which should be the most fun but Riptide GP2 winds up as a literal fish out of water as you find yourself constantly crashing and performing tricks into walls.  Some may argue the need to know the track and boost accordingly but the game became significantly arduous.
The developer Vector Unit has a good lineage with water racing games (XBLA Hydro Thunder) and should be absolutely ashamed of themselves for not putting the effort into extending the size the tracks for the PC platform.  A hall of shame inductee for sure because during the advanced stages, Riptide GP2 should be glorious and instead outed itself as nothing more than a huge washout.

A dark and thrilling tale of a young man named Geron travelling across the realm in hopes of reverting the dark prophecy bestowed on his land. He's no hero though, and everyone blames him for being the herald of doom which is obviously not encouraging at all, his journey neither easy nor glorious. As for the gameplay, it's not the most challenging quest out there, but at the same time the game never gives you clear hints to your actions so you have to pay attention. The storyline is really charming and has a strong "dark European medieval fantasy" feel to it (well, I suppose it's only natural, considering the Dark Eye setting), and the backdrops are breathtakingly beatiful, each scene working towards creating memorable atmosphere of the whole game. Voice acting was better than I've expected, but it's no Deponia. Overall, I'd recommend spending some time on this game even if you're not too keen on point-and-click adventures. It's an enjoyable experience similar to reading a good book.

This game is one of my favorite RPGs of all time. It has a really strong and compelling narrative and offers you plenty of chances to make choices that feel like they have some weight to them, though, perhaps not as much as the first game. The characters are mostly interesting, and the character development is definitely there. One of my favorite things about the story and characters is the moral ambiguity of it all. There is no clear distinction of good and evil between any of the sides. Simply two perspectives of what's right. The combat feels pretty fluid and I greatly enjoyed it. I liked how alchemy worked in the game, too. It's unnecessary in the first two difficulties, but in the higher ones, you'll find yourself greatly crippled if not using it. You cannot use potions in combat, so that adds some strategy to it. The game is absolutely beautiful on ultra settings, and it still looks pretty great even on lowers ones. The environment does at least. Nothing seems out of place in the world, the enemies are well designed and plenty creepy at times. They did a great job crafting the world.
That doesn't mean it's without its issues, though. The combat does seem pretty fluid, but in higher difficulties you'll find yourself rolling endlessly across the ground with your foes in hot pursuit. Blocking is often times useless, and there is very noticeable input lag on occasion. There's also a noticeable disparity between easy and normal difficulties. Easy being ridiculously so, and normal for new players likely quite challenging in the beginning. Also, though I enjoyed how alchemy works, it also leads to an obvious issue that can break the fluidity/immersion of the game. Since you can't use potions outside of battle, this leads most people to entering a fight to see which potion they should use for which resistances or buffs, loading a quicksave, and then using the potion. I love the idea and how it fits into the Witcher lore, but it needs some work. Also, either a pro or a con depending on your preferences, but it's not really an open world, and there's very few side-quests. You go from hub to hub, each having a few explorable zones mainly comprised of small passages. As far as the side-quests go, there's around 8 or so for the first 2 acts, I believe. Not really all that many. It leads to it being a fairly short game as far as RPGs go. Mentioning the choices again, I loved how they were worked into the game and they did "feel" weighty, though they didn't really mean much. You still end up in more or less the same situations with the same people doing the same things.
And then there's the much touted "Maturity" of the game. Yes, it may be much more so than many other RPGs, and it's definitely a dark game. The moral ambiguity definitely plays into this as well. With that said a lot of said "maturity" seems to stem from the idea that sex jokes are funny and adult. The characters way to often bring up "ploughing", at times it seems like every other sentence, though it's not really. It comes across as juvenile and cheap. There's mature themes throughout the game, though a lot of the perception of that seems attributed to the sexed up atmosphere. At least they removed the sex cards from the first game.
I probably missed quite a few things, this is just some stuff that came to mind. Might edit it on occasion.
I still recommend this game overall. It is quite enjoyable and the Witcher 3 is looking like a great game, so jumping into the series before that would probably be a good idea. It's on sale quite often, and even if not, it is easily worth $20 when it's not.

Nominated by myself for the "Test of Time Award", Hotline Miami was one of the first games I had purchased on Steam and quickly became one of the greatest games I had ever played. It's a simple game with simple objectives - go to a location and kill everyone in brutal ways by any means necessary. With straightforward mechanics like that you would be forgiven for thinking that this was some kind of 8-bit rendition of Call of Duty, but what really sets this game apart from many others is its difficulty - Hotline Miami can be extremely hard at points, but this is a trial and error type of game; go into a room, scout the area, immediately die, and respawn with the knowledge of enemy placements, behaviours, and weapons. This may seem like a waste of time to those who want to get in and kill, after all this is a pretty fast-paced action game, but it's definitely worthwhile. As for the "Test of Time Award", Hotline Miami is a game that, despite being only a small, short, indie title, offers a lot of replay value - new masks and new weapons are made based on points, and mission completion is graded - good luck with getting an A+ on them all. So, Hotline Miami is, for me, one of the greatest fames I have ever played and one that you can jump into and play for any amount of time, from 5 minutes to 5 hours. Fun, fast, brutally and beautifully gory gameplay with a killer soundtrack, if the movie Drive was a video game this would be it.

But as it stands, Mafia III is as repetitive as daily suburban life and it's far, far too stretched out to justify recommending. At its core, it's a ten-hour game that drags on twice as long as it has any right to. "Do you like hurting other people?"
Hotline Miami is psychotic, blisteringly psychotic, but yet subversive enough to penetrate through the fourth wall and have you questioning why, in fact, is this game so fun? The gameplay mechanics are simple: you come to the front door with a mask on and murder everyone. It varies in complexity, as the game gives you a healthy variety of tools with which you can use to make with the red splatters, and rewards you for utilizing your options with new mask choices--each one granting its specific boon. My favorite was Don Juan, the horse mask, granting me "Lethal Doors." In I would charge, typically getting gunned down or having my brains bashed in within seconds, and seconds later trying it again, only slightly different. You can get caught in loops where the same enemy kills you over and over and you insist on keeping the same pattern because it has worked so well until that point and you realize... well, maybe I should say I realized, that the whole thing seemed rather psychotic in nature, but why is it so fun?
"Why did you come back here? You're not a nice person, are you? You make me sick!"
The story lends the whole gameplay element about as much credulity as a handshake from a banker. But that is why it works so well. "Jacket," our unnamed player-character, is seriously unhinged from the start, living alone and, we learn, following instructions left on his answering machine.
"It's 'Dave' from Miami pest control. We need you. A client at SW 104th Street is having vermin problems. Try to handle it as quick and swift as you can. Someone else will clean up for you after you leave. Make sure not to bother any of the neighbors."
How curious our method is of "following instructions." However, Jacket has hallucinations, or maybe flashbacks, of three masked people sitting around him, asking him hostile questions, predicting the future with certainty, and generally being bizarre, which certainly doesn't explain anything, but it does add a bit of clarity to the situation. You are psychotic. All the neon colors, the pulsing retro techno buzz, the blood, the free handouts at every store you go to, the puking in the alleys. You start to see the people you've killed again, grotesque sinkhole foreheads dripping on the carpet. And then you die. Or maybe you don't. And then, once you've beat the game, it almost makes sense that the story is not over, and that you must play as someone you've killed. It would be easy to trust this "Biker" over Jacket, but when the final blood is spilled, it puts everything into question. Why did Jacket and Biker keep following the instructions on their machines? Could the whole thing really just be a couple kid's nihilistic game? Why is this game so fun?
"A picture is starting to take form here... I wonder if it's accurate. Some pieces don't quite seem to fit. Or maybe I just don't like the way it looks."
Hotline Miami manages to hook you with the one-more-try mechanic and a promise of an unforgettable fever dream of feral fantasy. Soak in this inspired indie game. Enjoy the brutality, enjoy the style, but most of all--enjoy the music.

I've been playing this game obsessively for a couple months now, and still can't get enough of it.  Learning the patterns of all the enemies is one of the most satisfying things I've ever done in any game.  When you start out, you're just fumbling around, faceplanting into enemies and getting torn apart.  If you practice enough, though, you'll be able to take on any situation without suffering so much as a scratch.  Every part of the game is very doable with the default equipment, so you're never just screwed because the right items didn't drop for you.  The weapons and spells that you can find all work differently and cause you to change your method of attack, but they're all pretty balanced.  There are a ton of different weapons types with their own unique advantages and drawbacks, rather than traditional "tiers" of weapons (1 damage, 2 damage, 3 damage, etc.)  And there's an instant replay feature upon death, where you can look and see what you could have done differently to save yourself (there's always SOMETHING).  This is quite possibly the most well-balanced game I've ever played, and I adore it.  Pick this game up right now if you can.
Edit: If you have any doubts, just look at how many hours I've logged on it ;)
Edited again, after launch day: Early access is over!  The game is complete and it's AMAZING.  I cannot believe how much better the game has gotten with time! This game is a fair upgrade from the previous version -- specifically the water physics is significantly better.  More watercraft to choose from, 13 tracks, and some nice graphical effects.  Water splashes on the camera.  Loads of acrobatic tricks to unlock.  Post times and challenge your friends to beat your mark -- you can even watch their ghosts as you make your run.
I'll recommend it for kids and people looking for a casual racer, but not for someone who is a hardcore racing fan or anyone bothered by shoddy physics.
[ONLINE MULTIPLAYER PROBLEMS]
I tried and failed on numerous occasions to get the on-line multiplayer to work.  There's no loading screen or menu, it just launches you into a game with seven random guys and then sits there trying to make all the pings match up.  I have yet to be able to actually race anyone else, so if you're looking for multiplayer racing, skip.
[MENUS]
The options menu leaves a lot to be desired.  There are no resolution options; their "resolution" area actually changes the fidelity -- not the resoltion.  My advice is to ALT+TAB out of the game -- which will make it a window -- and then size it as you see fit.  Also, I wish it had some sort of plot where it was you versus the other racers; the others are just names on computers.
[PHYSICS]
The water in this game is great.  When an opponent flies by you, he leaves a wake -- forcing you to make corrections or hit the wall.  However, while more beautiful and realistic than the first GP, the remainder of the physics leave a lot to be desired.
[AUDIO]
The audio is a mixed bag.  When you're in caves, the sound changes and you can hear the other riders better.  It's neat when you're so far out in front that all you can hear is yourself.  With that said, the guys over at Vector Unit need to google "cavitation" and "doppler effect".
[MISC]
Unlike the first game, there's no running the courses in reverse.  There's a reason why you can't run them in reverse, but I won't spoil that.  It's worth mentioning, though.  Finally, your riders are very stiff in their animations -- as if they were statues.  They could use some more animation.
All-in-all, it's a quality racing title and a ton of fun.  Feel free to friend me and see if you can beat my times.

I play classic point & click adventure games a lot and I also played The Dark Eye RPG in the pen & paper version in my youth. I cannot remember all facts and stories of the world Aventuria in which Chains of Satinav plays. Anyway I do not care whether the world is 100% reflected by the game. Nonetheless, the game designers have done a remarkable job to feel like being in Aventuria.
And also to create a really dense atmosphere with characters that you learn to love during gameplay. Like many Daedalic adventures the story is not a simple good vs. evil plot. Below the obvious surface (evil seer, ravens, dark creatures ...) one may notice thoughts about being determined in life though people don't support you or in general whether ends justifies the means (lies).
An important part of adventures are the puzzles and Chains of Satinav has a lot of good ones (especially in the faerie world). Unfortunately there are also times when the puzzles become easier again. Why? Although I appreciate that Chains of Satinav takes you to many places, the problem here is that some of them are very restricted. You cannot go further until you solve that handful of puzzles which makes it too easy sometimes and makes the game feel too 'vertical'. What was really refreshing however was the idea of having a destruction and (later) a repair spell in your repertoire which distinguishes the adventures from others a little bit. Those spells are also really well woven into the other puzzle sequences.
The world is drawn by wonderful fantastic sceneries which fit very well to the various places the adventure takes you to. The animations could be smoother though. The voice acting is done very well at least in the German version I played - whereas the music is let's say unobstrusive and could be diversified more and emphasize some events better.
A very underrated adventure in my opinion. All in all a game that I really enjoyed a lot. I will miss Geron and Nuri.

This is the best RTS I have ever played. I usually don't like RTS but I absolutely LOVE Dawn of War. This game has such an immersive, epic, dark and warmongering feel to it. You just enter battle and you hear the Ork soundtrack start with the drums and all in your mind is "Cleanse! Purge! KILL!"
This game doesn't feature all the races in Warhammer 40k but it does feature most of them, and the ones left out have been implemented into the game by modders, such as Tyranids. Relic surprised me with how accurate this is to the lore and the tabletop game. Even the resource costs of troops is the same as the cost for troops on the tabletop (in the tabletop you have X amount of points to spend in a battle for your troops and more powerful troops cost more points). I haven't actually played the Dawn of War and Winter Assault campaigns because I think linear RTS campaigns are among the most boring things in this whole world, but Dark Crusade features a unique and awesome campaign mode. (Soulstorm has this campaign aswell but in much larger scale.)
You start the campaign by choosing one of the races; Space Marines, Orks, Eldar, Chaos Space Marines, Tau, Necrons or Imperial Guard. All the races control different areas on a planet and then take turns assaulting other's areas with your hero, conquering them, gaining resources and honour guard (units that accompany your leader in battle who are more powerful than normal units) to spend on buying troops for all your areas or buying honour guard units. You can also unlock new gear for your hero, such as new ranged or melee weapons, better armor that give different perks, certain gear gives abilities like teleport and such, and to eradicate a race you have to assault their strongholds, and those battles have lots of different objectives and side objectives you have to do to win, like destroying different bases and if you want to, destroying bases that provide certain powerful units for the enemy so that the final push will be easier. I remember when I tried to take the Tau stronghold as Space Marine and the battle went on for like 1½ hour because they just kept harassing my base.
If you want a hell of a good RTS in one of the coolest, if not the coolest sci-fi universe out there, then this is totally the game for you. I'm not sure if it's still here but there's a platinum version of the game to buy which gives you Dawn of War, Winter Assault and Dark Crusade for 9,99€, I can't find it anymore though. If you manage to find it and you're a RTS fan, then do buy it because it's more than worth it, I assure you.

This game is well above average for the point-and-click genre of games.  It, like the sequel, weaves a beautiful story with beautiful artwork and music, and is well worth picking up ("Memoria" is the sequel and is also available on Steam).  Like all of this genre, there are some things to figure out which aren't necessarily intuitive, which can be frustrating.  This is no worse than any similar game, however, and didn't detract from my enjoyment of the game.
The interface and inventory are very easy to use, which is much appreciated in a land of complicated inventory management and skill systems and perplexing (at best) UIs.  For this genre, less is more in terms of making a player jump through hoops to work the interface.  This game does just fine at that.
I've heard others say that the story isn't anything unique, but as I've never run into a story quite like this before, I'll politely disagree.  There are some of the usual fantasy game tropes, but the overall story felt brand new to me.  At least personally, I felt it was a beautiful story with some parts that were heartbreaking (caveat: I am a softie, so I might be more emotionally invested in the story than some are!).
The characters were all nicely handled; I especially loved Nuri's simple naivete, which the writers made work nicely by not confusing simplicity with stupidity.  She is not stupid, even when her innocence about the "human" world gets her into trouble, and even when her inclination towards trusting everyone works against her.  "Your humans are angry with me, Geron!" she says after opening the cages of a town's entire animal population.  Her bafflement is endearing.
The artistry of the scenery and backgrounds is what really impressed me through both of my plays through.  The attention to detail and sheer beauty of some of the backdrop scenes really showed hard work on the part of the illustrators, and I respect that.  I have some screenshots uploaded from this game just because there were parts I went full-on tourist with the camera.
TL;DR: one of my very favorite games of the genre, beautifully done in terms of character, art, and music, and well worth picking up, along with the sequel, Memoria.

The Dark Eye: Chains of Satinav is a nice addition for anyone who´s into the point-n-click genre. Even though I´m not familiar with the Dark Eye World I found it an interesting setting. The story line is by no means original but the narrative still feels solid and keeps you as a player interested in seeing how the story will play out.
As other reviewers have done I will also recommend playing the game on hard difficulty since the game does become a bit to easy when played on easy with the help modes enabled. The main use I see for the easy difficulty is for those who wishes to play the game more like a visual novel, since the story and narrative is good this is a viable option. I found most of the puzzles to make sense and only the Fairy World may be considered a bit out of the ordinary in that department. The inclusion of a break/repair option was great since it creates more possibilities for item combinations without having to add more items to find in game.
On graphics one have to mention the backgrounds which look amazing and the character models are also great to look at when they are stationary. The animations are however not that good and both movement and facial expressions are jerky while the lip-sync in dialogues is even worse. Since one does get used to the faults and still get´s to enjoy the beautiful backgrounds the total impression on graphics is still very positive.
Music/Audio is for the most time quite nice even though I did find the protagonist Geron to be a bit whiny in the first chapters of the game. He does seem to mature or rather face up to the challenge as the game progresses which is a nice touch. The other characters, both minor and major ones, are well voice acted and adds to the overall positive experience when playing the game.
In short I will recommend this game for fans of the point-n-click genre and I would also view it as a good game for those who does not have much experience with puzzle games but want to try one out. The full prize of 20 € does feel a bit steep since the game is not that long but at a sale it´s good time value.

MURI is a great retro platformer game, very faithful to the PC games from early 90s or 80s.
The graphics are well drawn and use a fairly restricted color palette, simulating the early DOS games with EGA graphics card. The sound also simulates what early games sounded on the built-in PC speaker (there was no sound card in the early days).
The levels are also very well designed and have some secrets, although they are not too difficult to find if you spend some time exploring all areas. The secrets usually have some hints indicating there is a hidden passage or there is some puzzle-ish element (such as destroying some blocks). That way, they never feel "cheap" nor frustrating. In fact, they are quite straightforward.
Joystick is supported, but I had trouble configuring the D-pad in-game. Instead, I just used Xpadder (or Joy2Key) to emulate keypresses.
The gameplay itself has a brilliant touch: you can either play in 16fps, which really simulates the movement of early PC games such as "Duke Nukum" (the first Duke Nukem game). Alternatively, you can also play the game with smooth movement in 32fps, which feels more responsive and more modern. Either way, the game plays very well, the controls are very responsive, and the game feels balanced.

I only knew
series as a classic German pen and paper RPG until this point. After some research, I discovered that the realm of Aventuria has been turned into several cool pc games including
and
RPG series respectively. But I've never dared to expect an adventure game that takes place in a FRP universe! It has been a satisfying change of pace for a fantasy lover such as myself: enjoying the contents of fantasy without venturing into battle.
Our storyline takes place in humble beginnings, with Geron, the novice birdcatcher of the local ranger Gwinnling who lives in the silent medieval town of Andergast. Geron is considered to be cursed by the town populace, both disliked and feared with heavy prejudice due to an old prophet's dying words: "you will bring great disaster to Angergast!" Geron's unpleasant life takes an interesting turn though, when he is given the opportunity to get rid of the crows infesting castle's quarters. As he tries to attend this opportunity carefully, he meets Nuri, a fairy that will change his so far predictable life - and fate, forever...
I'll try and put my experience on the table shortly: I loved every single moment of this game! Characters are original, the narration is exquisite, and the story is incredibly well-weaved! On a fair notice, the art works are singularly amazing enough to buy this game! It gave me the thrill of old adventure classics like
or
. I found myself wondering the next bold move of our heroes in every pace, so I played the game in one single night!
Puzzles vary between 'the logically expected' and 'the brink of insanity', which sets a tone for every single environment by itself. The context of the game consists of the marriage of two separate themes: the dreamlike, abstract nature of fantasy and the heavy, forlorn quest for philosophy comes together to portray the world of Aventuria, a world worthy of getting to know surely.
If you consider yourself to be an adventure game player, please take note that this game - alongside its sequel,
- are modern classics to the genre. You will not be disappointed!

If you are a fan of either the Warhammer 40K universe, or RTS games, or both, then this game is for you. Out of all the Dawn of War games (excluding Dawn of War 2), this one is hands down my favorite. I have sunk a LOT of hours into this game, and I'm only about a quarter of the way finished with it.
Here's how the game plays: You pick a race (Space Marines, Chaos, Tau, Ethereal, Orks, Imperial Guard) at the start of the game. Each race has their own strengths and weaknesses. My personal favorite are the Space Marines, who are very versatile and can easily adapt to any situation. Once you pick a race, the game begins. It is set up like a board game, similar to Risk. Each race takes a turn, and on your turn you can choose where you want to move to. Where you choose determines what race you will fight in that area. Every territory also rewards you with Honor Guard, which are elite units (VERY powerful compared to your regular units). In addition to this, there are a couple territories that have special abilities, such as the Spaceport that lets you attack anywhere, or Forward Base which lets you start matches with some buildings already made. The game continues on like this, with you attacking and defending. Your commander unit also acquires War Gear as you play, which makes them even more powerful.
The real combat of this game is in the attacking or defending phase. The game plays as standard RTS fare. You gather resources, build structures, and grow your army. There is a lot of variety within a single race, which really helps to mix up the gameplay. You take over resource points and fortify them as your forces clash with your opponent. Once your army is built up enough, then you can obliterate your opponent and win the territory. Two things are important to remember, though. First, the way you leave a territory is what you will come back to when you are defending it. If you fortify it heavily, then you will be hard to defeat when the battle comes back to that area. Secondly, the special territories all have unique battles. The Spaceport, for example, has you gathering special units scattered across the map. The first side to collect 6 of these wins.
Graphics wise, this game is behind what you'd expect from a modern RTS game, but it gets the job done very well. The units are all very detailed, and pleasing to look at when you zoom the camera in. The only downside is that the terrain looks a little bland sometimes. However, this game is not about looking pretty, it's about the battles. And combat is really well done in this game. If you've played the other Dawn of War games, then you know how it goes. It's really cool to see the animations of units in combat, they don't just pummel each other until a health bar is gone, there is interaction between clashing forces.
In addition to the campaign, there is a skirmish mode that you can play to your heart's content. If you and a buddy have this game, then you can also jump online and play against each other in online multiplayer. All in all, this is a great game. Don't let Steam fool you, I've been playing this long before I bought it on here, and my hours in it are easily 200+. I like replaying the game as the other races to see what I've missed. If you like Warhammer 40K or RTS games, this one's for you. If you aren't sure, then grab it if it goes on sale. Trust me, it's worth it.

This game is one of my favorite RPGs of all time. It has a really strong and compelling narrative and offers you plenty of chances to make choices that feel like they have some weight to them, though, perhaps not as much as the first game. The characters are mostly interesting, and the character development is definitely there. One of my favorite things about the story and characters is the moral ambiguity of it all. There is no clear distinction of good and evil between any of the sides. Simply two perspectives of what's right. The combat feels pretty fluid and I greatly enjoyed it. I liked how alchemy worked in the game, too. It's unnecessary in the first two difficulties, but in the higher ones, you'll find yourself greatly crippled if not using it. You cannot use potions in combat, so that adds some strategy to it. The game is absolutely beautiful on ultra settings, and it still looks pretty great even on lowers ones. The environment does at least. Nothing seems out of place in the world, the enemies are well designed and plenty creepy at times. They did a great job crafting the world.
That doesn't mean it's without its issues, though. The combat does seem pretty fluid, but in higher difficulties you'll find yourself rolling endlessly across the ground with your foes in hot pursuit. Blocking is often times useless, and there is very noticeable input lag on occasion. There's also a noticeable disparity between easy and normal difficulties. Easy being ridiculously so, and normal for new players likely quite challenging in the beginning. Also, though I enjoyed how alchemy works, it also leads to an obvious issue that can break the fluidity/immersion of the game. Since you can't use potions outside of battle, this leads most people to entering a fight to see which potion they should use for which resistances or buffs, loading a quicksave, and then using the potion. I love the idea and how it fits into the Witcher lore, but it needs some work. Also, either a pro or a con depending on your preferences, but it's not really an open world, and there's very few side-quests. You go from hub to hub, each having a few explorable zones mainly comprised of small passages. As far as the side-quests go, there's around 8 or so for the first 2 acts, I believe. Not really all that many. It leads to it being a fairly short game as far as RPGs go. Mentioning the choices again, I loved how they were worked into the game and they did "feel" weighty, though they didn't really mean much. You still end up in more or less the same situations with the same people doing the same things.
And then there's the much touted "Maturity" of the game. Yes, it may be much more so than many other RPGs, and it's definitely a dark game. The moral ambiguity definitely plays into this as well. With that said a lot of said "maturity" seems to stem from the idea that sex jokes are funny and adult. The characters way to often bring up "ploughing", at times it seems like every other sentence, though it's not really. It comes across as juvenile and cheap. There's mature themes throughout the game, though a lot of the perception of that seems attributed to the sexed up atmosphere. At least they removed the sex cards from the first game.
I probably missed quite a few things, this is just some stuff that came to mind. Might edit it on occasion.
I still recommend this game overall. It is quite enjoyable and the Witcher 3 is looking like a great game, so jumping into the series before that would probably be a good idea. It's on sale quite often, and even if not, it is easily worth $20 when it's not.

I've had a lot of fun with this so far, but I am rapidly losing interest. I think the game takes itself a bit too seriously and fails in some very important ways.
Here are some questions you should ask yourself before you buy this game....
Do I have endless hours to dedicate to this?
How many times am I willing to fail a tutorial?
Do I like restarting, restarting, and restarting again?
Do I want to learn rocket science, without ever planning to be payed as a rocket scientist?
The learning curve in this game is HUGE. I found that challenging at first, but now I just want to do something fun. Tiny variations in mass and structure will cause you to scrap hours of work and start over. I've built over 30 rockets easily. 4 will leave the atmosphere. 3 of those will orbit Kerbin. 2 can fly by the mun. 1 can orbit the mun and return to Kerbin. This took me 80 hours of game play and it barely scratches the surface of what you can do in the game.
The navigation (maneuver node) interface is AWFUL. Everything is bunched together, making it exceptionally easy to push, pull or click the wrong directional indicator, causing you to scrap the whole thing, often with only a few seconds to perform the maneuver without repeating your orbit. Also, the 3 dimensional display must be navigated in a very 2 dimensional way, making it difficult to see what it is you are actually doing. I use a 51" flat screen tv as a monitor, set 12" from my face. I can't imagine trying to play this on something smaller.
So, is it fun? Hmm... are you a sadist? Does failure appeal to you? Would you rather crash and burn than travel the galaxy? Do you not have a life? Do you have an IQ of 300 and the dexterity of a brain surgeon? This game is for you!

This game, while also being one of my favorites, should be much more recognized by the community. While I understand that game review is subjective as all hell. Many people have shot this game down as it is different. Further concurring on the theory that innovation in video games is not truly desired by video gamers. This game is innovative, becoming it's own genre of video game that Steam does not have a tag for.
Notes about the game(I believe a pros and cons list to be inadequate)
-I, as an experienced StarCraft II player, have found commanding to be enjoyable, but slightly more dumbed down than a regular RTS. This is further multiplied by the simplicity of alien commanding. This, however, makes it easy for new players to pick up commanding
-The FPS action is incredibly tense, with the players having to turn off all other sources of sound or music to listen for footsteps or instructions from the commander.
-One concern I had when first starting was that I only liked playing marines, and I'm sure others have similar issues. I quickly learned that I could easily enjoy playing both sides. One must understand what they enjoy about each team before truly finding enjoyment.
-This game is- in my experience on the NA servers- generally underpopulated. However, as of the Winter sale of 2015-2016, their has been a huge surge of new players, strengthening the community and playerbase.
Helpful tips-
-Be nice to rookies. The one thing that solidified my enjoyment of this game was a kind player urging me to be my best and guiding me when I had just began. A little kindness towards new players can and will strengthen the player base.
-Carry a welder. Welders are cheap, available without any research, and can be truly vital in tense situations. Repairing a friendly's armor, or a marine in an exosuit can mean the difference between winning and losing.
-As a skulk, remember that your life is less valuable than higher life forms. Remember to never be afraid to initiate a fight, with a higher life form like a fade or onos following suit. You will most likely die but you have paved the way for your team to win a fight without losing any important or expensive life forms.
-Conceding can sometimes be the only option. Remember that there is always the option to concede by hitting x, and then selecting concede. Sometimes it is best, when new players join to just start fresh and hope for more even teams.
Final comments-
Natural Selection 2 is a fantastic game, made by fantastic developers that are constantly updating and listening to community feedback.
I would recommend this game to anyone that enjoys fast-paced action, is able to communicate well with others without getting in fights(my brother has this issue), and can be a good loser, because a loss can sometimes be inevitable

I've spent far too much time in a single night playing this game. It's unfinished right now, still having some placeholder art and more things being added, but the core is there and it's a blast.
There are two main components to the game - rhythm and pattern recognition. You'll need both to survive this game. The first is simple, just stay on the beat and you'll be fine. The second is the trickier one and more important one in my opinion. Each enemy has a defined movement and attack pattern, and you need to slip in at the right time and attack when you won't be hurt. Sometimes it's easy, like with slims that only move up and down, or skeletons who raise their hands before attacking.
Sometimes, it's trickier. Mushroom people who throw out AoE attacks. Dragons who move every second turn, or bats who I have yet to figure out the pattern for. Of course, if you get bit by a bat, it's likely not such a big deal, but missing the dragon could get you clawed or charred, a one turn death.
There's no "gotcha!" kills to this roguelike, though plenty of dying to do as things get frantic and you fail to keep up, misjudge the enemy attack pattern, and suddenly find yourself cornered, and you'll do more than a little dying as you learn the patterns of some of the more dangerous enemies.
Rarely frustraing, lots of fun, occasionally repetitive due to the single assigned song per level - hopefully this increases. The rest is headed in the exact right direction.

I have a hard time recommending this game in its current state.
First the things I like.
The games controls great using an xbox 360 controller.

What I don't like. and hope they are able to fix
First the sound.  I am a huge fan of hydro thunder.  And part of what makes that game so awesome is the whole background music and co-pilot talking to you type thing going on.  Sadly there is none of that in this game.  I actually really dislike the background music, it fails at making you feel like your on the edge of your seat like it does in hydro.
The sound effect used for wrecking your jet ski is just plain bad,  reminds me of broken glass.  seriously I just trashed a jet ski and the best sound they could come up with is the sound of dropped glass?
I could learn to live with the whole music thing, after all I can turn it off and play my own tunes, which I would recommend doing.  However after 37 races I am losing interest in this game very quick.  I have gone from this is really cool to this is really annoying.  We all know this game is a port of the mobile version.  The mobile version had in app purchases.  Now to their credit they did remove that part of it.  For the record I hate playing games that are pay to win or we are gonna make you grind grind grind.  Well that's what it feels like to me, a giant grind.
Yes this game is nothing more than a grind when you get right down to it.  I am on the third series of races out of 9 all together.  Within each series you have multiple races.  Each series requires x amount of stars to open and each race within requires x amount to open.   I  started to notice after the first series that I just could not compete anymore.  I spend what little money I have on upgrades and bam all of the sudden I am coming in 2 and 3rd.  I have reached yet another point in the 3rd series where I simply can not compete cause my bike is not good enough.  So what do I have to do, gp back to the first series of races that I can actually come in first place now and start racing them over and over again until I earn enough money to be able to compete once again.  An average race only lasts a couple mins so it doesn't seem bad really.  But let me give you an example.  I need 60,000 to unlock all 4 upgrades to my bike.  I would buy a new bike but to get a comparable one in stats it would cost me 100,000.  If you win a race you can make approx 1100 to 2200 if i recall a race.  if come in second or even third you get paid squat.  You do gain extra founds every time you level up as well.  for example if you reach level 8 you get a 8,000 bonus.  a thousand per level if I remember right.
My problem with this all is the fact I have reached a dead end in the game.  I can't win any more races to collect stars to be able to continue in the game.  The only way I can accomplish that is to upgrade my bike so I don't keep getting smoked by an average of 4-6 seconds.  And the only way to upgrade my bike or buy a new one is to grind out races I have already won over and over again.
Keep in mind I am only in the 3rd series, this may or may not get better.  I don't know and a may never find out because I am already burned out racing the same couple races over and over trying to earn money so I can upgrade my bike.

My original review of this game was to not recommend on the basis of the lagged gameplay sucking the fun out of the game. Having played quite a bit for a few weeks, I changed this to recommend with some misgivings. I have now gone back to not recommending it.
While the platform performance has improved, the developers have recently announced a major patch to the game to address various balance and item drop issues. Until this patch is in place, it is not possible to recommend the game as the fundamental level structure and so forth is broken.
While acknowledging the game is in beta, the issues faced by the game (e.g. survival is either impossible or trivial, siege vs bots is pointlessly easy, people disconnecting ruin PVP) are so central to its enjoyability, until they are addressed, this game is, essentially, pointless.
I hope these issues are fixed as I would like to recommend it as my hours clearly show. As is, I would spend your time elsewhere.

While the game does very little to innovate, it's a very accessible game, especially for people unfamiliar with the difficulty of older games. If you are looking for that challenge, however, there are modes to make that happen!
It's a very
game, in my opinion, but I think it's well done.

like it's from the 80s, as intended! Low-res, limited color-scheme, 16fps -- it's all there! (Although there's a 32fps version, which feels much better to play)
What you see in the screenshots is what you get. It seems very faithful to the era it's celebrating.
It also features color-coded enemies, each color representing a difficulty-tier.
Everything is well delineated, and there's never any confusion between what's an enemy, background and foreground.
The
follow the same route. If you like playing your own music while playing game, those can certainly be very annoying, but you should know what you're getting into.
There's one big issue, though, in the fact that there's no

And it's very unfortunate that MURI does not have any. There's a very short and looping track in the menu, but on its own, it does nothing to standout.
You could always listen to a podcast or something while playing it, though, without hurting the experience.
There are 4
in MURI. Each episode is self-contained, and has 5 stages, one of which is a boss fight.

Each of them has a Score Multiplier associated with it.

, just to see how it was. Normal mode should cause major problems to anyone. If you take the time to explore, you'll have more than enough lives and health pick-ups to carry you through. I didn't get any game-over in this mode. Hard will most likely be the most suitable for any more or less experienced player.
MURI, on the other hand, is more of a real challenge! There are not health pick ups nor lives anywhere. You'll have 3 lives for each episode, and that's it. This was certainly not the kind of experience I was looking for when I started playing MURI, but it's good to know it's there! (I have yet to play Volgarr the Viking)
Your health is restored between each stage, in all modes, which is very handy! It's also a small reward on the harder modes, to be able to take damage in moderation without it being an issue.
On every stage there are tons of secrets, in the form of fake and destroyable walls, hidden platforms, etc. for you to uncover, getting score pick-ups and lives as well as ammunition for the more powerful weapons. Your score is increased by picking things up and killing enemies -- a very welcome aspect is how the game tells you when you reach 100% Score for that specific stage! I think it's very fair. It doesn't tell you too much, but you can be sure to leave the stage without leaving anything behind, if you so want.
There are also hidden Cells. These will unlock the more powerful weapons for the Boss stage, but are also more challenging to get.
If you lose all of your lives, you'll get a game over screen, and "back to the menu with you"! Again, it should not be a problem in Normal Mode, at least.
I've covered part of this on the previous section. No worries, there's still a bit to talk about.
I've mentioned several weapons. These include your basic, infinite, slow shot. Then, there's Rapid Shot, MKV (Scatter gun), Laser gun, Explosive-shot gun, and a Crazy Barrage of Large Bouncy Shots gun. You'll be able to get ammo hidden through the stages. You always keep what you collect when you finish a stage -- except, of course, between episodes -- so exploration is highly encouraged.
Your active weapon is
the most powerful one for which you have ammo. I dislike this quite a lot. I don't see a reason for not allowing the player to switch between weapons, but I couldn't find one. This leads to you wasting very valuable ammo on the weakest enemies, and then having an hard time with the tougher ones -- note that this only made a difference in MURI mode, but still.

First off, the game constantly teases you by showing you pick-ups inside the walls. You know you
get there; all that's left is figuring out how!
The game doesn't try to hide many things. It's mostly very fair in that regard, as it gives you glimpses of possible secrets and fake walls every time.
Another way that I highly respect is that they
close a door behind you -- figuratively speaking.
There are no pits from which you can't get back, doors that close or anything of the sort. If you've left something behind, as long as you don't leave the stage, you can always go back to find it. This also goes hand in hand with the fact that they tell you when you reach 100% score. If they didn't tell you when you're near the exit, you've missed something -- Feel free to go back and explore some more!
There are lots of different enemies, each with their movement pattern, health, directional shots, etc. For its low length and amount of episodes, Muri compensates with the very varied enemies and levels in general. It'll never feel repetitive during the first playthrough! And if you're actively looking for this kind of game, I'm sure you can play through it at least twice without it feeling boring at all.
For each type of enemy, there are also different tiers, identified by their color. Green are the easiest, then Blue, Red and Grey, with these being the harder.
The enemies are well placed, and the game is never unfair. You can always see shots coming before getting hit. Enemies outside the screen still shoot at you and take damage, so you'll have to be careful.
One of the aspects characteristic of these old games is how methodical they are to play, and MURI is no different. If you rush, you'll probably get hit often, and end up losing a bunch of lives. If you play it slow, and be aware of the enemies' patterns, though, you'll be able to succeed with conviction.
If you've played NES or DOS games, you'll know whether this is for you.
The Boss Fights were also pretty fun, with multiple phases, as is classic. They also change depending on the difficulty you're playing on, which is always good to see!
I've seen some people unhappy with the lack of lives. I'd generally agree, especially in the easier difficulties, as it's very frustrating to lose a whole level of progress.
However, I don't think you have anything to worry about, in this game. MURI mode is there for the more hardcore players. If you're not one of them, exploration will reward you with plenty of lives. It's old-school design, but made more accessible. I do not think it poses an issue.

Hey folks,
I will keep it kind of brief:
Q: Do you recommend the game?
A: Yes, it is very fun to play, especially so with some friends.
Q: Is the game bugged/ under development? Any other problems?
A: For sure, it is EA and for sure you will find bugs and that sort of thing. Sometimes nothing appears to work. BUT, the devs are fairly quick in fixing stuff and almost none of the bugs really kill the fun. It is more the matchmaking that can be a pain. Other than the occasional "none of them online features works" periods, the core game performes well in my opinion. Single/Multiplayer/Coop all work fine, no in-game crashes so far, mechanics seem to be working as well.
Q: Does is feel like "Orcs must die"?
A: Absolutely. Traps, minions, castles, explosions, everything is there. Plus, you get a crafting system, new heroes with unique skills (quite a lot actually) and a new game mode (MOBA-styled PVP). I am also very happy that the devs are sticking with the charmingly funny tone of the game. A lot of effort was put into hero voicing, minions can be hilariously eager to smash stuff etc., you get the gist.
Q: But its F2P and I have had bad experiences with that. Does it affect the game?
A: Thats a matter of preferences and I guess this is the point where some of the negative reviews come from (except the "publisher rant"). We all had those games where the F2P concept ruined the core game. Surprisingly, this is not the case here. Of course, the devs need money. Thats why you have optional purchases. Most things are locked at the beginning and you need materials to craft stuff, and these materials drop in matches. Thats where gamers can be divided into those who want everything from the start and those who are ok with working on items. If you belong to the former, you might need to make a few microtransactions to get what you want. The latter kind of player, which I probably belong to, will be ok without, but new items take a while to craft. To the point: The game is free of charge and you can play as much as you like, which I think is incredible considering the quality and content you get. Everything else (pace of progression, access to heroes and items) only depends on you.
To sum it up:

Imagine a hypothetical "Orcs must die 3", multiply it with a couple of cool features, substract a point  or so for bugs and unplayability and divide the whole thing by F2P. The result is a authentic, fun game; charming and motivating, but depending on your ability to tolerate the F2P concept OR ... you know, just pay a few bucks to unlock something. Afterall, thats the stuff that keeps the devs going. Alternatively, you can always just try the game out and decide for yourself, cause, you know....it's FREE.

Designed to look, sound and play like a DOS game, this is a paean to the power of the aesthetic.  It could almost be running via DOSBox, such is the atmosphere of the game. A platform action game at heart with a lot of shooting, this is a fun albeit short-lived experience.  The graphics are suitably EGA like; there is no in-game music and the sound effects are pleasingly simplistic.
Some of the deliberate constraints may annoy those not used to playing old-style games: weapon selection is automatic - the most powerful weapon is always chosen.  The frame rate is choppy, but you can make it smoother in the menu.  There is no map or indicator of where to go next; fortunately the stages are not a sprawling affair - you can get through most levels quickly if you decide to.
There are some concessions which help make it less frustrating for some folk.  There are several small rooms hidden from view, usually with a power-up or scoring items.  You are briefly invincible when hit, enemies' bullets are large and easy to see and you can repeatedly bounce on most enemies to damage them.  There are several difficulty levels and the cut scenes can be skipped.  You have all this fun with no need to add commands like DEVICEHIGH=C:\WINDOWS\EMM386.EXE RAM into your AUTOEXEC.BAT file.

taps into a largely untouched nostalgia pocket, that of the DOS-era platformer. The gameplay & presentation feel wonderfully authentic, and the sci-fi theme is especially well executed within the stark EGA palette. MURI's pixel art awesomely captures the style of the time, and the same can be said of the crunchy PC speaker beepboops that may as well be forcing their way out the cracks of an IBM taking up your desk.
More importantly, though, each of MURI's levels are loaded with thoughtfully placed secret areas & collectible doodads, and the whole game features consistently satisfying shooty action platforming that fans of the original two Duke Nukems will feel instantly at home with.
If only Remar Games / Ludosity could chop the game down into a Shareware-style demo sold on a floppy at the dollar store, fanatical levels of period authenticity be damned.

This game has the ability to draw you in right away. Some of the biggest appeals are the story, beautifully fleshed-out backdrop, and the "close-to-home" fantasy lore that gives its fans exactly what they want in a game of its genre. The one thing that stands out as a possible set-back for some, perhaps is the cryptic and seemingly random nature of a handful of the puzzles throughout the game. Some puzzles seem obvious right away, others not so much. This game had me close out multiple times to eyeball a walkthrough to figure out what I was doing. I believe a good point-and-click can at least provide some clues that may be subtle and not deduct from the gameplay. I felt that this game was lacking that sort of "user friendliness" in some moments, especially when you are given items in your inventory that are used in highly unconventional ways. Maybe this is part of what makes this game interesting--testing out possible uses for an item with the interface or with other items...but where does it flip to tedium for the gamer?
The plot and art style of the game is what kept me hooked, there's a nice balance between clicking around just to explore an area and clicking around for items and descriptions of things to be used later.
I recommend this game for its engrossing easy, and fair amount of dialogue that doesn't wear you down. For those who get easily frustrated toying with different objects in order to advance to the next screen, this game probably isn't for you. Fantasy RPG fans, this one's for you.

This action platformer has tight controls, solid action, a fair challenge and rewards exploration with useful power-ups, no filler content anywhere (unlike many AAA titles these days). I was initially thrown off by the very dated graphics (this game was made to look and play like a DOS-era 2D shooter) but as the proverb goes "Do not judge a book by its cover" and for this game "do not judge a game until you've played it". Very pleasantly surprised. There isn't much music but the sound effects fit nicely what tunes there are fit the mood. The difficulty settings actually tweak some bosses to go along with the chosen setting and ensure everyone from the hardcore to the casual players (and the ones in between) can play this game end to end. The story is serviceable if at times bizarre. The levels are designed to be short and each act (which you can choose from when starting a new game) consists of 5 levels so the arcade experience and meaning of losing a life still holds.
TL; DR: Don't let the graphics throw you off, this here is a mighty fine 2D action platformer and shooter that just shows how much solid gameplay mechanics and outright fun trump polygon count any day!
