This is my review of Orion Prelude I will not be comparing it to its past versions Orion Beatdown or Orion Dino horde, nor go into the devs back story. You want to know about THIS GAME not of its past. Orion Prelude is a first/third person shooter where its main game modes are to kill dinos to survive or to try and kill an opposite team.

There are a couple pvp modes but there aren't many people(you may find one or two servers) playing. The only pvp mode that gets love is Vital. This is a interesting Idea and is fun, but can have problems. Vital you have two teams of five each of you have a generator which you must protect from the dinos which only thing they do in life is kill you and your generator.  As you kill you get credits you usually use them to upgrade yourself and get weapons but in Vital you can mess with your enemy's dino spawn. you can increase damage that dino deal, how many dinos spawn, and give them big dinos as a present and I feel its balance there. problems are with the players. It's doesn't have a balance system so instead it can be 4 old with 1 new vs 4 new and 1 old player its fun but you have to be careful . also this game mode will take you 1-3 hours(it may drag on) to beat and is really the greatest with a full team.

There are also three survival modes one named survival, conquest, and Slaughter. survival last around 40-50 mins in the most of the difficulties and your goal is to survival 10 rounds of dinos, how? by protecting your generator also you will have to go to outposts and capture them every 4ish rounds. You can buy weapons and upgrades in between rounds before the killing begins again.
Conquest is a copy and paste of survival but on a HUGE map, has 30 rounds, is 2-3 hours, and you can also buy jeeps, tanks, heles, and so on. It's fun but only use dedicated servers for if the host leaves then the game ends.
Slaughter is endless slaughter( I know what a surprise!) there are no rounds for you just keep getting hit by dinos you will be given guns and ammo over time and the longest I have survive is 20ish minutes and it's a good mode. in all, I play them at different times but each one is different and all are fun so I would suggest you try them all.
now that will give you a idea of the game itself I'm sure you have some other questions. (if I miss any please do not be afraid to ask for I will add it to the list, thank you.)
1. how does it run: it has always run well for me(60fps or higher) on ether of my pcs but I have heard that it runs better now than ever for some people who have had problems before.
2. sounds: Since 3.0 all weapon sounds have been redone/edited this has really made the games feel deadly. I have found one or two that I don't like but its an overall improvement.
3. graphics: Improved since 3.0, all maps look and feel better then they were and the new maps (2 which have been added in 3.0) are really well done.
4. how does it control?: good question, on mouse and keyboard like other good fps and controller
support is only for the 360pad, from what I hear its good there to.
5 modules: great don't have any problems with that. Although it's fun when the T-rex model flies in the air after killing it!
6. guns: you will see some guns that look semi normal but many are very cool and fun to just look at.
all in all its a great game. Its not a AAA title but you can sink some time in this. I would suggest this to poeple who loves first person and third person shooters. I feel  you would have as much fun with yourself as you will online. also there is steam workshop to make maps so If you like making maps then you might want to get this to. (Note: workshop is stuck in beta mode until a bug can be fixed)
7. score: 9/10. v3.0 really has made this game shine its not prefect but its a great game.

This game is one of my favorite RPGs of all time. It has a really strong and compelling narrative and offers you plenty of chances to make choices that feel like they have some weight to them, though, perhaps not as much as the first game. The characters are mostly interesting, and the character development is definitely there. One of my favorite things about the story and characters is the moral ambiguity of it all. There is no clear distinction of good and evil between any of the sides. Simply two perspectives of what's right. The combat feels pretty fluid and I greatly enjoyed it. I liked how alchemy worked in the game, too. It's unnecessary in the first two difficulties, but in the higher ones, you'll find yourself greatly crippled if not using it. You cannot use potions in combat, so that adds some strategy to it. The game is absolutely beautiful on ultra settings, and it still looks pretty great even on lowers ones. The environment does at least. Nothing seems out of place in the world, the enemies are well designed and plenty creepy at times. They did a great job crafting the world.
That doesn't mean it's without its issues, though. The combat does seem pretty fluid, but in higher difficulties you'll find yourself rolling endlessly across the ground with your foes in hot pursuit. Blocking is often times useless, and there is very noticeable input lag on occasion. There's also a noticeable disparity between easy and normal difficulties. Easy being ridiculously so, and normal for new players likely quite challenging in the beginning. Also, though I enjoyed how alchemy works, it also leads to an obvious issue that can break the fluidity/immersion of the game. Since you can't use potions outside of battle, this leads most people to entering a fight to see which potion they should use for which resistances or buffs, loading a quicksave, and then using the potion. I love the idea and how it fits into the Witcher lore, but it needs some work. Also, either a pro or a con depending on your preferences, but it's not really an open world, and there's very few side-quests. You go from hub to hub, each having a few explorable zones mainly comprised of small passages. As far as the side-quests go, there's around 8 or so for the first 2 acts, I believe. Not really all that many. It leads to it being a fairly short game as far as RPGs go. Mentioning the choices again, I loved how they were worked into the game and they did "feel" weighty, though they didn't really mean much. You still end up in more or less the same situations with the same people doing the same things.
And then there's the much touted "Maturity" of the game. Yes, it may be much more so than many other RPGs, and it's definitely a dark game. The moral ambiguity definitely plays into this as well. With that said a lot of said "maturity" seems to stem from the idea that sex jokes are funny and adult. The characters way to often bring up "ploughing", at times it seems like every other sentence, though it's not really. It comes across as juvenile and cheap. There's mature themes throughout the game, though a lot of the perception of that seems attributed to the sexed up atmosphere. At least they removed the sex cards from the first game.
I probably missed quite a few things, this is just some stuff that came to mind. Might edit it on occasion.
I still recommend this game overall. It is quite enjoyable and the Witcher 3 is looking like a great game, so jumping into the series before that would probably be a good idea. It's on sale quite often, and even if not, it is easily worth $20 when it's not.

Note: I've only played the alpha build, so some of this may be subject to change.
Crypt of the NecroDancer is an incredibly fun take on the Rogue-like genre.
At its core, NecroDancer follows the same tenants that most Rogue-likes do. You enter a procedurally generated dungeon with basic equipment and attempt to reach the exit. Along the way you defeat enemies, avoid traps, buy items, and make generally strategic decisions before you take each step.
NecroDancer throws an unusual wrench in the works, however. You're no longer allowed to move or attack unless you do so in sync with the rhythm of the current song. Doing well increases the number of coins you get from enemies, and missing a beat resets this bonus. Additionally, if you miss, the enemies essentially get a free turn. No longer can you sit and ponder your next move, you have to keep moving with the song. Additionally, enemies follow a generally fixed pattern and will only manage to deal damage to you if you neglect to keep this pattern in mind.
The result is a highly skill-based Rogue-like where decisions need to be made quickly, and mistakes are punished harshly. The game is definitely balanced around this mantra, as it's very possible to win without ever purchasing an upgrade for your character.
In order to cater to a variety of player-types, the game includes both a "standard" mode and a "hardcore" mode. In the standard mode you're able to purchase upgrades that permanently boost your character, and there are essentially checkpoints that allow you to start from later levels. In contrast, "hardcore" puts you on the first floor with no upgrades and requires you to clear the game in one go. There are time and score leaderboards for hardcore, along with character unlocks that serve to boost the difficulty even more. The terrifying "Aria mode" is unlocked at the end of hardcore, and features a new mechanic where any hit or any failure to match the beat of the song results in immediate death.
The end result is a very fun and refreshing game. Even in the alpha build the mechanics feel very polished, the enemies are varied and interesting, and the strategic gameplay is downright engaging. Much like Spelunky, you'll find yourself excited to die repeatedly as you learn to conquer the game's increasingly difficult floors. The less hardcore players will also likely find enjoyment in collecting new upgrades and unlocking new features as they slowly make their way to the end.
The music is also incredible, featuring the composer from Super Meat Boy. If you want additional variety or don't like a particular track, you can replace any level's soundtrack with an MP3 of your choosing. I haven't played around with this much yet, but it likely adds a considerable amount of depth to an already deep game.
Sadly, the Alpha Build doesn't have the 4th (and final) zone yet. However, if it is anything like what I've seen so far, it will be both devious and incredibly fun to play.
If you enjoy Rogue-likes or music games, this is a great purchase.

Over the past several months, I've had the pleasure of testing an alpha of
, a retro styled rhythm based roguelike.
Crypt of the NecroDancer is a procedural dungeon crawler where the player and enemies movie on the beats of the game's music tracks. That may sound like an eclectic mix, but it works. It works
.
You play as Cadence, a firey young woman who, against the better judgement of her elders, descends into the NecoDancer's crypt in search of answers. The intro cinematic shows Cadence prone, her head against a blood smeared rock whilst her narration says, "I don't know how I survived that fall."
Cadence is resurrected by the NecroDancer, who makes her heart beat to the rhythm of his music. Armed only with what she learned about the undead from her uncle Eli and the equipment she discovers along the way, Cadence must descent farther to find her answers and hopefully free her heart in the process.
Inspired in part by Spelunky, developer Ryan Clark has pointed out that they've tried to create something more accessible than typical roguelike, focusing on making the player feel like any deaths are their own fault rather than the game being unforgiving.
To help convey this, each enemy has its own behaviours which players can anticipate and respond to after learning their movement patterns. For example, skeletons move on every second beat, whilst ghosts move on every beat, but only when the player is facing away from them. The game's complexity is emergent and comes from the combinations of enemies which make each encounter feel unique and challenging. Each of the game's four zones is populated with its own enemy types, which become more varied as the game progresses.
As you play, Cadence comes across many weapons and items, each with their own behaviours that lend themselves towards different styles of gameplay. The properties of each item seems to be something you're expected to learn as you play, discovering that a broadsword will let you hit enemies on any of the three adjacent tiles, or that a karati gi will enable Cadence to move past traps without setting them off.
In addition to buying and finding items whilst playing, the game's lobby features a number of shopkeepers from whom items which impact on the game can be brought. Some items will be permanent buffs, such as health increases, whilst others will be more subtle like giving a particular weapon the chance to spawn in a chest within the game. Items from these shopkeepers are purchased with diamonds rather than the gold you buy items with in-game, and provide a way for players to feel a sense of progression as they complete the game's zones.
Rather than progressing onto the next zone when completing one, you are returned to the lobby area to find a staircase leading down to the next zone unlocked. In this "normal" mode, players are encouraged to explore and master each zone before moving onto Crypt of the NecroDancer's Hardcore and Daily Challenge modes which allow players to forego any items bought from the lobby shoopkeepers and play through the entire game with one life.
Beyond Hardcore mode and Daily Challenge mode, the game also offers some additional challenges and characters for varied gameplay.
The game ships with an absolutely rocking soundtrack from Danny Baranowsky (Canabalt, Super Meat Boy, The Binding of Isaac and Drifter, amongst others), but also features the ability to load custom tracks.
Currently, testers run a utility which generates beat definition files that the game uses to track whether your movements are done in time with the music. A Linux build of the utility isn't yet available, and there's some path/case issues which haven't been resolved yet, but the developers seem to be attentive and I expect these to be resolved soon. Eventually this functionality will be built into the game, but for now, there's a little bit of manual handling.
The game also offers game pad and dance mat support (if that's exciting, you can keep an eye out for some
) in addition to keybaord controls. I found that I had to configure custom bindings for my Logitech F310 gamepad and a "Dance UK" dance mat (which overrides the keyboard bindings), but after doing that, both were usable.
Crypt of the NecroDancer feels rich with atmosphere. Small things, like the subtle screen shake when striking a successful blow, or the shopkeeper's voice as he sings along to whatever music is currently playing really show the kind of attention to detail that is going into this game, and I find myself eager to see what each update brings.
Crypt of the NecroDancer will be launching on Steam Early Access on July the 30th (which is just over a week away right now).
There's no solid release date at this point, but it's expected to be released this year. You can find a few bits and pieces on the
(recently, they've been showing off some enemy art) and Ryan is quite active on the
.

I absolutely love this game: from the way the skeletons dance to the singing shopkeeper and amazing soundtrack! I would absolutely recommend it to anyone. I was hooked on this from the first moment I saw it, and 120+ hours later I'm still playing. If the rhythm aspect of it worries you, don't worry - the way the game is set up, the beat detection is forgiving and there is even a mode where rhythm is *not* a factor. This game is, as someone put it, "easy to pick up but difficult to master." You can learn how the game works fairly quickly, it takes a bit of time to get through all the Zones normally and unlock the items - but wait, there's more!! - there is a Daily Challenge, speedrun mode, Hardcore mode (requiring you to play through all levels with no upgrades and get to the last level without dying), and other challenge modes (Aria: 1 hit or miss a beat and you die; Bolt: everything is 2x speed). There is a huge amount of replay value, as the dungeon maps in this are randomly-generated and there is a wide variety of items (weapons, equipment, items, etc.) with a variety of effects. It's a different playthrough every single time. If that wasn't enough, you can even put your own MP3s into the game and play by just about any track you want, as long as it has a beat. I can't say enough good things about this game; if you are thinking about picking it up, you will not regret it! :)

You might wonder why you should buy this. If you are a developer then you are probably already using software that you like and are used to. If you are not a developer, you may think this software is just not your thing.
If you are though, like me, interested in creating a solid project quickly and without spending a fortune on assets, then this is one of the best software packages you can possibly find.
Why do I say this? Lets have a look at it compared to the big 2 engines:
1) How does it look? GameGuru does not have the ability to look as good as Unreal. It's not meant to. I would say that it does approach Unity at times however. Not quite, but enough.
2) How quick is it to create in? Well, if you want your program done in 8 months, use UnReal, in 4 months, use Unity, but if you want to have your game market ready in 4 weeks, you need this software.
3) How hard is it to learn? If you can use powerpoint, you can learn GameGuru as it has about the same learning slope. Unity takes weeks to become proficient at, Unreal, months, but GameGuru takes hours. Literally hours.
4) Cost. Unreal is free. Unity is free. GameGuru is not, but neither are the assets for Unreal and Unity. They are, however free in GameGuru.  Frankly there is no better bargain anywhere.
In summary, this product isn't for the experienced user. If you want to become a game developer this as a start woudn't be a bad idea. I love the software, the developers answer questions quickly, and there is no scripting required. None.
I give this a solid 8/10. Try it.
2016-11-24 I wanted to provide this update based on my personal experiences after using GameGuru seriously for while. I have purchased all of the DLC available and would estimate that with research and watching youtube videos on the engine, I've about 150 hours invested. I still like the engine and my 8/10 rating stands, it's quirky at times but fairly stable. I did discover a major drawback however. It's the heavily moderated GameGuru forums. When you encounter one of these GameGuru quirks it is natural to use the forum for answers. While there are several dedicated and wonderful people who do what they can to assist you, you quickly get the feeling that new users are probably not very welcome which must substantially impact GameGuru sales. Rather than being a place of fun and encouragement, it appears to have some very strict and unclear rules that new users simply would not know. If you inadvertanly break one of these rules, the impression given is that you are unwilling to follow the rules - not that you are a new user who doesn't know them. At least for me this can be quite discouraging. Reading through posts you will see a number of excited customers faced permanent user bans and locked down topics for unclear reasons, unlike other user forums. Dust: An Elysian Tail is a rare gem of a game. It might seem very childish or bland at a first glance, but beneath the surface is a true labor of love. The aesthetics are fantastic and the world is colorful and vibrant, which is a wonder considering it was made by a single man. The voice acting, while somewhat spotty at worst, was delivered by believeable and capable people, even if they may be amateurs, they never felt grating or cheesy.
The sound design, namely music, is top notch and fits the pace and the feel of the game very well. The rest of the sounds feel at home, and I can't recall anything that ever really popped out.
The enemy design is varied and interesting, although understandably each area only has a few enemy types each. The characters are interesting to talk to, whenever they have something to say, and listening to the vast amount of dialog the game offers is pleasant and interesting to listen to. The game tells you just enough about the world to keep you immersed, while leaving the less important bits aside.
What I might complain about would be the bartering system. There is no easy way to sell a large quantity of items, which forces you to hammer either the mouse button, A or D or the arrow keys repeatedly for literally hundreds of times, whether you're buying or selling.
The weapon augments and armors don't have interesting effects to speak of, and are very linear upgrades. Thankfully pendants and rings offer some more interesting choices.
And while the platforming is generally enjoyable, I at times felt that the character was somewhat floaty, or did not control as tightly as I'd hope, but it was a fairly small annoyance compared to the twenty hours of enjoyment I managed to rake in from this wonderful, beautiful game.
If you were to blitz through the game, you might expect around ten hours of gameplay, if even that. However, if you wish to go beyond 100% like me, you may easily get 15-20 hours or joy out of the game. Of course, if you hadn't seen any pictures or videos of the game, the game features anthromorphic animal characters aplenty, and if you are not a fan of them, you might want to ponder whether you can stomach it or not. The game nor the characters ever bring this up, however, so it's not exactly shoved in your face and down your throat. For people who love said style of characters, you are in for even more of a treat.

GameGuru is an ok engine for people who don't have any programming experience, however if you think you're going to make a serious game from it think again. While it may change names again in the future, it will always be in beta regardless of what the product states. While the loading times have improved from the original FPSC, there are too many issues tied to it's source code that probably will never be fixed. I'm sure many non-bias people who can think for themselves will agree if you look at it's history. I've actually lived through it since 2005.
Furthermore, this engine like it's predecessors seem to all have the same motive: making some quick money then going mia until people forget about it. FPSC, FPSC x9, FPSC X10, and now GameGuru seem to all follow this pattern since 2005.  It is however a great platform for new programmers to learn LUA, and the community is very helpful and knowledgeable. I will say it's the community in my opinion that keeps me coming back, but I regret investing my time and money into a dead end product. Also, the mickey mouse encryption which didn't exist before is ruining everything. If you're trying to protect a developer's intellectual property/content wouldn't it be a good idea to have it exist in the first place? What's the point of protecting something that doesn't exist? It can't even copy texture and basic text files right or even at all for that matter. GameGuru is the only engine where after I build my game, I have to go into the folders and manually check that it copied all the files over correctly. Then I have to manually copy the missing files over, and if an encrypted file was corrupted during the build I have to add and re-encrypt the whole build myself with a third party program.

I had been hearing lots of great things about this game, so I grabbed it along with the sequel during the Steam Winter Holiday Sale.
I haven't played any point-and-click puzzle/adventure games in a long time, but I am VERY impressed with this one. The sound track is great, the artwork is GORGEOUS, & I really loved the characters and story.
I played on easy mode, but even so I found the puzzles very challenging & difficult (maybe I'm just dumb though?), & it was very fun & frustrating to try to figure them out. The solutions are practical yet not obvious at all, which makes solving them deliciously satisfying.
The story ended in a way I did not expect at all, but that I loved. REALLY glad I decided to pick up the sequel at the same time I bought Chains of Satinav however, because the ending leaves you at a cliff hanger (in my opinion). I can't wait to check out Memoria & the other games set in this fantasy world.
I've noticed that some other reviewers are giving this game a hard time over the voice acting, but I personally found the voice work very enjoyable.
Absolutely recommended if you like challenging puzzles, lovely music and artwork, and an engaging story with entertaining characters.

A lot can be said about this game. It has its great moments, but also some very lame sides. First, the positive things about this game: It is a nicely done rpg with lots of costumization possibilities. You can not travel between cities and have to follow the plot of the game, but once you're in a city, you are free to explore it however you want to. There are lots of side quests and the main plot itself is very interesting. The side quests are also meaningful and mostly fund, not of the "fetch me this flowe" kind. The game is clearly made for adults, since there's a lot of brutality and nudity in it. This is nice to see in an era where almost every game is being made for all audiences. The crafting system is also one of the strong features of Witcher 2. You can craft weapons, armor, potions, traps etc.
On the other hand, there are some things which ruin the game. The checkpoint (aka autosave) system is a failure. You watch a cutscene, you listen to a conversation and then get to the fight scene. If you die, you don't get to fight again immediately; no you have to watch the cutscene again (which you can skip btw) and listen to the conversation (which you can click through). It is very annoying to constantly have to click your way to the fight after every death and it only adds to your frustration. There are also instances in the game where you don't control your main character, but you are rather given the control of a character in the story to fight. The game is almost telling you "Hey remember all those skills you gained through collecting experience and all? Yeah, they're gone. Have fun!". This is very very frustrating. In the end, you should make up your mind: can you endure the frustration of this game to enjoy its exciting plot and positive features?
tl;dr Witcher 2 is a beautiful game with some very annoying bull**** in it.

Now that I have a rig that can properly handle NS2, I think it's finally time for a review.
This game is incredible. I've been playing since NS1 but the devs completely outdid themselves with 2.
NS2 is extremely immersive and incredibly exciting. Strategy and teamwork are required and winning is very rewarding as a result. The graphics are rich, even on low settings and that only adds to how easily one can get zoned right in while playing.

If you have not played Natural Selection and are even just slightly considering this game, get it. If you enjoy FPS and/or strategy, get it. If you enjoy defending humanity against aliens or ripping humans apart with claws and jaws, get it. If you enjoy mech suits and jetpacks, get it. If you enjoy flying about and gassing humans, get it. With over 1000 hours logged and the solar system mastered, I can safely say that this game never gets boring or easy.
It is an incredible concept that the devs have put together extremely well.
In career mode you start off small and have to earn new parts, base upgrades and increase your own knowledge to master the solar system, starting off by launching just a few hundred metres up as you get the hang of the ropes and introduce yourself to the real-world physics of aerodynamics.
the feeling of accomplishment you get when you first achieve orbit, or step on another planet for the first time, your first successful docking of ships etc... there is so much to do and learn, and what i love about it is that it's all based on real world physics. You learn so much about actual space travel, orbital mechanics and the considerations you need to be aware about, such as there are no such things as straight lines in space, you are ALWAYS being pulled by something, the learning curves and challenges you need to overcome will keep you endlessly entertained.
When you achieve a milestone in the game you do get a real-world sense of achievement because it is genuinely difficult to do and you need to really ponder and challenge yourself as to how you're going to achieve something.
For example- you accept a mission to build a ship cabable of storing a lot of ore that you have to mine. you have to figure out how to build this ship aerodynamically, maybe it's too big for one launch and needs to be assembled in orbit? how will you do this? you have all the parts in your vehicle assembly building, you just need to apply some brains and creativity to think about how to achieve the mission, it's all up to you.
There are literally hundreds of insane mods for the game that make the in-space scenes amazing to see, the parts, missions and other ideas people have thought to mod make the game so much more interesting.
I give it 28/30.
The only annoying things are the bugs - or 'space krackens' that can randomly explode your ships when physics is enabled after loading etc can be annoying, do be sure to save.
Watchout with mods... if you install a lot which when you find out the incredible things on offer you probably will, don't do game updates for at least a month after it releases cause all the mods also need to be updated to work with the new version and any non up-to-date mods will stop the game from working since certain parts are temporarily locked until updated.
these are minor inconveniences compared to the pro's.

I gave this one as much time as I could muster.  It took me a while to really like Mafia 2 so I overlooked some stuff and tried to get through some of the story in this.  Just some thoughts by category follow:
Narrative:  Man, is it thin.  The build up didn't give me any time to care much about what happens to Lincoln's family.  Having played through Mafia 2 a few times, I thought they would give us a bit of background to play through as the character.  In this game, they just show you a cut scene.  A good one, to be honest, but that's about the end of your background on Lincoln.  I didn't find it particularly satisying, and by the time you're off to murder everything terminator style, you're doing open world fetch quests for characters that don't really seem to matter.  Certainly not to the character you're playing.  Also, so many of the "cut scenes" are just barely animated, static angles of you watching two characters jaw at each other in game.  Which would be ok if anything they said is mildly interesting or important, but they only serve to give you info on a character that only exists for you to lob a bullet or grenade at to gain some territory.  Underbosses aren't really characters as far as the story is concerned.  Since I was a fan of Mafia 2, I needed to know what happened to Joe, which the dev said they would cover.  They did, it's about two paragraphs of dialogue from Vito.  two wholly unsatisfying ones.  The acting in the proper cut scenes are great, but after the beginning, you barely see them until story missions.  And again, the writing is just ok at best, but it did nothing to move me to care about much I was doing.  and after 35 hours of gameplay, it's just not worth it to continue for any bit of the story.
Visuals:  I run a rig that currently maxes everything at 144hz 1080p.  Yes, the release was rocky and frame was limited, but they patched it fast.  The problem that continued to now with framrate is that using Vsync limits you to 60 frames.  The game tears pretty badly if that's not on.  It's fixable through it through Nvidia Control Panel, but I just shouldn't have to bother with that on any modern Triple A title.  Not this far in.  Also, the game looks super dated visually.  It lacks detail in the open world.  Anti-aliasing maxed out makes it look like everything has been rolled in lint, it's so soft.  Reflections are poor, when they work correctly.  Character models are hilariously limited.  I've started naming character models in mob camps.  There are about three or four for each faction.  Interiors are drab and cloned.
Gameplay:  Every mission to control an area is basically the same thing.  Blast through mob guys and kill or threaten on in particular.  Or, blow up crates and defintely take the stacks of money they leave in the open everywhere.  repeat ad nauseum.  There are some "missions" you come across while driving, but all you do is follow behind a car, wait until they get to the same mob camp you would've come across anyway, then you kill them.  There is a mechanic to crow bar doors that is the most boring minigame I may have ever played.  One wonders why they even bothered with it and didn't have you just mash a button like everything else in the game.  Story missions are the only locations that are of any interest gameplay wise.  and they're far apart.  It's just so boring to get to anything that matters.  Then once you do, it's a largely disappointing outcome.  Guns don't make any difference beside damage and aren't very different from one another.  Stealth is a waste of time, the AI is too poor to make that any bit of interesting.  You can sit in one spot and just whistle them to you one at a time.  It's a laugh, but gets sad and boring quickly.  and again AI is bad in a way I haven't seen in a long time.  Too easy to just take care of every one of your underbosses and make them happy.  It was just boring.  boring.
Conclusion:  Very stale.  Story is poor.  Visuals are dated and you almost certainly have to leave the game and make manual changes to make it look best.  Glitches quite often, one still exists that is glaringly difficult to get by and is a necessary mission (boxing level).  and overall gameplay gets boring fast and stays that way.  As far as addressing any social issues they hyped this up on, it seems more like an excuse to write in as many racial ephithets as possible.  It's clumsy at best.
I wouldn't recommend this to anyone until it's $5.

Overall I would rate this Game Creation Program as a 5/10...
Let me start by saying that I purchased this product when it was still in beta. When I first started using it, I expected there to be bugs or performance issues as the product was still being developed and software development is a process which gets better and better as new versions are released. The only thing is, this software is now released and no longer in the beta phase so I would expect a much more functioning and complete program than what it was in beta testing. It just fails to deliver on what it promises it can do. That being said, there are some very well developed features that work extremely well. But these great fetures are negated by all the issues that currently exist.
Pros:
Easy drag and drop interface for adding objects to the world
Very nice terrain editor
Support for custom scripting using Lua
Cons (Where do I begin?):
Performance is a HUGE issue. The IDE runs fine without issues but testing games is a bit of a hassle. Framerates are poor if you have any kind of special graphic effects such as Bloom. I would expect better performance on my machine considering I can run Skyrim on Ultra and Fallout 4 on Low with no issues at all. Also, the AI seems to completely lock up if you have too many AI entities (such as enemy characters).
My Machine Specs:
Windows 10 64 bit
AMD A10 APU 10 Core (4CPU + 6GPU) with R7 Graphics and CPU clock at 1.8GHZ
8GB Ram
Other Cons:
- No GUI for modifying the menu screens on standalone executables
- No native support for any type of objectives system even simple things such as a compass pointing towards where the player is supposed to go.
- No native support for any type of custom HUD
- Character entities are hard-coded to have a preset weapon which is a bad change from FPS Creator which allowed changing the weapon on character entitites to any of the weapons that were installed
- The AI is extremely slapdash and poor quality for 2016. I understand that AI can be customized through LUA scripting, but the majority of users expect at least decent AI by default. The enemy characters that have weapons just stand idle until the player gets pretty close to them and then they "activate". By that time, the player could have just shot them before they even "saw" the player. This completely eliminates the ability to add enemies that can "snipe" the player, or at least shoot from the same distance that the player can shoot them from. Also, as mentioned above, the player could just kill the enemy from a far distance - with a low accuracy pistol even - and the enemy wouldn't even react to being hit. You would expect the AI to at least cause the enemy to become aware that they have been shot at and move around or "search" for the player. Another huge issue is the AI pathfinding. Unless the terrain is basically completely flat, enemies have a hard time navigating small hills in the terrain. They often get "stuck" and end up just standing in one spot without continuing to follow the player and shoot at them.

Chains of Satinav is about a sassy dude who's constantly down on his luck, untill he must capture a fairy and everything gets much worse. Some of that may sound familiar... But it's hardly a bad thing.
This game is the second time I made a real effort to play a P&C Adventure, after I have No Mouth, And I Must Scream. Broken Age doesn't count, because it's short and unfinished at this time.
I'm putting this up front, Chains of Satinav is a great game, and it's baffling nobody ever talks about it. It's set in a world that now crosses over with multiple games from different genres, so there's a ton of worldbuilding through conversation and observation. The conversations themselves feel very real for a basic go-through-all-the-options dialogue tree system, mostly in part to the voice acting. The puzzles can be difficult, but make perfect sense in comparison to standard combine-items-to-see-what-works fare. Sometimes it makes use of options you don't really know are there, but the game does tell you what you need for the situation, you just gotta figure out how to get it. Sometimes you need to revisit characters after a puzzle portion is solved to try and advance the puzzle itself, which was annoying in that one section with a bunch of other characters fighting for screen time, but it never get's harder than that thankfully. No timed item puzzles or unsolvables. No deaths.
It's a really solid adventure game with endearing characters, sensible but difficult puzzles and a sequel I should get back to, as it looks like they've improved on the presentation even more. Memoria is the name, just to confuse people, but it is a direct sequel to this story and would spoil the ending almost immediately otherwise.
The only problem I had overall was the janky animations. It's the only thing that kept me from playing it through when I got it. Don't let it keep you away though, because it is definitely worth it.

DISCLAIMER: As a streamer I was sponsored with some copies of this game from the developer, however this won't affect my review of the game/program.
GameGuru was developed by the same people who developed DarkBASIC though the basic interface is much more visual when developing games rather than looking at an endless screen of coding you've just learnt to put a power up into a game.
Whilst it's indeed possible to create a game in minutes this seems to be based around the concept of taking one of the existing demo games included and modifying the variables, (such as health).
Creating a basic game environment is pretty simple in that you can create mountains by stretching out the ground environment, and picking up a weapon by selecting it from the menus and placing it on the floor.
For people who want more you can edit variables such as how much damage a weapon does, how much health enemies have, and even their intelligence parameters, such as whether an enemy will chase you endlessly or just patrol a set area.
The interface is easy enough to work with though sometimes it may take several seconds to open a menu or option.
There's a somewhat solid community of people where you can exchange ideas and community created content too which is worth a look-see.
To summarise; don't expect to create a AAA title within an hour on this, but you will be able to create a basic game to help learn the system with this, the developers sometimes stream live tutorials on Twitch).
It's a great way to learn how to create games and is fairly easy to dabble with, and fun too.

I am definitely a sucker for old-school point-and-click adventures. You know that kind of person who played through most of Lucas Arts and Sierra games during the early 1990’s and still thinks that LOOM was a great game and who, when someone says pirate, spontaneously starts humming the LeChuck theme? Yep, that's me.
Before we begin, it should also be noted that I have never played the pen-and-paper version of The Dark Eye. Save for my encounter with The Blackguards (another game by Daedalic) I have had no prior experience of the rich lore of The Dark Eye universe.
This review is based on my three playthroughs of The Dark Eye: Chains of Satinav (one regular + two achievement runs).
…are absolutely stunning, with a high sense of details put into the making of every 2D background. Nowadays you can expect to find this level of quality in many games, but in my opinion, 2D art truly comes to show in point-and-click adventure games, whereas it tends to be overlooked in other genres. In TDE:CoS the scenery seamlessly intertwines with the storyline. You can see that the sketch artists allowed themselves to be touched by the story... and possibly a wee a bit of fairy magic was involved as well.

…is also great, in all its simplicity. The tunes blend into the background so that you never take your mind off the storytelling. Instead of using their whole arsenal, the team who made the music carefully chose instruments that would mix well with both the story and the elfish concept art used in this game.
Most of the voice actors did a decent job. Overall it’s not that great, but good enough to do the game justice. Most adventure games let you down when it comes to the speech. Perhaps I'm too old-fashioned, but voice acting kind of kills the spirit, doesn't it? It almost always ruins the imagination for me. How does a beautiful fairy sound like? Or a talking crow? A brutish orc? Perhaps you have a tingling sensation of the sound in your mind, but forget about trying to mimic that sound with your own voice. The task of giving voices to magical creatures is a task best left for professionals and in TDE:CoS some actors were obviously more professional than others. Several characters does not sound anywhere near authentic (putting aside my subjective opinion of the matter, they simply sound way too scripted, which I believe most players would agree with). Then there are others with great voices.
Towards the middle of the game, you’ve gotten used to it. The female voice actors did an overall much better job than their male counterparts in this game. Or perhaps the dialogue was better suited for female voices, having been written and scripted by a woman?
As a side note: have you ever played the game called "
"? If not, I feel for you. It was a lovely little gem of its time and as every other game from the early PC/Amiga gaming industry it was (initially) released without voice effects. Save for a few sound effects and background music, you never knew how Simon, the mages, trolls or any other of the absolutely hilarious beings in that game sounded like. And that was... g r e a t. Later on, they dubbed it (of course). Which version do you think received the highest scores?
And I guess that’s my point; players have learned to expect mesmerizing graphics and all characters to have high-quality voices, no matter what. Some games try to come up with nifty workarounds (Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons comes to mind) but most such attempts fail. As a developer, you might not dare to let your product come off as a low-budget/indie game at first glance. But most of the times, less is indeed more.
…actually works! I didn't quite know what to expect when I started playing this game. I had not read any reviews prior to playing it but I have (sadly) learned the hard way to lower my expectations whenever I tryout modern fantasy adventures. But TDE:CoS felt more like a child's story, having been tucked away inside the writer's mind for many years before being put to the pen and shared with the rest of the world. With a box office budget, I'm sure that this game could have been turned into a decent movie script. As such, the limitations of a point-and-click adventure sometimes makes the story come off a bit crude and rough around the edges. But it's nothing that you can't polish up a bit with your own imagination (if you allow yourself to focus on the good stuff and ignore the rest).
My consensus after playing the game from start to end three times in just a few days is that the story is probably a lot larger than what could be depicted from this rather small game. As a player, I strolled along through the chapters but ended up craving more after each intermission (which is a good sign, right?) instead of the short cut scenes. Same goes, without a doubt, for the ending.
Perhaps the cut-scenes could have been more "layered" (in lack of a better word for it) to give them a bit more depth. Or perhaps the game could be filled with more dialogues, background stories and side-quest-lore that players could explore at their own leisure?
The single worst part of this game is irritably the part that should have been the easiest to get right: the coding and scripting of actions in the game. Although TDE:CoS should be more than able to run smoothly on almost any computer you could find today, it often slows down and feels sluggish between important actions and in scenes where the main character has to move from one side of the screen to the other. Why on earth did Daedalic not make this better? It saddens me to see such a seemingly easy task being carelessly ignored, especially when you consider the astonishing work made by the other members of the developing team.
Whoever cleared these animations should have their eyesight checked out immediately. Save from a few exceptions, I have not seen animated 2D stills of such poor quality since... gee, we’re talking pixelated 1990’s here. Forget all about expecting smooth 12 fps stuff. Honestly, people of Daedalic, I implore you to search for better animators for future titles. And to forego any quirky remarks; no, I haven't played the sequel (Memoria) yet and no, I have no idea if the animations improved later on in the game series. But I surely hope so. The story and its characters deserve it.
Had it not been for the lush scenery and music that straight off the bat inspired me to delve deeper into the game, I might actually have stopped playing TDE:CoS after just a few minutes due to the poor animations - that’s how bad they are.
But to everyone who has not yet bought the game: ignore all comments about the animations. Yes, sure, they
. Yes, they

So I see a ton of reviews stating that "This game is fun! This game is Awesome!! Best Co-oop ever!", but none of them give you any details at all. I see some that do, but it annoys me that they put up a 'release' video that has multiple reviews doing just what I hate. Don't get me wrong though, I do love the idea of showing the communities love for a game by putting their name on the video, but at the same time it's bad. I'll get to the point though, the review of the game via pro and con list.
Pros:
The game is 0.99c.
It has co-op in so many ways.
It has pvpve.
it has hordes of dinos.
It is satisfying to kill a bunch of dinos with a big gun/tank.
There are lots of weapons.
Conquest mode has a very interesting concept.
It has the old announcer styled "Double Kill, Triple Kill, ect".
Cons:
There is a bug that allows your "Private" server to become a public server without warning.
There is no way to change the audio for the Dino's seperately from the other audio so if your game volume isn't low the T-rex will kill your ears.
For all the guns, there are really only about 10 you will ever use.
If one person is killing all the dinos they get all the money, and can share it, but usually won't since the good weapons cost so much.
Getting a tank is a savior just as much as a death wish, as you can die in seconds to anything larger than the acid spitting dinos.(T-rex, stega, ect.)
Getting stuck on spots is very likely.
The tank's machine gun is ear♥♥♥♥♥♥much like the large dino roars.
The Mech is awesome looking but will die even faster than a jeep without a gun will.
There are turrets, but they only last for 60seconds.
They have an apc that does tons more damage than the tank, and has seats that are supposed to allow passangers to shoot from, but they do not, and it has a main gun that was apparently taken out so the main weapon has a non-functional cannon on it now.
The most viable way of killing dinos is running them over, but that will get you far far far less credits so you will be less useful versus large dinos.
There are still other bugs that have not been adressed.
Controllers still do not function properly with the game.
The new update has brought in even more bugs than before it seems.
This is supposedly the 3rd time the game has been 'redone' or whatever they would like to call it, and the ammount of change is so pitifully small that it's not worth mentioning.
So after putting all that in, I'll say this for my final words. I have played the game quite a bit, I'm lvl20+, which I didn't put as a pro or con because I didn't think of it as especially one or the other. I have used most of the weapons except for a select few that I just have not wanted to use at all. I've played all the co-op maps so far for survival and conquest. I can say this from my experience. I would not pay 99c to play this game. It is fun for a short while, but after you get frustrated with it, and after you realize how buggy and glitchy the game is. You and your friends will quickly move onto other games, and the fact that they have renamed it(for reasons I didn't look into as I didn't really care.) along side pricing it at 99c now, makes me feel like they have possibly given up on fixing anything with it, and just want to squeeze this lemon for it's last drops of juice. They put out a fancy trailer that recognizes the positive short review from the community, and left it at that.
So I say keep your dollar, and buy something else. This game will most likely rot in your steam library like it has mine. It has become that game that me and a few friends play for about 1hour every 2-3 months then forget it again because we hate the bugs and glitches.

I've spent far too much time in a single night playing this game. It's unfinished right now, still having some placeholder art and more things being added, but the core is there and it's a blast.
There are two main components to the game - rhythm and pattern recognition. You'll need both to survive this game. The first is simple, just stay on the beat and you'll be fine. The second is the trickier one and more important one in my opinion. Each enemy has a defined movement and attack pattern, and you need to slip in at the right time and attack when you won't be hurt. Sometimes it's easy, like with slims that only move up and down, or skeletons who raise their hands before attacking.
Sometimes, it's trickier. Mushroom people who throw out AoE attacks. Dragons who move every second turn, or bats who I have yet to figure out the pattern for. Of course, if you get bit by a bat, it's likely not such a big deal, but missing the dragon could get you clawed or charred, a one turn death.
There's no "gotcha!" kills to this roguelike, though plenty of dying to do as things get frantic and you fail to keep up, misjudge the enemy attack pattern, and suddenly find yourself cornered, and you'll do more than a little dying as you learn the patterns of some of the more dangerous enemies.
Rarely frustraing, lots of fun, occasionally repetitive due to the single assigned song per level - hopefully this increases. The rest is headed in the exact right direction.

Don't let my played hours fool you, I launch the game through a mod manager and so steam doesn't record my hours. I'm now a little over 4000 hours in this game, and still going. KSP plays like a flight sim, a management game, and a spaceship building game all rolled into one.
There are 3 modes, Sandbox, Science, and Career.
Between the different mods, online resources, and game modes, you can pretty much play KSP however you want.
Do you like building space ships, but don't like flying them by hand or managing money? use the mechjeb mod and sandbox mode.
Can't build for crap but love flying? kerbalx spaceship repository has your back.
you can play KSP how you want, it's totally open ended and down to your creativity.
the real benefit is it's physics. KSP models physics in such a way as to be relatively realistic, but also approachable.
Sure, that plane would NEVER fly in the real world, but if its center of gravity is behind it's center of lift, it's going to flip just like it would in reality.
the game progression feels pretty natural, and worthwhile.
highly recommended, probably one of the few games I own that could get a 10/10 even with their current bugs and limitations.
I'd buy this game again at full price in an instant if I ever needed to.

Pros:
-Wide room for adjusting your difficulty, from "only know how to press space" to "landed on Eeloo with 1 SRB."
-The fact that there is a mode that hooks you to collect more science and one for those who realistic management.
-So long as you have the know-how, you can get to any celestial body, and explore the surface of all except 2 (Jool & Sol)
-Modding community is amazing. You want more parts? Just drag a folder in. This just adds to it.
-You can adjust your resources accordingly, useful if you're using more than one source of fuel and need to balance.
-Aerodynamics provide both a challenge and a nice system to screw around with.
-There is no acheivement/medal, other than your own work and design. Land, or don't, you've still done something.
-The game is one big puzzle that you will never solve, and yet you'll always think that you'll have a "best craft/mission."
-Community is here for the game, and not fantasizing over a Youtuber/Streamer. They're generally optimistic people.
-Replay value is truly infinite. There is always another thing to do or another way to do an already accomplished mission,
Cons:
-The science system needs a slight amount of tweaking on Kerbin. This is just a personal view.
-The physics can rarely become ridiculous, but 95% of the time, its your doing, and not the games/computers.
-As much landmarks as there are already (won't spoil,) It seems to be lacking just a bit. This is also a personal view.

There are 12 tracks, and they all have a unique theme. Pretty to look at, but you don't have much time for that in this game.
It's extremely fast-paced. Stop for a second and you're going to lose.
There are a few shortcuts/alternate routes on (some of?) the tracks, but they're not the main point of the game. If that's what you love about boat racing/Hydro Thunder, then you won't really find much here.
But no, one of the main points of the game is to memorize and pull off cool stunts in the air to gain boost to go faster and beat your opponents. (In some cases, the clock is the opponent as well)
There is a TON of customization for your boats. Basic stuff like paint, upgrades, etc, but still, quite a bit of customization. So if you're into that, then I can assure you, it's on full display here.
The career mode is simple. You just play the various events, try to do your best, earn 1-3 stars per event, and use those stars to unlock further events to complete your career.
There's a time trial mode, and if you are a big nut for that kind of thing (like myself) then this game will offer endless replay value for you. Gotta keep trying to shave off a hundredth of a second here, another hundredth of a second there, and so on...
There's also split/screen multiplayer for up to 4 players! That's a fantastic feature that virtually no PC games have anymore. (I think) it only allows controllers in split/screen mode, though, so be prepared to gather up all your controllers, heh.
The online multiplayer is fun. I hope a lot of people end up buying this game, because we need to have more consistently full (6 player) matches! 1v1 can be fun but that's not how I want to play online boat racing. :(
Last, but not least, we have the controls...
They're OK. I'm used to games like Hydro Thunder, Split/Second, Burnout, and so on. The controls in this game aren't quite as... tight? responsive? as you're probably used to. You just have to hold down a bit longer than most games to get a tight turn. The track design plays OK with this kind of control, though, so it's pretty much all good. The main thing is just you, yourself, getting used to the controls. After you do that, they're fine.
Overall, I'd say 8.5/10. It's boat racing with a huge emphasis on tricks and boost, not too much else. Made originally for mobile devices, so it's not a very complex game with crazy twists and turns and huge variety, BUT it's still a very good game. Well made, fun to play for a while (especially if you like multiplayer or time trialing), and so on.
The game has a nice style and charm to it, but I'm a huge boat racing fan so I may be biased. You'll have to try it for yourself.
For $10 dollars ($7 during launch week) I consider it a steal, but that's just me.
I can't wait to see Vector Unit's next game! :)

MURI is as close as you can get to having a Shovel Knight or Cave Story for DOS platformers. Like the latter two, MURI takes old school aesthetics and mechanics and gives them a modern level of polish and accessibility while still being challenging. It's an excellently executed game from the creator of games like Garden Gnome Carnage and Iji.
Pros:
+ Authentically emulates the sights and sounds of DOS-era platformers.
+ Simple, but slick controls. I always felt like I had my character flawlessly jumping and shooting enemies. Shooting while moonwalking is a welcome addition.
+ Great level design. Each level feels distinct, has multiple pathways and is filled with clever secrets.
+ Tons upon tons of secrets for each level. MURI encourages exploration and completion for each level, showing when you have achieved 100% for each one. The secrets are well-hidden but gives enough of a hint to uncover them.
+ Fantastic pacing. MURI always knows when and where to throw enemies at you while giving you just the right amount of firepower and health to do so.
+ An interesting attempt at a complex story that juxtaposes well with the era it tries to emulate.
+ A female protagonist who's also a mother. You can never have enough good female leads.
+ Great boss battles. Each one tests the limits of your skills and make excellent climaxes.
+ Great value for about 2 to 3 dollars.
Mixed:
/ Inability to switch between weapons removes some choice, but it also keeps you from hoarding them, forcing you to adapt to any new weapon you get.
/ MURI makes an admirable attempt at a story that juxtaposes well with the DOS aesthetic, but unfortunately it ends up as difficult to follow.
/ The game takes about 2 to 3 hours to finish, but those 2 to 3 hours are so fun that you won't regret enjoying it.
Cons:
- Lack of 60 FPS. The max you can have is 32, but this doesn't detract from the gameplay at all.
- Somewhat short. It can be finished in about a few hours, but those few hours are very well-spent.
- Deserves a level editor.
Verdict: If you loved DOS games like Duke Nukem, Halloween Harry or Commander Keen, or you just love action platformers, MURI is right up your alley.

So, I don’t think this game is for everyone. I enjoyed it a lot, mainly because I really liked the car handling. I actually feel this might have the most enjoyable car handling in all of the open world games out right now, it reminded me of the old Driver games.
That was the best part of the game for me, driving around and exploring the city. Again I think this may have the best and most immersive city I’ve seen in terms of the actual layout and building architecture. It’s also a unique city for once and not just another recreation of New York that we’re all tired of. New Orleans (New Bordeaux in the game) has a nice variety of different districts and swamps that make it really fun exploring and taking in the sights.
The other thing I loved is that there are loads of enterable locations, restaurants, warehouses, houses, derelict houses, some public buildings, a church. GTA V could learn a lot from this, that had like f*cking 6 buildings to enter, where here it’s a lot more, I didn’t count but it’s like 50 to 100 enterable locations.
But that’s kinda where the praise ends. This has one of the most repetitive mission structures I’ve played through. All the missions play out exactly the same, go here, take out everyone stealthily (if you can) and then kill the gang boss. There is no variety to it at all except for the fact that it’s all in different locations. I tell a lie, there’s a few main story missions that deviate from that formula, but they are few and far between.
Since they patched it, the performance has improved a bit, they also fixed the weather so it behaves normally now and doesn’t feel like sunrise and sundown is sped up at 5 times the normal speed. It still doesn’t run that well though, so….
The game was rushed out though, some of the side missions are glitched, or show you can do them when you can’t, so you drive down to collect a truck to deliver, following the marker, and upon  arrival f*ck all is there. I completed all the missions in the game but it still shows that 2 aren’t finished for me cos the games bugged.
There are also small things that are unfinished, for instance a story mission building has these water fish tanks and these side wall pillar tanks that you can shoot out and shatter….but there’s no fish or water in them! And that building wasn’t under construction or anything, so there should’ve been some Nemo’s and Dory’s swimming around. Also there are shops, bars and supermarkets you can enter but can’t buy anything from.
Some people were praising the story, which I don’t really understand. It’s a generic revenge tale, where you just go around and systematically kill everyone. The writing and actors performances are top notch, but the actual plot is generic action fodder.
I guess where it deserves credit is the depiction of 60’s era racism. I’m not American, I didn’t live through the 60’s and I’m not black so I couldn’t tell you how spot on it is, but playing as Lincoln Clay you get to witness the discrimination and overt racism that only minorities usually get to experience. If you enter certain shops or bars people attack you, cos they have signs on the outside saying whites only and no coloreds allowed and sh*t. Also, every single cop you see in the game stares at you when you just walk around the city without doing anything, profiling you.
You can speed past the cops in a car though, going 120 miles an hour on the wrong side of the road and they won’t chase you, which goes back to this game being only half finished. Even when they do chase you it’s fairly easy to lose them.
Overall I would only really recommend this if you enjoy exploring open world games. I got it cheap, 50% off so I don’t regret buying it, but if you want a challenge gameplay wise then look elsewhere, I put it on the hardest setting and I breezed through it, there was no real challenge to any of the repetitious missions, and bear in mind that’s the WHOLE game, so you’ve been warned my fine feathered friend.

Aragami is a third person stealth adventure where you play as an undead assassin that has been invoked to seek vengeance.
You have been summoned by a girl with the purpose of infiltrating the army of light, and setting her free. Armed with your sword, and abilities to control the shadows, you must use your wits and powers to stay out of sight as you delve deeper into enemy territory. Whether you want to slay everyone that stands in your way, or move through the shadows completely unseen is entirely up to you.
The game reminds me a lot of Mark of the Ninja except it’s in 3D, and has co-op capability. Using any of your shadow abilities consumes shadow essence, so you can’t just spam them until your heart’s content. You’ll need to stick to the shadows to regenerate your essence, and avoid the light that drains it. Being able to teleport to the shadows, and violently stab as many enemies as I could was super satisfying. You can avoid enemy attacks if you’re quick enough, but you will get one-shotted if you aren’t careful.
The AI was decent for the most part, and they would sound the alarm if you got sloppy. Leaving bodies around was usually how I got caught, so I do wish there was a way to move the corpses. Later on, you get the corpse vanish ability, so that helps a lot. I played using the mouse and keyboard, and while the controls lack customization, the default bindings still felt natural and responsive.
There is also some exploration to find scrolls that award upgrade points. You can unlock 6 different activated abilities, however, you can only equip one at a time. You’re also limited to having 2 charges for each ability, but you can replenish the charges by visiting a shrine.
The game took me about 7.5 hours to finish, but I got stuck on a couple of levels when I was trying to do perfect runs. I’d expect people who are better at stealth games than I am could complete it quicker. Aragami is a solid stealth game with fun to use abilities. Whether you want to kill your way through the enemies, or sneak by undetected is entirely up to you. The AI could be more aware of their surroundings, but overall, it’s an enjoyable game. I’m completely satisfied with the purchase, and recommend it to anyone looking for a good stealth game.

Fallout Shelter is yet another great design by Bethesda that incorporates the survival in a post-apocalptic wasteland into a tycoon/simulator style game. There are countless hours of gameplay included, frrom desigining your own Vault, to exploring abandonded buildings that come across you while in the wasteland on a pure luck basis, I can easily see how people have devoted hundreds of hours into the game.
The way the tycoon progresses, with so many different options to choose from and full control over your own Vault, really makes me want to play more. It might not be very fun to sit down at it for over 2 hours at a time (unless you have a ton that you can do on the game) but it's a great time-killer or one of those things I check every few hours to see how my progress is going.
If I had to suggest one thing to the game developers, I'd have to ask you to place a timer on the buildings that you add in. It ruins the immersion to just magically have a power plant appear out of nowhere, and having a 1-24 hour timer on everything you can build would seem great. Another thing that I'd like to see implemented in the game is the ability to spectate your exploring wastelanders. It would take an immense amount of time to create and code, but overall I think the experience of seeing that fugitive slave who needed to be patched up would help the game seem a lot more enjoyable and realistic.
Lastly, I'll throw in the pay to win aspect. There are many purchases that you can make to help aid you, from lunchboxes, to nuka cola bottles, and while sometimes the game can require a lot of idiling and it will help a great amount if you purchase these items, you will do just fine if you do not purchase anything in the entire time you've played the game. I'd do it only to support the developer as there's no point in boosting something taht you can just awit overnight or go to work and come back to have it done.
Final words: please give this game a try. It's a great entry level game, it's a great time-killer. It's simple, runs great on a bad computer, and I promise that you will find some kind of enjoyment in building your own Vault.

I'll give this game a thumbs up because it sets out what it means to do - scratch that Fallout itch with a light-hearted take on this fallen universe.  The mechanics are simple and easy to learn within minutes, the dialogue is funny, and the art direction is colorful and fits Fallout lore, albeit repetitive on the quests.  It's great to pick up and play for just a few minutes.
The game does have its problems however.  I already mentioned the repetiveness of the quests and the combat is painstakingly SLOW at times.  There is almost variance to the enemies you'll defeat - get used to killing a lot of radroaches, mole rats, raiders and the occasional rad-scorpion.  I would be remiss not to mention that even though it is free to play, there really isn't a way to push through the game very quickly without spending some dough on nuka cola quantums and lunch boxes, which don't come cheap.  And getting all the legendary characters, weapons and clothing?  Forget it.
Still, if you like Fallout then this is certainly worth dabbling and having some fun with it.  If I wasn't into Fallout myself, my review might be a bit different.

On the negative, the combat system can be abused using  your special powers and you can easily wipe out everything from swarms of enemies to bosses without taking a hit simply by spamming the corkskrew attack through the air with your special power.  While the combat is more challenging at the beginning of the game, it loses that challenge as soon as you discover how to abuse your abilities.  The crafting system can also use some work being far too difficult to gather all the needed resources unless you buy them from the store.  But this is no problem because you seem to have an endless quantity of money, at least more then you need.  While I haven't finished all aspects of the game such as getting all the stars in arena or finding all the hidden chests, I followed the story to it's conclusion which is dramatic and well worth playing through to get, but it isn't a game I would pick up again for a few years unless I wanted to hear the story again.  Would I recommend the game?  Certainly.  The story alone is worth the price and it had it's moments of tenderness but facing the harsh brutality of the facts of life.

The Dark Eye: Chains of Satinav is a point-and-click adventure game that is the prequel to Memoria, as you play as Geron, the "birdcatcher", in his tale as the hero of Andergast.
I can't really say much without ruining the very indepth storyline, but this is a very fun puzzle-like adventure game incredibly similar to the playstyle of the Secret of Monkey Island series.  It is both artistically beautiful and creative, with a calm and soothing soundtrack, and a fantastic storyline.
Kids of the 80's and 90's will surely love this game, as it brings back a sense of nostalgia, yet it managers to cater to younger and older generations as well.  This game is well worth the $20, along with its sequel--although I highly recommend you play Chains of Satinav beforehand, as it really sets the foundation of this brilliant story.

Haven't gotten very far into the game, but there are a few things that I dislike immediately.  I use a PC, not an Xbox controller, so I'm immediately at a disadvantage.
First, the key definitions are completely different thant Witcher 1, and they are fixed (at least as far as I can tell), so you need to relearn them.  Some of them are the complete opposite, which really messes with trying to survive to get through the intro.  Plus, you cannot go into "options" and figure out what a particular key binding is.  You need to back out of the game completely, or tab out of it and pull up the help PDF, scan through it to find the matching key, and then go back into the game so that you can do something as simple as "sheath sword".  It used to be TAB.  Now it's the Zero key.  Yep, that makes sense.  Most of the other key bindings are equally insane, like they were thrown out there randomly, with no UI/CUA planning and definitely no QA testing.  If it were tested, someone would have said, "You know, changing everything around is really going to confuse people.  Maybe we shouldn't do that."
Next, this game, like many others in recent history, includes the new QTE (Quick TIme Events) for such things as brawling and so forth.  Letters pop up for a split second at random points on the screen, making it difficult as hell for those who are actually trying to pay attention to the opponent and actually win the fight (or those with vision problems).  You have to hit them in the right order to make the character survive the event, but because they appear at random places, you have to change your focus all over the screen in order to find the silly blinking letter.  It would be one thing if A or S meant "Left Jab" and you had to judge when to use it, but there is no binding to a particular function, it's just key mashing when the particular letter pops up on the screen.  This makes this game, like Tomb Raider, completely impossible for those who don't respond well to this kind of mindless action.  QTE's take all the skill and fun out of the game... and there is no way to get around them without repeating them 50 times until you finally manage to hit the right buttens enough to survive.  Great going there, folks.  You've destroyed a perfectly good game.

KSP is by far the most enjoyable game I have played to date. It is widely accessible and incredibly versatile. My six yr old nephew can enjoy himself by building and launching rockets and watching them explode without a care for the extensive intricacies of the game. I, on the other hand, can spend hrs optimizing a spacecraft's efficiency, gathering science to unlock the tech tree, and exploring moons and planets.
I also appreciate the active community the game has engendered. You can share vessels with friends, and various mods are available (and frequently updated) that help personalize the gaming experience. I do recommend playing the original game without mods just to get a feel for how the developers intended the game to be played. This way it keeps things simple early on, so you can focus on how to play the game and not get bogged down by 1000 different moving parts and complex automation. At some point, you will likely become increasingly frustrated as I did and begin to search out mods to make your life easier.
One aspect of the game that surprised me, and that I sincerely appreciate, is its STEM teaching potential. This game is an excellent option for parents desperately searching for a non-violent or educational gaming experience. KSP has been used in classrooms, and the developers have made it available to educators at a reduced cost. It's so effective; children don't even realize that they are learning the fundamentals of physics and orbital mechanics because it's just that much fun. The game also fosters a passion for scientific research and space exploration. Yes, it is a game at heart, but it can be so much more.
As with all games, my interest seems to ebb and flow. This game is no exception, but the high replayability makes me excited when I come back to it. Sometimes I will start the career mode all over again because I know I every spacecraft I build will be different and I will be exploring new places.
I cannot recommend this game enough, 10/10.

As a massive fan of Tenchu, I was super excited for this game and I have not been let down.
Aragami is a stealth based, third person adventure game that involves the use of shadows and has a very unique art style that I would compare to Mark of The Ninja, if it was 3D. While Aragami doesn't do anything too revolutionary in terms of stealth, it does stay true to it's Tenchu inspired design, and it plays very nicely. The AI is that classic blend of smart enough to be annoying but dumb enough to make stealth work like it should, the animations are beautiful, and the upgrades, while semi limited, offer some variation to the gameplay. I think this is probably one of the two best indie titles put out this year, only rivaled by Furi. The company behind it is new to the scene, and worked with a limited budget to create the most Tenchu reminiscent game I've played since Tenchu Z.
If you're a fan of stealth games, or ninja/feudal japan based games, give Aragami a shot. It's worth your time.

I remember being a teenager, spending hours with my friend playing the original Natural Selection, and loving every minute of it.  NS2 has taken the advice of its player community and updated its game without losing the charm and required level of skill of the original, and whether you're playing as a marine or an alien, it is always a unique experience.
Pros -
1) Fast-paced, skill-based combat (seriously, the learning curve is pretty steep, so be prepared to get annihilated by a good player who knows how to use a Fade or Lerk)
2) Entertaining evolutionary system for aliens and divergert upgrade paths for both factions.
3) Zero recoil on weapons (reloading at the wrong time will, however, lead to some very bad times)
4) Infinite replayability.
Cons -
1) The player community will be the first to tell you - this game is rife with skilled players stacking together on one team or the other and leading to heavily imbalanced (and often unenjoyable) matches.  This has been a problem for literally 100% of the games history, and it is basically canon now.  Expect lots and lots of team stacking.
2) Noted as a "Pro", if you're not a very skilled FPS gamer, the skill curve in this game can be considered as a "Con", and many players simply cannot master the higher alien lifeforms and will generally stick to "Gorging" (the builder class for aliens), or defending bases as a marine.
3) The game has a built-in voice communication system which - depending on the server you're playing on - can be a blessing or a curse.  Just like in every game (particularly FPS games), allowing anonymous strangers on the internet the chance to communicate with others will inevitably lead to some idiots creating a negative vibe in some of your games.  Be prepared to mute a lot of jackasses.
4) With a few major exceptions, there are very few active servers when compared to other FPS games, so you will find yourself spamming the refresh button on the server browser and filtering your game lists to find the populated games often.
Overall, nostalgia has kept me playing this game, and it's definitely one of those "why not!" games you'll find yourself loading up when you're bored and you've got 30 minutes to spare.  Finding a good server to play on and making a name for yourself with its regulars will be the difference between enjoying and hating this game.  I'd give this game a 7/10, and I'd rate it higher if/when the developers figure out how to fix the imbalance and poor server quality.  Better servers = More players = More servers = More fun!
