A Myst-like game in an omnipresent 2001 a space odyssey atmosphere. This review is about the RE version.
I am surprised that this game has so few reviews with many negative ones. Except for the voice acting, I found that it was quite an impressive and enjoyable puzzle game. The story was pretty interesting and directly inspired from 2001.
You are an astronaut. While working outside your space station, you see an enigmatic black cube floating close by.
Intrigued, you leave the safety of your station, trying desperately to catch it. Finally reaching it, you find yourself low on oxygen, unable to go back to your station. You lose consciousness, and wake up on a mysterious alien spaceship, named the ark by a previously rescued astronaut. Having no idea where you are, you start following the notes he left everywhere, trying to uncover the secrets of this spaceship, and maybe find a way to go back home.
To advance in the game, you have to solve a wide variety of puzzles (not one puzzle is the same). For this, you will need to read everything you find, and pay careful attention to your whole surrounding. Like Myst, Rhem games and the like, you will have to take notes. I never took so many screenshots in a game. Clues are just everywhere and can be anything. I had a lot of fun solving the puzzles.
Puzzles complexity is diverse and ranges from easy to impossible (for one puzzle).
Be ready to do a lot of trials and errors to solve some of the puzzles. Persistence is a requirement.
There is just one puzzle at the end that is way too hard to figure out by yourself.
In addition to the alien spaceship, you also have the possibility to explore two planets (and a satellite).
Because of the wide diversity of the environment, every rooms, places are different, you never get bored, and are just curious to see where you are going to explore next.
There are also two possible endings to choose from.
The background music also fits nicely with the surroundings.
The only thing I did not like was the voice acting, which I found pretty useless. An option to disactivate it would have been most welcome, or was there? There are two voices in the game, the previously rescued astronaut diary voice, and an AI voice (from your space suit?).
First, I did not see the point of having to hear the astronaut voice everytime one clicks on a section of his diary. It's more distracting than anything else, since one reads faster than the guy talks. Also, if you make the mistake of clicking twice on the section you want to read, the reading voice will start twice simultaneously...
So, I ended up turning off the sound while reading the diary. And just so you know, you cannot skip the reading part because the diary contains many clues to solve the puzzles. I would recommend reading the story of the other astronaut anyway since it is necessary to understand the plot.
Also, I did not really understand the true purpose of the AI voice. Was it intended to give us hints, or simply to keep us company while being all alone on an unknown spaceship?
It could have been seriously improved, since most of what she said was pretty obvious or just made me feel like a small kid:  I find a scalpel, and the AI tells me "leave it here, you could cut yourself!"; I look over some handrail, and she tells me: "be careful not to fall!". Oh well... It would have been great if it could have been funny...
In all, while looking past the voice acting part, I most definitely recommend this game. Puzzles were fun, the exploration and story quite interesting.
I am looking forward to the next games of this developper.
-------------------------------
The game ran flawlessly on a windows 7 laptop. But here are a few glitches I encountered:
- Simultaneous reading voices can be heard if you click several times on the same diary section (you are not supposed to do that, but well I did it...).
- on Planet Kepler, in one of the houses, I first found a locked door with a keypad on the side asking to solve some mysterious equation. When I came back later to try to solve it, the locked door and keypad had disappeared. At their place was a shelf. I first thought it was a different house looking the same, but I looked everywhere and never found the first house again. If anyone has any hint about this first mysterious house, I would be interested to know.

- after advancing in the game, some objects previously found, reappeared (copper wire, dark rock, bird fruit) and could be then needlessly used again.

A pretty neat adventure game inspired by classic FPA games like Myst and RHEM. It lacks some of the polish that those games had, but still has an interesting story, beautiful environments, and some clever (albeit easy) puzzles.
Pros:
+Extremely good prerendered animations and screens
+Unique sci-fi story told through diaries and the environment
+Very nice soundtrack
+Most of the puzzles are good
Cons
-Puzzles are mostly very easy...
-...with the exception of one puzzle near the end which makes absolutely no sense. Even after reading a walkthrough, I still didn't understand it. (this was the only puzzle I needed a walkthrough for)
-The game lacks polish; most of the animations don't "line up" with the screens correctly, so they just suddenly cut and start which breaks immersion.
-On the subject of polish, I found a prerender which contains a texture that has a very clear watermark on top of it. This kind of stuff really shouldn't slip through.
-Many animations show the player character from the third person, and some of the screens are shown from camera angles that the player character clearly couldn't be standing from. This isn't a big deal, it's just one of my pet-peeves as it breaks immersion for me. If you take a look at RHEM and Myst, these games always remain in first-person and all of the prerendered stills are always taken from camera angles that make sense for the player to be standing.
Despite some of its flaws, ASA is still a great adventure game. Definitely going to be giving the sequel, Catyph, a shot after this.

"GameGuru the easy game maker, no coding required." Whilst this statement is true you will not get a really good interactive game without coding, for instance you get one door script which basically opens and closes a door with input from the player, if you want it to use a key you have to define it in the editor through the properties but if you want the player to know which key opens which door you have to edit both the key and door scripts ( coding ), using one door and one key would be a really dull game so you have to make new scripts for each key and the door it opens, actually you rename and edit the original scripts which is very easy to do and with a little knowledge you can get really good interaction, I made a video of what I discovered and all the doors, gates, cupboards, drawers etc. are controlled with variations of the original door script. See the "Game Guru Doors and more" video in my videos link at the bottom of this review.
Note:- Don't be put off by the need for coding though as you can get ready made scrpts from the store and on the forum.

GameGuru is a developing package that certainly allows even the most novice game designer to produce a playable game. As said it is a developing system so the facilities on offer will only get better and there will certainly be more of them. Its wisiwig interface is doing to game designing what MS Work did for word processing. Now the game designer can concentrate on the intricacies of game play and worry less about the complicated programming. There is a comprehensive scripting system in the engine based on the LUA language that the designer can use to enhance the engine although there are a great number of ready written scripts plus many from the excellent community (see below) available in the Store.
What makes GameGuru really stand out are two factors not found to the same level in  other game engines. The first is the Forums where a large bunch of users are always ready to help with any questions. This includes staff from the company that produce GameGuru as many of then seem to be enthusiastic users of the engine. Rather like the staff found in Games Workshop stores in the high street.
The second big factor is the army of third party artists that continually produce amazing models for use in the engine in all manner of themes, fantasy, war, Sci-Fi, cartoon etc.  I should confess at this stage to being a member of that group. Although this engine is first and foremost a First Person Shooter creator it is also capable of producing educational games that can test such areas as maths, English, motor skills ETC. I personally as an ex IT Teacher would see this as a tool for the school both in the production of software and a teaching aid.
Perhaps one of the most innovated uses of this flexible developing engine is demonstrated by a the third party model developers, Wizard of Id with his Isometric Dungeons pack that allows the creation of Dungeon Keeper type games.
As I see it this software can only go one way and that's up. Highly recommended

Great game. I waited patiently for the full release ever since I first saw the tech demo a long time ago, and I was not disappointed when the full game was released.
This is not a game that everyone will enjoy, especially not those looking for a fast paced quick fix. This is a game that takes patience and planning. However, if you do have the patience, the time invested can be very rewarding. It feels great to finally get that last load delivered after going through hell just to get to your destination, or having to pull a fully damaged vehicle out of a bog or water and then tow it to a garage because you have run out of repair points in your utility kit.
The game is even more fun when played with a couple of friends, especially if you all have a fridge full of beer so you can take a break after getting through some rough terrian and take the time to grab a fresh can and roll yourself a smoke.
The addition of the editor is a good direction for the game, allowing users to create their own vehicles. I wait with baited breath for a map editor now.
There are some quirks, such as only one player getting an achievement for finishing a map in multiplayer, other players trucks being ghosts when not in use, savegames (sometimes) breaking between updates, but these will be solved over time.
Some additions I would like to see made to the game would be: larger and more maps, more variety of objectives, earth moving equipment so you could repair tracks, changing weather and different seasons.
Overall I recommend this game to anyone who likes the idea of driving trucks through mud, water and rough terrain.

Spintires is an off-road driving game with an exploration aspect that also happens to be set in Russia. (I presume, at least.)
This game is for a very small niche market in a genre of games that is populated mostly by Gearheads and therefore has a very strange appeal. In short, this game is something not many people will intitally be interested in but I think many enjoy after having played it. This game is what I like to call my "Calming Game." That essentially means this game is one where there is no real urgency to it's gameplay, there is no rush (it's a slow game, you really
go fast) and there is no sort of time limit. The save feature in the game is also quite nice; there is no time needed to save, it's almost instant and the loading times are very short. This alows the game to be easily picked back up and allows one to really slow down and relax. Now, onto the Good, Bad, and Ugly sections.
TL;DR: This game is something not many people would like unless you like big trucks or off-roading. That being said, this is the best off-road driving game out right now and is very calm and relaxing to play. There are some great maps for it and the feeling of driving is tight but can be wonky at times. The camera is your enemy; he wishes to never allow you to see where you're going in order to slow you down. Overall it is a game that needs some more polish but is not far off from being a gem.

If you're interested solely in the idea of driving offroad through fairly realistic mud/water/rocks then this game does that very well.  It's not realistic to the point of being punishing but it does a good job of staying very far away from being arcade and it's satisfying to watch the simulated mud moving around as you drive through it.
As for the rest of the game...it's more of a tech demo...you can load logs onto a truck from 1 or 2 log locations on the map and deliver them elsewhere to complete an achievement...you can take a trailer load of 'garage' parts to 1 or 2 spare garage locations on a map to unlock them(this is where you repair and get fuel trailers/change tires/change equipment on the trucks such as the crane attachment)....and you can offroad to "cloaking" places that obscure your map view in the beginning.  Outside of those few tasks the rest of the content has to come from you....maybe you got stuck and switch to another truck to come winch yourself out....maybe you broke a truck or need fuel so you grab yet another truck to bring repair points/fuel to yourself.....or maybe you drove through the same spot a few times and now the ruts have made you stuck.  Things can be a bit more fun if you have a friend or two(not random people) to play multiplayer with so you can convoy around together.
Over all the maps seem to be a bit small at roughly 3kmx3km(can take a while crawling in mud) and the lack of any additional missions or non-player AI means the game really does feel like a tech demo and given the terrible relations the devs have with the community I bet it'll stay like a tech demo.........BUT that doesn't stop me from recommending it to anybody that wants to do some offroading from the comfort of their home.

This game isn't particularly innovative from a design perspective, but it really nails character and tone.
- The soundtrack is second to none. Its not just a collection of the biggest songs of the era, though there are plenty of hits to be found, but it also has a ton of wonderful lesser known tracks that give an excellent texture to the world. The game also has a couple moments that trigger specific songs, and I found all of those to be pretty effective.
- The world also looks great, and has plenty of variety, including backwoods bayou areas, neighborhoods both affluent and poor, city centers, and industrial areas. The weather and sunsets also look great,
-The other thing I like about the game is the way it addresses the issue of race not only in the narrative, but also in the gameplay. There are areas in the game where you can get away with less, and be viewed with extra scrutiny based on the fact that Lincloln is black. This also effects the response time of the police, which is an interesting variable.
-The characters and performances are well delivered. Lincoln and his lieutenants are all well written and performed. Especially good though are the old preacher to whom Lincoln goes for guidance and help, and the manic government agent who agrees to support Lincoln in his quest to take down the mafia.
All in all I think this is a very decent open world crime game. It might not be able to hang with the best of the genre (things like GTA V and Sleeping Dogs), but its totally worth playing. I know there are complaints that it deviates too much from the Mafia 1 and 2 formula, but as someone who didn't play those I thought Mafia III was pretty good.

It starts out easy.  It invites you to reach a little further.  It'll be fun.  You're almost there, just a few more tweaks and you'll have it, next time for sure.  It is fun.

ASA: A Space Adventure - Remastered Edition captured me from the very beginning. I launched the game for the very first time and was treated to perhaps the
menu screen to leave an impression on me. I've included a link at the end of this review of a video of the menu screen.
Now I'm sure everyone is wondering what is so significant about a simple menu screen, and I will confess that the menu screen alone doesn't amount to much in any game. However it was what the menu screen represented that was important. Here you have a space adventure game, essentially Myst meets 2001: A Space Odyssey, and the first thing I see upon launching it up is a cinematic reel with short scenes that feel like they could be from a movie like 2001: A Space Odyssey and a chilling song to enhance the effect. Before I have even hit the play button I'm already asking questions about what's going on and the air of mystery and wonder has already been created.
So the question remains, does everything after hitting Play stand up to this menu screen I'm raving about?
In short, in my humble opinion, yes, it absolutely does.
ASA: A Space Adventure is in fact very similar to Myst, a slightly modernized version but still very true to the Myst style. A mysterious black cube appears nearby your spacecraft and lures you out, the next thing you know you're on-board a mysterious ship named 'The Ark'. From then on out, you are left to sift through diary entries left by one Philippe Forte and other clues to try and piece together what has happened on the Ark.
What ensues is a well paced science fiction adventure that hits all the right notes and maintains a good balance of feeding you parts of the story while maintaining an air of mystique. I was particularly impressed with the puzzles in this game. If you played many modern point and click style puzzle games you've no doubt come across a few puzzles whose solutions just seem inane. While some of ASA's puzzles tripped me up for awhile, at no point did I find any of the solutions dissatisfying, and in fact I enjoyed the problem solving process very much in this game. For many puzzles, figuring out the solution requires walking around and finding clues and taking notes. I have about seven or eight pages of notes, diagrams, and solutions that I had to write out, I even used a piece of graphing paper for one puzzle. The fact that I had to take notes alone was very satisfying.
The story in the game is just as impressive as the puzzling is. I found that throughout the game there is always a feeling of mystery and wonder, there are always questions, even at the conclusion of the game (there is a sequel in the works as of this writing called Catyph). Alien worlds, alien races, a gigantic mysterious ship...it is most definitely a full fledged science fiction setting. I have mentioned 2001: A Space Odyssey before, drawing similarities to the mystery and oddity of it all, but I also got Interstellar and Stargate vibes as well from the story. Regardless of influences or similarities though, I definitely found the story was well told and was fused together with the puzzles very nicely.
There is, unfortunately, very few games like Myst in today's market, which I find a shame as it's the perfect medium for telling mysterious science fiction stories via a puzzle game. This game is superbly executed and remarkably imaginative, and it's a shame that it's such a hidden gem since it deserves so much more attention and consideration than it currently receives. Anyone at all interested in Myst-esque games
science fiction adventures should not hesitate to give ASA: A Space Adventure a shot, it's a pleasant and interesting experience that is well worth your time.

I don’t change reviews but I had the pleasure of getting more time with the program. That is pretty much the key, time.
The more you use it the more you can see what it has to offer. There are lots of hidden gems in there. The biggest program is understanding them. There is help out there, but it takes some work on the user’s part to find it. That might be the biggest draw back and that is not the program’s fault in anyway.
Yes there are parts that can use some help, but feedback from users goes a long way. Lee seems to listen to what is being said, and I can honestly say not all developers do that. In that, that is the strongest part. Developers that listen. It would be easy to “make the money and run” but Lee and his team are still here hard at work.
The lag factor
That was one of my biggest issues. There is ways around that. You need to tinker with stuff behind the scenes. Camera angle and resolution are your friends. Some grass types add a fair amount of lag. Tinker with the right settings and I pushed my FPS 12-20. Sure that took some time, but if there was better info on the settings I would have been able to zip through it much faster.
This program ends up being perfect for:
Someone that wants to get into game making
Someone looking to learn how things work
Someone looking to be a part of an active community.
Someone looking to help grow a program

ASA is a broadly "Myst-like" (i.e. first person puzzle-heavy) sci-fi adventure game. If you're a fan of exploration and puzzle solving (studying notes to decipher passwords, exploring the world's nooks and crannies, discovering mysterious contraptions and figuring out their purpose, etc.), then you're bound to love ASA. logical - a rare feat for any adventure game.
I'm a big fan of Myst-likes, and having played a whole lot of them, from the Myst series itself to Zork: Grand Inquisitor or the more obscure ones like Schizm or Obsidian, I can safely say that ASA's puzzles and atmosphere are among the best in this subgenre.

I previously played ASA when it originally launched on Desura. The game features a slideshow style presentation similar to games such as Myst in which you move forward image-by-image rather than free movement as in a shooter. Although this might seem like a turnoff to many players this method of presentation is really one of ASA’s strengths. It allowed the developer to create very photo-realistic surroundings for you to explore and ensure you see all the sites from the best angles. The result is a game that makes the world feel more real as though you could walk into it and well realized enough that you would want to.
Like games such as Myst, ASA aims to challenge you with difficult but logical puzzles that you may need to write out to help figure out the solutions. The puzzles feel very natural to the environment and although you may struggle to figure them out are very rewarding.
The story for ASA is one that I found very engaging. During the game, you will find journals left behind by a previous explorer. You will explore the adventures of the previous individual through these journals while also making your own and learning a little of the history of a rather fantastic place that you will get to explore.

I loved playing this game. The medieval setting is great, the imagery is colourful and immersive, and the plot is extremely well done, complex and multi-lateral. The game has no shame in throwing you right into the thick of the lore and plot line, demanding that the player be not only interested in progressing through the missions but also be actively involved in the political situations and racial tensions, forcing you to make decisions that dramatically change the plot and entire world constitution. If you don't like plot-driven stories, especially ones that demand a lot of understanding from the player, then this probbly isn't for you and you'll get a lot less out of it.
The controls are a step up from the previous game, making them a lot more like typical ‘point-and-attack’ (or in this case swing and slash) video games, although strangely enough the interface took me a lot longer to get to grips with that the first game. The graphics are great too, though even the lowest settings make my computer want to melt into a puddle of molten goo. The voice acting is also decent in general, though if I hear some Scottish speaking dwarf yell at me “go plough your woeemaaannn!!” one more time…..
All I would have to say in general is that the game would really benefit from a jump button. Having to click everytime you want to go up or down something can get quite tedious at times.

What it lacks in overall features as compared to something like Unreal DK it more than makes up for in its ease of use and excellent interface. Entity placement is pretty similar to the Arma 3 level editor. It's also a continuingly evolving piece of software with people in its forums who have been creating AI scripts and such which keep pushing its abilities further on a steady basis.  If you have no experience with game creation and no coding knowledge I would say this is a perfect place to get started.

Key points at the bottom.
For a game in beta it's severely lacking in content. It also has a weird crafting system which is very off putting. Most of the things you will want require materials that you can only get out of a chest that you only rarely get which is really impolite to players IMO. Whereareas in league/smite you can just grind your eyeballs out and finally get the much desired champion/god you want, in this game you have to do that, but you have no idea when you will really get that thing that you want. Yes you can earn some of the currency as a daily, but the thing is that no other game limits you in such a way and you want to know why? Because it means that time you spend in the game is stunted. When you learn how crafting works you will only sign in to do dailies or you may get frustrated by the fact you cant' get the items you need. This means that you're not gonna play the game a lot.
In terms of gameplay, the game is orcs must die. You have hallways, you put traps in them and you funnel the enemies through the traps. There are some problems with this though. For example a lot of the trap placement areas are limited. I didn't really see many oppurtunities to throw enemies off edges or into stage traps. Most of those things were set up in such a dopey way. Like they are guaranteed to go down a hallway so there is a stage trap set up, but it's set up in the way of your own traps which you could put one there if it wasn't there. Also they're not extremely useful and some of them are one time use which baffles me. I'd have to say this game is up there in terms of disappointment alongside dungeon defenders 2 where a genre tries to fit in with another and does it poorly in the F2P market. There's actually quite a few skins already, which doesn't make a lot of sense considering how little content there is. There's also lots of missing stuff from the game.
Normally I'd say 'ehn, it's still in development' but it's in beta and open beta at that which means 'near release' which means that content is lacking and will be lacking upon release. I sense this game will fall to the wayside in a similar fashion to dead island epidemic. I would hope not honestly because the game is decently enjoyable and the pvp aspect brings the game up a notch above Dungeon defenders 2 in flexibility, but this game has even less content than DD2.
I played both modes for the game and I found them to be about the same in the deparment of how much I enjoyed them. Possibly enjoyed siege more because it was something new, but I feel the offensive minion summoning could use refinement. The other problem I seen is that of my games played about half of them had one or more player simply DC. This is pretty annoying to get in a game so new and there didn't appear to be a way to replensih ranks when you are down players in a survival game.
TL:DR - Frustrating system for unlocking things and a lack of content mean this game may not live very long.
Key reasoning behind review:
-Crafting system is frustrating and will turn off new players and there isn't enough to unlock to satisfy long term players.
-There is less than average content in a game that is near release.
-The game lacks a certain level of depth the previous games had as there are not placeable minions and stage traps are lackluster at best.

Quick review:  This is "Getting Attacked by Endless Impossible to Hit Flying Enemies:  The Game"
Seriously.  I can still hear the constant, endless, horrible screeching of the most annoying flying enemy I have ever encountered in a game.  It's Cliff Racers from Morrowind all over again.  I actually have fun playing this game despite the bugs, poor balancing, and lack luster presentation.  It has charm, like B grade sci-fi.  But those flying what-evers kill this game for me.  The guns are so hilariously innaccurate that there is no way you can reliably hit them, forcing you to listen to their screeching while they peck away at your armor, bit by bit, harassing you to the point of insanity.  Yes, my entire problem with the game is not the enumerable other issues that so many point out, but simply the fact that I spend the entire match beset on all sides by what amount to Cliff Racers.  No one liked Cliff Racers.  Not even the devs that made them.
If you like Cliff Racers, this game is for you.  If you don't, then get the game when it's a dollar.  Still worth playing with friends.

In the interest of full disclosure I'll say that I got this game on sale for $42 during the Autumn sale. I also had to cheat because I am bad at video games. This will factor in later.
This game is a little hard to talk about for me because I loved it but everything people said about it negatively is true. There's very repetitive missions that lead to a bloated middle half of the game that for some can be an absolute slog to get through. Features like customizing cars from Mafia 2 are gone and yes if you want to get technical this doesn't make you feel like an Italian mobster. That said though I think the game is worth your money and I will elaborate why.
First of all, the missions are very repetitive. I personally didn't really care for all the missions where you'd have to damage a district's funds to draw out the underlings. I feel like they could have been conveyed better with one big individual mission where you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥up and get all the money damage from that one mission instead of isolated incidents where you whittle it away little by little. However, when I wasn't doing the damage missions, I had a blast. I loved taking over a location, giving the location a boss, watching their henchmen arrive in color coded vehicles, and seeing the locations turn from ♥♥♥♥♥♥ hellholes to nice places. That and the missions where you go after the district bosses were amazing set pieces with wonderful character defining moments. So really when I say the missions were repetitive, I mean only 1/3 of the missions really feel that way while the rest are pretty fun.
This is where I have to disclose the cheats I used. Or more accurately cheat singular because it influenced how I played. Remember way up top when I said I was bad at video games? Well this game was no exception because even on easy I died a lot. That lead me to look up a cheat table for the game and using the infinite health cheat. With that cheat, my gameplay style was altered. I could pick a stealthy approach -and I often tried my best to do so even with the cheat active- but if I just wanted to go balls out and shoot some racist ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s with a shotgun I totally could. With the cheat, the game essentially turned into a fun and frantic time where it may have been slower and more plodding or just not completed at all had I not cheated.
The story in this game is unlike this transition because it's actually good. Really good in fact. It's so good that even if you're not like me and hate all the missions, I'd implore you to play through it anyway just to see the story unfold. Watching it on YouTube doesn't cut it because even if you're spoiled to the story like I was, seeing it happen organically is a thing of beauty.
It does not make you feel like an Italian mobster but the thing is, you don't play an Italian mobster. You play as a black man just as the Civil Rights Act passed in the 1960's in the deep south and society is just as ugly as you'd think with some places still having "No Coloreds" signs up, racial slurs, and the KKK in power. You're a criminal and you kill untold hundreds of people but you feel less like a mass murderer and more like a revolutionary sticking it to the man and fighting the power. Every district I overtook in the game, I felt like I was one step closer to taking the power back.
The long and short of it is this. This game is a great game in the shell of a good game. There's sparkles of brilliance here that are held back by repetition but for those of you willing to look past it, what lies beneath is one hell of a journey. Buy this. I don't care what the aggregate review score says if you listen to one review I hope to hell it's this one and I am saying buy this with your god damn money.

Retro parody is more popular than ever, and while the style and trappings of NES and SNES games seem to be the most popular among retro parody developers, the style of the classic IBM MS-DOS games goes largely ignored. Enter MURI, a retro parody game made in the style of classic DOS games around the EGA era (roughly mid 80s to early 90s) complete with 16 colors, 16 frames per second (with an option for 32) and PC-speaker sounds. In other words, a real gem.
The gameplay is very similar to the original Duke Nukem which is similarly episodic with multiple weapons and even has collectibles in the form of floppy disks and joysticks. It's a very fun and refreshing kind of game you don't see anymore, even among indie developers. I found it to be a very enjoyable, albeit brief experience even with four episodes. And lest not forget MURI has a score system which is not found in games of this type anymore, so even if you beat the game there is some replayability if you like getting high scores, especially as there is a multiplier based on chosen difficulty.
Overall a pretty fun game, especially if you're old enough to remember when games came on floppy disks. And it's very low in price too.

Arrow Heads:
~~~~~~~~~~~
This is crazy what I am about to tell you! Did you know that a chook’s favourite past time is. . .  archery? That’s right, archery - and some of those birds (or so I’ve heard) are bloody skilful! Crazy, hey?! Nevertheless, from now on every time I see a bird, I’m going to check to see if he has a bow and arrow on his back (I don’t want to be a recipient of an arrow through the head!
Arrow Heads is a multiplayer online and co-operative game where you control a chook (at first) through frantic archery battles.

There are two modes of play in Arrow Heads: Arcade and Arena. In the Arcade, you can play by yourself or with three of your friends on the same screen. The goal here is to eliminate twenty-five waves of enemies or order to win. Bear in mind that you only have ninety seconds per wave to do so. The waves are filled with bears! Some will run at you in an attempt to hit and shock you, while others will be armed with bow and arrows, harpoons and other crazy weapons. In this mode you’ll only have three lives or three chances to beat twenty-five waves. Every time you kill an enemy, he will drop yellow coins. Pick them as fast as you can to fill the spin gauge. When it’s full, you’ll be able to activate it and receive a better arrow for a short period of time, or even an extra life if you have lost one!  Personally, I like the rocket or the tesla coil arrows, as you can kill your enemies quickly. There are only three maps so far for this mode, which is too few in my opinion.
The Arena mode is basically playing online against three of your friends. Here, the first chook to reach ten kills wins the rounds. The difference in this mode is that you don’t have a spin gauge.  An egg will drop from the sky here and there, with one special weapon, and whoever picks it up first can become the most deadly bird around!
At the end of each game you’ll earn some coins which you can use to purchase either new customizations for your character, or bows and arrows.
The gameplay is far better by using a gamepad. Use the left stick to move your character around and right stick to draw your bow. It’s not that easy at first, let me tell you! You can also jump and dash which can be extremely useful to avoid an incoming arrow and to stun an opponent (with the dash).
The cartoon-style graphics are fun and well done, and I really the singing bird tenor. In terms of the controls, I prefer to play Arrow Heads with a gamepad.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Fun cartoon graphics
-	Co-op and online game
-	Fun and easy to play when you get used to the aiming system
-	Achievements & trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	 Needs to have more maps, especially on the Arcade mode
Arrow Heads is fun, fast, and you’re going to have a ball playing either with or against your friends.

Symmetry is sexy… or so we’re told. We’ve been conditioned by eons of evolutionary pressure to equate a simple formula: symmetry=beauty. Our primate brains are built for symmetry, since a significant portion of our grey matter is dedicated to the detection of it. We can discern within fractions of a second whether an object is symmetrical or not. This has profound effects on civilization. Generally speaking, people with highly symmetrical faces have more self-confidence, get hired more easily, are judged by workplace superiors to be more productive and intelligent, get more promotions, make more money, get more… well, you get the picture.
And what does this teach us about ourselves? That we’re a society of shallow sycophants? Yes, but it also teaches us that we are hardwired symmetry seekers; that we can’t help but be blindly drawn to symmetry like moths to the electric bug zapper. *Pop*. Fortunately, us gamers have learned to subdue our symmetry seeking boner missiles, probably due to prolific internet pornography fappery; okay maybe not due to that, but whatever the cause, we’ve learned the hard lesson that perfect symmetry in videogames is
.
Thus, most competitive multiplayer games have at least a little bit of asymmetry. The devs add just enough differences to the teams to produce faction flavoring, or they place the teams in asymmetric roles (i.e. assaulter vs defender, King of the Hill). All of this is just dandy, and we like to call it “gameplay depth”. However, treading too far down the wrong fork in Asymmetry Lane can lead to the developmental shantytown known as Balance Patch City: a dark domain in the midst of a constant process of buffing and nerfing that can leave the local player community distraught and burnt out, a community who’ve in turn been reduced a collective of fetal positioned, thumb sucking man-children babbling random strings of capital letter text that include phrases like “GAME=BROKEN”, “NERFPOCALYPSE”, or (Christian Bale’s favorite) “WHAT DON’T YOU ♥♥♥♥ING UNDERSTAND!?”
Thankfully, Unknown Worlds Entertainment has utilized their excellent navigation skills and have expertly trodden the full length of Asymmetry Lane. Aye, they’ve fought through the mines of Moria, passed the silvery towers Gondor, simply walked into Mordor, scaled Mount Doom where they threw a sheet of papyrus scribed with the word “symmetry” into the fires at the heart of the earth (a purely symbolic gesture, of course), and rode a disfigured gryphon all the way to Asymmetry Heaven. The end result of this epic journey? Natural Selection 2.
NS2 smashes head-on two opposing forces featuring polar opposite combat doctrines with an effect more dazzling than the quark-gluon plasma spewing forth from the Large Hadron Collider. Scientists are still baffled by its success.
Within this game you will take on the role of the Frontiersman, a Trans-System Federation grunt in a future where a space-faring civilization has taken a little time away from mudane tasks like warping space-time and building Dyson's Spheres to produce something so incredible that it is rarely seen in Science Fiction: a recoilless assault rifle. Mind blowing right? What will you do with this deadly accurate weapon? Like any good Space-American, you’ll use it to shoot anything that moves during an extra-terrestrial first contact scenario of course! We wouldn't want such a relationship to get off on the wrong foot after all, so you’ll be using your stand-off ranged capabilities to create interlocking fields of fire while taking solace in the knowledge that the word "questions" was removed from the dictionary three centuries ago. Watch those corners, watch those corners!
Alternately, you’ll be playing as the Kharaa, a misunderstood biomass collective of intelligent bacteria that can morph into higher lifeforms. Since you hate being roasted by the wanton use of flamethrowers, you’ll be using your biomass to morph into savage creatures with hardened carapaces, regenerating flesh, and poison gas for flatulence. No, not the Addams Family. Your cast of characters will include such melee-expert heavyweights as Skulk Hogan, Lerk Skywalker, Gorge Foreman, Walker - Texas Fade, and the dreadfully hideous Yoko Onos. You’re built for the ambush, so dark corners and high speed maneuvers augment your offensive capabilities.
NS2 takes this first-person asymmetry gaming perfection and kicks it up a notch Emeril Lagasse style. You take ¾ cups of FPS and throw in ¼ cups of RTS and BAM! You’ve got a full cup of “omg I can’t believe this actually works, what sorcery have you conjured to mix oil and water!?” hearty gaming goodness. That’s right boys and girls, one of you maggots (term used figuratively if you’re a Frontiersman, but very, very literally if you’re an incubating Kharaa xenomorph) is going rise to the call and transcend your mere 1st person existence to actually take semi-omniscient command of this needless bloodbath. The rest of you… well, you get to play your favorite units from Starcraft; that’s right, the indomitable SCV and the expendable Zergling. So grab yourself a welding tool Jonny Rico and go build my resource extractors! (Welding just not cutting it for you? Worry not because the Mutalisk, Ultralisk, Goliath, and Firebat also make faithful but legally distinct appearances in this title.)
As the commander you have access to the full suite of typical RTS institutions. There's the top down view, resource management, tech trees, upgrades, deployables, the left click, and the all important right click. You'll have your hands full trying to wrangle the units at your disposal. Only now instead of your units following your orders with unconditional obedience, you'll have to guide them through the delicate process of helping them arrive at the conclusion that, yes, sacrificing themselves in a suicide assault is good for them. Look, "Offensive Pattern Picard Distraction Phallus 8-D" is good for you because it's good for the team. Oh you get it now? Good for you... now run along and die like a good little Redshirt. Kay thanks.
Fortunately for new recruits, there are players who've played 2000 hours of NS2 and can teach less experienced competitors superior movement skills, map awareness, and gameplay knowledge.
Unfortunately for new recruits, there are players who've played 2000 hours of NS2 and will stomp less experienced competition with superior movement skills, map awareness, and gameplay knowledge. Whoa, déjà vu.
The point of that "it's a good thing/it's a bad thing" dichotomy was to highlight the fact that NS2, like almost all other games, has a learning curve. This one is fairly steep, so as a new player prepare to be overwhelmed. However, please unbind your Ragequit button and stick this one out; you need to keep in mind that you've entered a digital world that has never before been executed so flawlessly. No, not even the beloved Battlezone from '98 managed to mix FPS and RTS with this level of finesse (although, if you're looking for an excellent singleplayer version of this experience, that classic gem is a must play for you). You are now treading in uncharted territory never before probed by the gaming populace. With a little patience you too can navigate your way to enjoyable and memorable gameplay experiences.
My advice to new players: stick close to the guy with the shotgun. Unless your a Skulk, then run, run away from the gun with the shotgun! No! Don't stop to look behind you, HES RIGHT THERE! KEEP MOVING YOU IDIOT!
The bottomline: if you haven't lived vicariously as an ankle-biting, wall-climbing zergling... then you haven't lived at all. Play this mother♥♥♥♥ing beast of a game!

I do recommend this game for those who love point-and-click adventure games, but with some BIG caveats. First off, most of the voice acting really is not very good. The lead character's voice is very monotone, droll, and sounds like he just woke up. Some of the secondary characters are done well, however. Also, some of the puzzles are really, really obscure. This game will probably be good for those who are vey experienced with adventure games, but I would not recommend this to newcomers because of the frustration that some of the puzzles will cause.
The biggest issue for me is the ending. That's not to say that I'm dissatisfied with the final conclusion, but the ending sequence was literally as brief as "... the bad guy was defeated, and the hero went back to his home." Wait, what? I can't say anything else without spoilers; but for all of the questions that were created, you get no resolution and no explanation. You get a brief statement of what happened (literally just two scenes) and the game ends. Maybe some of those questions get answered in the sequel ("Memoria"), but as a standalone game I cannot express how disappointed I am in how the endgame story played out.
Still, I have a soft spot for hand-drawn graphics, which make the entirely of the game. Most of the world is colorful and vibrant; and those areas that are bleak are indeed grey and miserable. The art in this game is nothing short of gorgeous, and some of the unlocked videos show how some of the backgrounds were drawn, giving you a new appreciation for how much work goes into the art direction of the game.
So, if you really like point-and-click adventures, this is worth your time. Just don't expect too much of an ending and don't expect a lot of humor. "Chains of Satinav" is a very dark game. If you are looking for humor, the "Deponia" games, also from Daedalic, are a much better choice.

At first glance I thought this was just a rip off of the classic DOS platformer Duke Nukum, the similarity is mainly cosmetic. MURI has many differences that make it its own game.
First, the protagonist is a chubby Martian chick. Second, you can't save, although the episodes aren't very long so it's not a big deal. Finally, the controls don't feel nearly as solid as good ol' Duke: jumping is very weird and takes some getting used to, since you have to hold the key to reach maximum height. It feels more like a limited flight, and if MURI had a jetpack it would make sense. But I guess on Mars you can somehow jump around corners. However once you get used to it, it works pretty well.
Overall it doesn't feel nearly as sold as the original Duke Nukem, which is a little disappointing. I was expecting a hard-chiseled DOS platformer that felt like an old Apogee game. However it's not bad but in the end it just makes you want to play the old classics again.

MURI is a 2D platformer in the style of old classic DOS platformers like Commander Keen.  As such, the graphics and sound are intentionally limited to fit the restrictions of an old EGA video card with only a PC speaker for audio.  The controls are identical to those of the first few Commander Keen games, with Alt jumping and Ctrl firing, and the arrow keys for movement.
It claims to support gamepads, but wouldn't recognize my Xbox 360 controller.  It may be looking for older DirectInput controllers, but I didn't test that.  Any method you have for mapping controller buttons to keyboard signals should suffice if you want to use a controller but it doesn't recognize yours.
Given the restrictions it's placed on itself, the graphics and sound are very good.  It has a fairly unique visual style, and a font quite reminiscent of classic DOS platformers.
I wholly recommend MURI on two levels.  First, to anyone who enjoys 2D platformers, it's a solid experience.  Second, to anyone who liked classic DOS platformers, it's very similar in graphics, sound, and controls.  Also, if you like this game and want more of the same style, look up the Commander Keen Complete Pack to find the first five games in that series.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a fast-paced action platformer with some light Metroidvania elements. The game tells the story of an amnesiac known as Dust and his journey to figure out his past. Along the way he'll have to save various people and help out villagers. It's not the most unique storyline out there, and it's quite predictable for the most part. The game has full voice-acting, of mixed quality. You can tell that these weren't actors all from the same studio as the quality between character can differ greatly. There's some good voice acting, some bad voice acting and some that's in between, though I have to give credit for an indie game like this to even have full voice acting.
Gameplay is where Dust truly shines. Like I mentioned earlier, this is an action platformer. You'll explore a variety of unique locales and fight hordes of enemies. Combat is easy to learn, with a fair amount of depth to it. Dust himself can slash enemies with his sword, and there's a fair bit of combos you can create. However, the unique part of the combat comes from the game's secondary character, Fidget. Fidget has the ability to shoot various projectiles, which when combined with the dust storm technique creates devastating combos. It's a fast, satisfying system and I had tons of fun trying to rack up high combos. 
There's some light RPG elements as well, you'll level up and put allocate points into stats such as HP and DEF as well as equipping various pieces of armor. These elements accomplish their job decently enough, but I wish the equipment you crafted and found throughout the game was a bit more unique. As you go through the game, the equipment you find in the latter portions is almost always strictly better than what you had before, there's no equipment with unique modifiers or properties to encourage different playstyles, which I feel would fit nicely with the game.
Exploration wise, the game takes it's inspiration from Metroidvania titles, though I'd be hard pressed to call it a Metroidvania. For the most part, you'll explore an area, which usually involves a combination of platforming and combat challenges. These areas are mostly linear, with the occasional secret that requires a power you'll get later. There's a couple of towns in the game as well, with NPCs that will give you quests. These quests range from fetch-quests, to ones that will require the player to fully search out and explore an area for their hidden secrets. The sidequests provide a fun diversion from the main quest, and I enjoyed completing them all. 
Graphically, the game is beautiful. The backgrounds are gorgeous, and everything is animated spectacularly and while the anthropomorphic character designs won't appeal to everyone, it's hard to say that the technical aspects about them are bad
Musically, there's nothing too standout, sans one or two songs throughout the game, but everything fits the game well.
Overall, I highly recommend this game to anyone looking for an action platformer to play

Yesterday I purchased a four pack and played this with friends... that is where this review's experience comes from and the questions I want to answer are these to follow...
1: Is this a noob friendly game ...
2: Does natural selection have a good community a few years later after its release?
3: Is it worth it?
4: Machanics of the game..
Lets start with the machanics ... #4 : Natural Selection 2 is a asymetric RTS/FPS hybrid that pits two different species against eachother to battle for resources in order to gain map control and better tech .  The Marines side is best for startes , its more streight forward and self explanitory. If you like call of duty or Titan fall than the marines will feel at home with you. As a marine you will need to dodge , strafe and jump often to avoid the bites of aliens and their pesky projectiles that will murder you VERY FAST! so dtay afoot. Each side has a commander who will order you the player to make and construct buildings and power nodes to expand your region of power ( Map control ) , early and mid game sentries are amazing to stop or mitigate a rush to an expansion if placed right by the commander. Late game Sentries add to the horde of your firepower so dont hesitate regardless of what players may tell you , sentries can still kill people in the end game.
Now the aliens side... as the aliens you must spread infestation and build structures as the commander , they play much like the zerg from Starcraft. The aliens have a few distinct species , the Skulk who is what you as a player will initially spawn as. Skulks are fast if used correctly so wall jump often to build up momentum and use your speed to do circles around the ankles of a exo suit or marine to kill them becuase skulks have very low health. Than we have the gorge , a pig styled alien builder who can make or brake the aliens flow of battle by placing mini turrets called hydras , walls called clogs , minions to assist and tunnels to move the aliens a great distance to where they or you may need to be. Continuing on we have the bird ( cant remember the bloody name ) , a flyer who is very fast and cna bite / shoot projectiles to kill marines very fast , great for taking out a straggler or two on your way to a base. And onto the Fade , an assasin with a lot more hp  , use the fades ability to travel insanely fast around marines , confusing and disorientng them as you tear them apart limb from limb. Finally... The ONO'S ... a ultralisk - ish feel to them indeed as these tanky titans stampede through a squade of marines like scissors through paper , their only rivals being the exo suit and grenade luanchers which cost a pretty penny for marines and commanders alike.
Machanics in a gist , Team work is a massive need so listen to the commander and do as he / she tells you becuase YOU are the unit of this RTS. Map control and aggresion are key to victory. A good marine with a jet pack can turn the tide of a infestation in a jippy with the commanders support , likewise a good fade can end a large scale assult in the right hands. Skill and stratigy combine in this game.
Now is this Noob friendly... TBH , in my experience it is rare to find players who wont vote to kick you for being a new player , as a rookie your name will be green until you have reached a certain number of hours played on the game. So its very noticable if you are a new player. Even in " Rookie only servers " veterans will join and the balance that was once there will dicipate into a one sided fight very quickly. So If and onlly if the community was larger than yes this would be noob friendly but as of now , the community is quite small.
Community : Is it good??? TBH in the few hours ive played I thought about going back to League of Legends becuase players here are very hostile to newer inexperienced players like myself. Only one server welcomed my scrubdubbery with open arms and there i learned how to play.
Finnaly is it worth a buy???? Yes! , even though the community of this game is somewhat toxic , if you buy a four pack , its great with friends and great when you can actually play an all rookie game when you start out. the tutorial explains a good bit but not all of what you need to know , there is a low learning curve to the game and if you enjoy fps games , this is a new twist on a genre thats been stale for some time.

While playing my first PVP match, me and my friend realized a few things. Since this is currently in beta, if you see your team losing, there is absolutely zero reason to stay in a losing pvp match. Furthermore this game will almost certainly never be popular, so even when it is released people will just leave. Now you might argue that this is an issue with any online game, and I would agree, but for a less popular multiplayer game with only five players on your team, constant leavers will just grind on your soul until you give up on the game.
The PVE, as you may expect, was fine, although playing with random people will be an excruciating experience. I HEAVILY reccommend playing with friends over voice chat, as other random people will constantly walk into your lane and build in awful positions, ruining paths and mazes.
This game should obviously only be played for the PvE. If you do so, the maze/wall mechanics feel like a nice balance between the heavy mazing of Sanctum, and the very simple walling off of lanes from dungeon defenders. It did not appeal to me, but this may be enoyable for you.
+PVE with up to four friends is the same fun, hectic experience.
+More heroes to play gives more variation.
-I do not foresee any future for PVP besides groups queueing up together to smash uncoordinated groups. It may be fun when these groups clash, but otherwise I believe the random people will slowly just DC from the game and leave one by one (this was the case in the games I played that it looked like we may lose).
-Admittedly I did not play for an extended period of time, but the Crafting system where you pick up materials from fallen NPCs to unlock/upgrade your traps looks like it may take a long time.
-If you gain 65 Hero crafting materials from dailies, and 25 from leveling, from dailies alone the process for a new hero (450) would require about 7 days of playing dailies. However, in my specific case, two of the dailies required playing 10 games on two different champions. After about 8-10 games I was getting bored for the day, since the base gameply is fairly repetitive. This means for semi-casual players, the grind to unlock your favorite champion you experience on free week rotation may be an arduous process.
Someone once said (I believe it was TotalBiscuit) that once a game starts charging money, such as microtransactions, the game should be considered as released. Seeing as the developers have no qualms about charging in the in-game store,  I will consider the main mechanics of their game complete, with allowances for connectivity issues. I'm kind of a first impressions person, and can determine in the first 30 minutes or so if I will enjoy the game. I preferred dungeon defenders over this game for a multiplayer TD experience.

I have held off on this review for a long time.......
There is good and bad to this one and I'm trying to be as fair and unbiased as possible.
Firstly the bad...
I would not recommend anybody buy this unless you have a huge amount of time and more importantly, patience and passion for this engine. I backed this software when it was FPSCR and it showed huge potential but now I cant help feeling it has lost its way.
The fact you could build a collection of levels with this engine, call it a game if you wanted to is true, but the real point is that you wouldnt want to in it's current state.
At this stage in the developement there should be considerably more function than at present, Scripting is an intensley frustrating experience, the full LUA function set has not been fully implemented, added to that what works once is not guaranteed to work a second time and that probably sums up the whole experience, inconsistency.
There are still no camera controls, and the ability to create new weapons or FP animations etc is in the hands of the directx gods.
The store is an equally frustrating experience and at times shambolic, linking Steam accounts with TGC accounts has been a dogs dinner from the outset, the recent changes in the monetisation of the store have put a cost to everything,  Devs who had provided free content are now required to charge for a majority of it, albeit minimal, a charge is a charge. Customers are also limited to a certain number of free downloads a month, so if you find a free item there is a good chance you would not be "allowed" to download it. A minimum spend has also been introduced, and to cap it all there are constant issues with obtaining the content you pay for.
Very sadly there seem to be common themes when issues are raised, 1) That has not been implemented yet. 2) You can always vote for that in the features list. 3) have you checked the file integrity in your Steam cache. (The sheer number of times I have been required to perform this function is beyond me, suggesting a more deep seated problem with the software.
The current love affair with directx model formats is limiting to indie devs, this was dropped by microsoft yonks ago and must be a hang up from earlier TGC products, Where is fbx & animations, (something of a standard with most other engines) ?
The engine currently, in my opinion, does not produce superior quality to the previous offering from TGC, First Person Shooter Creator, (now gone open source) although over time it almost certainly will, the current out of the box experience is basic and clunky it would be an almost impossible task to monetise a finished product made with GG.
The engine has also been adversley affected by what is described as an nvidia driver bug, it is commented that this affects other games, so while technically not GG's fault it has extended the frustration with this engine considerably, I  mention this because at time of writing it is still an issue to be mindful of.
The Good...
The developer is a superstar, he appears to have single handedly built this from the ground up, sadly as the business has grown his developement time has reduced with the need for ever more "meetings" according to his blog..
The support staff in the forums are nothing short of superb, they do seem to be left out in a information vacum from time to time though !
The real stars of this show are the community, I have enjoyed incredible support whenever I have asked a question, the level of devotion shown by many to the continued developement of this software is commendable, TGC are lucky to have this level of support. The volume of new material posted to the store is great as well as a good revenue stream for TGC, there is no ranking or feedback mechanism for purchases but hopefully that will come.
Sadly however I will be shelving GG for the foreseeable future, TGC really must start to look at thier product as a whole, not silos where different areas look after different bits where never the twain shall meet, after all as a customer all I see is one forward facing interaction between myself and TGC.
I commend the decision to put the future developement in the communities hands (to a certain extent), but I never agree with building on unfinished foundations, I would question whether GG should have been declared out of beta when it was.

I give this a 7 out of 10.
The art style is pretty distinctive and makes the game stand out from other adventure titles.  I personally liked it, though I'd imagine it's not for everyone.  I do wish the animations during the chat scenes were a little less stilted.  All of the lines in the game have voice acting, which is a nice touch.  The majority of the voice acting is decent, though some of them sounded like they didn't want to bother with it.  The puzzles start out in a very logical fashion and can be figured out easily enough just by following the clues the game gives you if you pay attention to what's being said and what's going on around you.  Unfortunately, in my opinion that changes part way through the game, roughly about the time you enter the fishing town.  Suddenly you'll find yourself wandering back and forth repeatedly between the same few screens over and over frustratedly clicking everything in your inventory and speaking to the same characters for a thousand times to get that one oddball thing you missed.  This seems to build up to an incredible degree near the end of the game with what I found to frankly be the most bizarre puzzle solutions ever.
When you reach the final "level", things get a little more straight forward again, but that's mostly due to the fact that you have almost no inventory and there's not a lot of things that are clickable or screens to move between.  In spite of this, I'd still say to give this a play through.  The story made it worthwhile in the end and I'm looking forward to giving the sequel, Memoria, a try.

A few more notes I want to mention as I've played this game more.
I've spent a lot of time on the single player. It's fun to play for an hour or two at a time no problem. It may seem boring at the beginning, but like most other wave-based games, the waves get more difficult as you progress through them. And that's what keeps bringing me back. As I mentioned in my original review, it does get chaotic.
It's true that this game's local multiplayer is what shines. If you're looking for a local multiplayer game, then this is one I'd definitely recommend. If you want a game you can still play even once all your friends leave, then this game offers that. If you plan on never touching multiplayer mode, unless you enjoy facing wave after wave of enemies, this may not be your type of game.
Original:
I had a blast playing this game!
It's still new, so I understand the lack of online community. I'm hoping that changes, because multiplayer is a blast. I played local multiplayer at a local Toronto convention and even facing off against random people there was awesome! It didn't matter than I always kept losing. How can you not enjoy getting shot and then flopping around trying to annoy the person who shot you and stopping them from getting the win?
In terms of the single player, I enjoyed it. Yes, it is similar to most other games that have waves of enemies coming at you, but the projectile aiming gives it a different dimension. Maybe because my aim isn't great, but the sheer craziness of it all was great. Power-ups are very handy in the multiplayer arena, but they've still managed to include them in the single player to give it some variety.
This is definitely a game I'll continue to play. I can play offline multiplayer and single player, and as the community grows, I'll be playing more online.

The field of PC platformer nostalgia is a bit of an odd duck. There just weren't that many options in the 16-color EGA era; Apogee and id Games, primarily. Still, the four-directional (if a bit clunky) scrolling and rich diorama-like scenery provided an experience unlike the console platformers of the time.
MURI captures the feeling of that era without its missteps; Daniel Remar puts all his skill at well-designed levels full of secrets and gigantic boss battles here. The player character's slowness and limited set of movements doesn't feel unfair, and the enemies are challenging despite their own constraints.
The game is definitely short, about an hour from start to finish. Like most Remar games, the true replay value is in trying to get the highest score at the highest difficulties, a challenge once again relevant in the Let's Play decade.

The recent years have seen the rise of "retro"-style games, which seemingly attempt to recreate the look and feel of old games. From this, we've gotten countless NES—er, "8-bit" style games, whether they were created to honestly bring back the feel of an "8-bit" game or just to have an "excuse" to give for horrible artwork. Yet, very few designers have ever done the same with other consoles—or old computers. Daniel Remar (the creator of Iji) adds to this niche with MURI, a side-scrolling platformer which takes after the first Duke Nukem from the DOS shareware era of 1991 but adds and fine-tunes many features to make it its own game. Everything here feels authentic, from the PC speaker sounds to the choppy scrolling (which can be changed to be smooth from the Options menu if you feel like it) to the EGA palette (nothing in the game uses any more than the EGA card's standard 16 colors).
But it's a fun game, too, with movement that feels more fluid than you'd think it'd be and a difficulty balance that feels about right. The levels are of the exploratory kind instead of a linear sort, and it feels great when you find the way to an item that seems just out of reach. It's a rather short game, though, with five levels for each of the four episodes (a touch of the shareware era), even if they get longer as you progress.
Overall, it's a successful return to early 90s DOS and good way to spend ~2 hours of free time. The $3.99 price tag doesn't hurt, either!

This game is very under rated (not even, Steam has Very Positive feedback).  One of the original RTS/FPS hybrids (the sequel of anyways) with a unique Alien vs Marine gameplay style.  Aliens can climb walls, run through vents, fly, and expand their biomass throughout space themed levels, while Marines use assault rifles, shotguns, mines, and ultimately large exo suits to combat the infestation.  Different rooms on the map have power sources, and resource generators.  You can tell who controls the area you're in just by looking at it, as Marines require power so it will be lit up and look like a space station, whereas aliens will typically take the power out and darkness and emergency lights take over, and the alien hive spreads a visual infestation throughout the corridors, similar to the Zerg in StarCraft.
For as great a game as this is, there sadly seems to be no more than a few hundred people at a time playing, whereas at one time (at least during the original) there would be thousands.

There are two notable
to the game, though:
First, it is short. There's no denying it. 6-8 hours just isn't really long when compared to the likes of Monkey Island, The Whispered World, etc.
The second problem is that many puzzles are of the famed "moon logic" as some adventure games unfortunately are.
Sometimes, you basically end up combining everything with everything else and when you accidentally hit the solution, you end up thinking "well... that was weird".
Thankfully, the game has a built-in walkthrough, that can give you hints step by step without spoiling too much. This offsets the moon logic somewhat, so I'd say this is just a minor downside.

"The Inner World - The Last Windmonk" is the sequel to "The Inner World" and also a point & click adventure for beginners and advanced adventure gamers.
And even though not having played the first game shouldn't get in the way of solving puzzles and liking the game, I recommend playing the predecessor first.
The sequel shows the fantasy world of Asposia, three years after the first game's ending. After the so-called flute-nose dynasty and its survivors rose from being stone statues for years, they are now officially persecuted by a tyrann named Emil who wants to hunt down and execute all flute-noses, making them responsible for controlling the dangerous basylian monsters (basically flying mechanical dragons which were a creation of the last dictator who told his people they were living, dangerous creatures).
One flute-nose, young protagonist Robert, returns to Asposia, discovering the horrors to his family members and heavily controlled society. He wants to stop the persecution while also finding his love interest Laura from the last game and showing the people the truth...
As you can tell it's not quite a light-hearted story even though the game visually looks pretty cute.
But still, it's not a depressing story, instead it still contains enough humor (more like random, cute and sometimes even a bit dirty humor), amusing situations and entertaining characters to put the adventurer in a good mood.
Like in the predecessor it's an adventure game where you point & click your way through the story. You pick up items, combine and/or use them, talk to characters and explore places. There's no dead-end or way to die.
This time, however, you can control other characters more often (3 in total), like pidgeon Peck who can reach hardly reachable items better.
For advanced adventurers it shouldn't be a problem to solve the puzzles (only in chapter 5 it took me longer to figure out how to get further here and there) and also beginners can give themselves a try here but be prepared to find your solutions after a while since they are not that easy to spot and you'll have to think around the corner (or pay attention to characters' commentaries).
When it comes to graphics and animations, the creators really did step up here. They look way more carefully drawn, more detailled and just more beautiful.
The music, again, is also very good and contains a row of great background soundtracks outside of the well-known two songs from the first game (the title melody and the wind song).
The voice work? I can only tell you about the English version since this is the one I personally prefer. And it is quite fine, especially with these loveable accents and voices.
Is there something I miss in this game? Oh, sure.
Like the trading cards. There ARE some for this game. Unfortunately they don't seem to be activated or something and I'm not the only player having this problem. Hopefully this will change.
And since the story is also built on relationships between characters, especially protagonist Robert and his love interest Laura, I was looking for a continuation of their story but it's more like neglected. Like they see each other after three years apart and all we get to see is them standing in front of the other and talking. I was a bit disappointed. I didn't expect or want a soap opera but still more than that. A bit more heart.
So "The Inner World - The Last Wind Monk" is a very fine adventure with advanced graphics, animations and easy but not too easy puzzles for a couple of hours of fun.
If you're not familiar with "The Inner World", I recommend playing the first game first just to avoid confusion about certain relationships and connections to the story that happened before this sequel.

While playing my first PVP match, me and my friend realized a few things. Since this is currently in beta, if you see your team losing, there is absolutely zero reason to stay in a losing pvp match. Furthermore this game will almost certainly never be popular, so even when it is released people will just leave. Now you might argue that this is an issue with any online game, and I would agree, but for a less popular multiplayer game with only five players on your team, constant leavers will just grind on your soul until you give up on the game.
The PVE, as you may expect, was fine, although playing with random people will be an excruciating experience. I HEAVILY reccommend playing with friends over voice chat, as other random people will constantly walk into your lane and build in awful positions, ruining paths and mazes.
This game should obviously only be played for the PvE. If you do so, the maze/wall mechanics feel like a nice balance between the heavy mazing of Sanctum, and the very simple walling off of lanes from dungeon defenders. It did not appeal to me, but this may be enoyable for you.
+PVE with up to four friends is the same fun, hectic experience.
+More heroes to play gives more variation.
-I do not foresee any future for PVP besides groups queueing up together to smash uncoordinated groups. It may be fun when these groups clash, but otherwise I believe the random people will slowly just DC from the game and leave one by one (this was the case in the games I played that it looked like we may lose).
-Admittedly I did not play for an extended period of time, but the Crafting system where you pick up materials from fallen NPCs to unlock/upgrade your traps looks like it may take a long time.
-If you gain 65 Hero crafting materials from dailies, and 25 from leveling, from dailies alone the process for a new hero (450) would require about 7 days of playing dailies. However, in my specific case, two of the dailies required playing 10 games on two different champions. After about 8-10 games I was getting bored for the day, since the base gameply is fairly repetitive. This means for semi-casual players, the grind to unlock your favorite champion you experience on free week rotation may be an arduous process.

What can I say about this game that has not been said already.
Dust: An Elysian Tails is a beautiful game with a simple yet very well written story and an addicting combat mechanic that big companies could learn a lot from.
The game has that Metroidvania style, a big map to explore and RPG elements such as leveling up and distribute points to each stats, as well as equipment and items to help you along the way. The controls are solid and respond well to the commands, the keyboard is not an issue as the game was ported to have perfect keyboard+mouse set controls, but a gamepad is still the best option for this game. The main character, Dust, controls perfectly and very fluidly, you will never have a hard time slaughtering the countless monsters of this game unless you play on a higher difficulty. Which is something I'll have to address, the difficulty in this game is pretty decent on normal, but on hard mode the games punishes you in a way you will want to scream at the computer, two hits and BAM you're dead, you can only avoid this by leveling up and spending your points in your defense and using as much equipment as possible to avoid being killed so fast. Fortunately, you can't die in one hit if you have full health.
The art direction is by far the best part of this game, as you go on your adventure, you will often stop just to marvel at the background scenery, every drawing is incredibly detailed, even for a game as childish looking as this, the shadings, the lighting effects and the character and monster designs are also really good. The art style may take you by surprise, but being someone who grew up with Sonic The Hedgehog and old-school Disney cartoon, I don't mind one bit, and if you don't want to play the game because of its characters, then you're a close minded person and have no idea what you're missing.
The music is also pretty impressive, I don't know what HyperDuck SoundWorks are, but they did a damn well job with this game's music. It's all instrumental and it complements every scenery, dialogue, cutscene, stages and boss battles in a way that you will repeat these parts just to listen to the music.
The story is very simple, but that simplicity is really well written, making the story very interesting, with that 'I want to know what will happen next' popping on your head once in a while. The voice acting is okay, all characters you can talk too have voice acting, which is great since not every RPG have talking people, only dialogue boxes, but, not many voices are that good, Dust's voice for example sounds too young for someone as serious as him and lack a bit of emotion on certain dialogues, overall the voice acting is pretty okay.
Dust: An Elysian Tail, Great game, worth every penny I spent on it. BUY IT NOW!!!!

Garry's mod is a truly unique experience, helped somewhat by it's varied, if frequently mysogonistic and anarchistic, player and game showcase. Some of the most horrifying game concepts that would never survive outside this shell (Slave and concentration camp "Role-play") verses more diverse and original concepts (Prop hunt, Multiplayer versions of existing game universes.).
Garry's mod is the closest thing to a virtual reality universe-airport we have yet to make as a species, and part of the difficulty in reviewing this game is that there are so many possible adventures you could have while playing it. Garry's Mod is very difficult to honestly review. You might find the game you've always wanted, or you might find a reason to stop playing forever, but I recommend it.
