Dark Crusade is the second expansion to Dawn of War and advertised as a standalone expansion as well. It should however, not really be played as a standalone. The complete absence of any sort of tutorial or incremental introduction of units and technologies makes this an incredibly hard place to start for new players as you're essentially thrown into the deep end from the get go and just hope you learn how to swim before you get overwhelmed. To add insult to injury you can only use the two new races in multi-player unless you already own Dawn of War and Winter Assault.
The two new races are very nice additions however. The Necrons are a pure powerhouse, the immortal machine servants of a long dead empire, serving vicious and hungry gods. In game they play quite differently from the others, ignoring usual resources and tactics their build speed is determined by the number of strategic points you own making them a very slow starter, to compensate their units are unusually tough and sometimes even resurrects themselves upon death. Lategame they transform into a steamroller as even their Headquarters becomes a flying, teleporting doomsday machine.
The second new faction to be introduced is the Tau and they similarly play differently from the old factions although not quite as big a deviation as the Necrons are. The Tau are a strange mix of specialists, heavily armed but poorly armored weapons platforms and a variety of beastly allies. The biggest difference between them and other factions is the lategame choice of either going to the heavily armed but poorly armed weapons platforms or the huge beast allies they can also summon as choosing one path excludes the other.
The single-player changes gear from the previous installments and replaces the linear and scripted missions of Dawn of War and Winter Assault with an open campaign map in a Grand Strategy style. Each faction starts with a stronghold province and must conquer the rest of the map as you play along gaining various bonuses from their conquests including various pieces of wargear for their leader. The problem with this concept is all the maps in between the various strongholds are just plain boring, both in attack an defense. Although the map changes it all plays much the same and it comes down to pure grind very quickly.
The stronghold attacks however is where the game gets interesting. Challenging maps with multiple sub-objectives and small video sequences before and after makes them the only bright side of the new campaign.
In terms of graphics and sound it maintains the same quality as the main game. A thunderhammer still makes a satisfying thump when impacting a traitor's breastplate and the Ork's still scream out their one word with relentless fervor.
That feel that comes from the WH40K universe still exists, but the grind of the campaign makes it have much less of an impact than in the original. Still a good expansion, just not an exceptional one and definitely not one to be played as a standalone game.

This is by the guy who did Iji, Hero Core, and Hyper Princess Pitch, so if you liked any of those, you'll probably want this. Specifically, it looks and plays a lot like the original Duke Nukem from 1991, but it has a lot of cool features of its own.If you haven't played the original Duke, you're given about 16 decently sized levels you're free to wander around and explore in, grabbing stuff for points, getting better firepower, and looking around for secrets.
The game's pretty short, but each episode comes with a boss fight that gets tougher and more interesting the harder the difficulty you play it on. There's also always the drive to improve your score by looking for more of the secrets and getting better times, too, which is cool if you're into score attacking.
Personally, I like this game just for how authentic it is. Nothing in the game uses 16 colors, and even the sound effects come right out of the PC speaker. For some people, it might be a little tough to look at, but for somebody who grew up with DOS, it's a lot of extra effort that I feel makes the game really special. Not many games at all have ever used this kind of style, compared to how many NES-style games are out there, so I really, really appreciate it. Here's hoping for DLC, or better yet, a sequel.

I have to admit, I have some reservations about recommending this game. It's a beautiful old school point and click adventure game that keeps VERY true to its inspiration. The game looks nice and has an interesting, if not necessarily stellar, story, lots of puzzles, and loads of inventor items to fondle. If you like older adventure games like Lucasarts' classics than you should probably just go ahead and get this game. It doesn't quite have the humor those older games had, but the gameplay is much the same.
Unfortunately, many of the irritating aspects of those older games are very present here. Many of the puzzles require a good deal of "inventory alchemy," so you'll often find yourself spending time listening to the main character repeating quips like "What am I thinking" a dozen times in a row as you try combining every one of your items with every other item in an attempt to figure out what arcane combination will yield a helpful result. Puzzles are also rather hit-or-miss. Most are fairly logical, but as you get closer to the end of the game they become increasingly convoluted until virtually all sense of reason is lost. I'm not ashamed to admit that there is simply no way I would have figured out that last few segments without a guide. If you can put up with these irritations, than there is a good game here, but it is very much a diamond in the rough.
A note to achievement hunters: This game has some rather odd achievements for a point and click adventure game. First off, you will have to play the game multiple times to unlock everything (which I don't see any point in for this type of game). There are also a lot of achievements for performing arbitrary and time wasting actions like "click on this thing 10 times in a row." There is however, one interesting achievement I wish I had seen earlier. You can earn an achievement for using the "Hotspot Highlighter" less then 50 times in the course of a single play through.

MURI is a fantastic love letter to EGA DOS games that succeeds not in spite of its 16 color/16 FPS limitations but because of them. Minimalist and spartan it creates atmosphere with empty space, both visually and aurally, and succeeds in crafting a smooth dificulty curve through deliberate level design and the sequential introduction of new challenges and power-ups. The cherry on top is the surprisingly touching story told through tight dialogue scenes that don't overstay their welcome and explore themes of motherhood and sacrifice.
It's a short game, approximately an hour and a half long, but once you start it, it's hard to put it down, and if you have fond memories of shareware and floppy disks its presentation will absolutely satisfy. Game design has matured over the decades and it avoids the pitfalls that its forebears often succumbed to, and I would argue that it succeeds as an engrossing experience even without being viewed through the lens of nostalgia.

This may be a short game, but it's great all the way through. Four episodes, with four levels (plus a boss level) in each, and I did it in around 2 hours. For the price, though, I'm not going to complain, because it plays very well.
It's EXTREMELY reminiscent of the first Duke Nukem game. Fortunately, I like that game, so I like this too. The main difference with Duke Nukem is the addition of weapons, but other than that, the engine is almost identical (it could almost be a sequel to Duke Nukem, although that already exists). If you take Duke Nukem, mix in some Metroid style, and lowered your character's gravity so you can jump really high, that's this game.
The design is excellent: the weapons are varied, and you can't select them freely so you never feel like relying on any one weapon. On Normal mode, I felt that just as my health was getting low, a health pack would appear, so the levels have been designed well there. I also like the secret rooms to find, and a challenge to get 100% on the level. The addition of cells that open doors to power-ups on the boss level is a nice touch: you can ignore them, but the final battle will be harder, so it keeps you searching.
There are only a couple of negatives I can think of: there is no save function, which is odd for a game like this, but since each episode is done in around 20 minutes, it doesn't really bother me much. Second, I know the graphics and sound are supposed to be like an EGA game with PC speaker, but the music is just a rather dull theme song, then nothing. And the final negative? Not enough levels! It's not entirely a bad thing though, because if they released some more episode packs, I'd definitely buy them too. If you like Duke Nukem 1, get this!

You do not remember your past, but everyone else seems to remember everything of what you represents. Dust is your name, but who really are you? I do not usually care about the storyline in games, but Dust: An Elysian Tail has kept me very interested from start to finish.

Very early in the game you find a magic sword, who knows everything, but will not tell you anything! The magic sword wants you to take him with you as he will guide you on your journey ahead, and you use him for combat. You will be companied by a tiny, little, flying creature called Fidget who had been protecting the sword until you showed up. Fidget is my favourite character in Dust: An Elysian Tail. She is very adorable and makes you giggle, so cute. However she is not only there for the humoristic side, she is very helpful for combat and to learn new skills as you progress your game that are very effective.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a platforming game with simple RPG features. You follow your main quest while also being handed side quests that mostly are about finding missing people or finding an item and hand it back to that person. You earn experience and loot by completing quests and defeating enemies, which allow you to level up and upgrade one of the four passive skills. The game also offers a crafting system where if you find blueprints you are able to craft the loot if you picked up the required materials for it. The RPG element does not go deep in Dust: An Elysian Tail as it is very basic but otherwise is implemented very well.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a short game, but it is generally very enjoyable during the entire play through. I like how the story goes, how the game is being played, and I love the art style a lot. It is very pretty to look at, glittering and colourful. I especially felt dragged in during the snow levels, mixed with the soundtrack. Oh, and Fidget! Fidget, Fidget Fidget~!
My only complaint is that the cutscenes of Dust: An Elysian Tail. There are only like three of them, and they come at the end of the game, but they are very awkward to watch and not well done at all. Compared to everything else about the game, the cut scenes just fall hard and should not have been there. I was disappointed they had to resort to cutscenes. However it is a very minor complaint.

I played The Inner World with my 7 year old daughter a month or so ago and we loved it.  We were so pleased this sequel came out I bought it straight way.  We’ve spent some very enjoyable time together playing this.
We both loved the game; it was easy enough that an old ex-adventure gamer as well as a sharp 7 year old could enjoy it.   There is a mix of humour, like a good Pixar animation that adults and children can find amusing (for different reasons).  There were a few jokes I kind of cringed at thinking my daughter would ask why I found it funny, but they just went over her head luckily.  There were also a couple of slightly strong words used that I would have preferred my daughter not to hear, but honestly it’s probably nothing some of the kids use in the playground.
The hint system is great, as some of the puzzles seem just a little bit too obscure sometimes (but then it wouldn’t be an adventure game if it wasn’t!), but in some ways, the hint system is a bit easy to turn to.  It was also highly useful as we had a few days break in between sessions so sometimes had to remind ourselves what we were doing.. It starts off with a rough direction and gets more specific the more you click on it.
Would I play it on my own without my daughter, yes!  Would she want to play it on her own, maybe not, but an older child might.
If you are a casual adventure gamer, I would recommend you give it a go.  It’s not going to challenge a serious adventure gamer that much, but the graphics and dialogue are super cute – we especially love the tumble mice!

I didn't spend very long with this game before reviewing it and I didn't feel like I needed to. There were three big reasons for me giving a negative review, things that immediately stuck out and made me want to exit the game and uninstall.
First and foremost is the awful free to play model they've gone for. Something I really liked from the first two games was beating more and more difficult challenges to unlock everything. It felt rewarding! They've decided to replace that with a combination of extreme grinding and high prices. Take a look at the forums and you can see people already complaining about the grind.  What's even worse is that even if you do decide to dump $50 into this game that package doesn't seem to be enough to even unlock all of the characters, forget the rest of the stuff in the game that you may want. If you aren't sick to your stomach yet: The game is p2w as well. It seems like all the 'consumables' in the shop (which you buy with real money after suffering through 'exchanging' it for arbitrarily useless amounts of in-game currency) give distinct in-game advantages. Are you interested in spending real money to get a healing potion? This is your game.
Second, this game just doesn't 'feel' like an OMD game. It sort of plays like a shoddy knockoff. The graphics are either the same or worse than OMD2. In the couple levels I played your characters abilities just don't seem very impactful or interesting compared to earlier games.
Third, and I realize this tends to invite a lot of controversy/babyrage, but for the most part I found the character design to be cliched and lame. Nearly every female hero is a ranged/stealth/magic archetype. They mostly have the same predictable 'pornstar' body type with equally predictable battle-bikini costumes. Throw in some infantilizing style choices for the non 'sexy' character and you've got a well rounded roster of gross cliches.  I didn't look at every skin for every character but it seems pretty obvious from the loading screen/promotional art what they're going for. The male characters have a huge range of ages, body types, and even species! One of the male characters actually is somewhat scantily clad, but given his bizarre proportions it seems to be a comedic choice rather than sex appeal. Maybe you don't care about this and think it's fine. Good for you, I don't want to hear it. It was enough to contribute to deterring me from the game so I included it.
Yes the game is in Beta, but they seemed to think it was finished enough to show to the public. Unless their development plans involve completely replacing the f2p model and redoing all the art, I don't think these problems will get any better with time.

Fallout Shelter is a supervisor/mantinance/managment simulator, which puts you in the role of a Vault overseer overseeing a vault.
Fallout Shelter was developed by Bethesda Game Studios and released Mar 29, 2017.
There's not much to the story... well... not on it's own anyway. If you've played the fallout games there are plenty of nods to the lore within the fallout universe.
To put it simply, the fallout universe takes place after a nuclear exchange October 23, 2077, and now the people survive in complex underground systems known as Vaults.
In fallout shelter you need to keep your dweller's happy and content, maintain water, food, and energy levels, build new rooms, send dwellers out to gather resources, and much more.
The basic gameplay loop is "Make sure your stats are maxed"
, then slowly arm and equip all of your dwellers in the best gear possible.
I started playing Fallout Shelter to do something different with my time, and to wean myself off clicker-heroes.
If you're looking for a time sink; this is as good a choice as any. While not as complex and satisfying as other simulation styled games... I enjoy booting up the game, checking my stuff and then logging off to go about my day.

By far one of the worst games I have experienced in my 40 years of game playing.
I'm going to attempt a pro's and cons list... this won't be pretty:
Pros: Steam allows refunds! I love you steam.
Neutral: It's single player. Kind of disapointing for a first person arena shooter, but I can't hold it against them since it's honestly marked that way in the steam store.
Cons:
- The game has 1 level. There's buttons to change to others but apparantly they were never put in
- The game pretends to have 2 modes to play, but they are actually identical, just the same arena with you versus another insect
- No music during the game, cheesy repetitive sound effects (and very few of them)
- Gun variety? There seems to be 4 but they are all slight variations in the SAME model with just different lights, they function and sound all mostly the same. It actually took me a while to even notice that the guns were different occasionally.
- The game description says it's all about flying; but the "flight" button just makes you sort of jump and hover for a couple seconds. It's more about "jumping sort of not really that far" than it is anything resembling flight.
- This is a 1 versus 1 arena game.. that's it. There is litterally NO CONTENT.
- No in game feedback, the UI is void of anything that tells you what is going on. No kill counts, no death counts, no way to know what you are supposed to do or why. I mean sure the goal is simple "kill the enemy 10 times" but you don't even know how many kills you are currently on and no, counting for real isn't an option because:
- You have no idea if your actual kills were done by you or the environment. Both you and the enemy will die randomly to things completely not under your control. Walk near a gas cloud? you dead, Bump into a building and clip through it? you die. Walking too fast and the game bugs out? you die. If the world killed the enemy while you were shooting at it, you won't know.
- You will spend most of your time in this big empty arena (the only one...) waiting for the content to find you. Just one lonely bug walking over and shooting at you, over and over again.
- the enemy hit boxes are wonky. empty clip after clip into one body part or another and there's no feedback telling you if you are hitting anything (no bullets, no hit effects). the enemy just occsionally falls over dead (but then it does that even if you aren't shooting at it sometimes so you really have no idea if your bullets are effecting it)
- I could on about how bad the content is, but there's so little of it, what's the point?
- Beyond that it's technically put together badly. Game has lots of bugs, lots of clipping issues, lots of what you would expect from say an amateur gaming developer that hasn't been properly trained.
- Even the most fundamental game basics are broken here: you have to restart the game to change the sound effect levels; seriously?
- Game breaking here: Switching the screen resolution is on a "cycle" you litterally have to change and WAIT for the new resolution (and hope your system supports it) before you can "cycle" to the next one. If your monitor doesn't accept the next resolution in the list before you get to the one you want? Too bad, the game just goes black with no way to recover. Don't worry, it won't remember your resolution anyway so just force it closed. You get to cycle through every resolution every time you want to play the game. I haven't seen resolution settings this bad since DOS games were a thing back in the '90s, haven't we all learned how to make a settings menu that works yet?
I gotta stop, there's about 1000 more things wrong with this game. At it's very core I am finding it difficult to even call this a game. I have personally played student graduation projects with more content than this. At best this is a tech demo you might use to show the earliest stage concept of what your game is going to be about. But what you have here is a developer who made 1 big empty level and called it a full release product. And that 1 level was not even properly designed or tested.
Epic Failure in every way.
As a final note of just how poor the development quality is on this game? They couldn't even be bothered to name their launch file properly. If you open task manager while playing (which I had to do several times due to game breaking bugs that forced me to close the game) you will find the game is named: "Made with UDK"; that is litterally the default name for a file that anyone will end up with simply from launching the Unreal Development Kit.
This "game" could be made in a weekend for free by anyone simply by downloading UDK, uploading a few free models, putting in a basic menu screen and than launching the UDK movement demo to shuffle your models around.

Oh Binding of Isaac, how you've addicted me.  When I first started playing TBOI, I had no idea what I was in for.  I'd just heard the game was essentially about your journey to kill your insane mother.  I liked the concept and the idea that this was a dungeon/shooter/roguelike.  It seemed like an interesting game and the price was right so I gave it a shot.  TBOI is one of the most merciless games I've ever played.  As most roguelikes are played, when you die it's over.  Restart it and give it another go.  The great thing about the game is that it wisely gives you repeated incentive to revisit it's twisted world.  With achievements galore as well as some of the most fun weaponry you can imagine (Laser eyes AND guided missiles!) the game does it's best to keep you coming back for more punishment.
I would say the most endearing feature of the game is it's ability to make you feel simultaneously untouchable and utterly weak at the same time.  A few wrong moves can kill you instantly, but if you use your resources effectively, you can come out on top.  The game has quite a few different endings as well as the insane final final FINAL boss... But I'll leave these things to the reader to discover.  If you're a glutton for punishment and some very dark subject matter, give TBOI a shot, just don't expect it to hold your hand.
(+) Wide variety of power-ups, weaponry, and monsters.  The game will constantly keep you on your toes if you want to survive.  Some of the type combinations with weapons and Isaac create an almost comedic level of power against your foes.  These moments are some of the best in the game and will probably be the main driving force for future playthroughs.
(+) Surprisingly interesting and deep story to the gameplay.  It's not immediately apparent, but subtle (and not so subtle) cues give off the idea that there's more to Isaac's story.
(-) Probably my number 1 gripe is that there is no native controller support.  I just don't understand that omission but I'm guessing it was done as a cost/time saving measure.  Still a notable omission to an otherwise very tight control scheme.
(-) Sometimes the deck is just stacked and you aren't going to win.  It's to be somewhat expected in games of this nature, but you may find yourself in a position (many times) where you just don't have the tools to beat the game.  Better scaling with weapons and power-ups could have fixed this, but total randominity ensures that this is not the case.

My thoughts on MURI are pretty mixed. It's a fun platformer, but it's so short. I like how a game wouldn't want to over stay it's welcome or anything, but it can be beaten in under an hour. The game feels like Duke Nukem 1 (A 2D platformer) with less flaws. The problem is, is that it sticks too close to the same type of gameplay the whole game. You are never really surprised the whole game. It always plays it safe and never really deviates from the base structure. The game has some level design, but it's all a bit generic. If you are a fan of 90's PC games like Duke Nukem 1 or even Commander Keen and Duke Nukem 2, you should buy this. The games biggest flaw is that it feels too much like a 90's game, you could tell someone it's "The lost Apogee game" and they would believe it, there isn't much replay value (aside from tougher difficulties), and there isn't much variety. There aren't many modern features, I mean, there isn't any coop or anything. The graphics are alright, it looks like I could be running an old DOS game, and is pretty nice by those standards.
Well, overall, I may of sounded a bit disparaging on this, and I may of spent a lot of text talking about MURI's flaws, but it is a fun game which I really enjoyed while it lasted. I'm sure I'll buy the next game the dev makes, the dev has some talent. MURI is not the perfect game, but if you are a platformer fan who has three bucks to spare... Why not give it a shot? You know what, 7.5 out of 10 stars. I'd recommend it.
EDIT: Changed score from 6.5 since it didn't seem too fair. I'm playing it again and it's definately a 7.5. It's very enjoyable even with it's simplicity.

I played NS back in the day when it was just a mod. Was very glad to see it turned into a stand alone game.
Summary: NS2 is an asymmetrical shooter - humans vs. aliens, with a bit of base-building/RTS management thrown in. Each side has their own playstyles, strengths and weaknesses. If you've been looking for a fun FPS that's a little different than the norm then this may be for you.
Strengths: Asymmetrical shooter, variety of different "classes" to play, can choose to play as RTS base builder if you're the commander on each side. Very unique and best job at integrating the RTS/FPS genre. Good graphics, atmospheric maps with good level design on the whole.
Weaknesses: Poor commander can ruin the game for everyone else.
As I said I played the original in my dorm during college so I was very excited to see this released as a whole game. If anyone's played the original this has improved upon it. Better graphics, slightly revised weapons/classes. I really enjoy this game. WIth that said the RTS side is decent if you're in the commander seat. It can be a lot of stress to be a good commander, having to develop the skill trees for the FPS players, resource management, dropping health packs/ammo/turrets is great if you're a good commander, but the community is brutal if you're not. If you're not a good commander then everyone else on your team suffers so it can be a bit frustruating at times, but that's the price you pay for having an FPS/RTS hybrid.
The sides - Marines - The humans are the more straight-forward of the two options. Get guns, then bigger guns and mow down the aliens while expanding your base. As the base commander unlocks additional tech, each of the marines can choose different weapons, support (jet-packs!) and eventually the all powerful mechs. I personally enjoyed playing marines more (partially because I love playing as Bill Paxton and saying, "How could they cut the power, man? They're animals!")
Aliens - Aliens begin the game as more hit and run types in their basic forms. You have to use all of the vent systems to sneak up on unsuspecting marines to garner enough kills to mutate into the tougher variants. Definitely requires a little more skill to manage a successful alien invasion. It is very satisfying to get your kills as an alien, especially when you're tracking down that marine that thinks he can go off on his own and survive.
Recommendation - If you enjoy FPSes and have always wanted to try a combo FPS/RTS then this is the best one I've seen. If you've wanted to play an Aliens vs Marine game, then this is the best I've seen. Atmospheric, fun time to be had, just don't get frustrated if you get a bad commander.

This is a wonderful experience with a great combo oriented fighting style. The story is above average at best (though some parts of the story, especially at the end, are a bit inconsistent and hurt an otherwise decent story), and the humor is passable, getting a few chuckles out of me. But the true meat of the game lies in it's combat system, which is very combo oriented as I mentioned earlier, encouraging the player to combo as much as possible by not only giving you ways to break the "resting" frames that Dust has occasionally after chaining his moves together in a specific way, but also giving you a way to move across the map quickly, if blindly, in hopes of keeping that combo up.
Retracing my steps to get hidden collectibles became faster as the game progressed and I learned how the mechanics of the combat system worked (which is a huge bonus, because having to retrace one's steps can be such a boring time-sink in some games that I don't even bother with total completion), and was actually a little bit fun. Learning how to travel fast was the best part of retracing my steps, though, because I learned it myself just from playing around with the game. The developers knew that the mechanic was in the game, they even had a collectible that could only be gotten by abusing the fast-travel mechanic, but no one tells you, or even hints at, how to get that collectible and it's only through playing with the game and noticing the mechanics of the combat system do you figure out how to get the collectible.
All-in-all, I highly recommend this game. It only took me 20 hours to unlock and collect everything, but they were hours spent enjoying the game, which is more than I can say for a lot of other games that I've played.

First of all this game is not well optimised and is also not a very good console port.
The UI is messy and clearly still console, it runs very poorly when driving and drops fps on lowest settings.
On foot is decent enough to play with no visible lag but as i said driving is very different, not to the point its unplayable but its not as much fun as it should be thats for sure.
I have a mid/high range PC and run every other game in my library with high/ultra settings easily with solid 60fps and that also includes a couple of Early Access games that run far smoother than this game does.
The pedestrian AI is frankly quite embarrassing, just sit and watch what they do and it looks like i wrote the code for them, also very similar to the enemy AI they are about as dumb as i have seen in any game i have played.
All of the above mentioned are a real shame as the characters and storyline are excellent so far, its just hard to immerse yourself in something that regularly stutters when driving (which is rather important in a large open world) reflections and lighting are also done poorly regardless of settings.
If you needed more proof that this is a very poor console port then you only need to change the ingame settings to high from low and you will notice virtually no difference whatsoever to having it set on low apart from the fact that on low the game can actually be playable.
Steam really need to add another option rather than recommend yes/no to these reviews, i would reccomend it if you can handle performance issues, bugs, very poor AI, horrible UI and a serious lack of optimization for PC.
Otherwise give this game a wide berth.
TL:DR I cannot recommend this game in its current state.
if you can handle a game that stutters a lot and wont hold anywhere near 60 FPS and looks the same on low settings as it does on high then dive in, the story looks fun and the cutscenes and facial animations that back up the story and history are excellent and add to the gameplay.
If you are looking for a well optimised AAA game with an intuitive interface and decent AI then i strongly suggest looking elsewhere.

Fallout Shelter is a F2P game that originally surfaced on mobile devices a few years ago shortly before the release of Fallout 4. I remember completely failing at the task at hand and had my Vault and its Dwellers silenced forever due to a series of unfortunate events. I can only remember Deathclaws and my poorly equipped bunch valiantly defending their incompetent Overseer.

Recently the game was released on Steam and I thought it best to try and redeem this Overseer's tarnished record. The good news is that Vault 757 is flourishing nicely and has a lovely bunch of Dwellers who either wander around taskless or work 24/7 365 days of the year doing what they know best... constantly turning a valve.

I have to say that having had a fresh approach to the game, it is really accessible and it  is refreshing  not to have microfractions constantly pinging up asking you to spend more and more until your savings are  non-existent.  You can have it running in the background while you do some work or browse the latest news. Yes, tasks can be repetitive and you do have to wait to reach quests(Which is the interesting part). However I'm sure you have more important things to do rather than mindlessly click on tabs... If you get tired, you can buy a few  Mr Handys to automatically collect resources. Just be careful not to have them engage with raids or infestations as these lovely machines cost 2000 caps each to repair.
It's a neat little management game and I would recommend you give it a go. Just remember to keep those Stimpaks and RadAways stocked and you'll do just fine!

This game, this game is just so amazing. So many times when you see "retro" style games they are usually either throwbacks to old NES/SNES/Megadrive(Genesis) era games or a lazy excuse for weak graphics since they may look like a old game graphiclly but they don't often play like them. This game on the other hand looks and plays like a old dos era EGA platformer, most notably Duke Nukem 1 so much so I half expected to see the Apogee logo and a shareware registration page which sadly it doesn't have but it does have a quit to DOS option(no seriously, but sadly no Simulated DOS prompt pops up when exiting) and it even uses old PC speaker style sound and music(title screen), so when I say looks and feels like I do mean it, the scrolling is a bit chunky since back in the day smooth scrolling effects were done on the PC through moving 8x8 blocks to simulated smooth movement like arcade and NES games had.
Only downside it's a bit short since each episode is only 5 levels long and they could tweak the controlls a bit since if your shooting and then push back you don't turn but rather just move back unlike other games from the era it's emulating where you will always face the direction you press shooting or not. Prehapes this is intentional but it's still feels weird at least to me also there are no saves but since each episoded(4 in total) are only 5 levels long it's not a big deal.
So if you have fond memories of old shareware EGA side-scrollers from the 90's like Duke Nukem, Commander Keen, Bio Menece, Dangerous Dave and the haunted mansion and others then by all means give this a go.

When I launched ‘Chains of Satinav’ for the first time my, expectations have been pretty high. The game set in an almost legendary fantasy setting of "Dark Eye" (in some countries it's even more popular than 'Dungeons&Dragons' !), and above all an adventure, not RPG one, to me seemed like a guaranteed success.
Despite minor flaws like surprisingly low frame rate, and a few resolution problems, I've started the story, and meet our Hero for the first time. In ‘Chains of Satinav’ we take up a role of Geron, a young bird-catcher who bravely stands against dark forces threatening his home town of Andergast. The narrative we follow is a solid piece of work, with some surprising plot twists and believable, memorable characters. Not only the fully voiced dialogues, so important in adventure games, but also the world itself are designed with a great care for details making the whole journey a pleasant and memorable experience.
The riddles that fill the world of 'TDE: Chains of Satinav' are pretty good, some of them really witty, but overall not hard enough to discourage You from finishing the game. A huge plus is the fact, that they’re all pretty much logical chains of actions, which prevents typical adventure-game puzzle rage. An unique addition to the common point and click mechanics are two special 'talents' that Geron can use to his aid. Our particular bird-catcher is capable of breaking, and later even fixing some fragile objects, which allows him to solve some of the harder puzzles.
“TDE: Chains of Satinav” is a great adventure game, with beautifully drawn backgrounds and captivating story. The puzzles although not that hard, may provide just enough challenge to prevent You from blitzing through the game. Another great feature is an atmospheric music, perfectly accompanying Geron's adventures and enriching the whole experience.
-	A very good narrative with believable characters.
-	Set in a vast fantasy setting of ‘Dark Eye’
-	Need at least two play troughs to get all mutually exclusive achievements.
-	Unique atmosphere created by hand-drawn stills and amazing music.
-	Sequel already in store (check ‘Memoria’)
-	Surprisingly low Frame Rate.
-	Some common problems reported with game freezeing and resolution.
-	Puzzles are not that much of a challenge.

I bought MURI on a complete whim, going into the game not expecting much. Man, was I wrong. Remar has created something special here and I was nothing to short of being blown away. MURI is a side scrolling run and gun in the guise of an MS DOS aesthetic (seriously, as soon as I saw that DOS style HUD, I knew I was in for a treat) with plenty of things to shoot, plenty of power ups, plenty of levels, a ton of secrets and a phenomenal storyline. MURI is divided into four chapters and does a brilliant job of combining Sci-Fi elements into it's own unique telling, it's simply not enough to explain it here, I alone can do this game no justice. MURI is a special game, that does everything right, the MS DOS feel and aesthetic is beyond perfect, the story is original, the sound effects and what little music there is, is spot on. The game starts off easy, but it really does start getting brutal as it goes on... And theres a hard mode option, if you're feeling brave enough.
MURI gets zero complaints from me, it's an outstanding game that caught me completely off guard, and it's an experience I would happily share with anyone who is interested. To anyone who  is into the DOS scene, to anyone who misses the unique feel of these types of games, you have to try this. Great game, if all my fingers were thumbs, they would be up, but they're not. So it's two thumbs up from me! ;-) well done Remar. Highly recommended!

Some of the game modes require other players to play like: Gun Game, Rampage (if you want to be a dino), duel, etc. But Survival, slaugher, and conquest can be played by yourself. When I first picked up The Binding of Isaac, I thought it was a shallow dungeon crawler whose 'dead baby' motif wore thin after 5 minutes. But then I gave it a chance to change my mind and it succeeded dramatically. It plays very much like the old Legend of Zelda games on the NES but with a roguelike twist to the action.
You will die. A lot. But you'll make it a little further every time you try and slowly, you'll get better. There are hundreds of items that you will come across during your trials and they all provide interesting effects that alter the way you fight through the game. Since the game randomly generates each level, no two lives are exactly the same, providing for very powerful or very weak playthroughs.
Replayability? Tons. Each time you beat the game, you get something new. Keep beating it and the game gets longer and more difficult. When you first pick up the game, beating Mom (the first "final" boss) will be a monumental achievement but the gratification will quickly wear off when you discover that there's a new "final" boss to fight after you beat Mom and 2 more levels.
The game will never go easy on you (which can cause some very frustrating experiences!) but the sense of accomplishment never goes away. There are a ton of things to unlock, to beat, to pick up and to experience and if you really get into it, it's all to easy to lose 50+ hours to this $5 game.
If you enjoy roguelikes, if you enjoy randomly generated content, if you enjoy a challenge that ramps up each time you succeed, you owe it to yourself to pick up The Binding of Isaac.

The name Natural Selection describes this game perfectly. Certain species are meant to be superior to other species, and the developers made it perfectly clear that their race of aliens, the Kharaa, is clearly superior to the helpless marines that you will most likely end up playing as. The developers gave them a rediculously high skill ceiling compared to the marines, so while it is difficult to learn to play as them, the best of the best will play, and only play, as the aliens, leaving the all the newbie and mediocre players to fend for themselves against an unstopable force that they have no hope of stopping. Every game will end in an alien victory.
While the developers give the marines a fair amount of weaponry to fight with, including flamethrowers, grenade launchers, and mechs, all of them are rendered moot by the aliens absoultely absurd mobility and health. The game runs on a resource supply that you get from controlling certain parts of the map. The issue with this is that the marine weapons cost quite a bit of resources, and you lose them when you die. Seeing as though the aliens will win no matter what you do, you will always lose the weapon you paid for, leaving you to fight with a pea shooter assault rifle, a horrendous pistol, and an axe that's more effective at slicing cheese.
And then there are the aliens themselves. There's 5 of them, each of them unfun to play against. There's the skulk, which is what you fight at the begining of the game. Low health and crazy mobility. While a bad one is easy prey for the marines, a good one can literally slaughter a small group by themselves, and god help you if you face more than 1.
The gorge the least bs one there, but that's because he doesn't directly fight you. Rather, he corrodes your buildings from the safety of an nearby airvent and builds shortcut tunnels that help the aliens get from spawn to the corner they hopelessly have you pinned against in seconds. Lerks are just giant birds. They swoop in and bite at you until you are dead. This is the point where your guns start meaning nothing against them.
And then there are the fades. They teleport with a 2 second cooldown, they do high damage, and they sport an absurly high health stat. I've seen one take down 7 people at one time, all by itself. If any aliens is going to make you rage quit, it's this one. And lastly we have the Onos, a giant alien that's a tank. you're own mech is suppose to go up against it, but the thing is that the aliens more likely cut off your resource income by the time they are able to get to the Onos's, so you won't have an to spend on making your own mech. At this point, it becomes a victory lap for the aliens as ravage whatever is left of your base. Quite a sight to behold, actually.
I realize this game is suppose to be human vs alien, however these aliens make me wish there was a human vs human mode. It's absolutely rediculous. I can't recommend a game that's so unbalanced that it makes me wish it was just another TDM game. I mean, the RTS commander aspect of it is cool, but unlike a normal RTS game, your troops are actually human beings that can either be completely oblivious to what goes on around them, or god like players that you will love having on your team (Spoilers: They'll be on the alien team).
As thus, not only do the aliens portray a negative picture on how humanity is doomed as soon as it encounters aliens, it makes what could be a cool game a frustrating experience to play.

MURI is a platforming shooter designed to look and play like old DOS platformers such as Commander Keen or Duke Nukem < 3D. In fact, it's DOS-faithful to a fault, sporting rather loose controls, being less than visually pleasing, and boasting a sound library comprised of mostly farts and silence. However, if hunting for collectable floppy disks and super weapons behind false walls in a robot bunny suit sounds like your idea of a non-productive Saturday afternoon, you can do worse than this game.
Breaking up the action is a series of incomprehensible story segments with all the narrative finesse of an Iji, or a... you know what, I don't think I've found a video game story quite as ham-handed and inconsequential as Iji's. But MURI's certainly tries, in spite of its greatly reduced length. You may also find some replay value in the more crippling difficulty levels or gunning for the optimal score per level with a system that rewards both complete enemy destruction and minimum time elapsed. Because that's a point of pride among connisseurs of budget-priced, niche-retro-era-styled, other-gratuitously-hypenated-descriptors downloadable games. If you grew up playing this sort of thing on shareware disks or you have a secret-hunting complex, give it a whirl.

Mayhem Above is a musical score-attack game set in space. You play as a spaceship and as with other score attack games you have to get as high a score as possible. You do this by grinding the surface of planets, drifting the gravity field of planets, bouncing on the surface of bouncer planets, breaking planets by crashing into them at high speed, going to outer space and "tackling", read crashing into, enemies. Everything that generates score increases your combo meter, the more variety the more combo, which is needed to earn a high score amount.
As mentioned you can crash into enemies, but the enemies can also shoot at you, so you have to avoid their beams by jumping. If you get hit by an enemy beam your volume, the game's health system, will go down. Luckily you can recover volume by collecting volume cores around the universe.
Completing a map grants you XP based on your score. Once you have enough XP, you level up. When you level up you get perk points, which will help you gain better control of your spaceship and other nice perks.
The game uses a simple 2D art-style with a space theme. I had to play the game at the lowest setting, the potato setting, that is what it is actually called. The game is well optimized and will run smoothly on most systems with the correct settings. On high, the game looks absolutely stunning, I can not however run it smoothly at that setting, due to my PC specs.
The soundtracks fits the game perfectly. The included soundtrack has house, techno and trance music as far as I could tell, but I am not expert on music. The game also has the ability to use your own songs.
If you like score attack games, I would highly recommend this game. It is fun and it can be challenging when the music gets intense and the screen fills up with enemies.

Despite all that, my experiece was quite positive, the way everything feels, looks and sounds is exactly where my imagination goes when I think of such a title. The story is facinating, the characters are well developed and the performaces are memorable. The combat is fun and pretty fluent, hitting hard but taking hits hard yourself(which I really appriciate) If you get smacked by a giant monster whoose arm is the size of your whole body, you die. If a giant tentacle comes crashing down and pulverizes you, yeah your health is gone. That kind of realism, even in fantasy, pulls me in and keeps me there.
This game is not a casual RPG, it requires your devotion and your fully attentive mind to really enjoy the experience. As other reviews have stated, this game will not hold your hand, aside from the combat, the puzzles and mind games are some of the most worthy I have seen in years. This was a pleasant surprise constidering many games today have a nasty habit insulting the gamers intelligence. This mostly comes in the form of popup tutorials telling us how to identify simple patterns and basic logic that the avergae human does anyway, like...for basic existence. The opposite of just how smart we're talking here would be Skyrim. Remember those "Puzzle Rooms" where you would have to match this♥♥♥♥♥♥to that with the answers displayed blatently across the ceiling? Theres no such childsplay here. The Withcer will only teach you the basics and then your on your own. I would recommend this to anybody interested in a thought provoking challenge, that is based in a universe you believe is still thriving when you shut off the computer.

Daedalic has done it again. They've won me over with an absolutely charming story.
Now, let me start of by mentioning the drawbacks of the game. The voice acting is a hit or miss kind of situation. Some voices like the main characters, Nuri, Geron, and the Raven, were alright most of the time but others like that one eyed creature, the fairy queen, and the dwarf were so laughably bad that I had to turn down the volume. I just read the subtitles. But that brings up another problem. Something definitely went wrong with the english translation because there are a few awkward yet brief pauses and bad logical leaps with the writing. And the puzzles were a bit too easy to go through. The game also drops frames hard when real time texture compression is turned on.
However, the story and the characters were just so damn charming and endearing that I just had to know how things would turn out for them. The story has that same fantasy feeling I had playing through games like the Longest Journey and Dreamfall. The music and the art is also fantastic. If given the chance to buy the soundtrack and artbook, go ahead. It's not a bad move.
I would definitely recommend The Dark Eye: Chains of Satinav to anyone that loves fairytales and has the patience for the drawbacks I mentioned.

If you've played the early Duke Nukems and Commander Keens you'll immediately feel at home in this game. So far I've finished the first four episodes and they've all been a blast to play. The game not only pays homage to Apogee-style DOS platformers but develops them a bit further. The result is a more rounded game with a lot of secrets and some exciting boss encounters.
Sound
Instead of the PC speaker beepiness (which, admittedly, is faithful to the source material) I'd have preferred an AdLib-type soundtrack.
Graphics
The EGA graphics are fine, even though some of the enemy robots look a bit stiff. Because I played the DOS games I am quite used to the choppy scrolling, thus I haven't tried the smooth mode yet. Maybe I'll try it for the second playthrough.
Gameplay
The game is quite easy on Normal, though on later stages I died several times, in most cases out of carelessness. I imagine the harder difficulty levels are proper challenges. Finding all bonus items in a level provides some motivation to explore the entire level before moving on and later on there are some cleverly placed secrets. The first few stages felt a bit short, but they get more expansive in the later episodes. None of the ones I've played so far have reached the complexity of many Duke Nukem levels, but that is not necessarily a bad thing.
Summary
If you liked Duke Nukem and similar DOS platformer, chances are high you'll love this game as well. It's a short but fun nostalgia trip for a fair price.

There's absolutely nothing I can respect more than a game that knows what it wants to be, and Hotline Miami knows EXACTLY what it wants to be: fast paced violence! With tightly grouped rooms and corridors, this games level design allows for quick impulsive action to be the one true tactic.
When I had first played this game, I was super cautious, and was pretty much up to the epilogue until finally I just snapped (after dying for the 10 billionth time regardless of careful planning of the enemies behavior,) and just slammed through doors, rapidly pressing the fire key, slashing everyone and everything I passed by, and found that was actually making further progress. “Surely, this is just a fluke! Pure luck, added with strange level design!” I thought, but when I just simply let loose and mindlessly blasted through every level, I found it was the most effective way to play. Enemy AI is intentionally unreliable: changing patterns, braking rules that you find aren't so concrete, as they suddenly brake from their routine patrols, combined with varying reaction times from a wizened martial arts master to a handicapped rock. Add this to the fact that the respawn is instantaneous once you press the respawn key (matching the mood of when your just madly slamming away at the buttons going “woiehfpuhqwerp;oghbeipoqurhgvhdfgpovghjqpoerihjf;lbsdhg” because you died AGAIN) it is a game that punishes you for being slow and calculated, even literally, as waiting too long in an area will actually give you a lower score, whereas running into a room full of enemies and impulsively breaking each of their skulls in will reward you for your “boldness” at the end of the level, resulting in a higher score. It is a game that wants you to act like the mood it's trying to convey: impulsive, senseless, fast paced violence.
The only real “planning” aspect of the game is choosing from one of the many masks at the very beginning of the level, which will give you different abilities throughout the level, some to add more ease, and even some to add more challenge (there's one that only lets you see a few inches in front of you.) And these masks are ♥♥♥♥ing fun to play around with! My all-time favorite is one that you get for completing the game that lets you run SUPER fast, even further adding to fast pace of the gameplay. Other than these masks, the only best bet you have is twitch reaction impulse, and hopes that the enemy won't be even more hair-trigger than you are.
The art style also really puts you in the mood, as psychedelic mixes of invasive neon colors (namely red) fill the screen with pixel art that I feel does a good job of putting you into the time period, and it all gives this feeling of “These characters are quite clearly on drugs.” I know that to some, the whole pixel look is a bit of a turn-off, but trust me, I feel like with the setting of this game, it actually really works, and I've never been confused as to what I was looking at, so It's all clear enough to understand what's going on. And the color scheme is extremely refreshing to me, with so many games, some not even being as violent and dark as this, seem to have ugly, bland color palettes, whereas this one seems to put in extremely vibrant colors, probably to even further excite you as you play through.
So with all this talk of violence, blood, flashing bright colors, and impulse, you may be thinking this game is probably for the unintelligent spaz that you can easily find playing Call of Duty, drinking Mountain Dew with their Ritalin, and while I can certainly see those kinds of people playing this game, skipping through cutscenes just to get to the next level to kill more people, if you actually look through those cutscenes and listen to what's being said, this game actually has what I feel is a pretty fitting message: violence is pointless! “Whaaaat?” I hear you cry, “But you were just talking about how violent this game is, and how fun it is to partake in that violence!” Yes, but the game actually has a voice of reason in there that actually mocks you throughout the whole game. You don't play as a good guy, and it makes that known. The guy that you play as is doing things without even knowing or caring to know why, and it kind of makes fun of him for that, pointing out that all of this violence and killing can't be justified (okay, sure, I suppose the people you kill in it are also pretty bad, but I think that's more of just because this takes place in a world of bad people killing bad people.) I will admit: the message is pretty minimal in this game, and if you want to get more into it, you'd have to look at the second game, but trust me, this game actually does point out that there's no point or justification for what you do.
With a solid soundtrack, aesthetic, game-style, and level design, added with some decent writing to boot, I'd say that this game is a must have!
Also, before I forget: DO NOT GET THIS GAME IF YOU DON'T HAVE A CONTROLLER! Trust me, this is a great game, and I HIGHLY recommend it, but the controls with just a mouse and keyboard are beyond horrible, they're Donald Trump. Once you get a controller, it should be smooth sailing from there.

So there i was, booting up The Dark Eye: Chains of Satinav (TDE:COS hereafter) for the the first time. The game started straight away, a blessing after experiencing major compatibility issues with Daedelic's The Whispered World, and soon I was in game, launching into a somewhat abrupt beginning. Suddenly, the game stopped, seemingly frozen, before launching into dialogue, followed by the same thing EVERY TIME I spoke to someone. Now, I don't have an amazing computer, but I can handle fully 3D games just fine, no hangs. So I went to the options menu, turned everything down to low and it WAS WORSE! After some forum hunting I finally found out that TDE:COS needs to run in native color depth. So, I went to the configuration tool, changed it to 32-bit (from the lowest option, 16-bit) and, lo and behold, a fun game began to emerge.
I will say, that this was the most frustrating experience that I had with this game. The puzzles were fairly logical throughout the first half, with only a few leaps in logic towards the end, where some of the physics are more maleable. The dialogue ranges from stilted to quite engaging. The over-arching storyline has enough going on that I was fairly invested, though it did not bring much novelty. However, shortly after I worked through the aforementioned flaws, I began to really, REALLY, enjoy myself. The visuals are very effective and there is an ambience throughout the game that plucked at my fond memories of The Longest Journey.
Yes, this game is flawed. Yes, the graphics cause delays and hangs. However, once you look past that, there is a really great game here (anyone remember the flawed, but fabulous, Soulbringer?). Well worth a budget price.
Pros: Beautiful. Enjoyable puzzles. Fairly engaging story. Some of the voice acting. Solid musical score.
Cons: Running it. Some of the voice acting. A few of the later puzzles.

A 2D action platformer with RPG elements mixed in for good measure.
Dust, one of three main characters, has lost his memory and wakes up in the middle of a forest. He is immendiatly approached by Ahrah, a magic talking sword (Yes, you read that right) who guides him on the way to find out who he is. Straight after that, the Ahrah's guardian Fidget shows up and demands that the sword be given back to her. Dust declines, so Fidget follows along as dust tries to recover his memory.
It is a bit cliche, but the story changes gets significantly better very quickly. And the interaction between the characters can be hilarious at times. Especially with Fidget, who breaks the fourth wall several times over the game. The interaction between the NPC's can get pretty interesting too, depending on the situation.
Every character has brilliant voice acting, are all well written, and are all believeable people. Dust obviously has significant character development, Fidget is hilarious and the story has a very conclusive, brilliant, ending.
Dust: AET uses a three button combat system. Two buttons are used to make combos for attacking enemies with your sword, while the third is used for a projectile attack for low damage, rapid-fire, stun-locking attacks. However, the second button is what converts these projectiles into useful attacks, so sometimes a combo can be accidentally inturrupted by clicking Mouse2 at the wrong time. This isn't that much of a concern though, as button mashing can be semi-effective for those who find it too difficult.
Dodging and blocking are also in Dust: AET. Most of the time, I never thought to dodge that much, though that may just be me neglecting the ability. Blocking is tied to the attack button. This is fine, but sometimes I had felt that I would have preferred another button for blocking, as it is really just a timed 'counter' button. Either way, these are just nitpicks, and do not really affect the game
much.
There are many side quests avalable to Dust to complete or ignore. None of them are required to complete the game, though it may be impossible to only do the story missions due to a lack of XP. Some of the quests are simple fetch quests, while others can get much more interesting.
Leveling up and loot works just the way you'd expect. You kill stuff, you get stronger, you kill stuff quicker. It's a bit more complicated than that, but you get the point. Loot is aquired form slain enemies, which can be either sold or crafted into better equipment. Some will find the inventory screen a little lackluster, but it doesn't matter that much in the grand scheme of the game.
All of the keys can be rebound, there are many settings avalable to make the game run smoother or prettier, and all the menus are mouse driven. Though there is a tiny bit of lag with mouse movement in menus. If you prefer using just the keyboard, then the manus can be used that way too.
Overall, Dust: AET has a brilliant story, a great combat system, many side quests for the completionists, well implemented RPG elements and a good port to PC (I prefer console games, so take the PC port part with a pinch of salt). I think it's brilliant.
Note; The game was pretty much a one-man project, and has a quality that can rival most AAA titles. Keep that in mind when you're playing it.

You control it all, beginning with engineering and launching your first rocket and ending with building colonies and mining minerals from the other planets in the Kerbal solar system.
This game has a research tree in which you can purchase equipment upgrades using a secondary currency (science) which is earned by performing various experiments on and off the planet.
Ships, rockets, space planes, building upgrades... all cost money which is earned by completing contracts from the simple (test this engine) to the complex (put a base on the Mun.)
Overall, I give this game high marks.  I've sat down to put a satellite in orbit after lunch and had time run away from me, phasing out until the wife calls me to dinner.  You've been warned.

There's absolutely nothing I can respect more than a game that knows what it wants to be, and Hotline Miami knows EXACTLY what it wants to be: fast paced violence! With tightly grouped rooms and corridors, this games level design allows for quick impulsive action to be the one true tactic.
When I had first played this game, I was super cautious, and was pretty much up to the epilogue until finally I just snapped (after dying for the 10 billionth time regardless of careful planning of the enemies behavior,) and just slammed through doors, rapidly pressing the fire key, slashing everyone and everything I passed by, and found that was actually making further progress. “Surely, this is just a fluke! Pure luck, added with strange level design!” I thought, but when I just simply let loose and mindlessly blasted through every level, I found it was the most effective way to play. Enemy AI is intentionally unreliable: changing patterns, braking rules that you find aren't so concrete, as they suddenly brake from their routine patrols, combined with varying reaction times from a wizened martial arts master to a handicapped rock. Add this to the fact that the respawn is instantaneous once you press the respawn key (matching the mood of when your just madly slamming away at the buttons going “woiehfpuhqwerp;oghbeipoqurhgvhdfgpovghjqpoerihjf;lbsdhg” because you died AGAIN) it is a game that punishes you for being slow and calculated, even literally, as waiting too long in an area will actually give you a lower score, whereas running into a room full of enemies and impulsively breaking each of their skulls in will reward you for your “boldness” at the end of the level, resulting in a higher score. It is a game that wants you to act like the mood it's trying to convey: impulsive, senseless, fast paced violence.
The only real “planning” aspect of the game is choosing from one of the many masks at the very beginning of the level, which will give you different abilities throughout the level, some to add more ease, and even some to add more challenge (there's one that only lets you see a few inches in front of you.) And these masks are ♥♥♥♥ing fun to play around with! My all-time favorite is one that you get for completing the game that lets you run SUPER fast, even further adding to fast pace of the gameplay. Other than these masks, the only best bet you have is twitch reaction impulse, and hopes that the enemy won't be even more hair-trigger than you are.
The art style also really puts you in the mood, as psychedelic mixes of invasive neon colors (namely red) fill the screen with pixel art that I feel does a good job of putting you into the time period, and it all gives this feeling of “These characters are quite clearly on drugs.” I know that to some, the whole pixel look is a bit of a turn-off, but trust me, I feel like with the setting of this game, it actually really works, and I've never been confused as to what I was looking at, so It's all clear enough to understand what's going on. And the color scheme is extremely refreshing to me, with so many games, some not even being as violent and dark as this, seem to have ugly, bland color palettes, whereas this one seems to put in extremely vibrant colors, probably to even further excite you as you play through.
So with all this talk of violence, blood, flashing bright colors, and impulse, you may be thinking this game is probably for the unintelligent spaz that you can easily find playing Call of Duty, drinking Mountain Dew with their Ritalin, and while I can certainly see those kinds of people playing this game, skipping through cutscenes just to get to the next level to kill more people, if you actually look through those cutscenes and listen to what's being said, this game actually has what I feel is a pretty fitting message: violence is pointless! “Whaaaat?” I hear you cry, “But you were just talking about how violent this game is, and how fun it is to partake in that violence!” Yes, but the game actually has a voice of reason in there that actually mocks you throughout the whole game. You don't play as a good guy, and it makes that known. The guy that you play as is doing things without even knowing or caring to know why, and it kind of makes fun of him for that, pointing out that all of this violence and killing can't be justified (okay, sure, I suppose the people you kill in it are also pretty bad, but I think that's more of just because this takes place in a world of bad people killing bad people.) I will admit: the message is pretty minimal in this game, and if you want to get more into it, you'd have to look at the second game, but trust me, this game actually does point out that there's no point or justification for what you do.
With a solid soundtrack, aesthetic, game-style, and level design, added with some decent writing to boot, I'd say that this game is a must have!
Also, before I forget: DO NOT GET THIS GAME IF YOU DON'T HAVE A CONTROLLER! Trust me, this is a great game, and I HIGHLY recommend it, but the controls with just a mouse and keyboard are beyond horrible, they're Donald Trump. Once you get a controller, it should be smooth sailing from there.

My first impression was, what is the diffrence between this and the old Orcs Must die games? Well, after playing the survival mode for a couple of games, I headed to the siege mode. What is the siege mode?
The siege mode is like smite combined with the older classical versions of Orcs Must Die. It's 5v5 and is one of the most immersive and fun games I've tried in a while. The game style is MOBA, with a slight RTS feel, due to the fact that you can control which minions you wanna spawn etc.
That being said, this is not your standard MOBA like game, you can choose to have the defence trait or the attacker trait in the hero select screen. These will give your a certain trait to help you do either, as the name implies. As far as I've observed there is a defence and an attack lane, personally I've only really played defence, since I love placing traps and making fun little routes for the minions to die in, I like building stuff.
The obejctive is as in most MOBA games, to reach the enemy spawn point and take it down. Reffering to League of Legends nexus and Dotas whatever (I have never really tried Dota, so I don't know what it's called). The game itself is third person.
All around a fantastic game, that just recently really opened to the public. I look forward to what this game is gonna offer. Right now as it is, I am completly in love with this game.

Another example of action rpg (lite) tower defense hybrid genre killing itself.  First it was Dungeon Defenders 2 now Orcs Must Die Unchained.
Why a MOBA?  This game's style is not suited towards a MOBA.  Moreover, the popular MOBA's on the market don't require tedious grinding or microtransactions to unlock all hero skills/abilities.  DOTA2 only has cosmetic microtransactions.  Heroes of the Storm requires you to unlock heroes with gold which is slightly more tedious but passable.  OMD Unchained requires you to unlock heroes AND purchase unlocks/upgrades for traps and items to increase your hero's power.
Co-op Survival mode suffers from the same grinding feeling but the awkwardness of playing with four teammates.  Strategically planning trap placement is not something you want to do with four random players who often don't comunicate at all.  Never mind the fact the load times and 'waiting for player' queues are extremely frustrating versus OMD 1 and 2's drop in and get started right away.
A sad end to a great franchise.  I'd have gladly paid $30 for an OMD 3 that includes much of the same content (new heroes, traps, items, levels, even some grinding) but focused on single player and two to three person co-op modes.

Solid space simulator that doesn't take itself too seriously. Includes several tutorials that help the player get started, although after the moon, or Mun as it's called, the player is on their own.
In this game the player both designs the spacecraft for their mission as well as flies it. Both aspects of the game have their own unique challenges, although the biggest challenge and emphasis of the game lies in proper vessel design.
It's also possible to build and fly aeroplanes, although that part of the game is overshadowed by the space exploration part.
The difficulty of the game is fair at the default Normal difficulty, but the difficulty is also very customisable, giving extra challenge to the hardcore and a smoother ride for the casual.
Career Mode is the game's story mode and the objective is to accomplish more and more daring missions while gathering the three resources Science, Reputation and Money while simultaneously upgrading your facilities, coordinating your plans, and making sure your Kerbonauts are alive and well.
The progression is slower than in most other games, as gathering the Science resource is essential for unlocking new better parts, and sometimes gathering sufficient Science for the next essential upgrade can mean several nearly identical missions. This slugishness can be remedied by launching riskier, more daring missions with suboptimal parts, though, so daredevils might find the pace more acceptable. Gathering Science does also get much quicker once you reach the moons of Kerbin, Mun and Minmus.
Other than the Career Mode, there's also a Sandbox play mode where all parts are instantly unlocked and your resources are unlimited, and Science Mode, where Science is the only resource you gather. Personally I find these two other modes less engaging, though Sandbox is useful as a playground for testing wacky designs.

Perhaps the first "Action-Roguelike," Binding of Isaac combines the brutal shooting of games like Smash TV with roguelike elements such as perma-death, resource management, and randomly-generated dungeons. This offers near-infinite replayability, as it's never the same game twice. The game also parodies many classic and modern games such as Legend of Zelda, Minecraft, and Left 4 Dead.
Despite the initial impressions it may leave due to its simple, "cutesy" art style, BoI has lots of blood, disturbing imagery, a dark sense of humor, and plenty of religious overtones. I would not recommend this game for children, or people who get offended easily.
For everyone else, though, this may be one of the best games released in the last decade.

Quite an excellent game for the puzzle-minded.
You have to guide simple robots through obstacle courses, and do this by building basic circuit logic that they then have to follow, while utilizing motors and sensors and such so that your robot can navigate said courses. If you want a game that shows you how to use logic gates for basic robotics, and that gives you challenges all along the way to do so, then this game is for you.
It ignores the annoyances that you might have to worry about "in real life" regarding things like circuit engineering (as far as electricity and such, voltages, etc). Yet you can combine circuit logic to do some pretty cool things.
In the levels I have played so far, I have had to design robots that will navigate a maze of walls, that have had to follow lines, that have had to go around a curved table without falling off, that have had to follow a line to the end of an obstacle course without crashing into moving objects in front - etc. There's a fairly good variety in these levels, and solving them seems very simple in human terms, but getting the exact logic down so that your robot can do so is challenging. You manually have to decide what happens with literally every input and output with your sensors if you want to get anything done.
As one example, say you want to keep your bot between two walls (there is a level like this, at least one, earlier on), which curve on both sides to the end of a course. To successfully navigate such a course, you can put a sensor on both sides of your robot - so they face one wall each, and have logic connected to wheels on both sides that "turn" your robot the correct direction whenever you get too "close" or too "far" from a given wall (so you don't crash into them). This can be done by turning off the motor on the opposite side, or by simply reversing the direction of a motor, or by a combination of things if desired. In this specific case however, you could just have a sensor on one side, and have it try to stay within a "range" of distances by turning one way or the other to stay within a certain distance of it.
There's almost always a better way to finish a course, but I'm struggling most of the time just to get to the end at all. Yet finding a solution, or finding a better solution, in this game is far more rewarding to me than in most other puzzle-type games I have ever played.
I've gotten through about 17 hours of this so far, and most of your time in this game will be spent experimenting with every last thing, repeatedly redesigning a given bot to solve a level properly. You can try to solve a level with the bare minimum, or try to solve it "better" by trying to beat a given time or build a bot with less money required. Each stage has multiple of these "optional" objectives, which is sure to encourage replayability. I've only completed around 1/3 of the levels in the game after 17 hours, and I believe myself to be at least relatively intelligent (confirmation bias aside), so there certainly isn't a lack of time to have fun.
While the game is very difficult (obviously, this varies by the person), I find it very rewarding to play. When you successfully complete a level in this game, it really feels like you triumped over something meaningful. As someone who has messed around with a fair amount of robotics "in the real world," yet isn't about to go to the level of building my own garage and welding my own circuits again anytime soon, this game is basically the closest thing I've ever found to a good simulator of circuit logic.
Keep in mind as well that the game involves circuit logic and a limited number of places to put logic gates, so it can actually be more difficult to solve many of the puzzles than it would be if you were using "real life" modern electronics (which often have full software integration, allowing for much more complex commands). This limited nature of the game makes it all the more challenging, and also educational. My poor memory means that I have to be very careful when designing a given circuit that I color-code each wire for given "segments" properly, and I'm nearly to the point where I really am going to need to start writing down my circuit logic on paper before trying to put it into action in the game.
Yet all of this is great fun, if you're patient. If, on the other hand, you don't have the patience to learn - this game might end up being highly frustrating for you. I highly recommend it to anyone who wants a good challenge, and who ever has had an interest in circuit logic. It isn't for everyone, but it certainly is worth a shot.

Are there bugs? Yes, more than just a few (but not enough to make it a triple A). Are the controls difficult? Bottom line is, this review is pretty bad because it's way too subjective, but it's one of my first reviews ever so I'll use that as an excuse.
