I like it, but I'm also a sucker for logic puzzles.  I'm an engineer by trade and this kind of game is right up my ally.  One of my favorite games of all time has been Banjo Kazooie: Nuts & Bolts if that gives you a hint into what I think is fun.
I'm not going to call this a puzzle game or a programming game.  The puzzle is "How do I beat this level?"  The "programming" is figuring out which gates to use and how to wire them up.
Here's what I do like:
* It's an objective based robot creator!  It makes you use your mind to figure out how to beat each objective.
* There are tons of parts and logic board configurations that you can play with.
What I don't like:
* Levels get pretty tough to the point you want to just quit and you can't skip them.
* Laying out wires should have been more of a click-and-drag function instead of a click-click function.  It's very difficult to see if the wiring post is clicked on or not.  Click on a post and drag it to another post would have been easier.
* There is no ability to do a simulaton senor check without using a "on/off" switch gate on your board, which takes up slot.  It is especially annoying when your board is near full with gates and you have to run wires too.  See above for why running wires is not a great method.  If an option was included to "turn on the senor with a given input" then it would really help trouble shooting your boards.  A little model of the bot doing the function in the corner would be great too instead of having to go to the actual challenge to troubleshoot.
Little story for the last point... I was doing the level where you have to design the bot to turn when it reaches a colored wall.  Thankfully they set it up so that a left turn and a right turn had different colored walls.  If your bot goes off course onto the red flooring you would fail the challenge.  I kept trying to rig up the board to do a 90 deg turn with the gyros, with a count gate but I couldn't see what circuit board and values were doing.  Gist of the logic function I was going for - IF SENSOR IS ON COUNT TO 90 USING GYRO OUTPUT AND TURN THE CORRECT WHEEL AT THE SAME TIME THEN RESET COUNTER AND GO BACK TO BOTH WHEELS ON.  I finally had to setup another set of senors to adjust the wheel motor directions when they went over the red flooring because I couldn't see what the gyro and counter were outputting.
For the current price, $20, it's not a bad game.  I've spent more on AAA games and have gotten less play time.
If you like a mind challenging game and like mechanics/electronics, then I recommend this one.

Another quality adventure title from Daedalic. The story was very good and much darker than any of their other games I've played. The puzzles were extremely well designed. The main character has a special ability to break certain things with a spell and then to fix them which made for some very clever puzzle solutions. The dialog did a great job of directing you too so that you always knew what your objectives were. The voice acting was hit and miss, but mostly miss.  This is too bad because the writing is very good and there is a major disconnect between what you the player are seeing/feeling and how the voice actors portray this in their performances.  The animation style took a little getting used to.  The had drawn artwork is beautiful so it is too bad that the animation doesn't live up to it.  It was kind of distracting for the first 30 minutes or so and then I either got used to it or it got better. Chains of Satinav is a point-and-click adventure developed by the German Daedalic Entertainment and based on The Dark Eye RPG world, also German in origin. Both Daedalic and The Dark Eye have had difficulties with gaining currency in the English-speaking world, but based on this adventure (my first contact with Daedalic) the fault may lie in the Anglo-American cultural attitudes, for Chains of Satinav was absorbing and challenging in equal measure.
Unlike in so many adventures, the lead is not a wisecracker but rather a serious young man hexed with bad luck and shunned by society because of this. Yet the game feels more like a Grimm story than a typical fantasyland, either in high or low mode. Since "gritty, mature fantasy worlds" usually mean dwarves with liver cirrhosis and bisexual elven terrorists I am happy with this design choice. There is a general feel of sadness everywhere and the themes deal with innocence and corruption.
The graphics fit the above naturally and the hand-crafted scenery are lush yet clear. Colors are never garish nor murky and the visual presentation is an exact fit to my personal tastes. Animations are slighly limited, true, but that did not lessen my gaming pleasure. All sounds good too, especially the melancholy soundtrack which avoided the fake epic stylings so prevalent in many other titles. Settings are varied as well, from a crime-rotten port town to another plane where normal logics are superseded by fairytale equivelants.
Puzzles are typically logical and the solutions are within reason but occasionally the clues are rather obscure and this can lead into confusion, especially in the fairy worls already mentioned. There are limited help options of which I used the hotspot highlighter, meaning that a button push shows all the interactive parts of the screen. Dialogue is more clear than flowery or punning and despite being based on a pre-existing RPG world there were, incredibly, no lore dumps anywhere. Since the story sees a downbeat young man protecting an innocent young woman I am unsure how the feminists would see that aspect but I did not see misogyny anywhere, nor other prejudices.
As a whole this 10-hour game was a positive first taste of the Daedalic adventures and I will most certainly play the other ones as well. Definitely recommended for adventure fans.

The grind is real (see bottom)
OK, so first you have to sign up for a Robot account with your email. Second, you have to find your friends all over again because it doesn't use the Steam system.
But that's not the worst part. The grind is real. I need hundreds more items before I can do my first crafting.  You have to play the same things over and over and over again.  This might not be so bad if you like PvP, which is what this is geared toward, but my preference is co-op. So my co-op partner and I have to do the same 3 levels over and over again to get to the point where we can craft items and get to the next level.
The game might be sort of OK if you are into PvP (but still not nearly as good as OMD2 as explained below).  A lot of the best things about it are only available in PvP, like the minion cards. But that just makes it worse for those of us who prefer solo or co-op play. You can see some cool things that you can't reach unless you are playing PvP.
Here's an example from OMD2.  In that game, you could buy archers and swordsmen and put set them up to help you with your traps.  You can't do that in SP or Co-op.  You get a single guardian, and when that guardian dies, it dies for all the upcoming waves too.
Another example of going backwards is that in OMD2, you had a lot of options of where to put traps and a huge variety of traps.  Trust me, you won't get nearly that many different traps in this game unless you put hundreds of hours into it or pay real money for upgrades. Alright community, I've decided it was time to update my review seeing as how the Developers poured alot of time into new updates and model packs. Keep in mind that I will not be grading this on the same scale as I would a game, because this product specifically allows users to create their own games, without needing to know HOW to create a game. Instead, I will be grading it based on how well it executes its goal.

Keeping that in mind, GameGuru is amazing. The very simple editing window makes finding and placing your content quick and easy. Considering that this is a Drag and Drop style creator, what it does it does very well.
Editing Sprite is easy and based on a Dynamic/Static system, allowing the user to quickly decide whether or not an object should be able to be moved, destroyed or stationary. This makes creating NPC type characters very easy, and the options for the entities allows the user to add voice files, scripts or chance certain properties very quickly.
Designing terrain and editing buildings has been added since my last review and works fantastically. Obtaining models packs is simple and adding them to the editor is automatic.
The only real limitation here is the user's imagination. Here's the problem with that, however. Most indy game devs with no coding experience will use this engine and the base model packs without even attempting to learn the scripting language used by GameGuru or create their own original objects and animations. This means that many of the game produced by users of this engines will be rehashes of more popular RPG style games with unoriginal graphics and dull stoy modes.
; This would have scored higher, but the lack of HD graphics seems to be holding this editor back from becoming a full fledged engine that could crank out serious titles, which is okay. What this software does, it does extremely well, and could be the first steps many indie devs need to get their feet wet in the game developing world.

It's not a Pay to Win.
Here's what's changed from OMD2: in addition to killing orcs with traps, two new strategic changes have been made. The combo system is now much more important to success, and can't spam tar and arrow walls to win like before; you'll be broke and ogres will be trampling over your tiny baby-man corpse. You will have to vary the traps you use and keep in mind the damage properties of the traps (and sometimes even heroes) to maximize funds. The second major change is that rerouting orcs to where you want them to be
is key to success. Barriers will become your friend, and sappers will make you cry tears of blood.
Here's why it's not Pay to Win.
List of Things That Cannot be Purchased With Real-World Money:
- Traps
- Trinkets (called gear in this game, same thing)
- Guardians (some can be obtained if you buy the packs for the game, but otherwise not for sale)
- Traits (passive bonuses to your character)
- Minions (PVP)
- Bosses (PVP)
- Materials
List of Things That Can ONLY be Purchased with Money:
- Skins
Consumables and characters can be bought, but they can also be crafted. However, it is important to note that the materials needed for crafting characters are not found in low level maps and it will take you a while to reach the point where high level enemies spawn to find those drops.
Almost all of the negative reviews come from people with 4 hours or less of gameplay, so they don't really understand how this game works, they just played it, saw it wasn't OMD2, and downvoted it and started crying about it.
It is not P2W, it's very well made, if you like OMD2, you will like this, as long as you have the patience to level up a lot before being able to hit the big leagues with fancier upgraded traps and consumables.

** This was written AFTER the performance update. **
Background:
Male, 11 years of programming experience, mostly C/C++.
Used T3DGC, DB, DBPro, FPSC, and FPSCX10; Beta tested FPSCX10, even got a lovely christmas-card from TGC.
Disclaimer:
The harsh language and comparisons made should be taken lightly, as I am exaggerating for the sake of exaggerating. That being said, the complaints are legitimate complaits.
On to the review:
Remember the time you wanted a Game Boy for christmas, and you got a Super 30-in-1 off-brand "Game Boy" instead?
That is what this software is to other game creation suites/tools.
Admittedly, you can have very much fun with a Super 30-in-1 off-brand "Game Boy" but you still know it's not a Nintendo Game Boy.
First off, performance is terrible, even after the sought after performance update.
I mean, I can run GTA V, Fallout 4 and Metal Gear Solid V at the highest graphical settings in 1080p at a rock steady 60FPS, but my computer still drops frames when playing a demo level with Game Guru.
I'll admit that the update GREATLY improved performance, but as stated above, FPS drops still happend.
Secondly there is the standard assets.
It's the kind of bland, poor-quality nonsense regulary reserved for early PS2 low-budget shooters.
I bet comparing the GG player/enemy models/rigs/animations with the ones from FPSC Classic would exhibit remarkable similarity.
I clarify my view on the standard assets later in the review.
Some pro's and con's:
Pro's:
- Easy to use (Double edged sword)
- Terrain modeling
- LUA Scripting
- Good for beginners
- Have a game up and running (albeit with unstable performance) in seconds
Con's:
- Easy to use comes at the expense of de facto game development standards
- Performance
- No hitboxes (this has bothered me since FPSC Classic)
- Editor layout
- Out-of-the-box AI is broken (but can be improved easily through LUA)
- Explosions are sprite based (I swear, I'm not making this up!)
- Depth issues related to the use of sprites (i.e. explosions, blood, and so on)
- No editor ability to tweak/add/remove shaders
- Adding/making custom assets can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥br> - Did I mention that explosions are SPRITE BASED?!
- You can't distribute multiplayer games (yet)
To clarify:
Sprite based visual effects:
When I say sprite based, I mean it as in ONE LARGE SPRITE, as in Doom or Duke Nukem 3D.
I can appreciate that GG is a work in progress, but the explosion sprite from FPSC Classic looked SOOO MUCH BETTER. I mean, it looked like a dream compared to the current one.
Standard assets and game engine:
Many argue that the standard assets are just there as an example, a template if you will, and that you can get much more out of Game Guru by making/adding custom assets and utilizing them in conjunction with LUA to make more use of the engine.
Although this is very true, if you have the knowledge to make your own character models, rig them, animate, export, and script accordingly using LUA, you obviously have a good understanding of how these things work, and you might be better off utilizing a true and tested enging like for example Unity or Unreal Engine.
If you're a beginner/aspiring developer you likely have little to no scripting experience, in which case the ability to customize game mechanics or other aspects of the game through LUA would be lost on you.
Though there is many other things I could have picked on, I refrain from doing so as it would not make my point any stronger, but instead serve to paint me as a "hater."
Final thoughts:
This product has potential, just like The 3D Game Creator had potential, then FPSC Classic, then FPSCX10.
I've owned many TGC products, including but not limited to:
- DarkBasic
- The 3D Game Creator
- DarkBasic Pro
- FPSC Classic
- FPSCX10
- DarkGDK
Every product by TGC that I've used, I've only used for a short period of time, with the exception of FPSC Classic.
FPSC Classic had a fantastic community, which later became even better with the release of the game engine source code, which many improved on to such a degree that the engines modified by the community became paramount to developers using FPSC Classic.
FPSC Classic was simply the best WYSIWYG game maker at the time, but that slowly began to change when FPSCX10 was released and the community was split between two camps.
Trying to reinvent and rebranding the steel every X years will not improve the product, but going back and improving the steel by adding other elements to make it stronger, better and more suited for the constantly changing environment in which it is used; That will improve it.
I hope that is what TGC are going for with GG, as I fondly remember tinkering with FPSC Classic and DarkBASIC Pro, which inspired me to get into C/C++ with DarkGDK, and today I make my daily bread from C/C++ programming.
What I think is the strike of genius with the release of GG is that it's deployed on steam (with all the advantages that follow), and the community feature vote; Those two things will help in making GG better.
I hope that the GG community will thrive soon, and that it will become the new FPSC Classic and inspire many to pursue a career in game development and/or programming; But I simply cannot recommend GG to anyone at the moment of writing this.

Rating: 7/10 at this tiime
As you can probably tell from my hours of using GameGuru, I've very much enjoyed using it, and still do. You can make some nice looking levels fairly easily, and there is lots free and paid assets to help. The Forum support people and Devs are helpful, and if you don't want to do anything but make levels and plop in included entities and 3d models, or buy some from the GameGuru store, this is a good choice to start with in level/game creation. And mostly an enjoyable hobby.
Be aware though, that if you wish to go further than that in GameGuru, you will be leavinng the "easy game maker" part and you will need to:
1. Learn Lua and what it can or can't do in GameGuru. I enjoy learning new things and already have a background in coding, so this is not a minus for me, but may not excite you that much. Also be prepared to hunt down the sparsely documented, scattered and limited GameGuru function calls and try to find how to use them. The GameGuru forum sometimes helps, but other times you will be googling constantly for help as the GameGuru Forum search ability isn't that great. And unless you know exactly what you are looking for, searching may be a long process.
2. Learn 3d modeling, animation, texturing. About the only free option for any of these is Blender, and it's not a "learn in two days" thing, and neither are the paid expensive options. You will have to be very dedicated to learning for a long time before it really benefits you.
GameGuru does though come with a basic model importer (DirectX files the only really viable option at this time) and limited character creator (Limited human race choices, ages, sizes, body types, not much in civilian clothes and no civilian or other clothing available in DLC form at this time). Still, an improvement over nothing at all.
Of course you'd also have a learning curve with any of the free game engines, so there's that.
I bought GameGuru with some DLC in a bundle for around $2.00, so I'm not complaining about the price!
I should also mention that although you will still be limited (even if you do learn LUA and 3d modeling stuff) in what you can do with GameGuru, the creators appear to be trying to improve things, and add more options (as evidenced by the latest update to C++ and group selections in the level editor).
At this time, I give GameGuru a 7/10 as it now has no save/load ability for the standalone games, day/night cycle, does have difficult dialoging/text options, no vehicle option beyond static or moving a static car with custom lua scripting, poor mele and missing other things you'd normally find in most games. But if the Game Creators actually update GameGuru to even half of the requests (there is a page to vote for the next addition to GameGuru), I will be the first to give it a 100/10 (and it's starting to look like I will be doing that eventually).

I have had my eye on this game for a while as actually building robots can be very expensive but I always wanted to try my hand at it.  The game was very recently ported to Linux and as such I snapped it up immediately, I was not disappointed!
The game is superbly well designed with a training area, a sandbox mode as well as a career mode with some pre-defined challenge levels in each with acheivements to complete (like time to complete, no of parts used and cost).  Those levels are pretty simple in the begining but quickly start providing more and more of a brain teaser as you go on.   There are five areas in the career mode and I have only just completed the last level in the first area today! The last level in the first area looks deceptively simple but is actually a real head scratcher when you start getting into the detail.
Finding any negatives in this game is pretty hard I would say, it will obviously significantly tax your problem solving skills but realisitcally if you expected a game like this to be easy I would say you need to re-evaluate those expectations.  The only real negative I can think is that in order to progress to the next levels you cannot just complete the previous levels but must also have completed a certain number of acheivements in the earlier levels.  It might be nice to be able to progress to the next level without having to acheive a lot of the preceeding challenges first.  Still its a pretty small negative in the grand scheme of things and it may be possible the devs will amend this at some stage in the future.
I would say if you are looking for just a bit of fun with some robots the sandbox area will give you that and if you are looking for a real challenge for the mind then the career mode gives you that.
Overall the game is not only fun but gives a great experience in development and puzzle solving skills coupled with some genuine learning about electronics and robotics.  I can highly recommend this game, a well deserved 9/10.
Also as a last point if you are a Linux user I can confirm that this game worked flawlessly on my Debian based OS.  The hardware stats on my gaming pc are pretty minimal too so I would say this is a superb port to the platform!

So here's the story:
Got super excited when I found an Aliens VS Humans game(been looking for a tactical one like this for a LONG time), so I bought it for 10 USD.
Started it up after installing: takes about 10 minutes to start up--and that's just the loading screen. No joke. I'm thinking, "Oh, maybe it just needs to load the files for the first time." Yeah I was wrong.
Get to the menu, and I'm getting 7 FPS. Why? I've got over the system requirements and I'm running 7 FPS on medium settings, wth? Turn all the settings down to low, 720p resolution: get 15 FPS.
Go to server browser and see if it's any better(by that I mean maybe it'll run faster in game). Find a server, try to connect to it. It's not full, and it's not connecting. Thought maybe a lot of stuff was happening in the server so it needed to process and load it all; nope. Wait about 5 mins and I close it out. Go to another server and try to connect, nope, after 5 mins again, I'm stuck on the dang loading screen.
Finally decide to try the quick game option, and asks me if I want a tutorial. Hadn't ever played, so I clicked yes. And it takes around 10 mins to load...AGAIN. After it loads it's running 17 FPS(btw I have my Steam settings so I can see my FPS in game)...on lowest settings. My gosh...talk about not being optimized. So I start to hear the narrator and this is what immediately comes to mind after he's done speaking:
'Background noise in the recording, you can hear the click to stop the audio from recording at the end, and there's a lot of static and it ends like it cut off; because there's not background noise in the game.' Can't believe that was the final audio recording for that, I have audacity(a free audio recording/editing program) with a $40 headset that sounds 10x better than this. I record it, if there's background noise I remove it ENTIRELY, and I have a cardboard box for my "professional" recording. Like really, this is the best you get when you release the game? That's one of the worst audio recordings I've ever heard in a game, it's rushed; unfinished and could have of been better made if you took your time.
Enough about the audio rant, next, it tells me to build an armory, then kill some enemies. I start shooting the enemy(let's just call it an alien rat, first glance that's what I thought it was), and guess what happens? I drop half of my 17 FPS while fighting. I don't know why.
I go back into my graphics settings after killing the alien rat and make sure everything is down, and turn the resolution down to the lowest. I decide to see what would happen if I turn up the quality on some things, because in some games it happens to run faster on higher settings; don't ask why, but they do. Anyways I literally JUST click the little arrow so that the texture quality is medium, and what happens next? Drop half of my 17 FPS again?, no. Increased FPS?, no.
All of the dang HUD disappears off my screen. Nothing at all. No text for the settings menu, and no HUD whatsoever in game. Wth? I click the left arrow(arrow that decreases the quality) on the button-area I had clicked, and nothing happens. I hit apply: nothing. Not a single text is on my screen. Empty rectangles and empty boxes.
I proceed to close out the menu and reopen it to see if it was glitched for a second. *sigh*...This keeps getting better and better, doesn't it? After I close the menu again my game freezes...comepletely freezes. It's sound is looping and locking at a certain point(that indicating it's completely frozen), I open task manager to close the process...and I don't see it. Because of course, the stupid application is covering my desktop and I'm blind to everything there. I tried for 3 minutes to get the stupid task manager to work, finally I found an option where I can "move" it by right clicking on its icon on the Windows bar. Move it over to my second monitor, and close out the application.
TL;DR: Game froze, HUD disappeared, terribly optimized, bad experience. Had high hopes that I could play this but NOPE! I'm also REALLY ticked off that I'm above the recommended requirements, and that the requirements lied to us. I should be able to get a solid 30 FPS on min requirements on the lowest settings AT LEAST. NOPE!
Bad game, uninstalling and not playing again.

Orcs must die is a franchise of puzzle - third person action games. You solve the puzzle - defend your base from a horde of incoming orcs - by setting multiple trap combinations and shooting the surviving orcs in the face.
This game, on the other hand, is not.
It has two game modes, survival, the "classic" one where you team with 4 other players to defend your rift, and the new and "exciting" 5 vs 5 mode, siege, a mix of attack, defense and moba. And that's what kills survival mode: You have the level up mechanic and the moba-ness forced into it.
Survival it's a hollow experience. You can't put traps wherever you want, like in the previous games, you can only set them in the designed blue spaces of the map. You're not solving a puzzle, you're filling that blue spot with traps and hoping for the best. There is little planing and no creativity.
Remember the "shooting the surviving orcs in the face" part? You will do that - over and over. The orcs have too much life (or your damage is too low) and you feel powerless.
Now, this part will only affect you if you've played the other two games:
Did you like swapping weapons on the fly? It's gone. Your character has 4 skills and a passive (does that ring a bell?) and that's everything it's going to get.
Did you like headshotting with Maximillian's crossbow? Or turning the orcs one against another with the enchantress rod? It's not here.
Maybe you enjoyed the great variety of traps and changing them inside the level? Nope, at least not for free (or without farming).
I can't properly comment on siege, just played two matches with a friend and we didn't have any fun. In fact, we got progressively bored. It's a moba: instead of buying items, you place traps. That's it. You level up and get perks that make you a little more powerful. It is dull.
But well, at least the humor is still there.
On a more technical aspect, the game feels slower,  and uglier than the previous games, even on maximum graphics and running at solid 60 fps sometimes it's not fluid. I guess it's ok for a beta.
The game is free, so if you think you'll like it, give it a try. Just don't expect orcs must die 3.

While it does deliver the same topic in a different way, it is by no means a rip-off. It's a story completely capable of standing on its own two feet as something that should be remembered in the history books.
If you enjoyed the first game, you should definitely buy this one. Obviously you didn't like the first game for its combat, so it shouldn't be much of a surprise that there was a complete overhaul in the fighting methods. Rather than click and dodge like before, it's become a more sophisticated sword fighting simulator. While it does have its glitches, it does remain fair once you can get into it. Sometimes. Other times, the difficulty on normal seems ridiculously hard and the loading times can discourage you from playing forward, what's more, is that easy difficulty is ridiculous in its own rights. Normal is like playing dark souls, whereas easy is like playing a game that you payed your big brother to play for you.
But you shouldn't want this game for the combat, it's the immersion, the story, the artwork that really draws you in. You have to pay close attention and learn as much as possible in order to follow the story, but if you manage that, it becomes one of the most well crafted tales you will ever hear, with numerous factions all desparately trying to wriggle out on top.
tldr: buy this game if you want an epic continuation of an already beautiful series, only if you enjoyed the first game though.

Hands down, favorite Nancy Drew title EVER. We finally see a humanized Nancy with an emotional backstory, and the story line is SO edgy that it really keeps you engaged. I think that by the time this title was made, HERInteractive realized that many of their players skew older than originally intended, because this storyline honestly contains "thematic elements" as they call it in the movies. You really feel like a spy in this one, and I mean like an action-movie spy, not just a teenage detective. The flashbacks are awesome, it's fun to travel around Scotland, and the characters are colorful and multi-dimensional. Definitely recommended for longtime fans and newcomers alike, though I would caution parents to maybe check out the bioterrorism-type theme before you decide if you are comfortable with your 10-to-12-year-old playing this one. There are other, milder titles to try first (like Secret of the Old Clock, which was my favorite when I was young and a great first title). So much fun, though!

The Good:
Great visuals at time of release and superb art direction and immersive detailed hubs and environments to explore. A truly interactive and mature story with an excellent branching narrative and compelling decisions to make that matter to the plot, characters, and player, all of which are interesting in their own right. Good replay value to see the various routes situations can be completed in. Many side quests have their own contained narrative to them with various resolutions.
The Bad:
Erratic difficulty curve, often very hard or very easy. Some mechanics behind the Swordsmanship skill tree feel as though they should have been fundamental to the combat while others feel useless. The user interface feels designed for a controller. Combat is only serviceable, has depth but lacks responsiveness and control.
Verdict:
The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a beautiful looking RPG with an engrossing story full of interesting characters and a compelling plot with many layers. It has short comings in various areas, most importantly its average gameplay, but it's not enough to deter my recommendation in the slightest. The Witcher 2 may have the best implementation of a branching narrative in any video game. If that interests you then you owe it to yourself to play this game.

Nancy Drew is one of the most well known fictional detectives in literature. Many grew up with her books and games, and even if they forget the name, Nancy Drew can easily bring up an image of a teenage girl detective solving mysteries. For her 29th adventure in her game series, it gets a little more personal. In both her books and the games, Nancy’s mother is not looked into nor given any extensive backstory. All we know is that she died when Nancy was young. So what happens when Mrs. Drew is the mystery?
With Mrs. Drew’s bare backstory, Nancy Drew: The Silent Spy builds on it to give her more character. Named Kate Drew, she visited Glasgow, Scotland after getting a phone call eight years ago. She never returned and died in a car accident.
Eight years later, a mysterious letter is delivered to Nancy from a MI-5 organization named Cathedral asking her to go to Scotland. Kate’s death is not what it seems and has gone unsolved since. Soon learning that her mother was a spy taking down a terrorist organization called Revenant with the cost of her life. But Kate’s death is believed to have been intentionally caused by Revenant. Nancy soon finds herself taking her mother’s place as Revenant starts to rise again.
As she arrives in Scotland, it seems like the few people she meets is nice and immediately wants to help her. Each character has their own quirks that I could not help but love. Other than the repeating characters of Carson and Ned, both wanting Nancy to get home safely and giving you information this time around, there are only a few characters. There is Bridget, a friendly native that takes an instant liking to you, Moira, a woman who has a close connection with Kate, Alec, a skip tracer, and Ewan, your Cathedral contact that assists you throughout your mission. Don’t put too much trust in them, after all everyone hides secrets.
A lot of the characters are likeable, my favorite being Bridget, and you do get the feeling that they are hiding something from you. Bridget in particular gives off an energetic vibe, mostly through her great voice acting and writing. In fact, everyone is written and voice acted well. While I do not know my Scottish accents, all of the people that is supposed to have one does have a constant and natural sounding accent. None of them suddenly changes it for no reason and you can hear that they share the same accent.
The dynamic of Carson and Nancy is heartwarming. They both miss Kate, but they have different ways of showing it. While Nancy agrees to go to Scotland to learn of her mother’s true lifestyle, Carson wants Nancy to be safe. He does lock up some of Kate’s papers but it is to keep her safe as Carson knows her drive to solve mysteries. When he realizes Nancy will not go home till she finds out, they both have a heart to heart and Carson goes along with it.
With Nancy, you do see why everyone wants her to go back home. Nancy is the only one not caring about the harm that can befall her, mostly seen with Revenant contacting her. You can decide to do the activities Revenant gives you to gain more information about your mother and thus show how far she is willing to go. She also gets to do some cool spy stuff with the gadgets she gets. A few flashbacks to Nancy’s childhood when Kate was still alive is also nice. It further connects her to Kate and makes it more believable.
You get a lot of history of Scotland through books and newspapers, some optional and others used for puzzles. With one of the ways you can get money making cookies at the stand outside of your hotel. Though you only get a few areas to go to. I’m disappointed that Nancy did not go to where Kate had her car “accident”, especially since she went mostly for her mother, or try to dig up any reports. Most being inside, with one of the pubs not able to enter. It would of been interesting to have a lot of areas to go to branching off of the train station to give it a more of a Scottish feel rather than just locations.
There are a variety of puzzles for you to enjoy. Some puzzles go with the Scotland area such as having you figure out the names of Scottish food and recreating and recognizing a tartan design. Others use logic as you try to figure out various codes or arranging letters to unlock something. There are interesting puzzles scattered around, one of the most memorable ones contain you having to understand sheet music. Only a few puzzles are timed and they give a good amount of time in relation to what you need to do. Be careful, as most have an implied timer. You can always start over if you are caught.
Though why is Cathedral using the same passwords from eight years ago, especially when Revenant needs the information Kate has to rise again. There had to be someone in Cathedral that knew, or could of hacked into, her password just in case Revenant figured it out before Nancy.
There was one puzzle that did not work out in their favor, the Jabberwocky puzzle. Early on you find out one of the papers in your suitcase was a poem Kate kept called the Jabberwocky. Once you receive a colored version, all you know is that it is a regular poem. Though suspicion is raised with some words being colored and most not. This is when it gets muddled. Nancy Drew games are designed in a way that you can do steps out of order if possible, so you do get some wiggle room. The problem with the Jabberwocky puzzle is that you will know it is a puzzle, and not just a poem, if you skip to the last clue. Kate left a recording of her giving instructions on how to decode the message, and even Nancy says there is a message hidden in the poem, but you can not solve it yet. You have to get told to follow those instructions on a note. This could of been handled with the note not being needed to start decoding but for the player to use it as a reference, like the books you get are. I am also disappointed that you can’t find all the letters yourself, as it already writes down the letters and puts spaces where it did not specify in the recording. It would of added another way for the player to take the role of a detective.
+ Strong story
+ Good voice work and soundtrack
+ Puzzles
+ A few easter eggs scattered around
+/- Limited locations
– Some unanswered questions
– Jabberwocky puzzle
Nancy Drew: The Silent Spy is a great game in the Nancy Drew series. It was interesting having a game where Nancy is driven by her personal need to know what happened to her mother. Everything is handled seriously and you can feel how the Drew family misses Kate. It was a risk giving Kate Drew this backstory and having the player not believing it from the other family members, but it does work out. If you have not played the others, or only played some of them like I have, this is a good entry point.

The Binding of Isaac is the quintessential roguelike dungeon-crawling shooter. The player will take control of Isaac, a crying naked young boy trying to escape the basement of his home. Isaacs mother, instructed by god to take his life as a test of faith, is the final boss in the game. Each level is a unique randomly generated dungeon, with 6 to 10 rooms and a boss fight. There are six playable characters that can be unlocked, and more than a hundred different items to discover and use during each random adventure. The gameplay is simple, consisting of dodging enemies attacks and firing Isaacs tears and dropping bombs as a means of offense. The game has a dark sort of humor about it, with each stage seeming to become more and more dangerous and depressing for little Isaac. The gameplay is solid, though the story is quite simple. There are no NPC's, no quests, and no real RPG-like qualities. It is a simple and entertaining romp with a high degree of difficulty, that requires a fair ammount of luck. Created by Edmund McMillen and Florian Himsl, The Binding of Isaac is beloved amongst fans of indie games and dungeon crawlers because of its pick-up-and-play nature and simple setup. For casual players, the game will find a place as a quick and easy shoot-em-up that passes time. Hardcore completionists will have plenty to work for, with a collection system that tracks every item the player has found and many varying and difficult achievements and characters to unlock. The game is single player only, and derives much of its value from the procedurally-generated levels and humorous yet difficult gameplay. If you'd like to see some gameplay, check out
.

LogicBots
Released
Incandescent Games
Incandescent Games
3D Simulation
8th of February, 2017
Singleplayer
Incandescent Games made a hot game for engineering/robotics fans. Pun intended and as far as I’m concerned, LogicBots can be enjoyed even by a “neophyte” such as myself, who would sooner learn a few more foreign languages than pick up a college-grade maths textbook. Yes, I did volunteer to review a game who’s topic doesn’t really fall into my area of expertise, yet I am always eager to learn new things. Exact sciences may be more or less of a mystery for yours truly, yet curiosity could only be sated through a constant push towards bettering oneself. It goes without saying, that the dev team have started off very well with their Steam debut.
LB cannot really be categorized as a video game with a storyline, since you don’t have a set location, cast of characters or action/intrigue. What you do get though, is an open-ended campaign of sorts, in an undisclosed area and time frame. Creativity plays a secondary role to more in-depth knowledge about electronics. The drones or robots you shall build from scratch, are to be tested around specially conceived tracks within warehouses and you must constrain yourself to a given budget. Success is measured in advancing to bigger facilities and  more equipment at your disposal. So stop looking for a story and enjoy the game regardless. Lots to learn so it might just as well be fun, right?
Fully 3D simulators have been on Steam for many years already. Some look subpar indeed, but fortunately for LogicBots, its dev team skillfully used a handful of assets and they focused on them until you couldn’t complain about any low-res textures or performance issues. Apart from a few typos (such as “fucntional”), I could find no cons to this title's looks. The robot parts, the assembly & testing locations and even the circuit boards you shall wrap your head around, all feature the right amount of details and sufficient feedback, for even the most pretentious of gamers.
Sounds are a hit & miss, sadly. LogicBots only has a few sound effects and a repetitive soundtrack that shall force you to listen to your own songs soon enough. Or mute the sounds altogether and focus on programming in a quiet environment. I can’t imagine real life engineers listening to elevator music while tinkering away on a contraption or another.
That’s where LB’s spark is displayed in all its glory. The gameplay is unique since I haven’t had the pleasure before, to step into the virtual shoes of robotics enthusiast outside of a Sci-Fi setting. LogicBots is as grounded into reality as you can expect and by the looks of it, you start out small with seemingly simple designs (consider them highschool projects), only to quickly advance towards drones of a complexity I couldn’t have imagined. And unfortunately, so far we don’t have any flying/hovering blueprints, so all projects shall be land-based and rolling around one wheels of different types.
The well-explained tutorials should keep you busy for an hour or two, as you definitely can’t argue with their invaluable help. If you’ve never seen the insides of robot before, you probably can’t reach very far in this game without LB’s tutorials to hold your hand. Don’t even get me started on the circuit programming. If it feels like making/defusing a bomb, you’re on the right track. It’s both complex and as intuitive as it’ll ever get in a video game. I won’t bore you with the details pertaining specific parts, but rest assured that LogicBots is anything but arcade or flimsy.
It’s a fleshed out simulator approaching its rarely touched subject, with a user-friendly demeanor and also sufficient complexity without alienating the folks which build such machinery as a real life hobby. Skilled robot assembly and testing, are the ticket to early recognition for many young students and enthusiasts. It is an expensive hobby to boot but as with most things in life, as long as you’re finding peace of mind and pleasure in it, no price is too high.
I sincerely admire those who can create such gizmos in their spare time and out of their own pocket. It shows the kind of dedication to knowledge and constant improvement, that are not that foreign to me, despite my lack of applied technical proficiency. Ambition carries many masks and you cannot disrespect the labour of those which turn notebooks filled to the brim with diagrams and mathematical formulas into something very palpable and ultimately, enjoyable. The muscle has its well defined role, but it shall never hold a candle to the brain. The game is fully worth its price tag. Go buy it.

NS2 is basically StarCraft FPS; Zerg vs. Marines. The aliens and marines fight to capture and hold resources while upgrading their team to ultimately destroy the opposing teams base(s). The Aliens upgrade by evolving new powers and abilities, and the Marines upgrade through new and improoved technology. One player on each team takes on a command role, issuing orders to the other players, delegating attack, defense, and building infrastructure, all through a top-down RTS style command interface. Though the commander may issue orders, players maintain their free-will to follow or ignore those commands. Communication and team cooperation is key to a winning team.

This is one of the best open-ended puzzle games I have ever played. I might enjoy it even more than the Zachtronics games (SpaceChem, etc.)
Granted I already have a lot of experience with logic cirtcuits and can solve these puzzles by doing crazy overkill things like building state machines out of nothing but NAND gates... this experience might not be as enjoyable if you're just learning what a NAND gate is (or heck- maybe it's even more rewarding!). But I'm amazed by how much fun it is to use those skills in this game. It does a great job of removing (almost) all the annoying busywork involved in building something and leaves you with the core of engineering- designing something to solve a problem (including the fine-tuning of your design to handle real-world complexities). The various different goals for cost, speed, and component usage seem well defined and make it enticing to think through several different designs for the same puzzle.
This is catnip for engineers.

I picked up this game shortly after I heard it was going off of Steam, and its price went down to just $3. For what I paid, I really enjoyed the game. In short, its got an interesting story, unique enough combat, and a few heart racing moments that make it worth a playthrough.
Going a bit more into the story...Alan Wake is different from other games in that it tells the story in an episodic format, like a TV show. Combined with the game's horror/mystery genre, this system makes for some great cliffhangers that make you want to keep playing. The characters are diverse enough, and do actually play major roles in advancing the story at certain points. What I commend most of all is Remedy's ability to retain the whole mystery theme throughout the story. While you'll probably understand what you're fighting against, what you're fighting for is never made clear. The ending wraps up some of the story, but leaves the player to solve the mystery for themselves, adding a whole other level of depth.
The gameplay and graphics are decent. Nothing too special here, but they're both good enough not to hamper the experience. The variety of enemies is respectable, and you're put into some situations that provide grounds for unique combat scenarios. There are a few collectables, but I personally don't see the excitement in replaying the game just to retrieve these. The graphics have aged a bit, but on the positive side help the game to run well on lower end systems!
If you somehow have this game and haven't played it yet, give it a go. While the somewhat repetitive combat and dated graphics hamper the game slightly, Remedy's unique take on blending literature and gaming to tell a mystery is quite refreshing, and I'm sure you'll appreciate it!

To start, I have played this game on both PC and X-box 360, the PC version had slightly better graphics and better optimization and will focus more on that version.
Alan Wake is a third-person psychological horror game which follows a popular writer of the same name. He is looking to relax from the big picture and stress of popularity and writer temporarily so he and his wife Alice plan a get-away to Bright Falls, Washington. Not long after arriving, strange things begin to occur and seem somewhat familiar to him. The events that unfold are taken from a story that he began writing, but never finished.
Overall, the experience was wonderful and gripping. The story was not as predictable as it sounds and captures the right sides of a true psychological horror experience. Many times throughout, the music, setting, and atmosphere put me on edge and made me jump numerous times. On a side note, the soundtrack is great and have listened to it separately from the game often. The combat and general mechanics work great and do not feel clunky or misplaced. I encountered very few problems with the game and I am having trouble coming up with negative things to say about the game. I thoroughly enjoyed it and would recommend it to horror fans or fans of Remedy Software.

Truth be told I was not sure what to expect with The Binding of Isaac.
Thematically you can push the notion that it's an imaginative biblical study, or one that focuses on mental health crisis's in families, or that it's a reflection on childhood trauma...

With that being said, if you are a fan of the first Zelda's combat (which only really improved with A Link to the Past) and are admittedly skilled enough to get through the game without much trouble, then I am certain you'll have a better time with this than I did.

Wonderfully written story, perfectly delivered dialogue, yet god awful combat. The Witcher began as an extremely unique franchise with a darker twist to the univeresally known Lord of the Rings saga. While it does deliver the same topic in a different way, it is by no means a rip-off. It's a story completely capable of standing on its own two feet as something that should be remembered in the history books.
If you enjoyed the first game, you should definitely buy this one. Obviously you didn't like the first game for its combat, so it shouldn't be much of a surprise that there was a complete overhaul in the fighting methods. Rather than click and dodge like before, it's become a more sophisticated sword fighting simulator. While it does have its glitches, it does remain fair once you can get into it. Sometimes. Other times, the difficulty on normal seems ridiculously hard and the loading times can discourage you from playing forward, what's more, is that easy difficulty is ridiculous in its own rights. Normal is like playing dark souls, whereas easy is like playing a game that you payed your big brother to play for you.
But you shouldn't want this game for the combat, it's the immersion, the story, the artwork that really draws you in. You have to pay close attention and learn as much as possible in order to follow the story, but if you manage that, it becomes one of the most well crafted tales you will ever hear, with numerous factions all desparately trying to wriggle out on top.
tldr: buy this game if you want an epic continuation of an already beautiful series, only if you enjoyed the first game though.

I would love another Myst-like game, but unfortunately Quern is marred by stubbornly bad technological decisions so I couldn't even bother to play it. It has such bad performance even the starting menu caused my fans to run hot just idling.
After trying to get it to work at an acceptable level for an hour over a few days so it doesnt cook my hardware, I crawled the discussion boards for ways to improve the performance outside of the very limited graphic options in game but didn't find anything of value. It's nearly unplayable in terms of minimum requirements and I can't reccommend it to anyone as it looks and plays worse than 5 to 15 year old games that have a good design phillosophy.
Quern is anything but modern, it is made in Unity5, but I don't believe it's Unity's fault the game runs so badly. Quern's unreasonably taxing on any hardware is due to how the devs built the game like 2 ton weights dropped on your GPU and RAM and if your PC can handle the strain the devs consider it 'optimized' which is far from it.. The hardware specifications are very misleading even when hitting the recommended settings, and honestly if the game was made properly it wouldn't need anywhere near them. Indie graphics are one thing but this sort of sub-par performance is another.
Watching the trailer you would expect to be able to run it no problem at at least a solid 30fps when you have played more visually impressive games like I have, but you would be wrong. The game is about 15 hours from the developer's mouth, but they decided to load nearly everything at once on the island into the engine making the game entirely bruteforcing your hardware and it has zero smart use of optimization methods. There's only maybe a maximum of 2 splits in loading Quern. Good luck If you dont have over 8+GB of RAM as it loads everything on the island with no game loading afterwords. The per-pixel realtime rendering (that you cant turn off) causes GPUs far too much work that tanks fps unless you play in tiny fuzzy resolutions because the developer have chosen not to use any modern technique like culling.
Performance wise is anything but good... when brought up repeatedly, the only thing the developer keeps saying is play it on the lowest resolution at 600x800, avoiding the elephant in the room that the game isnt optimized in the slightest capacity and they actively chose a method that is antithetical to optimization. It has been a year since release... and the optimization patches months apart only make bandaid changes. The dev gave excuses or goes silent when pressed about atrociously bad optimization when compared to other modern or older games. When looking around for reviews, Quern even has big problems and can drop fps to 10-20fps on the recommended specs (again no use of culling, as it tries to offload everything to the GPU all at once)
There is absolutely no justification to making a game almost entirely bruteforced. It's been the standard for decades, even in the case of big taxing games, to split loading rooms, cutscenes and swap assets out for lower quality ones so this sort of thing doesnt happen. Quern needs to be entirely reworked for a smarter workload to allow seamless loading between much smaller chunks with portals and or allow you to turn off the per-pixel based realtime lighting for baked lighting or pre-rendered scenes, but as is the only video options they allow you to tweak to get better fps turn the game into a gray pixelated mess or a fuzzy tiny window. Instead the devs pursued getting 4k support into the game and leaving lower to middle end hardware out to dry.
Nothing in Quern justifies the excessive demand on the hardware, it's just held down due to bad development decisions and until the developer treats these issues with more serious care than just relying on Unity patches I'm giving it a thumbs down. Quern deserves better than this and it's the team's responsibility to deliver on some quality assurance.

The Good:
Great visuals at time of release and superb art direction and immersive detailed hubs and environments to explore. A truly interactive and mature story with an excellent branching narrative and compelling decisions to make that matter to the plot, characters, and player, all of which are interesting in their own right. Good replay value to see the various routes situations can be completed in. Many side quests have their own contained narrative to them with various resolutions.
The Bad:
Erratic difficulty curve, often very hard or very easy. Some mechanics behind the Swordsmanship skill tree feel as though they should have been fundamental to the combat while others feel useless. The user interface feels designed for a controller. Combat is only serviceable, has depth but lacks responsiveness and control.
Verdict:
The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a beautiful looking RPG with an engrossing story full of interesting characters and a compelling plot with many layers. It has short comings in various areas, most importantly its average gameplay, but it's not enough to deter my recommendation in the slightest. The Witcher 2 may have the best implementation of a branching narrative in any video game. If that interests you then you owe it to yourself to play this game.

Nana in the Dark is a small story driven adventure game which bases off the ‘survive each night’ scenario. First thing that stood out whilst playing this game was the calm relaxing music when you begin the game, unfortunately day doesn’t last forever… At night you have to defend yourself with your dog side companion Candy who fetches you batteries to help survive the night.
Interestingly the ghosts, unidentified things attack you; the torch is used as a weapon to burn these creatures but their never ending all night! The game restricts you from staying inside the apartment for too long which is a great game mechanic, especially when you are searching for sparkles to forward time. Time after time I kept replaying levels because simply they were too challenging, found the game addicting as a result.
To the developer’s credit ‘Nana in the Dark’ is fun, challenging with user controlled cut scenes. But there are some features which should be nerfed and implemented to improve the overall gameplay experience.
-	Firstly, the unidentified things spawn too often which can cause performance issues and makes the game too challenging at times especially when retreating indoors.
-	Secondly, Candy provides batteries too often making it rare to run out
-	Lastly, the map is too small with little area to move
Unfortunately there are some slight performance issues on my GTX 960, sometimes the game would slow down or freeze but fixed itself.

Overall Nana in the Dark is a game with fun, addicting core game elements and room for improvement, if you have a day spare, don’t mind the price and like what you read in this review I would recommend picking the game up.

This is my first negative review on Steam.  I always give a game a chance.  I find things to appreciate because I recognize I'm toying with someone's hard work and creativity.  That said, here's my review:
The premise and story are contrived, and the puzzles and visuals are uninspired.  In short, the game is lame.
Note:  I didn't play the game all the way through because after having made significant progress with little effort, the game suddenly lost all direction.  It was like, is there even another puzzle for me to solve?  What, where?  More to the point, why do I care?  The game gives no sense of urgency to the player for making further progress, and then it refuses to give any indication of what to do next.  That's not the kind of "mystery" you want to design into a game like this.  I didn't care enough to look up a walkthrough online, I just stopped playing and never looked back.
Pros:
-Self-updating map screen
-Awesome "Journal" feature that allows you to take pictures (as "sketches" on each page), to which you can add a brief note.  I used it extensively as I went, as if it really was my own journal, and I have to say it was the most fun I had while playing.  Yes, that's as sad as it sounds.  The document I created by myself was the best part of the game.  What does that tell you?
-The voice acting isn't terrible.
Cons:
-Lazy design work.  For example, every tree on the island is a pine, and it's the exact same model for each.  The size doesn't even vary.
I give this game a thumbs down not because anything stood out as extremely bad, but because nothing stood out at all.  If it had been a bold but failed experiment, I could at least have appreciated the attempt at innovation.  You get a lot of indie games like that.  They're trying hard, but it just doesn't work.  Quern is not even trying.  The creators seem to have picked up the formula for how to construct a puzzle game from the greats that pioneered the genre, and then put their own project together in color-by-number fashion.  Mechanically, they built it competently enough.  But no love went into the game.  Therefore, I consider my time and money wasted.
4/10

I have been considering getting a raspberry pi computer and a robots kit to build a mobile weather station (my own 'Mars rover') just for fun. But I hesitate to spend a couple of hundred dollars on a project that I might not have the talent or persistence to complete. Then I saw logicbots on Steam. For a fraction of the cost of real parts I could practice building robots and circuits before laying down the serious money.
I am only three hours into the game, but I can already see it meets my expectations. The tutorial is a very good introduction to boolean logic and simple circuit board construction. There is an extensive campaign with increasingly challenging tests, and a sandbox mode to just mess around.
Building the robots, and designing the control circuit is very interesting.The robots look realistic, and the building on the circuit boards has a simple but realistic feel. The only thing missing is writing code. The puzzles can all be solved by logic; unlike many puzzle games the difficulty is not created by making you try random guesses. The interface could be a little better designed: it often takes multiple clicks to do what I feel should be acomplished in one. But I haven't encountered any game breaking bugs.
I have read several negative reviews that fault the game because there is a small random factor in the tests: what this means is that if you repeat the same test with the same robot you might get different results. This situation is described in the tutorial under the reliability heading, and ways to engineer around it are discussed. The random factor is a deliberate part of the game, to simulate real world situations. In the real world it is almost impossible to control all the variables, so real devices must be over engineered to cope with the unexpected. Personnaly I  like this approach.  This randomness is not just luck, it is a design challenge that can be overcome by careful analysis. However, if you are looking for a strictly mathematical game with no random factors, then you might find this approach to be annoying.
I think the game is well worth the price if you are interested in programming and robotics. And much cheaper than the real thing.

I'd recommend this game for adults, or persistent teens.  I'm only about 10 levels in.  So far the game does an excellent job of letting you build and run robots through a variety of common obstacle course.  The robots are realistic, meaning you work with the kind of components you'd expect in a school's robotic lab or from an electronic retailer.  Chassis, wheels, various bits of metal beats, sensors, etc.  The logic part is pretty limited, which is part of the challenge: it's quite a bit harder to program collision avoidance with a few basic logic gates than an Arduino.  That's part of the challenge, and if you don't enjoy that, you might not find this as fun as, say, Matlab.  But I'm enjoying it.
It isn't yet polished, and I find some of the construction process tricky due to UI limitations ... but I have yet to find an actual bug in the game, which is refreshing.

Nowhere near as bad as some people are making it out to be.
PW2? No more  PW2 as TF2 or League of Legends is.
Siege Mode? Kind of like Siege mode for SMITE but with the added layer of trap management.
Survival Mode? Honestly, it doesn't quite hit that sweet spot that OMD2 did very well. For instance, you can't headshot crit enemies. You cannot double jump. Equipment that you equp to your deck isn't as interesting in the early game as it was in OMD2. But on the bright side, I can now play with more people than just one other person and defend Gondor against the onslaught of the Orcs. Early game trap variety is low, but looking at all the traps that are available later on, I can safely say that there is a lot of trap variety, and once you nlock the ability to modify your traps, it will add even more variety, you just have to spend the time and grind to get there (or spend a few hundred dollars on chests for crafting components) But actually you are literally gated by time as well becuase you have to be a certain account level to actually upgrade your items.
Crafting? It will require some grinding, yes, BUT, the grind is nowhere near as bad as grinding for new champions in league of legends. NOWHERE near as bad. Sure grinding for a new hero might actually take as long as it takes to grind for a champion in League of Legends. BUT, the crafting materials you do amass are different types, which means the crafting materials you are gathering can be used for other things like traps, traits, and upgrades. Crafting is a double edged sword. There are a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥to collect, some of which don't appear to do anything at first, but in the bright side, they don't overlap. usually. However, Rift crystals are used to craft champions, Guardians, and traits.... I kinda wish that rift crystals were used exclusively for heroes so unlocking them would be a bit easier...
Other thoughts: The progression grind may appear to be hilariously long. But if you really think about it, there is no real end game to this game. It is all really about your choices in traps you unlock and upgrade as you go to kinda build your own repertoire and specializations. By the time you unlock everything, there may be nothing to do. the 5 v5 siege mode is interesting, but I can already see that it will never ever reach that competetive level League and Dota2 have.
Honestly, I think Robot should focus more on the survival aspect like they did in their previous titles. I also think they need to liven up the skills of the heroes and perhaps decrease attack speed but increase the base damage of every hero to make them feel more impactful. This game is still in Beta (though really it feels like Season 1 of League of Legends to me) and given how drastically they have changed OMDU in its previous iterations, I am willing to bet that Robot is in fact receptive to feedback and will make changes that are not only beneficial to their bottom line, but to the player base as well.
I urge people to give Survival mode a chance and play matchmaking mode. You may actually have fun on the harder maps (for your level). The game gets quite challenging and the placement of your traps actually matter.

Updated december 7th 2015:
I've taken another look at the software after a recent update, and I definitely see improvements. I'm also amazed how quickly and seriously the devs do listen to feedbacks (something great, not a lot of companies do). So that already is one point that made me think again.
One great new thing is the list of really-quick (between 1 and 5 minutes each) tutorials, appearing right at the start of the soft. Tutorials which are very basic, but the basic infos is what was needed before that. From "Editor basics part.2" it as it explains well each part of the editor, and most importantly: the controls, which may not seem very intuitive.
This game-making software will not make you able to create an amazing game full of stuff and with next-gen graphics. But at the same time it's a 20€ game engine, so at that price you dont expect next-gen software either.
This engine costs 20€ and allows much less than for exemple Unreal Engine 4 which is free. But at the same time, the lower-level graphics, and the 'lighter' soft allows anyone to use it: no need for hyper-expensive configs to run it and use it the way you want. (I forgot to take this into account with my first review)
There are indeed features that are lacking, like for exemple being able to put water on different hights level. But I saw how quickly devs listened to feedback, and I've also discovered the "vote for new features" button hidden in the 'help' menu, and judging by the requests, the basic needs are probably already on the "to do" list. So I have no doubt it will improve.
Now is it worth it ?
Well, no, but yes at the same time.
No:
-maybe not now, because some features are lacking, and as I've seen in the comments some major updates are planned.
-it is what it claims to be, an "easy game maker", so no fancy UI (for now), and you will of course not be making AAA games with this. If you're looking for professional tools it's clearly not the way to go (again, maybe "for now").
-Graphics. Graphics are counter-strike:GO level, so not that good, but enough to play without burning your eyes ;)
-some elements are not apparent. Apparently you can change terrain textures, sky, and even scripts (which all could solve for exemple the texture quality problem). Haven't found any of that in the soft yet. The on-start tutorials are a good start on a more understandable software tho, so they need to keep improving that part.
Yes:
-features will come as the engine is updated.
-it is what it claims to be: an "easy game maker". You get what you pay for, and it may be confusing, but it's pretty simple to use indeed. Probably not for professionnals, but if you're just looking for something to try game making without having a really powerful computer or a lot of money, and maybe get something out of it, then you should really give it a try. 20€ is cheap enough, and it's not an empty powerless software at all.
-The basic stuff, the most important one you'll need to have fun, is here. Scripts, textures, all that stuff goes beyong the "easy" part, so I understand that it's not a priority for now. Water-level and menus/saves/UI features areprobably gonna be the next thing they add, and after that you'll have a complete little game maker.
Unlike previously, I do now recommend this product. It's not totaly complete yet, but it got my attention and I'll definitely start trying to get things done in it ; I am also interested to see what future updates will bring.
Clearly not for everyone, so think about what you really want from a game making software before buying it. But if you wanted a simple tool allowing you to do basic games, or just to have fun with world editing tools without knowledge of game making, nor a lot of money to spend on software/hardware, then you cant go wrong with Game Guru.

I want to give this game a "neutral" rating but I have to pick positive or negative and I think the negative is more apt.
I don't have the same complaints as other people - the siege mode doesn't bother me (I got it to play the PvE mode with friends) and I don't care about the micro-transactions, I just feel like it doesn't do OMD2 justice. It feels like a different game.
None of my complaints are things that can't be balanced before the full launch and I'd love to come back and recommend this game as things progress but as it stands right now after playing 4-5 matches with my friends I have issues with the following things:
1) The gate/guardian mechanic is weird. OMD2 was corridors to place traps in and create kill boxes. I find that more often than not in a 4 player game we wind up just wailing on enemies that are wailing on a blue barrier. This stems from my second complaint -
2) There isn't nearly enough room to place traps. Nothing in OMD2 was more satisfying than setting up a bad♥♥♥♥♥killbox that you got to watch enemies evaporate in for a wave or 2. You don't get that in this game. You have little tiny restricted areas in which to place a few traps and it's not enough to really make much of a dent in the later waves of enemies. The traps feel like an after-thought instead of a core gameplay mechanic like they were in previous games.
3) Along with there not being enough room to place traps the balance of money earned on waves and trap costs is way out of whack. The fun factor of this game would increase 10 fold if we got more coins per wave and were given more space to place traps. The trap power feels pretty okay (frost vents are still trash, always have been, tar for life) but it just feels like you don't have much room for creativity, nor the cash to be creative with trap placement.
3) Hero balance is way out of whack. Melee level up at least 2x as fast as ranged because they can hit every single enemy while the ranged shoot the melee in the back (thankfully no FF) instead of hitting enemies.
4) All hero power is way out of whack. They are all far too weak to be fun to play. Even the most basic enemies take way too many hits to the kill to the point that you don't feel powerful just annoyed that nothing dies in a timely fashion. It would be a lot more fun to be able to kill enemies faster but have more enemies to kill, with the exception of the classic exceptions which are supposed to be really tanky and hard to kill. I know the game has the different gear and traits but honestly looking at them none of them look very exciting. 12% more damge to ogres - hold the phones did someone say 12 whole percent? Against a single enemy class? Whoopie. I think the heroes should all be baseline probably 2x as powerful as they are, the amount of enemies increased to compensate, and the traits changed to more creative/engaging buffs. Faster movement speed after X number of combos in a set time period, chance to set fire or slow or freeze enemies on hit, chance to trigger double damage against certain classes, etc.
5) The special abilities are all really underwhelming. I haven't played every hero but the ones I have tried have all had really underwhelming Q and E abilities, and the V overcharge type ability is really underwhelming. There are some exceptions - I liked the fire ladies dragon's breath type channeled ability and Hogarths damage reduction is super handy but his leap ability? It's non targetable and practically a death sentence if you leap into the wrong group of enemies. I'd rather something more useful like a frost breath frontal AOE slow or a ground stop type stun. Especially with the lack of trap placement taking away most of the killbox gameplay the characters should have more CC available.
6) The respawn timer is too long when you die. Probably 2x too long. Drop the initial cooldown WAY down and make it increase with each death IMO.
7) Please for the love of everything good and holy give Maximillian the shotgun back. That stupid bow is total trash.
I think it has a lot of potential and people new to OMD might like it but for people who've been salivating for a 4-5 player co-op OMD since OMD2 are going to be disappointed. A great start but could use some tweaks to make it more fun.

UPDATE 2/18/16:
After a few months of use I have more new positive and some negative thoughts. Again my favorite part of the engine is royalty free. You just don't see that often and its really good, because this engine has great potential and there are now hundreds of scripts and mods that you can download free or purchase (Depending on what it is) and use them in your game royalty free and can sell your game. There are scripts that you can even make a full blown RPG on the gameguru store. Its a really good engine and I highly recommend it. Me and my team are currently working on a retail game using GG and we've coded our own work arounds and patches to make the engine much more flexible to our needs. TGC have been doing a fantastic job updating and fixing the engine to remove the early bugs and other problems and it even runs alot better on older hardware, which is really good because eventually this engine could even replace FPS Creator Classic (Which in my opinion is still the best FPS creator in the series).
My only negative thoughts is the GUI and change of server policy.
