The good:
GameGuru provides a fast, super easy way to build "a game".  It includes a pretty good set of models to get you started.  You can import your own models and animatons the Lua scripting language allows you to create various detailed game mechanics without any heavy programming.  It's fairly easy to throw something together fast, then come back and add details later if you want.  The dev is friendly and will usually respond if emailed.  If you don't want to learn anything, or do anything impressive, exciting, or original, this is for you.
The bad:
As I've spent more time with GameGuru, I've found that EVERY concept I've started to explore has run into bugs or crippling limitations.  I'm amazed that they release this software with so many broken features.  I can't understand why they designed the software with so many obvious limitations.  I didn't buy this software thinking is was "Unfinished/Early Access", but that is really what it is.  I guess the devs think that documentation will scare new users away, so they don't offer any.  If you make an error in a Lua script, it can go unidentified and causes the software to crash.  If you want to do something original, and your willing to learn, then look elsewhere.
6 months later:
They have changed the version number and introduced a FEW new functions.  I've discovered even more limitations.  Bugs I reported over 6 months ago have been confirmed by other users, but are still not even acknowledged by the developer, and most definately NOT FIXED.  There is no real system for reporting bugs, only a forum that is seemingly ignored by the developer.  Some of the included models got broken at some point, and have not been fixed.  They have improved framerates, but even with framerates around 90-100 FPS I still have jerky movement that looks like im getting 20 FPS.  They still don't provide any proper documentation, only an online guide through Steam that is still missing many functions, and lacking critical details of the functions that it does cover.  The few "support staff" type people usually can't offer anything useful(if they respond at all), and any real help comes from other users.
Recently I've spent more time testing a few new features and I've found that none of them allow me to take my project any further.  There are still just too many basic functions missing.  The "lead developer" is now claiming he's the "only developer" and that's become the go-to reason given for the lack of progress on anything meaningful.
Development goals come from a list that users vote on.  Unfortunately since they have marketed this to users that don't understand even basic programming, the development goals that are voted on are mostly things that can be done through the existing scripting language even with it's significant limitations.  There are a series of youtube videos that explaing how to do various things. Users that don't care to look at the videos, or unable to follow examples of even the simplest methods can simply make a feature request.  Lee, the solitary developer, is all too happy to add these simple requests to his 'feature vote" list(maybe because they will be easy to check off this list, and this list is his measure of progress).  In this way, Lee has made for himself an endless list of simple tasks that make the software more "idiot friendly", but do nothing to make the software more capable.  I'm afraid he's chosen to "rearrange the deck chairs on the Titanic" with the community driver feature vote.  It's clear that this software isn't going to get the basic features that it still needs to be a "real" engine any time soon.
In a recent email to the developer(Lee), I asked about problems I was having due to "gimbal lock" and the fact that several bug reports I made had been ignored.  His response was to ignore the bug report question completely(what a surprise!), and he offer explanation about Euler rotations while acting like he didn't understand what "gimbal lock" is as he dismissed the issue and even claimed it was a "feature".  He said "Strangely, you're the first to quiz this feature of the engine", and he said gimbal lock is "an engine choice that works for most uses".  His implication was that he had not heard of this issue, and could not conceive of a situation where this might be an issue, and IF it was a problem, I was the only one complaining about it.  I gave him some examples of how gimbal lock was limiting what I could do, but he never responded.
A quick look at the "Feature Vote" list:  At this time(7/29/16) I can see that if we're lucky in 3 months, Lee will be working on "implementing" a function that already exists and was explained in a instructional video 7 months ago("Quest Givers").  6 months from now he might be on to another function that was also explained 7 months ago("Inventory").  After 9 months we are literally back to square one("Quests").  After maybe a year, he'll get around to another one that was covered 9 months ago(Lifts and Conveyors).  The features I mention here are all things that are easy to do now.  The "Feature Vote" list is a bad joke.  Most of the "features" on the list are things that are already present, or things you can't believe GameGuru still doesn't have.
With this product even a monkey can make a really bad game!  I've owned GameGuru since it come out on Steam, and I just haven't seen any progress in the direction I would like to see it go.  It has, at times, been interesting to experiment with and find ways to try to work around the many limitations of this software, but ultimately it's been a complete waste of my time.

Short rating: 6/10
First of: The game in itself is a lot of fun.
The graphics are pleasing, the mechanics work smoothly, and the riddles are mostly fun.
But!:
-Your inventory WILL get cluttered
-Some riddles are a chore to solve (run around, check the entire area, and remember 20 things at once)
-It often feels like you're too busy to scroll through the abundance of mostly useless items to actually focus on what the clues might mean
-Some riddles don't give you any clues at all, and feel random when you finally solve them
-There's little to no consistency regarding the riddles. Some are impossibly hard to solve and require you to check the ENTIRE island for clues, and other riddles are basically just "Click this 3 times."
Everything else is great, though. It's a satisfying game to play.
Do I recommend this game?
Yes, but barely.
It's a well made game, but a lot of times it's simply frustrating to play.
The game tries too hard to implement riddles, and shoves usable items down your throat before it lets you even attempt to solve a puzzle.
And by the time you get to an area where you need said items, you've already forgotten what you have in your inventory, and what ost of the items even do.
Who knows, I might just be too dumb for this game, and it's meant for really smart people who can micromanage and keep track of dozens of things at once.

I just completed Quern. What an amazing journey. Since falling in love with MYST and Riven, I've been a on an endless quest to find a game possessing the same story-rich, fully-immersive qualities. Thank you for such a beautiful and HUGE gaming expericence.

A really enjoyable Myst clone, though probably a little bit simpler and not as bang-your-head-against-the-wall. A bit more linear, probably has a lot in common with The Room too, though the feel of the place is very Myst. The puzzles were intuitive and fun, with many that I hadn't seen in a puzzle game before, and others that were comfortingly familiar.
Ran smoothly for me, and the visuals are decent. No mindblowing graphics, and the draw distance is kind of sad, but it being a puzzle game, this isn't that important. The actual aesthetic is lovely, if a bit desaturated.
The game has been updated since its release -- comparing my own experience to a Let's Play -- improving some puzzles to avoid you wandering around lost for what to do, and also adding some optional guidance (press Alt to highlight interactable objects, or click the Hint button for inventory items).
The voice-acting is a little bit weak, but these are also one-sided conversations, so it's hard to go all out on them. The backstory of the world is pretty cool, and it's nice that you get some payoff for what's happening in the story. The music is also pretty nice, as is the sound design - it's nice to have the auditory feedback.
For colour-blind players: There is currently no colour-blind support within the game, and a few of the puzzles DO rely solely on colour. (Thinking specifically on the Alchemy section.)  It is not integral to the gameplay, and most puzzles that incorporate colour also have other visual signifiers. It's still playable, and the developers have said they wanted to add colour-blind modes, but as of now they haven't. Keep this in mind.
For deaf players: There's at least two puzzles that rely on sound -- one pitch-based, and one volume/sound-shape based. They have visual representations, so you can solve them easily by looking up a walkthrough, but it's kind of annoying. Beyond that, all voice-acting has subtitles.
With that all in mind, it is definitely worth buying while it's on sale, and probably even when it's not.

###############Original Review#############
While the game is fun and interesting to play unfortinatly I can not currently reccomend buying this game. I enjoy these type of games, and this one has potential but with one major turnoff in its current state, the same turnoff that made Bad Rats a bad game... you can run the exact same robot with making zero changes what so ever and get three entirely different results. It seems the calculations are tied to the frame rate, but when VSync enabled still bounces the frame rate between 60-61 (200+ with Vsync disabled) that 1 FPS bouncing back and forth at different times ends up making the same robot without being modified at all do different things each time.
If they can get the Bad Rats issue out of this game I would fully recommend it, but when a game about making minor tweaks to fix issues can not even keep the same results when running the same thing over and over it makes it more of a game of luck then of actually making the perfect tweaks.
It has potential, it is fun even with that issue, but I just can not recommend it fully until that gets sorted out.

So if you woke up in the middle of a land you’ve never been to and have no idea who you are? You’d probably wonder, but what if… you had a magical talking sword and a little companion who doesn’t know how to shut her mouth? You’d probably be confused or more the less, terrified. Yeah, welcome to Dust: an Elysian Tail.
Dust: an Elysian Tail is a 2-D indie fighting game that is good-looking, fun, and has a really fine story. First off and most importantly: the gameplay is really satisfying. The combat system in the game is original and unique in a way that you can rack up to 100+ combos in seconds. Rampage destruction on your enemies and take them out first before they take YOU out. Be warned for if you’re not careful in the battlefield, you will be taken out. The gameplay is distinctive like that so you’re not completely this invincible warrior taking people out with one swing like in most games. Of course, the common enemies you find here are quite easy to kill; but also quite dangerous when they start grouping up on you. At first the game lets a few slips here and there, but as it progresses, it gets more and more punishing for each little mistake. But when you push out and get over countless kills, it’s all-the-more satisfying. When you get to that boss and take him/her out, nothing has ever felt more satisfying. Though, from time to time, the game will push you to your limit and you must push though. It’s excruciating at times, but it is genuinely worth it.
As a reward for this, if you complete combos or take out a group of tough enemies, you will be given experience. The level-up system in the game is interesting for you can level up certain things every time you do so. So you can continue your path of terror. Like Skyrim, Dust: an Elysian Tail gives you that rare thing to be able to level up anywhere you want to, unlike most games where you have to level up certain things to be able to proceed correctly. Now, let’s move on to the graphics, where it’s about as good as the gameplay.
… if not better.
Dust: an Elysian Tail has about the finest hand-painted world. Yes, you heard me, everything in this game was HAND MADE. This is mostly Dust’s strongpoint; the world, characters, and even down to the details in the menu are beautiful. The flora, the towns, the strongholds, and even that flow of lava that’s going to kill you in a few seconds, are all gorgeous. This amazing art-styled graphics are combined with anime-style characters; to add to that, they’re animals, furries if you will. Now I can already see some of you already turning away from the game. Personally, though, this doesn’t change anything at all. Personally it goes well with the overall game, makes the game’s visual presentation more effective. The story is also quite wonderful…
Now, the story is about…
Hah, I got you there didn’t I? I’m not going to spoil it (or much of it). But I’ll say that the story is purely wonderful. It has the perfect blend of characterization, humor, and masterful storytelling. Just get the game; I will say it’ll be worth your time.
Downsides?
Not much, besides a few bugs and a few A.I. glitches. Sometimes the game can get irritating to get by, but overall not much going against it.
So just get Dust, it will be worth it.
Personal Gamer Score:
9/10
Recommend this game for those who want an awesome game with a good story, art/graphics, and an excellent game with good gameplay. But I may not recommend it for those who dislike anime-style graphics or sometimes time-to-time irritating gameplay.

GameGuru is a very particular piece of software, as in "there is nothing like it or close to it": A 3D game creation program with a VERY low learning curve. You can piece a simple FPS together in less than an hour using only the assets and prefabs.  If you put your mind into it and fiddle around (as I did), you can achieve quite beautiful landscapes with enough content to actually make a descent looking game. Now, as the negative reviews are stating, the drawback of creating a tool that is meant to be easy to use is, of course, some limitations. My biggest gripe currently being the terrain painting tool which is too basic in the editor, you actually have to test your game to change the textures and ambiance. You can import your own assets, again, the process in doing so is, to say it lightly, a pain in the rear, especially since it uses the rather obselete .x format files as its only option. But then again, you can modify the scripts (LUA) and obtain some interesting results. The guys at TGC are working on a 3rd person camera view (already partially working) and the integration of the FBX format for assets. So it's all a work in progress and updates have been popping up pretty much every month.

Over the last couple months, i been using gameguru, first off id like to mention how amazingly easy is to get the hang of , i had it figgured out the day i got it , the lua scripting (assuming your experienced in any scripting) is very easy to learn and if you are not experienced , in my opinion lua scripting would be a great place to start, as so far it seems to be easiest scripting language to get the hang of. for example i took one of my gsc scripts i wrote for my codwaw mod , and rewrote it in .lua , so i would have it in gameguru, now when i had originally wrote the script , to make it work bug free , it took about 4 or 5 hours , and was just over 500 lines of code , to do a script that does same thing in .lua (and of course have it working bug free) , it took me just over an hour , and uses less then 100 lines of code. So you can notice what im saying when i say lua scripting , is deff easy to get the hang of , and a great start for people wanting to gain the knowledge of coding...
As for the community for gameguru , i have to say in my opinion , its hands down the best modding/scripting community ive come across, and ive come across alot of different modding/scripting communities. An amazing feature offered at the gameguru website aswell is the zendesk , which ive never seen at any modding/scripting community , where the creators of mod tools or said software , are able to be contacted for support , you can directly message them , and get a very helpful reply reasonably quick , for instance , everytime i've message them my wait time on reply has never been more then a day.
Game-Guru Software has a variety of useful , easy-to-use , & helpful tools , including character creator & import model , which character creator is a very use way to design you own characters with a variety of character creator assets and custom assets can be made and added to use , and import model speaks for itself , but the really cool part of this feature , which i find very unique , is the ability to actually do the model scaling and settings all in the one screen.
On top of all that, there is also an asset store , where users can buy very cool assets (guaranteed to work great) for a reasonable price, not to mention with this software , your not just making a mod on game already created , you actually make your own game , and to the point where you have rights to sell of you want to, there is not much else i can say other then check it out if you have not , its amazing & you should :D

The Witcher 2 world is simply wonderful, picturesque, varied and vast, incomparable to any other role-playing game.
It isn’t open world game. But don’t worry, you won’t run along the paths on both sides limited by invisible walls. CDPR replaced them seamlessly with natural obstacles like chasms, giant trees or very thick bushes. Locations are very diverse. These are cities, villages, open areas, and covered with dense vegetation and ancient elven forest where tree crowns blurring high in the clouds. All amaze diversity and ingenuity. The new proprietary engine Red Engine perfectly shows a play of lights, creating a magical atmosphere, paradoxically also realistically.
Combat plays crucial role in the game at any moment we have the opportunity to duel difficult opponent and even take part in the epic battles. The fighting has changed since the first Witcher. We have stronger and more powerful attacks to choose from, varied by passive and active skills. There are three paths of character development: swordsmanship, alchemy and magic. Generally, fighting system is fun, scenic and rewarding, it requires constant attention and feline reflexes, because sometimes we literally have only split seconds to activate protective emblems or attack an open enemy. Not everyone will like this rule, since some players might get frustrated fighting larger groups or one difficult enemy.
Overall, The Witcher 2 Assassins of Kings is a beautiful game with modern graphics and addictive gameplay, with its emphasis on realism, psychologically complex characters, original and surprising missions, elections burdened consequences, rewarding combat, good music, humor, sex and climate. First of all, the climate! All these elements form a coherent whole for making up the unique atmosphere. We have, moreover, to deal with the so-called immersion, true masterpieces in terms of visualization and scenario.

Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is a lobby-based tactical shooter developed by Valve Corporation. Players join either the Terrorist or Counter-Terrorist team and complete objectives to win the match. CS:GO’s most well-known game mode sees Counter-Terrorists fighting to stop Terrorists from planting a bomb at a designated sight by eliminating them or defusing the explosive. At the start of each round, players purchase weapons using money earned from previous rounds. CS:GO’s community has developed an abundance of custom maps and game modes that expand or reinvent default gameplay. A huge assortment of in-game weapon cosmetics can be acquired by playing the game to distinguish yourself from other players.

Now I realize this might have appeal only to a specific demographic, but it's a demographic that's rapidly growing. Do It Yourself hobbies are on the rise and climbing faster everyday. Leading the charge is the world of electronics. I myself am a relatively new inductie. About 8 months ago, while plugging in my phone charger at work, staring at the powerstrip under my desk it occurred to me that I don't know very much about electronics. I consider myself a learned guy, college grad with a degree in philosophy and a view that an education carries far more worth than it's potential monetary value down the line. And I LOVE all things science so to not know much about something so pervasive as electronics didn't sit well at all.
Two weeks later, two dozen books later with 1000's of various components bought online and I was well on my way to learning everything I could. The end result, cutting a long story short is that I just finished my first semester back in college working towards a second degree, a B.S. in Nanoelectronics and all this stemming from my plugging in my charger. I mention all this because this game has been exactly the kind of game I've been dreaming/searching for ever since then. I just finished taking DC Circuits, C++ programming and well Chemistry tho that's less applicable here, but after 4 intensive months, I still managed to learn something new within the first two tutorials. But what's more is that it's really damn fun.
I, and I'm sure I'm not a lone, have my fair share of guilt whenever I spend more than a reasonable amount of time, (however we each define it), playing games when I should be learning something, anything. So to have a game that not only challenges/works out our critical thinking, problem solving, analytical reasoning skills, introduces concepts found in electronics, engineering, physics, and programming and is a really fun puzzle game to boot is a win win...win.
I especially enjoy the set up to each challenge. "Here's the course, the problem, challenge, puzzle or what have you, now go make a robot that can maneuver the challenge". And you're off building, testing, rebuilding then putting together circuit boards utilizing  boolean based logic gates and the like,  having fun all the while. This is the kind of game we should support.
Let's be honest, for many of us, gaming is an escape from the world beyond our monitors. And there's nothign wrong with that (in moderation). I admit that's why I game. But we all have to return to the larger world sooner or later so why not taking something away from our time spend in escape? That's my two cents anyhow

(An exerpt from an essay I used to get into college.)
"Hotline Miami takes place in a gritty alternate reality, one where the Russians, not Americans, are the world’s dominant superpower. In Miami, tensions between Russians and Americans are high, culminating with vigilantes intent on ridding the city of its Russian mobs. However, these vigilantes are controlled by anonymous phone calls, and many of them carry out the will of a higher organization out of fear of what would be done to them if they didn’t comply. The game revolves around discovering the truth behind the phone calls and the true motivation behind the attacks of the vigilantes. With tight game mechanics and a pulse-pounding house music soundtrack, Hotline Miami is a frustratingly addictive masterpiece.
While highly praised for the intensity of its gameplay, Hotline Miami has more than just murder and mayhem to offer to the gamer. The game has a deep, intriguing storyline hiding beneath the gameplay.  The plotline of the game is in anachronic order, meaning the gamer must piece together the story for themselves as they push through each successive level. And, with every level, tidbits of the personalities of the vigilantes are revealed. For example, the gamer must dissect the motivation of the protagonist when he goes from systematically taking out the Russian mobs to attacking a Miami police station. Was it only a means to an end, discovering who was behind the phone calls? Or had the brutality of his actions warped him into a madman who killed for sport? The game offers a structurally complex story for the gamer to decode for themselves."

TLDR: A fun (While somewhat flawed) FTP MOBA/survival co-op 8/10
Mind that the review below is mainly on the survival mode, as I only tested out the MOBA portion a bit.
Pros:
1: Stays true to the trap elements from OMD1-2 and mixes it up a little bit, even unlocking the traps isn't too grindy. Overall a good job on the traps.
2: With the multiple gamemodes, and the ability to have a five man team, there's a lot of variety avalible.* (See later)
3: The new hero set up and abilities work alright, excluding a few OP skills for certain characters, its relatively balanced (For beta) and has a good feel.
4: Combat is nice and fluid, the skills and combat blend well
TLDR: I get kinda ranty, ranged combat needs to be tweeked, and map/launcher
Cons: (Mind that many of these are nitpicks, I'd rated most of these as .3 of the pros above when it comes to importance)
Combat negatives
1: A grave loss from the original series.... Headshots don't deal extra damage anymore, they flat up state it in the tutorial. Now I don't care if its a moba-esc game, but come on! Give headshots a mild buff like 1.2 damage.
2: Spam to win nature of ranged characters, with the loss of extra headshot damage, the only thing you need to do in close quarters (Even long range) is hold M1 and use abilities while back peddling. This is absolutely terrible, Though the combat feels alive with the abilities/traps, you need *Something* to give the player a reason to aim carfully, to consider his next shot. OMDU does not currently have this, and it shows.
3: (really minor... But its important to me okay :(  ) The ranged weapons of both the original mages, feel almost exactly the same, there's no meaty sound effect for the crossbow, and there isn't a real difference in projectile speed for the wand. Don't get me wrong, they're different, one has an arcane effect and the other has just physical, they impact enemies very differently.
But If it were my game, I'd want them to feel different.
4: *You will end up repeating the same maps a good few times until you level up, which is good and all since at least 1/5 players has probably done the map before, so he/she knows some good trap spots. But it sucks being the player who's done the map 4 times in a row(Mind that the maps are big and detailed, so if you get bored of mid, switch to left, or right, or back etc).
5: The game's launcher is disgusting(No, not the weapon), it opens a new window behind the original instead of fading the game into the launcher window. It just lacks style you know?
Again, 8/10 game, but needs to fix its combat system up a little bit and possibly put some more stages (perhaps user created stages? (That get approved)) into each leveling segment to add variety to the map pool.

There are some things that I really like about Game Guru and some things that I think could use some improvement.
Pros -
The complexity is managed exceptionally well in this title. The editor is extremely intuitive. There's very little chance of really screwing up your work. The editor is in a very early stage of development. There’s a great amount of effort spent on communicating with users, both listening to complaints, requests and compliments. There is also a lot of educational material produced and a nice BLOG to keep up to date on how the product is developing. The pace of development is quick. There are thousands of expansion objects available for purchase to help start projects. You can import externally created objects. Lua scripting support is getting better all the time!
Cons -
The engine isn't as polished as others. Performance isn't that great. (But is being worked on heavily at the time of this writing.) What can be produced is limited to what's supplied in many ways and extending the tool beyond it's original feature set is still somewhat painful. More comprehensive help/documentation is needed.
Conclusion -
The engine isn't for everyone. It is for people interested in making games who want to focus on design / strategy more than technical details. Coming from a software engineering background, I've developed a great appreciation for the amount of work that goes into making products that simplify processes in a smooth and intuitive way. I have been and continue to be impressed by this project.

This is my very first review on steam. Even though I have a few dozens of games in my library, i played every other game with certain expectations and it was matched (for the most part). Quern on the other hand blew all those expectations out the window. As an induvidual game developer and a real enthusiast of this genre of games, I have tried my hand at it only to be met with varying results of success. Quern on the other hand feels almost like a AAA puzzler created by an indie studio.
There are a few minor flaws but as a huge fan of the Myst series, this is the sequel we should have gotten to Riven. Myst 3: Exile is a competantly made game but really easy at times. With Quern, i found the right balance of figuring out puzzles really quickly and being stumped at certain points in time unable to progress. The comparison to Riven is inevitable as the whole world of Quern is one entity and compeonents from different parts of the world solve puzzles in another. This is a solid effort from an indie studio and it never feels like it. This game was the best $5 i have ever spent on steam since the Talos principle (which is also an awesome puzzle game..with it's own game mechanics). Immensely recommended for all fans of puzzle games and especially fans of the Myst series!

In all it is a good game, but I would recommend it for young players or players that are new to puzzle games.

The following review was written long ago during Early Access. The game has improved, with community features such as Steam Workshop now built-in to the game, more fun things to do, and an optimized core for smooth play. This is a fantasic game for builders, thinkers and puzzlers, but don't just take my word for it, read what my former-self said about the game before it weas even complete:
What is LogicBots? This is a sandbox simulation where you get to build autonomous robots to do your bidding. The core gameplay is a huge set of 'levels', each with several potential goals. You review your objective(s), then with a set budget and assortment of bot-bits and coloured wires you set-out to custom-build a bot-to-order. The construction requires both the physical conformation as well as a circuitboard with the logic-gates that define how your bot's inputs manipulate it's outputs. Once you think you've got the right mix of form and function, you press a button and the simulation takes over: your assembled bot is thrown into the level and left to it's own devices.
Each level's 'sub-quests' will futher challenge your imagination as you work to improve your bot and are forced to dream of more efficient and clever ways to achieve your goals. If you want to play socially, it's fairly easy to export/import your bots to share with friends - the game generates a PNG thumbnail and XML text file that makes it a snap.
Although this game is still in 'beta' it has kept me challenged and engaged for hours on end. While there is a steep learning curve for a person like me, the challenge doesn't become stale. I've always been a fan of sandbox games, so I'm sure I'm a bit biased, but this game has huge potential. The developer is active in the Steam Community forums (Fall 2014) and very responsive to feedback.
Undoubtedly worth the current $20 buy-in if you enjoy games that challenge your mind. Heck, you'll save that much in solder and wire after just a few bots!

I never thought that the combining FPS with MOBA elements would be such a great combination, but Paladins pulled it off. While many say it's a cheap knock-off of Overwatch, I've never played the latter, so I can't really say.
What I CAN say, though is that Paladins offers gameplay that will appeal to people interested in the strategy (MOBA) aspect of the game, AND to people who just want to jump in and start shooting stuff.
The games also don't take too much time, so the it can act as a quick intermission without really messing your schedule up.
That said, the game is not without bugs. The interface doesn't show you the ping of the region server you're choosing, so you won't know if you're lagging or not until you're actually in the game already. The latest update also activates the 'Auto Buy' feature, which is a pain in the a$$.
I've also encountered several hackers while playing the game – it's a massive bummer to go through an entire game with zero kills and like 20 deaths (all from headshots). The devs say they're working hard to fix this (and I hope they do), but in the meantime, it's a major buzzkill.
All in all, I highly recommend people to give the game a shot. It's fun, easy to grasp, and free to play (although I got impatient and bought the 'all characters' pack lol).

(An exerpt from an essay I used to get into college.)
"Hotline Miami takes place in a gritty alternate reality, one where the Russians, not Americans, are the world’s dominant superpower. In Miami, tensions between Russians and Americans are high, culminating with vigilantes intent on ridding the city of its Russian mobs. However, these vigilantes are controlled by anonymous phone calls, and many of them carry out the will of a higher organization out of fear of what would be done to them if they didn’t comply. The game revolves around discovering the truth behind the phone calls and the true motivation behind the attacks of the vigilantes. With tight game mechanics and a pulse-pounding house music soundtrack, Hotline Miami is a frustratingly addictive masterpiece.
While highly praised for the intensity of its gameplay, Hotline Miami has more than just murder and mayhem to offer to the gamer. The game has a deep, intriguing storyline hiding beneath the gameplay.  The plotline of the game is in anachronic order, meaning the gamer must piece together the story for themselves as they push through each successive level. And, with every level, tidbits of the personalities of the vigilantes are revealed. For example, the gamer must dissect the motivation of the protagonist when he goes from systematically taking out the Russian mobs to attacking a Miami police station. Was it only a means to an end, discovering who was behind the phone calls? Or had the brutality of his actions warped him into a madman who killed for sport? The game offers a structurally complex story for the gamer to decode for themselves."

First off I been on Steam for a really long time, and this is the first time I have written a review. Not because this game is better than every other game I have played, but because I feel like there needs to be more people playing this so that it can really go far.
This game (if you can call it that, more on that later) might be in Early Access, but it is one of the most complete games I've played in early access. I have only ran into one bug that happened twice in my first 10 hours of game play. That bug being that it crashed when starting the simulation. Otherwise everything works as expected.
The reason I would maybe not consider calling this a game is because it’s not designed to be some easy pickup and play. It’s a robot simulator, well maybe not even that. It’s a circuit simulator that happens to have robots.
If you don’t understand Boolean operators, AND, OR, NOT, or XOR then this game might not be for you. This really did take me back to basic circuit building.
There is only a sandbox piece to the circuit building. To use the robots you have to play through all the levels and unlock the components. Another downside is there is almost no community around this game as of this writing, so if you get stuck on a level your SOL. At least for now, I really hope that changes and we see a bigger community.
Go play it! Have fun building and then re-building.

After playing this game for a short while, I have decided that it is finally time to do a review on this game.
First off, I would like to talk about the graphics and visuals. For a game that is only in its beta stage, I am very surprised at visual modelling of the weapons, maps etc. It is surprisingly stunning. However, I have noticed that some of the player models when holding certain weapons don't exactly look too pleasing. Specifcally the remington pistol, as it appears that the player model's right hand goes through the gun. (I am talking about third-person stance.) This is an easy fix for later updates.
Next, I would like to talk about the damage of various weapons. The balancing is decent for the time being, except I feel snipers like the M24, and other cheaper snipers, still one shot in the arm and leg. Personally this is rather off putting, and I would suggest that the rifles do less damage on arms and legs, therefore forcing the player to improve their aim by going solely for body and headshots. This is separate to the SVD Dragunov sniper. As of being semi-automatic, this rifle was balanced fairly well by making it 2-3 shots in body and arms/legs, and 1 shot in the head. The balancing for that is fine. Pistols are also a problem some time. I am finding myself hitting too many headshot 1 shots with pistols at long range, which does seem really unfair for the opposing team. If this was reduced to two or three at range, it would be much better. (Unless I am headshotting enemies that have already been tagged.)
Furthermore, the running speed of the knifing is causing the player to glitch, by causing them to 'climb' other people and elevate them. Whether this is a glitch with collisions rather than running speed, the speed that the player travels when sprinting with the knife should be lowered a fraction.
Finally, I'd like to talk about the maps. I recently played a map called 'factory' (I think), and it appeared to be a complete reskin/remodel of the middle area, t and ct spawn, long and bombsite A of the Counter STrike: Global Offensive map, Dust II. This was rather surprising, but I was disappointed at how small the map was, therefore for maps like this, I'd suggest increasing the map size, and maybe alter it so tunnels and bombsite B were present too, but add extras around the map, like higher platforms accessible by ladders, or underground tunnels etc.
Overall, I am really suprised at how well this game looks, and will continue to play the game. I even intend to make a video sometime soon on this, and give more feedback.

Phenomenal. This game was an absolute blast to play through, especially for a genre I generally don't enjoy (this being the Beat-Em-Up aspect of the game, not the Metroidvania aspect of it). The world is highly open and fun to explore, with absolutely incredible atmosphere and a slightly cliché though very well polished story. The music as a whole is solid, though admittedly I only really found myself truly attached to a few songs in the game. It fits the world though, and it knows when to pick up and when to slow down. The characters are pretty enjoyable, each of which having their own unique qwerks and characterization to make each individual character in the game so compelling. It helps that the voice acting is honestly pretty good. The anthropomorphic-animal-type character design is offputting at first, but it really didn't detract from anything.
All of this is topped off by one of the most fluid, reactive, and satisfying combat engines I think I've ever played. Combos are given to you relatively early so you have plenty of time to practice using them, and I'd be lying if I didn't say I haven't sent chills down my spine for some of the absolutely insane stuff I've been able to pull of. Despite having one weapon (two if you count his companion Fidget), Dust has a huge variety of ways to handle pretty much every enemy in the game, and very rarely does mowing down hordes of minions ever get stale. The artstyle helps ludicrously in this department, making each hit feel rewarding and managing to maintain a long-lasting combo stupidly satisfying. This game has its share of Action RPG elements in it as well, with stuff like shops, level ups, and various equipment options to choose from as the game expands.
All of this made the game such an absolute thrill to play, and if you can manage to snag it for the deal I got it at (Three and a half dollars!? What!?), there's no question as to whether you buy this game or not. This game is nearly flawless.
Oh, and pretty much all of this game was made by one person - Dean Dodrill. Incredible.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a fun action-adventure game with plenty of secrets and references to other indie games. At the start, you are discovered by the sword, Ahrah, and it's guardian, Fidget (a character vaguely reminiscent of Ruby from LUNAR 2: Eternal Blue.) It's really fun to whirl through the air and through hordes of enemies on your way to discover your identity and purpose. While the first half of the game is a stroll through plains and mountains that look very similar, the second half takes you underground, through hallowed ground, over snowy peaks, and into a fiery volcanic basin. There are only a few bosses and the enemy design is sometimes bizarre, but mostly a standard cast of trolls, minotaurs, goblins, et al. Regardless, the art style is coherent and enjoyable. The game is not very difficult on the standard difficulty and there are no instant fatalities (i.e. there are no pits and lava/spikes only cause nominal damage.)
Overall, I was reminded of the feel of Super Ghouls 'n' Ghosts, if Arthur was an unstoppable flying anthropomorphic mink/fox. This game is definitely worth the few hours of your time to play if you generally enjoy platforming and hack-and-slash mechanics.

This is a pretty ingenious game that has very good controls and a (predictable) really engaging story. You play as Dust, a warmblood who awakens with no memory of who he is or how he got there. He meets Fidget and a talking sword named Arrah and the three embark on an adventure to discover who he is and what he has to do.
The game is a 2D/3D hybrid, much like the style of Shadow Complex. The game has a map system, hidden treasures, and powers that you must acquire in order to go back and find things you might have missed or need to progress.
There's also an element of RPG, where by killing enemies, Dust earns XP and can upgrade his stats using skill gems, in the area of health, attack, defense, and Fidget.
The combat is very enjoyable and is friendly to people who just like to button mash and those who like to use combo moves. The game rewards you with bonus XP for higher hit combos, so it's in your best interest to not get hit.
You can earn money and materials to buy and craft new items to make Dust quite a force to be reckoned with.
The voice acting is a little cheesy at some points, but it's pretty enjoyable, and most of the actors they got fit their parts.
Some say if you don't really like Anime or "Furries" then you shouldn't play this game. I say, that's really not true. Whether or not you're a fan of either, the game is a lot of fun. It's probably a solid 10-11 hours of gameplay if you just want to get through the game, more if you are a completionist. Highly recommended.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a game unlike any other I've played before. Alone, the many parts that make up DustAET are extraordinary. Together, they form a whole that is definitely more then the sum of its parts.
The artwork of DustAET is spectacular, nestled firmly in the "Disney" category in terms of style. Don't let the cute art style confuse you, though. The story going on behind the scenes is suprisingly mature in terms of content. The story of DustAET is one of genocide, terrible crimes, redemption, and eventually, sacrifice. DustAET holds a rare place in my list of games as one of the very few games which have brought genuine tears to my eyes at the ending. I won't spoil that ending, but it touched me in a way that very little does these days.
Moving back to the artwork, DustAET is beautiful from start to finish. Each level is lovingly hand-drawn. Each character and enemy is hand-animated. It all comes together in a feast for the eyes. The music, too, is a feast. Done by HyperDuck SoundWorks and Funky Rustic, the soundtrack is one that I've already listened to many times and likely will for much longer. Each level has music that fits the art perfectly.
The combat system of DustAET is fluid and simple, but surprisingly difficult to master. Two buttons let you make combos. Combined with the one of the secondary character's magic attacks, you can unleash partile hell on your enemies. The combat would be the one area, though, that is a bit lacking. Enemies aren't overly challenging, but in the final level, there's a new enemy type that defies all the rules of combat tought to you so far. It seems more then a bit unfair, but it also is explained by those enemies being professional soldiers, so I'll let it slide.
The boss fights were lacking as well. Nothing overly special up until the final boss. The final boss, on the other hand, is a three part affair, ending in a map with hugely damaging environmental hazards. The final boss is so tough that it almost feels broken at times. The satisfaction of beating it, though, is worth it. Turning the difficulty up doesn't do much for bosses or enemies. They use the same A.I. and are vulnerable to the same combos. They just have more health and do more damage, making them more annoying instead of more challenging.
There's a fair bit of side content in the form of treasure, secrets, and side quests. There's little incentive to do them, though, unless you really love your achievements. The amount of backtracking required to get them all is a put-off for me and probably anyone else who isn't OCD about getting 100% completion.
The RPG elements of DustAET are weak and could almost be ignored, but they do add some spice to things, particularly the gear and crafting system. They're there if you want to take advantage of them, but monsters will drop gear from time to time and you can probably get by with that stuff.
The only other point worth mentioning is the voice acting. The entire cast of characters are voiced, which is impressive. The voice acting suffers a bit, with some characters sounding far too happy, while others seem a bit stilted. One voice actor in particular clearly had a bad microphone. None of them are bad enough to ruin the experience, though. It's just an annoyance, and a minor one at that.
Dust: An Elysian Tail puts many AAA game developers to shame with its content, reasonable price, and stunning art and music, more so when you consider it was the work of one man, plus the sound team. Even more amazing, DustAET is a port from the Xbox 360, but it certainly doesn't feel like it. DustAET is a PC port that feels like it was born on PC to start with, another thing that puts almost all AAA developers to shame.
Dust: An Elysian Tail is clearly a work of love and passion, and it shows. For $14.99, the game is more then worth the money you'd pay for it. Highly recommended.

First and foremost I am honoured to be the first to review this game on steam, it's as old as I am, but is a favourite classic.
Zork: Grand Inquisitor is an old point and click adventure game (If you like Deponia or anything by Humongous Entertainment, you may enjoy this.) It was the last official Zork game released and one of the few graphical ones.
Being released in 1997, this game does show it's  age, particularly during cinematic cutscenes. However, despite being 20 years old, and at a reduced resolution, the graphics hold up well during standard gameplay.
The graphical style is panoramic 360 pre-rendered 3D images, similar to the Myst franchise. As such, it requires very little processing power, which is always a plus. The cinematic cutscenes feature both 3D CGI and live action, and are quite charming, despite their now low quality.
TLDR Graphics: Nice, but heavily aged
Zork GI features plenty of voice acting, plenty of sound effects, and a nice instrumental soundtrack. Good quality that should have no issues, despite the age
As mentioned above, this is a point-n-click adventure. Although in a 3D style, it functions like a 2D game. You click on arrows to move to the next room, or to interact with your environment or inventory. it mostly features clicking or clicking an object to select it and another to try and use the two things. Quite simplistic, but even an older, inexperienced or casual gamer will have no problem playing this. It's 90% mouse/trackpad and barely any keyboard.
This game is very puzzle oriented. That being said, simple controls belie a deceptively challenging puzzle game.
TLD Gameplay: You basically just need a mouse
The story, in typical Zork fashion is quite ridiculous, funny, cliché, but charming. To avoid spoiling much, basic plot is a tyrannical leader by the name of Mir Yannik takes over the land of Zork and outlaws magic, to make way for his regime in the scientific age. He imposes insane laws on the land (and suggests that you FLOSS REGUARLY) and vows to destroy any magic contraband. You, the player, happen upon a brass lantern early on, which contains the trapped soul of your travelling buddy, the former Dungeon Master of Zork, Dalboz of Gurth. He is basically the magic king. Your job is to travel to the Great Underground Empire of Zork (which is literally underground) to recover 3 ancient artifacts, that will have the power to restore magic to all of Zork: The Skull of Yoruk (I knew him well), The Cube of Foundation, and the Coconut of Quendor. The game is broken up into several definable chapters, but the second part, the main part, takes place where you and Dalboz the lamp explore the underground in search of these relics. This will be about 80% of the story.
Armed with a magic lamp, whatever you find and can carry, and a small assortment of saved magic spells, you point and click your way to victory!

I normally don't write reviews, but I've been seeing a LOT of unfair reviews for this game, so here goes.
Many people have written bad reviews based solely on the partnership with Gameforge as a publisher. I agree, it was a poor choice, but giving a great game a bad review because of the publisher is ridiculous.
Also, many people have complained that this game is a MOBA. That's also ridiculous, because that is ONE game mode. Survival is the classic tower defense that we all know and love from OMD and OMD2, except that we have the option of playing it with a larger party if we wish (the level will scale in difficulty based on party size). Also, the MOBA-ish game mode that is Siege just happens to feel like a natural next step for the game. "Hmm, I wonder what it would be like to be on the other side of this, trying to get MY minions INTO an enemy rift...?". Well now we know. It's a load of fun! :D
I've also seen the complaint that it's pay to win. How? Consumables that you can also craft and/or get randomly from chests that you sometimes get after a game? I have a load of consumables that I haven't used any of. Sure they can make the game a little easier, or give an edge in a match for a short time, but they're not THAT big of a deal. edit: And you can't even use consumables in PvP.
I love this game, and while it can be somewhat grindy, the materials for unlocking heroes can be easily obtained through daily quests. It may take a couple of weeks to unlock a hero, but that's no different than any other free to play game that I've played.
If the grind is too much for you, then throw a little money at the game. I have yet to actually pay a dime for this game, but I probably will at some point. These people have families to feed, and that's why they made this game.
I do have minor complaints though. One is that I feel considerably less effective as a hero than I did in OMD and OMD2. The thing is, I understand that we have to be weaker than before, considering that there can be up to 5 people on a team. The other complaint is that if someone leaves or disconnects, your team can be left in a pretty rough spot. I assume they're working on a solution for this, like an AI bot that can take over or something, but that's why games go into beta.
TL;DR: It's free, and fun.

Formerly known as FPS Creator Reloaded, this game engine is undoubtedly the easiest game maker in its class.  When I say 'class' I mean that it is up there with other engines that allow you to create realistic 3D worlds and populate them with realistic characters.  The software is currently aimed at FPS enthusiasts.  However, it is versatile enough to create fantasy, RPG, children's games and more, and the developers are branching into these areas more and more.  It also makes an excellent virtual reality engine.
The software isn't free but it is cheap and, unlike with many game engines, you are free to sell any games you make without purchasing any licenses or paying royalties. You are not even obliged to include any logos so in theory no-one need know your masterpiece was created by such an easy game engine!
Although easy, the software is very powerful.  You can easily create stunning landscapes with cliffs, water-bodies and many different skies.  You can choose from a selection of different terrain types (such as desert, lush, ice, forest, cartoon...).  You sculpt the landscape just how you want it using a set of very easy sculpting tools.  You can really unleash your creativity and artistic talents with these. Once you've created the terrain you can paint on ground, mud rock and sediment.  Then it's time to populate your level with entities and characters.  Adding these is a simple matter of drag-and-drop.  You can customise how each entity behaves by simply editing its property panel.  You can also change its Lua script and if you know how to code in Lua then the sky's the limit.  However, no Lua knowledge is required - you can produce quality games without it.
The software comes with stock characters.  However, you can very easily create your own unique characters using the built-in Character Creator tool.  You can even use a photo of your own face to paste onto a character and the result will look very realistic.  Making a new character can take literally a few minutes.
The software comes with an impressive library of assets such as models, Lua scripts, sounds, music, terrain types, textures, etc. but you can use your own for added customisation. There is even an importer for you to import models directly.  And if you don't want to make your own, there is an ever growing Store packed with them.
The engine is still in Beta and is currently undergoing major improvements to performance and visuals.  The development team recently took the very courageous step of converting the whole engine from Dark Basic to C++ to boost performance. Talk about radical and brave!  It speaks volumes about what the team's mission is: They are determined to create the ultimate game making tool in terms of quality results and ease of use.
Testing your current level is as easy as clicking an icon and you can even edit the level in Test mode using powerful editing tools.  The test level will just pause while you make those crucial little adjustments.  Of couse, you can also save your whole game as Standalone.
In terms of ease of use, this engine is miles ahead of the likes of Cryengine or Unreal.  In terms of quality results (ie, great games with stunning visuals and great AI) it isn't quite there but it is catching up.  There are many improvements in the pipeline and many great features due to be implemented in the future. Plus, we the users get to choose which features are implemented first!
In conclusion, this is a work in progress but already a very impressive piece of kit.  They've come a long way and I see a big future for this engine, both for the hobbyist (by the way, it's so much fun to play with) and those with ambitions of creating games for the commercial market.

If you look at the promo screens, this one looks like a generic crap shooter with "zomg! dinosaurs!!1" added in to appeal to 12-year-olds. If you get around to play, it will feel much like that, too. The ingame physics are rather laughable, especially when flying dinosaurs move around like broken kites, repeatedly crashing into mountain sides and generally being jokes. There also appears to be no proper clipping, so you can freely walk through fallen enemies, and get stuck very badly between crappily-textured rocks. This all spells "unprofessional" in big letters.
But I'm still playing it. Guns are done rather well, and the overall game architecture is not bad, if you can look past the bad physics. It's actually fun to deal with the waves in survival and buy better gear, then go to secure a mission objective. Classes working together with their special abilities are quite appealing, too. The game still needs a lot of polish, especially work being done on the glitches, and it certainly is at the upper end of what you can charge for this at 15€. But if you get it on sale and play with some friends who just want to have fun with a silly multiplayer shooter, this might be for you. It has a store for ingame purchases, but you can safely ignore that.

Alan Wake is a third person thriller that puts heavy emphasis on the story and its presentation. The game was originally meant to be an open world game, but the developer changed it to a linear game since they felt that an open world game could potentially destroy the pacing. Still, many maps are surprisingly open for a linear game and I've appreciated that very much. You take control of Alan Wake, a popular writer that can't write a word anymore and is getting heavily frustrated about it.  With his girlfriend, Alice, he is going to a little village to take a break, but something is strange about this place...
The darkness is your biggest enemy and only the light can save you. Naturally, your flashlight becomes your best buddy. In order to weaken the enemies before you can kill them effectively, it's adviced to shine the light at them before shooting a single bullet. Besides of the exploration and a little puzzle here and there, that's what Alan Wake is mostly doing. However, some people say that this game is too repetitive and the whole gameplay can be seen in the first 2 hours. And for the most part, this is true. It didn't stop me from finishing the base game and both dlcs, but I felt that the game urgently needed some diversity. Adding new gameplay mechanics or go as overboard with the maps as with the mind♥♥♥♥ing story would have helped a lot.
+ great premise
+ solid presentation
+ very good looking environment
+ it was cheap
+ flashlight makes for a good atmosphere
+ FOV slider
+ friendly AI that isn't useless for a change
+ ammo is scarce

Women have romance novels, men have the Witcher Chronicles.
THE GOOD
Beautiful game. Definately makes my top 10 of most rewarding games. Story motive is whatever you make it, ie revenge, love, liberation. Characters are worth remembering and are tied into the story. Decisions are left to the player. Great streamline, there is an ending and you are working your way towards it. A large demographics appeal. Fantasy, Romance, Mideval. Sweat, Sex, Magic, and Mayhem. Player character is extremely comfortable, not annoying. Narraration is done in a different style than the game so you don't feel like you are in a history/literature class. Two melee weapons either/or can be quick drawn at anytime. I think there were 6 magic spells, also at anytime. And 6 throwing weapons, if i recall correctly, at anytime you want them. Upgrading and crafting I am torn on, some aspects are truly innovative.
THE BAD
Difficulty level has too large of a margin. Cinematics are over used and way too story supportive, causing a lot of down time that you can skip but will cause you to probably never know what the game is about. Graphically demanding, but not a good transfer ratio. I felt that with all the requirements to run the game that the graphics would have been better, ie less stutter, clipping. Intro is about as long as the entirety of the "game". Talent system gives no noticeable effect, though it will probably have extreme effect at higher difficulty settings. Too open for a closed environment game.
THE UGLY
I hated this game at the start, never really gave me a point as to what was going on. I felt as though I was just bumbling around to where the mini map was telling me. I was even agrier after dropping 4.5 hrs in this game to see the start of chapter 1 begin, that confirmed that I had simply been bumbling around. But after taking a long break from this game I came back with the notion that I owed it to myself to complete a such highly regarded game. I was very pleased. Not until about 3 hrs left in the gameplay did I realize that the story of the main character was the story I had created through interactions/conversations. So this game won me over with only about 3 hrs of gameplay that I actually understood the game. I became enthralled with the story and even more so with the story interactions of supporting characters.
Graphics 10/10. Even though I was expecting more its still some of the best I've seen
Story 8/10. 2 pts for not making it apparent to the player
Controls 10/10. Common melee/magic mix with a quick hud
Mechanics 9/10. 1 pt for making one of the key features, alchemy potions, inaccessible during combat.
A fantasitic engine for game design with an easy to grasp, fully visual creative flow. A great starting program for ones interested in game creation/production.

The story is complex, the decisions are also so, and though there isnt a right and wrong choice, each one has a strong repercussion. You shape the game as you play. Great fun, and at some points i was stuck for minutes trying to decide who to help or which path to take.
By the end of it you will be itching for part three, and if not, you are dont have a pulse or are a drowner...

A very, very addictive game/physics sim.
If you like heavy transport with the best modelled exquisite detail? Then this is the game for you. There's a reason it has external cameras; you will be constantly enjoying the vehicle bucking and twisting as it goes over rocks, branches and bogs down in ruts full of mud and water. The game is pure eye candy!  Water physically Pushes against Your truck and cleans mud off your caked wheels.  Loading logs is pretty easy with an Xbox controller and gives you another sense of the passion that Oovee have put into this. The truck will move as it's loaded up or as you lift loads with the crane. it will physically sit down in the mud or on its suspension. It will also quite simply topple over if it's limits are exceeded. Very realistic indeed. Gameplay is a bit cheesy with' cloaking ' points needing to be uncovered to view hidden vehicles or tracks/roads across water or which are the "correct" path, which are otherwise completely black on the map view. The game truly doesn't need this as the true battle is finding your way across terrain or water, that will in an instant trap your vehicle or drown it! Meaning you have to try and recover it to a garage by towing it, or clicking it back to a garage you have unlocked or in the worst scenario, starting the map all over again. The pleasure is managing your fuel, putting tankers in strategic points on your route and using correct vehicles to both deliver your load and pull your vehicle out of drastic situations. Once you finish the maps you will be crying out for more!! You want expansion packs, more trucks, challenges, cranes, punctures, business model, trains, real roads like ETS2 etc.  The list is endless, it leaves your craving tons more. You end up watching real Vids of Russian trucks hauling logs or *anything* mud related; hill climbs for eg. The sad thing is there is nothing in the pipeline at the moment. Oovee have released the truck editor and soon a map editor, but it's like they have passed the buck to the community to keep this, very unusual, sim alive. It's frustrating along with a very,very annoying trait that every time Oovee release an update, it wipes out your game saves. Leaving all those maps as if you've never been there.. Somehow you are still drawn towards it but it will no doubt test the patience of gamers unless they sort this issue out. Try the demo out, which was at Oovee site.
Edit: Some very good truck models on the workshop that have extended the life of this, but sadly nothing further in the way of anything pc related future expansions.. The consoles appear to be the primary target now. How sad...

Being a lot like Overwatch, this game still holds its place with where it stands, but from what I've seen from playing it, a lot of things still seem to feel rather un balanced and, most of the times, almost cheap. I can't really give this game a positive score or a negative one, as, while it is rather fun, it's almost always infurating to play at times due to not being able to switch the character that you are playing during the match. While some may say that this is a good feature to be having, I think that it's, in all honesty, not that great, due to how unbalanced some teams may end up feeling within the first minute of actually playing.
Much like TF2, this game can easily leave you with a sour taste in your mouth. There's no actual voice chat, from what I've seen, and the ingame voice commands feel as if they'd take a good week to learn to begin with. In addition to all of this, the menu itself just feels kinda off, and definitely takes some getting used to
In the end, I still can't really give this game a good review, or a bad review. With the 5 on 5 matches you have, teams can really be unbalanced in the roles of the characters, and with the skill level in general sometime, although, that can still apply to anything. If you've yet to play this game, with what I mean about the unbalanced factors, is that your team may end up feeling like a game of TF2, where you have 8 or more spies on your team. And if you haven't played TF2 enough to experience something like that, I'm honestly rather surprised to say the least. If I were to give this game a score, it'd have to be a 7/10. Mainly due to the balancing that has been put in place, and how unfair it can be. Most games end up being a one-sided match, and that's not fun. I've only played a handful of matches that felt fair for both teams, those were fun.
One flaw I definitely see with this game, is character balancing, and hitboxes in some cases. Some characters in this game, in my opinion, ruin the game and only make it fair for the person playing them. These tend to be the flankers from what I've seen. In addition to this, some characters, in general, just seem to be a lot better than others, and make some characters in the game useless, as they can easily counter many characters the game has, and don't really have counters to them.
The game is free, and I recomend playing it if you want a fun experience, but you'll probably grow to have a love-hate relation with this game. As some things kill you before you can respond, and some ults don't seem to work the way that they're intended to, which is rather silly (much like the flankers, which I've found one of; in my opinion of course.) This is, again, all my opinion however, so you can feel free to feel however you want about this, and the game itself.

If you look at the promo screens, this one looks like a generic crap shooter with "zomg! dinosaurs!!1" added in to appeal to 12-year-olds. If you get around to play, it will feel much like that, too. The ingame physics are rather laughable, especially when flying dinosaurs move around like broken kites, repeatedly crashing into mountain sides and generally being jokes. There also appears to be no proper clipping, so you can freely walk through fallen enemies, and get stuck very badly between crappily-textured rocks. This all spells "unprofessional" in big letters.
But I'm still playing it. Guns are done rather well, and the overall game architecture is not bad, if you can look past the bad physics. It's actually fun to deal with the waves in survival and buy better gear, then go to secure a mission objective. Classes working together with their special abilities are quite appealing, too. The game still needs a lot of polish, especially work being done on the glitches, and it certainly is at the upper end of what you can charge for this at 15€. But if you get it on sale and play with some friends who just want to have fun with a silly multiplayer shooter, this might be for you. It has a store for ingame purchases, but you can safely ignore that.

"Kane & Lynch 2" is perhaps a more blunt approach to how we view violence in videogames than the kind of sly manuevering we've seen in other titles like "Spec Ops: The Line". I hate to compare it to that, but the comparison feels appropriate.
It was a little ahead of it's time with the aesthetic. The cellphone camera back in 2010 existed, but I don't believe it was to an extent that we now live with today. We see this on the news, horrible crimes being committed on cell phone cameras, this past year being amongst the worst. Watching the game play through the lens of a pixelated, digital camera gives this a level of authenticity that makes the violence hard to swallow at times.
The whole game leaves you feeling uneasy, and the two protagonists are mutilated, their goals are destroyed, and it's hard to feel empathy because they are rabid dogs attacking everything that moves. This downward spiral into hell ends without a lot of fanfare, which is fine, as it fits with the overall nihilistic approach to everything the game has to offer. Life is pointless, violence happens, people die.
Controls are a little finicky and some of the earlier weapons seem to have an issue hitting anything at all. However, I enjoyed this title as a piece of underrated art, something to experience. It's a short playthrough, and if you're getting it for the current price of roughly a dollar(Steam Winter Sale), it's more worth it than the garbage movies that pollute our theaters these days. At least this gives me a little more to chew on, even if my teeth are shattered and my mouth is bloody at game's end.

GameGuru may be seen as three different things, depending on the eye of the beholder:
1- It is a good game builder tool in general, which may favor styles like first-person and third-person RPG games, as well as first-person action games.
2- It is a great FPS builder. Which is of course logical, since it comes from the same creators that gave us FPSC.
3- It is a superb learning tool, giving you the very basics and leaving you to go into game making as deep as you want.
This is my very first review on Steam. However, I am quite confident it will be a fair one, since I've been a gamer all of my (long 39 years) life, and I have worked in the gaming indie industry for the last 4 years, mainly in the music and sound department. And I will start the body of this review with a hard statement: building crappy games is easy, but building good games is hard. Hard as in: it takes a lot of effort, a lot of study, and a lot of time.
When you first start Gameguru, you will find a set of tools that will allow you to VERY easily modify your landscape and add entities to populate your world (from buildings, to rocks, to people, animals, weapons, and even some heavily armed rabbits!). In the few minutes that takes learning how to use them, you will be crafting plains, mountains, plateaus, moors, lakes, villages, towns, deserted towns, and whatever your imagination wishes to design.
Once your world is populated, you will want to bring it to life. In order to help you achieve this, Gameguru offers you a nice variety of assorted scripts with different functions. A script is, basically, a really little file (in this case, LUA files) with some lines of code, and it will tell your rocks to stand still, your doors to open and close, and your characters to stand guard, patrol, shoot, follow waypoints, and quite a lot more tasks.
Of course, this is not the end of it. Maybe you want to add some entities into your game that are not included in Gameguru's core software? No problem at all. There are some expansion packs waiting for you (some of them are very good; I personally did not like one of them, but it may be because I find no use to what it got me). If they do not include what you are looking for, you can always check the Gameguru store, where several users upload their works, be it 3D art, decals, audio, scripts and other stuff, so that you can purchase it at prices that come from fair to ridiculously low. Some of them are even free! If, even then, you cannot get what you want, you can always make it yourself and import it into Gameguru through fairly intuitive interfaces.
But what if you do not know how to do the things you want to? This is the part of "learning" I was talking about. Gameguru is a game making engine, however, it is impossible to anticipate every single thing its users will want to build. If you want to add your original 3D art, you will have to learn how to handle third party software that allows you to craft it. The same will happen with sound, music and scripting. So, can I make a game with no coding involved? Sure! I can make a hundred of them. Can I only use the art and music Gameguru brings me? Yep. In thousands of different ways. Can I make an AAA game with original art, amazing soundtrack, innovative mechanics and things like a day-night cycle, intelligent wild life and a nice save system? Well, of course! BUT, in order to do that, you will have to study or pay other people to make what you cannot. Is this a big disadvantage? Not really, not at all.
I'll give you my personal example: since I started fiddling with Gameguru, I've been using it to make an educational project based in the history of my country (a country where videogames are, by far, NOT one of the important industries). Since it is very hard to find people willing to sell their work cheap, not to mention for free, I've been learning how to use Makehuman and Mixamo Fuse (character developers), Blender (3D art), Rigmesh (3D mesh creator), MapZone (texture creator), just to mention a few. Yesterday I managed to successfully build my very first LUA script, that will allow me to activate characters in order to make them tell me something. A simple script, indeed, but a great step for me in videogame craft learning. I've had put 157 hours in Gameguru, but I have learned more in the last 3 months than in 4 years inside the industry. Gameguru is an excellent way to see if you have what it takes to make a decent game, learn the necessary skills, pay for what you can build and, finally, be proud of your creation.
Since this is a work in progress, Gameguru will occasionally present some kind of bug, but not really often enough to be annoying. If this happens, or you just have some questions about anything related to the engine, you can always ask the customer service. They are the most polite support team I've had the pleasure to deal with, they answer fast, clear and easy. Also, they take some of their time to broadcast live on Twitch once per week, streaming interactive tutorials and answering any questions you may have, always with a very good mood added to it (I am personally a fan of GameGuruRavey and his jingles, he's just hilarious).
Of course, if you don't want to learn all of that stuff, you can always make simple game levels. Most shooters are not that hard to build, and you can even make cutscenes using any video editor. It's very easy to make simple games. And Gameguru makes it clear that, using some bucks, you can start to understand why the most famous games take millions of dollars to build.
One thing to notice is that Gameguru does not support a large variety of formats for 3D and audio. That is my only issue with this software. However, I was told in a recent Twitch broadcast that they are already thinking on adding support for more file formats. Also, the team is right now working on a faster, more efficient engine that will render objects more efficiently, as well as add many performance boosts to it.
In synthesis: if you want an easy way to build your own 3D first-person (and soon 3rd person too!) games, in a very easy, fast way, that will allow you to explore and improve your capabilities, Gameguru is your software of choice. If you want to build a GTA5 clone with no knowledge at all... well I'm sorry son, you really should follow a career not related to videogames. Gameguru is a great way to have fun, build, destroy, rebuild and learn.
And, as a forum member said, "Learning is what it's all about. Isn't it?"
