Women have romance novels, men have the Witcher Chronicles.
THE GOOD
Beautiful game. Definately makes my top 10 of most rewarding games. Story motive is whatever you make it, ie revenge, love, liberation. Characters are worth remembering and are tied into the story. Decisions are left to the player. Great streamline, there is an ending and you are working your way towards it. A large demographics appeal. Fantasy, Romance, Mideval. Sweat, Sex, Magic, and Mayhem. Player character is extremely comfortable, not annoying. Narraration is done in a different style than the game so you don't feel like you are in a history/literature class. Two melee weapons either/or can be quick drawn at anytime. I think there were 6 magic spells, also at anytime. And 6 throwing weapons, if i recall correctly, at anytime you want them. Upgrading and crafting I am torn on, some aspects are truly innovative.
THE BAD
Difficulty level has too large of a margin. Cinematics are over used and way too story supportive, causing a lot of down time that you can skip but will cause you to probably never know what the game is about. Graphically demanding, but not a good transfer ratio. I felt that with all the requirements to run the game that the graphics would have been better, ie less stutter, clipping. Intro is about as long as the entirety of the "game". Talent system gives no noticeable effect, though it will probably have extreme effect at higher difficulty settings. Too open for a closed environment game.
THE UGLY
I hated this game at the start, never really gave me a point as to what was going on. I felt as though I was just bumbling around to where the mini map was telling me. I was even agrier after dropping 4.5 hrs in this game to see the start of chapter 1 begin, that confirmed that I had simply been bumbling around. But after taking a long break from this game I came back with the notion that I owed it to myself to complete a such highly regarded game. I was very pleased. Not until about 3 hrs left in the gameplay did I realize that the story of the main character was the story I had created through interactions/conversations. So this game won me over with only about 3 hrs of gameplay that I actually understood the game. I became enthralled with the story and even more so with the story interactions of supporting characters.
Graphics 10/10. Even though I was expecting more its still some of the best I've seen
Story 8/10. 2 pts for not making it apparent to the player
Controls 10/10. Common melee/magic mix with a quick hud
Mechanics 9/10. 1 pt for making one of the key features, alchemy potions, inaccessible during combat.

First of all: Would I recommend this sofware? Definitaly. I think every aspect of the software is great. You can make your very own game within minutes and without any programming experience. There is a lot of media downloadable (free too) in the store and the DLC's contains massive amounts of objects to add to your game. Besides GameGuru contains already a large library of objects.
In the (very) beginning I also experienced a lot of errors, but they got quickly fixed everytime there was a new update and as for now: I haven't experienced problems for a long time.
Why am I so excited about GameGuru? It is already a powerful game engine and the features list is very promising. I'm very excited to see DirectX11 and Anti-Aliasing together with the performance update!
You can not, indeed, customize your game very much, but that doesn't matter as GameGuru is still in an early stage of development. As Lee Bamber said on the forums somewhere: "In the end, we want you to be able to customize every pixel on the screen". I'm looking forward to that.
But it is not as bad as you would think. There is still a LOT that you can change like the entity's properties, audio... You can even create your own character and import your own models with just one click of a button and if you dig deeper into the
folder you'll find out that you can change a lot, especially when you can program in LUA. Don't worry if you can't:
- First of all, it is simply not necessary because GameGuru lets you change a lot of things already
- There is a large amount of scripts shipped with GameGuru
- LUA is not that hard
- There is always a team of experts who help you on the forums
Something that I would really like to see is an API or SDK or something. I am programming my own menu for the game, but I cannot access things like KD-ratio, shots fired, accuracy. I also want to change the gun specs from within my menu so the user can apply upgrades and such. Maybe a way to implement the character creator into my menu... Enough examples because I think you know what I mean.
Something that is nessecary for a shooter game these days are hitmarkers. Unfortunately these are not added (yet).
Overall I find this a winner! I read in another review that TheGameCreators still not learned from their mistakes, as FPSC Reloaded has the same problems as there predecessors.
That statement is completely not true! Indeed, the older FPSC X9 and X10 contained a lot of errors and sometimes you were unable to make a game. I can agree on that one, but nothing is easier than GameGuru. I had absolutely no problems using it. I start it, I choose some objects from the library, I place them and that is literally it. There you have it, your very own game, created in just minutes. It also runs like a charm!
And then the other aspect of the engine; gameplay. So much better than the older FPSC's. The AI is absolutely amazing already and you have a wide range of enemy characters. I especially like the Zombie pack for its level of detail!
You can not only create FPS games, but also third person shooters. You can choose between these genres;
- Modern day
- Medieval
- Sci-Fi
- Fantasy
- Cartoon
There are many objects included for each genre and if you still don't have enough you can buy extra DLC's. And from my point of view: They are very good priced as you get many objects and they still keep going as you don't buy your DLC once, no, you also get free updates for them...
Final verdict:
Software: 9/10
Support: 9.5/10
It is really a great piece of software, so easy to use, yet a lot of aspects you can change without any knowledge of programming or modelling. For people who still doubt:
.

So be ready to die. A LOT. This game will demand crazy fast reflexes and sometimes, careful planing. But there's no better feeling than finally nailing that level you've been stuck in for an hour.
And the soundtrack! Oh THE SOUNDTRACK! It's hands down the best OST I've heard in a game ever, period. The retro synth music really puts you into the 80's vibe of the game and it keeps you pumped during the levels, enhancing the gameplay.
As I said before, the story is deceptively simple. But if you delve deeper and read between the lines, you'll find a very amazing and interesting plotline. Plus if you collect every puzzle piece found within the levels, you'll gain access to the secret ending of the game, which I'm not going to spoil for you.
Overall I'd recommend this to anyone who likes fast-paced action games, with a side of retro violence.

ORION: Prelude. Previously known as Orion: Dino Horde, and previously known before that as Dino Beatdown. It's a nifty little FPS about...well, the mass killing of dinosaurs.
The name changes, despite what the developers will claim on their forums, are repeated attempts to avoid their perpetually low metacritic scores.
Each iteration of this dino slaughter game is merely just a shameless repackaging, in an attempt to shed it's horrible metagamer score. Perhaps neither here nor there, but it does give you an idea of how dishonest this publisher is willing to be to ensure the game continues to sell.
The game has a glaring lack of polish, tends to run at very low framerates, even on powerful machines, and has the nasty habit of crashing...repeatedly, for no apparent reason.
Notably, some people only rarely experience these crashes, but for many people, the game is rendered unplayable. And of course, when you're not crashing, your friends are disconnecting.
Playing through a single match of any appreciable length becomes rather difficult.
Pair that with the repetitive music and downright embarrasing voices the humans feature, you get the distinct feeling that there was a notable lack of love going into the visuals and sound in this game.
Seriously, though. The voices are reminiscent of an athsmatic in a bathroom with seasonal allergies and a horrible headcold. (Looking at you, support class! If you call me "homey" one more time...)
Notably, the lag and the crashes and the disconnects are issues that have persisted for me and my friends over a year, since the game was called ORION: Dino Horde.
If you are among the lucky people who can play this game without crashing non-stop, then I suggest you immediately stop to thank your lucky stars.
The game features a variety of modes, but most modes involve slaughtering dinos. (There are a few that allow you to play as dinos.) The game contains 3 classses of humans you can play as, support, assault, and recon. (Think of a clunkier version of Tom Clancy.) While assault is fun to play as with his jetpack, and the recon is nifty with her invisibility, the support class wins hands down, with his ability to heal himself and others....to an extreme degree. He can tank just about anything with his healing gun.
Even though the support class is massively overpowered, playing the game as any other class is quite difficult.
Between massive dinos that create unavoidable earthquakes, or even bigger dinos that merely swallow you whole, ORION exists on a strange difficulty spectrum.
So long as one uses the support class, and uses the turrets on the backs of the vehicles you can ride, the game seems relatively easy. If you, like me, decide to explore what else the game has to offer, you'll run back to your support class/turret combo relatively quickly, as you find that the world of dino horde is quite a cruel one indeed.
In short, Orion: Prelude, under any name, is a glitchy, laggy, poorly thought out PVP shooter/dino killing game/dinos vs humans, that attempts to excuse its mediocrity with a low price point.
Considering the legions of pvp shooters out there, you're probably better off picking up any one of those and leaving this one be.

When I bought this game I expected a mildly entertaining imitation of Myst, full of questionable puzzles and unoptimized technical performance, like so many of it's indie cousins. Instead, what I got was a game so well made, it's actually a better Myst than Myst.
Everything about the visuals, the music and the sounds scream Myst, but upgraded to modern standards. Quern uses the same structure: solved puzzles unlock new areas with even more puzzles. They are all logical and even the more difficult ones are never unfair in retrospect.
The story is well told in a series of 'encounters' and letters you'll find along the way.
The game looks and runs great. The island environments look beautiful and are very detailed. I was surprised a game looking this good didn't have performance problems. Many Unity engine games suffer from horrible frame pacing (microstutter). Not this game.
I really can't think of anything negative to say. If you are a Myst fan, buy it. You won't be disappointed.

Alan Wake is a phenomenal thriller game that will entertain and hook you whether you're a horror fan, a thriller fan, an action fan, or someone just looking for an entertaining game with fantastic story and gameplay harmony. While it may no longer be available to buy, if anyone still has inventory copies you owe it to yourself to try and secure a copy.
Failing that, your best bets are hope that Remedy/Microsoft can actually renew the musical licenses (hard as that may be considering who's within) OR buy a used physical copy for consoles.
5/5
The game starts off simple enough; you begin within a dream while en route to the location of the game. Within the dream you're taught the mechanics of the game, from running and dodging to aiming, reloading, check points, and some do's/don'ts. It doesn't really do a lot to educate you on collectables or other out of the way things, but that's acceptable in my eyes as you should be learning and experimenting with that yourself.
Running is smoothly animated and rarely if ever has issues. Unlike the sequel, unfortunately, he's about as in shape as a typical veteran regular at Friday Magic. Admittedly, this works for the story, as Alan is a writer and thus more brain than brawn (Though being a New Yorker, I'd think he'd have SOME physicality...though I guess at least he's slim). Thankfully even if you're out of stamina, dodging is not limited or hurt in any way. On that note, dodging is a relatively fluid and solid tool, and usually comes with leeway when it comes to attacks that arrive within 2-3~ seconds of the dodge's start.
As for combat and interactables, personally I've never really had much issue with properly using switches or levers or even the opening of supplies. Generators have been smooth and if I ever failed it was always frame skips on my computer's part or me screwing up a timing. Cars aren't Forza quality, but they're solid for the rarity that they're truly used. Reloading is reliably usable (even abusable some might say) and they feel good and impactful to use. The mechanic of using light to burn away poltergeists and darkness, or remove an enemy's immunity shroud, is ingenious and something I wish more games could figure out ways to imitate and reimagine.
And there's
as satisfying, whether its your first panicked run or your 5th veteran replay, as standing your ground in the darkness without light and simply relying on endless dodges and managing enemies vulnerable states while blowing them away with shells and bullets galore. If you grow addicted to it, I highly recommend American Nightmare's arcade mode.
The soundtrack, both original and licensed, is hauntingly beautiful and perfectly fitting. Of particular note are episodes 4 through 6; 4 ends with the full version of an original song integral to the story called "The Poet and the Muse" by in-story band Old Gods of Asgard. Poets of the Fall, using their real band name and sound, also do Episode 5's "War" (I highly recommend the music video for fans of this game). Episode 6 ends with perhaps the most hauntingly fitting song; David Bowie's Space Oddity. Sadly this song alone almost guarantees this game will likely never see the light of relicensing again.
Beyond the perfectly chosen end credits of the episodes, the environmental sounds and songs are  well chosen and articulated. From the subtle change of quiet night sounds and background music to strong winds and accompanying diminishment of light to the sudden swift drop of the aforementioned peacefulness for yells and slams or even the slicing of the air by an axe as it embeds itself near your feet, the sounds are all crafted to help encourage you to keep yourself moving. Always forward, never looking back, and always fleeing by the skin of your teeth; all this, along with the writing and gameplay, ensures you're moving at the dev's pace. And what a fast chaotic pace it is at times. As fantastic as the writing is, without the wide ranging sound effects and BGM this game would be nothing.
No matter how great a game's gameplay, if its a game with a purpose or a story the writing must be on point. Alan Wake achieves this gloriously while also subtly critiquing both itself and real world contemporaries of the same style. An especially high prevalence is given to Stephen King and his quotes and books regarding thrillers and horror. The game's also a great boon for aspiring writers to learn some lessons of literature if they've struggled to learn in the past. It gives you not only the definitions and explanations but easily experienced demonstrations in action.
From the personal growth of Alan and the slow dawning realizations of various characters to how The Darkness™ manipulates people and events, this game shows Remedy knows how to craft a solid story. It combines with gameplay and sound to form a perfect trifecta of panic and speed; you feel compelled to rush ever onward and ever faster, as not only will the story pick up but the sounds signaling hordes of death become more commonplace and the gameplay becomes more frantic and even at times borderline chaotically panicked.
But despite the seemingly rushed pace of the story, its actually well paced and developed. They take strides to leave clues and hints of the world around in the form of TV/Billboard adverts (another underused ingenious pioneer of game dev, this time for publisher/funding money) and radio collectibles. The radio collectibles involve characters from throughout the town, most of whom you meet over the course of the story a varying multitude of times. From out of the way paths offering local plaques of history and manuscript pages actually being fully written to the idle chatter and optional conversations with rare instances of characters being around you, there's so much more to experience in the game...even if it takes you more than 1 replay to find and digest them all.
If there is a downside to the writing, it would be that some of the supporting cast seem a bit too easily believing of the situation. However to contrast that, they explicitly mention they know the town has a history of weirdness and there's also the live action mini series' that preceded the game's original release. Alan's growth and self realizations could come across as "too fast" to some, but I felt as though there were hints of it being less "development" and more "mostly return to his former self with a small helping of personal growth". If accurate, its certainly less concretely put on display than other parts of the writing.
Very pretty, and they hold up quite well even nearly 8 years later. You will regularly find yourself stopping to marvel at the pure beautiful of their Pacific Northwest. From distant mountains and hills to boundless forests and quaint log cabins; from a myriad of camping grounds to historically accurate ghost towns once home to bustling mining operations, its clear their countless trips to the US for research and authenticity paid off in spades. You're almost sure to even find yourself gaining a sense of remorse for so many locales clearly past their prime left to wither and disappear; a truth of the region to this day.
However, the same cannot be said of character models. While some hold up better than others, they all suffer from occasional awkward lip syncing. Their fingers and hands, while not remotely San Andreas levels of stiffness and actually being individually articulated, seem vastly underused. It's clear the best part of model development was facial based. While the quirkiness of the models can be grown accustomed to or even loved, the true graphic staying power of this title rests in the landscapes and environments. And in that alone, it soars...or perhaps spookily floats.

If I would have played it on release I probably would have been amazed by the graphics, because the look of this game is something special. Even though it's getting fairly dated it still packs a punch. The lightning in Alan Wake clearly carries this game to such an extent that the age of the game hardly matter and you still sit there enjoying the visuals. But yeah, you can still see that it's getting dated. Textures, characters and cutscenes got that bland 2010 look and the monotone forests that you traverse will eventually become dull and lifeless. As I'm writing this review I've gotten very spoiled with more recent releases that I sometimes forget myself and why I got intrigued by this game. The use of lightning.
The gameplay is simple to say the least. You will encounter zombie-like people (that are not really zombies, but people warped by a pretentious dark presence thing) that you will have to focus on with your always present flashlight to remove their defense and then simply gun down. You will retrieve a small arsenal of weapons, including flares and flashbombs, that'll make your life a lot easier in your walk through Bright Falls as you're casually shooting shadow-beings. Don't get me wrong, the game have many good things going on and the first half has a nice feeling to it, but as you're progressing the gameplay will get so monotone that it's almost comical instead of thrilling. Also, objects will fly at you and it sucks.
The story start out pretty good. You're a famous writer on a trip to the american paradise Bright Falls to help your writing block and shet goes down pretty quickly. It's intriguing, and as you're traversing the very interesting locations you will get sucked in. But then the story goes deeper and deeper and deeper, until you're sitting there wondering what and why you're even playing this game. The story goes from intriguing to pretentious and cliché, in my opinion. It doesn't help that the game is seperated into 6 episodes with a recap of what've happened at the start of the next one, trying so hard to make it feel like you're experiencing a grand tv-series. Though I have to say the game have a touch of Twin Peaks in it which isn't all that bad.
I'm saying cliché because when you're in the thickest of things the game will still present you with a bit of humour in the shape of Barry, your right-hand man. I love comic relief in games, but I really wonder how this game would have felt without the dad-jokes and sassy remarks. It's one of those factors you don't really think about seeing you secretly enjoy them when you're playing, but they do kind of ruin the serious life-threatening story the game is trying to tell us. Especially considering the end of the game, which I will not spoil, you will be struggling to realize whether you've experienced an epic or a sitcom.
It's a good game. It got good things going and if you enjoy a bit of an older title, pick it up on a sale. You might enjoy the story more than I did.

I have put a lot of hours into game guru and so far, I have mixed feelings about it.
The updates are good. The editor has come a long way over the year and that is good to see.
A lot of the proccesses are straight forward to use and you can throw together a level fairly quickly.
Editing the game files is fairly easy and if you are a complete begginer with game engines this is definitely worth taking a look at.
But...
I cant help but feel that the direction of game-guru is slightly off.
Is it a game engine? is it a game maker? yes but there are so many features missing it's difficult to call it anything more than a level creator.
You are limited with customisation of terrain textures and they are not as easy to change as a lot of other editors out there.
Things stop working. Features such as importing custom models can just stop working and that is only the start of the problems with importing custom content.
Unless you have some knowledge of lua. you are going to run into trouble with making anything more than a basic: go from point A to B collect/ destroy something along the way and finish.
Game-Guru does have some nice simple features, such as: being able to change environment settings while testing although why this option is not available while acutally in the editor is beyond me, but never the less it is easy to use.
When the importer does work it is good to see your custom models in the editor to create your own custom environment.
This software is WIP... there are bugs and it can be a pain but still, I'd say it's worth a go and it has potential.

I think explaining the mechanics of the game is SPOILERS, but many of the negative reviews talk about them anyway, so here are my thoughts:
Many of the choices in the game will seem irritating to people who are used to games granting them agency. Similar to Bioshock Infinite, the point here is that the player character has no agency in the situations affecting her, or even in how she reacts. The player is not in complete control of the main character: she is not even in complete control of herself. The best you can do is ride the waves.
Making decisions based on incomplete information seems unfair. I think this could have been an interesting mechanical framing if it had been driven home harder in the narrative expositions: if it had been made clear that the narrator was changing her mind, and not writing the whole truth.
This game was an interesting experiment, and while it left me frustrated immediately after finishing the experience, I'm starting to come around to it a few hours later.

is a narrative game about a girl trying to cope with multiple problems in her life. Gameplay is limited to walking and text choices so it is kinda like a 2D walking simulator. The story and drama are very down to earth so it won't appeal to everyone. I usually stay away from a game with no gameplay but good writing and fantastic music won me over.
Journal is like writing your own story. Your character is innocent unless you decide otherwise. It seems that not everyone likes the main character but I think the point of the game is that you create who she really is.
According to some reviews, the choices have no weight to them because they have no impact in a long run. I don't think you can change the ending but you can change side events before that.Sometimes our choices have an impact on us but perhaps can't change certain things in our lives.
When I played this game I genuinely cared about the characters. There are some multiple choice answers that will affect your relationships and it will have an impact on this short journey. You will have to play the game about 3 times to collect all extra story cookies.

Honestly, as soon as I heard the music I knew I would love this game. Without giving away spoilers I will just say that music progressively changes to match the plot. From a sound design point of view, everything was flawless from sound effects to music and voice acting. Not only the music was good but it really complemented the tone of the game.
Only about 10% of the game is voice acted from a perspective of the main protagonist. Personally, I prefer games not to be voice acted completely because reading makes me more engaged. Text walls are not too big but If you do not like reading there is no point in buying this game.
Obviously, this game has Kid's drawing vibe to it. When you walk to another screen it flips the page which gave me a weird nostalgia of Sega's Comix Zone ( not related in gameplay obviously ) It is a simple presentation and yet very powerful. Backgrounds have a bit of a surreal take which makes you wonder if the world is real. I guess you could argue that animation could be more fluid but I think it was made clunky on purpose.
I am not saying this game has impressive graphics but the art style is used in a way that makes the story more impactful.
I enjoyed this game a lot because I could relate to the story but it is not for everyone. If you usually skip text walls and looking for an actual game you probably won't like it. Journal has a good message backed up by good music, creative looks, solid writing and good atmosphere. I would estimate the length around 3 hours if you actually read it but it gives you a reason to play it twice. This game made me cry and I am not afraid to admit it.I felt that a lot of heart went into making Journal, something that only few video games get across.

ORION: Prelude. Previously known as Orion: Dino Horde, and previously known before that as Dino Beatdown. It's a nifty little FPS about...well, the mass killing of dinosaurs.
The name changes, despite what the developers will claim on their forums, are repeated attempts to avoid their perpetually low metacritic scores.
Each iteration of this dino slaughter game is merely just a shameless repackaging, in an attempt to shed it's horrible metagamer score. Perhaps neither here nor there, but it does give you an idea of how dishonest this publisher is willing to be to ensure the game continues to sell.
The game has a glaring lack of polish, tends to run at very low framerates, even on powerful machines, and has the nasty habit of crashing...repeatedly, for no apparent reason.
Notably, some people only rarely experience these crashes, but for many people, the game is rendered unplayable. And of course, when you're not crashing, your friends are disconnecting.
Playing through a single match of any appreciable length becomes rather difficult.
Pair that with the repetitive music and downright embarrasing voices the humans feature, you get the distinct feeling that there was a notable lack of love going into the visuals and sound in this game.
Seriously, though. The voices are reminiscent of an athsmatic in a bathroom with seasonal allergies and a horrible headcold. (Looking at you, support class! If you call me "homey" one more time...)
Notably, the lag and the crashes and the disconnects are issues that have persisted for me and my friends over a year, since the game was called ORION: Dino Horde.
If you are among the lucky people who can play this game without crashing non-stop, then I suggest you immediately stop to thank your lucky stars.
The game features a variety of modes, but most modes involve slaughtering dinos. (There are a few that allow you to play as dinos.) The game contains 3 classses of humans you can play as, support, assault, and recon. (Think of a clunkier version of Tom Clancy.) While assault is fun to play as with his jetpack, and the recon is nifty with her invisibility, the support class wins hands down, with his ability to heal himself and others....to an extreme degree. He can tank just about anything with his healing gun.
Even though the support class is massively overpowered, playing the game as any other class is quite difficult.
Between massive dinos that create unavoidable earthquakes, or even bigger dinos that merely swallow you whole, ORION exists on a strange difficulty spectrum.
So long as one uses the support class, and uses the turrets on the backs of the vehicles you can ride, the game seems relatively easy. If you, like me, decide to explore what else the game has to offer, you'll run back to your support class/turret combo relatively quickly, as you find that the world of dino horde is quite a cruel one indeed.
In short, Orion: Prelude, under any name, is a glitchy, laggy, poorly thought out PVP shooter/dino killing game/dinos vs humans, that attempts to excuse its mediocrity with a low price point.
Considering the legions of pvp shooters out there, you're probably better off picking up any one of those and leaving this one be.

You may see many comparisons to the Myst series in other reviews and these are not hyperbole. Myst is the standard bearer that many, including myself, measure first person puzzle-adventure games. Few games measure up and Quern - Undying Thoughts is the first in several years that gave the kind of experience I remember from playing Myst growing up.
The experience is more guided and linear with the gating puzzles presenting themselves readily as you explore. This may result in an easier experience for those well versed in this genre. However, I felt the experience was still extremely rewarding. The puzzles are varied and well designed. Moreover, the puzzle and world design blend together for a compelling aesthetic.
A fantastic experience for new and experienced puzzle gamers.

Quern is, in essence, a spiritual successor to the Mysts and Rivens of olde. It is absolutely chockful of puzzles, interesting lore, and unique architecture. It will make you think, make you frustrated, and provide that wonderful elation when your brain finally comprehends the mechanics of a specific challenge.
I was deeply impressed by the sheer density of the puzzles in this game; a few rooms alone contained as many puzzles as all of Obduction (a deep disappointment despite its unique aspects) and roughly 95% of my time in-game was spent solving puzzles or exploring the area. Only 5% was spent looking for the next puzzles and feeling stuck without something to work on. The only time I would encourage someone to look at a guide is if they cannot find what to do next at all...don't look at a guide to get through a tough puzzle!
I can't recommend this game enough for anyone who enjoyed Cyan's early games or loves puzzle/mechanical games in general. This is truly a hidden gem.

TL;DR Better than the last, but still lacking. Neither game is worth it.
Sequels work like remakes in a way. You learn from the past to build a better future for something you love. Sadly Kane and Lynch 2 didn't learn enough. It made good changes but sacrificed other things in return. Some things it did change wasn't enough. Gunplay is much better, but get's boring easier. The art direction for the camera and colors I like, but is nauseating. The story got better, but is still bland and got boring.
I want to touch on gunplay first like my review on the first game as I want to at least give credit for this. The gunplay isn't always innacurate now. Up to a certain range you are 100% accurate. Excpet for the fact every weapon long range is the worst thing to use. even the snipers are slightly off and don't use a scope anymore. Why? I don't understand why not using a sniper scope with ones that have one is a change needed. However they did change the cover system. In the first the cover system was non-existent. It was there but never worked. So I found myself hiding behind pillars while aiming. In this game it's now a button you can press instead of waiting behind something. However cover is useless as enemies get the weirdest shots on you. You know when you slightly see someone's head poking out and get a shot like that? That's what ALL the enemies do. But you can't be directly in the center of an object. So they will always shoot your foot, or hand. But it isn't a constant  problem I'll admit. But is annoying when it happens. This happens most often in the helicopter section later in the game.
Ahh now the story. It got better. But not in the way I wanted it to. Plot holes are still a thing. At this point, if you hear a topic get brought up, forget it was mentioned no matter how awesome it sounds. They won't talk about it, nor how Lynch got over his blackouts from the previous game, or was able to move on and meet a new girl. It even brings up new people who still don't get a background of any kind. Even in this game with no knowledge of the main 2 characters from the previous game. The only time you get a clue of what happened is how they mention the first game as "The incident". To be fair, I still don't get why lot's of stuff happened in the first game.
The levels are thrown together. I'm saying it. They feel like someone threw cherios ontop of a piece of paper. It was so bad that I thought one of the consturction sites was a blocked off area that was for decoration/scenery. It wasn't. it was this huge empty lot with barely any construction equipment placed in this awckward way that in no way had any cover from gun fire. But it got worse. I figured out that killing all enemies isn't required to complete a level.
Ya that's right, it's not required lot's of the time. I got so bored of this game, I started to speed run through the horrible gunfights. Sadly they still plague this game being mundane. But it suffers from the Destiny disease of thinking enemies with more damage and more health= boss. It doesn't btw. different abilites or different ways of taking them down, or hell, having a uniqe interaction with mutliple diverse stages is a boss or mini boss or something. The only other variation was attack helicopters if you count them. Even the climax when you confront the main enemy is scripted. You don't have a gun fight like in the 1st game (as boring and easy as it was), you just get a cutscene you can't hear. So make sure to have subtitles on. Why? this is why
*wind*
I have
*wind*
see
*wind*
deal with
*wind, and sees Lynch shoot a gun*
that's w-
*wind*
*end scene*
How do you get away with doing that? Honestly how? That's not even the end, you then have to fight through an airport. I cared so little at this point I just turned the difficulty from hard to easy and ran past everything.

Even though this game is free, I cannot recommend it.  The critical bugs and poor mechanics can't make up for it being free or even that you can have some fun playing it.  I do play it a lot, but it has become monotonous and at times extremely frustrating.  TL:DR at end.
The most problematic bug that goes unaddressed is the one that will corrupt your save files leaving you to start anew.  While the game says it uses the cloud, your saves are local and if they are corrupt there's nothing that really can be done.  There are no saves on the cloud to rescue you.  You have to manually back up your saves frequently.  The bug occurs if you're playing the game and your computer shuts down, either by power loss, blue screen of death, frozen and you have to reboot to do anything, if you can't exit the game normally your saves will be forever lost.  What makes this most insidious is that if you paid money for the lunchboxes or colas then they, too, are gone forever.  Bethedsa will not give you back the items you received from them.  It becomes lost money.  Steam will not reimburse you either.  So spending money on the game is a gamble.  You must make those manual backups daily to protect yourself.
Another bug is actually with buying these items.  While I have never spent money on the game, so many others have and when they buy items it becomes stuck in their inventory without the ability to get the in game.  Steam will tell you to go to Bethesda and they will tell you to go to Steam.  You have to go back and forth in order for Steam to reimburse you and you only get that with proof of going to Bethesda, having the items in your inventory, and showing how they can't be brought into game.  It's a real hassle and so far I've only seen a few actually get their money back.
The last frustrating bug I'll discuss is when you send a group on a quest, there's a chance for you to become stuck into a cycle of click on the group to enter the quest and then getting sent back to your vault instead of the quest location.  You have to select the group again, try to enter the quest again, and hope it will send you to the quest location.  On average I must repeat this cycle about 5 times before getting into the quest and it happens every other day.  There are times I've been stuck in the loop 10 times before I give up and exit the game, restart, and then try again.  I have better luck with it working then.
The mechanics that I dislike are how you loot, how the focus and zoom automatically changes on you during events, inability to see who's wearing what eq in a list form, poor ability to search for people, radscorpions leaving the room they are fighting in to go to another in your vault.
On quests you can loot containers and bodies, but frequently your dwellers are in the way and it can become a pain to do this as when you try to click on them you get a dweller not the lootable item.  I've learned to loot containers after I've left the room to make it easier, but you can't loot bodies unless you are in the same room.  It becomes a game of moving people out of the room and back in to try to get them to reposition so you can click on the feet of the bodies, because that works best.  Sometimes the bodies fly into other rooms, or the wall because there is no room and you can't see them.  So you just have to click on the blackness to make sure there was nothing there.
Whenever there is an event the focus will immediately go to that event and zoom in.  This is highly frustrating.  When you have 170 dwellers, 100 rooms, an you're trying to train people, move them around, level them up, change their eq, it's the biggest pain your patootie to have the focus move from the room you were in to the vault door because of ghouls that will be stopped by your guards in seconds.
While you can find your dwellers on a list, it's hard to get them to focus.  Sometimes a double click on their name works, sometimes right clicking, other times, nothing will work.  There's probably some bug with that too.  But when you get to having over 100 people it's really hard to manage them when you can't find where they are wandering around.  And those events that pull focus make it harder.
When your dweller has a baby it will move the focus to the top of the vault even though you were at the bottom.  So if you happen to have a population boom at the bottom of your vault you're going to be annoyed with how many times you have to move back down to the bottom of your vault to click on the next pregnant woman.  Issues like that keep coming up.  The game decided you should be zoomed in and over here even though you don't want to be.
On your dweller lists, it does not allow for outfits or weapons.  So you can't see who doesn't have them and who does.  You can see by looking if they are wearing something, but not if they have a weapon.  So you have to click on each and every dweller to make sure they have a weapon.  This is annoying and added to that the focus change stuff it makes you want to pull your hair out.
Then we have the radscorpions.  I don't mind them, but one behavior is downright buggy maybe.  If you have an attack at your vault door you have x amount of time to kill them before they move to the next room.  This continues until they're dead.  No problems with that.  If something pops up in the middle of your vault, dwellers in that room will fight it until it's dead or they die.  If there is no one in the room and no one comes to fight it they will spread to other areas of the vault until all killed.  Still not a problem.  Radscorpions drain energy like crazy.  If they appear in a room without dwellers, you will have a problem.  Even if you send dwellers in from next door and have a robot fighting it from the very beginning the radscorpion (if not almost instantly killed which is very hard) will leave the fight and appear in another room.  Even if that room has dwellers and fighting starts right away, it will keep leaving the room and appearing elsewhere until it pops up into a room with 6 people it in that can kill it rapidly.  By the time this is done you have little energy.  I don't think the mobs that popup like that should be able to relocate while you are actively engaged in fighting them.  It seems to be a bug since it doesn't happen with other creatures that pop up in your vault through the ground.
And finally, after a while, the game becomes boring as it's just the same thing over and over again.  I have fun in the beginning setting up my vault and trying to train everyone, but the quests are the same.  You don't do anything but click on the rooms to send your dwellers and then click on the loot.  Sometimes there's a question you have to answer, but they're all the same.  I now dread the daily maintenance of questing because it's long and boring.
The good is that it's free.  The base building is limited, but designing what goes where is important and there is strategy to that.  There is no pause for a bathroom break, so just exit to the main menu to prevent an event that might kill your dwellers if you're not there to click on their healing.  There's leveling up and level stats on characters, outfits with different stat mods, weapons, and you can craft your weapons and outfits from blueprints you find on quests.  So, there's some fun to be had and I've played it for a while now.
TL:DR  Don't pay money on this game.  You MUST manually back up saves daily or risk corrupted games and lost purchased items forever.  Bugs and mechanics make it frustrating and tedious.  But some fun to be had for a little while if you are not invested in the game.

Short, choose-your-own-adventure-ish type game. As with many indie games, this one has a heavy ending that slaps you in the face with drama. Sometimes that works, sometimes not. Here, it works.
I say "choose your own adventure" but that's not quite right. You don't really influence the story outcome that I can tell, at least in any significant way. I'd have to do a second playthrough to know for sure, so take that for what it is.
The game and artwork are as presented in the screenshots - you play the role of a girl with missing journal pages, and the story itself fills out over time as you learn more about what is going on.
Gameplay-wise, I only ran into one bug: when streaming, the gamepad would not work on my Steam Link unless I unplugged the gamepad from my streaming machine. Once done, it was fully playable with the gamepad.
The story is more interesting than it first lets on. I did have an urge to stop early on because it seemed a bit dull, but I'm glad I stuck it out. As time went on, I thought "hey, I'm playing a truly bad girl who doesn't realize she's bad". I would frequently be given choices that were, in a manner of speaking, all bad choices. That would have been a unique twist, but it wasn't the full story. In the end, it all made sense and I'm glad I stuck to it. My only complaint, I suppose, is that the game did feel a bit repetitive and long for what little gameplay and story there is.
This may not be everyone's cup of tea, but it was a nice change of pace for me. Recommended 3 out of 5.

I received this as a gift for my Birthday, and I have to say after weeks of use, I love this game maker!  The interface is easy to learn, and the developers have YouTube tutorials and a weekly Twitch broadcast to help the community learn the finer points of what you can do with this engine.  Out of the box you can make a FPS with no coding, and if you love FPS type games, then this engine is definitely for you.  With learning the scripting language (which is Lua, the scripting language many MMOs like WOW use for modding) you can do a lot more.  You can create other types of games such as RPGs.
Many of the negative reviews seem to be from Early Access, and I have to say when looking back on the Developer blogs and News Page on the Gameguru website, it looks like many of those negatvie reviews were addressed with updates and patches.  The developers seem really invested in this, and they do listen to the community.  They also created a Feature Vote page so that whatever gets the most votes will be implemented into the game (right now they are doing a major overhaul to speed up the engine, and after that the next thing to be worked on based on the Feature Vote is saving and loading).  Updates to the engine have been happening almost weekly.
As a sole developer who wants to make small indepent games mainly as a feature for my art, this engine already does so much that I can focus most of my time on creating assets.  As someone with some background in PHP, learning Lua and the specific game functions is extremely easy.  A lot is planned for the future of this engine, and I look forward to what I will be able to do in the future.  While waiting for the Feature Vote stuff to get implemented, I can focus on making assets and levels.  I can also pour through pages of information on their website forums to learn new tips on what is currently possible.
Still not convinced?  Keep an eye on the updates and go through the backlog of news and updates that have been done, and you will see this is a product that evolving to become one of the easiest, cost efficient (no royalties if you sell with this) and fairly powerful game makers out there.

Journal is a piece of interactive ficiton about a young girl going through a troubled time. The game is divided into short chapters which focus on an event in her life. Within each chapter the girl deals with her confused feelings regarding that chapter's event and your input comes in the form of deciding between two choices that come up during dialogue: you can either respond positively or negatively. The choice doesn't seem to affect the overall outcome, but it affects how the character comes out. There is no puzzle-solving, you move from character to character, exhausting dialogue choices till the plot moves you forward.
I am a bit torn on what I feel about the game. I picked all positive choices during my playthrough, and oddly enough, it felt jarring. The character is meant to be portrayed as a troubled girl, and me making her respond positively to everything felt at odds with the writer's intention and the character he is trying to portray. I didn't like the girl very much either throughout the game, whether she responded positively or negatively. The message is that she is young and troubled by events in her life, but what I percieved is the cruelty and selfishness you see in many insensitive children. Frequently through the story, we glimpse from her inner monologues that she doesn't really have any remorse for some of the things she does. Maybe it makes her more human, but it makes her less likable.
Despite that, the game's psychedlic finale has been slighlty redemptive to me. The girl becomes more of a sympathetic character and the game's allegory is demystified. The music in this game (and the finale, in particular), is truly great at setting the tone.
This game is so frequently on sale that it is hard not to give it a recommendation despite my mixed feelings. Playthrough is about 2 hours.

I don't know. I really don't know.
It's hard to say whether I enjoyed Journal or not. Like Omikron: The Nomad Soul, there were certainly a lot of things I did like, but just as many things that I just didn't enjoy.
"Journal" is a game that follows a young girl suffering problems after an emotionally traumatic and pivotal moment in her life, and you proceed to play as her for the five days that follow.
For starters, I really enjoyed the visual aesthetic... to a certain degree. I love the hand-drawn look (reminds me of "Close Your Eyes", which I played and beat very recently). I like how you actually play in a 3D journal, and as you unlock areas, the items that cover their entrances are removed and set beside the journal. I like the little shadow shows that describe the different carnival members between the days. It feels like I'm going through someone's actual journal and looking at their personal thoughts.
It seemed strange that the world looked all cracked and broke when I was played, but after being revealed the big spoiler and seeing the ending, it actually made a lot more sense that in the girl's imagination, the world would look that way. So good on the designers for making that.
However, I'm not a fan of the characters' art. They all lack faces and proper voices to make them feel real. They just look like puppets. Perhaps another layer to the way the girl perceives the world, but it was one I didn't enjoy. I felt like I could have been immersed more if all the characters had voices.
I also found the portion where you control the girl walking off the pages and across her room a little goofy. It's just weird to see this tiny hand-drawn girl walking across a 3D rendered world. I found something funny in it. And I didn't enjoy how preachy the game got about it's point. I like the little subtleties that support the underlying point, but I also believe that underlying point should be something subtle. Something that you let the player discover for themselves.
Along with that, the music was just... okay. It wasn't memorable. It felt like a person hitting different keys within the five-finger space he had for each location. Even the big, momentous, reveal feels mundane and ordinary because of the music. Along with that, the sound on the girl's voice is terrible. It sounds like she's in a recording room with a mic in front of her. The guy who talked during the carnival shadow shows sounded great, so it seemed odd that her audio quality was so low.
While the world and the character designs did follows the mentality of the girl after this big moment in her life... it doesn't feel like the story relates to it in anyway. It just seems like you walk around and talk to people with little consequence, because the game ends with a text crawl and a montage of a family that had no signigicant important to the writers, it seemed (as their last names are different. But who knows? Maybe Melissa Royall's last name is marital.)
Along with that, the controls just suck. You slide too much to the point that you might leave one area and slide into another one right after without intending to. And there were a host of glitches in the game, from conversations cutting off randomly, to the interact button appearing over things I couldn't interact with, to certain text just being a ton of random letters (Although, I think that was intentional, but I don't know. It was never explained in the story).
I can't say I hate Journal. I just feel apathetic for it, but within my apathy lies just a little bit of sympathy. And maybe you can find some empathy within me for that. I just hope there is no antipathy between me and you, dear reader.
What I mean by that, is that this game has some good stuff that outweighs its flaws, but it just didn't do much for me. However, I know it could be effective for anyone who's gone through a traumatic event in their life and can relate more. I never went through anything similar to the girl, so that might be why my heart doesn't go out ot Journal that well. I can see people loving this game, but for my money I just didn't. I'm giving Journal a 6/10

High amount of mechanical and deciphering puzzles with a fairly simple but well brought out story.
None of the puzzles are overly complicated or time consuming as some of those in Myst or Obduction. The balance is quite good here. The map is also quite compact and you can walk very quickly by holding the shift key, so no need to constantly walk back and forth for minutes on end. Compact doesn't mean less space for puzzles though. There's plenty of things to figure out. And I mean, really, a lot!
Graphics are very decent. They've put a lot of details in the puzzle items/mechanics themselfs but the landscape is somewhat on the rough side. But at the same time, it also had some surprisingly impressive moments.
Usable items are clearly visible and you can even use the alt key to highlight everything you can interact with. So no need to pixel-search for anything either. There's also a nice in-game notebook you can use to draw pictures of the things you're looking at. While technically, this is just a screenshot mechanic, they've added a nice touch to it by making it visually look like pencil drawings which is both cool and fitting in my opinion.
This was certainly a very enjoyable experience.

I'll start with the problems I experienced during my playthrough which as I'm writing this is probably about 80% of the way through.
Performance:   The initial loading screen after selecting 'new game' had me thinking the game broke.  It took about a minute to load the last 20 seconds of which was a frozen screen.   This happened each time I loaded a save, but it would eventually load with no further signs of performance issues during gameplay.
Puzzles:  Most were fairly straightforward and made sense, but there were  handful, probably 7 in total, where I lost patience, eventually cheated by watching a playthrough and either was angry with myself for overlooking something obvious or annoyed that my line of thinking did not match that of the developers.  For instance, and I will try to avoid spoilers by changing the details of the puzzle, I see a set two sets of symbols which I correctly identify belong to an object however, my thinking is I need to find pieces to place over lights to recreate the symbols to unlock a key.  That was not the case and I was supposed to look at the symbols and move the lights to match something in the symbols.  There were other puzzles that I unlocked unintentionally and unknowingly because I didn't realize it was a puzzle and was just touching buttons to see what they do and then didn't understand that I had already unlocked the puzzle.
So with the complaining done, I enjoyed the storyline and despite my above frustrations found myself continuing to play because I wanted to see how the backstory would conclude.   The music had a nice ambient feel that changed as you went through different areas.  The color scheme is kind of gray and bland.  I generally prefer vibrant colors in these types of games, but the textures were nice enough to overcome that.  Inventory is a bit wonky as I've seen stated in other reviews, but was certainly not game breaking.  So while it didn't match my ideal puzzle game standard, I would still consider it well made, well thought out, and worth buying.   I bought it on sale for $12.49 and thought that was a good price for it.

I picked this game up on a sale and it had been sitting in my list of games in a backlog for a long time. Decided to finally play it. Put around 8-9 hours into it. I was kind of misled. I was sold on the notion that this had super metroid elements. This game definitely does NOT have those elements. Exploration is fairly linear; and what there is to see or find isn't really worth your time. The game has a 2d platformer feel similar to that of games of Odin Sphere. Also has a similar art style too. So that's a plus in my book. Gameplay is particularly mindless, but satisfying if not boring after a while. It's essentially a hack and slash. No deep combo systems or anything to speak of. You have a companion called Fidget who can cast spells that are useless by themselves but combined with Dust's special ability can cause screen filling chaos. Other than that, it's a press and hold X to win kind of game. That's fine if you are into that, but just know what you are getting into.
Enemy AI is pretty terrible. They don't really do anything to avoid you. They mindlessly rush into your flurry of slashes and have no way to really keep you from doing so. Pretty large oversight in my book. I played on Tough, so I didn't play on the difficulty after that which is as hard as it goes. Maybe it gets better/harder on the 5th difficulty, but I doubt it after my experiences on the 4th difficulty.
The story is pretty nice. I won't really get into it, but it's a solid little adventure. Can't really fault it there. It kept me interested enough to play through the game. The ending was kind of cheesy, as well as the last 3/4's of the game, but it wraps up nicely.
The voice acting is decent. The guy who voiced Dust tried to hard to sound edgy and mysterious, and Fidget annoyed the ever loving♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me. I also hated how Fidget kept trying to be witty and break the 4th wall. I just learned to skip through all her dialogue. She never said anything relevant.  Everyone else was fine though.
Art style and what not didn't bother me. I actually found the in game graphics very pleasant to look at. I also liked how they handled dialogue with the animated 3d renderings that talked out their part. it's a nice little touch and very appreciated.
The game ran fine on my 5 year old laptop. That's saying something I suppose. The achievement list encourages at least 2 playthroughs. I don't see why anyone would want to after you beat it once. The game honestly doesn't offer much enjoyment to go through again.
I know it seems like I was really hard on the game. Fact is, it just isn't anything spectacular. It's a mediocre experience. However, I can still recommend this game to people on the basis of if you like mindless hack and slash 2d side scrollers, it's worth a purchase if it goes on sale again. Just don't go in expecting anything like a metroid journey or whatever people say about it. it's not true.

This game is great.  It's a game that me and my 3-5 year old son have been playing off and on for the past year or so.  It has a kid-mode so he can experiment and learn without being too hard, yet the game actually has some interesting platforming and combat.  The platforming is assassin's creed ish, where you have to move and hold the "hop/jump" button to complete the jumps.  It's great for kids learning the basics of platforming, they can focus on timing, or positioning, but don't have to worry too much about both ALL the time... although sometimes.  I help him with some of the combat and with some of the harder platforming sections, but the combat is also really nifty.  You use different colors, red/green/blue based upon which button you press matching that color B/A/X and can do combos, leap smashes, hard punches, etc.  The red is just damage, the green is fear, and the blue is a stun.  It's actually pretty fun and cool.  There are also little puzzles where you move a little mushroom buddy, play music, and other little things along the way.
My only gripe is that the saving system is too far apart for me, and especially for a kid playing.  Sometimes you have to play 30mins or so between stretches before saving, which is waaay to long without a manual save method.  I also wish the dialogue was voiced!  I know that was probably a budget constraint, but it would have been pretty cool, especially because my kids can't read yet (although when I was sitting with them I would read it to them, which is not the worst thing in the world).
I am so glad that I found this game and have had a blast playing it with my kids.  I was playing the Shadow Tactics game demo, looked up the developer, and just so happened to be looking for a game to get for me and the kids to play.  The music is fantastic too!  Which it was separate DLC and I would buy it.

Journal is a narrative-driven adventure game presented in a very unique way - the game itself takes place inside a diary and while it can be found in a 3D room the stages within are presented in 2D, hand-drawn pages. As you go from one "screen" to another a page is turned revealing a new area. If no further progress can be made the game just puts a post-it before you to see that particular area is yet to be revealed.
Basically, each chapter consists of exploring the surrounding area and conversing with the individuals encountered. The basis of the story is your protagonist's problem: suddenly, all the things she'd written down in her journal disappeared. She sets out to find answers but then the game focuses on things such as friendship, love, family issues, problems in school and things that eventually make you reminisce about your life and your childhood. Some of the conversations can feel eerily nostalgic - but then again you have to be in the right mood to play this game.
The game is, unfortunately, quite short, but tells an interesting story with memorable characters and great accompanying music. Again, I would like to emphasize the presentation - this hand-drawn world with its faceless characters can be very intriguing. The only downside for me was that when I was presented with a choice during some key dialogues I did not really feel the result of my selection. These choices can be the polar opposite of one another: you can be nice to your counterpart or can hurt your relationship with that person picking a more harsh response. Still, in the end it didn't matter, at all.
As much as Journal looks like a game for children it is actually for adults. It is very difficult to categorise it - to tell who it is for. I can easily imagine most people will find this uninteresting or quite the opposite - it can evoke emotions that will eventually make you uncomfortable and quit the game.
Nevertheless, I like giving such games a chance and I think you'd better do the same.

Where to start with this software? Well let's start with the Pros,
- Easy to use (I set up a test level in about 5 minutes, I got used to it MUCH quicker than Unity),
- Smart A.I system (You can set paths, they can find you when walking around securing the area, AND they can shoot you),
- Character Generator (This is the reason I loved RPG Maker VX Ace so much, you don't have to spend 4 hours creating a good looking character, think of what you want to see, find the clothes, move a few sliders to perfect it and voila a cool looking character in about 10 seconds),
- Easy stacking (I know it may not sound like much but believe me, when making something ontop of a table, it is SO simple, I remember FPS Creator didn't have that),
- When making a steep hill, it creates rocks automatically (again, may not sound like much but, try making a rocky cliff by hand, it's not easy, this does basically the same thing the Cry Engine does, after a certain angle it creates a rock texture),
Okay, time for Cons,
- Beefy computer needed (I have a decent computer nothing special, but the game lags on lowest settings so yes, you need an upgraded computer),
- One level games (One thing I liked about FPS Creator was the fact you could make 1924 levels and EVERY level and I mean EVERY level would be put into the files, this you get a level, I went to create a game where you had to infiltrate a building and it would do a level transition from outdoors to the building interior, and found it only exports one level, just what I wanted The Game Creators),
- The actual game runs even slower (This is an even MORE annoying thing than the last two Cons combined, because I went to load up a level that aparently passes for an .exe file, and the menu alone lagged, didn't think much of it until I pressed "Start", it went to the loading screen, said "Not Responding" and needless to say, I never got to play that game).
Okay, so the Cons kind of outweigh the Pros (not in numerical value, in how annoying or good something is), but if you're a new game developer and have a good computer and no knowledge of programming, I suggest you start here, you can even play multiplayer games!

KSP is a perfect blend of realistic physics with tongue in cheek silliness. Set in the Kerbol system (an analogue for our solar system) you run the Kerbal Space Centre on the planet Kerbin (discount Earth) and attempt to explore the solar system. I say attempt because timing is so crucial and there is such a big learning curve that you can be certain you will suffer your fair share of disaster. Due to this learning curve and the precise nature of maneuverers I know that this game will not be for everyone. you need to know going in that it will take you a while to get used to the game and hundreds of hours to master. I am still a rookie myself and have yet to land on Duna (discount Mars) so I say this with no air of arrogance. However, part of the fun of this game is the emotional roller coaster it takes you on and the lessons you learn from your many (and I mean many) failures.
From the joy of sending up your first rocket to the anguish of watching it hurtling back towards earth. The pride you feel when gaining your first orbit to the dread of realising you forgot to extend the solar panels and are out of electrical charge. The elation of finally landing on the Mun (discount Moon) to the grief of watching your favoutrite lander design crashing violently into the surface of another planet. It's all part of the experience.
There are also plenty of mods which add great extra content. From adding better atmospheres and textures to nuclear and antimatter reactors there are mods for almost everything. Mech-Jeb is a great mod for slightly ironing out the difficulty but you then have to get used to using the mod. I would suggest playing the vanilla game for a while before using mods.
If you love space games then this is a game for you. If you love challenging and complex games then this is a game for you. If you love sandbox games then this is definitely a game for you. The game gives you complete freedom, within it's three modes, in what you want to do and how you want to go about doing it. There are no missions, no set goals and in sandbox mode there are no constraints on finance either. If you love realism then this is probably a game for you too. As I mentioned at the start, the realism contrasts with the light hearted and slapstick tone of the game which gives it it's charm. The little Kerbals (discount humans) are cute and the in game descriptions will give you some chuckles.
I hope you can gauge from my review whether this is a game that you would enjoy. The price of £29.99 is relatively expensive and I did pick it up in a sale, however at the moment it never seems to go down below around 25 - 35% if I remember correctly. All I can say is that for me it's worth the price because of the hours you will put in IF you enjoy these sorts of games. It's one of those games you will always come back to. It's charming, challenging and it's in Space, and Space is cool.

The Witcher 2 is a masterful RPG for the well written story and several choices, the fantastic gameplay, which is a huge upgrade from the first Witcher, and the wonderful graphics which my computer couldn't handle. (I mostly played on high settings and 1366x768 resolution. Althought I could do 1080 if I lowered the graphic settings and turn off aliasing.)
The story follows a few months after the events of the first Witcher game, which itself serves as a sequel to a series of books by Andrzej Sapkowski. I haven't read the books myself, but I ordered the first on Amazon, it should be in the mail soon alongside a copy of Season 1 of The Americans on blu-ray, a great show that everyone should watch.
At the beginning of the game, you see a cutscene of King Demeved being assassinated, and in the prologue, King Foltest is assassinated, with Geralt being blamed. The prologue is in the point of view of an interrogation made by Vernon Roche, a blue-stripe. A sort of secret police for the king. Anyway, the prologue sets up the game with all the mysterious events and deceptions coming from characters that were involved in the battle in the opening, more characters get involved as Geralt travels east in Chapter 1, and even further east in Chapter 2, and even further east in Chapter 3.
I don't wanna spoil anything beyond the Prologue, just know that the story is fantastic. If you wanna know, there are separate paths to take in the game, I mostly followed Vernon Roche after he helped Geralt escape from his prison cell. The other path is with the squirrels where you fight for the non-humans.
I would say there if there was any game to come as close to Game of Thrones in terms of use of political situations and deceptions and not holding back on showing♥♥♥♥♥♥ torture and nudity, The Witcher is that game.
The gameplay is a huge stepup from the first game, which was mouse clicking combos and hours of potion making, it was kind of bland, but the story made up for it. The gameplay in Witcher 2 is just brilliant, and actually benefits if you use a gamepad. The fighting is similar to Assassin's Creed for the parrying and dodging. There's a weapon and power wheel, and really, every button is put to use.
I shouldn't have to say anything about the graphics, just look at how gorgeous it is from the store page. In game, there are a few textures that pop, it might have been the camera that forced the popping, I wasn't really sure, but that's pretty much it in bugs.
Definitely can't wait for The Witcher 3: The Wild Hunt

Quern is a super enjoyable puzzle game that I'm surprised I hadn't heard of before I played it. It has a lot in common with the Myst series (including some definite nods to the franchise), but it's still it's own game. It's like if the original Myst was turned into an adventure game with an inventory. A lot of the puzzles are very self contained--as compared to something like Riven where understanding the world is the puzzle--but there are points where you need to go back and re-use tools from before but in a different way with your new knowledge. Frequently, you'll find yourself approaching some complicated machine and needing to both figure out how it works and subsequently what you need to make it do, which will be familiar for anyone who's played Myst. My one general criticism of the puzzles is that it felt like too many of them revolved around just finding a solution written nearby and spending a little time interpreting it.
Overall, it's a wonderful game with a cool world and lots of cool puzzles, and I would definitely recommend it to anyone who enjoyed Myst, The Witness, or any sort of adventure/puzzle game.

This game is indeed very much like the Myst series, and as such, shares its good and bad aspects.
Pro:
- Graphics are excellent.
- Puzzles are varied, challenging, and interesting.
- In the item window, there is some optional help to suggest what the item is for (for those of us with limited imagination).
- There is an option to highlight usable objects, even when the focus is not on them.
- There is a map (although it's not used in the last part of the game).
Con (hardware usage):
- For a game with very little real-time action (some would say none), it needs surprisingly heavy resources. On my system (i5-3330 + GTX 950 + 12GB RAM), at 1600x900 resolution, I got a decent 50 fps, but the 4-core CPU was at 85%, and the GPU ran at 80C. Even at that, there were often gaps when panning/moving. Changing the graphics quality from Ultra all the way down to Low seemed to have little effect, if any.
- The game checks your hardware on install, and sets the graphics options to what it thinks is best. Unfortunately, once you change them from that, there's no easy way to get those initial settings back. In light of the point above though, this may be irrelevant.
- Controller support is not complete enough (yet) to be used alone - you still need the mouse and keyboard for some things. In the end, I found the best experience was in Mouse + Keyboard mode (only) configuring my Steam controller to mimic the native controller layout (with a few personalizations).
Con (the game itself):
- Like Myst, the story doesn't make much sense until near the end, and even then it's not very deep.
- Again like Myst, it is often very hard to know where to go next, or what to do when you get there. There are clues, but they are often subtle and easy to miss. Many of the clues are relevant to other locations, so unless you have a near-photographic memory, you spend a lot of time re-checking everywhere you've been to see what clue you might have missed. At first, I had to rely heavily on a walk-through. As things progressed, I got better at knowing what to look for and remember, and how to interpret it, so I needed the walkthrough less and less, but I was never able to do without it completely. Let's have a round of applause for those good folks who devote the many hours of time and effort it takes to create those walkthroughs!
- Even a walkthrough can't help with some of the hard puzzles that use random combinations that reset when you fail. Summary: Worth a purchase when on sale.
Quern takes the best of the Myst gameplay and improves upon it. The graphics and audio narration is refined. The setting is lovely. The puzzles are challenging. In fact, the puzzles are so varied you will undoubtedly need to reference external material (guides and spoilers) to pass some of the more challenging puzzles. But, Quern goes one step further than Myst ever did, introducing some puzzles that are randomized.
The most frustrating of these was a 12 step simon says. By itself, it was challenging but not overly so. Add in a pencil that kept breaking 6 times and a written mistake for the 7th time (using a pen)-- you (like I) may find yourself incredibly frustrated. Still others require a lot of thought and attention to detail.
Quern also features a save system-- although my experience was that it saved back to a recent save point in the story rather than to exactly where you saved it.
Overall, I was pleased with Quern. I recommend it. I got it on sale and thought it was a bargain. If puzzles aren't your thing, don't get it. If you might be frustrated by the RNG and overly complex puzzles, then buy it only on sale. At full price, it's a bit pricey for the amount of playtime you're going to get. So I do not recommend it at full price.
