Basic functions of the map editor are pretty intuitive and after less than 10 minutes of tutorials I was ready to start creating my own map. So this really is the Easy game creator. As the tutorials state, playing with the map editor is actually fun (no sarcasm here). After playing with the editor for the first 30 minutes I already had a scene with a river, some trees and houses and a couple of bad guys, and I was ready to play my map through. Easy, fast and fun. That's for the basic functions. The advanced functions are not quite as intuitive and since there is no documentation, it took awhile to figure out for example how to play music or make player jump to another map. Fortunately there is live support and friendly community that can help newbies onward.
Graphics are nice and it's easy to change the amount of details. Frame rate was kind of low at first, but removing unneccessary graphical elements such as shadows and grass helps a lot. The engine always uses the resolution of the operating system, so playing the games on ultrabook with 2560 x 1440 resolution might not be the best possible idea. There is a way to force it to 800 x 600, but this feature is not visible in the editor and can only switched on from the setup.ini file on a stand alone game. Also game menus and loading screens can only be changed by editing the files in the stand alone game directory.
Possibilities to edit the gameplay such as weapons and player controls are limited. There are several actions player character is able to do, namely walking, running, jumping, shooting, reloading, aiming and crouching. As far as I know these can't be altered. This pretty much limits the possible game genres to different kinds of FPS:s. It is possible to change the view to third person, but currently there is only one model that can be used as a third person player character. The most unpleasant limitation of the games created with GameGuru is the lack of save/load game options. It is probably possible to create a way to save and load by LUA scripts, but it requires some imagination. However the development of the software is ongoing and the community of users can vote for new features.
There are a couple of ready made and fully functional materials (entities) that come with the editor. The selection is limited though: for example there are only two kind of building blocks for custom buildings (warehouse and asylum) and three kinds of enemies (soldiers, zombies and medieval things). The appearance of the entities can't be customized, but their behaviour is controlled by LUA scripts which provides theoretically unlimited possibilities. There is also inbuilt Character Creator for custom character design, which has a small set of hair/hat, face and body graphics and an option to import custom face graphic.
The default collection of graphics is just enough for simple war-, zombie-, fantasy- or cartoon game but pretty much exludes other themes. More entities can be imported from .x or .3ds files (there are certain rules the texture files must follow in order to work properly) and they can also be bought from GameGuru Asset Store or Steam.
Positive:
+ easy, fast and fun
+ has everything you need for a complete war-, zombie-, fantasy or cartoon game
+ LUA scripting
+ community vote for new features
Negative:
- low frame rate
- difficulty to locate certain features of the software
- limitations (can't edit textures, other graphics, player commands or game mechanics)
- no save/load game (although this can be created with LUA scripts and some imagination)
Do I recommend GameGuru? It depends. If you are a skilled programmer with a professional team and an intention to create the greatest game of all time, you might want to consider other engines. If you are a non-programmer with an attention span of a goldfish, this software is probably your best change to get something actually done.

Another thing people complain about is the textures, but get ready to have your mind blown guys! The textures can be as good as you want to make them! GameGuru allows you to make your own textures for maps, and I have seen textures for terrain on the store as well. Another thing that people have used as a point against GameGuru is that the AI is terrible. I myself can admit the AI does need a little bit of work, but get ready to have your mind blown twice in the same hour! The AI script itself is editable and if you feel like you could make the AI better or just want to add something to it you are free to do it and no one is going to complain. The staff as far as I can tell in this game are just amazing they are really helpful and always try to be there when their customers need help. Even if you can't model or lua code you can still make some pretty nice levels on this software and there is always a community store/forum full of free models and scripts that can help you out or just add an extra flavor to your level. I have to recommend GameGuru and look forward to using it for years to come atleast. I wish I could do a so-so option, because the thumbs down feels a little harsh in this case, but a full on rec wouldn't sit right with me.
I'm not judging this like how I would an adventure game, first off, because that'd be unfair and also quite silly. I'm judging this purely on what it is: a walk in a person's shoes during a difficult time.
As that, the way the game is done is a great concept. The carnival stories between the chapters were a great idea, and done to good effect. The every day objects "blocking" off places was a very cute idea. The designs, the plot itself, all of it is really interesting, again, as a concept. But in execution it just really didn't hold up for me.
There just.. wasn't really enough to do. Secrets to find, optional and hidden parts of the memories as simple as earnable dialogue, would have boosted the experience considerably.
Another issue is not being able to reason out the truth of anything going on with any of the events until we're told, when the avatar herself does know. Denial doesn't cause a lack of knowledge, so to use what we quite literally don't know anything about in order to Surprise us about specific actions didn't work for me. (it was, however, used to great affect for the last reveal) Maybe if she seemed surprised when it was revealed too, like if the missing journal pages manifested narratively as the avatar in the journal not knowing either until it was repaired, it would have. But I don't know.
It's just.. a very good idea executed too blandly for me to recommend it freely. I don't regret buying the game, and I would probably recommend it to creative friends who'd get something from the concept on it's own, but other than that it's just... okay.

The Witcher 2 is a masterful RPG for the well written story and several choices, the fantastic gameplay, which is a huge upgrade from the first Witcher, and the wonderful graphics which my computer couldn't handle. (I mostly played on high settings and 1366x768 resolution. Althought I could do 1080 if I lowered the graphic settings and turn off aliasing.)
The story follows a few months after the events of the first Witcher game, which itself serves as a sequel to a series of books by Andrzej Sapkowski. I haven't read the books myself, but I ordered the first on Amazon, it should be in the mail soon alongside a copy of Season 1 of The Americans on blu-ray, a great show that everyone should watch.
At the beginning of the game, you see a cutscene of King Demeved being assassinated, and in the prologue, King Foltest is assassinated, with Geralt being blamed. The prologue is in the point of view of an interrogation made by Vernon Roche, a blue-stripe. A sort of secret police for the king. Anyway, the prologue sets up the game with all the mysterious events and deceptions coming from characters that were involved in the battle in the opening, more characters get involved as Geralt travels east in Chapter 1, and even further east in Chapter 2, and even further east in Chapter 3.
I don't wanna spoil anything beyond the Prologue, just know that the story is fantastic. If you wanna know, there are separate paths to take in the game, I mostly followed Vernon Roche after he helped Geralt escape from his prison cell. The other path is with the squirrels where you fight for the non-humans.
I would say there if there was any game to come as close to Game of Thrones in terms of use of political situations and deceptions and not holding back on showing♥♥♥♥♥♥ torture and nudity, The Witcher is that game.
The gameplay is a huge stepup from the first game, which was mouse clicking combos and hours of potion making, it was kind of bland, but the story made up for it. The gameplay in Witcher 2 is just brilliant, and actually benefits if you use a gamepad. The fighting is similar to Assassin's Creed for the parrying and dodging. There's a weapon and power wheel, and really, every button is put to use.
I shouldn't have to say anything about the graphics, just look at how gorgeous it is from the store page. In game, there are a few textures that pop, it might have been the camera that forced the popping, I wasn't really sure, but that's pretty much it in bugs.
Definitely can't wait for The Witcher 3: The Wild Hunt

I've just finished this game. And i have mixed feelings. In this game you are taking role of young girl, who has diary, has problems, etc. First day (the story is divided into 5 days), you can walk around a little bit, talk to 3 people. So far, so good, and i was trying to pay attention to dialogues, names, also choices while talking to those people. Second day, new locations are available, with more people (every day will add new locations and new people). Yeah, you can see the relationship between them, you can interact with them, but nothing really matters. Your "choices" can change only few lines of text, nothing more. And in the end, none of those interactions really matters. It is there just to fill some time, or just to show you that girl has some serious problems. But those problems are actually nothing to worry about, everybody has some problems in his life. What is really important in this game, is actually Day 5, the last "chapter" of this game. Change of atmosphere will tell you that something is not right, your mum will send you to a special place, and you will uncover the truth. The main problem of our protagonist. Well, the ending was really hard and strong, and also started some processes in my head (because as i said, everybody has some problems, and i have some now), but after finishing game, i realize that most of the game was useless, and it should not be there as it gives you nothing. But yeah, without content, it would be more shorter, and also price would be lower, and maybe that's why developers put everything in. I don't know, it is already short enough (and ask 10 euros for that is really ridiculous, real gametime is around 2-3 hours. Yes, i have 6 hours on record, because i actually fell asleep for a moment).
But let's summarize it. Soundtrack is not bad, it is actually good, even as backround music, it helps to create the right atmosphere. The controls, well, you need only 3 keys (space, <- and -> ). Animations, well, there are not any real animations, maybe those "carneval" things (short stories between the days, not really related to protagonist - maybe a little). Hmm, graphics. You can see screenshots from the game, that's all. It is probably hand-drawn, so it does not look bad, but as i said, there are no real animations, so it feels cheap. And for 10 euros, it is really sad. I know, it is an indie game, but still.
There are also some achievements (i've got most of them after first ending, but for 1-2 achievements, you have to play game again. And as there are zero replayability, you can just ignore dialogs), and also trading cards, if anybody interested. But you can't buy that soundtrack. As i am looking at game's price, i don't want to see soundtrack's price (it would be probably 10 euros too).
I don't know, i still don't think it is a good game for 10 euros. Maybe 2-4 euros at max, but no more. So if you want this game, you'd better pick it on sale (-75% or even -87%, then the price is right and that's when i can recommend this game). I still have that bad feeling that developers just wanted to grab money from people, who loves these kind of games, especially with that description about "A journey through the life of a young and troubled girl as she tries to face up to the choices and responsibilities that come with childhood. An experience that questions the reliability of how we choose to remember events and explores the truths hidden within our dreams.". Well, yes, it is there, they are not lying, but i was expecting something more, that's all. I am not saying that this have to be same for everybody, it is just my feeling about it. I have played much better adventure games, with better stories, gameplay, soundtrack, etc, and for less money. And only good thing about this game is just that ending, which nobody sees coming, because the game keeps it as an secret. It will show it to you only at the end. I don't know, do as you want, it is your money :) I just wanted to warn you, as lot of people (80% of them) are recommending this. Maybe they can see something special about this abstract game, or it just helped them in hard times. Yeah, maybe. But there are many alternatives :) Just saying.

Quern - Undying Thoughts is beautiful.  It is a Sisyphean task to create a puzzle game that will appeal to all since the challenges must be surmountable but involve enough thought so as not to roll down into a clicker game.  I personally like to have my grey matter stretched but I do not enjoy having to combine calculus with chess and hope that I noticed a word on a wall discoverable only within the first 2 minutes of gameplay.  I will say the puzzles were tilted towards the mechanical side of the equation as opposed to the theoretical, which is true to the story as they have been physically created as both tests and a guide.  The puzzle progress is linear, but this remains true to the theme of the story.  I did hit the forums near the beginning of the adventure at one point where I could not determine where there even was a path to follow, but in retrospect, there were clues.  This keyed me into noting what might guide me later.  If you are looking for the New York Times Sunday Diagramless, the puzzles might seem dissapointly easy.  However, I enjoy feeling the satisfaction of solving challenges on my own rather than just clicking along to a walk through so I found them well ballanced.  If you want a gorgeous environment with enjoyable puzzling all wrapped up in a capable story line, Quern is a gem.

A solid Myst clone, although the story doesn't compare.  Like Myst, here you wander around an alien environment and figure out how to make things work. The puzzles are very challenging, and it's quite segmented by "area"--you can't progress to the next area until you finish the one you're in, and so on.  I tend to prefer more "open world" concepts, where you can work on numerous puzzles simultaneously (taking a break from one when you get stuck to go work on something else). That way, you don't have to completely stop when you get stuck. This one was very chronological, and the "choice" at the end wasn't nearly as witty or interesting as Myst. Mostly, the "letters" you encounter along the way were redundant. It would have been nice to have a more likeable character to follow. All this being said, if you need a "Myst" fix, this is a great choice. The puzzles were mostly solveable without help (although I did need a hint or two here and there), and the mechanics were intuitive (which is to say, there were enough hints that you could figure stuff out.  Nothing more frustrating, say, than a door with a code and no hints whatsoever about how to find the correct code. Trying thousands of combinations is not a fun way to waste hours of your life). Overall, I enjoyed playing this, and thought it was well worth the $12 I spent on it.

This is a beautifully made puzzle game in the Myst tradition. If you enjoyed the serenity of being on your own on an island in Myst, you'll love Quern - Undying Thoughts. It actually seems to pay a number of hommages to Myst with its visuals and puzzles that often are represented as mechanical devices.
The graphics are great (not perfect, but easily good enough for a very immersive experience). The soundtrack is very atmospheric as well. I really appreciated the automatically expanding map and the notebook which allows one to not only capture snapshots (sketches) but also to write one's own notes so that one can browse through them later to see whether a new found object can be used in a previously visited location, for instance.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys exploring abandoned worlds and have only a few suggestions for improvement: I found some of the puzzles rather easy as such, but very obscure to approach. In other words, it was not obvious a couple of time what to do next and there were far too many options to make a trial and error approach to exploration satisfying. In hindsight, every step is logical, but as a matter of fact, other steps would have been logical as well and I don't enjoy trying all those options. Most of the time, one receives enough hints (through notes and drawings left behind, or through properties of objects) that one has a motivation to find another item or attempt a task, but a few times I found there were gaps in driving the next move. Sometimes the search space was confined enough to make educated exploration feasible, but sometimes it was just too vast for my taste.
I would also have loved to see more organic puzzles. Some of the puzzles in the game are of this type, i.e., you are just trying to create or fix something that someone else would have done as well, if they just lived in that place. But many puzzles involved elaborate machinery that had not other purpose than to present a puzzle to you. Why not, say, fix an elevator that looks like people would use, rather than operate a contraption that purely appears to be an obstacle made for you as a puzzler? The narrative of the game justifies pure puzzles in your path, but still, solving those hurdles does not feel as satisfying to me, compared to accomplishing tasks that actually make sense outside a pure puzzle challenge.
A bit more story along the way would also have been appreciated. This would have added to the urgency, the desire to see what's next. As it is, one basically already knows the path from day one and there are no major reveals on the way. At one point a bit of interest is added but that then remains static as well till the end. So for the vast majority of the time one just wonders what the next puzzle will look like.
In conclusion, my criticism is a bit of nitpicking at an extremely high level. I thoroughly enjoyed this game and couldn't recommend it any more to the republic of puzzlers. :)

One of the best things about pc gaming is all of the awesome indie games you can buy extremely cheaply, and then get just as much fun and as many hours of play (or more) as any "triple A" title. The binding of isaac is one of those games. At first it seems to be a fairly innocent arcade-style dungeon crawler, but in reality it is anything but.
The binding of isaac is about a boy named isaac (and maybe other unlockable characters...) who jumps into his basement while fleeing from his mother, who is on a mission from god to slay her only son. The game has other pretty dark and sacrilegious referrences, but that just adds to the fun. The gameplay is about you controlling isaac as he walks around the dungeons and fights monsters by shooting his tears at them.
As you progress through the dungeons and defeat bosses, untimately attempting to kill mom, isaac will level up various skills and gain new abilities with the various items you can collect. If you make it to the end, you'll feel like a complete badass rushing around killing enemies easily with your upgraded tears and items.
In the end, this game is highly worth $5, but if you aren't willing to pay even that little, it often goes on sale with the various steam sales. I got the game and the dlc for less than $4 on one such sale.

This is a great editor for creating your own small games. This is especially usefull when you don't want to learn to code or spend a long time coding and modeling. If you are just looking for a basic editor to create a small game for your own enjoyment or for your friends as well, this is a good place to start.
The thing I don't like about this, is that it is very limited. In the base editor (without dlc, so for € 20) there are very little assets. Of course I get that if you seriously want to make a game and release it, you should make your own models, but I use this one just for myself, have a bit of fun making small levels etc. But there is just too little to really make some good levels.
There are some (not a lot) of buildings, but they don't work well together. There are a couple of medieval weapons, but almost no scenery to go with it. I wanted to make a very small medieval styled level, but the only building that fit in is a church. So there is a church in the middle of nowhere, plus some hills and trees. The models that are in the editor are pretty good though.
There are some add ons you can buy, but those are very limited as well. They don't offer much assets either. I wouldn't really recomend this, unless you can make your own models or can get some models elsewhere. There is a store where you can get models, but very little are free and you end up spending 5 times the amount you paid for the editor if you really want to create something nice.
So overall, I would not recommend this if you are looking to create a nice game. It's a bit of fun to mess around with (place a lot of medieval enemies and killing them all with a shotgun is really fun) or try out some ideas you have and later make it in another editor or engine.
One thing I would like to add is that levels without much or none buildings and set in a more forest or hill area are very possible, but still limited by the few enemies and weapons (and the terrible AI).
EDIT: It appears the devs are actually interested in improving GameGuru (just look at the comments on this review), so it might just improve.

IN SHORT: This is a wonderful game if you like colorful worlds, a nice (and surprisingly touching) story and easy-going gameplay. It is a smooth ride with the occasional challenge here and there. Clearly the makers put in a ton of love and it shows this everywhere.
Full review below.
Pro
+ Vibrant and colorful world, bitesize levels which fit together coherently.
+ An easy and relaxing ride.
+ Nice story with some clever morals (great for kids as well!)
+ If you look carefully, eastereggs + collectables.
+ Good mechanics around fighting and solving puzzles.
+ Amazing soundtrack!
Con
- Not for people who look for the ultimate challenge.
- Not exactly "platforming", this is automated platforming.
Playing The Last Tinker was a great experience. It reminds a lot of the platform games of old, like from the N64 period. But let's get one thing out of the way straight away: this game took a simpler approach to platforming. In terms of gameplay this means 2 things.
1: It removes all challenge for the real platforming fans out there.
2: this means the game needs to deliver in different areas to make it up.
In my humble opinion I would say it does the latter nicely. The charm of this game is unmistakeable. The game is set in one big colorful world split up in bitesize levels and is really fun to explore. At some point in the story the world is attacked by the "bleakness" which is draining all colors. This means you usually get to see 2 versions of a level. One filled with bleakness and one where it has been cleansed. It is rewarding to return the world to its original looks.
The game has a great story which dares to touch our world's problems (racism for one). Also I could not help but start caring for the inhabitants. Even though communication is done via simple text clouds, it manages to convey the message how the creatures feel about all the happenings. Some are scared, others angry, others sad and hopeless. Not only does this fit with their colors, but it also makes sense and is relatable.
Apart from the "platforming" the game offers just enough combat varience and puzzles to be entertaining. Think along the lines of opening doors by pressing buttons, lowering bridges, guiding helpful creatures with their own abilities (like exploding), finding keys or items, etc. Nothing new, but entertaining anyway.
I also like how the creators experiment with different genre types (even trying "noir" at some point), and how they created some mini-games which actually complement the story.
To top it all off, this game has an amazing soundtrack. Each part of the world is complemented by its own instrumental style. I especially liked the music from the noir level and the blue world in general.
I would say this game is just long enough for what it tries to accomplish. I have had a great time and even felt some genuine emotion here and there. Technically this game also performs great. I had no bugs or issues at all, had steady FPS (though to be fair my pc is quite strong), and found the controller support excellent.
As I wrote above, this game clearly shows the creators invested a lot of love.
Therefore I would recommend The Last Tinker to any gamer looking for a relaxed experience.

False advertising at it's finest people. This software promises that the "Characters are smart and equipped to navigate the environment and hunt you down" which couldn't be farther from the truth. Just playing their demonstration maps, you can see even the developers themselves could not create a half-decent FPS experience.
The enemy AI is some of the worst I have ever seen, half of them do not move no matter what. They will not pursue you, they will just stare at you and fire at you if you get close enough to them. Some will occasionally decide to chase you which looks hilarious. The animation is a disaster. I don't know if the AI is horrible due to bad scripting on their part or if it has something to do with the engine itself since the same enemy can be placed into a map multiple times and yet they all act a bit differently despite using the same scripts.
GameGuru also brags about a powerful "game engine [that] is optimized for efficient use of memory, frame rate performance and graphic card compatibility". Again, lies. This engine, even with hardly anything in a map, chugs so damn slowly on a modern gaming rig it's pathetic. Loading up one of the demo maps and the frame rate (with all settings on lowest) is 30 at best. This seems to effect the controls as aiming becomes much harder when the frame rate drops. Changing graphical settings hardly improves the frame rate which suggests that the engine is simply inefficient when it comes to rendering the scene.
Now onto the most unforgivable aspect of the engine: the IDE. While on the surface it seems simple and easy to use, it really lacks some basic features and can be a real chore doing simple tasks like copying parameters from one entity to another. There seems to be no quick method for doing this, nor a quick method for placing entities, you have to click on the entity in the list every time you want to place one down. The best they give you is a "spray tool" which isn't very useful for most cases.
You only get 4 textures to work with when it comes to the ground, which isn't so bad as long as you are using entities for all other grounded structures which would increase the entity count by a lot. There is a major lack of options and choices in the IDE which is the most disappointing part of the IDE. There isn't much you can customize to your liking. There are ways to change things like the HUD, player settings and such but it isn't explained or built into the IDE. You have to go through the engine folders and edit various files just to change weapons and other major aspects of "your game". In other words, it's not very flexible.
They do allow the use of LUA scripting but they don't provide a lot of variables or useful functions for you to use and applying the scripts is limited to placing one script into one entity. Still, editing these files and having to script is the opposite of "the easy game maker"concept. It really feels like you have to rig a broken system just to get things to be barely passable. That being said, I would imagine it taking a ton of work and editing just to create a "game" with at least a mediocre playing experience. For the rest of the user-base, they will be creating complete garbage with this thing.
So, to conclude this review, I have to say it is not worth it. It's cheap for a reason and even for a dollar it isn't worth it. This software is not ready for release, yet here it is, like so many other awful products on Steam recently. It's poorly optimized, awfully coded AI, hilariously bad animation, effects and weapons, as well as it's lack of user control in basic elements of the game keep this from having any value what so ever. I hope that they can improve upon this and consistently update it with new features because it is a decent foundation but it is far from being useful to anyone who is taking game development seriously. You have been warned.

This whole little game that Richard Perrin was working on for 10 years is actually about memory, and how definitely subjective it is. Any event, any occurrence that we either live ourselves or solely witness, will be retold through a certain perception. There is no such a thing as the truth once an event is recalled from the memory. There is only our own experience, thus, any narrator is eventually an unreliable narrator.
is a perfect example of this notion.
The narrative centers a 5 day period in a nameless teenage girl's life when she's been trying to deal with both expected troubles of growing up, establishing a character, making choices, learning hard earned truths and living consequences; and a specific, singular disaster fundamentally too heavy for her young being to deal with. Through detached and off dialogue options, abhorrently selfish exclamations and numbing expressions, we take a walk.
is an interesting, yet eventually surreal and nettlesome experience.
The artwork is hand drawn, picking a thin balance between beautiful and creepy, and that many would basically define as being eerie. A melancholy, water color environment combined with slender, faceless characters do create our setting. The whole display screams detachment and an inability of adaptation with the world. A failure to emphasize is written all over the artwork. The music changes as our heroine change places within a side scrolling environment from "feeling blue" to "something's off" any minute. We are given short stories told with shadow plays between chapters to declare some bitter life lessons now and then, and complete a whole playthrough within 2 hours.
I do adore story driven or narrative games mostly. But defining
to be either story driven, or narrative would be an understatement and probably even a completely wrong definition. In this collection of personal expressions, the narrative is completely subjective with little to no room for diverse character progression. Contrary to player expectation with the choice options presented in game, our protagonist already displays a precognized set of actions. Her mentality, her actions and reactions are not actually alterable. Any and all events that we encounter within the game, are already lived, thus categorized and concluded within the mind of our heroine. We are solely there to witness her personal recognition of events rather than having a gameplay. She is a bitter, troubled, detached, numb child; stuck in an existential crisis.
Is this a bad thing for us to witness in a game? Quite possibly not. This game was one of the best examples of "unreliable narrator" in any game I've seen before. Yet, it also comes with the direct obstacle of constantly misinforming the player, making him/her walk into dialogues with semi-truths, wrongly presented information and endless defense mechanisms, evading for any kind of truth to be discovered. Being trapped within the narration, you are doomed to make wrong choices inconsequentially. Thus, there is no immersion, no character sympathy or even empathy, no control over any outcome. You are forced to witness endless apathy directed through stereotyped declarations.
The game is most definitely a great art project, and managed to accomplish what it has come to aspire: an ode to memory, perception and illusion of understanding. Yet, I find myself failing to recommend the game in the end. It is not fun to play. It is impossible for one to actually emphasize with the setting. It all is fleeting, surreal and numbing... as it was probably intended to be so. I most certainly appreciate it, yet fail to recognize the beauty of this kind of existentialist numbness as gameplay. There is no hate, no love, no fear, no bravery... "Nothing" wrapped in pretty colors. Pick it on sale if you'd like to take an unusual experience with the grand illusion of choice.

Kane & Lynch 2: Dog Days is such a strange game that it almost seems like an elaborate prank or creepypasta. Everything about it just feels
. Not enough to make it unenjoyable, but just enough to make your skin crawl while playing it. The controls are just janky enough to make aiming more of an effort. The enemies behave somewhere between robotic and realistic, making them seem almost inhuman. The music is a far cry from other third-person shooters' hard rock soundtracks - aside from a couple licensed tracks, you're treated to pulsing background noises that get more and more unsettling as the protagonists' situation worsens.
The story of Kane & Lynch 2 is pretty simple - the titular characters reunite in Shanghai to oversee an arms deal. As expected, things don't go as planned, and the two are forced to fight for their lives against Chinese gangsters and corrupt police officers. It's a straightforward crime drama and revenge story.
In terms of gameplay, Dog Days is a lot like Spec Ops: The Line without any twists. You get two guns, you hide behind cover, and you try to coordinate attacks to take down enemies. Gone are the grenades and explosives of the first game, though propane tanks can be used as improvised bombs. The game's arsenal is pretty diverse and includes a lot of Chinese guns, which are sadly uncommon in a lot of shooters today. Unfortunately, the difficulty scaling is terrible. In hard mode and extreme mode, enemies can absorb entire magazines of MAC-10 ammo and kill you with a couple stray pistol shots. Normal provides a decent challenge, but anything above that is mindlessly-frustrating and hard to enjoy.
There is a multiplayer mode for the game, but it's mostly dead unless you can organize a game yourself. Thankfully, bots are included in the game, so you can enjoy the Fragile Alliance mode without getting a party together. It's a fun little diversion where you and your team rob a place then try to escape without getting backstabbed by each other.
The tone of Kane & Lynch 2 is odd. It almost feels like a psychological horror game at times. Enemies have little to no combat dialogue and top-tier aiming skills, while you will struggle to fight back against them and try to get clean shots. You're constantly treated to the worst humanity is capable of throughout the story. The plot is extremely abrupt and makes the player question what they experienced. The main characters are hard to like, and their actions are questionable at best. And we already went over the "music" the game has to offer...
You'll either love Dog Days for its brutal, uncompromising story and direction, or you'll hate its wonky mechanics and bullet sponge enemies. I personally liked it, but I can't say that this game is for everyone. If you like third-person shooters, you may enjoy this game. I cannot recommend buying it outside of a sale, as the story is on the short side. The DLC all relates to the game's multiplayer modes, so don't bother with it unless you are interested in them.
With all that in mind, think carefully about whether this game seems right for you. If it sounds like a game you would want to play, remember to avoid buying it if it has anything less than a 75% discount.

Kane and Lynch 2 is a game that gets a lot of flack and for rather good reasons. It's abrupt ending, repetitive gunplay and unlikeable leads. But at the same time. I feel that's all in service of itself. Creating a sense of being a spectator into a dark world we don't understand nor do we want to.
The game uses a granny handheld camera style. In the vain of 'Man Bites Dog". It creates this dirty and distorted vibe that you'd expect in an unmarked VHS snuff tape or odd YouTube video you'd come across randomly. Made by these clearly unstable men you'd never want to come across yourself. The savage brutality sells that fact as you shoot someone in the head and see censor pixels rather than blood. As if it's too gruesome to actually show
There is no character development. By the end of the game our two main leads learn nothing from their experiences even after losing loved ones and spilling countless ammounts of blood, and it's clear will probably continue their mass rampage somewhere else. It speaks true to how real psychopaths act. There is no true way to understand a broken mind. And thus we can only view it from a distance like a horrific train accident.
Kane and Lynch 2 is not for everyone. It's a sloppy, rough around the edges shooter with no real value once you finish it. But I would recommend it as an audio-visual experience rather than as a normal video game. For it's short length, it fully immerses the viewer into a psychedelic horror show of neon lens flares and graphic violence. Whether it was intentional or not, it's lack of gameplay polish also really helps to sell the dark World IO Interactive is trying to build. A world's built around nihilism, full of nothing but human monsters that♥♥♥♥♥♥ torture and kill as a means to an end.

NOTE: This is an "Early Access" review meaning that this review was written in its beta stages.
The easiest way to explain this game is that it's a free version of Overwatch. Thats pretty accurate too. Most of the key elements of Overwatch will be present either modified or straight out ripped from Overwatch. Which isn't a bad thing (mostly)
Each round you need to defend a control point until one team has reached 100%. Once a team has reached 100% on the control point a payload will spawn in. The team that got 100% will need to push the payload to the other teams side while the other team needs to defend the payload. The payload process lasts three minutes plus additional "overtime".
The champions in the game are mostly good but I feel it is incredibly unbalanced and some champions are complete rip offs from Overwatch that they don't even try to make it look different. The graphics are nothing great and are sort of like what you would find in World of Warcraft or CS:GO. This isn't so much a bad thing but they do look very childish especially in the Jungle map. At this point there are only three maps in the game. I wish there would be more but the maps are well designed and they're good for now.
Pros:
- A big and diverse range of "champions"
- Fast paced and fun gameplay
- Game searching is very quick
- Rewards at the end of each game
- Its free
Cons:
- Some Champions are obvious rip offs from Overwatch
- Only three maps
- Graphics are sort of like World of Warcraft or CS:GO. Meaning not great but no so bad.
- The overtime system is horrible. Its horrible in any game. This should be removed.
- The control point percentage system is weird. It goes up 3% at a time every 2 seconds. It should only go up 1% every 2 seconds.
- Unbalanced as ♥♥♥♥
- The time to respawn is too long. There shouldn't even be one.
- Lots of bugs.
Final verdict: the game is brilliant for a free game. It's something you can play for hours and hours. It can run on almost any system from this decade. I really recommend this game. Especially since its free. It's fun, it goes at a fast pace.
At this point I give it a 7/10 becuase of the lack of brilliant graphics and only three maps. I also wish some of the champions weren't direct rip offs from Overwatch. Maybe this will change when the game comes out of beta.

Journal is a game that can't be fully explained with words on a review page. It is a game that's better to experience for yourself. Just to be sure that someone wanting to buy the game is reading this, I will include no spoilers whatsoever.
The summary of the game states: "Enter the pages of the hand painted world of Journal. A journey through the life of a young and troubled girl as she tries to face up to the choices and responsibilities that come with childhood. An experience that questions the reliability of how we choose to remember events and explores the truths hidden within our dreams.
Journal is a narrative driven adventure game by Richard Perrin, the creator of Kairo and the white chamber, with art and writing by Melissa Royall."
Well, it certainly is everything stated right there. This game is something that hits hard with reality. It doesn't put anything unrealistic or stupid in it, but rather truthful and depressing subjects that hit hard with many who play it.
The story, the ending and the characters are all brilliant! The only thing holding this game back (Which lots of people have mentioned already) are the slippery controls. You know every ice level EVER on a platform game? Where you're sliding all over the place and the controls are so sensitive? That's this game for the entire thing. But after about an hour into the game, I stopped paying attention to the slippery controls and fell in love with the story. Another con would also be that the games too short for a $10 game on Steam. I got this on sale for $1.39 and it was a bloody bargain.
If you, the reader, aren't aware of my rating system it goes like this.
BURN IT! (1-2/10)
Refund it politely then wonder why you ever played this game (3-4/10)
Buy it if it's on sale (5-6/10)
Buy it anytime and complete it (7-8)
BUY IT THEN REPLAY IT OVER AND OVER AND OVER AGAIN! (9-10/10)
So, this game is totally worth buying and it only take 3 hours to complete, but I think you should probably get it on a sale. This game also has a secret ending so, there's more for you.

In general, The Witcher 2 is extremely well executed and I sincerely enjoyed nearly everything about the game (minus a few miniscule things, which I will detail)
The GOOD things:
- Plotline is superb. The Witcher 2 is based on a novel and the story is top notch quality writing. Real LOTR  type stuff.
- The choices you make throughout the adventure determine how the game ends. The Witcher 2 actually has 8 different endings depending on the choices you make, and these choices are actually impactful (for example, MAIN characters can live or die depending on what you do). You can easily play though this game multiple times and get a different story line/ending each time.
- Characterization is probably the best I have seen in any game of this scale. It is hard not to care about what happens to the cast in this game. You either love or hate the characters because they have fully realized personalities and motives. If you consider how many main characters there are, along with all the of the different plotlines which are occurring, then this could not have been an easy feat to accomplish.
- The combat system is well executed. It is not sluggish or boring and it allows you to fight in many different combat styles if you choose to do so.
- The visuals in this game are simply stunning. If you compare The Witcher 2 to Skyrim, which came out within six months of eachother, The Witcher 2 blows Skyrim out of the water in terms of graphics and visuals.
The BAD things:
- There is no fast travel feature. There is a lot of walking around. It's not so bad that it breaks the game, but it is quite noticeable and it begs the question of why such a simple time saving feature was not placed into the game.
- Again, like in the original Witcher, you don't ever use the crafting/gold/enhancement items you collect unless you spend a lot of time and go out your way to do so. I felt like this was a big area the designers could improve on from the orignal, but it never happened.
- Some of the difficulty in the game is not quite balanced. For example the first chapter is probably the hardest one because you have zero gear or defenses and the mobs will just♥♥♥♥♥♥on you. As you progress and get better gear and talent points, the mobs literally become meaningless because you scale above them so drastically. Better balance was needed for sure.
Overall though, again, The Witcher 2 is excellent. The most important aspects of the game (the story and the actual combat) are executed extremely well. After playing The Witcher 2 I find it hard to believe that Skyrim received so much praise even though they were released within six months of eachother. The main thing Skyrim has over Witcher 2 is better  character combat/thieving customization, but the story and characters in Skyrim are just horrendous. I suppose it depends on what you are looking for in a game.The Witcher 2 takes about 20 hours to finish.

This is one more of those cases like Portal where the first game felt like a real PC game and the next one feels more like a console-optimized interactive movie. (To a modest degree, but in that direction.)
Yes, the production value might be high, the story might be interesting, but I'm not reviewing a movie here, but a game.
While in the first Witcher game, I liked the style, all its strong points so much, I could easily overlook the various weak points, but in this game, from the very beginning, I saw little but its flaws.
And because I saw way too many to edit them elegantly, here is a list of notes of the things that bothered me, in no particular order:
- Dithered lighting!
- Anisotropic filtering is enforced in the nVidia driver (since the game doesn't seem to have the option), but it still runs on trilinear!)
In these two points the graphics in Witcher 2 are actually worse than in the first game.
- Almost immediately vanishing corpses. (Same in the first game, but come on! Go with the times!)
- No graphics engine or keyboard config settings in game, only via launcher. The first game had all of this.
- Some fast-mouse-click QTE (quick time event) minigames are unnecessary and kind of harm immersion (sometimes practically "click now or die" - especially one scene in the prologue was annoying, since it was multi-phased and involved a sudden 180° change of camera view) - It makes little sense to expect very heightened adrenaline-pumping awareness while watching a cutscene and feels more like harassment.
Even the relatively lame fist fight mechanics of the first game I found more appealing than mere WASD button pressing on command.
- The precise-aim crosshair for daggers and such is almost invisible.
- Some quest/dialogue progression in the prologue doesn't make much sense, i.e. leaving continuity holes
- Selectable dialogue texts don't really match the Witcher's response that well. It's generally difficult to lead a conversation according to your true intention. You might end up accepting a task without wanting it. I often had to reload and try all options to at least get an idea of what I was doing.
- Some dialogue barely audible because mumbled, need to reduce music volume (e.g. inn), but might be too low in other cases then.
- Blood and dirt splatter on screen in cutscenes - harms immersion (4th wall breaking)
- Some gold bags might be untouchable due to usable objects nearby.
- An occasional geometry flicker issue that I saw in the first game, too, but no other game. Also some texture gaps.
- Not being able to take a killed guard's sword during a prison break is kinda stupid, and it's not like it would be overpowered in that situation.
- Game crashed before boarding a boat in one scene - couldn't save in that segment for some non-apparent reason, so had to redo and loot all the stuff I took there.
- No launcher bypass possible using witcher2.exe or via other means. Launcher then places a symbol in the task bar just to add annoyance to the whole thing.
- Inventory UI is kind of stupid in that it shows no stats for items in the list while highlighted, and menu items change size when highlighted, which impairs usability.
- The game package doesn't even include the manual. It's just 7 MB, but I had to download it separately. Also outdated!
- None of the 4 inventory sorting icons (whose meanings I had to find out by myself) gives you a value-for-weight sorting.
- Inventory sorting keeps reverting to time-of-pickup.
- Dropping an item from the inventory scrolls the whole list back to the top.
- Key-based inventory scrolling doesn't use Windows settings. Repeat rate and trigger delay is way too high for my convenience. Also, PGUP/PGDN have no function.
- Voices during conversations often have a strong reverb that doesn't match the environment at all.
- A more general issue that was already in the first game: You can take stuff out of storage crates and such, and none seems to be owner-tagged, although most of it should. In a game that seeks to create immersion, this common RPG trait is always disturbing that.
- Message "item cannot be sold" when trying to put it in my storage. Thus, unsellable items cannot be put in storage. Apparently the storage is just a crudely repurposed vendor.(which can lead to bugs)
- Quest texts go ahead in time, telling what's gonna happen later or supposed to happen. The player doesn't seem to be considered relevant in these things and it feels like a bit of a spoiler.
- Wavering camera during dice minigame is unrealistic and annoying.
- Missing comparative feature of inventory item stats with worn item stats.
- Fight club quest - when I'm asked to lose, I cannot decide to just quit, only accept the scam or fight (to win) anyway.
- Often repeating NPC lines. Less would be more (immersive). They say the exact same thing every time you pass after an area has loaded.
- Dialogue response timeouts - stupidest thing ever. For most dialogues it's perfectly fine or you to think about what to say for as long as you like (and I don't see a problem with that, and it's often necessary because the dialogue options are so unclear), but for some reason I don't see some dialogues will default to whichever option your cursor is on after a few seconds. If you don't notice the timer icon right away, you won't even know what you just chose.
- When moving through the world, occasionally there's a loading symbol in the lower right corner, but loading is almost lag-free, so that icon is distracting, because when it briefly flashes, I keep thinking I just walked over a lootable object.
- Geralt looks straight and not down when he's talking to a dwarf.
- Small things like cursor not staying on menu when exiting to main menu with intention of selecting quit game. UI usability sucks in this game.
- At least one quest didn't allow me a proper outcome in the journal and a quest tied into that one was absurdly unrealistic regarding changing a shop owner's conscience.
- I am led through endless cutscenes that last long enough to let any potion run out and then right after that I'm in battle with a boss enemy, without potions. (Maybe the timers halt, but if they do, that would actually harm immersion again.)
- First boss battle sucked, because while the game wants to look like a movie, the difficulty style is like hardcore indie games where you are likely to fail dozens of times, which I literally did. I must have tried 30 times. I felt like an actor and the director was shouting at me because I didn't do every move exactly according to script. I had to concentrate more on the "click now" like symbols on the screen than on the boss itself. I also at first didn't know when exactly the battle started and had to reload just to be able to drink potions in advance without wasting some of their meager 10-minute effect. Then I was frustrated because it used the wrong trap, despite me having selected the special trap for the boss. I eventually realized after several tries that I was supposed to left-click the marker with my mouse to place it. During the battle with a gigantic menacing boss, crows were sitting on a nearby corpse as if nothing was happening.
- Many events could be enacted in a non-instantly-lethal way and especially in normal game mode. But instead: cutscene after cutscene. One time I was to play another character in a short event and fought someone in a duel. I fought well. The moment I defeated him... cutscene where I fail. This is disappointing and borderline insulting to the player. Don't let me fight if you intend to cheat me out of my deserved victory.
Bottom line: This game often feels like it's trying to make me its trained monkey and has its fun toying with me, like I'm just an employee meant to move the story forward.
A lot about this game is the same stuff that put me off about games like Castlevania LoS 1+2 (of which I played the demos).
It gets surprisingly easy later-on though.

I've put 8 hours into this game and I want to put more into it. I like playing it alone and as I've not played the other Orcs Must Die I thought I would give this a try due to it being free. I've yet to play Multiplayer, even in survival mode, and I don't know if I ever will, but I know that I'm enjoying what I've seen thus-far.
However, I still would not reccomend this game. The price-gating is silly, worse even than Heroes of the Storm. Whereas Heroes of the Storm gives you one resource to grind (Gold) and that can unlock all of the non-cosmetic content in the game, OMD:U gives you about 20 different resources to be used in crafting everything from traps to minions to heroes. It is cumbersome just trying to figure out what resources are needed for what content and the amount being asked for a lot of these crafted good, ESPECIALLY the heroes, is way above what I would consider to be reasonable.
8 hours in I've had no issues with traps. I've made do and honestly with the hero I've been maining I don't think I need many more at this point, but I don't own this hero and if she moves out of the rotation then I'm stuck and my setup that has been doing me very well suddenly becomes a lot less viable.
I am willing to grind to unlock stuff. I've not spent a penny on Heroes of the Storm, but the cost of the heroes is staggering, the cost of everything else I can see some justification for, but the variety of crafting materials is unhelpful, the crafting system is hard to get a handle on, and I feel if I were a less patient guy this game would just be too much for me to stand.
So I can't in all good faith recommend this game. If the team drastically revamp how the crafting works, and the pricing on the heroes, then I may even put some money into it, but as it stands I can't and won't pay for a game that so transparently wants to inconvenience me into paying.

Orcs Must Die! was a game that changed the scope of dungeon defense games by making you part of the action and focusing on giving the player both a sense of urgency as well as control. You needed to be both fast and precise in trap making and actually combat with the hordes of unrelenting orcs. As you procede and earn rewards, you unlock new trap types, unlock new levels, and you can spend skulls as you wish to fit your own style of gameplay. Orcs Must Die! 2 simply impoved upon this by adding new traps, new enemy types, new magic charms, a new playable character and, best of all, two player co-op. So, to me, it only made sesne to be excited when seeing the trailer on steam for a new free to play Orcs Must Die game with up to 5 player co-op. I expected to see new traps, new characters, new enemy types, and a new story line. As soon as I launched the game, I was met by all but one of these things: a new story line. Instead of a story I found unresponsive controls and a tutorial that broke the fourth wall and treated me like a child. After finishing the tutorial, I was treated to a screen very reminiscent of League of Legends and I realized why the War Mage (Apparently, now known as Maximillion?) kept calling the orcs "minions" and my fears had been realized. Orcs Must Die! Unchained's introduction of 5v5 pvp was not an added bonus as I had originally thought, but the new focus of the game. Orcs Must Die! Unchained is a moba. Even the tower defense option is treated as a moba. The developer's of Dungeon Defenders tried to make their tower defense game into a moba which completely flopped and they tossed it, so why did Robot Entertainment think that it would work for Orcs Must Die? If you want to play a true tower defense game, spend the cash and buy Orcs Must Die! or Orcs Must Die! 2. One of the best things about pc gaming is all of the awesome indie games you can buy extremely cheaply, and then get just as much fun and as many hours of play (or more) as any "triple A" title. The binding of isaac is one of those games. At first it seems to be a fairly innocent arcade-style dungeon crawler, but in reality it is anything but.
The binding of isaac is about a boy named isaac (and maybe other unlockable characters...) who jumps into his basement while fleeing from his mother, who is on a mission from god to slay her only son. The game has other pretty dark and sacrilegious referrences, but that just adds to the fun. The gameplay is about you controlling isaac as he walks around the dungeons and fights monsters by shooting his tears at them.
As you progress through the dungeons and defeat bosses, untimately attempting to kill mom, isaac will level up various skills and gain new abilities with the various items you can collect. If you make it to the end, you'll feel like a complete badass rushing around killing enemies easily with your upgraded tears and items.
In the end, this game is highly worth $5, but if you aren't willing to pay even that little, it often goes on sale with the various steam sales. I got the game and the dlc for less than $4 on one such sale.

NATURAL SELECTION 2:
This game is outstanding! I played the original Natural Selection MOD for Half-Life and this is a gorgeous looking game through and through. It's aesthetic cohesion and replayability make this something that can be played time and time again.   Between Marines and Aliens, and the many maps and technologies and lifeforms and upgrades and the cooperation and coordination is key. Then there is the COMMANDER role that turns this already grand game into its own RTS style interface, a birds-eye-view of the action; needing to listen to your troops/hordes requests and concerns. Communication is the cornerstone of this game, so having a good headset is a must.
This game is only a few years old, but has a very strong very (generally) helpful community of players. However any game community that is independently created, crowdfunded, and operated always needs more new players to keep it alive, so thats where I URGE YOU to BUY THIS GAME!
Don't be swayed by those that say it has a "massive" learning curve, don't get me wrong there is a learning curve, but in the best way possible. There are so many things to get good at, and strategies that can be done on the various beautifully made maps, there are so many weapons, and classes that you can be "good" or "bad" at. So it'll probably take a lot of dying before you learn how to land those "bites" or "bullets" correctly in order to secure those kills and better help protect your team and push for further command points.
The strategic and coordination element of this game is out of this world, so many ways each match could be played. There are skill levels that get calculated based upon a variety of factors, namely kill/death , win/lose, attack/defend, build/destroy, time spent/rounds etc ratios. It blew me away how many variables there are in a given game, that its not just a BAD commander or a BAD player, or even just a BAD team; literally a dozen other things that could have affected a game to go one way or the other. So in the middle of a game if your losing and the team all blames the commander for not doing this or that, or the commander is blaming the team for not listening to commands or being ''noobs'' or whatever, so in short don't be scared by any learnign curve, or anything that anyone else says isn't good about this game, because they are wrong. It is filled with solid individuals from all over the world who unite together and fight in this beautiful space epic. Natural Selection 2.

Quern is a puzzle game which takes place on a island with puzzles based around language, number, herbology, element and machines, This is a really good vertical slice of what a modern first person puzzle game is. Nothing is too hard, I got lost not knowing what to do next a couple of times, but that is all part of the fun of the hunt and exploration. What starts out a mysterious and unknown becomes familiar and puzzles which start out perplexing will become mastered by the end of the adventure. Like a lot of games the player is presented with a choice at the end and it is very arbitrary as to which yo choose, which is a shame, but Quern's story is interesting for the most part.
Graphically it is a very nice looking game with the exception of a few textures here and there. The soundtrack is quite muted, which is a shame because there are some good tracks. My biggest gripe with the music is that it doesn't reflect the environment very much and when you move between areas the soundtrack doesn't blend like it should do in this kind of game.
If you are a fan of first person puzzle games, or even puzzle games in general, I can highly recommend Quern.

It feels kind of harsh to judge a game on what it isn’t rather than on it’s own terms, but like many others I bought City of Colours on the strength of the description. Inspired by Banjo Kazooie and Jak and Daxter. If you’re going to namedrop to sell, then you can’t be surprised when you’re compared directly to those games.
This game shares almost nothing with those classics except for a twee art style. Those games are defined by platforming, collectables and an open structure, where players can take on challenges in whatever order they wish. The Last Tinker is an entirely linear game with no jump button. Platforming challenges consist of nothing more than holding a trigger and moving the stick forwards, similar to Zelda games – it’s almost entirely automated and thus entirely unengaging.
The rest of the game consists of tepid, unchallenging puzzles punctuated by perfunctory batman style combat. Occasionally there’s an utterly rote boss fight. I know this is a game aimed at children, but even by those standards the game is coddling and witless. It falls in that uncomfortable middle ground where it’s far too childish for older kids whilst being too mechanically complicated for little ones. If you’re wanting a 3D platformer of old, give this one a miss – it is not what you want it to be.

Enter the pages of the hand painted world of Journal. A journey through the life of a young and troubled girl as she tries to face up to the choices and responsibilities that come with childhood. An experience that questions the reliability of how we choose to remember events and explores the truths hidden within our dreams.
Journal is a narrative driven adventure game by Richard Perrin, the creator of Kairo and the white chamber, with art and writing by Melissa Royall.
As the summary says, in this game you play as a troubled young girl, facing her responsibilities and the consequences of her choices.
The game plays relatively well, aside from the controls. It feels like they made this game, intending it to be a point & click, but instead decided to use keyboard controls half way through development. I really think the game would be better if, instead of keyboard controls, they used point & click mechanics. It would even go really well with the game; in its current state, you have to navigate with the arrow keys (which are a little too responsive) and space to talk to people or interact with the environment. So, naturally, point & click controls would help with the over sensitive arrow keys and also allow you to simply click on a person to walk over to them and talk to them.
The story is a really well made one, despite it being only around 2 hours long. The premise is that suddenly, the pages of your diary are blank and you need to find out what happened to them. By playing through each of the 5 days, you collect the information that has disappeared. If you like games where the character has a mild case of amnesia, or is needs to find pieces of his/her memories as they progress, you will enjoy this game. The secret ending that you can get after you play through the game once is worth your time to find ;)
Has beautiful hand-drawn visuals and a soothing soundtrack. The perspective of this game is strange: you (as the girl?) are sitting at what seems to be a desk in your bedroom, looking into your journal, playing the game, looking for the missing words of your journal (journal-ception?!). When you complete each day, the perspective changes, and you are greeted by a shadow puppet show that tells a unique story. The main part of the game consists of wandering through your British town, talking to people, completing tasks, resolving troubles, and taking part in school life.
Some actions are influenced by your decisions, but I think you get the same ending no matter what choices you make during your first playthrough.
There are 10, easily unlockable achievements that took my 2.3 hours to unlock (one is sitting at the menu screen for 10 minutes xD). The price is high for only 2 hours of content, so I recommend you buying this game on sale for under $5, unless you really want to play it. Overall a really enjoyable game that plays sort of like a visual novel. I got it for $1.39, and I couldn’t be happier.

Journal is not a video game, there is no actual "game" involved: no puzzles, no skills required, no choices. It is just a mildly long story -  nearly 3 hours - that unfolds as one clicks endlessly the same button and travels the same places.
The story is not great either: It starts in a terrible way and gets mildly more interesting as it approaches the end. However, dialogues are quite boring and sometimes they feel inconsistent.
Journal could probably be transformed into a decent comic book, but it is not a good video game. This is somehow sad to realize, because it seems to me that the game means a lot to its authors for personal reasons.

A short and sweet story with an intriguing art style. Very much an Angsty Teenage Girl Simulator, but in a good way.
P.S. if you decide to play this, I STRONGLY suggest starting a second playthrough after finishing your first one and unlock the secret ending. Worth it.

I'm not really sure what to say about this game. I feel like I should probably wait a day or two before writing this review, but if I do that, the emotional charge that's in me will go away.
First of, this isn't a puzzle game. Or even a game really. It's an interactive story with dialouge choices along the way. Some of these choices (or maybe even most of them) don't really hold much consequence and most of the results are quite predictable. This isn't a problem however. It's the moment that you make the choice that really matters. You sit there weighing the options next to eachother, knowing fully well what will happen when you choose either one. Just like in real life.
Nearly all of the choices we make in life feel predictable to ourselves. We understand that when we lie, either someone will discover the truth or we will be wondering whether or not someone will discover the truth for the rest of our lives. Once we actually follow through with the lie howerver, we constantly think about what would of happened if we told the truth.
Which, in my humble opinion, is this game's greatest strength. It makes all of the choices feel like choices that we one day could make ourselves, and shows us how people may or may not react to those choices. I found it to be extremely compelling.
The story it's self is quite uninteresting, particularly the first two days. It comes across as rather uninspired and pointless and I was rather underwhelmed. Keep in mind while trudging through it, that it is actually pretty important and you should pay attention. Although I found it rather dull, it's quite complex and the characters come across as quite relatable and human. You'll know someone just like nearly everyone you meet in this game.
Something also needs to be said about the art style and music. Although it's nothing that would drop a jaw, it suits the mood and story very well. The world looks and feels tense, which makes the later parts of the plot seem much more interesting. The whole game you're wondering why everything is so depressing and dim until you finally reach the ending where everything falls nicely into place, bringing forth understanding for certain design choices.
This game isn't for everyone. Not even for most. There are no puzzles or gameplay, only walking around and making choices. But the choices themselves are what made this game worth it for me. I sat in this chair at the end thinking about why I do what I do and considering the effect these choices are having on other people. If you're looking for an experience similar to the one I just described, then I heartely recommend this game to you.

I have been using GG for 3 months now, so it’s about time for a review.
From the first day I used this I was very impressed at how easy and user friendly it was.
You can get instant visual results with this package, straight away without having to read manuals or have any background in modelling or coding.
Now its 3 months later and I am enjoying it more each day.
I recommend this package to anyone from the first time gamer to, wannabe game makers, like myself.
You can create your own 3d models and use them in game with ease.
The scripting language is easy to learn and comprehend, it basically a descriptive logic language.
I recommend that you also learn how to do 3d modelling and scripting as well.
To gain an all-round enjoyable experience.
I also do recommend that you put some time into exploring and understanding how the package works. This will give you the realisation that this package has great current and future potential.
Don’t be afraid of editing files and scripts to understand how things work. If you break something you can just re-download a new set and start over, but its best to work off a copy of the original files.
This has been the best value for money purchase i have every made.
I also need to make special mention the generosity of the community and the developers and moderators in the forums support, and the stores.
It is exceptional, there is always someone around and prepared to help you out with any issues.
Make sure you take the time to browse the forums. There is a wealth of information within the forums.
Not to mention 1000's of free 3D models made by the community members and there are 100's of scripts for free as well.
Enjoy.

In general, The Witcher 2 is extremely well executed and I sincerely enjoyed nearly everything about the game (minus a few miniscule things, which I will detail)
The GOOD things:
- Plotline is superb. The Witcher 2 is based on a novel and the story is top notch quality writing. Real LOTR  type stuff.
- The choices you make throughout the adventure determine how the game ends. The Witcher 2 actually has 8 different endings depending on the choices you make, and these choices are actually impactful (for example, MAIN characters can live or die depending on what you do). You can easily play though this game multiple times and get a different story line/ending each time.
- Characterization is probably the best I have seen in any game of this scale. It is hard not to care about what happens to the cast in this game. You either love or hate the characters because they have fully realized personalities and motives. If you consider how many main characters there are, along with all the of the different plotlines which are occurring, then this could not have been an easy feat to accomplish.
- The combat system is well executed. It is not sluggish or boring and it allows you to fight in many different combat styles if you choose to do so.
- The visuals in this game are simply stunning. If you compare The Witcher 2 to Skyrim, which came out within six months of eachother, The Witcher 2 blows Skyrim out of the water in terms of graphics and visuals.
The BAD things:
- There is no fast travel feature. There is a lot of walking around. It's not so bad that it breaks the game, but it is quite noticeable and it begs the question of why such a simple time saving feature was not placed into the game.
- Again, like in the original Witcher, you don't ever use the crafting/gold/enhancement items you collect unless you spend a lot of time and go out your way to do so. I felt like this was a big area the designers could improve on from the orignal, but it never happened.
- Some of the difficulty in the game is not quite balanced. For example the first chapter is probably the hardest one because you have zero gear or defenses and the mobs will just♥♥♥♥♥♥on you. As you progress and get better gear and talent points, the mobs literally become meaningless because you scale above them so drastically. Better balance was needed for sure.
Overall though, again, The Witcher 2 is excellent. The most important aspects of the game (the story and the actual combat) are executed extremely well. After playing The Witcher 2 I find it hard to believe that Skyrim received so much praise even though they were released within six months of eachother. The main thing Skyrim has over Witcher 2 is better  character combat/thieving customization, but the story and characters in Skyrim are just horrendous. I suppose it depends on what you are looking for in a game.The Witcher 2 takes about 20 hours to finish.
Oh, and Philippa Eilhart is such a babe.
