This is one more of those cases like Portal where the first game felt like a real PC game and the next one feels more like a console-optimized interactive movie. (To a modest degree, but in that direction.)
Yes, the production value might be high, the story might be interesting, but I'm not reviewing a movie here, but a game.
While in the first Witcher game, I liked the style, all its strong points so much, I could easily overlook the various weak points, but in this game, from the very beginning, I saw little but its flaws.
And because I saw way too many to edit them elegantly, here is a list of notes of the things that bothered me, in no particular order:
- Dithered lighting!
- Anisotropic filtering is enforced in the nVidia driver (since the game doesn't seem to have the option), but it still runs on trilinear!)
In these two points the graphics in Witcher 2 are actually worse than in the first game.
- Almost immediately vanishing corpses. (Same in the first game, but come on! Go with the times!)
- No graphics engine or keyboard config settings in game, only via launcher. The first game had all of this.
- Some fast-mouse-click QTE (quick time event) minigames are unnecessary and kind of harm immersion (sometimes practically "click now or die" - especially one scene in the prologue was annoying, since it was multi-phased and involved a sudden 180° change of camera view) - It makes little sense to expect very heightened adrenaline-pumping awareness while watching a cutscene and feels more like harassment.
Even the relatively lame fist fight mechanics of the first game I found more appealing than mere WASD button pressing on command.
- The precise-aim crosshair for daggers and such is almost invisible.
- Some quest/dialogue progression in the prologue doesn't make much sense, i.e. leaving continuity holes
- Selectable dialogue texts don't really match the Witcher's response that well. It's generally difficult to lead a conversation according to your true intention. You might end up accepting a task without wanting it. I often had to reload and try all options to at least get an idea of what I was doing.
- Some dialogue barely audible because mumbled, need to reduce music volume (e.g. inn), but might be too low in other cases then.
- Blood and dirt splatter on screen in cutscenes - harms immersion (4th wall breaking)
- Some gold bags might be untouchable due to usable objects nearby.
- An occasional geometry flicker issue that I saw in the first game, too, but no other game. Also some texture gaps.
- Not being able to take a killed guard's sword during a prison break is kinda stupid, and it's not like it would be overpowered in that situation.
- Game crashed before boarding a boat in one scene - couldn't save in that segment for some non-apparent reason, so had to redo and loot all the stuff I took there.
- No launcher bypass possible using witcher2.exe or via other means. Launcher then places a symbol in the task bar just to add annoyance to the whole thing.
- Inventory UI is kind of stupid in that it shows no stats for items in the list while highlighted, and menu items change size when highlighted, which impairs usability.
- The game package doesn't even include the manual. It's just 7 MB, but I had to download it separately. Also outdated!
- None of the 4 inventory sorting icons (whose meanings I had to find out by myself) gives you a value-for-weight sorting.
- Inventory sorting keeps reverting to time-of-pickup.
- Dropping an item from the inventory scrolls the whole list back to the top.
- Key-based inventory scrolling doesn't use Windows settings. Repeat rate and trigger delay is way too high for my convenience. Also, PGUP/PGDN have no function.
- Voices during conversations often have a strong reverb that doesn't match the environment at all.
- A more general issue that was already in the first game: You can take stuff out of storage crates and such, and none seems to be owner-tagged, although most of it should. In a game that seeks to create immersion, this common RPG trait is always disturbing that.
- Message "item cannot be sold" when trying to put it in my storage. Thus, unsellable items cannot be put in storage. Apparently the storage is just a crudely repurposed vendor.(which can lead to bugs)
- Quest texts go ahead in time, telling what's gonna happen later or supposed to happen. The player doesn't seem to be considered relevant in these things and it feels like a bit of a spoiler.
- Wavering camera during dice minigame is unrealistic and annoying.
- Missing comparative feature of inventory item stats with worn item stats.
- Fight club quest - when I'm asked to lose, I cannot decide to just quit, only accept the scam or fight (to win) anyway.
- Often repeating NPC lines. Less would be more (immersive). They say the exact same thing every time you pass after an area has loaded.
- Dialogue response timeouts - stupidest thing ever. For most dialogues it's perfectly fine or you to think about what to say for as long as you like (and I don't see a problem with that, and it's often necessary because the dialogue options are so unclear), but for some reason I don't see some dialogues will default to whichever option your cursor is on after a few seconds. If you don't notice the timer icon right away, you won't even know what you just chose.
- When moving through the world, occasionally there's a loading symbol in the lower right corner, but loading is almost lag-free, so that icon is distracting, because when it briefly flashes, I keep thinking I just walked over a lootable object.
- Geralt looks straight and not down when he's talking to a dwarf.
- Small things like cursor not staying on menu when exiting to main menu with intention of selecting quit game. UI usability sucks in this game.

That name used to mean something less than a year ago. It wasn't a game, back then. It was an ideal, a game that existed only because we wanted it to. The world would be better with it's presence, we thought. Gaming would never be the same if it appeared; like an atom bomb, it would change the way we looked at things forever.
It has now been over a year since that name was brought from shadow, to spotlight, and now discussion. What do we have now, six DLCs down the road and plenty of time to sink in hour upon hour?
PROSITIVES:
THE COLOR BLUE: While New Vegas might have been in a dusty desert, brown in excess is never a good thing. Fallout 4 finally gives us some richer colors to stare at. Metal foundries turned Raider Strongholds have fiery hues to inflame our anger towards injustice. The countryside has pleasantly clean skies and lush vegitation in the remains of old highways and parks. Rad storms and the poisoned Glowing Sea cast a harsh green glow onto the landscape, flashes of lightning jolting us from our idle stares into the maelstrom above.
ACTUAL SHOOTER COMBAT: At long last, 3D Fallout shoots like it should. We can sprint for the first time, quickly moving from cover to play that deadly game of bullet ping-pong. Recoil feels right, and moving guns with a controller isn't linear and stiff, but fluid and responsive, allowing for quick manuvers of sight-hip-repeat. Grenades can be tossed with your rifle out, allowing you to coax opponents out of cover and into your waiting line-of-sight. These tenets of design may be standard on other shooters, but they were lacking in Fallout. And now, it's here and (almost) perfect.
A USE FOR EVERYTHING IN THE GAME: Cigarettes, electronics, and chemicals won't be the only things you pick up anymore. Bethesda has put purpose behind every coffee cup, every discarded glass, and more. To let your creative desires flow in your canvases of guns and housing, you'll need the right materials. Every peice of junk you come across has little salvagable components within themselves that you can then use to make useful things. Want to construct a wonderful bungalow for your character out of a gas station? You'll need steel and wood-and both of things exist in clipboards and tin cans. With the exception of folders, you'll find yourself reaching for whatever isn't welded to the floor.
AN ARSENAL AS CREATIVE AS YOU: Previously, every raider has the same rifle as a soldier. Fallout 4's crafting system allows for what New Vegas tried to do: mods that made your gun yours. Enemies can have weapons creatively-tuned or plain as paper; one raider's ramshackle rifle has a tuned receiver or a hair-trigger, while another's Pipe Pistol is just a tool for the job. But with the right perks and parts, you can make very special armor and weapons for yourself. Why have a Standard Laser Rifle when you can tweak it to scatter beams or incinerate to disintigrate? Why have just a Leather Chestpeice when you can shadow it to sneak and stab? Your character can be as unique as your tools.
BETHESDA'S BEST ARMOR SYSTEM YET: Fallout 3 and NV had only three slots: Face, Hat, and Body. Skyrim got closer, segmenting the body into Greaves, Boots, Torso, and with Necklaces and Rings to boot. Now we have something magical: from top to bottom, Hat, Eyes, Face, Left arm, Torso, Right arm, Left leg, and Right leg, and a new "underarmor" slot for close-skin clothing that can be worn underneath your armor. Mix and match for effectiveness or looks, but regardless, it's diverse.
BEYOND THE BIG FINALE: The game will go as long as you let it. No DLCs required to expand the level cap-it's already cranked up to infinity. Build the most impossibly powerful individual for as long as you keep playing. And when the ending hits, your survivor keeps walking to mop up leftover quest and locked perks.
FROM COMPANIONS TO SOULMATES: Past games had their share of good pals to support the sadness of the wastes, and this game keeps that bar high. Each companion has their own stories, likes, dislikes, dreams and hopes. They routinely make subtle movements and little dialogue quirks that bring real people out of virtual constructs. And with their perks being unlocks rather than presence-based, you're welcome to try them all.
A FLAVORED CAST OF VOICE ACTORS: Bethesda's past ventures often had small crews of common voices, but they've done something with this one that prevents dialogue from going stale audio-wise. I can't quite put my finger on it...bigger cast? Similar voices? Regardless, it's better here.
PLASTIC SURGERY REFINED: The character creator in this game's absolutely phenomenal. Dials and numbers become a stretch-and-pull plethora of wonderful options of any face and body shape you can think of. Channing Tatum or horrible scar-rack? Your choice.
CONNATIVES
THE STORY: Truth be told, it's not that bad. It has about one good twist, but that's it. Granted, the main story wasn't the spotlight in these games.
PRESTON AND HIS MERRY MEN: Alright, the Minutemen are a great way of discovering workshoops and places to build settlements. This is ruined by the fact you have to babysit your territory while the okay-companion Preston is forced to become a pez-dispenser of "do this' quest. Trimming down the quest he gives or the amount of workshops you can have and use would easily make this better to bear, but presently it's a pain that hinders your desire to build in different places.
POWER ARMOR: In addition to canonicly making no sense at all, the Power Armor system, while cool and interesting, isn't extrememly needed or even utilized. You can mix and match peices onto a frame, and there's an alright system in place for making your own extreme exosuit, but your parts can take damage and break off of you, requiring more scrap to fix. You're also slower in it and using it will require Fusion Cores, a costly fuel source that makes constant use an impossibliity. By the time you have plenty of gas, your player will often be stronger apart than with Power Armor.
OLD PROBLEMS THAT LINGER: New songs sit in the radio-about two of them. The rest are re-used from older games, leading to a quickly-annoying earworm generator that's even more grating than the previous titles. AI still gets stuck in places and onto things, animations are still not flawless (but better.) This is the only Fallout game I had where I actually completed every quest in one run, leaving nothing to do. The Armor system doesn't allow you to wear EVERYTHING (would it kill to make all common clothes underarmor?) And of course, bugs on bugs.
THE DIALOGUE WHEEL: In an attempt to trim dialogue, Bethesda made every encounter have four dialogue options. This wouldn't be as bad as it is if every option you choose is described in two words or less, so you'll never know exactly what you'll say. The biggest gripe is the "sarcastic" option. It's never described as "yes" or "no", just "sarcastic." It's ridiculous.
THE VERDICT
APPROVED-Worth a buy.
A year later, this game is still giving. Still, I find new things to do, new contraptions to build, and new adventures even after plenty of hours more than my friends. Though all in all, I have to say this is a weaker RPG for Bethesda. It's a greater shooter, no doubt, but it's no RPG, and for some people, that's all Fallout was. I understand that frustration.
But in all of the bad, remember this: this game almost went the route of No Man's Sky. Hype infatuated so high, hopes set to an unreachble bar, that when the product finally dropped, the flaws that were there clashed so intensly with our impossible ideal. Now, UNLIKE No Man's Sky, this game actually did meet many of it's promises, thankfully. But make no mistake, this is not the game you see in the Announcement Trailer.
At least, not without Far Harbor.

Numerous games come to mind playing this.
Everything by Rareware, Psychonauts, Little Big Planet, Paper Mario. Yes, I'm using the "it's like <all these great games>" description that's usually a bit scammy. I'll pick one then, it's like Beyond Good and Evil. Linear, not terribly complex, but downright fun.
- It's not a platformer.
- Don't expect puzzles. It's just lever-pulling and repeating a sequence.
- A bit of (self-)referential humor at times, don't expect a lot.
- Linear as all hell, except for a single optional collectible. There's also gems to buy moves with(or as a key item at start), but that happens automatically. There is no backtracking whatsoever. ~8 hours.
-- Possible because of this, an excellent hint system. Just ask your buddy and he will fly almost the exact route you need to go.
- Combat is not difficult,
. I went for the "instant death" difficulty, thinking it to be a cooler name for "nightmare". It is not. Things will gib you continuously, even things that only knockback on other settings. Does not make the game more fun, just more annoying. No achi either. Just don't.
-- The cargo rails. What I thought was a scenic trip through the wonderfully crafted world was instead a quick time event in disquise. Especially on instant death. Bah.
-- Enemies(outside of boss adds) do not respawn. Even instant death is quite doable, the regular levels. Bosses still require a lot of trial and error until you completely know the attack pattern.
-- You gather three colored powers over the course of the game,
. The first quarter of the game is simply"hit it until it dies, dodge if it attacks". They also give a superpower usable once a bar is filled. But this doesn't add any depth to boss fights, as they still need to be hit X times in the weak spot.
- It's cartoony. Some people use that as a pejorative, but it's simply a description. Like romantic comedy. Some people never like romantic comedies, most people need to be in a mood for it. Just like with cartoony. It feels cell-shady, everything is bright and un-brown.
- "Everything in this world is made of paint, paper and glue", and it shows. Text balloons are in gamespace, some are static, so you can view a textbox from the side to see that sinusoid cardboard thing, and you can view them from behind where they're blank.
- The world is beautifully made. There's dissapointingly much lore, as you don't ever see e.g. the inside of a dust refinery, or a rainbow factory where colors are made. On the other hand, you can often peer in a random direction and see detail without the quests ever taking you there.
- The characters. Banjo-Kazooie-like creatures just ramble on in their voice, gesturing, no matter their actual text. Each race has a "voice", and some unique characters have their own. There's quite a few different expressions. The three races look nothing alike, not just their bodies but their districts as well, each has their own architecture. Especially the spirits look great, Green was amazing.
It was a fun experience. I loved the characters, I giggled, I facepalmed at the cheesy story, I enjoyed the scenery, I raged at instant death(just don't).

: This British choice-driven youth drama has plenty going for it.
* A solid premise -- find out why the teenage protagonist's journal is suddenly filled with blank pages.
* Goreous art direction -- hand-drawn graphics; clever use of real-world design elements to put spatial limits on the levels, as the story goes on; paper-cut shadow plays during the cut scenes between days (chapters)
* Believable, well-realized characters -- fun fact: without even trying, I unlocked all of the personality-related achievements without a guide during my first playthrough, just by asking "What would Angela Chase (from
) do?"
* Intriguing setting -- a surreal, dream-like version of an otherwise unremarkable British small town during the bleak early days of the Tony Blair era.
: Lack of options, maybe? You explore the town, talk to people, and figure out who you're meant to interact with next. Not a lot of variety in terms of gameplay. Theoretically, it would be possible to port the whole game into Twine, using hyperlinks and text descriptions to move between locations. (Thankfully, the characters and the central mystery are compelling enough to keep going.)
Also, if you're not into family drama or coming-of-age narratives, you should probably avoid this.

The original Myst series is quite sacred to me. Any game claiming to be inspired by it is going to be held to a very high standard. This title meets that standard and beyond...it is an impressive, artful, and well executed piece, and it brings me great satisfaction and enjoyment. The puzzle difficulty is just perfect, and the puzzles are intertwined beautifully. Each breakthrough brings a bit of excitement, as new areas and possibilities unfold, revealing new mysteries and challenges.
This work is everything Myst could have been, had the technology existed in its time. The setting, themes and story line are original, though clearly inspired by Myst, but you do not have to be a Myst fan to appreciate the quality.
The developers paid very close attention to little details, and it makes such a difference. The voice acting, lore items, maps and story art are sumptuous, and they have innovated a great new notebook feature that allows you to sketch a screenshot. It is the first time I have seen it in an adventure game, and it's a beautiful idea.
Speaking as a Myst fan myself, I was thrilled to discover this title. It is indeed a childhood wish come true!

Been using GameGuru on and off since it was under another name.  It has pros and cons just like any engine.
Pros:
-Easy terrain editor and GUI interface.
-Save and load game feature written in LUA
-Easy to make standalone EXE, although needs more work.
-starts up a lot quicker than some other engines.
-Can import entities .X etc, FBX is still under development
-Lots of stock available on the store as well as enough default stock to get on with.
-Comes with stock LUA scripts but these are quite basic.
-Has a basic character creator but you can super impose your own faces onto the models
-Has game test mode and in test controls
-Has some basic documentation and videos, but not very technical, good for beginners.
-Great forum and friendly members with a wealth of technical/artistic knowledge and experience
Cons:
-You will need to do a lot of LUA scripting to get any sort of game mechanics that are unique to the game you are developing.
-AI stock scripts are quite basic and behaviour of AI is not great, you will need to improve on existing scripts to get better results.
-lack of 3rd person weapons.  Only comes with wizard staff.
-cannot create your own weapon projectiles, projectiles hard coded to use stock media at present
-Features can take a long time to get implemented and there is a big list on the feature vote list, not a huge fan of public feature voting systems.  A lot of engine functionality missing.
-Not enough technical documentation
Overall:
GameGuru is ideal for outdoor levels, once the eagerly awaited (for some) EBE (Easy Building Editor) is released in the next version, users will be able to build their own buidlings etc for indoor levels.  Whether AI will be able to go above 0 height is another thing.
Recommended if you want to scuplt terrain and throw in a few entities.
Not Recommended if you want indoor levels and high performance and great lighting.
Next update will be 1.132 (without the EBE as it still needs more work), this will see FPSC characters in GameGuru.
Version 1.132 released, some updates/fixes plus lots of converted FPSC media and example maps.  No EBE just yet, more to be done on it.  Check out Galaxy Seed, awesome artwork and animated spheres.
Summary:  GameGuru is in it's infancy still even after 3 years of development.  Has a lot of potential for being a good engine.  At the moment, only consider purchasing if you want to create outdoor levels.  Probably the best choice engine if you want a lot of stock media to start with.  Very good value for money.  If you are able to work with the limitations of GameGuru, I'd say buy it, try it and learn LUA for more complex stuff.  You haven't got anything to lose.  Good for getting game design experience, as the GUI is pretty easy to use.  Gets the thumbs up from me, but needs more features of which there are many still to add.  For a small team, they are doing pretty well so far.

Well I must say after spending some time with this software it's one of the best products for making quick games with. I picked this up a few days ago and started playing with it, getting a feel for the program took me no less then ten minutes. Now, I've played with the mainstream engines UDK, UE4, CE3, Unity4-5 and I was never able to get something done so fast with any of these Unreal Engine 4 is a bit easier than the other two I've mentioned but this is still easier. If you don't want to take the time in learning complicated game engines like the ones I've listed above then this is probably the best twenty bucks you will spend. It literally took me an hour to get something to look good and very playable.
It's intuitive, easy to learn, good quality visuals, and fun! You CAN import your own .x and .3ds model files so I don't know where these other reviewers come off saying "You can't use your own content." This is something I highly disagree with. A shout out to those people: do yourself a favor and find some plugins for 3ds Max, Maya, or whatever else you use. Blender exports to these filetypes natively and it's free, so why not get started with the cheapest, and in my opinion the best way to get started in game making without needing to worry about silly royalties because you can sell your creations without worrying about losing any money.
I mean sure, Unreal Engine 4 and Unity are free but they are complicated engines to use. UE4 has a 5% royalty but offers plenty of ways to make a game without needing to program. Unity is good as well and royalty free but this package forces you to code everything as far as game funtionality is concerned! CryEngine 3 is $9.90 a month, royalty free and a pain to use, not too mention the silly crap you need to download to get things to work properly and if you cancel, you can no longer use it, AAA studios getting you again. When it comes down to it and you just want to make something this is a good place to start if you're just getting your feet wet. Otherwise I would advise more professional level folks go after the engines I mentioned above. This software is no slouch and is still in the works and I would reccomend this.
But yes, buy this software you won't be disappointed!

Hard to give a bad review, though it's hard to give a good one too.
Game Guru is not for pro nor total amateur. There're scripts and if you don't use them, you'll do nothing. And if you don't modify them, you'll do the same as the other GG users.
Modify a sentence, modify a sound, or rewrite the whole script or a part of it, or BUY scripts on the store. That's what I did. Plus the ones you find for free in the forums. you'll also need entities (3d model). Again: your own, GG store or the same everyone owns.
Pros:
- Easy game maker (you don't have to know how to write a script)
- If you're creative, you'll have possibilities.
- If you know scripting, you'll have possibilities.
- If you love simple things at the moment, that's what you need.
Cons:
- For an easy game maker, it's not that easy at first because tutorials only shows the basics for now.
- It's not that easy when you don't know what a script is.
- Lots of bugs. Unstable (the map is huge, but if you want to make a street alive, your CPU will suffer.
- Not worth the price I paid (not the steam 20$, but a 100$ when it was called FPS creator reloaded)
- Careful what you wish for

Fallout Shelter. Now, this game is only really enjoyable if you are into these kinds of games. I, for one, love games where you can run your own certain place, like amusment parks, towns, and in this case, your own vault. And this game did everything that it said it would, and almost everything that we hoped it would be. So, what did I think of the game?
Well, for starters, let's go ahead and say a few positives. I love how you can make as many vaults as you want because of how you have to choose a number when you start a new vault. It allows you to make several vaults and still have tons of room left for someone else's vault. Another positive, as you know, is that the game doesn't have any paywalls or time constraints. You only have to pay if you want more lunchboxes, which allows you to obtain more items. Yet another postive is that the design of the game is fun and familiar. This game's cartoonish style is appealing to almost anyone of any age, which allows the game to be enjoyable to see every time you load up the game. Plus, Fallout players will recognize the style from some of the games, which appeals to them as well. One more positive is the ability to choose the babies' names. As overseer, you are able to choose the names of babies that are made in your vault. This allows for endless fun and creativity because of how often you make babies and how many possibilites are available. You can name them after celebrities, people you know, or just random words. It's really fun. Last but not least, the game's free. What more do I need to say? It's free to play.
All right, now let's dive into some negatives. First of all, much like the Fallout games, the game moves relatively slow. Now, Fallout players will be used to this, as the game revolves around what you do, so the game moves slow in the sense that you have to move it forward. This game, however, moves slow for a little while until you get more people or you get lunchboxes. This might make the gamers who are only playing this game because its free relatively bored because of this. It made me bored, to be honest, because it took me a while to get more people, lunchboxes, and different types of rooms. I actually quit for a few days before getting back into it because I would rather play a game that goes fast or at least doesn't go too slow for me. My last negative is more of a dumb thing, which is the possibility of failures. What I mean is that in the game you are able to rush certain things, which increase in the likelyhood of failing every time you do it. What I don't like about it is, for me at least, is that sometimes is happens even though it is only a 34% or even 16% chance of failing, but it still fails anyway. Honestly, it's an extremely amazing feeling when you have a 74% chance of failing, but still get a success.
Anyway, from all of these things, I would give this game a 7/10. It's a really interesting and cool game to play if you're into this genre, and plus, it's free. So even if you're not, you can try it out anyway. You might even like it.

My Review after over 10 hours of playing this symphony of fun and frustration:
First of all the game is still in development (beta) so of course there are bugs and all the well known things (lags, sound suddenly stops, ...) in the game. This does not count as a con like the developers are going to change and improve the game.
So when we leave all the bugs away I would say it is a very nice version of "Orcs Must Die!" with a very high potential.
- There is still the well known rift defending mode where you need to kill all the enemys before they get to your rift/s. It is new that you can now play all modes and missions with up to 4 other players. (friends or just anyone)
- The new mode "Conquer" (I hope its the right translation) feels very much like "League of Legends". Here you can either play against NPC's or other players trying to take over the enemys rift. The tricky thing is that your team needs to defend and attack at the same time. Of course you defend with your character and loads of traps. Attacking you do with spawning troops of orcs, swordsmen or whatever, leading them through the enemys traps, killing the badass guards and gates until your troops can enter the enemys rift. Furthermore there are (like in "LoL" too) specific side tasks to do (depending on the map) which allows you to send in a boss with your troops once per task.
- What surprised me pretty much is that they built an ingame shop where you can buy new characters or equipment for real money. Of course you can chraft everything you can buy in this shop, but this needs a lot of time searching for the specific loot. But still I hate games with shops where you need your debit card. Anyways I cross my fingers hoping that they will take it out again. I more like paying for the game instead of geting it for free and then paying ingame for all kind of stuff. But I guess im not the only one with the opinion. ;)
However, I'm a big fan of "Orcs Must Die!" and I would definitely recommend it.

Do not be fooled by my hours. I did not have internet for months so Steam could not track it. I've logged in around 50 hours with this software. My review has been updated to reflect my experience with the original release (which I purchased), and the Developer version, which was provided by the Devs.
Version reviewed - 1.111
____________________________________
GameGuru (GG) is created by The Game Creators. These are the same people that made another game creator called "First Person Shooter Creator" (FPSC). You can easily tell as they are basically the same thing. I mostly bought this cause I mostly wanted to see if they have learned from their mistakes in FPSC, which I have used for roughly 30-60 hours (when it worked,) but could not actually produce anything due to it huge errors and problems it suffered from.
GG lets you make your own First Person games. You can't go too far beyond that. You will mostly be stuck with making FPS games, as that is what 90% of this content is made towards. Comparing this to FPSC is almost 1000x better in just about every way imaginable! The most welcoming part it actually loads 99.99% of the time, and runs on new systems! FPSC is limited to running on Windows XP only, and FPSC 10x went to it's early grave and was never finished.
____________________________________
GG is a "Drag and Drop" style game maker, which is it make it easier for beginners or young kids to make a game. You will be using pre-made assets and models to create your map/level to how you see fit. The addition of a built in terrain editor is nice as well. The sculpting tolls are simple to use. The in-game testing also has nice features, like allowing you to edit while in game! GG has a lot of features that I never expected to be seen from TGC, which is really amazing.
You are also able to use SOME of the older FPSC Model packs as well, but only SOME of it. Most of the older content packs will either error out or will cause the engine to crash. They also made DLC packs to help those expand on their asset library. BE WARNED THOUGH! Much like FPSC, the model packs are nice, but they are VERY hit or miss in terms of quality. Some models look like they came from the year 2000. Same goes with any music and sounds. Also want to point out that some of the GG models and DLC include models from previous FPSC model packs.
GG includes a Character Creator as well. At the initial launch, it was extremely limited and no where near finished. As of current testing, it has greatly been improved and have added in more assets to play/edit with.
TGC also have an "Asset Store" which can be found on their website. I have not purchased much from there, so I can't say too much to what it has to offer. Much like every other Asset store though, be prepared to spend a lot of money. From what I could find, there was hardly any free items.
____________________________________
During the initial review, this software could not run on my potato of a laptop, and only worked on my Desktop. My first run at this software was not exactly a nice one. I crippled the entire engine permanently within 7 minutes! I did not have good experience in the initial launch and because of that, heavily swayed me to tell everyone to not purchase this software.
After getting access to the Dev version, I am able to run this on my potato (though at slow rates) and have been able to test out and try more things than I was able to before. I was not able to test this on my PC because of life problems, and the lack of Internet at home, so my laptop was my only choice in being able to download this and give it another try. I will say it does seem to work MUCH better and haven't had any issues in running GG. I did crash it trying to open the controls page, otherwise no other crashes or engine breaking errors.
My only fault with it that I can see is the lack of "Options/Settings" for the engine. I was hoping I could reduce the quality or settings to help improve performance, but you can't change any settings. Since there is only 1 option setting, GG takes about 20 min to boot up on my potato, and suffers a bit of lag when I try to add lots of objects on the screen.
____________________________________
Do you want to create a AAA Quality Video Game? Well you came to the wrong place. GG will help only the new comers to video games, or kids wanting to try out "Simple" game building.
As quoted from Lee Bamber [DEV] "GameGuru is more for users who want to create games quickly, have a little more fun doing it and skip the coding part if you want to. Even though it has a powerful LUA scripting system built-in, it will never replace professional games programming/modeling/design, but as an introduction to game making it's a great place to start."
I've stated before, the quality of assets/sounds tend to jump everywhere. If you have the talent though, try to use your own content. Making a game with your own creations always looks better than just paying for things. Much like any other game making software, it all takes time if you truly want to make something great.
The AI still tends to be dumb and stupid. Zombies get stuck on obstacles, enemies don't always shoot at you, the typical simple AI.
I have not made anything special as of yet, but I might possibly make something or other and release it on Gamejolt or ZeoGames, just so I feel I got something out of it.
____________________________________
Wait, after talking so much praise about this software, why the Thumbs Down? Let me explain.
You see, there isn't really a "Demo" or "Trial Version" of this software. I purchased this before the whole Steam Refund policy was a reality, so I was stuck with this software. I only bought it because I wanted to see how much it faired with FPSC. As there was no Demo or Trial, I had to buy it.
Now, after purchasing this software for $42 (Premium Pack when it had ALL the DLC and a discount) I felt burnt from it. As I stated I was not happy with the initial release. Most issues have been fixed since then, but I know why I don't enjoy it.
To really try and explain this, I have to mention Doom Builder, which is software that I've spent hundreds, if not thousands of hours on.
Let's say you wanted to build a small town square. In GameGuru you would simply drag and drop all your pre-made assets into place and place out decorations with what you had. In Doom Builder, you had to draw in everything and paste textures on everything. This is why I enjoy Doom Builder more, because I am not limited to what models I have. If I wanted to make a room and keep tweaking and changing it as I work on the game, I can do that. If I wanted to change something in GG, I have to search for a model to find something close to what I want, or try to make my own, which spoilers, I suck at modeling. This is why I PERSONALLY can't recommend this software, it's just not meant for me. I prefer being able to draw out my world/game than drag and drop. If you are like me, then you probably already use Unity or Unreal Engine (which are free.)
My Final Verdict:
6/10

I´ve been playing Overwatch for a while now (Level 115) and I decided to give the controversial "Overwatch Rip Off" a try, and♥♥♥♥♥♥that was fun.
I think while being similar, they are also very different and I´ll tell you why.
To start with, Overwatch totally depends on your ability on a character, nothing more, nothing less; however in Paladins you have those "cards" for each character that can give you advantage over the enemy if you manage them well, and also you have in-match upgrades that can be a game changer.
By example, imagine the enemy team has a lot of heroes with shields, then you can upgrade you character to inflict more damage on shields, therefore you´ll be able to carry your team easily. These kind of things are what give Paladins a great strategic feel, and I liked it. You could also decide to upgrade your reloading speed, etc... that can be a vital change in the battleground.
On the other hand, there is one thing I didn´t like, but It´s normal due to it being a Free to Play and Overwatch a Paid game, I´m talking about microtransactions. Yes, Overwatch has microtransaction, but it´s totally optional, as I´ve gotten a ton of Legendaries without having to buy crates, but in Paladins you got those crates that can almost only be purchased via real money, and that´s a shame because the skins that can be got by normal crates are kinda lame (just same skin with diferent colors)
In conclusion, I think this game is great, (I still prefer Overwatch due to characters, etc...) and It´s totally not P2W, something positive looking at nowadays F2P shooters, and if you want to give it a try, do it, it´s free!

The game is a little rough around the edges, but works well enough to enjoy.
Linux performance is not good. With my humble GPU and a 6 core CPU everything has to be put to low or off in the quality settings. If you have Windows, there's only one real choice: Don't play in linux!
Windows performance is approx 75% better and can get in between med and high quality with the same hardware.
But performance in general is just horrible compared to AAA titles with far greater draw distance and detail. Edit: With linux this is how I feel. In Windows with the higher quality settings the game looks better than it did at first. It has grown on me and I kind of like the way it looks now. There are some well done parts later on and some glitchy parts as well.
Anti-aliasing is horrible here. Enabling it removed jagged edges but makes objects highly blurry. Tree detail becomes that of the blind.
The story is interesting (maybe 1-2 minutes of story in about 2 hours). Is it done in a way that is anywhere near that of Myst? Not even close. Later on the story gains more ground and I found myself quite bored during it because of the way its done - a rather import part and long part of the story was done in a really boring way.
There's jump ability but plenty of invisible walls. You can't fall off of anything despite having jump ability and so far it feels like they just left it in instead of removing the ability. It has so far only helped to get out of a boat without trying to walk in a different angle. After 20 hours I've seen no real need for jumping excet to get out of glitchy spots where the player gets stuck.
I do like the fact that you can view letters and close them while the voiceover continues.
Arrow keys are default bound
Its rather bland looking. Edit: It improves later on after some areas are unlocked and further from there. There are some really nice looking places and its not all rock and overcast sky.
What about the puzzles? You start off right away with one. Every door seems to be locked! So you're solving puzzles opening doors to new areas. They are varied and kind of interesting. Some are more like adventure games where you put an object into the holder or whatever and that's the puzzle finding where it goes. Then there's sliding blocks around to get the blocks in a certain place or directing light. And more.
Some puzzles are really annoying. Some are fun. Some puzzles are redone. Some puzzles will make you confused. Some will not be what you wanted but its what you get.
There's one puzzle where you literally need to use the zoom click of the middle mouse button to read the symbols well. Not terriblly fond of that, but its functional. I'm sure someone will liken it to a magnifying glass in the real world but whatever.
The inventory ... edits.... Sometime after 2 hours I realized that the scroll wheel allows srolling through a use inventory. So that the object chosen is the one that is used in the world. This is necessary at times when there's multiple objects in the inventory as sometimes multiple objects can be used with the same use point.
The game can't be completed without using the inventory in everway possible.
Edits... After 20 hours (took 23 hours for me to complete) and seeing how the game changes, being longer than I expected (so many puzzles everywhere, more and more) and the better performance and quality provided by Windows, I still recommend this game and at 20 hours have not completed it yet (and I feel I'm solving every puzzle at a good pace).

A very joyful and colorful 3D Platformer, that honestly anyone, at any age can enjoy. It wasn't a very long game, nor was it very hard one, but when I finished the game, it left me with a overall good experience, and it makes me want to go back and find the remaining collectables and get the last few achievements.
The game isn't very hard. Which allows for anyone, at any age to play and enjoy the game. There is no precision platforming, because it is removed by some "almost automatic" jumps. There are a ton of save stages, which means if you die, you don't have to start all over again, and if you ever get lost, then you can always ask your little helper to show you in the right direction. Some people would say that this makes the game too easy, but I honestly don't mind.

The Last Tinker is a charming game which quickly got me emotionally engaged and made it really easily for me to relate to the protagonists on my journey.
The story is an all-ages adventure with exciting characters which all have their own motivations and place in the game world. I really liked the colors and the animations.
There is no jump-button. All you need is to step off a ledge for example and your character will jump automatically. Similar to the jump mechanics in Zelda games.
Almost all of the negative reviews of this game are complaining about this aspect because buyers were not aware of it beforehand.
It is a solid game with some easy puzzles, a bit of character leveling, some secrets placed around the levels and enemies to fight.
This kind of game is rarely found on the PC and I thoroughly enjoyed it.
I suggest this game to players that are open towards all-age stories that come with lots of humor and some popculture references.
It is uniquely charming and gave me a warm fuzzy feeling inside.
Buy it cheap on a sale or at full price. You will likely not regret it.

As a game itself, Garry's Mod is incredibly hit or miss. Essentially, it is a lawless sandbox akin to Creative Mode from you-know-what or something akin to the Spore planet editor, so expect things like that. The game is overflowing with creative content ready for download at no charge. Garry's Mod is perfect for creating GMOD films(you know, the hysterical ones on youtube, shoutout to EthioMod) but otherwise, if you don't enjoy playing God, then single player may be one of the most boring experiences you can go through.
Compared to the two former editors, Gmod is horrifically inferior. It is not endless in scope, as is MineCrap, nor does it allow terraforming, easy model building, or basic programming, as Spore does. Don't expect to easily become immersed in "your world", because it will almost certainly disappoint you if that is your goal. Single-player offers no goals or guidelines. Its pretty endless, but then so is the boredom. If you don't intend on making aforementioned hilarious videos of TF2 Freaks, cringe fandoms, or just about anything else, then do not buy this game for the singleplayer.
However, GMOD truely shines in the multiplayer factor. In fact, I can say that it more than redeems itself. Hilarious physics, malicious intentions, and a whole buncha internet losers, n00bs and trolls, all in one place-what could possibly go wrong? Answer: a whole lot. And its a whole lotta fun, I may add. If you're not into hilarious and mindless madness with your siblings, friends, or fellow internet weebs, then you have many other options. MANY. OTHER. OPTIONS. There are an incredible amount of gamemodes availiable in GMOD, and they are a diverse set, too. Many are so fleshed out that they feel like actual games. Aside from competitive play, there are many excellent RP servers to join. The community of GMOD is kind and intelligent(lol), and this reflects in the multiplayer servers.
Overall, is GMOD good? Yes, it is. Though its singleplayer is an extremely specific selling point, its multiplayer is well worth the experience. Though you must be at least marginally sociable to fully ejoy this 'mod', you will find that such behavior will ultimately pay off.

I will admit it: at first, I didn't like Journal. The main character comes across as an unlikable narrator. As other negative reviews have mentioned, she steals, lies, and hurts her friends. It's hard to find anything to like about her as you begin her story.
But then the experience broadens, and you begin to see some of the reasons why she is making poor choices. One of the girl's regrettable experiences hit home so much that I was emotionally jarred. Perhaps because I was also once a teenage girl, I found myself relating heavily to her story. You watch as she struggles through the realities of divorce, relationships, death, and the daily nonsense of life. It is an extremely personal tale, and I was floored by what the game achieved. I could have easily been that girl, through some of the ways she related to others and the choices she made. I didn't like myself then, and the girl in the game doesn't like herself now. Journal is in some ways a tragic work. How much you like the game will possibly depend on how much you relate to her and her journey.
There are some minor flaws in the experience. It can be difficult at times to determine where the next conversation trigger is, so that you may talk to some individuals multiple times fruitlessly, trying to figure out what you're supposed to do.  You will wander over the same settings again and again, although this is accomplished at a pretty brisk pace that never feels too cumbersome. Some of the dialoge choices could be clearer; at times, I was unsure what my character was getting ready to communicate by the options.
Still, for the flaws, I absolutely recommend Journal. It blends painful realism with touches of imagination that create a story that can stun you in the accomplishment of its narrative arc. I applaud Locked Door Puzzle for what they've made: Journal is a piece of art.

my final verdict is simply, if you like puzzle games and something relaxing, then i definatly can recommend this game.

Enjoyable action platformer - the combat system is simple but fairly effective, the enemies are a good combination of decently sized hordes with a few more varied enemies to make fights varied in different chapters.
Story is enjoyable, if not particularly original its delivery is good. Doesn't take itself too seriously but avoids taking it to the ridiculous just for the sake of 'humour' like a number of other similar games in the genre.
The RPG elements of the game, crafting and leveling are okay, not great though. They are not particularly varied, leveling up one attribute to the exclusion of others is impossible as you have to keep all 4 within a certain range of each other. Crafting is satisfying but again there is no real choice, simply craft the best gear possible as it drops.
The platforming is good, trying to find all the hidden areas and treasures is satisfying but challenging enough, abilities are also gained during the storyline opening up new areas for exploration.
Duck Game is always fun every time.

This game hurts me as a long follower of the OMD! games. I played OMD! 1 and 2 through, even the endless maps ontop, so much fun did i had with the games. But this, this is not the sequel i wanted nor needed.
It looks like OMD! but, it feels so wrong, so very, very wrong. And maybe thanks to Gameforge, did i just now learned about OMD! U. And thank god for that.
Pros:
-Interesting Heroes to choose from, once you unlocked them either through grinding or RNG shop with money
-All the traps from the earlier games are there! But not all, you have to unlock them again through grinding or RNG shop
-The levels and survival maps (runs? Missions? Not sure how to call them) are nice and fitting into OMD! But there are only few now, and the few are getting boring quickly.
-Good ol' OMD! humor is inclusive and free!
-Ummm...skins for your heroes? No, wait, you have to unlock them through leveling and RNG shop too.
Cons:
-Almost all the mentioned points up there
-Graphics are looking horrible
-Tutorials are stuttering! No joke, my pc is able to run The Division on ultra smoothly, but the tutorials of this game are stuttering for no reason!
- GRINDING! Everyone playing this game can assure you, that if you want to play free, you have to grind, ALOT.
-Crafting. Yes, the tedious amount of crafting is a con too. You have to craft almost everything in this game.
-MOBA. Sadly yes, the MOBA aspect is a con too. Other players with money can unlock early on Heroes, you don't know and know how to fight. Put in the level imbalance and upraded Traps imbalance, that can happen, and your game is over.
-It feels like you have to put in cash to get somewhere in the game, into a shop to buy chests with RNG. Great.
-As some others mentioned, the Community isn't happy at all about Gameforge and Robot, ignoring and stealing ideas for Patches and more.
Overall, ignore it, or better, play some round first, than get back here and give it a negative Review. This game doesn't have deserved it, to be here on Steam, insulting the OMD! series. Kill this game out of mercy, not out of hate.

Despite its flaws this is my favourite game of 2016.
I own both Mafia II and III and spent 15 hours on Mafia II (which I got on a sale)  before I decided it wasn't for me. I spent 96 hours to finish part III and enjoyed every minute of it. Yes, the gameplay is repetive but no more so than closing umpteen Oblivion Gates or killing a seemingly never ending horde of dragons in Skyrim.
Mafia III is much less about a criminal building an empire than it is about a biracial black man embarking on a journey of revenge. Said revenge gets ditched out in droves, from
to
. I will not soon forget those moments and likewise the entire story of the game is memorable because it pulls no punches in portraying racism.
It doesn't hold back on telling how ♥♥♥♥ed up the world is either. It tells the truth about the racist war on drugs and how it became to be and it even references MKULTRA, a CIA programme that attempted to implement mind control by using LSD. I love how Mafia III blends in controversial facts with fiction.
What I dislike are poor design choices like how well your guns handle, how much ammo you can carry, and how much health you have depend on how much you subordinates(!)  like you. It would have been much better if you got a bigger discount buying stuff the more they like you because the ammo and gun prices are pretty ridiciculous. Also I really missed the lack of a hard save. And I regret that it is a poor port that ran at 60 FPS after the framerate got unlocked but stopped doing so after a "performance patch" got released.
But all in all I can't help to love this game.

It's a shame this game isn't being sold currently due to it's music license expiring in May. Aside from the combat becoming somewhat repetitive, and there being a lot of product placements in the game, it is a well crafted horror game.
The atmosphere of the game is very suspenseful for the most part. There are certain parts of the game where you can tell what will happen next, but for the most part, it keeps you guessing as to what will be Alan's next move.
The combat system is unique in that you have to weaken enemies with light in order to defeat them, but it does become a bit of a drag after a few chapters of doing that.
The soundtrack in this game is marvelous. From the licensed songs from artists such as Roy Orbison and David Bowie, to Old Gods of Asgard(Poets of the Fall), the soundtrack is perfect for the game.
All in all, this the best horror game I have ever played in my life, and it's saddening that it's not for sale currently.

Performance issues were mostly resolved through various patches by the time I actually started to play this, and was able to hold a steady 60 FPS most of the time, but I was still getting drops to 40 FPS in the French Ward with an i5 6600k and a GTX 1070.
Overall, the game is generally underwhelming, massively repetitive and lacking a number of the features that made previous Mafia games great. There are a few nice set pieces, but they're few and far between, and the stealth mechanics are super easy to master, making most of the game a cakewalk.
That said, if you can get this for like £5, maybe £10, worth it for the mission to take out the KKK meeting.

There is some very slight puzzle solving in AER, but it’s mostly a narrative game that looks pretty and has a cool flight mechanic.
You could almost call AER an open-world version of Journey or ABZU. Its price, length, and main appeal are about the same.
The moment in AER that initially hooked me was towards the beginning upon emerging from a tutorial cave, immediately transforming into a bird, and flying towards a wide open landscape with a village just emerging into view on the horizon.
Possibly the main thing AER does really well is environment design. The landscapes look pretty and enticing, with interesting locations stretching off into the distance. The world in AER has an almost GTA San Andreas-like quality of looking and feeling big without being too big to quickly traverse. The individual locations all display a highly detailed quality despite AER’s choice of a low-poly graphic style and simple, solid-color textures. The central village looks lived-in and believably arranged; there are ruins everywhere that tell stories just by how they’re laid out. Seeing all those locations both from up close and from high above while flying elicits a cool sense of scale.
The central mechanic – transforming into a bird to fly across a sea of floating islands, works well. Flying is simple, but also fast and empowering for those who enjoy exploration. It can be a bit tough to accurately land, and the on-foot controls feel a bit janky, but not prohibitively so.
The main story just tasks players with tracking down a few temples and solving some simple puzzles within them. What I like about AER is how, as an exploration game, its characters give players just enough direction to know where they’re going. It actually feels pretty similar to The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild in that regard, only offering clues to locations with no waypoints at all. All the game offers is a simple compass and a map. The temple interiors are also impressively intricate.
If you can pay $15 for Journey and $20 for ABZU, AER is a nice-looking, soothing, but oddly empowering four-hour adventure through (and over) some well designed environments.

Journal is a very simple game that tries to give you some food for thought in regards to depression, social anxiety, loss, friendship and how things change through life.
While not completely successful and lacking a certain cohesion it is still a very interesting, albeit somewhat limited, experience.
-really nice art style
-good classical soundtrack
-touches on several interesting themes
-the sudden change of mood made the last chapter very emotional
-divided between a simple, somewhat ham-fisted, storytelling in the first 4 chapters and some deep, sometimes cryptic, narration during end of the day cutscenes and day 5
-pretty short and linear
-when using a controller the stick feels very sensitive while choosing conversation options
-I couldn't advance the ending scenes using a controller and had to fall back to keyboard
Journal seems to be at an empasse on what it is trying to do.
The first days are full of day-to-day teen problems and simple musings on the problems the character faces: the conversations are pretty simplistic and somewhat trite in dealing with how everyone feels.
The cutscenes at the end of the day start as somewhat cryptic, almost philosophical takes on the feelings that were simplistically addressed during the day: story wise they are explained after the ending but I was left with the feeling that they were designed as a more detailed take on the events of the game.
Without spoiling anything, the ending presents a sudden change in mood with a good sense of urgency paired with a good view on loss and the scars life puts on us: it might seem an unoriginal view overall but it was still emotionally powerful.
I guess different players'd appreciate the game in different ways...people in their teens'll probably sympatize with the problems and fears the character faces but might feel the cutscenes and ending shift too much into a deep and dark territory. More mature gamers'll probably feel the daily chapers are pretty boring and unoriginal in the way they represent teen problems and will be more interested in trying to understand whether the cutscenes act as metaphors for something deeper: they'll also probably feel very connected with the ending.
Despite the problems regarding its identity Journal was a meaningful experience for me, one surely worth its sale price of 2$.

The following is a quick overview of Natural Selection 2 for a full review please check out my website at -
Natural Selection 2 is a first-person shooter combined with a real time strategy game, resulting in the ultimate competitive experience. The game can contain any number of players completely based on the number of players the server can handle, however, in tournament events they appear to use twelve players per games while the average server is around sixteen to twenty players per game. Natural Selection 2 is almost completely an online experience but does offer an offline training mode to help new players understand the game without having to figure out the basics in a competitive environment. The game was developed by Unknown Worlds Entertainment using the Spark source engine (which was also developed by Unknown Worlds Entertainment). Natural Selection 2 was released to the public as open source code to help players develop modifications much easier. By the game's title its pretty obvious that Natural Selection 2 is the second game of the Natural Selection series the first of which was one of the ten most played Half-Life modifications but was never released as a standalone. Unfortunately it is only available on PC but is purchasable on steam. The graphics aren't really top tier but aren't terrible either, they just need a little more work so they stand out a little more. The in game experience of Natural Selection 2 doesn't actually offer any music and the SFX are a little poor in some places. The designers of Naturals Selection 2 decided that they shouldn't really mess around with a storyline, instead allow the player to just jump straight into the game itself and as a result the game has little to know story line at all. The game is however, updated quite regularly and does offer some DLCs that allows the player to customise the texture of the in game characters for a small price. The options in this game are also pretty impressive with the ability to not only change video and audio options but also proformance settings and experimental proformance settings as well. The gameplay is very intense within the game forcing the player to practise strategy, game knowledge and mechanical skill to master the game making repetitiveness not really a factor. The competitive side is still growing within esports and should be a very impressive once it has. Overall I gave the game a 7.7/10 final rating as the game play, options and content just make the game. The audio is really lacking and the graphics aren't top tier either, but with updates this could really improve.

This is the game, that made me like multiplayer games again. It is an adult game - the game will give you no badges, no better weapons, no loot or anything for good behavior - only team victory. You are the sole judge of how good you are doing. People who like to learn, will have something to learn for few hundreds of hours. People who are narcistic will think they are good, while contributing nothing to the team. New players will be too shy or too overzealous in their actions. It is every team member's responsibility, that out of the twelve random players you get some teamplay emerges.
The "Natural Selection" name is very apt. Some say, the game has steep learning curve. I think that is not true. I think it has long learning curve. It will teach you very quickly your failures through death and defeat. First you need to get your aim straight, then some confusing movement going, then you maybe try some alien side play, then you learn the structures and maps, then some soft skills and using your mic effectively, tactics, strategy, using map and navigation, enemy weak spots detection... the list goes on forever. At every step you are usefull to the team, if they are able to use you. If there starts some shouting and arguments, you know your team is going to lose and deserve it. If you are getting good leadership and good intel, you know you are going to win - > thats teamplay not simple DBUTT and aim like other games are trying to tell you!
On top of that there is a RTS-like Commander, that builds structures for you and pretty much looks out for you from above. In this game you will be defending/assaulting places YOU think are strategical and not some random waypoint or something, like in other games. You decide what place is important for victory as a team and suffer the consequences of your decisions!
If you are SICK of games just repeating the same every round and that are extorting money from you through game mechanics, if you don't like the game telling you how good you are for killing 1000 enemies - games with oversimplified goals, games where players are just slightly smarter bots for you to play with...  well, simply if you are in mood for some enjoyable challenge and social experience, this is the game for you!

Just an FYI, I'm going to be spoiling story stuff in this review, so for the spoiler-free review, all I have to say is:
Journal is a story-based game with good voice-acting, music, and art assets, but I found the story to be muddled and confusing, which is bad for a story-based game like Journal, as there is nothing else for the game to fall back on, and for that I can't recommend this game.
Spoilers from here on out.
I was drawn to Journal because it is a story-based game, and in general I tend to like story-based games like this. Other than that I came into Journal with no other preconceptions, so I was essentially walking into it with an open mind with very few preconceptions about what I'd find.
I went through the first couple of days of the game and for the most part enjoyed myself. I enjoyed walking around the town, meeting new people and having conversations with them and piecing together information about this world. However I did not enjoy having to take certain actions before I had all the information about the situation, which I felt was the case many times when dealing with the bad things the character did. In the story, we discover that the main character broke a window at school and blamed her friend for it, cheated on a Math test, and stole a snowglobe from a charity shop (what I'm assuming is the UK version of a Goodwill), and every time I had to make a decision about the situation only to have the revelation of what had happened be revealed after I had made those decisions.
Day 4 takes a darker turn as you find out that your parents are going through a divorce because your mother was caught sleeping with the park groundskeeper, and you come to this realization while your mother is pressuring you to say something at your grandmother's grave, with whom you had a shaky relationship with before her death.
The fifth and final day drops the big whammy that your sister was critically injured on a carnival ferris wheel, and the fifth day is the day you say goodbye to her for the last time. This is the point where I'd say that story fell apart. Day 4 already felt very disconnected from the 3 previous days, and Day 5 was even more so.
To sum up my feelings of the story of Journal, is that it left me both confused and bored. At the end of the game, I did not really care for our protagonist, she came off as a bratty teenager, and that is not a character type that I enjoy or empathize with. As such I did not care that her sister had died, and I did not care that she had attempted to re-write her journal to remove the pain of losing her sister from her memories as part of her journey through the grieving process. All I could think of is that I would be one of those people who would say "I'm sorry for your loss" that she expressed frustration with.
The main creative force behind this game is Richard Perrin, who had previously done the game Kairo, which is a game that I had played for a little bit, but I can honestly say that I didn't "get" that game, and that seems to be a trend for me with his games. I don't "get" Journal. Maybe Richard Perrin is pretentious, or maybe I'm not the kind of person who can understand his games, but either way, I don't "get" Journal.
Because of how lack-luster I felt the story was, I can't recommend this game. It wasn't a bad game, but it certainly wasn't a good game either, and if you went your whole life not playing this game, I wouldn't say that you missed much.

The Binding of Isaac is a game which is incredibly addictive despite being ridiculously challenging at some points.
During the beginning of the game, you will fail a lot and you will have to restart, but that is just how it is, you learn from your mistakes and you gradually get better and better, as you traverse the different floors, you unlock new things and learn new tricks and secrets. The rooms are randomised every playthrough, which really gives the game a lot of replayability factor, because you never know what is going to turn up in every room, and that goes for everything (bosses, items, general enemies).
The soundtrack is superb and adds greatly to the overall experience of the game. It's very fitting and it's very catchy.
Also, the DLC 'Wrath of the Lamb' is a must, just because it adds so much new content including new bosses, floors, items and pickups called Trinkets. However, most content is focused around the later part of the game, so new players will probably not get the chance all of what it has to offer until they get to the very late stages of the game.
Overall, The Binding of Isaac is a great game and definitely worth the price it is being sold for. I personally picked up the game and expansion on sale for £1.99, which is a STEAL.

Despite the graphics being not exactly state-of-the-art, and the lack of anything resembling a "story", I must confess that I have rarely played such a complex and rewarding game. It did, of course, take quite some time to learn all that stuff you need to know in order to not have all your rockets go kaboom shortly after liftoff. Youtube videos from users like Scott Manley can be really helpful in that regard.
And then, when you finally manage your first manned mission to the Mun and back (without rapid unscheduled disassembly during the landing), you finally get the courage to plan a mission to another planet. After carefully assembling a complex multi-stage rocket, and getting it into orbit (which, in and of itself, is not quite easy), you still wonder if you didn’t forget something important. Is there a sufficient amount of fuel on board? Are there enough parachutes and batteries? Is the staging correct? Really small details can make the difference between a successful mission and a catastrophic failure. This can either mean having your Kerbal die an explosive death, or leaving him/her stranded on a foreign planet, or somewhere in space, for all of eternity. Unless, of course, you send a rescue mission.
And when you get tired of all these complicated orbital mechanics and staging issues, you can just switch to sandbox mode, and do some weird stuff. Framerate-destroying explosions and random spaghettifications can be quite funny.
This game is also responsible for restarting my interest in all things concerning space, rockets, moons, explosions, physics and the like.
Things I have learned from this game:
> When you’re in orbit, and want to go faster, you have to slow down
> Never forget your parachutes!
> Check your staging!
> There is no “overkill”!
> When your rocket is wobbling, add more struts
> When your rocket is to slow, add more boosters
> Jeb doesn’t quite understand the concept of “danger”
> “Science” is a scalar quantity measuring the amount of single-use multi-purpose knowledge that can be gained from a specific situation

If you've read any other comments, you've already seen this at least once, but if you haven't, WARNING: THIS GAME IS EXTREMELY SLOW. There isn't a whole lot of gameplay in this game. It's not a Metal Gear situation, either, where about 50% of the game is awesome cutscene and the other 50% is awesome gameplay. This game could probably last about 2.5 hours on a normal playthrough, and about 80% of that was cutscene.
So, let's get down to gameplay and story. First off, this was made in RPG Maker. It's not some amazing thing, but it's not bad, either. You can't move diagonally, or anything fancy. The controls are very simple, and you never have more than four buttons besides the arrow keys (A, S, Z, X) that do anything. So, what's the story? Again, pretty simple: Blue Bot wakes up in a pod. He's drowsy, fading in and out of consciousness, but eventually he breaks the glass pane of his pod and crawls out. And thus, the adventure begins. As Blue Bot, you'll wander the world for a while on your own, then you'll suddenly hear the only other voice in this world. The first puzzle begins: Dig up crystals that will power the teleporter that will hopefully lead you to the source of this new voice. And once there, you meet Blue's companion: Red Bot.
So, at this point, I should digress to mention why my play time is lower than the play time I suggested to be an average. It's because the puzzles are optional. Yes, you read that right. 50% of the gameplay (10% of the whole game) is optional. Why? Because this game is supposed to be simple.
If the puzzles are too complex for you, like a few of them were for me, or you don't want to spend your time on them, that's alright, you can skip them after a few failed tries, because Wanda isn't intended to be complex. The game's two stories (one told through the cutscenes, and another told through the collectible photgraphs) are very simple as well, using imagery clearly to indicate what's going on in each scene, so you can relate that easily to other scenes.
Y'know what, whatever. I'm done trying to be accurate, or sound fancy. I'm recommending this game because it's the most heartwarming experience I've had in the last week or so. I'm a sucker for simplistic storytelling, and as far as that goes, Wanda takes the cake. Wanda isn't even a simple game, really: It's a simple story, told in a relatively simple way. And if you don't love that, that's alright. I did, though, and if you think you would too, this game deserves your money.

It is a B-movie game. You know, all these brutal movies with low budget actors, unnecessary gore and violence, with a lot of random action shoot-outs. I wish I'd liked this more, but ultimately there are way too many things I didn't like and nothing that I loved.
The art style is pretty, the characters are well designed, and the flying is great. I spent a lot of time just flying and doing stunts, and that's definitely the game's big strength. The theme music is nice, if you like its take on "With Or Without You"-era U2. If you like what you see in the videos, and if that's enough for you, go for it. Although I love a lot of "walking simulators" where all you do is go from A to B and press a button to unlock a gate to do it again, I can't put this alongside, say, ABZU. It's not pretty enough to get away with this and didn't tug on my emotions at all. It has a lot in common with this year's Rime, visually and thematically, but Rime is much better in every regard. On top of that, Rime has a much better line in easy but well-crafted puzzles.
One of the things I didn't like was the amount of waffly lore. Rime communicates just as much as Aer about its old world and fallen gods, and a lot more besides that, without ever saying a word. Aer had me speedreading and jabbing the A button as quickly as I could to get past the surfeit of dialogue boxes, and no amount of extra writing was ever going to make me care about what was going on.
The loading breaks are an irritation, too. Even with an SSD, the fact that there are so many of them and that they take so long is a hindrance to your enjoyment (and it must be much worse on a HDD).Every time you step into a cave, it's a black screen and a progress bar, and maybe you only peeked in there to see if it was a cave you'd visited before. How, you wonder, can it take so long to load the contents of one small room? There are also noticeable hitches when you move from zone to zone in the sky. I was prepared to give the game the benefit of the doubt -- perhaps they only had a tiny team and couldn't afford to make the game invisibly load around you like other open world games, I thought -- but I was shocked to see the huge credits list at the end.

Pleasantly surprised.
I launched this game only to collect the trading cards, but something in me got me to stay put and try this game out.  I honestly thought it was just another adolescent trash story, but, no, it's not that at all.  It's actually a mature story.
Basically, you control a young female who goes around wondering where her journal pages went.  As you begin to ask people about this, you begin to discover there are other more important things going on.  You quickly discover that all bad things that happen is your fault.  Eventually, I began to question what the heck is going on?  Why is the character I control doing these things??  By day 5, it all comes out, and wow...  I was moved.  Truly, the writer did an excellent job presenting this story in the manner she did, from the perspective of an older woman re-telling the story of herself as a  young person who is shielded from a very dear and important truth, and acting out because of not knowing.  I was deeply moved.
This is a gem amidst♥♥♥♥♥♥♥  If you can overlook the simplicity of the gaming aspects, and take this as an interactive novel more than a cheesy game, then I highly recommend this.   It's a very good story for anyone of any age, from pre-adolescent on up.  I was moved.  You might be too.

Binding of Isaac has the dual distinction of being my most-played Steam game and one of the cheapest games I've ever bought. 90+ hours for $2.50? Not too bad!
The randomness of each playthrough and touches of dark humor make the game endlessly replayable. I should also mention that I am terrible at twitchy, fast-reflex type games, yet it doesn't stop me from doing a quick BoI run almost every day. Buy it!

While the control differ greatly from Witcher 1 and combat is tricky to get the hang of, the graphics are prettier and the story continues to be quite intriguing. Due to the key decisions the player has to make, it definitely has a high replay value.
The fact that there are only 35 levels and a similar amount of talent points to be distributed across a much higher number of skills, while a nuissance, it not an actual hiderance on normal mode. On higher difficulties it can easily be remedied with a number of mods.
One minor disappointment were the sex scenes. While romancing everything that looked somewhat female was a huge and admittedly entertaining part fof Witcher 1, it is neither entertaining nor exciting n Witcher 2. All the scenes look the same and there is no sense of accomplishment as one "collects" them. It might be a nod to the criticism that Witcher was sexists, and its female characters too loose. But as a woman myself, I was still highly entertained by this conquest element.
Still, even as a slightly more monogamous witcher, Geralt still walks the line between good and evil, without truely knowing which is which. To me, that is what makes these games. I highly recommend them.
