The Binding of Isaac is a game which is incredibly addictive despite being ridiculously challenging at some points.
During the beginning of the game, you will fail a lot and you will have to restart, but that is just how it is, you learn from your mistakes and you gradually get better and better, as you traverse the different floors, you unlock new things and learn new tricks and secrets. The rooms are randomised every playthrough, which really gives the game a lot of replayability factor, because you never know what is going to turn up in every room, and that goes for everything (bosses, items, general enemies).
The soundtrack is superb and adds greatly to the overall experience of the game. It's very fitting and it's very catchy.
Also, the DLC 'Wrath of the Lamb' is a must, just because it adds so much new content including new bosses, floors, items and pickups called Trinkets. However, most content is focused around the later part of the game, so new players will probably not get the chance all of what it has to offer until they get to the very late stages of the game.
Overall, The Binding of Isaac is a great game and definitely worth the price it is being sold for. I personally picked up the game and expansion on sale for £1.99, which is a STEAL.

The witcher 2 is set in a fantasy medieval world inspired by polish and Russian mythology and based on Andrzej Sapkowski’s books. You play as Geralt of rivia, a witcher. Witchers are mutants engineered to be professional monster slayers and are generally feared and looked down upon by regular people, Geralt uses two swords, a silver sword to fight monsters and a steel sword for humans. Because the game is a direct sequel the opening prologue puts you right into the action and new players to the series can get a little lost, however you don’t need to play the first game to fully understand what is going on, plus the witcher 2 has an extensive journal with all the information. The prologue starts off with Geralt imprisoned after being framed for assassinating the king during a siege, he’s being interrogated by the kings special forces and you play through his memories as he explains what happened during the siege. Later you manage to escape from the prison and your quest to clear your name and find out who’s really behind the series of assassinations begins.
The story will take you to a number of different kingdoms and cities and you’ll meet lots of very interesting characters, how different events happen during the story is based on the decisions you make, As the story goes on the plot gets deeper and deeper, and the bigger picture becomes clearer ,who will geralt save? who will he kill? who’s side will he choose? the faith of entire kingdoms can be directly or indirectly be affected by the choices you make, the line is blurred between pure good or evil and there’s no clear morality, you do what you think is best, sometimes choosing the lesser evil in the name of the greater good, The role you play in the game has a very heavy effect on the story. The game has 16 very different endings and fully completing it will take you around 40 hours. Also i have to mention the game and story touch on drugs, murder, torture,♥♥♥♥♥♥ incest, racism, nudity and more, however they all fit very well into the witcher universe and make the game feel very realistic and mature. If i was to compare it to a tv series it’s like game of thrones but with a richer world and with an eastern European flavour added to it.
Gameplay wise the Witcher 2 is in third person and you fight in real time, combat is not easy, Geralt is not invincible and a group of knights could easily kill him if you’re not careful. Geralt can you use a number of potions and traps as well as his mutant abilities to give him an advantage in combat, potions can help him do more damage to certain monsters or improve his health, while his mutant abilities can be used to deflect arrows or stun opponents.
The witcher 2 is a fantastic sequel, everything that was great about the first game has been immensely improved, the combat, the story, the characters all have been improved to a degree that is almost unbelievable, graphically it is one the best looking games ever made. The game is truly a masterpiece with a rich and detailed world, good gameplay and a deep and interesting story.

AKA break all the doors. I like it, I guess. You get tickets depending on how well you do on a challenge, basically, you will get more tickets if you get gold than getting bronze. Tickets can be spent on game modifiers for multiplayer, as well as some hats and a key to the basement of the arcade (the single players really small overworld)! getting all the hats and modifiers (with the exception of the shoes and helmets modifiers) will grant you access to buy the ultimate champion hat, 466 tickets!!! I know I can't argue about this, but still, you can't play against computer opponents in the regular multiplayer mode. I don't know if it is exactly impossible, I don't know if there are game that utilize AI's on this kind of game, so I really don't expect some kind of VS. CPUs mode.
OVERALL SCORE (YET AGAIN WITH SOME THINGS I HAVEN'T MENTIONED ABOVE!)

CONCEPT: 7.5/10 Really simple, really good.

SINGLE PLAYER: 7/10 There needs to be more challenges though!
OVERALL SCORE: 8.5/10 This game is worth every penny. No really. This is the definitive party game, and it has ducks. Which might attract some people. I honestly don't know what else to say, so I'll end it here.

Ever wanted to make a game but were too intimidated by coding or modeling? Gameguru is a great way to get your feet wet in some suprisingly deep game development without having to worry too much about the nitty-gritty details.
I think it's important to note that Gameguru, as with ANY game engine, is only as good and rewarding as the user is. Yes, you can make a game in a matter of minutes, but to make a GOOD game (which Gameguru is already capable of), you will need to dedicate some time to learning it's quirks and features. The good news is that Gameguru is easily the most user friendly product available at the moment. Invest some time into it to learn how it works before starting your own projects. The old saying is true, "You reap what you sow." The more time and effort you put into Gameguru, the more you're going to get out of it.
Finally, I have to commend the developers and commnuity around Gameguru. The devs (our fearless leader Lee Bamber) respond to user input almost immediately and seek community requests as the main focus of the product. If you have a problem or a really sought after feature, speak up! Chances are they will hear you!
The community is spectacular. Many of them provide free assests and tutorials/lessons on the forums, which is virtually unheard of in other engines/communities. If you genuinely want to learn a thing or two about game development (i.e. not just begging unfairly for free stuff) then you will find a warm and welcoming community not too far.
Gameguru isn't perfect in it's current state, but it showed promise early in its life and has only capatilized on that potential. Based on my several months/year of experience and watching it grow, I am confident that it will grow past its already impressive state into a heavy weight engine capable of standing tall next to industry standards.

It drew me in with the promise of a beautiful flight mechanic, and I stayed behind to look out for a dying world.
Mechanically speaking, the game is short, sweet, and lives or dies by what you put into it. There is little resistance put between you and advancing the plot; The keys and main temples are marked by a few, simple puzzles, none of which stopped me for long enough to lose momentum.
And then there's the flying. I don't think it's possible to exhaust how intuitive, organic, and downright
the mechanic is. So much of my time spent with it was in arbitrary play, learning how to coast indefinitely without flapping, or climbing to the highest possible point and then diving. Definitely break out a controller for this, if you have one!
In terms of the story you set out to piece together, the game hits a very specific niche.
Your bouts of flying are marked by discovery, and how much you want to see is ultimately up to you. The wider story is presented in scattered fragments; Now, since I'm a sucker for reading every memo left behind in an Elder Scrolls game, this was a lot of fun for me. These fragments are not nearly so exhaustive, but in a sense they're also not really optional, since the act of finding them is a major part of the game. They can sometimes beg more questions than they answer, and this may invite you to look for more than is actually there. I didn't personally mind, since I like to speculate.
I found the story on the whole rewarding to follow. The game opens with a bright sense of hope and freedom, which shifts as you understand more and more of the world around you and the responsibilities of your pilgrimage. I won't spoil anything, but it left me feeling as full and empty as its scattered islands. I can only think of one honest gripe I had with the writing, and it was with the semantics of using the term “spirit animal” out of context.
In the end, it hit a very specific place in my heart that most games have only teased with minigames or subplot. It probably won't change your mind if you don't like reading piecemeal exposition-- worst comes to worst, you just bought yourself a really, really good flying simulator-- but if you've been looking for this as long as I have, I think it'll hit, and hit damn hard.

While GameGuru is still young in the development cycle and has a long way to go, it definately holds huge potential for an awesome game dev tool.

Just wanted to add that the Game Guru forum is a huge asset to this product.
Not only are there plenty of projects in development that show what can be done with some time and effort, but it is one of the few communities that actually want to help people get the most out of Game Guru - and not treat you like an unwelcome noob.
If you want an engine that allows you to create the next awesome game with little or no time put in then Game Guru IS NOT for you.
But if you love learning, want to push the boundaries of your own skill set, and are willing to put some work into making your game concept come to life, then Game Guru, along with its awesome community is definitely a great choice imo.
2017 holds promise of some nice improvements to this still young engine - and for the price, along with a truck load of media to get you started it is almost a give-away.
But if you don't want to put time and effort into learning the software and the art of game design then I would suggest juat playing games made by others.

is a touching story about two little robots finding each other in a seemingly lifeless world.
The graphics of the game are a bit old school, but I found myself enjoying them. Some of the animations were super adorable. It kind of reminded me of the cuteness of To the Moon.
Gameplay for
is pretty simple. You use the arrow keys and Z most of the time. During the puzzles, a few more keys are thrown in. I admit, sometimes I forgot which key went to what, but that's more of a personal problem than something wrong with the game.
Now the puzzles in the game are pretty well thought out. I did skip of few of them because I was more into the story, but none of them are unbeatable. The first few are easy, with the rest being a bit more challenging. I'm sure with enough time, anyone can figure them out.
Lastly, the music...the original reason I bought this game. The music is very lovely, and fits in well with the game. Usually I turn off the music for video games and listen to my own, but
isn't really a game you're supposed to do that with. I could listen to the soundtrack all day. It gets a thumbs up from me.
In the end, I really enjoyed the story this game told. So if you like stories and puzzles coming together to form something that makes you think a little, I definitely recommend that you pick this little gem up.

GameGuru is the type of game creator I always wished for. It’s got the tools to make a game without having to code or create 3-D models. A lot of software seem to aim toward easy game creation, but what sets GameGuru apart is not only the easy-to-use tools, but the possibilities they come with. A few examples: The terrain system, the character creator, and multiplayer.
Also, it’s important to keep in mind this software is still being updated on a regular basis. So many more features are planned that expand on the already promising list of available tools.
You can jump into the community and request features you really desire to use for a project you have in mind as well. GameGuru runs on its own community, one I recommend jumping into as soon as possible for the reason I just mentioned. Who knows, you may be one who requests a feature not yet mentioned that does get added to a future build. It happens.
One huge thing I’m personally always excited about is the GameGuru store. So often are new ready to use scripts, characters, weapons, buildings, etc. are added to expand on your resource library. It’s true you get more than a handful of game ready assets out of the box, but one look at their store and you’ll understand why it’s worth a big mention in this review. The game-ready assets aren’t only cheap, but are quality.
The main idea to take from this software at this time is that it’s not only one if not the easiest to use, but the tools are giving people the ability to create 3-D video games that have quality results. I’ve been using GameGuru since the first beta (when it was called FPS Creator Reloaded) and I can assure you it’s come a long way and the team behind this game creating gem has proven to me they are  truly dedicated to the software, and will continue to add more amazing tools. I’ve backed the project with a gold pledge and have been impressed with what it has become ever since. And, of course, with how it continues to grow today.

The island is gorgeous and huge, but it never feels overwhelming. The game does a great job at subtly directing you towards your next objective. The puzzles totally hit the sweet spot for me. Great mix of object interaction puzzles, clue deciphering, and good old fashioned logic. The puzzle difficulty will no doubt have you leaning back in your chair, arms folded, for a nice think quite often, but there are almost no instances where you'll think to yourself "that puzzle was unfair". Each puzzle is also elegantly designed and will have you bursting with glee at every "ah-ha!" moment.
One aspect of the game I did not expect to be drawn into was the plot. Quern is a very unnatural place where its inhabitants don't age or require nourishment, and to them, time outside is frozen. The location sets up many interesting questions about the importance of mortality and the corruptability of man, in addition to being the source of friction between two interesting characters, both steadfast in their beliefs but neither with the clear moral high ground.
This isn't just a game for Myst lovers. This is a fantastic play for anyone who can appreciate a quiet moment, amidst some very pretty scenery with the waves crashing gently in the background, to get the ol' brain working and figure through some sweet puzzles.

Parts of the game are very good, but when you encounter a 'boss fight' be prepared to be VERY frustrated!
The problem is difficulty spikes. One minute you'll be easily slicing through enemies without taking a hit, but the moment you face a boss you're dead in seconds. Many people have commented that they have to drop the game down to Easy difficulty to defeat the bosses just so they can progress. This should not have to be done!!

The gunplay is good, the atmosphere is good and (mostly) authentic, and the story (so far 21 hours in) is reasonable. That was all the good things i have to say about Mafia 3.
The graphics and driving mechanics are a huge step down from the (six years older!) predecessor, and the protagonist is amazingly even less relatable and interesting than was the case in Mafia 2. The idea with you having "underbosses" to help you is good, but the execution is almost laughably bad, none of their bonuses really add anything, apart from the one you get when you originally acquire them, and leave no reason for you to care about which boss you choose. Naturally the game is far from reliable, with quite a few crashes straight to desktop, in seemingly random places, and even though the graphics are notably worse than Mafia 2, the game still has really bad problems with unstable, and generally poor, framerates. All of this is pushed in the background, however, when it comes to the missions. There is NO and that is _*NO*_ variation at all, in the missions after the introduction of the general mechanics of the game. Every single mission is: Drive to this highlighted place on the map, shoot everyone there, and pick up anything that glows green in your magical see-through-walls-vision. That's it. Nothing else. And even though this seems like a rather easy thing to manage, the game engine still manages to mess that up, repeatedly removing the icons from the map, never to be seen again (until you restart the game anyway), and the AI of enemies is beyond stupid, with them wading slowly towards the sound of me, completely oblivious to the ten dead bodies of their allies lying in the exact same spot, where i can just point my gun and wait for them. The design of the shooting galleries is rather bad as well, with virtually no levels that has more than one or two entrances, and almost no possibilities of playing a more stealthy approach.
All in all this game is on a level i expect from a €10 game from some backwater startup developer, who bit of more than they could chew, not a fully priced AAA-title from a company that has shown that could make superior games half a decade ago!
Avoid this game like the devil, until it's on sale dirt cheap, it's really not worth the price!
UPDATE:
Now, more than 40 hours in, and with all missions completed, it is clear that nothing changes for the better in the later stages of the game, it's just more of the same.
UPDATE2:
Now i've also tried the racing "DLC" and oh my, it is absolutely awful! Not only does it showcase how painfully poor the driving is made in the game, the opponents are also equipped with elastic bands, making sure that even if they flip over their cars, they're magically right behind you five seconds later. If you fall behind it is just as painfully obvious, i've been within the same distance of the opponents while being 8 seconds ahead of the map record, and 20 seconds behind it.. The traffic (on races with it) is painfully badly made, and makes sudden lane changes constantly, as well as driving across the street with more than 60 mph .. in the middle of the city.. yeah right. Finally the FPS is horrible in the races with traffic, especially the one with the roundabout, _EVERY_ time you exit the roundabout and start going uphill there is 2-4 seconds where the game drops to 4-6 FPS, regardless of graphics settings. I will not be completing all the races, don't bother either, even with a controller the handling just isn't up to the task of being a racing game.

Growing up, I remember playing the original Myst and all of its sequels and taking the time to understand all of the puzzles, consider all of the good and bad endings, and generally explore as much as I could. I remember agonizing over some of the choices about who was good or evil, and even with the old postage stamps graphics I still find the original game beautiful and compelling.
I didn't necessarily get that with Quern. It is a beautiful game and very much follows the Cyan idiom of worlds that have just the right combo of realistic and implausible details to force you to think how the game wants you to. However, the storyline felt a bit forced at times. The puzzles were a mix. In the beginning, some of them are stupidly hard or just feel like you're running around to fill up time, but the final few puzzles feel very simple (although I can't say I've ever needed to do algebra in a puzzle game before).
Overall, I think it's a fun game that's worthwhile to play, if nothing else than for the pretty visuals and immersive soundtrack, but maybe try to grab it on sale if you don't necessarily have nostalgic memories of this genre.

I wonder how many people who are going to start their career in space/rocket science in the next several years came to it through this game. There are already
, but it's better to wait a couple more years so some of the players finish their schools/universities. Just hope they don't rely on the game too much, it's not
and also real-life rockets cost a little bit too much to be prone to rapid unplanned disassemblies.
As for the game, gameplay-wise it is quite hard in the beginning, but then it becomes absolutely do-what-you-want. The moding community is pretty large, if you want something, there is almost always mod for it (though you might need some help to find it). Because of them, KSP has almost infinite replayability as once you are finished you can just get another star system, or other rocket parts, or other atmosphere stats, require life support systems or all at once. After you feel comfortable you can easily adapt modlist to your liking or just try some of numerous community challenges. The game is obviously playable (and pretty good) without mods but they just add a whole lot of possibilities.
Beginner's tip: you will probably need some video guide on game. Your mileage may vary, but
are a great start. And not only these ones, he makes a lot of awesome content.
Visually game looks pretty good for me, but it's usually recommended to use
and
and some other mods if your computer can handle them.
In-game music is atmospheric and enjoyable. Some tracks were even used during SpaceX pre-stream music session.
Physics is where it gets a bit weird. KSP is sort-of infamous for all the numerous physics bugs and not so much for replicating
ones. Some of the most weird ones got a collective name of Kraken and it stroke suddenly and destructively. After numerous victims and erecting him a monument, most of their kind were eliminated, though they are still easily found by
who want it (and sometimes those who don't). Anyway, in recent versions I don't remember encountering any of them.
Beginner's tip: kerbals can survive high-speed falls if they land on their helmets. Kraken knows what they are made of.
Performance is somewhat another issue. After Squad at last released stable 64-bit version and polished a lot of code most problems were solved. However, the game is still CPU-intensive especially if you use a lot of mods and/or parts at once. In that case you should be prepared for awesome 3-4 SPF (seconds per frame) slideshow. This example is pretty extreme, but my play sessions are usually about 10-15 FPS. I must admit though that I use about 109 mods and I saw that coming. Unmodded version runs much smoother, but I didn't have time to test the limits with some gigantic space station.
Beginner's tip: if the game is too hard on your RAM, launching with "-force-opengl" additional parameter is probably the only solution since all mods that were usually used to increase performance are heavily out-of-date now.
Of course, educational value is
KSP really shines. Want to learn basic orbital mechanics? Base game is a great playground! Wondering why there are so many different rocket engines? Take your time comparing stats and experimenting. Thinking "Noone launches rockets with manual controls in real life"? Choose one of

and have some fun with programming! Want to know how stationary orbits and Lagrange points really work? Grab some
and you're good to go! Just started your space geekiness but didn't manage to memorize the timeline yet?
and upcoming Making History Expansion DLC will help you! And so on, and so on...
Also, whenever there is a big update to the game, mods and savefiles tend to be broken. Fortunately, this game has no DRM so you can just copy the game directory elsewhere and continue your game. Also, previous versions are now available in beta-versions section of in-Steam preferences.
Overall, this game is very worth its price (except when you are not interested in the genre altogether) and allows for a very fun, sometimes intense, sometimes sad (I try my best, but my self-made KIA Kerbals Memorial keeps expanding) experience.

I feel like this game is getting a lot of semi-underserved hate for not just being more of the same ol' OMD (and some deserved hate for the F2P elements)! It's resigned to be a 5 player co-op experience, and a 5v5 competitive experience. If you've played the previous games and are wondering about this one, here's what you should know...
--Classic Gameplay--
The classic "defending against waves" format is back in the form of Survival Mode. With this you can team up with up to four other players to defend against waves of enemies. The places you can construct traps are a little more restrictive, and the traps don't quuuiiite have the pop they did in previous games. This is because, hey, there's 5 of you. That's a lot of firepower from the heroes, so the traps seem more toned down. Still, they are essential, and plenty of fun. Most of all, it's a lot of fun to actually get to play OMD with more than just 1 friend, and I think overall the mode feels balanced and is a lot of fun...with friends you know. Random groups...less so.
--Siege Mode--
This is the competitive 5v5 mode. It is very similar to a MOBA like DOTA2 or LOL, but also pretty damn different. There are still traps and minions, but now each team is leading their own minions to their enemy's rift. It'd be hard to explain everything, but you gain points to power up your portal(s), allowing your team to summon better and better minions (which you get to choose just like your traps). Each hero has really well defined strengths, and you even chose your roll before the match starts, giving you actual bonuses based on what you intend to do. Compared to most MOBAs it's pretty simple, but the added tower defense mechanics make it a surprising amount of fun once you get into it.
--Unlockables--
I think this is a sticking point for a lot of people. This game is F2P, so prepare for microtransactions. You can certainly get by without paying anything, and you'll still be able to eventually unlock every hero, trap, minion, and item. But it's fairly slow going. After the tutorials and about 5 siege matches I managed to unlock 2 traps, 3 minions, aaand...well, that's pretty much it. Unlocking heroes  take forever, and there are only 5 free heroes in rotation at a time (out of like...12, so, not a huge deal). The real kicker is unlocking items requires the classic skulls...AND materials, of which there are a pretty big variety. They drop randomly during matches, and are rewards for logging-in, quests and leveling up, buuut if you aren't lucky it might take forever to get the Radiant Gears you need to get that new trap. Plus traps/items/minions are rated by rarity, and the rarer ones require even harder to get items. What's worse, you can buy heroes, but you can't buy traps, minions or items. You can just buy chests that MIGHT contian the materials you need. It's an ok system if you plan to play a lot, because it'll give you a lot to constantly strive for, but for a lot of people I can see this being a deal breaker. Frankly, I don't blame you if it is.
TLDR; It's different than the previous OMD games, but there's a lot to love here. The gameplay is exactly what it needs to be. However, if not for that great gameplay, the grind required for unlocking all those sweet traps/minions/items would be almost unforgivable.

This game I quite enjoyed. First off, I was surprised that it was by the same developer(s) as crafted Kairo, although in retrospect, it made sense storywise a bit. Definitely demonstrated some variety in their ability to craft games. The secret ending is something they like to do, and it seems to be more about their whimsy than about being part of the actual game, which I appreciate.
Anyway, as to the actual game. This is a curious blend of interactive novel and point and click adventure. It was very well written in my opinion. The 2-D design was fairly perfect for this game. The artwork itself was very cool, in that it seemed to be sketchbook art given life, which I thought was pretty neat.
So, in the game, you play as a high school teen who seems to be having some issues in her life. Her friendships are strained, her family relationships are strained, her schoolwork is suffering, etc...As you explore this world, more is revealed, and it leads you on a bit of a path to self discovery. However, what I thought was even more interesting was the Sixth Sense (movie) approach to story telling in this game, which is to say that everything that happens in the game has a greater prupose that, upon finishintg the game, will all fall into place seamlessly and present an entirely different picture after than you might have thought was happening during the course of events that led you through this experience. I thought that was particularly well handled, especially considered that this was obviously a cathartic experience for the games writer as well
All told, I think this game deserved about a 7.5 out of 10, but I also think that depending on your real life circumstances prior to playing this game, the ratings could easily be higher. I was glad to be given this window into the writers mind a bit. There are also some very nice film reels at the end of the game that also give some real life perspective to the in game story....and that secret ending....make sure you see it. It's really easy to accomplish and will only take you about 5 minutes longer to take the necessary steps (which can be found in the Community Hub if you dont feel like exploring...but basically finishing the game unlocks new dialogue towards the beginning of a second playthrough which will allow you to unlock the secret ending without having to play through the entire game again).

AER: Memories of Old is a good game in a lot of ways, but is lacking in others. A few (potential) negatives about the game:
It is very short. I completed the entirety of the game in just shy of 4 hours.
The game doesn't always perform well. A few points in the game (for example, a cave with a lot of particle effects) brought my framerate to a crawl, and I suffered from audio crackling and framerate dips when facing towards too many islands at once.
The game doesn't really test your skills. The flight controls take a few minutes to get used to, there are a few platforming scections, and there are light puzzles in the "dungeons". Your reflexes and fine motor skills won't be particularly challenged by AER.
However, there are good things about the game (and even about the points I mentioned above).
The game has a consistent tone & theme, and uses the few resources it has to communicate them well. The narrative of AER's world is very overtly about appreciating beauty in nature and the world. I would argue that this is a little too on the nose when it comes to the written story, but AER's gameplay and world design convey this idea very well. It is enjoyable to fly around and explore the islands: even if you don't find the key or item you need, there are often easter eggs, story fragments, or just little details that make the exploration feel rewarding.
The game's brevity makes it a quick play that doesn't overstay its decidedly shallow mechanics. I listed shortness as a negative, but this can just as easily be spun into a positive light. The game being too much longer would be tiring, but the game is just long enough to explore the mechanics it does have while telling its story.
AER is a relaxed experience. The game is willing to let you explore its story at your own pace, and doesn't demand much in the way of mechanical skill.
With this in mind, I'd recommend AER: Memories of Old if:
You are looking for a game that values telling a story over crafting tight gameplay, and you're okay with not being mechanically challenged. If you like the experience of exploring and finding little secrets and details in the environment, even better.
You're willing to spend the price of the game (17.99 CAD at time of writing) on a ~3-5 hour experience. The price is steep, especially considering the time:price ratio of many games, but the game manages to make those few hours more dense than most. I'd wait until a decent sale.

I have been playing around with GG with over 1500 hours put in. I feel it is a vary good game making tool if you understand it's limits.
I cant tell you if GameGuru is better or worse than another game engine, because I have never tried any other engine. But I can tell you I have made decent scenes, have a little ( A lot more now ) knowledge of lua scripting now, talked to very helpful people in the community and had a lot of fun doing it.
Good:
- Vary good/helpful community. This is the best community I have ever seen. ( This is still vary true )
- Using the editor is fun.
- I have learned lua thanks to GameGuru. That says a lot to me.
- Lots of tutorials, from Steam, GameGuru website or in the editor, you will find what you need.
- The shop.. You can buy scripts and assists in the shop for a really good price. This is a huge help! You can also sell things yourself on the shop. All the items on the shop are 'player' made.
A shop sounds bad. But really it is the best part. If you know nothing about 3d modeling and animations, the shop will be one of the first places to check out if you get GameGuru
- GG has an okay character creator to make npcs. You can't do as much as you would want to. But it's still okay, for some games I see it being vary good. For me personally it worked out for my projects. But it is vary limited at this moment.
Bad:
- I like the dlc's. But it should be noted that they plan on making more and some people may say "cash grab" ( I love the dlcs, I have them all )
- No crafting mechanic. ( I don't care about this, but I know some people will )
- texters on everything seem a little outdated. ( Vary true )
Ugly:
Simple features are missing at this time. You could script them but will take scripting knowledge.
Not a default feature:
- load/save games. This has been added!!
- Questing, no way to make your own npc that gives a quest. Once/if you try to learn lua, this is one of the easiest things to make.
- No inventory system. This is needed with most games people want to make. I understand it is hard for gameguru to make an inventory system that fits all needs. But as of right now they don't even have a basic feature for devs to work with. Coding an inventory system is hard for beginners. Making a loop that checks all the slots to then put the item in the next empty slot is not something beginners will understand.
So, my rating for GameGuru is, 7/10    ( Vary fun to learn, Hard at times, Vary nice people to help you, lacking basic features)
Edit: I changed my rating to 8/10. If it was not for Gameguru I would not know as much as I do about coding in Lua.

Kane & Lynch 2: Dog Days is a game that's way ahead of it's time.  It's an interesting 3rd person cover-based shooter that has the right idea and aesthetic.but unfortunately it's bogged down by frequent lankiness and weird bugs.
The game play is similar to that of Gears of War in that you "snap" in and out of cover and for the most part, it works well! I only had one weird instance happen where I was stuck hopping from cover to cover and Lynch just wouldn't budge out as a helicopter was shooting at me.
Another highlight is the destructible environments. Almost everything you or your enemies shoot breaks down into small debris. This keeps the gun play fun to look at as well as frantic since you're constantly on the move from cover to cover. There's also scripted events where they bust down a wall and it all just looks gorgeous against the grimy neon-drenched Shanghai.
Speaking of which, the graphics are certainly the highlight of this game. While the game play is still solid, the atmosphere of Shanghai is breathtaking. From the blinding pink neon to the disgusting brown grit from a basement, there's a lot of variety to make you literally feel the city.
There are some odd choices the art designers went with though which may or may not appeal to you. For starters, the ENTIRE game is "filmed" through a camcorder which goes in-hand with the completely annoying shaky cam which is left on by default. While this effect is cool, it's also very nauseating and that's incredible for me to say since I never get motion sickness - not even from VR games.
Continuing on, the game is supposed to look like it's being filmed live as everything is happening. With that comes overexposure on bright areas, weird artifacts during movement and dark areas, etc. Everything you'd see in an amateur YouTube video.
Adding on to the atmosphere, the soundtrack is just nothing short of amazing. It's a weird blend of drone sounds mixed with Asian drums and synth rumblings that really adds to the tension. The soundtrack is available on Spotify and YouTube so I recommend a listen ASAP.
A huge problem the game has is its weird glitches. Multiple times I witnessed my co-op partner spaz out, get stuck inside walls, or go through doors, I'd see a gun on my screen but he wouldn't see it, and vice-versa, and, annoyingly, aiming for one level was completely broken (as in, we'd be looking in one direction but firing a completely opposite direction).
As it's worse though, is the crashing. We've, so far, have had two big crashes during our co-op sessions that required us to restart an entire level.
That being said, we both got this game for dirt cheap and if you see it for less than $5, I highly recommend this game to play through with a partner. A lot of fun and I see the potential this series had.
Unfortunately, it came out way ahead of it's time. I'm a firm believer that if this game came out now with the amount of polish Square Enix requires now, that it would be a top seller!

What can be said about this game?  As I've read on other review sites, this is a game that could only ever exist (and be profitable) on PC.  This is a game that shows how unique PC gaming can be.  There is litterally a "simulation" for almost every type of activity out there, most bad but some unbelievably good.
Spintires is just such an example.  It takes such an obscure subject, logging in Russian forests, and manages to make an amazingly entertaining game out of it.  It defy's logic how something so obtuse can be made to be entertaining but somehow the dev has done just that and delivered a piece of stunning and well made gaming excellence.
If you haven't already heard or read about this game it can be summed up with the these simple points:
I once called this a "tactical" driving game to a friend and that is exactly what it is.  It's surveying a potential path, recognizing what the truck you are driving is capable of, consider the load you are carrying and (after weighing the potential consequences of your choice) slamming the throttle and pushing through whatever obstacle may be in your way, be it mud, river, forest or whatever else this game decides to throw at you.
It truly is a test of endurance and will leave you wanting more.  So far I have completed 3 maps and plan on finishing them all before toying with the plethora of mods available.  The dev has made an offroad simulator that has far surpassed anything I've ever played.  I no longer desire smooth ashphalt and carefully contoured corners, I want the most brutal conditions mother nature can throw at me and seeing if I'm able to tackle them in the meanest, rustiest, ugliest trucks ever designed by man.
And I have...barely.
On a side note, I have noticed a lot of negative reviews about people complaining about the progress of the game, and there have been issues between the dev and the publisher.  Those seem to have been ironed out and, while progress does seem slow, they are getting there.  I only see good things in the future for this game and am glad to be on board to see how it comes.
I suggest you get on board too!

This game...
My biggest critique would be the audio.  Its strangely missing in some cutscenes (footsteps, sword slashes, punching noises, ambient noises), under-delivered in other instances (some crowd noise seems weak and out of place), with some dialogue drowned out by music or other ambient noise (Geralts voice actor, while awesome, is sometimes inaudible due to acompanying audio).  Audio is the #1 thing in games, where if done wrong, can remove me from the experience.  Animations are #2.  Outside of pre-rendered cutscenes and combat, character animations are stilted and ugly.  Don't go into this game expecting to see facial animations either, because they don't exist.  There is just barely lip sync.  While not entirely impactful on my experience with the game as a whole, I would like to critique the level design in the final chapter.  Loc Muinne is a maze with very few landmarks.  It was just kind of a pain getting around that level.  I look forward to the sequel which promises to be open world.  That would suit a game like this better.  Linear level design just feels wrong.  Also, the pacing in this game is off.  I didn't find myself invested in the story until the end of chapter 2, which is 2/3 of the way through the game.  I may be to blame for not playing the first game, or reading the books, but really... as a game designer, you have to have a plan to bring new players into the fold, and to get them interested in your story as well.
With all of that said, the game is very good.  The combat is great.  The story is well layered, and well delivered.  In fact, its well supported as well.  I found myself spacing out during several cutscenes and afterwards saying, "OOOOOOKKKKKKK... WTF just happened again?"  No problemo.  Open the journal, read the journal entry for the mission I am on, and the cutscene is well summarized right there.   With the awesome journal, I was able to keep up with the story, and learn a little more about the game's story.  So, definetely a recommend.

Ugh... so many thoughts after finishing this game.  The truth is, I'm not sure how to feel about it.
Do I recommend the game?........... Yes.  I think it's worthy of recommendation.  This recommendation does, however, come with a caveat.
The game, to me, was very disjointed.  It was as if every day's journal entry was completely unrelated to any others.  It also seemed that despite the choices made and what was said during some of the many conversations throughout, the outcomes seemed a bit unexpected and almost illogical.  I found I was often confused when, as the protagonist I would be having a seemingly pleasant conversation with someone only to find I was suddenly forced to defend myself over something that was not apparent.  But I guess, after thinking about it more, maybe that's one of the themes of this game... not everything happens as expected.
In the end, you do sort of find out, in an abrupt sort of way, the premise for the game itself and why some things happened the way they did.  It still doesn't explain everything of course.  I was still very moved (to tears) by the ending as it comes almost out of the blue and it hits you like a ton of bricks, but I was also still a bit confused with some of the prior events since they did seem very mashed together.
Aside from the story, I like the graphic style used.  The voice acting was top notch and helped me connect a bit more with the main character.  The music was also very well done.
So once again... I do recommend this game, but you really do have to play it without expectations.  It is still a touching story.

This is an intimate game.
An interactive narrative, more than a game, it tells a sad, sober story about a tragedy viewed from the eyes of a teenage girl. No, you don't play this game for action, you don't play it to min-max the endings, you play it to find out what is bothering the girl so much she doesn't want to comprehend some things she talks with others about.
Some interactive plot choices do change the ending dialogues with key actors, but nothing you do (or at least I didn't find anything) can change the outcome of the main narrative.
The visual style - everything drawn like with children's crayons is beautiful and few screens out of the house it hides a dark and foreboding background, making the exploration interesting and sense of dread palpable, like in the best of horrors.
If you want a short deep narrative with some interactive elements, you can't go wrong with this little gem.

First, comparing this game, Journal, to Richard Perrin's previously popular game, Kairo, is to compare fire to ice. Not as opposites so much, as simply defying comparison. Beyond an obvious regard for thinking-gamers, please consider them seperately when deciding on the selection of either.
If at first we think to compare this (apparently unnamed) protaganist to our own experiences, we soon find out how wrong we are. While there are, no doubt, some young lives closely matching that in this game (perhaps every life has some immediate comparisons) what makes this game MOST remarkable is that it starts out to seem anything BUT. Just a young girl, misunderstood as are most people. By gradual steps (or more frequently, sudden starts and stops), we find out she is NOT us, and therefore, if we expected validation, we may begin to lose faith in this game. But if we continue, we find out in surprising reveals (conversations, experiences & titular journal entries) that inwardly she may be almost exactly like us, no matter our age, background or gender. NO life is truly ordinary. Or easy.
But this game's real theme is regret. Choices have, not so much results, but consequences. Our "heroine" frequently laments her choices, while other characters, in word and act, confirm the irreversable, often heartbreaking, permanence of "The Wrong Choice" made. There is no SAVE.
The artwork was strategiclly minimalistic, changing to become more haunted to match our protaganist's life. I don't recall much sunshine (if any, but this IS supposed to be the UK.) Rain was part of the story, as were the gritty streets and coffee-cup rings on some "pages". Temporary barriers between locations were made "young girl's life" obvious, including a band-aid. The "busy" dialog was effective and amusing. Aesthetically, a very pleasing game.
The stories built into the game were a wonderful, welcome touch, though never explained specifically. Did they even exist "in story"? Perhaps leaving them, and their source (mostly) ambiguous, except quite probably from our heroine's subconscious, was more interesting in retrospect. Particularly if they were driven additionally by interest in her friend Trevor and his oft-mentioned comic. If indeed retrospect is to be considered in our analysis and/or appreciation, we may find this game to be absolutely filled with subtle (and not) hints and clues. Dare I say, almost in a David Lynchian sense? (Please understand, "Journal" is NO "Mulholland Drive".) This game, like many great ones, may truly be better appreciated AFTER completion.
It had some moments that, at the time, felt like minor flaws in the game. Now I'm not so sure. Is something that only SEEMS like a flaw less a flaw, despite having taken us momentarily out of the game? I can't go into detail about either of the two (spoilers) I noticed, but they were moments where cause and effect were reversed. Something happened that, at the time, made no sense. But when the reason was learned minutes later it seemed that, if characters had been encountered in a different sequence, actions would have felt to have occured normally. Having finished the game, I just don't know anymore, except that it seemed unfortunate at the time. Perhaps it was nothing more than a plot device. Foreshadowing maybe, or a jaring of our comfort zone. Or I got the game sequence reversed by selecting the wrong topics from the wrong people in the wrong order.
There was one instance that seemed otherwise flawed. The protaganist went to talk to a teacher about a family member, but when that person is selected as the "topic", there was no discussion available. But as far as I could tell it had no major impact, except to (regretably) draw notice. Perhaps the intent WAS to say nothing, but that might have been better indicated.
Also, I wish there had been a way (other than rapid spacebars) to avoid repetative dialog, if desired. (Perhaps a color change if nothing was different since prior selecting.) And I'm not sure why we were allowed to continue going into places that no  longer had importance (particularly the Post Office, which had its brief moment of signifigance.) Perhaps simply to intensify the game-critical feeling of "choice". The promised opening of the package never happened, and as such felt forgotten in the story. A contrivance, essentially, but relatively minor (not even important enough to be considered "spoiler".) Perhaps other player choices would have had more satisfying, or complete, results. Another was far less minor (i.e.: "spoiler" level), but just as abandoned. Also, there may be players unhappy about the lack of a SAVE feature. Well, life is like that.
I'm glad I played it.

I want to recommend this game, I really do, but the gameplay detracts from the story too much to actually make me want to tell someone to sit down and play it through. First off I bought this game for maybe $2 on a steam sale. It was something I'd seen a few times and passed up because it didn't look like my type of visual novel. But it was; it was just executed poorly. First off your decisions barely matter. Only if you want the losing a friend achievement does it matter what you choose along the way (and I just so happened to toss myself down that road in my first playthrough) and even then losing a friend doesn't change the outcome. The ending is pretty much disjointed from every event along the way. Sure the ending explains her rotten mood, but the ending is more of a 'this is why I'm acting so sour' kind of backstory than it is 'these are the consequences of my actions' which is what you would expect a series of choices to lead you to. I could live with that (even though the completionist in me wants to truck through and read all the dialogue for every option) if it was the only downside of the game.
What really gets me though is not the lack of options in the game. It's the feel of the world itself. The MCs voice is very nice and I can appreciate the music of the game, but switching from page to page is a bit of a headache. The pages seem to shift in a very awkward manner looking like it's flickering between the two pages before you finally settle on the second screen and half of the time the MC jumps when she gets there. If she was at the edge of the screen when it was flickering all of a sudden she's in a middle as if the game was trying to disorient you. Day 3 was the worst of it due to a bug that can jump you into the journal pages of Day 5 (except you can't interact with anyone and then you get kicked out of it and think you were doing something wrong and kicked yourself out of Day 3's plot). Overall I felt like I was tussling with the journal pages more than working with it to immerse myself in a story line.
On top of the bad scene transitioning is the disjointed day transitioning. Each day ends with a screen shift into what looks like a puppet show telling you a 'story' that is supposed to connect with the main story line. On most days it feels as though the author of the game forgot where we was going with the story and abruptly cut it short before the final conclusion. At first it seems like an isolated event, but once you get to the end of the game you realize that the end of day stories are like most things, cut off without a proper end. There is never an explanation of the package, or her grandmother's behavior, characters like Heather are briefly mentioned and treated as if they'd been there since day one but are really never there at all. The whole incident with John is never flat out explained either-- it's the only piece of the plot that it seems as if the author purposely avoided saying and yet it is the only piece that you can logically draw a conclusion to because everybody knows what really happened.
On top of that the game forces achievement hunters to go back through day one all over again looking for a secret ending that adds no depth to the story at all. As if the gameplay wasn't frustrating enough the first time they developers make us take a motion sickening gander across day one all over again to try and 'cheer us up' with a whole bunch of nothing.
If you get it on sale, the story (despite it's holes) is cute and will leave you feeling a little heavy, and the achievements are easy to get if that's all you're looking for, but the interface and scene changes just aren't worth the story in my opinion.

This is a very nice game, very pleasant, but you may want to note that my 5-hour playtime was a full play of the game, exploring every corner, trying to find every ghost, getting exploration achievements, etc. In other words, I was hardly speeding through it--5 hours is pretty much the most you're going to get out of it.
The game is suitable even for small kids. There are brief glimpses of something scary, and many bad things happened in the past, but nothing unpleasant can happen to the player--there is no fall damage, for example--and in general the game is peaceful and relaxing. There are several jumping puzzles but nothing too hard, which is good, because jumping is kind of erratic. Flying around is a lot of fun.
The flight controls could be better documented.  Just remember that, like a real bird, a steep dive will speed you up, and a steep climb will slow you down. The biggest problem people seem to have is "how do I slow down so I can look at islands or make a precise landing?" Either climb up until you stall and then level out, or try to bank right and left at the same time (press both mouse buttons simultaneously), which will slow you quickly. Flapping wings seems to build up speed cumulatively so only flap as many times as you think you need to. And if you hit ground--or a tree, or a rock, or a sheep, or anything else--you'll change back to human, so a landing doesn't have to be super graceful.
Also: F for lantern! The game DOES tell you this, at the beginning, but it's easy to miss. You should basically have the lantern on any time you're walking around on land. Long falls will extinguish the lantern so don't forget to turn it back on again.

Negative reviews of Alan Wake rightly point out some of it's problems, the main one being the pace of the game, which seems to be padded out. Parts can be repetitive, game mechanics seem clunky, and I suppose it's not - for the most part - particularly scary. For these reasons, I don't think it quite holds up to widespread acclaim it recieved at the time of it's release (2010)...
But despite this, I thoroughly enjoyed it. The first episode was probably the most mundane in terms of gameplay, but things quickly become more interesting as the episodes progress. The narrative progresses in the same sort of way that the TV series Lost does, with an array of possible explainations for the games events which leave us constantly questioning what it all means, even until the very last episode. It's very successful in this sense.
Where Alan Wake succeeds the most, however, is probably in it's creation of an atmosphere. I loved the town of Pacific North-West town of Bright Falls and it's odd residents and traditions. I loved the creepiness of it's world, and little additions such as the radios and the TV shorts you can watch ingame add another dimension of the game. So much effort went into these features, which are clearly a labour of love. The characters are entertaining, the references made me smile, and the scenic cutscenes are stunning.
Alan Wake isn't for everyone, and some will be a little put off by the first episodes gameplay, but it's definitely worth giving it a chance to explore the world it so expertly builds.

This review was written in English and Russian
I recommend to buy Wanda ONLY WITH DISCOUNT.
Wanda is an indie game with some nice puzzles and a cute story about two robots' adventures in a post-apocalyptic world. The game tells us a story of Blue Bot (male, no doubt) and Red Bot (female, for sure) walking in wastelands from one puzzle to another one with some check-points (save spots).
The robots speak fictional symbolic language (devs say it's Hyrulian language from Legend of Zelda) so I can't understand a word but I can still feel that the story is about friendship, love and hope in wastelands (or in a big-big world for Green Bot and Yellow Bot).
Pros
1. Rather good music. Sounds of bots reminds me about Wall-E.
2. Interesting and well designed puzzles (well, some of them) which you can skip anytime.
3. It's easy to unlock all of achievements in one playthrough if you're careful not to skip any of the puzzles and collect every data shards (square-shaped objects with a glowing green circle) along the way.
Cons
1. There's no in-game menu and you can exit the game only by using Ctr-Alt-Del buttons. There's no save/ load system.
2. The game is so short that you can end it in less than 3-4 hr. so the game is overpriced.
3. There're a lot of cutscenes which you can't skip. In fact there're more cutscenes than gameplay itself (solving puzzles and searching for collectible data shards). And devs call their game "a short film/ novel".
4. Some puzzles are not logical and well designed, e.g. puzzles with portals (you can't see the spot where you should shoot).
5. You don't understand the whole story if you don't know Hyrulian (fictional language).
The game is a little cute thing but there're better games about robots in the wastelands, e.g. Machinarium.

Я рекомендую покупать Ванду ТОЛЬКО СО СКИДКОЙ.
Ванда - это инди-игра с несколькими головоломками и милой историей о приключениях двух роботов в пост-апокалиптическом мире. История рассказывает нам историю о Синем (Голубом) боте и Красном (Розовом) Боте. Как видно из цветовой дифференциации, один из роботов - парень, другой - девушка, и оба они двигаются по пустошам от одной головоломки к другой, между некоторыми из которых находятся чек-пойнты (места сохранения).
Роботы говорят на выдуманном символическом языке (по словам разработчиков, это какой-то хилурианский язык из Легенды о Зельде), так что я не понял ни слова, но все-таки чувствую, что эта история о дружбе, любви и надежде в пустошах (или в большом-большом мире для Зеленого Бота и Желтого Бота).
Понравилось:
1. Неплохая музыка. Звуки ботов напомнили мне фильм "Валл-И".
2. Интересные и хорошо сделанные головоломки (ну, некоторые из них), причем, вы можете пропустить головоломки.
3. Легко получить все достижения за одно прохождение, но только если вы не будете пропускать головоломки и найдете все осколки информационных карт (квадратные объекты с мигающим зеленым кругом).
Не понравилось:
1. В игре нет внутриигрового меню и выйти из игры вы можете только через три кнопки. Нет также и системы сохранения, записываться можно только в чек-пойнтах.
2. Игра настолько короткая, что вы можете не спеша закончить ее за 3-4 часа, так что цена игры завышена.
3. Много сцен (анимационных вставок) на движке игры, которые вы не можете пропустить. На самом деле, этих cценок больше, чем игрового процесса (разгадывания головоломок и поиска осколков информационных карт). Да и разработчики называют свою игру "коротким фильмом/ новеллой".
4. Некоторые головоломки нелогичны и плохо сделаны, например, головоломки с порталами (вы не видите то место, куда следует стрелять).
5. Вы не поймете историю полностью, если не знаете хилурианский (выдуманный язык).
Игра - забавная вещица, но имеются лучше игры про роботов в пустошах, например, Машинариум.

This game puts on many hats. It has an element of storytelling and an element of puzzle-solving. The game is centered on a robot wandering through an unknown apocalypse of the robot civilization and meeting another surviving robot. The story centers on their relationship while providing puzzles to solve which require the player to swap between the two robots in order to solve it.
The gameplay is not terrible, and there were no bugs that I encountered whatsoever. The game did live up to containing puzzles. What makes this game so difficult to enjoy deals with the ratio of cutscene to gameplay combined with the inability to understand the story at all due to the made-up language. Either of these story delivery methods would be acceptable in isolation (few and short cutscenes with made-up languages OR long cutscenes with easily understandable lore), however, the combination serves to present feelings of agitation as one waits for the gameplay to begin while observing cutscenes that lack any non-verbal gesturing to make up for it. With the asking price being approximately $10 USD, this game falls short. If you would like this kind of game I would only recommend it with a considerable discount.

A good example of a game that is carried by it's atmosphere and writing. As they did with their 6th-gen classic 'Max Payne', Remedy show excellent attention to detail and fans of contemporary horror will really enjoy the little easter-eggs and nods to popular media (my personal favourite was their faitful homage to Serling's The Twilight Zone). The very Stephen King sense of small town dread mixed with Cascadian scenery (taken straight from Lynch's Twin Peaks) makes exploring the environments pretty enjoyable. I just wish there was a little bit less focus on the woods surrounding the town, as this got a bit same-y after 10 or so hours.
The game is paced pretty strangely, mostly due to pretty irritating combat. This can maybe make the game seem as though it is dragging out a few hours longer than it needed to be. Also, some of the humour falls a bit flat - maybe that is a reflection on my sense of humour though.
Overall, I would recommend this game if you enjoy a good story. It may be derivative and clearly wears its influences on its sleeves, but its fun nonetheless. It is a shame that the game is no longer able to be sold due to music licensing issues - I hope Remedy is able to secure the rights back otherwise this modern cult favourite will become pretty obscure/difficult to play.

I started this game right after I finished the first Witcher game, so I was still very impressed with the first game and had really high expectations of this one, however, I found The Witcher 2 to be incredibly different. In so many ways. And I am not a person who likes change upon something I already loved so much like the first Witcher.
I had to push through the incredibly difficult prologue, the different combat system which really disappointed me because I loved the time based sword combat in the first game, and the change from classical painting art style for cutscenes to comic art. I was really bitter about it. However, it all changed after the end of the prologue and the beginning of this incredibly complex story that had so much going on that I was really immresed in it. Moreover, the further you go in the game, the better it gets in terms of story, gameplay, graphics and art style, music, and EVERYTHING. This game wasn't really what I hated anymore, the story kept getting deeper and all pieces from the previous game and this one were coming together somehow. I found that despite all the differences between the first and second Witcher games, they still kept the core of what made The Witcher series what it is; a story about greedy, ugly human nature when politics, beliefs and money and thirst for power cause conflict. I completely fell in love with this game, and I can't wait for the third installment.

EDIT:
After many patches and a serious shift in direction, OMD!U is finally shaping up to be worthy successor to OMD2.  While still not perfect, I find myself regularly returning to OMD!U for a couple matches of Orc smashing goodness.
Progression, while still heavily grind-y, feels more rewarding now.  With more ways to earn your loot, including daily "quests" and match completion rewards, what once felt like a helpless grind now feels more like playing a slot machine.  While that is still leaving your ability to upgrade your traps to RNG, it definitely feels better than the previous systems.  More direct avenues for upgrades would be much preferred, as working for a chest only to have it give you more cards for a trap that you'll either never use or have already maxed out is still pretty annoying.
My other main complaint is that the higher difficulty levels almost require you to play with a group of two other players to be successful.  I understand the game is designed to be played co-op and that the more allies you have the better, but I tend to play most of my games solo, including OMD1&2.  So it would be nice to have a real chance to complete Master and Rift Lord difficulties while playing solo without having to power level well over the recommended rank to have a chance.
Aside from those main complaints, I do feel that there are many more minor changes to be made, including certain underwhelming traps and characters, some difficulty balance on certain levels (being either unexpectedly difficult or easy within their difficulty tier), and endless levels being too few and far too difficult, even when extremely power leveled.
While I do have some negative things to say, I am mostly pleased with the game that Robot has provided through these update.  If you like Orcs Must Die 1 or 2, then I suggest at least giving OMD!U a try.  It is a free to play game, so at worst the only thing ventured is your time.
While there is still a lot of room for improvement, Robot's demonstrable effort to change the game for the better gives me hope that this game will one day be the successor that OMD2 deserves.  Good on you, Robot Entertainment.

As someone who has over 200+ hours in OMD2, I really love this franchise.  With that being said, OMDU being FTP really concerned me.  Most FTP is poorly implemented and done in a way that punishes the player if they don't dish out several games worth of money into them to make progress.  And based on what I was hearing, it sounded like OMDU was going down that exact path.
Unfortunately, it looks like it really was.
OMDU plays better than ever.  The gameplay is great, the new roster of characters is a nice change of pace, and the new abilities and traps are a welcomed addition.  I am already addicted to the gameplay and would love to keep playing.  But, the problem is, is that most players will never experience 1/3rd of what this game has to offer due to the INCREDIBLE cost of literally everything in this game.  Want a new trap?  Better hope you have either a padded wallet or 30 hours of grinding on your hand.  A new character?  Well that costs even more, better pick which arm and leg you want to give up.  The costs are absolutely astronomical and brutally punishing.
Which is incredibly disappointing actually, because all of the charm from OMD was leveling up, getting new traps, getting new gear, getting new weapons, upgrading it all and trying to find that PERFECT setup for each specific level.  But with OMDU, it's just "This is what you have, grind match after match after match and MAYBE, JUST MAYBE after a couple days you can get the base variant for a single new trap if you're lucky."
It's such a flipping shame, because I would've gladly paid full price for this game and enjoyed the living heck out of it had they not gone the FTP route.  But now, I am honestly questioning whether or not I will continue on with this game knowing that I either have to shovel truckloads of money into it to make any progress or grind for weeks and weeks and weeks just to get a decent variety of traps and characters.
Hopefully Robot will decrease the insane cost to make progress in this game.  If not, they're likely to lose a longtime dedicated fan.

I was severely disappointed to find that I am glued to the ground and that the platforming is simply holding down a button. The game is incredibly simple and easy. Combat is braindead, the path is extremely railroaded, and collectibles aren't very difficult to find for the most part. Because you are glued to the ground and the paths are railroaded, you will often find the collectibles right in front of your face. The "specials" I have gotten have mostly gone unused, as they are unnecessary (unless the game requires them to be used). Your "life" and "health points" are pointless considering you respawn about 2 feet from where you once were due to generous checkpoint placement, and the fact that there isn't a "gameover".
However, the game isn't a bad game. Being simple and easy does not mean that the game isn't fun. Contrary to this, I have been thoroughly enjoying the game once I got out of the "This isn't a 3D platformer" mindset. The designs of the characters are very interesting and cool (you can't tell me that Koru's scarf isn't awesome). The art and music both are beautiful! Colors are vivid and lush, sound effects are satisfying, and the story is interesting enough to me that I want to know what happens. And even though the combat is incredibly simple and easy, I still have fun with it due to the sound effects, colors, and animations. The animations being incredibly fluid and fun to watch.

Alan Wake is an interesting premise. It doesn't escape a lot of the 3D action-shooter cliches—namely long stretches of going from A to B, repetitive enemy encounters, and a lot of buffer material that lengthens the gameplay—it's still a fairly solid game all-around.
The writing is coherent, most of the time, and does a good job of placing you in the shoes of an author who is living out his own nightmares. I believe the screenwriter, Sam Lake, also worked on Max Payne, so you should anticipate the same level of surreal and bizarre. I wouldn't call it the best story I've read, nor is it the most original, the way it is narrated does a great job setting the atmosphere of Alan Wake: dark, somber, sometimes ironic, and sometimes incredibly strange. It's no surprise to me that Sam Lake appears to be a fan of Twin Peaks.
The weapons function well with the light mechanic, and the game can be pretty fun and intense at times. The shooting gets boring after a while though. I think the most interesting use of mechanics I've found in Alan Wake is actually from the DLC expansion. If you end up liking the base game, give the DLC a shot.
All in all, I think Alan Wake is good enough to recommend. It wasn't amazing, but I certainly enjoyed it.

As much as I would like, there simply isn’t enough to AER memories of Old to give it my recommendation.
It is a shame, because the concept in itself is promising. AER. is a lay-back type of game, focused on exploration and puzzles in which you unravel the mystery of why the world is broken into tiny bits. As a bonus, you can shapeshift and fly around as a bird, a mechanic which was quite polished in my opinion. I also really liked the graphics; I certainly became addicted to the low-poly high-res style of AER after a while.
The problem start at the contents of the game; after 4 hours I have seen EVERYTHING in the game. Every memory (a.k.a. the glowing symbol-dudes) , every scroll, every achievement except one because of a bug. This really undermines the whole exploration gameplay, which is one third of the gameplay you get to experience.
The second element of gameplay, the puzzles, were also a let-down. I found the puzzles to be extremely simple. No complex mysteries or intricate mechanisms, but simple platform-to-platform jumping and pushing some buttons will solve about all puzzles in this game.
The last element, and the showpiece of AER, the ability to fly is barely used for anything else than getting from A to B. it is used in only 1 puzzle; a severe underuse and waste of resources.
The game is absent of physical fighting, which isn’t a bad thing but it doesn’t really provide an alternative way for you to really feel like your battling an ominous antagonist. AER - Memories of Old is a game that leans entirely on its visual style. While some may find substance in exploring its small world, the bulk of the game isn't very engaging or even intuitive for that matter.
Gameplay:
AER's main focus here is exploration with puzzle solving and platforming taking a back seat. You have the ability of flight to explore floating islands in the sky. While not mechanically deep as there are no combat or simulation elements to flying, the controls are fluid and zipping around while exploring various islands from above is quite fun. The islands themselves don't hold a lot of interest upon landing on them. While many hold pieces of environmental storytelling, lore from ruins/tablets/scrolls and dialogue from NPCS, everything is expository. There isn't much of a scripted story that surprises or grabs you while you play. You just go from island to island reading these notes with platforming that feels floaty and puzzle solving that's too easy. While many will argue that this is the type of game you can relax to, the lack of engagement makes this game come off as boring. Furthermore, the lore pieces or blobs of text for that matter aren't logged by your character in a journal, neither are items or directions. So if you get lost or are trying to get a grasp on the lore of the game, not having a journal makes the process more frustrating. Not having a interesting narrator or character that intertwines with your own story rather than just spouting dialogue about something that you never experienced yet are told to care about also doesn't help.
Visuals & Audio:
This game is whimsical. It has an amazing art style and great environmental music. The visuals look straight out of an abstract art gallery. There's a ton of color in the design which helps keep the game visually appealing but it isn't overdone to a point where everything is an eyesore. The biggest problem I have is the lack of bioms for the islands. You pretty much have 3 and most of them
are just your typical green trees, blue lakes, vanilla island. I like the drearyness of the snow islands though. You also have sanctuaries and caves which have there own moments of great music which comes off as calm and quiet, almost somber in a way. There is a bit of a Zelda vibe for the visuals overall. A mixture of Wind Waker & Skyward Sword. Wind Waker for it's cartoony and simple environemnts, models and textures, skywards sword for it's color design. I'd say all of this makes the game really interesting to play, at least for a bit.
Content:
This game is unfortunately quite short. It's about 4 hours if you find everything which seems decent for a $15 game. However, a lot of that time spent is just wandering around trying to find out what to do or where to go. While I feel the exploration is solid, therea aren't a ton of interesting places to go to. You do have a lot of secrets/eastereggs and the environmental design
is interesting to comb through, but if you're expecting something that doesn't feel padded or shallow, I'd look elsewhere or for when this game drops in price.
Overall I don't think AER is a bad game because it has few strong points going for it. Those strong points can hold their own but when you dive into the meat of the game there isn't much here. Little touches like having a small index to save navigational instructions and lore pieces would have added a lot to the game. By the end of my play session I had no desire to continue the game. While I liked flying around and exporing I felt nothing towards what the game was trying to build up.

Myanmar-based Kodots Games describes “Wanda” as a “tale of … finding companionship, love and hope in a wasteland.” The game introduces itself through a blue robot that somehow avoided damage, emerging out of its pod before starting its journey in search of anything that responds. About a third of the way through, we meet another robot, this time red, and our small band of robots continue their journey in search of… anything.
“Wanda” prides itself in being a “minimalist story-rich puzzle,” and rightly so. This game has no dialogues at all, only running with a series of robotic sounds and unknown symbols. Paired with the game’s soundtrack and a few bits of sound effects, the players are left on their own to observe and draw the story out for themselves. But is it really effective?
I have to admit, there’s something inherently sad about a robot repeatedly making the same sound more than 50 times, which I assumed meant “Hello,” only to get no response. The beautiful artwork accentuates the feeling of sadness, leaving you to wonder what really happened in that world. It’s clever, really, to make the player feel a sense of tragedy with everything that’s broken on the ground, only to juxtapose the scene with the beauty of the starry night sky. It’s a conflicting feeling, to say the least.
However, I’d be lying if I said that “Wanda” hit me in my emotional sweet spot. Yes, I felt bad for our blue robot, cheered for him when he met the red robot, and felt bad for them when they’re being scared by thunderstorms, but I never quite connected with them as much. Their journey did not feel normal to me - it felt controlled and contrived. It felt as if their travels were simply a means to move the story along.
