I played Myst and Riven as a kid, and while I was too young (and probably not smart enough) to beat those games, I always found the sense of mystery and otherworldliness truly amazing. I finished Quern a few days ago (as an adult and possibly smarter) and must say that I really enjoyed it! However, there are a few issues that takes away from the experience.
The first two or three hours of this game are great: stunning visuals, great sense of mystery and excellent puzzles. Walking around the strange world of Quern and noting the different puzzles, clues and locked doors is an amazing experience. The puzzles are varied and range from easy to quite difficult. The best puzzles are those that require you to remember something you've seen in another location and combine, alter, or place items in several different locations.
After a few hours, you will go from being
. At this point, the game takes a turn for the worse. For some reason, the puzzles go from being varied and very clever to being highly repetitive and almost completely based around
. It feels like ZadBox just ran out of ideas for the puzzles. Some puzzles are so difficult at this point that I end up googling them. They are mostly based around logics or maths, and require you to write down equations. While this is a cool idea, I feel like it's going a bit too far. I don't mind spending a long time solving a puzzle, if it involves walking around the world looking for clues. I just don't enjoy standing around in one place, trying different combinations and writing down sequences (not when you have to do this for every puzzle).
Eventually more of the story gets revealed, and it's just not very good. It feels forced and boring. Up until this, my imagination had run wild: where am I? What is this world? What's the backstory? Then I found out and it was just "meh".
I would definately recommend this game, and am looking forward to ZadBox's next game, but hope they have learned a few things from Quern! I would give this game 7/10, but want to acknowledge that it could have been a 10/10 if the puzzles kept the same quality throughout the game and the story wasn't so disappointing.

Wanda is a beautiful game, there is no doubt about it.  You plays as a robotic survivor of a lonely wasteland. The plot seems like a typical post-apocalyptic game at first, but trust me on this : It get juicy later on. Yeah, Juicy is the word for this game.
What I like about this game is that the entire narrative relies on subtle character animations in the cutscenes. There are no readable dialogues in game, except a few tutorials. Your main protagonist and his cute little buddy only speak in some sort of robotic language. The cutscenes are plentiful and they are all well done, especially the later ones. In fact, the game is 70% cutscenes, telling you a very touching story.  The music in each cutscenes are simply awesome. They are not your usual looping background music. I noticed the music is perfectly timed with the scenes. A perfect fit for the game’s art style and narrative.

The puzzles in the game are well designed. It’s not sophisticated physic puzzles. But rather, very creative wide array of puzzle. You have to disable the force file. Dodge the lighting balls. Use portal guns to create way and at one point, the blue one become tiny to add more flavor in gameplay. They aren’t mind-blowing puzzles but quiet impressive and well made for a game that focuses on story-telling. The game is flexible with puzzle too. You can skip them on repeated failures. A plus point for me.
This game is rather short. But the novelty is strong with this one. Do you enjoy playing unique artistic games with “juicy” narrative that will leave some thoughts for you to ponder even longer after ending credit? If yes, I’d totally recommend this game!

Story: Do not go into this expecting a true sequel. Consider this a spin-off title. There are only two characters from Mafia 2 that are involved or even appear in this game. No links to Mafia 1 whatsoever outside of a mention of Lost Heaven briefly in a mission. As it stands by itself? It's a decent story. A story about a guy needing to avenge his family and the lengths he's willing to go and the demons he's willing to inherit (or defer) to meet those ends. (Though a word to the wise, in the final alteraction, being a pacifist will do nothing for you I proimse. Take the shot, I wish I had. You'll see what I mean.)
Art: The game is visually gorgeous and, after some patching work was done, the lighting seems to have been relatively fixed. If you have the hardware to turn your visuals all the way up, definitely do so. The few lighting issues that do still appear don't last long and they don't impact immersion all that much. The environment is gorgeous and incredibly immersive.
Sound: The music in the game is great and the ambiance in each area is fantastic. You really do get the late 60's feeling of the south. The environmental art works very well in tandem with the ambient noise.
Gameplay: The action and overall gameplay is great but level design in respect to playability is terrible. Mission design is even worse. Every mission is only as open ended as the designers wanted it to be. Trying to sneak into a fort from the complete opposite side of the area in whcih you started the mission is not possible because brush is palced in leiu of a wall to artistically attempt keep with the realism, but to prevent you from going anywhere the designers didn't want you to. Since bushes and plants are used as barriers throughout the bayou region, ALL bushes and plants are cement walls to your car. Do not try to drive your car into a bush, especially at high speeds. You will regret it.
NOTE: For everyone excited at the opportunity to have complete freedom in a game from the Mafia series, tone down your expectations. Your actions seldom matter unless you're explicitly told to make a choice. Stealth runs in missions are completely unacknowledged and your lethality really doesn't determine anything outside of certain key enemies you choose to knock out or kill. I played through an entire mission without even being seen once or even interacting with a single enemy, and when I arrived at my target's location, a rocket launcher was shot at my face and the entire scene erupted into chaos. The cutscene that followed the completion of the level explained that I ran around killing everyone in the building and that I left a "Bloodbath" in my wake. Even though I didn't kill or touch a single enemy outside of my target.
Summary: If you want a truly open-ended crime drama where you get to be the boss, I'd honestly look elswhere. If you're alright with jumping into this and ignoring the illusion of choice this game provides you, then please buy away. The action is great and the story (as a standalone tale) is pretty good for what it is. Just do not try to equate this to Mafia 1 or 2 at all. It's nothing like either (aside from the fact that shotguns are still pretty much nuclear rifles with minimal spread).

Whoa, this game is savage. Completely badass. I cant believe i forgot about this game. I don't see how a single person could give this game a bad review.
Incredible graphics. Even in 2017. It might not be apparent at first, but keep going. Wait till you get to the decrepit/scary back parts of the city with the flooded muddy courtyards. Absolutely badass. I love the detail and all the postprocessing effects used to give the atmosphere a unique tone. i wonder what game engine this game uses because it looks great and runs very smooth as well.
The amount of assets and small little objects used to detail the maps really show that great care went into this games atmosphere. The graphical effects are so creepy at times that It almost feels like a horror game. (And this game is quite old so it goes to show that you dont really need ultra 4K res textures to make a game look great)
And kane and lynch are just a match made in heaven. Freaking obsessed with these guys. The things they say to eachother seem like a pretty damn accurate depicition of what two full grown men would say to eachother in a similarly ♥♥♥♥ed up situation.
**GAMEPLAY**
-Awesome selection of guns that i've never used in video games before.
-Satisfying gun sounds and bullet hitting environment effects
-Surpringly good AI. They will stay aimed at the last position they saw you which is cool for creating diversions or flanking enemies. It's not like most games where the enemies automatically know where you are at all times. Plus enemies advance and retreat accordingly. And hitting them in the body armor stuns them for a bit which is quite realistic.
Gunplay itself is fine. But i can understand why some would find it quite medioce by todays standards. However that is easily overshadowed by the amazing story, action sequences, and most importantly the badass dialogue between kane and lynch.
The gunplay consists of nothing more than firing bullets at your enemies and seeing a small white hitmarker when a shot lands. At first i can see why there are so many negative reviews to the gunplay because the first level gives you these UZI's which are absolute trash and you can barely hit a dude that is 5ft away. This made me think the game had terrible gunplay at first. Worry not..You will be introduced to a quite large selection off off-beat/unusual/unique chinese military and police weapons including sniper rifles, LMG's, Auto-shottys, Grease-gun looking things, desert eagles, etc.
Once you get the hang of the weapons and learn to crouch before firing every shot, then you will really appreciate the gunplay 10x more. I get headshots all the time now. Otherwise for casual players the guns are quite inaccurate and can definately lead to beginner frustration.
There is not much more than shooting however. No grenades, no weapon melee or takedowns, no rocket launchers or grenade launchers to use. The only two kind of cool things are being able to toss explosive gas canisters and shoot them in maidair. The first Kane & Lynch wasn't a very good game. It had bad guns, a broken cover system, and odd design choices, such as putting you through an entire level of combat before the tutorial level. Kane & Lynch 2 isn't
, but fixes some of the problems the first had and manages to be a decent timekiller.
Mechanically, this is your basic, bog-stander cover-based third person shooter. You have guns, you shoot them, you duck behind crates. There really isn't a single mechanic or idea that you wouldn't find in any other game of this genre, and yet it does these things reasonably well. The shooting is satisfying and responsive, the cover system actually works this time around, and the arenas generally give you enough room to maneuver. Cover deteriorates, so you have to keep moving and switching up your strategy, which is good. I found that some encounters seem to rush you just a bit too hard with enemies, but overall there's a good challenge on Normal difficulty. It makes you work to progress, but isn't overly difficult.
The graphics aren't amazing on a technical direction, but I loved the atmosphere and design of the Shanghai environments, and there are some cool stylistic flourishes. The game is supposed to sort of look like a digital camcorder video, so darker areas, and areas with smoke or haze actually have the kind of blocky compression artifacts that you would see on a youtube video. They never have an in-game justification for this and no one is recording anything in the plot, but I thought it looked cool overall.
The plot is really the big weak point. As with the first game, the story is kicked off, and largely progresses, because Kane and Lynch are idiots who do stupid things. This is sometimes called an "idiot plot" because the plot can't happen unless someone violates common sense, and boy to Kane and Lynch do this over and over. The story itself is only vaguely interesting and not very fleshed out, with several scenes ending abruptly and jumping to the a completely different place. There's nothing to really hold your attention either, and the audio mix in several cutscenes is quite poor, so be sure to turn on the subtitles. To say something positive, Kane and Lynch are much more bearable this time around, being less abrasive (and Lynch is on medication now, so he's not quite as unhinged), and they both carry a sense of remorse for some of the things they've done. One upside is that you really don't need to know the events of the first game to get this story, there's really only two brief references to it that aren't plot critical, but overall I just couldn't invest myself in caring about the plight of two nasty idiots who makes things worse for themselves.
The big criticism surrounding this game is that it only lasts about four hours, and at a $60 price point, I can definitely understand being unhappy about that, but I got both games in a combo pack for 6 bucks, and you can get just this game for $2 in the current Summer sale. I think the game's short length is actually a benefit at this price point. I just wanted a short, simple shooter that I could beat in a day because I didn't feel like investing in something longer and this game scratched that itch perfectly. Even though it's not an amazing or particularly creative game, it's still a competently made shooter that's fun enough in the ways I want a shooter to be. It's actually the length that's the main reason I'm reccomending it: Kane & Lynch 2 is the perfect filler game. It gives you a sort of big-budget shooter experience in microcosm, for a very low price. I don't think you should rush out and play it right now, but I think it's worth having this sitting on your Steam account for one of those rainy days where you want to beat something, but don't want to commit 50 hours.

Put over a hundred hours into OMD2. Not a big MOBA person so was a bit worried at first with OMDU.  Survival in OMDU though is awesome.  If you're new to the series and just attack it as a brawler or like a MOBA in Survival, you're in for a rough ride.  But when you get with a group of strangers having to improvise a killbox together, putting all the tricks together (different traps to combo, killing in killbox to combo, creative walling to delay waves on one side so you can rotate over later, etc.) it is awesome.
After getting a perfect score on the hardest difficulty on all the levels in OMD2, I had gotten used to the carefully planned killboxes, knowing exactly what was coming every wave.  With the random minions/doors each wave, the improvisation and cooperation really make OMDU Survival mode a standout.
If you're a MOBA fan, I haven't tried much siege mode as it's not my cup of tea.  I can guarantee that it is different than any other MOBA you've tried. This isn't a LoL/Dota clone.
If you've never tried an OMD game, there's a bit of a learning curve on Survival, but the community is friendly and there's nothing more satisfying than beating an especially hard match.
If you're an OMD1/2 fan, matchmaking will take away a lot of the control you're used to.  You'll also have to be patient about unlocking some of your favorite traps.  Still, the new heroes (omg, all the smolder damage with her unique trap), more traps, more types of enemies and supersize maps make OMDU Survival something special.

A beautiful, charming, and fun "platformer" game... But why the quotation marks?
Most complaints seem to be that it has no real platforming, as it is all done automatically while holding the jump button, and that apparently makes it a bad game because it's not like the games it says it's inspired by.
However, that is pretty much the only thing missing, but even then, it's only a problem if you're closed-minded enough that it stops you from caring about what the game IS.
The world and characters are beautifully colourful and varied. Cartoony looking, and yet still so detailed and smooth. Playing this game is like eating candy with your eyes!
The gameplay is fairly linear and easy, but addictive. While I can appreciate the desire for the accurate platforming of old (I love the PS1-2 classics myself), the auto-jumping helps the game flow nicely, while you focus on exploring, and figuring out how to proceed through obstacles, with occasional small puzzles and alternate paths. There are also multiple collectibles hidden in the levels, which unlock fun little extras, like big head mode, concept art, and more!
The combat, while simple on the surface, grows more complicated and fun as you learn different attacks and powers, and encounter new enemies that require different strategies to defeat.
And finally, the story is light hearted without being childish, yet the theme is deep in ways that are very clear.
So don't focus on what it isn't, look at what it is. When a game is inspired by something, it doesn't need to be 100% like that something in every way in order to be a worthwhile and memorable experience.

I enjoyed this game and will come back to it to finish. I have made it far enough into the game to feel I would comfortably recommend this game. It's a fairly inexpensive title which I wasn't sure about in the beginning. It feels like a Jack and Daxter as far as the silent protagonist, loud mouthed best friend, colorful levels, and quirky supporting characters. However, it's sort of a platformer with no controlled jump and Arkham Asylum style combat. This makes for more of a beat em up with a few flaws but overall a quirky story, solid combat, and a fun world.
Graphics: They set out to create a specific style and succeeded beautifully. For the overall aesthetic, they nailed it. Everything looks like it's painted and when the world starts going "bleak", the lack of colors is very apparent. As you take damage, you seem to be drained of color which is a nice effect. The speech bubbles are actually cut out signs on cardboard which are only written on the front of. I do have a problem with the speech bubbles, as fitting as they are. Sometimes, they don't appear until you are right next to a character. They are large enough that I find myself having to move the camera to read them. This could have been corrected by making them pop up a bit further out, but then it wouldn't feel like the characters were talking to you. Overall, it's my only gripe about the graphical presentation.
Music: This soundtrack is amazing. From the stealth areas where the music changes dynamically when guards are getting closer to you to the standard area themes being unique and fitting. The music you get on the farm feels very twangy and laid back while the combat music is more up beat and intense. Every area's music is not only appropriate, but also something I would go out of my way to find and listen to while relaxing at home. It's a stellar example of matching the visual aesthetic to the auditory aesthetic.
Gameplay: The game offers a variety of difficulties without forcing you to unlock them which seems less common these days and I am glad to see it. The difficulties range from Kid, where most attacks are one hit kills, to One Hit Death, where every hit you take kills you and HP means nothing. That being said, all the difficulties seem to be arbitrary increase in damage against you and damage enemies take. There are no AI modifications or spawn rate modifications which I noticed. The AI, in general, is very basic, but this is not a bad thing. Each monster acts it's own way and never react based on other monster's movement. It's a very NES/SNES style of programming AI. The smaller melee guys just rush you. The larger AI guys rush you. The ranged guys stay ranged and never move. The shield guys disappear and reappear waiting for you to stun them. No monster will surprise you by doing something you don't expect. But it works Trying to time your attacks so you hit the small guys, dodge the big guys, ranged attack the ranged guys, it all adds to that chaos that made those earlier games fun. The issue I have is the checkpoint system. It doesn't maintain a state that the game is in, merely a respawn point. What this means is, if you are in a particularly nasty fight, you can run in and kill as many guys as you can until you die, respawn near by, run back in and the only monsters there are the remaining monsters of that wave. Every fight can be done like this, including boss fights as far as I can tell. There are no numbered lives so there is no way to lose the game. As far as the platforming with no jump button, it works. There is a run button. If you are holding it and you reach a ledge with something you can jump to, it will jump. They work in a lot of timing systems into when to progress to the next platform and when to stay back. With ranged enemies covering these platforms, sometimes you find yourself bouncing from one platform to the next and back again while waiting for another platform to come up and trying to not get hit by the ranged guy. The challenge is there if there was an actual reason not to die.
Overall: I really do like this game and would recommend it, if only as an example of a game with a fully fleshed out concept. My issues are generally surface level. It could use a life system or a full respawn of enemies on death. As it stands, maybe playing it on One Hit Death can serve some challenge, but I see it ending up as more of a test in ones patience, really. Ultimately, a fun experience, albeit an easy one.

Edit: I've officially beaten this game and am happy to say I stand by my review. It held up through the end. Definitely pick it up if you enjoy the AC: Syndicate style of gameplay. If you have questions/concerns, wait for a 50% off sale and grab it 7.8/10.
24 hours in and still going. I feel comfortable giving a review on this game now.
This, as you've probably heard, isn't going to be for everyone. It's not a successor to Mafia 2. It's nothing like Mafia.
After one of the best intros in recent gaming memory (the first 5 hours are really incredible from a tone and storytelling perspective) Mafia 3 settles into an AC: Syndicate type of pattern: kill baddies, capture territory. You'll be fighting everyone from the KKK to street racers. In between all of that you'll get elaborate boss fights. Those are a lot of fun, from shooting it out with the italian mafia while Johnny Cash plays as the soundtrack to taking down a klan rally, it's all really well done.
Your mileage may vary. Some find this stuff repetitive. And to be fair, it is. But it is always fun for me. Sneaking into bases with silenced hardware and taking down the enemy without raising an alarm is a challenge and a rush. There are some really tight shooting mechanics on display here, and the physics from the bullet hits are satisfying; there are also some brutal takedowns with the combat knife (though, you can choose non lethal takedowns too).
As you've probably heard, this game isn't that well optimized. I'm happy to report that in 24 hours of gameplay, I've only had one crash. I also get 40-50 fps on medium settings (with a few high) depending on where I am and what I'm doing. I'm playing on a GTX 960 with an i5 and 8gb of RAM. I know that there are those with much better rigs than me getting much poorer performance. All I can say to that is that this game remains a crap shoot. You're rolling the dice. It may work well for you and it may not. Luckily there is the two hour return policy on Steam for just that reason and that's more than enough time to figure out how it's going to pan out.
The graphics in this game range from beautiful to ugly. Just depends where you are and at what time of day. The skyboxes are hilarious and sometimes when the sun rises it looks like a nuclear bomb is going off 3 feet from your face. Really wonky stuff here and there.
I'm reccomending this game because I am enjoying myself, a lot. Like I said, the shooting mechanics are really tight. I enjoy the AC: Syndicate style of gameplay. The writing is really well done, with great voice work. The boss fights are awesome. Oh, and the soundtrack is my favorite in any open world game ever--sometimes I'll just sit on the menu screen and let All Along the Watchtower play.
Anyway, I hope this review helps some of you make up your mind one way or the other.

When I first saw videos for Spintires back when it was Early Access I assumed this was similar to the Farming Simulator 2015 games that you just drive farm equipment around and do meaningless tasks.  Then when I read that the point of the game is to drive around and haul logs I thought "this game can't be that fun..."
It turns out after purchasing it I found myself stuck playing it for a few hours at a time.  Something about driving big, dirty, smoke-bellowing, diesel trucks through mud is entertaining.  The trucks look amazing, and there are some crash physics for when you rub against a tree or a large rock and watch the bumpers bend permanantly.  The mud and water physics aren't perfect, but they look absolutely amazing for a video game.  Sometimes it feels like you are watching a video of an actual truck.
The lighting can be goofy and I find it's defintely easier to drive in the dark with the headlights off than with them on, which limits the view to only the cone in front of you.  But for as generic as the gameplay seems, it definately keeps you entertained for a while.
My first time trying multiplayer mode was a complete blast.  Having to help tow your friends out of a mud bog was hilariously fun.  I have many screen shots of flipped over trucks with my friends' names hoving above them.
The game is still a work in progress, but I have thouroughly enjoyed my purchase of this game.

What happens if you mix peaceful exploration like in ABZÛ with a large pixel, minimalist style? You get AER Memories of Old. The Steam debut for developer, Forgotten Key and an enjoyable experience for gamers of all ages. Daedalic Entertainment is the game’s publisher and they confirm that aerial-based adventures are their hallmark, so to speak. Part of the Deponia series or not, AER represents an adventure, first and foremost.
While it’s never fleshed out as much as I would have preferred, AER Memories of Old has a unique story of its own and since it’s a narrative-driven experience, the game trades replay value for a compelling albeit somewhat restricted tale. Why do I consider it so? Well for one, the female protagonist is not properly introduced nor does she have a lot of NPCs to interact with. Auk is a shapeshifter, the last of her kind and she must undertake a pilgrimage that will culminate in the banishing of an evil entitiy that has lingered for far too long within the fractured fantasy realm known as the Land of Gods. The Void, as its name may suggest, seeks to destroy everything in its path. It was defeated once, but apparently it is in resurgence thus sparking the selfless quest on which Auk has embarked.
Auk may change her form at will and turn into a bird which may or may not be an eagle. Regardless of that insignificant detail, she’s not a bird of prey. There is no violence depicted in AER and I honestly didn’t miss this feature one bit. It’s not like you won’t find a violent video game on Steam within several seconds of browsing your library or the Store. The lack of a challenge through conventional foes however, is felt and may prove to be the one element that will feel amiss in an otherwise consistent gameplay. No sense of urgency and by no means, can players fail in their mission or get hindered by in-game “deaths”. Falling or flying from the invisible barriers within Land of Gods, simply transports Auk back to the last “nesting” place unlocked during the current region she’s visiting. Basically, autosave points which are well distributed across the map.
There are few characters or creatures and even fewer enemies, yet the gliding/flying mechanics which take island hopping to a whole new level, will surely compensate for the lack of a proper threat and an antagonist worthy of Auk’s efforts to restore her homeworld to its former glory. Esentially still a linear story (imposed by its objectives), AER Memories of Old at least offers players, the freedom of choosing which task to tackle with at first and the fairly large map is opened to exploration within 10 minutes of starting a new game. You can’t really restrict a game about flight in this day and age and there are obviously, no time constraints either or an impending doom that might force you to rush at any point. Feel free to dash through the clouds and visit every single floating island. No matter how small, there’s usually something to see, everywhere you look and the game encourages thinking outside the box.
In more ways than one, AER Memories of Old reminded me of a game I had reviewed one year ago. Windscape has no flying around or the smooth gameplay found in AER, but the visuals on both titles are proof that “less is more” can be applied in gaming as well. And they’re both powered by the Unity Engine, if it has any importance to you. In my case, it does. It almost guarantees flawless stability even on 4K resolution and AER has not disappointed in this regard. Or at all, to be perfectly honest. No glitches whatsoever, nor frame rate drops or any crashes to desktop. I took over 100 screenshots and most of them have been posted on Steam as well. It goes without saying that I’d never link so many to my Steam profile, unless I thoroughly enjoyed what I was seeing.
With Vsync enabled, it never strayed from 60fps even by a single digit. Sure, you’ll probably point out that the textures themselves can’t put a strain even on older PCs out there. I wouldn’t call that a disadvantage or claim that anything other than the most detailed and crisp textures might affect my keen eyes. No, most indie titles make good use of minimal visuals and I wouldn’t have them any other way. If you want eye popping and hardware punishing visuals, Skyrim mods are just around the corner. Including a low-poly version that’s guaranteed to run the game even on a smarthphone (if only). AER still looks better than that one.
With no voice acting at all, AER had to focus on its soundtrack and while the songs were just as relaxing as the gameplay, they didn’t stand out in a particular manner. Still, I have to admit that not all stories need a voice or more. It didn’t bother me that I had to just read dialogue boxes. Overall, it was a pleasant set of sounds that never hindered nor improved the storyline.

Yes, with no threat at all and a big baddie that barely shows itself, Auk has all the time in her world to explore and fly in every direction and corner of the map. Apart from unlocking new Steam Achievements as you discover hidden symbols and creatures across the smaller floating islands, you’ll also have a chance to get acquainted with the mythology behind the story, as you read from scrolls and also interact with a select few, talking animals. As already mentioned, ABZÛ and AER share at least some common elements. They both unravel tales relating to Atlantis counterparts. While the former takes this quite literally, the latter features an archipelago suspend forever among the clouds.
Divided into several regions, each with its distinct topography and climate, AER Memories of Old will certainly keep most players entertained and on the lookout for new clues while in search of salvation for the nearly abandoned world. What I didn’t really appreciate is how abruptly it all ends, without the proper closure or even giving players the option to keep flying and witnessing for themselves, how defeating The Void has now freed Land of Gods from any signs of taint and destruction. So no particular replay value and an ending that seemed rather rushed. Just take my advice and search every nook & cranny before commiting to the main quest which will have you exploring the entire map anyways.
I wouldn’t consider it a cliffhanger type, but it may leave room to interpretation and perhaps, even a sequel one day. it's not like I would mind playing an AER 2, of that much I'm certain. Such relaxing titles that don’t require players to kill or harm anyone or anything, are a niche genre which is surely needed in gaming. The ultimate goal of defeating evil, musn’t always entail or enforce the use of similar, underhanded measures as the antagonists had no moral qualms about. An excellent debut, Forgotten Key!

I was interested in playing this game for two reasons initially: 1) I really enjoyed playing Kairo (also made by Richard Perrin, creator of Journal), and 2) I found the way in which the protagonist was being negatively described in various reviews to be intriguing. More often than not, I enjoy games in which I cannot fully sympathize with the main character because it helps you to understand things from new and unique perspectives. That being said, due to my own life experiences I was actually able to empathize with the character in this game in some respects,  which actually  made my experience all the more personal. This is a fantastic game, deeper than most.
The game reminds me of interactive fiction, in a lot of ways. It's telling a story, a very complex one, using both stunning visuals, beautiful music and powerful written word. But unlike a typical visual novel, this game allows for freedom of movement within the world of Journal and more variance in choice of responses. The main story is juxtaposed perfectly along with a shadow puppet play which acts as a sort of philosophical intermission between chapters.  There is a sense of doom lingering throughout the game that hints toward something tragic, which is also expressed via a gradual shift and general sense of unease in the atmosphere and setting of the game.  Nothing you do changes the outcome, however, and this was the hardest thing for me to accept. Nothing leading up to the end can truly prepare you for it, and it's quite a heavy conclusion to deal with.
I can see why some people might view the main character in this game in a negative way. She's young, has been through a lot, and makes many mistakes. But she's trying to come to terms with it all, and you are right there with her the whole time. None of the mistakes I mentioned can really be prevented by you, although you can gently guide the main character into more apologetic or thoughtful responses. Sometimes it's truly painful and cringeworthy to witness the main character going through such turmoil or causing it, but it's that brutal honesty that makes the game what it is. Journal is a journey, a dreamlike one that slowly transforms into a nightmare right before your very eyes.

A modern Myst quality game, with Myst-level difficulty and length (or maybe slightly easier). Worth the purchase. I never felt like I was lost or mislead, never felt like I was stumped or stuck, but I did have to spend a little time on each puzzle 'puzzling' out how to get to the right answer.
An in-game note-taking feature is provided right around the same time you need to have one. Regarding the puzzles themselves, they're a bit reliant on 'find object, use object in proper location' in many places, and others require you to run across the island for 10 seconds to go grab some other item, etc, but the true 'puzzle' puzzles are good quality without being overly difficult. I did feel like I brute-forced one, and stumbled through another rather quickly.
The game is easier the more you pay attention to things in the game. The entire 'story' is that nearly every puzzle is intentionally designed by someone who wants you to solve it, so there is always an answer to be found or puzzled out.
The voice acting is indie-quality (which means that it works, is functional, isn't terrible, but you're not getting Nolan North or Jennifer Hale). Graphics are pretty to look at. Sound is good. The soundtrack is nice background music, but nothing to write home about. A very solid, indie title.
A nice little diversion for 8+ hours if you're a puzzle game veteran or enjoy those 'escape the room' games. However, be sure to check the length of time others played the game and compare to my time, as a person who was watching me play the last hour commented that he was 'surprised how fast I was solving the puzzles at the end', so I may have a more puzzle-oriented mind than most.
One of the hours on my 9.1 hour record MIGHT have been spent AFK with my girlfriend, so I think it was mostly a 8 hour game for me.

Everyone who has played them looks back at Myst and Riven with nothing but positive memories, because they were outstanding games. I didn't hear anything about Quern before, it popped up in the puzzle section of Steam as a game similiar to Myst and Riven, so I checked it out, read some reviews and finally bought it during the sale. Looking back I didn't have to wait for a sale because this game is absolutely worth it's base price.
Quern has everything you would want from a spiritual successor to Riven in particular. Alone on an abandoned island? Check. Having no idea at all how it came to this or what to do? Check. A mixture of tribal buildings and stuff and steampunky machinery? Check. The satisfaction of finally figuring out a puzzle and being able to advance? Check.
Some puzzles may be a bit tedius, others may be a bit hard to find the solution for, but that's really like 3 out of 100 puzzle moments. I also would have liked some kind of hint catalogue like you have for the Myst games to give you a little push towards the right solution, at the moment you can only inspect the items you have on you what can give you an idea at some occasions though.
The graphics are also very well done, you can adjust the settings during the game and see the result instantly and it looks really beautiful.
All in all a clear recommendation. Play!

The Last Tinker: City of Colors is a character action platformer with light puzzle elements. You play as a totally adorable monkey.
The city you explore is wildly colorful and vastly vibrant. This is game developed by a small team and is styled in the vain of older style platformers such as Banjo Kazooie. While exploring and traversing the main areas the game does not actually have a jump button. Its more of a run at the ledge and it'll auto jump. Mildly Zelda-esk. And because of that it makes me a feel a little weird calling it a platformer however it's still relatively apt.
This is a nice little casual game with a lot of character. Each area of the city and its citizens has a specific color that represents an emotion. The issue is some of the colors are absent and everyone is getting a little too into their own color. Its up to you to bring back balance.
The puzzles are not terribly difficult, nor is the platforming. The combat is little shallow but there are upgrades to give it a little zest to keep it from becoming tedious.
All in all, a very nice short fun casual game great for that time in between larger more intricate titles.

A long winded approach - as usual - but this demands a special space. Read on.
In a reasonably detailed response to a query I posed at the forums the dev (Lee Bamber, a 20 year veteran) listed his intentions, his ideas and his dreams. But he was rather non-committal to a time-frame or even to what will be in the final package.
You might ask, is this a good thing? I'd have to answer yes, absolutely.
Let me explain.
No. There's no dot point roadmap that will promise Feature X by Date Y so if that's what you expect (what we might ALL expect from an Early Access project) then walk away now.
Yes. Early Access projects require input from users and in this you have a receptive and responsive dev who is NOT locked in. In my view, any potential developer who wants a rapid development environment - almost custom made -  would see the advantage of this.
Very easy. A bit boxy when you try to get very smooth edging but overall, simple with a free flight mode down to a reasonably small resolution. A nice feature is doing a walkthrough (or a fly through) and being able to to move a rock, turn a tree or flatten a mound or hill on-the-fly. No possibility of dynamic maps although I've heard hints there might be. (It's obviously coded because a random map generator is available via the IDE for some mountainous terrain - that needs smoothing.)
Easy enough but lacks fidelity. 4 brushes in total and grass. If I want a desert savannah with dry grass and rolling hills with lush vegetation on the same map, it's not going to happen. Some great terrain assets are available at a good price but it's all or nothing with each package, not mix and match. Ultimately your level designs are based around what is possible - not on what you want.
LOTS of options here. Not entirely optimised for performance as it stands but bloom, fog, ambience, surface and colouration (restricted to 1-100% rather than 255 but that may appeal to you). It's easily configured with easy to use sliders giving an RT view of how you want everything to look. Combined with lots of nice included and purchasable skyboxes, THAT look is right there.
I'm still fiddling with atmosphere and day/night scripts and have a couple of issues with light source positioning but it appears (at this stage) that it will do the job. Some scipts are already available for environmental effects although rain etc. is not available yet (that I could find).
There's a nice music engine scoped in but simplified access is a bit limited atm. It's easy enough (with some basic maths) to get cued ambience/background music fades across a range of tracks and it's all easily triggered via zones or objects or even scripted events etc.
Media zones can be used to trigger effects, music shorts or even videos. They lack some of the tweaking options you might want but again, based on what is available (but not "available") this will be easily done. Scripting events is my prefered option anyway rather than a canned stepping plate. In short, it caters for all.
LUA. (aren't they all?) No integrated environment but it's not a major issue as most coders have a preferred IDE. To link an entity to a script is a 2 second job via the entity properties.
I have had some real issues with having scripts triggered by zones stopping when out of range. It's easily worked around by applying the script to an object using the  "always active" option. If this were applied to zones...
Another issue for those who prefer tight access to what's being run. If you put down 20 objects with the same script attached, that code will run 20 times and you really need to have your head around this because debug can be a real nightmare. Half your time will be spent writing detection/stop flags (and debug dumps to find out wtf is going on!).
For those wanting a linear, call on demand approach... Wait some or get down and dirty. Coding can be fun right?
A more serious issue is no ability to dynamic reference map entities. I'm positive it's coming. The demand is high and no dev could possibly ignore the cries for addressing via name reference. (Lee, are you there Lee?)
Short answer. Throw it out and code your own from scratch. The tools to address characters are powerful enough to really have fun with this but what is currently available is not going to interest any SP FPS game developer much. It's predictable, mundane, stilted and well.... awful. If you just want a plug and play zombie (literally and figuratively) then it's good enough.
Waypoints, while available are a bit off. No circular patrol. Start, get to end, turn around and retread same path. Fixable? Probably, I haven't spent much time bothering tbh.
Do you know a good modeller/animator? In fairness, give it time.
Note that this is based around CURRENT, not potential, so it's subject to change.
2D Platformer? Nope. This is 3D :)
FPS MP shooter where you and a heap of mates can frag each other all day without all the BS? THIS is a must. You'll love how fast you can do this. With a bunch of different quality weapons available as included assets and/or store assets you get lots of choice. MP access needs some love (that will come). Make a map, throw around some trees, buildings, blinds, towers etc. and bingo. If you're conversant with IDE we're talking a solid day at the keyboard. 2 at the most. You'll be the toast of the town.
Want an RPG/Puzzler? Quite probable at this stage but you're going to have to get your hands dirty in code. It doesn't seem to be a big priority (by choice or development stage?). The tools are there and good scripting fills the gaps but AI, current characters etc. mean a very lonely trip. If you know a good modeller and animator and you're a good coder or visa vie? THIS will do the job. At worst it will make an excellent world concept test platform because it's so quick to hack something together.
Survival genre? I doubt it. Moving, building, rotating etc, although scriptable is a PITA. It's simple enough to create environmental effects and food/drink scripts etc. but with no terrain destruction the inevitable mine, gravel pit and towering 5 story castle is just not there. Will it come? I don't know. See my comments re: roadmap above.
Kids games? A few more assets of a "cartoony" nature would be fun. I've already done a couple of collecting and shoot-em-up hacks with mushrooms and rabbits for my kids and everytime I hear the bouncy soundtracks I made to go with them, well, I smile to myself. Having someone play your game - by choice - is a great feeling.
..oo00oo..
In summary, given that the passion for this by the dev is tangible, the support excellent and the open scoped project feel to this is actually a positive aspect.

This game partially restored my faith in the video game industry.
For some time, the video game industry has been churning out games plagued by the effects of operant conditioning, where the player is metaphorically pecking a button to get some corn over and over again. First-person shooters flashing numbers on your screen telling you how many points you got for that l33t 720 noscope; multiplayer games with loot boxes begging you to crack open a box and get that instant-gratification; that next turn button sitting down there in the corner that you just gotta hit one more time; Setting off into the world of an MMO, not because you want to experience the world, but because you need to kill 10 boars, gather 12 apples, deliver a letter, and because you can turn all these quests in at once to get those juicy experience points in the least amount of time. Why bother experiencing a game when you can just accomplish short-term goals to get rewards?
AER Memories of Old is a game this industry needed, and this industry needs more games like it. The entire premise of the game is pure exploration. Not subjugating other people in PvP, not winning a round, not reaching a level cap, not making a lot of in-game currency - just exploration. The game has a story, it has an end-goal, it even has some puzzle elements, but all of these things are secondary to the concept of exploring this beautiful world the developers have created for us, and you use exploration to experience the aforementioned elements. Developers need to learn from this game and design their games around making the game good as opposed to just keeping the player's attention.
As said, the game is about exploration. The player will be able to do this as a human, or as a bird, switching back and forth at any time, unless you're indoors. You can't use bird form indoors. Luckily, this restriction was only put in place for the sake of solving the minor puzzles as a human. Honestly, I was almost never tempted to use my bird form indoors, so it didn't get in the way, especially since I spent almost all my indoor-time at a walking pace, only running normal-speed when a certain puzzle eroded my patience away. Most of your time is spent outdoors anyway. The transition between human and bird form is smooth, as is pretty much everything else in this game, and the flight mechanics are great. Pressing the jump button while airborne transitions you into bird form, the X button is to flap your wings (Which simply increases your speed), the triggers are for yawing left/right, and you can airbrake by holding them both at once. I don't want to go over too much because this game is best experienced first hand.
The only shortcomings this game had was its lack of a toggle walk button, and puzzles. A game like this — a game about taking in the world and stopping to smell the roses — needs a way to lock your character to a walking pace. Luckily, there is controller support, so walking is at least possible. I used an X-Box 360 controller and just tilted the thumbstick halfway to walk instead of run. It was a bit of an inconvenience, but it was doable and it's mostly a knitpick. As for the puzzles, this game didn't need puzzles. I was actually disappointed when I realized there were puzzles in the game. They're not hard puzzles, just inconvenient. I don't want to be focused on puzzle-solving when I would rather be focusing on taking in the atmosphere and appreciating the world.
As for whether or not I would recommend this game to someone, it depends. If you're an art enthusiast, an escapist, or like exploring, I can definitely recommend this game to you. If you're one of those people that eat up games like the ones mentioned in the first paragraph after the heading, this game probably isn't for you and I can't recommend that you buy it. Looking at the few negative reviews attached to this game, I can say with confidence that those people just missed the point of the game.
I have my entire playthrough saved as a Twitch highlight, so that can give you a better idea on how the game looks and plays. Don't worry, I don't ruin the recording by talking over it or anything. Obviously, there will be spoilers starting an hour or two in, so try sticking to the earlier parts.
This game now stands alongside Witcher 3 and Stardew Valley in that I'm glad I paid full-price for it because the developer deserved my money.

If quality was measured by potential then Alan Wake would be a great game.
Unfortunately, an interesting premise is held back by poor voice acting and character models, repetitive gameplay with interesting set pieces few and far between sitting uncomfortably amongst clunky controls and movement.
The story itself would have been this game's saving grace had it decided whether to be as hoaky as its Twin Peaks inspiration or as serious as it tries to be. It sadly can't seem to pick either one. It has a hard time balancing Alan Wake's personal dilemmas, his marriage and struggle with fame as well as the aligorical battle against darkness for his wife throughout the game, and the ridiculously cringey set of supporting characters within the unbelievably lame and uninspired setting of Bright Falls. Where Alan Wake, despite being horrendously voice acted, is a serious protagonist I actually found myself routing for with a surprising level of developing complexity as the story unfolds, the characters alongside him are such exaggerated archetypes who are crudely surface level individuals with little-to-no character evolution. The story has some interesting minor twists but nothing mind blowing and the resolution ultimately means nothing due to the 'special feature' levels offering a soft ending tacked onto the original.
Gameplay-wise, it's quite odd to see the design fundamentals of Max Payne 1 and 2, Remedy's previous defining masterpieces, thrown out of the window despite them actually being ideas that would have greatly helped this game avoid being a tedious bore throughout. The Max Payne games emphasized freedom of movement and fluid controls. Alan Wake implements the very opposite of that and not in a 'wow the low stamina and snail's-pace movement and aiming is really immersive and interesting' kind of way. Resident Evil is a series that does slow clunkiness well. Alan Wake is a clunky game made by masters who have show cased their fluent understanding of fluidity and speed, resulting in a game that just doesn't feel like it's hitting the right notes in regards to movement and shooting mechanics as it doesn't seem to be the developers forte. I'm not saying it should have been a Max Payne set in a forest type game but it would have benefitted the gameplay had they taken some of the fundamentals used to make the gameplay in Max Payne fun and implemented them here. The 'fight with light mechanic' is actually quite neat and the aid of torches, flairs and even flashbangs help add dynamic to each fight but these are items that don't really help that much due to either their scarcity (specifically flashbangs) or due to the fact that they really aren't that necessary as each encounter is easy to blitz through, resulting in a stockpile of items that make later encounters even easier until the game strips them from you. That being said though, it was a neat idea that might have carried this game had it been less of a gimmick.
Level design is okay, sometimes interesting but mostly okay. Two standout moments, the stage on the farm section and the battle through Bright Falls all the way to the chopper with the sheriff are thoroughly enjoyable. Other than that you'll just be getting your fair share of trees and lumber lodges with groups of enemies lazily sprinkled here and there. In terms of level progression and pacing, it's all over the place. The final level prior to the 'special feature' levels is just god awful and boring. Excessively long driving sections and on foot sections devoid of moments do little to propel the player towards their final goal. This is odd because the game actually does a good job of building up pace towards the end. The fight through Bright Falls, the rendezvous with the sheriff and Barry after the helicopter crash. It did help me find some motivation to fight through the final moments. Which is why it's so puzzling that the end level is just mind-numbingly boring, especially it's first half being the very definition of 'there can't possibly be more of this driving section' followed by 'yes there is way, WAY more of this driving section.'
Enemy design isn't that interesting: Regular grunts, speedy grunts, projectile grunts and grunts who take more damage. The boss fights are against possessed utility vehicles and it's as interesting and engaging as it sounds. It isn't a hard game in terms of combat, at least when you're kitted out properly, in which case it's a cake walk. There just isn't the same kind of dynamic in the combat scenarios that Remedy are known for with their prior games. Go here, combat, go a little further, combat, further, combat. There aren't a variety of memorable moments. The only scenarios I found the game to be difficult, and in some part quite cheap, is when enemies creep up behind you and knock you around with a two or three hit combo, dicing off most of your health after the camera pans towards an enemy in the opposite direction. This, paired with the moments where random objects hurl themselves at you in quick succession can grate your nerves. Other than that the walking simulator that this game tends to be is just a boring jog through the forest. (Also as an inactive geek even I could sprint faster and longer than Alan Wake does my god is he a cardio disaster.)
Visually the game isn't too bad but then again how far wrong can you go with dirt paths and copy pasted trees. Every now and then you do get a nice look at the mountain range and the flickers of light that dot the levels. The character models aren't great and lack any emotive ability. Facial animations and body expression are extremely weak here. This would have been ok if games like Half-Life haven't highlighted the effectiveness of such methods years ago.
Overall - it's a shame that Remedy hasn't put out anything worth the kind of attention Max Payne 1 and 2 received when they came out. This could have been just as good if not better. Cheap on the grey market or steer clear of this entirely, when there are other games that nail what Alan Wake tries to do, it isn't even worth scouring key resellers to hunt down what is essentially a brain melting walking simulator.

The game is like a nice, cool breeze during a hot summerday. It invites you to take a deep breath and relax, read some, explore and just enjoy a while. While it does that it also tells us a story of a dying world. The ambience on the game reminds me of Shadow of the Colossus - how quiet the world is and how there are traces of civilizations long gone, with nothing else left than memories and scrolls to tell the tale. Simplistic, yet beautiful graphics support the unique feeling the game has, and there is a lot of diversity between different islands - snowy landscapes were my favourite with their little stars and heavy snowstorm.
This is not meant for players who like to achieve a lot and proceed through games quickly with adrenaline pumping through their veins. It's for players who like to take their time, enjoy little nyances the game offers and just relax.

This is my very first review on Steam and, unfortunately, I will not recommend to buy this game. I purchased the game some time ago but I had problems with my NVidia + Linux combo until a few days ago when I updated my drivers. The first experience of going through a training is pretty OK-ish, but when it comes to the multiplayer, the game can be thrown away.
Constant timeout errors prevented me from connecting to ANY of the game servers. I have NEVER had any problems with OTHER online games. This game requires a VERY SPECIAL treatment for the multiplayer to work. I am not kidding here, the official support forum actually has quite a lot of posts on how to tune/configure your routers to be able to play this game. Have you ever seen anything like that? You need to configure your router to be abler to play a game (i.e., to workaround problems of poor software design and implementation of the multiplayer components of the game).
Considering that the multiplayer is the main backbone and the main problem of this game, I can say - this game is unplayable. Considering the size of the NS2 dev team (9 ppl), the amount of patches (200+) they delivered on Steam and the fact that the problem is still (after several years) not resolved, I can say - the problem will not be resolved (i.e., it will require resources that the dev team does not have since they already in the maintenance mode and money are not coming anymore).
To summarize: the game is broken, dead and abandoned. Do not buy it.

The progression system of the game which involves getting random crafting materials which you can get when a match ends for PvP, or during and after the match for anything that isn't against other people, is a bit... hard to really track how much better you're doing or progressing.
Most of the stuff for the more interesting traps/heros is stuck at high amounts of rare resources so atop of them having a low drop rate in general, there's also a low rate dropped any time they actually are recived which causes a 'you have to get lucky on a possibly 40 outcome dice roll to get an item you want then get it in a 'higher' amount'
Instead of the old progression of doing levels, then occasionally getting a new trap, most of the classic traps are given to you then the mid-tier traps from the previous game have to be made, along with what i think are new traps which are much harder to craft. You can get randomly a trap/various things to help you in the game, premade at random but the odds seem to be inherintly low.
The game is still good for a time killer when you and a friend want to murder orks, though survival is not 'up to 5 players' but is 5 players which means you'll get somewhat cramped trying to build traps coherintly and someone will run by and throw down something in the way thinking they're helping. The campain which is somewhat hidden in the menus will allow you to do 1 to 5 people but the way the game works on it's strange mixture of leveling system means that you actually have to have a hero that is near the same level to do decently enough, along with the fact that the game assumes you'll be running 3-5 people some of the maps will have 4 lanes that need to be defended at once which leads to what I personally dislike the most about the game.
Traps don't do as much damage and arn't as generally effective from the other games, heros are much more of a prominate feature and are the bigger focus. Heros have their own prebuilt abilities and specials along with a 'iconic trap' that you always have for playing them, so instead of OMD2 where you played more for a main weapon, you more play for a set of abilities or type. Such as tanky, higher damage, and such. In PvE type activities you're mostly just going to be hitting mobs and letting traps help damage unless you manage to make a very good kill box that will typically kill the spamy enemies but won't really stop anything heavty from walking through.
While I don't enjoy PvP based games I am at least happy with the fact that it's doing it's own  thing, and isn't just going to copy leauge/dota type of play with there being three lanes and such. Instead there's three roles, which all get tiny bonuses, defense/attackers/pliagers. Which pilagers are really just junglers with a different name, though instead of attacking neautral camps of creatures it's mostly helping out attackers and defenders. While people can have a role you arn't locked into it, you can go anywhere you want on the map and do generally whatever you want but you get benefits to doing what your roll claim is, i'd go into more detail but the tutorial does a good enough job at explaining it. If you like mobas but dislike the sameness they get, there is at least an interesting difference in the map setting and how the 'tower defence+attacking' mixes.
Want to kill orks with friends and not care about what happens, try it out
Going to be mad that the progression system in a f2p game encourages people to spend real money to get shortcuts and claim it's pay to win when it's almost entirely pay to skip grind and get things that people won't really know/have counter things, don't try it out
Honestly I find the mixture of trying to keep the game's PvE and PvP system close as possible together neat, but it does mean that throwing 99 dollars into it to buy like 20 things that can be hard for people who are new to the game... My recomendation is to basically do PvE for the most part unless you want to try PvP and go in knowing that people might have bought their way into systems they know and understand.

If you're looking for a chill experience while being bundled up in your bed, this game might just do the trick. It takes aproximately 2 hours, and it's a quite interesting experience. I wouldn't recommend it to anyone, but I would recommend it to ME so I guess that's what this is all about in the end, right?
The graphics are enjoyable, I loved how everything remembered me somehow of the little town I grew up in. You start by being a quite forgetful young lady, in highschool, not knowing what she said a few days back and most of the times being an annoying little brat. I didn't like the main character specifically, but it turns out she was actually having a lot of STUFF going on. While you talk to your friends and family, things seem to unravel and you get some clues that there may be more to this story. You hear that something's wrong, but WHAT is it?
There is actually a story-within-a-story too, as between chapters you get small bits of the life in a carnival,  that will tie all the loose ends in the final chapter.
The music is pretty enjoyable, and the whole game has an "old" feeling to it, like something happened in those days you weren't born, but you see on postcards in your parent's keepsake drawer.
The only thing I would've wanted is more voice-overs, as only the girl's monologue is actually spoken, the rest is written.
This game does go into that niche, weird, hipster game zone, maybe more than other indie games. But I really enjoyed it, and I hope you will too. P.S. I wouldn't pay 10 euros for it, but 5 and less are an ok price.

This game is a masterpiece and I cannot recommend it enough. I was mostly drawn to this game due to the artistic style, and that certainly didn't disappoint. Journal has an aesthetic that I've never really seen anywhere else, and it makes good use of it throughout.
While I came for the aesthetic, I stayed for Journal's narrative and writing. It's a game where the character you play as is an actual character: she does things you don't want her to do, she says things you don't want her to say, and she keeps secrets from you. Constantly. It also is a game about choice, but also not. It's really just a game about life and living and how consequences will always be there, no matter how hard you try to outrun them or erase them.
Journal is, at its essence, about the human experience of storytelling. It's about the stories we tell ourselves about ourselves to try and make sense of ourselves, our worlds, and our lives.

This game was actually somewhat frustrating for me to play. Maybe this experience is my own, and nobody else has had any of these problems, but I felt that I should share nonetheless. The story is definitely the most appealing part of the game, but the design behind it is really lacking. Most of it is played through text, and sometimes you'll have to respond to what people have to say. You'll normally be given a couple of choices. Sometimes it's hard to know what choice you pick is going to result in what actually happens. The options are sometimes just vague one word descriptors, and aren't the easiest to follow as to what your character is going to do or say next. This isn't like Mass Effect where it'll give you a diagrahm showcasing which ones are your good and bad choices, which makes it a lot easier to know which route your going in the game. Instead, the options in this game are placed right next to each other with no kind of color indication or anything to specify which one's your 'good' choice, and which one's your 'bad' choice. Maybe I'm just spoiled by how other games have designed their games, but it felt like there could have bee some kind of implementation of that in this.
This game also has its fair share of backtracking. You have to talk to everyone (or at least it feels like you have to talk to everyone) if you want to advance the game, and sometimes if you do things out of order (like I guess I must have done...?) then this results in you going around and talking to EVERYBODY AGAIN and going through all the dialogue options AGAIN until you finally find the right person you needed to talk to. Even then sometimes it feels as if you have to talk to some of the characters twice, because for some reason it seems as if there was a dialogue option that wasn't there the first time, unless I'm just mistaken.
Also, there was a point in the game where I made a mistake in my choices, but I couldn't go back because the game doesn't have a save system. You can't save and load from wherever you want, instead the game saves and loads based on checkpoints. It would have taken me a few minutes to get back and make the change I wanted by replaying that certain section, but if the game utilized a normal save system, that mistake easily could have been avoided.
There was also this strange graphical glitch where the entirety of the text was replaced with these rotating and shifting characters that looked like the text was glitching out to the n'th degree. I don't know if this was intentional or not, but it happened in a few areas of the game, and with dialogue that I don't think I was supposed to miss, so it must have been some kind of glitch. Game breaking, no, but definitely something that was very confusing, and ultimately just led to more frustration.
All in all, this game feels very sloppy and poorly designed which broke my immersion into it about halfway through. This made me frustrated and not really care much about the story, which is what the game is all about. Don't get me wrong, I'm fine if a game is all story (I loved Gone Home), but this art style and engine were not the best route to accomplish the story they wanted to tell. There could have been a much better way to tell this story. Overall, if you think the game looks like it has an interesting story, pick it up when it's cheap. Otherwise, give this one a pass.

Duck Game may be one of the most violent 2D platform games out there. I'm surprised PETA ain't after these guys for their representation on Ducks. I've played a lot more with friends than I have alone.
Then again, Ducks have never been able to hold guns before or wear knight helmets. The object of this game can vary game mode to game mode. The
itself is not too bad although quite simple. Generally in multiplayer, players will have to kill one another to be the last one standing. Multiplayer can be played locally with friends/family or can be played over the internet. The movement within the game is decently well rounded. Ducks can jump and sort of have the ability to "fly" (more so glide). They can flap their wings but never gain any altitude, only slow their descent. Ducks may also grab (either items, explosives or guns). You can also trip yourself in game (which I'm assuming is for dodging. Although it's a little weird and doesn't exactly make sense). Strafing is also a feature in the game as well as the ability to quack. Yes, being a duck you can quack.
Levels themselves come in all shapes and sizes. This is a great feature because it really can make the difference in the game. Some levels are super small while others have some good length to them. Weapons available for pickup are scattered throughout the maps. Some weapons require you to unlock a door before you can proceed to pick up the weapon. This can cause a race between players to get the only weapon on the map. Weapons themselves are drastically varied. They come in the form of pistols, muskets, net guns (don't do damage but displace the player or allows you to throw them off a cliff), machine guns, shotguns, grenades, grenade launchers and rocket launchers. Some weapons take time to reload while others simply run out of bullets and force you to pick up another weapon. The game is unique in the sense of it's score keeping. Between "x" amount of games, there will be a cut-scene where your ducks are throwing their "marker" (be it a rock, a hat, a helmet or a log). This cut-scene is meant to show who is in the lead. After the games are set and done, players can watch a televised "news re-cap" of the previous games. This is actually quite neat to watch some of the replays with friends.
Single player resembles multiplayer but will throw the occasional mission your way. You may need to raid a specific location, grab a specific item then leave the level in one piece. You will be rated either gold, silver or bronze depending on the speed you complete the mission. You can visit a booth to buy small upgrades in order to speed up your mission progress. The
themselves are as basic as NES graphics but try their best to display every little detail. This may sit well with some while others may not be able to get over the simplistic graphics. The
are okay but I feel a little more variety regarding the explosions and maybe even quacks could have been added. Muskets and other gun shot sounds are as accurate as NES sounds can get.
Overall, not too bad of a game. I think the price is up for question but on a sale I would recommend grabbing if you got a few friends on standby to play with. 1 player mode is fun but local is a lot more fun. Some may find this game neat while others may find it repetitive. I'll give it a recommendation but with caution as some may find it boring after playing a few games.

This was an amazing game all around. The cinematic cuts throughout the storyline were brilliant and really kept me captivated in the story, despite being how technically simple and one-directional it was. I found out about this game via their launch day imgur post. Right away I was quite interested, but it still took me a few hours to decide whether or not I actually wanted it.
Well, I did, and I haven't regretted it at all. I'll put it cleanly, though; it's not for everyone. It's a very simple game, with technically little content like items and dungeons, whilst featuring a soothing flying and exploring experience.
Effectively it has a number of things:
- Casual jogging
- Jumping
- One-sided text box conversations and book/scroll/tablet interaction
- Casual puzzles. Hints here and there, but even without those they're pretty easy
- Stories to be found all over
- Flying
- Flying
- Did I mention it has flying? well, it has great flying. Smooth as heck, and a fun tool to explore the flying islands
What it doesn't have:
- Combat and by extension, enemies
- Loot
- Forced map routes
- Highly detailed textures
- Cutscene galore (There are some cutscenes, but the majority of the gameplay so far is flying / walking / bit of talk-reading / interacting with certain elements)
The terrain and models are basically low-poly textures and models, leading to a rather simplistic look. The colours and shading still make it look pretty decent, though. Save for the clouds, Those could be better. At first I thought it were 'locked and undiscovered' islands, until I tried landing on one.
The music is very fitting. Non-intrusive, yet present and fun to listen to.
Flying can be done after you exit the inital cave. It's very simplistic, just like the overall game, yet also very fleshed out and smooth. You can start flying by jumping and pressing [E]. After that you can steer with WASD for main controls, LMB/RMB for banking, LMB+RMB for slowing down, space bar for flapping your wings and accelerating. If you happen to hit something, you get reverted to your human form. However, you maintain intertia, so if you simply bumped into something, it's very easy to go back into bird mode and continue flying.
Overall, I certainly think it was worth the money, and if looking at the trailer vids and screenshots piqued your interest, chances are you'll enjoy it. Simple but soothing game without forced elements.

The Witcher and The Witcher II are games that have a lot of character building.
This game is based on a set of novels by a Polish author and has become popular enough for 3 games. The 3rd will be out soon and the support for it is astounding.
I've fallen in love with Geralt of Rivia, a witcher, which are an order of people who were genetically modified as children to be faster, stronger, more resilient humans who can cast spells called signs to help with combat. They are monster hunters who stay neutral (or try to) through out their adventures.
Geralt is also the desire of pretty much every chick he runs across. He gets a lot of tail. Tastefully of course. But seriously this guy is a bush master.
So, the main combat style is sword fighting, which he is VERY good at, in many different ways.
Throughout the game, you're forced to make choices, which change the game in significant ways and give you different outcomes and endings. It's similar to Fallout or Mass Effect in this way. It still has a linear story line, with optional and required sub storylines.
It's written beautifully. I cannot WAIT for the 3rd and final game.

Things I liked:
Graphics are top notch and music is good. The inventory system is a fun addition to puzzle games, and the picture taking with the journal to type in game notes is better than some puzzle game implementations of just taking a picture. This game certainly has a lot going for it.
Things I didnt like:
There is a line between giving clues and giving solutions, and unfortunately Quern steps over this line frequently. Most puzzles felt less like puzzles and more like "follow the instructions". For instance, the code to the first combination lock you come across, maybe 5 minutes into the game, is found on the first 2 notes the professor gives you. No clues or anything, you either brute force the combination or are given the solution. That trend continues throughout the entire game (I could give tons of examples, but don't want the review to be too long), though it does somewhat redeem itself in the latter portion once you lower the tower and access the underground area (more on that later). I also wish the inventory system was utilized more, pretty much all of the things you manipulate in it are keys with moveable parts in order to fit into the key hole. Thats not really a puzzle, its a toddlers "match the shape" game.
The story is also very flat. The notes the professor leaves for you gives you very little story other than "I discovered a thing and want to share it, and I've decided the best way to do that will be to trap someone here and make them solve puzzles culminating in completing my work because I left it incomplete due to boredom" (literally all he had to do was wait for a computer to finish a calculation, but that was too big an ask for him). There is also another npc who gives you somewhat of a lore dump later in the game, that can be summarized as "the discovery is dangerous. Seal it away instead of sharing it" only done in an over dramatic way. And the end of the game is a let down no matter which advice you chose to follow.
Conclusion/Going beyond the thumbs up/down:
I really wish the entire game played like the latter portion underground as a lot of the puzzles there felt like actual puzzles. My favorite is a key with 4 places to put differently shaped segments, only unlike a lot of other keys in the game you don't manipulate it in your inventory. You have to figure out which segment goes where, and instead of spoon feeding you the answer the game simply gives you 2 rules on how to figure it out. Its great stuff! If the underground was its own game, I'd recommend it in a heartbeat.
But its not its own game. Its stuck on the end of a rather boring "follow the instructions" gauntlet of weak game play, and the entire thing is layed on top of a weak story. As a result, I find it hard to recommend the entire game. The graphics and music are great, but it takes more than that to make a great game.
