This is great conceptually, but I wouldn't exactly call it fun or relaxing to play.  It is less of a game, and more of an interactive story about a young girl coming to grips with the more unpleasant things in life such as accepting responsibility for her actions, dealing with hard truths, acknowledging her limitations, and accepting that sometimes bad things just happen.  It's a well-told story, and it was trying to accurately portray human brokenness, but after a while it kind of felt like "Empty Apologies: The Game."
Gameplay involves simply walking around town and talking with people.  (There is a jump button programmed into the controls, but you never actually do anything with it.)  Occasionally you will need to interact with an object, but for the most part you will be dealing entirely with dialogue.  You are only able to marginally impact the outcome of events, however, and many of your "decisions" are merely for flavour.  This makes sense story-wise, but as a player it is a bit frustrating.
The art style is interesting.  It is made to look like the animated pages of a child's sketchbook, with office supplies like post-it notes and paperclips blocking off unavailable paths on the map.  I thought this presentation was clever, and added to the immersive atmosphere of the game.
Additionally, the voice acting was strong, I liked the secret ending, and I enjoyed the silhouette cutscenes between chapters (although I wish I'd been able to skip them on subsequent playthroughs).
Overall, I found this game to have high production values and an intellectually stimulating premise; however, it was taxing to play through, involving heavy-handed doses of both school and family drama, and only minimal gameplay.

The creator told you a major event at the very end of the game, to show you how cowardly she/he was, and how she didn’t want to face it, and ran away from her past. On the bright side, this game had an art style that I wish more games were like, which lead me to why i bought the game. Let me start off by saying this: The game is goregous and plays smooth. It's lovely to look at and if that's enough for you, that's enough for you.
It saddens me to dislike a 1-man blood, sweat, and tears effort like this, but I had way too many problems with this game to like it. My main problems were with the story, and unfortunately the story is thrust into your face so much that I couldn't ignore it enough to enjoy the game, even with the skip button.
The game wastes no time throwing every cliche in the book at you. You wake up with amnesia. You have a cute, squeaky, (nauseating) companion. There's a talking sword driving the first objective. And, of course, there are monsters in the way. Not a great first impression.
Which I could ignore if the writing and voice acting were good. As it is, the main character sounds like he's trying to squeeze one out with every line, and the little flying companion is...well...exactly as annoying as you'd expect. I don't fault the voice actors this time around though. The writing itself is horribly cliche in that way that puts voice actors in a no-win situation. You have to be really good to pull off bad dialogue.
The final straw was the first boss fight. They introduce a parry mechanic right before the boss fight that is pretty vital. It's also clumbsy, using the attack button and holding it. Why couldn't we just have a parry button? It's not like the controls are overwhelming. But anyway, the boss fight. It's fine, aside from one move this boss does: The Stomp. For some reason, this move connects when the foot starts moving toward the ground, rather than when the stomp hits the ground, (you know, like every other game). Really really undermines the whole parry system.
I didn't play farther than that, so for all I know, the game might get better further in. All I know is, I'm not gonna be finding out! Sorry Dean.

:  This is one of the best spins on adventure games i've played in a while. It reminded me of ye ol' Jak and Daxter and Ratchet and Clank, where you have just a simplistic complication, but don't let that fool you as there is more to this game then it seems.
:  Being one of the few members of the town outside the major districts, your little community takes in all kinds of color'ed people and the town acts as a neutral settlement for people afraid of their own districts. Majority of the game revolves around the complications each of the 3 colors present to one another;
most commonly known for anger and rage is well represented through the Red characters.
, the curious types of people who turned coward, have more of a technological side with their robust defenses and how they live boarded up in their homes away from all the outsiders.
was the trading hub of color, which in this world was the biggest product that everyone needed and used. Although due to complications they all turned sad and depressed.
At the very start it may seem slow, but if you pull through the excellent tutorial that is given and move towards the big twist that even I did not see coming, the game draws itself a quite nice narrative.
:  The combat after you reach the fighting part of the tutorial seems very bland, sort of a button mash really to kill most of the enemies early game. But I digress as the further in the game you play you can purchase upgrades and combo's for your attacks and also increase duration of abilities. This allows for people with different playstyles to work more efficiently and perhaps change the gameplay to suite individual people.
The parkour element, a MAJOR part of the game is very well produced. The smooth maneuvering of jumping around on boxes and planks really feels fluent. It may be hard to understand at first but once you get through the basic of how to jump around without stopping to look around it becomes a fun experience jumping around and exploring to find collectibles.
:  A combat/parkour game must have a big majority of the focus on the controls, without doing so it could make the game feel troublesome to control and overall a bad experience. From what I have played of the game using my Xbox 360 controller (
) it is very difficult to get used to from the average buttons. The interact button is what would strike most people as the most unusual, as on the 360 controller it is (Y), and you will see why it is as you progress through the game.
The combat portion of the controls amongst the parkour is also very fun to play with. It has a dodge mechanic which seems very functional when needing to dodge attacks, and can also be used to initiate combos and reach platforms if performed correctly.
:  This game may not be as extensive as the old PS2 games that this game seems inspired off, it does bring a nuance in this genre with its unique parkour concept and the difficult combat found later in the game. I greatly feel this game is well worth the $4 spent and is a must pickup if it goes on sale for lower.

I knew this was just a conversion from the mobile application, therefore, my expectations for this game should have been low. It is impossible, however, not to feel some excitement when engaging with new material from the Fallout universe - and excitement walks hand-in-hand with high expectations. Fortunately, Fallout Shelter has, to a great extent, met those expectations.
Why? This game is so simple to play, which makes it perilously addictive. Everything can be controlled with just the mouse. For instance, to assign vault dwellers to specific roles, you just drag and drop them to SPECIALised rooms. That’s right, the pun was intended. Your vault dwellers have the S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system, just like Fallout, and some of the rooms have a preferred S.P.E.C.I.A.L.s. The Science Lab required high Intelligence, for example. While it isn’t compulsory to adhere to the assigned S.P.E.C.I.A.L., doing-so will make you vault dweller very happy; and happiness, as you will find, is very important.
The rooms of your vault, weapons and armour will be limited in the beginning, but your options quickly grow with the growth of your vault’s population, which can be increased in two ways: you can build a Radio Studio to attract dwellers from the Wasteland, or, in a more novel way, assign a male and female dweller to a Living Quarters, then sit-back, and let the amorous spectacle commence. Fortunately, for those sick-minded individuals out there, the game won’t let you force incest, or exile a pregnant dweller.
As for the graphics, they are, of course, basic, but not repulsive or retro-feeling. In fact, the endearing Vault Boy cartoon-style pervades the game and makes each dweller quite endearing. The power armour suits, though, look a little compressed, and a little too comical.
The replay value of the game is somewhat limited, which, of course, is because Fallout Shelter was intended to be the launch-pad for Fallout 4. This is evident in the missions, which, after incorporating some witty dialogue in keeping with the Fallout universe, fail to vary and challenge the player: the management in combat is limited, the same half-a-dozen locations become dreary, and the enemies equally so. In short, the missions can become something to run in the background, in order to gain revenue, whilst being more attentive to another task in your Internet browser.
Overall, this game is definitely worth playing, but only if you looking for a bit of light-hearted fun. The serious gaming, and long-term gaming, remains with Fallout 4, or for more avid Fallout fans, like myself, Fallout: New Vegas.

The control aren´t perfect. The way the dots move (specially on close angles) is unreliable and if you’re not in a flat surface the direction the jump bottom will launch you seems randomize, that said, they work well most of the time.
Each level is theme after a fond an its historical context, giving each typeface a personality and character of their own and making each “zone” feel unique not only on gameplay but in tone, a must-play for atmosphere enthusiast.
Scattered throughout the levels are asterisks that unlock texts explaining the development of the technologies and arts that lead to each typeface, and while I usually don’t like when gameplay is interrupted with text, these are interesting on their own and mark a breather in-between the most frustrating parts of the platforming. If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I never bother to review games.  This is literally the first game I have ever written a review for, and there's a reason I chose to start with Quern.  The reason is that Quern is that damn good.

The physics aren't zany, off-the wall, and sometimes glitchy. Hero characters can't equip multiple weapons to create unique play-styles. Hero attacks are "balanced" instead of just letting you be a maniacal orc killing machine. The strategic/puzzle element of the game at the harder difficulty levels is gone. There were some levels on nightmare my friend and I played like 7-8 times before we finally figured out a winning 5-skull strategy and that was really rewarding, then we'd check online and other people would have completely different solutions. Bought this game while on sale (was buying horror type games) and definitely enjoyed it.  I am also from Washington State so it's cool to see a game based here, even though the town is fictional.
PROS:
-The story is awesome.  Elements really remind me of the Vanishing of Ethan Carter (A writer's tale) and Silent Hill 2 (paranormal town, searching for your wife, etc.).  Both are highly recommended titles, the former can be found on Steam.
-It has a healthy mix of action, horror, adventure, and comedy.
-A wide range of weapon choices with a large supply of ammo and equipment.
-Driving cars are really entertaining and hilarious while mowing down taken.
NEUTRAL (kind of nitpicking):
-Character graphics and movements could be a lot better.  Though the environmental textures do look great.  To be fair though this game did take Remedy 5 years to develop (released in 2009) and they're a smaller studio.
-Fighting can get really repetitive (this could be a pro or con if you like or hate this type of thing) since there are only a small variety of enemies.  So you're facing the same taken and doing the same fighting strategy over and over.
-You lose your whole inventory of weapons and equipment on a regular basis (and have to recollect again).  Sometimes it makes sense with the story and other times it doesn't make any sense.
CONS:
-Wake's stanima is pretty bad.  I wish it was better or it would increase as you progress.  This gets really annoying when you're being forced to survive with little or no ammo/weapons, getting rushed by enemies, and need to make it to the next checkpoint/light only to have Wake get gassed after 5-10 seconds.
-A form of healthpacks/first aid would be nice to have (for quick health).  You gain your health back by standing still or standing in a checkpoint light.  There is no time for this especially when you're continously getting rushed by enemies and there is no checkpoint around.  This is a poisonous mix combined with the bad stanima.
-There is a form of Taken that are really fast (not the bosses) and almost nearly impossible to take down.  Sometimes you get rushed by 2-3 of these guys and they just run up behind you and stab you in the back.
-Controls can get a little clunky.  You still walk a little bit even after you've stopped clicking W.  This gets frusterating when your jumping or trying to balance while trying to avoid falling to your death.

This game may be "myst like", but it is not like Myst.  Myst is a coherent whole with many interlinking parts.  Quern is a loose narrative delivered in cryptic notes from a meglomanaic.  The puzzles have nothing to do with the narrative, except for the stated "to delay you".    I can't see why:  the guy has been gone for 100 years and probably dead by the time You "complete his mission".  Why slow you down, if it will benefit everyone?   I never bought into the story he presented.  Gamana, on the other hand, told a compelling story of how absolute power, and its concomitant corruption, destroyed her world.  It took me 27 hours, and using hints, to complete this game.  Without some of the hints, I would never have finished it.  Maybe I'm not the brightest bulb on the string, but I enjoyed Myst, Riven, Uru and got through those without hints.  I complained a lot about Obduction, but even it is more logically put together than Quern.
Now, having said all that, I will say the game is good looking and sounds good as well.  I understand how difficult it is to produce new sorts of puzzles and tasks to make a game different and enjoyable at the same time.  In that respect, Quern has broken some new ground.  Some of these puzzles are so complicated it sometimes seems impossible to do.  If you like a challenge, though, this is just the game you've been looking for.  Take notes, take lots of "sketches", and refer to them often.  Don't leave the game for long periods without playing it:  A lot of the immersive thinking and history fades and it just makes it harder.
I'm giving it a thumbs up for innovative thinking, a good challenge, and nice environmental looks, sounds, and music.

Journal was fairly disappointing.
The attempt to create a plausible yet unreliable narrative character is a rather difficult accomplishment, and Journal
didn't manage to get it right. Firstly she constantly tells you what she is doing wrong, there's no guessing the ambiguity of her statements and the final twist to the tale, comes as completely unexpected, there are no hints, or eureka moments of "Oh this is why they included that!" In short the game does not encourage reflection, or analysis, it (like so much other modern material from films to books) hamfists you with the truth it wants you to realise rather than allowing an individual interpretation, or playing to multiple meanings through ambiguity. This is no more clearly recognised than when the characters speak in a sequence of randomized letters, that conveys their dialogue without conveying meaning. It's an opt out of revealing subtle clues to the player and feels lazy on the part of the writers rather than illustrating her mental blocks or incapacity to handle her situation.
The art style is very childlike, in fact it seemed a bit too childlike considering the adolescent phase the protagonist is portrayed as going through. Yet it has a certain charm, the blurring lines of movement, the overall conceit of playing or moving her through her life as she writes her diary is clever, and the transferral of blocking objects to background desk additions after each daily diary entry is completed are innovative.
The support characters are completely unoriginal, from a stay-at-home Mother, who does nothing, to the cliched cast of school characters, it again felt somewhat lazy on the part of the writers, not one character feels truly original or effectively offsets the protagonist, so that her character is actually revealed, not even her selfish interactions with her primary friend Elena as this is contradicted by her opposite interactions with others.
As an unreliable narrator we would expect her opinions and interactions with others to be offset by  actual scenarios in the game, but this does not occur at any point. It is also not helped by the stereotypical character designs employed to illustrate these other people, faceless or not. We are shown her perspective and all the events tie in to her persepctive rather than show her to be a delusional liar, which would make far more sense considering the psychological condition of denial they attempt to portray her as being in.
The bridging story of the Carnival, intrigued me at first, although I cringed through the monotone of the male voice-over narrator for these parts. I wondered at first at the symbolic significance that they were attempting to use with the portrayal of the carnival, and although it does serve this in a minor capacity the ultimate integration of the carnival into the main storyline, simply destroyed any symbolic function it could have served and denigrated it into a literal truth.
The gameplay itself is fairly smooth and reliable, and area transitions occur quickly without any long delays or interruptions allowing the story to continue at a fairly rapid pace. The only issue is that once the story is completed there isn't much replay value, as interactions don't seem to affect the outcome at all, in fact the only reason to replay would be to try achieve a 100% completion of achievements. In short there is not much longevity to the title.
Overall I don't recommend Journal, it's not as poor as I make it out above, but neither is it actually good. In short it is fairly average title, without replayability that means you're probably better off spending your money on another title or buying this only when it's on sale.

A missed opportunity.  That's all I can call it.
NS2 isn't a bad game.  In fact, despite not personally recommending it, I still think it is a good game.  The problem is that it isn't a game I can recommend to others.  If you look at my hours I'm not someone who hasn't given the game a chance.  In fact, I beta tested the original NS1 mod.   When NS2 was announced and they asked for help to fund it, I purchased a few copies of Zen of Sudoku (another game they produced).  Then, when they were near finished NS2, I pre-purchased the game, sight unseen, long before release.
So I do support the game and the makers.  I just can't recommend it anymore.  Why?  Well the answer can be found in the game's development.
The big failure of the game is exactly what happened with NS1.  Basically the developers allowed a small--but vocal and intolerant--minority of players dictate the direction of gameplay development.  These 'pros', are basically the people and clanners who play games competitively and/or in tournaments.  Now I can see wanting to appeal to the 'pro' gamers as a means to generate interest, but there needs to be a balance between competitive and casual play.  Sadly, there never was.
In the end, the difficulty and learning curve puts this game well out of reach of all but the veterans.  New players are quickly steamrolled and wonder how the heck it happened.  What's worse is that they released the game without a trainer or tutorial mode.  While there is a basic 'sandbox' mode that helps to get a player acclimated to the game before they play, it's too little too late.
I saw this all happen in NS1, and it saddened me when it happened here.  The competitive gamers basically co-opt the game, and casual players are forced to play at that high level or they don't play at all.  In my opinion, the logical way to develop the game would have been to introduce a 'tournament mode', with increased difficulty, for those dedicated players.  It could have been finely tuned to appeal directly to their form of play, while still leaving the game with a 'casual' player base that could actually play the game.  Unfortunately, the developers objected to this concept suggesting they didn't want there to be 'two games'.  But the reality is that difficulty levels are part of gaming.  That doesn't make it "two games", it makes it one game with two difficulty levels.
With the development team basically abandoning casual players, this basically meant that no matter how many sales they made, the new players never stuck around.  If you look at the history of the game, you will see that from the release in late October 2012 until the end of 2012, there was a large player base that bought the game and was playing.  Since everyone was still learning, it meant there was the potential for developers to cater to that casual player base and build their numbers further.  Instead, they went the other way, abandoning the casual player base in favor of the competitive and tournament players.
Over on Steamcharts you can see just how the game started strong and then flamed out in a spectacular fashion.  (
)   The all-time peak number of players online was just a bit shy of 10K.  At time of writing there were ~200 playing.  It's sad, it really is, since this could have been a much better overall game.
The nail in the coffin for this game was when development for 'game balance' was put in the hands of volunteers.  Since the game is easy to modify (in the LUA scripts), balance changes didn't have to be hard coded into the game.  As such, a bunch of people who felt they 'knew better' how the game should be developed were able to markedly influence balance changes by verbally bullying anyone who disagreed with them.  Anyone who dared question those who wanted to make the game harder were verbally ridiculed and harassed.  The game forums became toxic as a result, and casual players began their exodus.
Well, those competitive players got what they wanted.  The game is exactly how they said it should be balanced.  It's too bad there is hardly anyone left playing now.
What's worse is that the more appealing elements of the game--the highest level 'upgrades'--only show up when the outcome of the game is predetermined.  (which happens within the first few minutes)  Users who look and see the marine 'mech' robots and the 'rhino-size' alien don't realize that they will likely rarely if ever get to play them.
This game is a good example of what *not* to do when developing a game.  While I can see the appeal of competitive gaming to a game like this, it can't be at the expense of casual gamers.  Otherwise you kill the potential for the game to grow.  Look at TF2.  A game that is 'easy', but that can be hard based on the skill of the players.  That could have been how NS2 ended up.  Instead, the game is harder than ever.  What's worse is that they added a ranking system to which isolates players based on skill.  New players will find game choices limited as a result.
Simple example of a poor balance choice?  In TF2, if you need to get health, you can pick up health kits (on the field or in spawn) and also be healed by the doctor.  In NS2 it used to be you could go to 'spawn' and heal up fully (health and armor) at the armory--like a med cabinet in TF2 spawn--and you could get health-only medkit drops in the field.  If one was away from spawn, armor could only be repaired with a welder. (like a medigun, except anyone could carry one if they bought it.)  However, the competitive complainers cabal (I love alliteration) pressured the person doing balance work to make it so the armory would no longer heal players.  In other words, once you lost armor you needed to be welded, and you can't weld yourself--other players have to do it.  The outcome of this change was that it made it that much harder for players to stay alive unless they are highly skilled.
In the end, I still play NS2, and I would recommend it to anyone who I felt had the skill to survive.  However, there aren't very many people who fit that description.
Unless you are someone who considers themselves an exceptionally good FPS player, I would advise you give the game a pass unless it is deeply discounted and you're willing to take the chance the game may not be fun for you.
While NS2 is--on the surface--a good game, it missed its chance to be a great one.

I know at the time of this writing I only have a few hours in this game, but all of the negativity aimed at it solely for it's microtransactions are obscuring some of the other things that should be talked about here. Yes, this game will obviously be a grind without paying actual money for materials, but everything that effects stats or traps can be earned. The rest is cosmetic. This is pretty common with this sort of game and uncommon for it to be any other way in a free to play multiplayer title. I hate to make the argument "well it's free" but, hey it's free. So as not to rant, I'll do the normal bullet point pros and cons.
PROS
- The game you love, Orcs Must Die, is here and still fun.
- It is much easier than the last 2 iterations in the series to set up a co-op game.
- You do not have to play the MOBA portion of the game
- Working together is important and there is a lot of meta-strategy, but it's easy to get the hang of.
- It looks better graphically than the last 2 and performs better on lower end systems.
- The gamepad support is top notch.
CONS
- Sometimes games will boot you at the loading screen. You can hop right back into your game though, much like League of Legends.
- The client is super glitchy. Sometimes your cursor does nothing and then other times buttons will refuse to load.
- There really isn't a way to mess around with graphics setting. All you can do is change the ratio. This NEEDs to be fixed.
- The pricing on the microtransactions are hardly "micro".
- The drops rates for some of the crafting items are nearly non-existent.
I think this game is getting an unfair rep and I'll revisit this review somewhere down the road.

Journal...how do I describe Journal.
Journal is a game that focuses on the story. The only keys you use are the right and left arrow buttons, and then the space bar. It's more than enough.
Journal...is something different.
When I first started playing the game after buying it on sale, I'll admit. I wasn't that impressed. I thought it was a bit odd, and I liked the art style. The story was simplistic and seemed to have no point. Then a window got broken. Then you find out YOU broke the window.
You make all sorts of descions in the game that all pertain some sort of importance, though some are miniscule and others are...game changing. Literally and metephorically. You change the course of the game with each move you make, and then you also change the story itself, to a point. At first it isn't all that interesting and honestly a bit confusing, but then things fall into place. it's like a puzzle and you have to put it together. Piece by piece, word by word. You'll have to stop a couple times to figure it all out, though it isn't an inconveinance. Little puppet show stories are between each...chapter? Page? In your journal that sort of help you understand, while also delivering a seperate lesson and helping piece things together.
The most remarkable thing about this game is the ending. The ending made me think, made me sit back and stare at the screen. At the last sentance for a good ten minutes, just wondering. Wondering, thinking. Appreciating. This game gets a whole lot of credit for its ending; you realize what the whole game was about, why you did what you did, what your motiviations and everything else were for your actions and the truth behind the puppet shows.
This game is more of an experience, and it's a real good one. I reccomend it to anyone who wants to be surprised and enlightened, and who doesn't mind contomplating things.

If I were to describe this game in 2 words, they would be: Spyro Nostalgia.
Yes, this game is simple, easy, short, limited and childish; but the same could be said for most classic childhood games. It has small subtle elements of games like Jak and Daxter, Ratchet and Clank, and Crash Banidcoot but more than any other game, it reminds me of Spyro. The gameplay, the progression, the story, the characters, the enviroment, the little annoying squeaky follower that talks on your behalf because your character is either a mute or an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The list goes on...
Back in the day when games were short and simple this could fly but nowadays it is much harder to compete with modern games. There I both recommend and not recommend the game based on the following:
-IF you never had a childhood (Probably adopted by sterotypical overachieving Asian parents) and never got to play Spyro or other games like it then this game is probably a waste of your time and money.
-IF you did have a proper childhood (Thank your parents) and/or still are a child AND played similar games such as Spyro or whatever then I definitely recommend this. Let's face it, the older games seemed like classics because there was nothing better to play then and in many ways are just plain and simple great fun. In many ways those games are arguably better than The Last Tinker and actually have more to them BUT they don't make them anymore. If you're anything like me you've milked those childhood games dry over time through Playstation 1, Playstation 2, Playstation 3 HD remakes and even Playstation emulators. The Last Tinker is the closest you'll get to reliving those types of childhood games.
That nostalgia aside (the main selling point), the graphics aren't bad. The game has a very colourful, vibrant look but that is also due to the story line. No framerate issues that I've noticed nor any pixelation. No bugs or glitches. Simple controls, enemies and powers to learn. Decent soundtrack. Replayable missions if anything was missed. Easily completed steam achievements. Fun unlockable visual modes (Small heads, Big heads, Black & White, Colour Reverse, Mirror World, God Mode, Arena). No real overall downside to this game, only things that not appeal to your game tastes.
P.S. This is my first review. Sorry if it was unhelpful, unagreeable or too long.

Review:
The Last Tinker: City of Colors has got to be one of the best indie games I have ever played. It isn't the most difficult of games and not necassarily the best of the indie franchise, but it certainly has had some work put into it and it deserves to be recognized. And with that, let's get into this review.
So to kick things off, let's talk about the story. The main character that you play as in The Last Tinker is Koru, who suprisingly enough, is the Last Tinker. Weird right? The place that this all takes place in is Colortown, where three factions of people live together; blue, red, and green. A race is held anually in Colortown and Koru always competes. But the night after the race, things go terribly wrong. A purple color element turns the world into bleak or in other words, white and gray. Now Koru most bring together the factions and their elements to stop the bleak from destroying Colortown. Although I may have left a few things out, I personally though that this story was although very simply and relatively childish, it was still fun and I thought it added to the game very well. Not much else to say about the story. Next, the gameplay.
Ahhh, 3D platformers. Oh how you made my childhood amazing. This game is very reminiscent to me of Spyro: Dragonfly Dojo and Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. The gameplay is sort of an action 3D platformer. You also get new abilities for each element you collect and for each move you buy from the fighting expert. The combat was pretty unique too because once you got further into the game, you were given many options on how to take on your enemies with the power of the elements granted to you. There are also puzzles which you know aren't the most challenging thing, but you know... they're there :P. Now one thing I am sure people will want to know about this game is what are the controls like and should I have a controller? Gladly, the keyboard controls are good and a controller is not necassary. If you are a pleb like me, you don't have a controller for PC games. Althought the controls felt a little bit contradictory near the start of the game, you eventually get a good feel for them. Onto the look of the game!
Honestly, this would probably be the main reason I like this game so much. The visuals are absolutely amazing in terms of variety and color. And that is what made me want to play it that much more, so I can restore color to Colortown so I can see the color again :D. Now of coures the game isn't exactly on my top list of best graphics, but man these visuals just draw you in that much more.
The last thing I would like to issue is how the game is $20 at original price which brings up the question, is it worth $20? Well my personal answer to that question is no, no it is not. Although all of the things I said were good for the most part, this game is not worth $20. My first reason for it not being worth that much is because the game doesn't really have enough playthrough time and if you'd ask me, the game doesn't have much replayability. I consider my self a relatively average platform player and my playthrough was only like 5 to 6 hours. With $20, you could go buy something you can pour many hours into like *cough *cough Rocket League *cough *cough. I got the game on sale, so I would say I got worth out of it. Honestly, my best calculation of worth for gameplay is $2 = 1 hour. The second reason I would say this game is not worth $20 is because of the fact that there is much more time and value you can get out of 20 dollars. Unfortunately, this $20 price tag for a game that was released a little over a year ago for an indie game with a small amount of play time just makes the game not quite worth it. The Binding of Isaac is a game in which you send a crying naked boy down into a hellish underworld to be terrorized by legions of flies, maggots, spiders, and miscarried undead children. You must dig through piles of poo for resources and make use of whatever garbage you can find to improve your chances of survival, often through self-mutilation or devil worship. All of this must be done to escape your mother, a schizophrenic Bible-thumping Christian zealot who believes God commanded her to sacrifice her son to prove her faith. Needless to say, it's understandable that a lot of people might be turned off on the game moments in due to the horribly disturbing concept and imagery.
Unfortunately, they're the ones missing out here. TBoI is by far the best roguelike I have ever played. Combining all the best aspects of The Legend of Zelda style gameplay with surprisingly nuanced controls, well-executed gallows-humor, and a mountain of randomized content that just refuses to get old (I'm about 117 hours in and counting at this point), it holds appeal for both casual gamers who feel like dumping a couple hours into something on a lazy afternoon and hardcore players who insist on getting every achievement (There are a lot of these. You will never see most of them). While I can't ethically twist your arm if you find Isaac just too horrific to handle, anyone else should give it a shot.

I am a person who likes to try out different game development softwares. I own four as of right now, RPGMaker VX Ace, GameGuru, Leadwerks Game Engine (With C++ Addon), and Axis Game Factory AGFPRO 2.0; alongside several other programs to model, texture, etc. I must say, I would recommend GameGuru to friends who want to get into basic game design as it does not require any programming (although you MAY edit in Lua). It's simple to use, and you can create multiplayer games to play with your friends. Now, this is NOT for a person looking to make a professional game. For that, Leadwerks is where you'd want to go. GameGuru is still a very good game engine, and good for starting developers who just want to have some fun and make a small game. GameGuru has a lot of potential, and even though its in early access there aren't any crash bugs or any bugs that I've encountered.
The only downside to this program is the asset store, paying up to another $25 for extra textures etc. But you can import your own, I believe GameGuru supports blender files? (Don't quote me on that one), you can texture them and add detail in Substance Painter, or Substance Designer. Alongside make textures in Bitmap2Material. I own all of these programs and they are great, costly, but great. And in conjunction with GameGuru I can see someone making a game that people would buy. Graphics can always be improved but of course you'd have to take the time to do that yourself.

The writing is extremely subtle, and without a solid grasp of comparative literature most of the metaphors will go over a typical player's head. As a consequence people who dislike Alan Wake truly ARE idiots- of course they wouldn’t appreciate, for instance, the open-endedness in Alan's existential catchphrase “Its not a lake, its an ocean” which itself is a cryptic reference to Absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing Nothing. I’m smirking right now just imagining one of those addlepated simpletons scratching their heads in confusion as Sam Lake's genius prose unfolds itself on their computer screens. Alan Wake is a game about the world's greatest liar and serial killer.
You play as Alan Wake, a writer who writes Max Payne fan fictions or something. Alan and his wife Girl-Lady travel to the town of Bright Falls because Alan spent the last few years seeing if he can beat George Martin's record of not doing anything.
But not all is well in Bright Falls and soon Alan finds himself in a sticky situation, surrounding by an evil force and it's minions. It's up to Alan and his bumbling manager Barry to save the day and shoot ancient evil entities in the face.
Alan Wake is a third person shooter developed by Remedy Entertainment, mostly known for the Max Payne series. Or atleast the first two.
Your most common enemy in Alan Wake are a force known as the Taken. The Taken are possessed humans covered in shadows, they're invincible until you can pierce their shadows with a source of light, with stronger lights being able to kill them outright. With their shadow pierced, you can now get to the sweet gooey human center, where you can then fill them with holes with one of the several firearms Alan picks up along the way.
The combat works, which is nice. You can focus the beam of your flashlight to cut through the Taken's shadow faster, and then just shoot them. You also have defensive options such as flares to gain some space when you're being swarmed, and flashbang grenades which just flat out waste everything save for the largest enemies.
You also gain a flare gun every now and then, which acts as the rocket launcher of the game.
The one thing I noticed though, was that location damage doesn't seem to be a thing. I've tested various times and aimed at every body part, but you always do the same amount of damage no matter what. Regular Taken always take three revolver shots to kill, the fast ones take two, and the brutes take six. Elite Taken like the Sanic fast one usually take six as well.
It makes it simple to just aim at someone, break their shadow, and then just light them up, but it's also strangely basic considering Remedy's past games.
Alan Wake also fancies itself a horror game, but it's more like a saturday morning cartoon. Both the Darkness and the Taken are just...Silly, and that's coming from me. It may just be that the developers have no experience with the genre, but there honestly isn't a scary bone in this game's body.
Unless you count rambling men with knives as scary, in that case you should come visit sometime.
It's still pretty good tho, there's a bunch of really neat design stuff here. Things I didn't notice when I played this on the Xbox back in 2010.
Like the draw distance stuff. It kind of works as a foreshadowing device, you can see locations that you haven't visited yet in the story just looming in the background. During the beginning of the game, you can also see the gas station you're supposed to go to anywhere on the map, making sure you can't really get lost. Not that its easy to get lost or anything.
This game, however, I don't think was meant to be played with a mouse and keyboard. Don't get the wrong idea, the game works fine and controls great. It's just that you basically turn into the greatest dead eye of the west now that you don't have to play with a controller.
Alan goes from “I've barely ever shot guns before.” to “I will not hit my target firing behind me without looking and also drinking this glass of water. The dude hits his mark at any distance as long as your flash light is focused on it, it's kind of amazing.
Should you play Alan Wake?
You should, but you're not going to find it on Steam, though. Its not really scary either, but they at least give you guns. I played Outlast right before this, and if I had to pick between two not-scary horror games, I'd go with the one that at the very least lets me shoot at my attackers, at least then you have more gameplay options.
Check this game out if you're looking for a competent shooter with a campy story. And maybe wait for the sequel that might come out.

Quern is beautifully philosophical, it makes you think about how important is for a Proffesor his own research and what it means to him to trust you with it. In the game you follow Prof. William Maythorn's guidance into an elaborate puzzle inside a world filled with his great discoveries and investigations.  What i like most? It's how he is preparing and training you, like his dear student. Honestly he was like a father figure in some way. He trust you and he teach you what he has learned through letters and his own experiments that you use to solve his own puzzles.
Honestly i've never felt so deeply inspired with a game since Life is Strange. Usually puzzle games don't have great stories but QUERN really has an emotional story without using annoying cutscenes and without telling much about it: it's just the game as it is, it has an inmersive soundtrack and when you beat the game it leaves you with a great moral question. I can appreciate games with more focus on storytelling rather than gameplay (I even like Gone Home which a lot of people hate), but I did not like this game. It's not a bad game, the voice acting is good and sketchy artstyle is really appealing but I could not sympathize with the unnamed protagonist nor did I have any interest in her. She's a troublemaker who lies, cheats, and steals... and breaks windows. Even if you pick the positive moral choices, it doesn't affect the outcome of the story and as a result, she's still a ♥♥♥♥♥.
Throughout the whole game, you're left wondering what it is that she's going through that has caused her to behave this way. I felt like the story was a bit of a muddle and that it wasn't really going anywhere as they leave out details for pretty much everything, such as her parent's divorce, her grandmother's sudden change of behaviour, and the package you have to pick up from the post office. They don't really contribute to the story as the ending explains why she has been acting out.
The ending (which I won't spoil) was very cheesy and it was clearly meant to be sentimental but it just happened so abruptly. Nothing in this game has lead to the events of the ending, except for the carnival interludes maybe. I feel like I would've sympathize with the character more if they told us this in the first place rather than trying to make it into a huge twist.
Is this game trying to tell us a story about the life of a teenage girl or was it meant to be deeper? Either way, the disjointed narrative structure of the game just shoehorns more mysteries and it was all pointless. They try to tell so much story within the short legth of the game. I bought this game with my disposable income of £1.74 as the game was 75% off. You can complete this game within an hour and a half and the achievements, as well as the game of course, is very easy. Unless the game is at that price, I would avoid. It's a love it or hate it game but one with no incentives to play it through the second time.

After being disappointed with The Witness, I was eager to play a truly Myst-like puzzle game. I happened upon Quern, which I had not heard of before, and it was exactly what I was looking for.
Although the beginning of the game relies too much on finding "key" items or solutions to ciphers that will allow you to progress if you can simply figure out where to use them, the real fun is in the creative puzzle machines scattered across the world. These are introduced about a third of the way through, and get more elaborate as the game progresses. At 15 hours (YMMV; about 10% of that time was me wandering around frustrated, which I'd consider smooth sailing for a game like this), Quern was neither long nor short, and kept me wanting more.
The graphics are great, although I would have appreciated more environmental variety, and the music provides nice atmosphere. The story is pretty boilerplate--just an excuse to throw puzzles at you, really--but the voice acting is good, which is always a relief.
Honestly, though, I don't even need a story--just give me a big brass pipe-organ-looking thing with levers and lights (and no instructions) next to some locked vault-like door, and I'm happy. The bottom line: Quern had enough of those machines, big and small, to keep me interested.

I know at the time of this writing I only have a few hours in this game, but all of the negativity aimed at it solely for it's microtransactions are obscuring some of the other things that should be talked about here. Yes, this game will obviously be a grind without paying actual money for materials, but everything that effects stats or traps can be earned. The rest is cosmetic. This is pretty common with this sort of game and uncommon for it to be any other way in a free to play multiplayer title. I hate to make the argument "well it's free" but, hey it's free. So as not to rant, I'll do the normal bullet point pros and cons.
PROS
- The game you love, Orcs Must Die, is here and still fun.
- It is much easier than the last 2 iterations in the series to set up a co-op game.
- You do not have to play the MOBA portion of the game
- Working together is important and there is a lot of meta-strategy, but it's easy to get the hang of.
- It looks better graphically than the last 2 and performs better on lower end systems.
- The gamepad support is top notch.
CONS
- Sometimes games will boot you at the loading screen. You can hop right back into your game though, much like League of Legends.
- The client is super glitchy. Sometimes your cursor does nothing and then other times buttons will refuse to load.
- There really isn't a way to mess around with graphics setting. All you can do is change the ratio. This NEEDs to be fixed.
- The pricing on the microtransactions are hardly "micro".
- The drops rates for some of the crafting items are nearly non-existent.
I think this game is getting an unfair rep and I'll revisit this review somewhere down the road.

I don't think I can recommend Duck Game enough. If you like platformers, competitive games, shooters, to laugh, or just something you can pick up and play for a few minutes, this is for you.
Despite looking incredibly simple, there is a surprising amount of depth in the game. Weapons are unbalanced, but in a way that no one weapon completely trumps another. It's all about your situation and quick thinking. You got a laser that will bounce down hallways and demolish all below you, but you're completely exposed to attacks from above. A six shooter can shoot threw doors and blocks, but if you miss and fire again, you'll be shooting at an angle (which can be used for your advantage). Flamethrowers are a nightmare for your opponents, but just as dangerous to you. You could have the ultimate laser that fire a huge beam that fries everything in front of you, but while charging up, another player could run up to you and take you out with a single-shot pea shooter.
You can play dead using the fumble button or use it to grab a ledge to make that extra little distance to make that little extra distance to make the jump.
You can throw items at other players to make them drop whatever their holding. Are they holding a roman candle? Throw a pistol at them and watch as the fireworks fly out of your opponents hand and possibly light HIM on fire. Someone got a better weapon and charging at you? Throw a box at them before they can shoot and they'll be defenseless.
And of course, there is the comedy. Good lord, I laugh so much while playing this game. Whether it's a player stepping on a mine he set himself, two players shooting each other at once, leaving the game with no victor (which happens A LOT), or if you celebrate your victory to early and then a gun in the middle of a fire heats up and misfires, killing you just milliseconds before you're awarded a victory. Even the little things make this game funny: The way that the ducks squak and quack when they're set on fire, when they're hit with an item thrown at them (and in those cases, sometimes it's bleeped like they said a swear, which gets a laugh out of me everytime), or how close shots cause feathers to fly off the duck.
I love this game. It's very simple and easy to pick up, but gets very deep with how those simple controls and functions work, and half the joy is learning how to use them. (When holding a sword, run towards a player with a gun, hold the attack button, and press down to slide. Keep holding down the attack button and watch what happens. If only you could have seen my face when I found this out.)

There's a kernel of something good in this game, but it still needs a lot of polish for it to come through. I guess $5 was cheap enough to risk it, but I can't recommend it unless you're feeling super open minded.

I bought Spintires when it was first offered on Steam in late 2013 or early 2014 (I forget exactly when it was first offered). Back then it showed a lot of promise and even though it was still being developed, I could see it was going to be a great off-road game.
This year however the game has gotten worse. What use to be somewhat challenging has become too easy. Even in “Hardcore” mode you can almost go through any of the provided maps leaving the shifter in auto and not using AWD (All Wheel Drive) or the Differential lock. They even modified some of the more challenging areas in a few of the maps such as the angles of a few hills, tree placement (most notably near one of the unlockable garages on the Coast map).
The saving graces of the game are the visual aesthetics and the number and quality of third party mods. So, if you’re looking for an off-roading log transporting game that isn’t too difficult to master, you’ll be very happy with this game. Alan Wake is a game about the world's greatest liar and serial killer.
You play as Alan Wake, a writer who writes Max Payne fan fictions or something. Alan and his wife Girl-Lady travel to the town of Bright Falls because Alan spent the last few years seeing if he can beat George Martin's record of not doing anything.
But not all is well in Bright Falls and soon Alan finds himself in a sticky situation, surrounding by an evil force and it's minions. It's up to Alan and his bumbling manager Barry to save the day and shoot ancient evil entities in the face.
Alan Wake is a third person shooter developed by Remedy Entertainment, mostly known for the Max Payne series. Or atleast the first two.
Your most common enemy in Alan Wake are a force known as the Taken. The Taken are possessed humans covered in shadows, they're invincible until you can pierce their shadows with a source of light, with stronger lights being able to kill them outright. With their shadow pierced, you can now get to the sweet gooey human center, where you can then fill them with holes with one of the several firearms Alan picks up along the way.
The combat works, which is nice. You can focus the beam of your flashlight to cut through the Taken's shadow faster, and then just shoot them. You also have defensive options such as flares to gain some space when you're being swarmed, and flashbang grenades which just flat out waste everything save for the largest enemies.
You also gain a flare gun every now and then, which acts as the rocket launcher of the game.
The one thing I noticed though, was that location damage doesn't seem to be a thing. I've tested various times and aimed at every body part, but you always do the same amount of damage no matter what. Regular Taken always take three revolver shots to kill, the fast ones take two, and the brutes take six. Elite Taken like the Sanic fast one usually take six as well.
It makes it simple to just aim at someone, break their shadow, and then just light them up, but it's also strangely basic considering Remedy's past games.
Alan Wake also fancies itself a horror game, but it's more like a saturday morning cartoon. Both the Darkness and the Taken are just...Silly, and that's coming from me. It may just be that the developers have no experience with the genre, but there honestly isn't a scary bone in this game's body.
Unless you count rambling men with knives as scary, in that case you should come visit sometime.
It's still pretty good tho, there's a bunch of really neat design stuff here. Things I didn't notice when I played this on the Xbox back in 2010.
Like the draw distance stuff. It kind of works as a foreshadowing device, you can see locations that you haven't visited yet in the story just looming in the background. During the beginning of the game, you can also see the gas station you're supposed to go to anywhere on the map, making sure you can't really get lost. Not that its easy to get lost or anything.
This game, however, I don't think was meant to be played with a mouse and keyboard. Don't get the wrong idea, the game works fine and controls great. It's just that you basically turn into the greatest dead eye of the west now that you don't have to play with a controller.
Alan goes from “I've barely ever shot guns before.” to “I will not hit my target firing behind me without looking and also drinking this glass of water. The dude hits his mark at any distance as long as your flash light is focused on it, it's kind of amazing.
Should you play Alan Wake?
You should, but you're not going to find it on Steam, though. Its not really scary either, but they at least give you guns. I played Outlast right before this, and if I had to pick between two not-scary horror games, I'd go with the one that at the very least lets me shoot at my attackers, at least then you have more gameplay options.
Check this game out if you're looking for a competent shooter with a campy story. And maybe wait for the sequel that might come out.

It's very easy to see why Paladins got tagged as an OverWatch clone, due to the really close similarities. Some people here even call Paladins as "Poor Man's Overwatch."
From what I can see they've got plenty of differences. Let's discuss a few. First of all, in OW, you can freely switch heroes/champions in mid-game, but in Paladins you're stuck with your champion choice until the game ends.
Paladins also has a unique card system in place that boosts abilities or stats, which adds a dimension of unpredictability. For example, one of Skye's cards grant her an extra amount of HP per level, which in turn can help that player survive an otherwise lethal attack. You won't know what the other's player's card loadout would be until you actually start the game (you can check once the game starts by pressing Tab then selecting the Loadouts sub-tab, although not many people do that). There's also in-game items that push those stats/abilities further: let's use Skye again as an example. You can unlock the Nimble Fingers card for Skye, which allows her increased reload speed upon successfully landing her Poison Bolts skill. Now set that up in a card loadout, get it to level 2, then pair that with the Deft Hands item, level Deft Hands to 2, and you've got yourself a Twilight Assassin that dispenses punishment at the same rate Tracer's Plasma Pistols unloads clips. Overwatch doesn't have these two features, as far as I know. Thus, OW heroes can be 'predictable', in the sense that you'd have an idea of how much punishment they can take before they bite the dust - and be confident you'll pull it off.
Then we've got the champion similarities. I mean, come on - Fernando and Reinhardt. Aren't the shields alone huge giveaways? HOWEVER, the play style is radically different. Reinhardt's shield can be deployed multiple times with zero cooldown, but Fernando has to wait 8 seconds before he can deploy his shield again once he puts it away. Another example? Pharah and Drogoz. Sure, both can soar and hover, use rockets as their primary pain dispensers, and are generally annoying once they get to the air. BUT, they've got key differences too: Fareeha Amari's ult enables her to, I quote, "justice rains from above" on multiple targets. On the other hand, Drogoz keeps to his draconian roots and picks out JUST ONE unfortunate sap who will, I quote, "behold the dragon's fury." Last example I'll give for this section would be the snipers, Widowmaker and Kinessa. Both have sniper rifles that fire in auto mode in close to medium range, they can both use mines, and have a way to get to high ground - but that's where the similarities end. Widow can use one Venom Mine (explodes and deals poison damage) at a time (IIRC), while Kinessa can unload up to a maximum 3 Oppressor Mines (deals continuous damage and slows targets, default is 2 mines) at one time. Widow uses a grappling hook to traverse the map and get to high ground, but she needs line of sight to do so. Meanwhile, KInessa uses a teleporter to get to high points, and she doesn't necessarily need LOS (although you'll need to have a good estimation of where you want to land, otherwise you'll miss your spot and fall to death). Then their ults: Amelie gains infrared vision, shared with teammates, and sees ALL enemies through walls for a certain period of time (this is actually closer to Cassie's ult) while Kinessa gains double damage if/when she hits an enemy's upper body, and is an almost-guaranteed critical hit.
We also need to consider the time differences. Quoting Kinessa,
.
.
All in all, OW and Paladins are two different games with close parallels. It's like comparing apples and pears. That said, Paladins is still a fun game to play, especially with friends.

This is a very strange game.  When I first started I thought that it was a game with a decent narrative that was very poorly executed.  You end up being confused and it seems like information that can even seem irrelevant is being shoved at you in the wrong order.  It turns out that this is exactly what Journal is trying to accomplish.
I think that if you go into this game with an open mind, try not to play it like an RPG but rather an experiencial narrative, and know that everthing that seems confusing is intentional, It's possible that it will bring you a very personal and emotional experience that only certain Indie games are wont to do.  To the Moon is the other game that comes to mind as a personal and emotional journey, although the two are drastically different in execution; just like To the Moon it is best to play this game in one sitting so as to experience the entity as an undisected whole.
I don't guarantee that you will love this game, but take a chance and you just might.  It's definitely not for everybody, but if you enjoy the Indie narrative subgenre(or adventure game without the obsessive clicking as I like to think of it), I would suggest giving it a try.

Thoughts, in no particular order:
It's an OK game, but it's not as good as Mafia 2.  And no where near as good as Mafia: City of Lost Heaven, which is the best of the three by far.
It doesn't really have much to do with the mafia, at least not like the first two games.  All three games are tied together in a way which I think is neat (I don't want to spoil it).
The graphics are cool.
The soundtrack is cool.
The gameplay is soooooooooooooooo repetitive.  Every mission that progresses the story is the exact same.  This means that a few hours into the game and it becomes stale as all the missions become the same.  Go here and interrogate this guy.  Then go there and kill the guy he told you about.  Then go kill the guy above him.  Then move to the next area and do the same.  And then the same somewhere else.
The side missions are different, but you don't need to do those to finish the game.  And even they get repetitive (go here and pick up liquor, go there and pick up weed, etc.).
The game lacks the immersion aspects that made the first two games good.  Your car doesn't really get damaged that much in Mafia 3, no matter what you hit.  Cops don't chase you/pull you over for speeding - even if you're driving past them at 130mph.  Your car never runs out of gas.  You can't close doors after opening them.  You can't flush toilets.  You can't drink beers at bars.  All of which you could do in the previous games.
The game is very long as well - which isn't a good thing in this situation since the game is so damned repetitive.  Took me about 40 hours to beat it and I wasn't really doing the side missions until after the game was finished, then I did a few of them (you can keep playing after beating it).  40 hours would be fun if there was a big variety of missions, but since they are all virtually the same it becomes incredibly taxing and boring.  I had to force myself to finish it just because I wanted to see how the game ended.
Parts of the game are like a "choose your own adventure" book in the sense that you can choose to go down one path or another and it will alter the way the game plays out.  This offers some good replay ability in order to see all the various story arcs... but again, since the game is crazy repetitive there's no way in hell I want to sit through another 40 hours of gameplay to see what would happen if I opted to do
instead of
.
I'd recommend getting it when it's on sale.

I feel like this game is getting WAY too much hate that it honestly doesnt deserve. I will probably get flack for saying this, but honestly I think a lot of people are being extremely harsh on the game simply because they are butthurt over the fact that you are not playing as the traditional italian Mafia. The fact that this game ahs more negative reviews than positive is just flat out silly. Its REALLY not a bad game. However, if it had come out during the last generation, I think it would have been recieved more favorably.
Mafia 3 has a great setting, great atmosphere, AMAZING soundtrack(and not just the songs. The ambient and combat music is also stellar), nice cars, a very cool anti hero protagonist(he is basically a 1960s Punisher), a brutal revenge plot, entertainging and satifying combat, and great voice acting. The game has an EXCELLENT foundation. And overall, i found that there is an undeniable sense of "fun" to it. Trust me, when the music kicks in and you are blowing Sal Marcano's guys to hell along with a few mob buddies, you'll be having a good time.
The games graphics aren't anything spectacular, but they aren't "that" bad. I was actually quite pleased with them tbh. There are just some weird lighting effects from time to time and every looks kind of blurry for some reason. The game is also a bit buggy and the AI isn't especially smart. However, where this game really falters unfortunately, is the execution of the narrative. Mafia 3 is VERY repetetiv. You are basically just going around doing the crap over and over again with an occasional cut scene in between(though the cutscenes are very good). Majority of the game is basically you just going around destroying rackets and elimating underbosses over and over again. The saving grace is mostly the very enjopyable combat and the cutscenes that happen occasionally. Other than that, its not particularly interesting.
Despite the game's shortcomings, its really not as bad as some of these people are saying. Again, I do believe a lot of the disastisfaction stems from the fact that you are not playing as an Italian mobster in a more traditional authentical "mafia" storyline. I do reccomend playing it. It is fun and the story is engaging despite the repetetive gameplay. Also, Mafia 2 is overrated. It was not a masterpiece folks. I had an engaging story and thats about it.

After playing this game the first time, I literally said "F this game." I constantly got destroyed repeatedly, aliens were literally the hardest thing to get a kill in (outside getting a Onos) and I just didn't understand the game.
After my "Second" tour of duty, I gave the game more than a 2 hour shot. Looking back on that 2nd shot, I'm happy I did. Once getting past the STEEP learning curve, I was able to hang with pack. No longer getting destroyed everytime I encountered anyone or anything and was able to really appreciate what this game is... RTS mixed with FPS.
It's really a great an idea, you live and die with your commander or hive leader. If you don't listen to their orders, you lose. If you do... you have a fighting chance depending on his skill level. This game requires you to work together otherwise you get dominated by groups. Remember that, cause if you don't... you'll soon learn. With that aspect brought up, I've really felt a sense of accomplishment when we slowly started pushing across the map and constant yelling over the coms to get to the "Computer Lab, we're under attack there". Once you arrive in the computer lab, you'll know what this game is about. Cluster F*** of Aliens and Marines just trying to "win" that one spot for your team. If you win it, you have a sense of "We did it" but that sense slowly drifts away once the enemy re-directs it attention else where.
You'll have choices to go help that next area or punch them where it hurts and push forward. Sometimes your commander will make the call, other times you have to know whats best for the team. With that being said, I give this game a 8/10 and a recommend buy if at a discounted price. ($25 dollars is a pretty steep cost for the amount of learning curve you have to deal with).

I don't think I can recommend Duck Game enough. If you like platformers, competitive games, shooters, to laugh, or just something you can pick up and play for a few minutes, this is for you.
Despite looking incredibly simple, there is a surprising amount of depth in the game. Weapons are unbalanced, but in a way that no one weapon completely trumps another. It's all about your situation and quick thinking. You got a laser that will bounce down hallways and demolish all below you, but you're completely exposed to attacks from above. A six shooter can shoot threw doors and blocks, but if you miss and fire again, you'll be shooting at an angle (which can be used for your advantage). Flamethrowers are a nightmare for your opponents, but just as dangerous to you. You could have the ultimate laser that fire a huge beam that fries everything in front of you, but while charging up, another player could run up to you and take you out with a single-shot pea shooter.
You can play dead using the fumble button or use it to grab a ledge to make that extra little distance to make that little extra distance to make the jump.
You can throw items at other players to make them drop whatever their holding. Are they holding a roman candle? Throw a pistol at them and watch as the fireworks fly out of your opponents hand and possibly light HIM on fire. Someone got a better weapon and charging at you? Throw a box at them before they can shoot and they'll be defenseless.
And of course, there is the comedy. Good lord, I laugh so much while playing this game. Whether it's a player stepping on a mine he set himself, two players shooting each other at once, leaving the game with no victor (which happens A LOT), or if you celebrate your victory to early and then a gun in the middle of a fire heats up and misfires, killing you just milliseconds before you're awarded a victory. Even the little things make this game funny: The way that the ducks squak and quack when they're set on fire, when they're hit with an item thrown at them (and in those cases, sometimes it's bleeped like they said a swear, which gets a laugh out of me everytime), or how close shots cause feathers to fly off the duck.
I love this game. It's very simple and easy to pick up, but gets very deep with how those simple controls and functions work, and half the joy is learning how to use them. (When holding a sword, run towards a player with a gun, hold the attack button, and press down to slide. Keep holding down the attack button and watch what happens. If only you could have seen my face when I found this out.)

Natural Selection 2 puts such a large spin on the whole 'Space Marines vs. Aliens' genre with such a massive success. Never before have I played a Human/V/Alien game as balanced and well tweaked as NS2. Dead Space 2, the humans would shred any Necromorph team that wasn't pro, and in Aliens: CM, the Aliens practically floored the Marine team 9/10 times. NS2 however, puts matches at a grinding stalemate which can last for at least 30 minutes, but don't worry, this is why it is so fun. The whole objective isn't your lazy 'TDM', but instead you must actively push against your foe over a power struggle for the map, as you creep your way closer to their HQ which you have to destroy. Every game is an exciting war of attrition.
Gameplay: TEAMWORK! That is the tagline of this game. NS2 doesn't want your 'lone wolf' cr*p. If you try to be a hero, and not a soldier, you'll either be mulched beneath Alien teeth or blasted to bits by Marine rifles. NS2 is unique in the sense that it merges the core FPS gunplay with RTS elements with a hitch: on each team of 12 (Can be 24 on some servers!) 11 of you will be the soldiers fighting the other team in fluid, energetic and fair FPS combat, the 12th however becomes the Alien/Marine commander, entering the command station and turning THEIR game into the RTS element. The commander has full access to the entire map, watching over every one of you. The commander can do many jobs, including planting structures for you to build, setting waypoints for you to follow, research technology/evolutions to develop your fighting against the enemy, or even little things like dropping ammo/health for you. Be wary, as skill and patience are required to be a commander, otherwise you'll find yourself ejected by team vote. resources are vital, as they form a personal currency for personal upgrades, weapon purchases, and for the Aliens, developing into more evolved life forms. Resources build up over time, but increases the more Harvesters/Extractors your commanders have placed.
Marines: The brave Frontiersmen are your generic space marines. They have 3 weapons which pack many punches before upgrades are even mentioned. Relatively slow starters, your strength is in technological investment, so hope your CMD keeps his eye on tech requests. Phase gates can be buil, allowing you to teleport en-masse to certain areas as long as a Phase gaate has been built there. Over time, the marines will have access to new toys to experiment with, including shotguns, flamethrowers, jetpacks and even F*CKHUGE exosuits. When marines get to the peak of their tech, unless the Aliens are equally evolved, they will be utterly steamrolled beneath their metal boots.
Aliens: The Kharaa are considered the most fun of the two races, being the fact there is so many ways to play them. Spawning from an egg, you start off as the basic Skulk, a wall-walking little b*stard with teeth, though weak in direct combat, and likely to get trampled, a true Skulk player will manuever through vents and hide in shadows, ambushing with lethal force. Resources for Aliens are used to evolve to bigger, better and uglier life forms and also purchase upgrades. Gorges are the engineers of the Aliens. These fat buggers can build slimey walls to block routes, and create plant-like turrets. Lerks are flying monsters, designed to f*ck the marines' sh*t whever they fly. My personal favourite is the Fade, a humanoid assassin that teleports across the map, sowing fear and having the marines bombard the team chat in fear. Everybody loves the Onos, the biggest and hardest b*stard in the game. This 2m tall bull charges and flattens whatever it runs into, something short of the entire marine team is needed to kill one.
Graphics/Animations: Graphics are great for an indie game like this, and the design of the aliens are anything but generic, these aliens, though simple, instill the perfect feeling of disgust when you see them/hear them click and slurr to each other. Animations are great, when your marine comes through the infantry portal (respawning) it truly feels epic.
Community: The community is alive and kicking, no doubt about it the team chat will be exploding as sh*t goes down, you'll be hearing enemy positions, commander requests and simple smack talk o players getting seriously involved. It really is a great feeling being a part of a community like this. People are friendly and consider every game fair and just. I've encountered so few ragers, it doesn't compare to CoD or GoW. Albiet, lag issues are quite the problem in NS2, the framerate can drop to ludiocrously low levels in some servers, but that can't be helped.
If you love teamwork, a great FPS and the average RTS, and of course, Marines vs. Aliens, then Natural Selection 2 deserves a nice warm spot in your library.
