I don’t want to be writing this review on The Binding of Isaac at all. Because to write a review on this brutal, disgusting, brilliant, frustrating and amazing game; I have to stop playing it.
The Binding of Isaac has been the single most difficult game for me to put down since I accidentally downloaded Path of Exile back in March and lost a month to it. Last night I was supposed to be working on Batgirl combos (The latest DLC character for Injustice – Gods Among Us) but instead I found myself signing up for a run through Isaac’s creepy basement once again.
I had seen this game on Steam and I knew it was created by  Edmund McMillen who designed Super Meat Boy. I had seen the screenshots and saw the original Legend of Zelda-esque layout and the creepy art. I saw that it was cheap as all get out ($7.99 if you get the DLC, $5 on it’s own) and was well received by the community. But for whatever reason I had never gotten around to downloading it.
Well obviously, that has changed. The reason for this is because The Binding of Isaac still climbs its way up the game ranks on Twitch.tv.  Seeing a game in the Top 10 with over 2,000 people watching streams for it makes me wonder. It makes me think, “there must be something more to this!”
For a quick overview if you haven’t played the game. The Binding of Isaac is a 2D top down shooter  randomized Zelda-dungeon-crawler RPG monstrosity. The story provides a psychotic and gruesome backdrop for McMillen’s ‘cutesy and disgusting’ brand of art direction. You play as Isaac, a poor kid whose mum went mental from watching too much Christian broadcast and has now been told by God that she needs to sacrifice (Read: Kill with a kitchen knife) her innocent little boy Isaac. Isaac finds a trap door in his bedroom and escapes to the basement of his house in an attempt to get away. There he fights all manner of evil, monstrous and disgusting creatures ultimately working his way towards the final boss. Yeah, you’ll never guess who THAT is.
The Binding of Isaac is bitingly satirical, sadistically humorous, and stays true to it’s predecessor Super Meat Boy by being ridiculously difficult. The dichotomy between  brutality difficult and sheer entertainment strikes a perfect chord through the game’s randomization system. No two play-throughs are the same with maps, enemies, bosses and items being randomized within a loose floor by floor structure.
The basic gameplay is simple enough. Shoot enemies in a room, dodge projectiles, doors to the room will open allowing you to advance, collect any loot, rinse repeat, find the boss, kill the boss, go to the next floor. The fun and surprise is in the combination of the weird and wonderful items and how many different ways there are for your character to get stronger. On top of this, the sheer difficulty of the game makes defeating every floor a reward in its own right.
To speak to the difficulty, there is no ‘easy’ or ‘hard’ option. The only choices you get are as you slowly unlock characters through different actions in Isaac’s basement. When you run out of hearts, you die. There are no checkpoints or autosaves, you just die.  This is a purely skill based game, and although occasionally you’ll get completely hijacked by a wickedly designed room right before the final boss, ultimately you’re responsible for a success or failure. ZeroGamePlan on Twitch.tv claims to have had 168 successful runs on Isaac without dying once.  Watching him play makes me believe this without a doubt.
The hook for me is that every time I die in the game I am compelled to play again. Maybe I get a more powerful item this time, maybe I’ll get lucky and end up in an Angel or Devil room early on for some fancy upgrades. Maybe, just maybe, I’ll make it to the end.
According to Steam I’ve dropped about 15 hours into the game so far and I’ve only managed to get a full clear twice. The game’s final character unlock is after 10 successful play throughs, and then there’s the 10 challenge modes with set items, buffs and debuffs you’re forced to contend  with.  Even beyond that the game has a healthy and thriving community on Reddit that has all number of challenges proposed through the use of Cheat Engine or other limitations like ‘No Bombs’ or ‘No Treasure Rooms.’
If you’re a fan of challenging games like Dark Souls, Monster Hunter, or Super Meat Boy you’ll love Isaac. This game is not for the faint of heart or the easily discouraged. The twisted humor and grotesque style of The Binding of Isaac certainly won’t appeal to everyone. Underneath however, is a cleverly designed game that is fun, addicting, and worth every penny of it’s $7.99 price tag.

This game is at the same time easy and hard to recommend. What it does well it does very well, and the concept itself is intriguing and applicable to anyone who has played around with texttypes in Microsoft Word or other word processors. Due to my mixed feelings about this game, this will be a long review, so here is the short of it: some mechanical aspects bog this game down and makes the actual gameplay frustrating, but the theme and creativity carries it past that to be an overall enjoyable experience. For the longer version, keep reading:
Firstly, we have the problems, and it comes down to mechanics. In the game, you are playing as two dots that are connected invisibly like the wheels of a bicycle. You are progressing through the history of the written language, with a focus on typography. The two main mechanics are jumping and walljumping in order to progress and collect letters (collectibles) and stars, that unlock pieces of texts that give you information on the different types of text.
The problem is how the game mechanics interact with the environment. The jumping is a bit floaty and it is difficult to accelerate without "picking up speed" on the ground/platforms. The environment, however, has a lot of small platforms and edges, since you often are progressing on top of letters. That means that you can get stuck with one dot on each side of an edge, the walljump mechanic can fling you backwards when you bump against an edge or the jump can simply have different height for seemingly arbitrary reasons. This leads to a lot of frustration and spamclicking, since the game requires you to precision-jump in an environment that often kills you if you're not fast (read; lucky) enough to get past the specific obstacle.
The checkpoint system can also screw with you; sometimes it's fine and gets you back to exactly where you wanted to go, sometimes you miss a star and it checkpoints you right after the specific jump, with no way to get back without restarting the entire level. This would not be as bad if not for the choice by the developers to hide the letters and stars with their use of color; the letters and stars are white, and in almost all of the game the background is also white, so they are barely visible at times. They further obscure them by adding smoke and other effects, making actually seeing the bloody things a nightmare. I personally missed a few stars and letters, and I have no clue WHERE I actually missed them, since I didn't see them in the first place. So to get them would require a whole new playthrough, which I feel is bad design.
So why do I recommend it? Well, while the mechanics are annoying a lot of the time, the rest of the time they are highly enjoyable and cleaverly used in the puzzles available. Basically, when the game mechanics work, they really work and feel truly great. The actual puzzles themselves (disregarding the frustrating platforming) are mostly creative and fun, leaning heavily on the environmental design which is top notch. The theme is incredibly strong, making you feel like you are actually progressing through time, with a lot of clever references and sometimes minigames that made me smile. The sound design is stellar, with every stage (or time period rather) having a distinct feel in both estethics and sound effects.
The environmental hazard can be a source of frustration, but the rest of the time they are imaginative and constantly engage you, with cogwheels spinning, platforms lowering or elevating you, blocks of text that you have to slide around and more. Every new thing the environment throws at you fits with the time period in a charming way that is hard to describe. The environmental and level design is truly fun, and it's difficult not to appreciate the theme as you desperately spamclick to get past that one little ledge that is stopping your progress. The information you get through text is a bit dry at times, but succeeds in making you appreciate the environmental design even more.
This game feels like a labor of love, with it constantly playing with its own mechanics and stylistic approach. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't, but the good parts were good enough to be the parts that stuck to my memory in the end. It is unfortunate that the problems weren't picked up through playtesting, because without them this game could've been a true little gem and a great game. As it is, it settles on good, and still worth a playthrough.

It does have a nice sense of style, but there are some serious issues. The early game is too easy, but at least it is causal and relaxing. The later parts of the game become incredibly frustrating, because there are some minor issues that add up to a game that is frustrating rather than challenging. The physics in the game is a little too unpredictable and a slight jiggle between the dots can cause you to miss a jump and die as a result. Other times there are timed puzzles where you can’t see all of the puzzle, so you just have to hope your timing it correct. I was even respawned on a deadly block and died immediately. On the other hand, it is only $5 and if you can grab it on sale, it is worth picking up.

I really wanted to like this game, but I really didn't. I loved Amnesia and was sent in the direction of this game by somebody who said this game was similar. Well, I thought it was very clear that Alan Wake was trying to be Amnesia, but it really wasn't hitting any of the right points. (For reference, I completed the story but did not play any of the special missions I think were added later.)
The first problem with this game was the perspective and movement. It was a too-close third person perspective, where the playing character took up too much of the screen. It also was an awkward over-the-shoulder angle, so I constantly found myself moving slightly off to one side of where I wanted to be because centering the destination on the screen meant I was pointing Alan's shoulder where I wanted him to go. Movement also felt clunky and the fact that Alan couldn't run more than 25 steps (not an exageration, I counted) before an  invisible stamina meter ran out was infuriating. Adding to this aggrivation is the fact that the enemies (who you are expected to fight, since you can't hide from them) can run faster than you and for far longer. You can dodge their attacks a little, but the dodge button is also the sprint button, so once your stamina is gone you're out of luck.
Moving on to the combat -- I like the idea. The enemies you're fighting are possessed by darkness, so you need to make them vulnerable with a flashlight before you can shoot them and kill them. This is a neat concept. The execution, unfortunately, is pretty bad. I've already mentioned that the enemies are much faster than you are. This is made worse by the fact that you slow down even more while boosting the flashlight, which needs to be trained on each enemy for several seconds before you even consider shooting them. Even once they're fully vulnerable, though, it'll probably take three or four shotgun blasts before they're down. Meanwhile, five other enemies have come at you at all sides and you haven't even managed to train the flashlight on them yet. Your hitstun is almost twice as long as theirs, so if you get hit once you're probably dead -- especially if you're hit by an enemy holding a meat hook, as they can attack you three times in rapid succession. Boosting the flashlight (necessary to make enemies vulnerable in any reasonable length of time) drains the battery. It does recharge slowly, or you can replace it with one of the many batteries found around the map. The problem with that part is that changing the battery is slow and it doesn't fill the flashlight meter all the way back up, so it actually doesn't save you very much time over just waiting for the recharge. Reloading the guns is also slow and you'll need to be able to do that many times per fight. If you were faster than the enemies, it would be alright since you could put distance between you and take the time to reload and recharge. You're not, though. Even if you were, about half the enemies have an unending supply of axes they can hurl at you with impressive accuracy over a large range. Finally, every time a new enemy spawns camera control is wrenched away from you to focus on these new enemies for several seconds. I cannot count how many times I died because the camera was focused on a new enemy while an old one was hitting me. Sometimes that new enemy was the only danger and I died anyway because camera control came back so late I had no chance to react to their attack before I died.
The overall story was an  interesting premise that I liked, but again the execution was poor. The game was repeditive and predictable. Alan regularly said, "You've gotta be kidding me," and I often parroted him when I saw the exact same setup for the dozenth time. At one point, I literally yelled at my computer, "Enough with the ******* birds, already! They're not scary, they're just ******* obnoxious!" It was lazy and aggrivating.
Also lazy were the graphics and backgrounds. To some extent, I can forgive graphics issues -- especially on five year old indie games. There was no reason for pre-rendered cut scenes to have people clipping into each other and into walls, though. There was even one cut scene where a character somehow got stuck in a door. How is that even possible when it's pre-rendered? The environments also seemed like nobody had really given them much thought. The one that really made me roll my eyes (and convinced me to bring this aspect up in my review) was a bathroom that had nothing in it except for two rolls of toilet paper and a bottle of asprin. I know it's a nit-pick thing, but it wouldn't have taken much effort to add a towel and toothbrush and make it look like some actual thought and effort had gone into it.
My final thing to complain about was the blurring that occurred during all of the fight scenes. It's clear the developers were trying to copy the distortion that appeared in Amnesia when you looked at an enemy for too long and your sanity started to slip. That worked in Amnesia because you were hiding, though. Here it was far too much distortion when you were trying to aim a revolver at somebody swinging a chainsaw at you. It added nothing to the ambience and was merely yet another aggrivation.
All in all, I really liked the ideas behind this game, but the game itself just didn't live up to the promise. It wasn't scary by any means, merely frustrating.

Journal is a very enjoyable inde adv game, It requires no real skill other than a willingness to explore the world and converse with the NPCs in it.  Journal tells the story of an unnamed women, looking back on a difficult time in her child hood through her journal, which you are helping her write as you play.  The unusual premise and the beautiful hand drawn children’s story book graphics are worth the price of admission alone.  The story elements (divorce, death, friendship, coming of age) are never handled to deeply, but it was enough to cause me to think back on my life more than once as I played which is something very few video games have ever accomplished, its more like a good novel or movie in that way.  The only game aspects are how you chose to answer questions (aggressive, guilty, positive, pessimistic), how much of the world you interact with, and how that changes your relationships along the way.  None of this ever really changes the outcome, which will make sense once you play it and the story even addresses this at a point.  If you enjoy adventure games and can have some empathy with a main character in fiction then you will enjoy Journal.  Oh, and it plays great with a gamepad too.

Okay, so when I heard there was a new OMD in developement I was fairly excited because I loved the first two. Then I find out Gameforge is publishing it in Europe; my excitement goes straight out the window. But of course I still had to give the game a chance (even if I now regret that decision).
Basically what has happened is; Robot has hopped on the "sub-par, everyday MOBA train" in an attempt to hitch a ride to "Money Town".
After a very brief time playing I found the game to be repetitive and boring but, don't worry, if you're not a fan of grinding you can unlock EVERYTHING in the game by throwing your money at it.
Now, you may think a game that offers 5 player co-op would be fun, but you'd be wrong. Having 5 players drops the difficulty level to zero, again adding to the boredom of grinding. And while the idea of having a selection of characters also sounds good, it is poorly executed.
All-in-all Orcs Must Die! Unchained had everything it needed to be a great Tower Defense game, maybe even a decent MOBA, but it was completely ruined by the reliance on a HUGE "pay-to-win" scheme (seriously, if you think the £50 of DLC advertised on steam is a lot - it's nothing compared to the in-game store) and an incredibly poor choice of publisher.
If you're looking for the true Orcs Must Die experience (or even just a good tower defense game) get OMD2.
If you're looking for a good MOBA play literally any other one you can find.

So, here we are again with another resurgence period of point 'n' click adventure games. We had Haven Moon, Eyes of Ara, and from the company that started it all; Obudction. Now, we have Quern, a game that follows to that age-old formula so well it might as well be counted alongside those classics were it not for a few glaring issues.
In Quern, you get the full "Myst"-esque package, haunting melody, amazing scenery, challenging puzzles, great voice-acting, and much more.
When I first started playing it, I knew it was something special, so much so that I can't deny the effect the few faults here and there had on my overall experience and in the end had me wishing they could've been ironed out beforehand were the developers to have had the time and resources to do so.
As great as the game was, using Unity for it was a bigger mistake than Cyan's decision to customize Unreal Engine 4 for Obduction. A regular issue that pops up with increasing regularity in Unity developed titles with actual effort put into their visuals is the speed and optimizations which were to me, unsurprisingly, deplorable.
Add to that an issue in later chapters of the game with a certain scene (No spoilers) that was animated using hand painted sketches rather than actual complete art that would've served much better and just served to show just how little time the developers had to develop that scene than they should've had.
Add to that a rather lackluster ending sequence that is underwhelming even in comparison to that of the original Myst and you have what I would call qualms about whether the game should've simply been an homage to its predecessors or if it should've taken a step further and innovated the genre as many other titles are doing.
All in all, I had a terrific time playing it. I WILL replay it, eventually, and I can only hope that the developers make more of the same. In time, I'm pretty sure they'll hand us a gem that'll remain in our hearts and memories as do the classics.
Should you wish to be transported to a magical land where zen and your mental fortitude are the tools of your survival, then look no further than Quern. It feels like what would happen if you package a jigsaw puzzle and a sea smelling breeze in a compressed can.

<Quick Overview>
pros:
fun
fast paced
team work based
cons:
Game is possibly abandoned (no regular updates)
extremely long load times
servers are empty (hardly anyone plays this game anymore)
non stop yelling

<Indepth Review>
In Natural Selection 2, you play on the side of the Marines or the aliens.
The two sides use a combination of RTs style structure building (the commander) and first person shooting (everyone else). The two sides have upgrades, structures, team work, and their brains to best the other side.
This game is fun, It'll kill sometime if you're bored. However, it gets old very fast for a large number of reason.
1) You can tell from the "Christmas splashpage" on the title screen, that this game does not recieve many updates. It is nearly February and we are still being shown Christmas images.
2) The game's connection and loading speeds are awful. In order to connect to the "tutorial", I was subject to an unbelievably long time period. I was able to boil some pasta and prepare myself a nice carbonara before it was done loading.
3) When connecting to the server list, one can see many servers. Unfortunately, there are only 10 or less servers that are actually being used. On average, the servers hold 10 people. This is a good indication that this game is dead and plaers have abandoned it for its many flaws.
4)Advanced players of this game have no room for beginners. They will scream and belittle anyone who doesn't understand the game mechanics immediately. The only reason they won't kick you, is because there is strength in numbers.
If you'd like a "get yelled at" simulation, then this game may be for you.
5) Aliens have an advantage in this game. The aliens are capable of very quick movements. WIth how shooting is implemented in this game, it is disasterous for the marines. Therefore, everoyne wants to play on the alien side and you are left with an unbalanced team.
<Conclusion>
It's a fun game, but save your money. The many flaws of this game has led it to lose its player base.
I'd consider it if it was on a great sale (75% off and up) and if I had many friends that were interested in playing.

Duck Game is that rare competitive gem where I have just as much fun losing as I do winning. It's hilarious and absurd and doesn't take itself seriously. It's a lot like TF2 in that respect, right down to the crazy number of hats available. There are some bugs, and it can certainly be challenging for new people to get into it when playing multiplayer against more experienced people. But in my opinion it's worth it because of the sheer amount of fun I've had--certainly more than any other game I've played on Steam.
Controls are tight and responsive, right up there with 16 bit platformers like Mario, Megaman, or Sonic. You can see from the video clips above that the graphics and sounds are pretty solidly retro-inspired and fit the game well. Rounds are short, sometimes just a few seconds, There is, indeed, an irresponsible number of weapons, and their interactions with each other and with different setpieces lead to a lot of interesting gameplay. I'm a little more than 50 hours in and still learn something occasionally. The basics are easy to learn: pick up a weapon, aim it at a duck, hit the fire button. Yet all the interactions of the different mechanics make for a very high skill ceiling, and the vagaries of online play combined with all the different ways to kill a duck (or accidentally kill oneself!) lead to great replay value. Consider that a round lasting for a minute is a big deal, and there are people posting reviews with over a hundred hours in-game. That's a
of Duck Game.
I feel I would be remiss if I didn't mention that the community, so far, has very few toxic people that I've seen. Sure, every game has its share of jerks, but I just don't see them very often in Duck Game. I think a lot of it has to do with just how
the game is, and how easy it is to laugh off a loss. Sure, winning is cool, but Duck Game is just so damn fun I don't care if I win.
I have enjoyed my time with Duck Game more than I have any other game in many years. It is pure fun, pure joy.

GameGuru aka FPS Creator Reloaded is a product from TheGameCreators, best known for DarkBasic and other game development tools like AppGameKit. Think of GG as sort of a game development sandbox. GG offers a fairly easy to use editing environment, extensible through LUA scripting.
I've had experience with other TGC products as well as the beta for FPSCR/Game Guru before it launched on Steam.
It's actually hard to rate this game with a thumbs up or a thumbs down. The dev team for TGC is fairly dedicated so it has the potential to become something great. At the moment though, it's missing a lot of core features as well as import/export functions.
Does it deliver on it's claim to create games you can play in minutes? Yes. It works. But it's missing a lot of the features and polish that would make it truly shine.
The dev team is very active and also actively listens to community feedback. If you're willing to tough out the rough patch of EA to get to the good stuff, then buy it. If you're not sure or undecided then maybe hold out until it's a more fully fledged product.
A lot of people have compared GG to other game engine/platforms such as Unity, CryEngine, Unreal, etc. If you're actually proficient with some other higher level game engine/programming language then you should definitely use that. If GG looks like something that appeals to you, then maybe give it a try.
There are plenty of videos on youtube that show off the program and walk through the process of making sample games/levels. While GG comes with some basic content, keep in mind that if you want to replicate some of the eye-candy you may have seen created by others that you'll probably need additional content to make it happen, which can be purchased in packs from TGC or imported as models.

First off, let's call this what it really is: a level editor. You don't so much create new games with it as you create new levels for an existing game. But it does this limited task very nicely. The terrain editor is extremely easy to use and it's nice to be able to take a first-person view to tweak it. You basically run through your level as if you were playing it, you hit F9, and you're able to edit the level from the player character's perspective. It comes with a small, but usable collection of assets which the developer promises to grow over time. Additional assets can be purchased from their store and a few are free. Lacking is any way to produce your own assets or even instructions on how to convert external assets in various formats to theirs.
So, if you're happy with a generic first person shooter for which you write all the levels using mostly pre-made assets, GameGuru can be quite a lot of fun, especially if you get to play them with friends. But you shouldn't expect a complete game authoring system. At the end of the day, what comes out of your pipeline will be a generic first person shooter. But it's a really short pipeline using this tool.
